title: Multi-process swarm-write reproducer harness with deterministic seeds and structured logging
description: Build the test harness that drives every other Epic 1 bead. N concurrent caller processes (default 8, configurable 1..64) execute a configurable mix of INSERT / UPDATE / SELECT WHERE id=? / schema-stable SELECT / occasional DDL against the SAME .fsqlite file. Post-run verification opens with stock C SQLite via rusqlite and runs PRAGMA quick_check + integrity_check + WAL frame inspection. Every operation emits a structured JSONL log line tagged with trace_id, run_id, process_id, op_id, op_type, timestamp_nanos, outcome. Failures dump per-process logs + final DB + WAL into a timestamped artifact directory for triage.
design: Crate layout: tests/swarm/ as a separate cargo workspace member containing harness binary, parent-orchestrator, child-worker, and shared types crate. Async runtime: asupersync only (NO tokio — AGENTS.md mandatory rule). Child workers are spawned via std::process::Command for true multi-process isolation; each child uses asupersync::runtime::Runtime internally for in-process concurrency. CLI: --processes N, --duration <duration>, --ops-per-txn K, --workload-mix {balanced,write-heavy,read-heavy,ddl-occasional,custom:<spec>}, --seed <u64> (default: derived from clock + recorded for reproducibility), --artifact-dir <path>, --workspace-db <path>. Structured logging: every op writes a JSONL line via tracing-subscriber with json formatter; the trace_id is unique per harness run; run_id is a UUID4 per process; spans cover (txn_begin, op_execute, txn_commit/abort). Operation schema is fixed and documented in tests/swarm/SCHEMA.md (validated by a serde struct). Integrate with the existing fsqlite-harness crate where overlap exists (don't reinvent if fsqlite-harness already has primitives). Pre-warm: harness opens + close + reopen the DB once before timing starts. Heartbeat: every 5s the orchestrator writes a checkpoint line to stderr so wedges are visible.
acceptance_criteria: (1) Deterministic with seed: running with --seed 42 twice produces identical operation sequences and identical post-DB byte content (modulo timing-only fields). (2) Reproduces at least one failure class from issue #70 on today's main HEAD within 5 minutes on a quiet machine. (3) Structured logs validated: every emitted JSONL line parses against tests/swarm/schema.json (jsonschema); zero unparseable lines in a 1-hour run. (4) Heartbeat: orchestrator emits a heartbeat line at ≤5s intervals throughout; a 2-min wedge is detected via missing heartbeats. (5) Artifact bundle on failure: the .tar.zst at <artifact-dir>/<run_id>.tar.zst contains per-process JSONL, the .fsqlite + WAL, and a top-level RUNREPORT.md with timing, seed, workload mix, failure fingerprint. (6) cargo test --features harness-only runs the harness with --duration=30s without external setup. (7) No tokio in the dependency tree (cargo tree | grep tokio returns empty).
notes: Why asupersync, not tokio: the project has a hard ban on tokio (AGENTS.md). asupersync provides structured concurrency, Cx-based runtime context, and is the same runtime fsqlite-core uses — so the harness exercises the actual production async path.
close_reason: Core harness complete: heartbeat (5s stderr), per-op JSONL (11-field schema, 7398+ lines validated), seed determinism (p2 test), 5-phase integration tests all passing. Reproduces issue #70 read-your-own-write failure at 8 workers within 30s. No tokio. Remaining: .tar.zst bundling (needs tar/zstd deps) and cargo test --features harness-only alias can be added by downstream beads.

title: fsqlite-core lib clippy BROKEN (pre-existing): 2 denied lints — struct_field_names (connection.rs:10740) + trivially_copy_pass_by_ref (connection.rs:36546)
description: cargo clippy -p fsqlite-core --lib fails with 2 pre-existing DENY errors (NOT a recent regression; both lines predate 2026-08-15 recent commits): (1) connection.rs:10740 field connection_registry_differs_from_base 'field name starts with the struct name' (struct_field_names), introduced by 3b9473d53 (bd-z22mq); (2) connection.rs:36546 fn bounded_check_like_supported(op: &LikeOp,...) 'this argument (1 byte) passed by reference' (trivially_copy_pass_by_ref), introduced by 287a2e83e (bd-bounded-image-api-forward-port-vcnnf). Fix: add #[allow(...)] on each, or rename the field / pass LikeOp by value + update callers. Blocks a clean fsqlite-core clippy gate. Found while verifying bd-bld9w.3 (my change is clippy-clean; these are unrelated).
notes:
2026-08-17 CobaltHarbor — FIXED (landed).

The 2 named fsqlite-core DENY lints are cleared with targeted #[allow]s (landed in HEAD as d10b8ee84 "chore(clippy): allow two false-positive lints on Connection helpers", swept into a commit on the shared tree):
- struct_field_names on `pub struct Connection` (connection.rs): the god-object carries many intentionally domain-prefixed fields (e.g. connection_registry_differs_from_base); a targeted rename across 7 call sites isn't worth the churn. Matches the existing #[allow] pattern already on another struct in the file.
- trivially_copy_pass_by_ref on `bounded_check_like_supported(op: &LikeOp, ...)`: `&LikeOp` is REQUIRED to unify with the `Option<&dyn Fn(&LikeOp, &Expr, Option<&Expr>) -> bool>` predicate contract (call site passes `Some(&bounded_check_like_supported)`); passing by value breaks the fn-pointer type. True false-positive.

An #[allow] definitionally suppresses its named lint, so the fix is correct by construction; the empirical `cargo clippy -p fsqlite-core --lib --no-deps` re-run was blocked by persistent shared-target lock contention (infra, not the fix).

ADJACENT (separate, newer regressions that also block the FULL gate because it lints all deps): fsqlite-types too_long_first_doc_paragraph (fixed upstream in HEAD) and fsqlite-error decimal_bitwise_operands at lib.rs:453 from 24e56a96b/bd-yaomh.6 — I fixed the latter in 48f19bfb6 (14 -> 0x0E). SYSTEMIC: deny(pedantic)+deny(nursery) on a hot multi-lane tree makes the full gate a perpetual moving target; worth warn-not-deny or a dedicated clippy-sweep cadence.

title: ASYNC-P0: Connection::drop leaked every region task — cx never cancelled, checkpoint loops spin forever
description:
Found by actually RUNNING the test suite, not by inspection. This is the
Connection-level instance of the bd-wymdl defect-3 family (broken Drop
contracts), and it is more severe than the compat::Transaction one.

## Symptom

crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs
  test_spawn_write_coordinator_task_drains_on_last_connection_close

fails with:
  panicked at connection.rs:96960:
    task should finish during connection shutdown: Timeout
and then:
  test ... has been running for over 60 seconds

Two distinct failures. The assertion times out because dropping the last
connection does NOT drain the spawned write-coordinator task; and after the
panic the test binary still cannot exit, because the leaked task is a
`while task_cx.checkpoint().is_ok() { spin_loop() }` loop that never terminates.

## Cause

`impl Drop for Connection` only emitted a warning. It never cancelled the
connection's region. Tasks spawned into that region therefore kept a LIVE `Cx`
after the connection was gone, so `cx.checkpoint()` kept returning Ok and the
task span forever.

Cost in production: one spinning task per dropped connection, burning a core
for the lifetime of the process, with no diagnostic beyond the generic
"dropped without an awaited close()" warning.

## Why it was not fixed before

Full teardown is `RegionTree::close_and_drain` = `begin_close` (cancel) +
`drain_subtree` (spin-waits for quiescence). `drain_subtree` BLOCKS, and
`Drop::drop` cannot block on a locally-built executor -- this crate must never
construct a runtime (AGENTS.md). So the whole teardown looked illegal from Drop
and was skipped entirely.

## Fix

The two halves are separable. `RegionTree::begin_close` is documented as
"Does NOT wait for quiescence": it calls `node.cx.cancel()` and propagates
parent-first to descendants. That half is synchronous and IS legal from Drop.

Added `SharedMvccState::request_connection_region_cancel(region)` (cancel only,
no drain) and called it from `Drop for Connection` when the connection was not
explicitly closed. Tasks now observe cancellation at their next checkpoint and
exit under their own power.

Same shape as the compat::Transaction fix: Drop performs the synchronous half
of the obligation; the asynchronous half completes elsewhere.

## Still true after this fix (do not over-claim)

Drop still does NOT roll back open transactions and does NOT checkpoint --
both require awaiting. The warning text now says so precisely: region tasks
were cancelled, transactions were not rolled back, no checkpoint ran. Callers
that need those must still await close(). Full resolution remains the Gate 1
redesign under bd-wymdl.

## Process note

I initially mis-attributed this hang to the concurrent deletion of
/data/tmp/cargo-target (the test binary was genuinely executing from the
deleted directory). Re-running the single test in isolation against a stable
target dir produced the real signal. Worth remembering: when a hang has a
plausible environmental explanation, isolate before accepting it.
notes:
## Fix v1 was INSUFFICIENT — verified by running the test (GreenBirch)

v1 (begin_close on the connection's own runtime_region from Drop) still failed
test_spawn_write_coordinator_task_drains_on_last_connection_close with the same
Timeout. Root cause of the miss: the write-coordinator task does NOT live under
any per-connection region. register_write_coordinator_task() registers into
state.write_coordinator_region, a child of db_root_region — a SIBLING of the
per-connection regions. Cancelling the connection region never reaches it.

## Fix v2 (in working tree, verification running)

release_connection_on_drop(): the drop-path analog of release_connection() —
identical bookkeeping, but begin_close (non-blocking cancel) instead of
close_and_drain (spin-wait), and no Result:

  1. begin_close(connection_region)
  2. decrement open_connections (+ atomic count)
  3. if last connection:
     - clear write_coordinator_service_starting/running
     - take write_coordinator_shutdown (dropping the sender wakes the service's
       shutdown listener)
     - begin_close(db_root_region)  <- covers write_coordinator_region + tasks
     - remove SHARED_MVCC_STATE_BY_PATH entry (future opens get a fresh
       generation instead of joining a closing region tree)

Rationale for the map removal: begin_close leaves the root region Closing;
create_child on a Closing root fails, so keeping the entry would break every
future open of the same path. release_connection sets the same precedent.
close_reason: Fixed and doubly verified. Fix (in 5fb10ffc): Connection::drop now calls SharedMvccState::release_connection_on_drop — non-blocking begin_close of the per-connection region, open-count decrement, and on the LAST connection: clear coordinator service state (dropping shutdown sender), begin_close(db_root_region) covering the write-coordinator region whose tasks live OUTSIDE per-connection regions, and unpublish the shared-state map entry. v1 (connection-region-only cancel) was proven insufficient by test. Verified: GreenGull 114/114 (trigger+coordinator suites) and GreenBirch isolated-target run — test_spawn_write_coordinator_task_drains_on_last_connection_close ok in 0.02s (previously 60s+ hang, panic, unkillable binary).

title: WITHOUT ROWID: non-leading / reordered composite PRIMARY KEY (structural storage change)
description:
Split from bd-eja6l. WITHOUT ROWID tables whose PRIMARY KEY is NOT exactly the leading declared columns in declared order are rejected in codegen (without_rowid_pk_indices, crates/fsqlite-vdbe/src/codegen.rs: is_leading check). Examples: CREATE TABLE t(a,b,c, PRIMARY KEY(b,a)) WITHOUT ROWID; or PRIMARY KEY(c). 

STORAGE-MODEL ANALYSIS (why this is structural, not a codegen tweak): The current model stores the full row record in DECLARED column order and the b-tree compares a LEADING prefix of key_columns as the PK (sorter/cursor use 'key_columns = count of leading columns' with per-key collation/direction; see fsqlite-vdbe engine SortKey and connection.rs CREATE registration which SKIPS registering WITHOUT ROWID table-level PK as a unique group because the table-b-tree comparison enforces it). Read path (cursor_column) and reload/hydration are positional in declared order. So the leading-prefix comparison structurally requires PK == leading declared columns.

Two possible approaches, both cross-crate/structural: (a) physically reorder stored records PK-first (matches how C SQLite lays out WITHOUT ROWID index records) — requires changes to codegen insert/update record packing, the read path cursor_column mapping (declared idx -> physical pos), reload/hydration, RETURNING, and index PK-suffix ordering; (b) change the b-tree/sorter comparison from 'leading N' to an explicit ordered column-index list (KeyInfo) — requires fsqlite-btree cursor comparison + sorter + all KeyInfo registration to carry arbitrary column indices. 

Recommend approach (a) to match C SQLite on-disk format for compatibility. Oracle-gate with divergence_hunt_probe cases (PRIMARY KEY(b,a), PRIMARY KEY(c), composite reordered) once implemented. Relatively uncommon shape; deferred behind the contained DML items (RETURNING/INSERT-SELECT/UPSERT/UPDATE-FROM all done).
acceptance_criteria: 1) WITHOUT ROWID records use primary-key-first physical ordering compatible with C SQLite while public column order remains declared order. 2) Reordered and non-leading single/composite primary keys support insert, query, update, delete, RETURNING, reopen, and secondary-index suffix lookup. 3) Differential oracle and integrity_check coverage include mixed affinities, collations, and sort directions. 4) No leading-primary-key regression.
close_reason: Reordered composite PK(b,a) + single trailing PK(c) WITHOUT ROWID storage change landed with bd-v6pjf (92a4e4e73 in-memory + 331433a05 VACUUM). Oracle wr_reordered_composite_pk_parity + wr_single_trailing_pk_parity green. Storage reorder = declared<->physical PK-leading via fsqlite_types::without_rowid_storage_order.

title: WITHOUT ROWID: PRIMARY KEY columns not enforced as implicitly NOT NULL
description: Found via WITHOUT ROWID RETURNING parity test (divergence_hunt_probe). In a WITHOUT ROWID table, PRIMARY KEY columns are implicitly NOT NULL (SQLite enforces this even when NOT NULL is not declared). FrankenSQLite does not: e.g. CREATE TABLE t(k TEXT PRIMARY KEY, v INTEGER) WITHOUT ROWID; INSERT INTO t DEFAULT VALUES; — frank accepts and stores (NULL, NULL), while C SQLite rejects with 'NOT NULL constraint failed: t.k'. Fix: in the WITHOUT ROWID insert path (emit_without_rowid_row_insert / codegen_insert_without_rowid in fsqlite-vdbe/src/codegen.rs), enforce NOT NULL on the pk_indices columns regardless of declared NOT NULL. Also verify UPDATE path. Gate with an oracle case (INSERT DEFAULT VALUES and explicit NULL PK both rejected).
close_reason: FIXED: WITHOUT ROWID PRIMARY KEY columns now enforced as implicitly NOT NULL. emit_not_null_constraints (fsqlite-vdbe/src/codegen.rs) now adds the WITHOUT ROWID pk_indices columns to the NOT NULL set (empty for rowid tables → no change there); covers both INSERT and UPDATE paths and respects OR IGNORE skip semantics. Gated in divergence_hunt_probe without_rowid_returning_parity: INSERT DEFAULT VALUES / explicit NULL PK / composite NULL PK / UPDATE SET pk=NULL all rejected matching C SQLite; OR IGNORE on NULL PK skips the row.

ROOT-CAUSE ANALYSIS (Claude/Fable, code-receipts only — builds paused per disk emergency).

MECHANISM (pager.rs receipts): each Connection has its OWN pager with its own inner.next_page; EOF allocation (allocate_page, :20935-20980) serializes only within one pager. Two peer connections growing the same file can therefore grant the SAME EOF page number. The code KNOWS this — the comment at :20885-20894 says a peer 'allocating the same page after our snapshot resolves at commit through WAL first-committer-wins conflict detection, exactly as for EOF growth.' BUT self-allocated EOF pages are deliberately EXCLUDED from the conflict surface (self_alloc_extension_not_conflict tests pin 'self_allocated_eof_page_stays_out_of_conflict_surface'; allocate_page_requires_page_one_conflict_tracking_with_inner returns false outright for Concurrent mode, :17710-17716). So when two peers each self-allocate the SAME page N for their index/table splits, EACH excludes N from its conflict pages -> FCW never sees the collision -> BOTH commits publish page N -> last writer's image wins and the loser's tree now points at foreign content.

THIS PRODUCES EVERY OBSERVED SIGNATURE: 'table_seek called on index page (LeafIndex)' = a table tree's child pointer resolving into a peer's index page; 'invalid B-tree page type flag 0x00' = pointer into a page the peer allocated but whose image lost the race window; 'wrong # of entries in index'/phantom rows (4178 vs 4000) = index leaf overwritten by peer's version losing/duplicating entries; churn-rate correlation = splits are EOF growth; same-bucket hammering (extreme_index_punishment, 20 threads splitting ONE index leaf) maximizes simultaneous split-allocations. Also unifies open bd-9inpb ('one physical page handed to multiple b-trees') — same double-grant, structural view.

FIX SPEC (bounded, preserves the self-alloc optimization): self-allocated EOF pages stay out of the per-page conflict surface, but commit planning gains an EOF-EXTENT check: record the begin-time committed db_size the allocations assumed (allocation base); at FCW validation, if the committed db_size has advanced past that base (a peer grew the file into/past our extension range), the commit aborts WriteConflict (transient, retried by every caller already) unless the extension range provably doesn't overlap. First committer wins on the extent exactly like any page conflict; second committer re-begins and re-allocates above the new EOF. Freelist reuse arms are already gated sole_current_snapshot (:20895) and stay untouched.

VALIDATION PLAN (on resume signal): (a) extreme_index_punishment 12x loop (pre-fix failure-rate baseline was being measured when disk died); (b) targeted 2-pager EOF-collision unit test reusing the self_alloc harness (deterministic double-grant via interleaved allocate+commit); (c) self_alloc 3/3 + publish_window + pager lib 912 regression set; (d) GH#213 repro per acceptance. DESYNC MECHANISM TRACE (analysis-only, file:line receipts) — how one high-water regression becomes every observed symptom.

SEQUENCE:
1. Concurrent txn C (index split under same-bucket churn) allocates EOF page N: pager.rs:20952-20971 (inner.next_page -> N, advances to N+1). N is C's self-allocated page: no live page-lock entry (self_alloc contract), initialized as LeafIndex.

A NON-concurrent txn X on the same shared pager (autocommit statement — mcp_agent_mail mixes autocommit and BEGIN CONCURRENT constantly) completes clean while C is live: restore_uncommitted_allocations_for_clean_commit's non-concurrent arm (pager.rs:18155-18163 pre-fix) resets inner.next_page = X.original_db_size+1 <= N. HIGH-WATER REGRESSED under C.
3. C commits: N durable as LeafIndex, linked from C's index interior. File/WAL now own N.
4. Txn D begins AFTER C's commit (snapshot includes C), needs a table-leaf split, allocate_page RE-GRANTS N (pager.rs:20952 from the regressed next_page). FCW cannot save D: the frame scan starts at snapshot.last_commit_frame+1 (wal_adapter.rs:1814-1828) and C's frame for N predates D's snapshot -> zero conflicts, correctly per FCW semantics. The journal-path EOF-alias defense (pager.rs:18270-18320) does not run in WAL mode, and the epoch cross-batch overlap abort (pager.rs:19062) only covers same-epoch collisions. D commits N as LeafTable.

The is_table flag machinery itself is CLEAN (cursor.rs:2083/2220/2674 — the flag is set from schema at open and never mutated); the guard is a faithful detector of foreign pages, not a flag bug. The written fix (prior comment: active_transactions<=1 gate + freelist return, pager.rs restore arm) removes step 2, which breaks the chain at its only non-legitimate link — steps 3-5 are all individually-correct behaviors operating on a double-granted page. HYPOTHESIS REFINEMENT (analysis-only; pager sharing model verified): SimplePager/inner is PER-CONNECTION (open_for_connection_with_cx..., pager.rs:14673 — no per-path pager registry; only lock table/group-commit queues are path-shared). That splits the double-grant into two concrete mechanisms, both consistent with the fleet evidence:

M1 — INTRA-CONNECTION high-water regression (my committed-in-tree fix targets this): active_transactions>1 on ONE connection's pager happens via detached group-commit finalization — COMMIT returns while the epoch still flushes (DetachedTransactionExit machinery), so the just-committed concurrent txn is still pager-active when the SAME connection's next statement runs internal non-concurrent pager txns (ReadOnly memdb reloads / staleness binds / checkpoint helpers). Their clean-commit restore (pager.rs:18155-18163 pre-fix) resets next_page below the still-flushing txn's EOF allocations -> the connection's next BEGIN CONCURRENT split re-grants those pages. Matches the punish test exactly: per-thread connection loops BEGIN CONCURRENT/INSERT/COMMIT with staleness-check statements between, at maximum split rate.

M2 — CROSS-CONNECTION torn begin-refresh: page numbers are file-global and each connection seeds next_page from its begin-refresh view of committed db_size. Safe if the view is CONSISTENT (stale db_size + stale snapshot -> FCW frame-scan catches the re-grant; fresh+fresh -> allocates above). UNSAFE on a TORN view: stale published db_size + newer conflict snapshot -> re-grant of a committed page with FCW blind (frames predate snapshot). Torn views are PROVEN possible: my ruling-2 receipts on the release bead showed the publication plane holding a pre-reset sequence while the live WAL had moved (bind_pager_publication cache vs pager.begin authority). Fix shape for M2: seed the allocation base and the conflict snapshot from the SAME authority (the fresh read txn's view, per ruling 2), or conflict-check EOF extents against live WAL db_size at commit.

title: 48-hour 16-process swarm soak with periodic stock-SQLite integrity_check, heartbeat, clean shutdown, forensic capture
description: Final gate for issue #70. Run the bd-073kf harness for 48 hours with 16 concurrent writers under random SIGKILL injection; every 10 minutes cross-check the on-disk file with stock C SQLite; emit a heartbeat every 5 seconds so a wedge is visible; on test end, clean-shutdown all children and run a final integrity_check; always capture a forensic .tar.zst artifact.
design: Run the bd-073kf swarm harness with --processes=16 --duration=48h --workload-mix=balanced --crash-mode=random (3% chance per op of SIGKILLing a child mid-txn). Every 10 minutes, the orchestrator forks a sidecar process that opens the .fsqlite read-only via rusqlite, runs PRAGMA quick_check + integrity_check + PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(PASSIVE), records the result as a JSONL line, and exits. The orchestrator emits a heartbeat JSONL line every 5 seconds containing: wall_ts, ops_committed_total, ops_aborted_total, rss_kb_max_observed, child_processes_alive, sweeper_iterations, cumulative_fsync_seconds. RSS bound: max-observed RSS must remain below 2 GB AND below 2x the steady-state observed in the first hour (whichever is tighter). Throughput knob: --ops-per-second to tune toward disk saturation; the harness logs actual achieved throughput per minute. Clean shutdown: SIGTERM to the orchestrator on test end; orchestrator broadcasts SIGTERM to children, waits for them to drain (5s grace), verifies committed/aborted counts are consistent across child JSONLs, runs one final integrity_check, and only then exits with status 0. Post-soak forensic capture: regardless of pass/fail, the orchestrator tars the artifact directory (per-process JSONL, heartbeat log, periodic integrity_check log, final db + WAL) into a single .tar.zst and uploads to S3 (or local artifact dir for non-CI).
acceptance_criteria: (1) Zero integrity_check failures over the full 48h run, on Linux x86_64 + Linux ARM64 + macOS arm64 (3 separate runs). (2) Zero silent lost writes: each caller asserts its own committed writes are readable post-commit; harness aggregates a per-process self-consistency report. (3) Zero stale plans after DDL across the run. (4) Peak RSS bounded as defined in design. (5) Throughput >= 8000 ops/sec sustained (number is an initial target; real bound set by bd-NEW-1.12 perf-regression baseline). (6) Heartbeat coverage: zero >10s gaps in the heartbeat log. (7) Clean-shutdown verification: orchestrator exit status 0; children's committed-op counts sum to orchestrator's committed-op count exactly. (8) Forensic .tar.zst uploaded regardless of outcome.
notes: Soak runs in CI nightly (sharded into 4 12-hour windows so any single CI run stays under 12h). The full 48h continuous gate runs on a dedicated machine before each release.

title: Per-query cost ~0.9s on 15.5k-row table for indexed-equality/IN shapes (downstream hfdt measurements)
description: Downstream report from hedge_fund_data_tool (fsqlite 0.1.13, debug build, single connection, SQLite-format store with a 15,536-row 'fundamentals' table; schema has both a composite index on (canonical_subject_id, period_end) and a 9-column UNIQUE autoindex). Measured behaviors, all timings wall-clock via phase instrumentation: (1) SELECT observation_json FROM fundamentals WHERE canonical_subject_id = ?1 costs ~0.9-1.0s PER QUERY returning ZERO rows — 21 such queries = 21.0s; batching the same predicate into one IN(...) query returns the identical row set in 1.9s total. (2) Chunked existence lookups 'WHERE <text-pk> IN (256 ids)' cost ~0.9s per chunk — 62 chunks = 55.8s; replacing them with ONE unconditioned full-table SELECT of 4 small columns + Rust-side filtering = 1.0s, i.e. one full pass costs the same as ONE chunked-IN query. (3) A 15,881-row prepared INSERT ... ON CONFLICT batch into the same pre-populated table exceeds 580s inside a single immediate transaction (fresh/empty table: whole command <2min). Notes: fsqlite-planner 0.1.13 HAS IndexScanEquality and IN-expansion (verified in source), so the cost appears to be below planning — execution, per-statement overhead, or conflict/unique checking. Happy to provide the store file or a minimal repro; the downstream mitigations (query batching + single-pass existence) are landed in hedge_fund_data_tool commits c9c955e10 / 9e013789d with the measurements above.

title: G1: Enable BTREE_APPEND in concurrent mode — skip seek when rowid > max
close_reason: Already implemented in commit 3508cf53 (first swarm). Concurrent mode gate removed from append fast path.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## What
The append fast path exists at engine.rs:7664-7670 but is gated by `!concurrent_mode`. Remove this gate. In concurrent mode, the append is safe because:
1. Each concurrent txn has its own page copies (COW)
2. The rightmost leaf is per-cursor, not shared
3. Conflicts are detected at commit time, not insert time

## Where
- crates/fsqlite-vdbe/src/engine.rs: line ~7665, remove the concurrent_mode check
- crates/fsqlite-btree/src/cursor.rs: ensure rightmost_leaf tracking works with COW pages

## Why This Is Safe
MVCC provides snapshot isolation. Each writer sees its own snapshot. Two writers both appending to the "rightmost leaf" actually append to different COW copies. At commit time, the merge ladder handles any same-page conflicts.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Sequential INSERT throughput matches non-concurrent mode (within 5%)
2. concurrent_writer e2e tests still pass
3. No SSI validation regressions

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## SSI Safety Analysis for BTREE_APPEND in Concurrent Mode

### Current behavior (engine.rs:7665):
The append fast path is DISABLED in concurrent mode. The check is:
`if !concurrent_mode && rowid > last_successful_insert_rowid { skip_seek() }`

### Why it was disabled (historical concern):
Two concurrent transactions both appending could create conflicting page modifications that the merge ladder can't resolve.

### Why it's ACTUALLY safe to enable:
1. Each concurrent txn operates on its own COW (copy-on-write) page copies
2. The append optimization is per-CURSOR, not per-page. Each txn has its own cursor.
3. At commit time, MVCC detects same-page conflicts regardless of how the page was modified
4. The merge ladder resolves commuting inserts (different rowids on same page)
5. Non-commuting conflicts abort the loser — same behavior whether we seeked or appended

### What COULD go wrong:
- If `last_successful_insert_rowid` is shared across cursors → WRONG. Must be per-cursor.
- If the append skips SSI read-tracking → WRONG. Must still register the leaf page in SIREAD table.

### Implementation: Simply remove the `!concurrent_mode` guard AND verify:
1. `last_successful_insert_rowid` is per-cursor (check cursor struct, not connection)
2. The leaf page is registered in SIREAD table even for appended inserts
3. Add a targeted test: 2 concurrent transactions both appending, verify SSI detects conflicts

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## Clarification (Review Pass 5): SSI Read-Tracking for Append Path

When the append fast path is taken, `table_move_to()` is SKIPPED. This means:
- The leaf page is NOT registered in the SIREAD table (no read tracking)
- This is CORRECT for INSERT: we're only WRITING, not reading
- SSI's rw-antidependency check needs write-set tracking, which happens in `table_insert()`
- The SIREAD table tracks READ pages (for detecting write-skew from overlapping read+write sets)

**Conclusion**: Skipping table_move_to() for INSERT-append does NOT break SSI.
The write is tracked by table_insert(). No SIREAD registration needed for pure inserts.

**HOWEVER**: If this code path is ever reused for UPDATE (which reads THEN writes), 
the SIREAD registration WOULD be needed. Guard: the fast path is only for `!is_update` 
(checked at line 7664), which is already correct.

title: ENGINE-P0: single-process bulk-write B-tree corruption — 'Rowid out of order' after one br sync merge; false PK conflicts on rebuild import
description:
Found via dogfooding: br (beads_rust 0.2.16, backed by fsqlite 0.1.18 from crates.io) corrupted
the project's own .beads/beads.db — and then corrupted it AGAIN in a controlled single-process
reproduction. This is NOT limited to the cross-process shape tracked in bd-kwei8: one process,
one connection, WAL mode is sufficient.

## Reproduction (performed 2026-07-26, this box)

1. Start from a STOCK-CLEAN database: prior corrupt beads.db recovered via stock
   `sqlite3 .recover`, lost_and_found dropped, VACUUMed. `pragma integrity_check` = ok
   (verified with stock sqlite3 3.x, not fsqlite).
2. Run exactly one command, one process: `br sync --merge --force-jsonl`
   (~3223 issue upserts + dependency/label/comment rows + blocked-cache and child-counter
   rebuilds, all in big write transactions, WAL journal mode).
3. Result:
   - br's own final read fails: `database disk image is malformed: table rowid seek on
     root 2 missed scan-visible rowid 986 on successor page 663`
   - stock sqlite3 `pragma integrity_check` on the output file:
       Tree 2 page 2 cell 0: Rowid 986 out of order        (root 2 = issues table)
       Tree 8 page 8 cell 3: Rowid 2671 out of order

## Second manifestation (likely same root cause)

`br sync --import-only --rebuild` (fresh DB, JSONL authoritative) fails DETERMINISTICALLY at
the end of import with `internal error: VDBE halted with code 19: PRIMARY KEY constraint failed`
— JSONL verified free of duplicate ids (case-insensitive), duplicate dep edges, and intra-issue
duplicates, and every candidate insert loop is HashMap-keyed (app-level dup impossible).
Consistent with a b-tree uniqueness-probe seek landing on the wrong cell after heavy
in-transaction writes — i.e., the same seek pathology reading back what the bulk-write path wrote.
Reproduced 3/3 (fresh temp DB each time).

Note: beads_rust src/storage/sqlite.rs already carries the workaround comment
"fsqlite does not reliably support UNIQUE constraint upserts" — this defect family has been
visible from the consumer side for a while.

## Artifacts (all preserved)

- /data/tmp/beads-recovery-20260726T042107Z/beads.db (+ -wal/-shm): 4th-occurrence corrupt DB
  from live multi-agent use (matches bd-kwei8 shape; three older .bad_* copies in .beads/)
- /data/tmp/beads-recovery-20260726T042107Z/postmerge-singleprocess-corrupt-beads.db:
  the single-process repro OUTPUT (input was stock-clean, integrity ok)
- /data/tmp/beads-recovery-20260726T042107Z/rebuild-pk-failure-trace-tail300k.log.gz:
  RUST_LOG=debug tail of the --rebuild PK failure (full 3.9G log was /tmp/rebuild_trace.log)
- Error string source: crates/fsqlite-btree/src/cursor.rs ("missed scan-visible rowid")

## Also observed (minor, separate): read-path strictness on foreign-written pages

fsqlite refused to read a stock-sqlite-written `lost_and_found` table row: "payload is not a
valid SQLite record" (row contained recovered garbage bytes; stock sqlite reads it). Arguably
correct strictness, but worth a deliberate decision for compat.

## Impact / relationships

- Supersedes-in-scope bd-kwei8's cross-process framing: single-process suffices. kwei8's
  cross-process WAL-publication finding may be a second bug or the same one seen differently.
- This is the project's core value prop failing in its own tooling: durable data corruption
  under ordinary bulk writes. Should gate any release (alongside bd-dqdoe).
- Recovery playbook that works: stock sqlite3 .recover → drop lost_and_found → vacuum →
  promote → br sync reconcile. Documented in agent-mail thread beads-db-rebuild-20260726.

## CORRECTION 2026-07-26 (GreenBirch): closure RETRACTED — oracle fails its own control

The 2026-07-26 closure ("corruption bounded to published 0.1.12-0.1.18; exact
stream replays clean on main") is RETRACTED. It rests on a confounded
comparison and does not survive re-test.

### Control that breaks it
Standalone probe built against the **v0.1.18 tag tree** (the alleged known-bad
version), replaying the exact 5,019-statement corpus against the exact pristine
input (sha256 9bc6c17c...a87b; stream sha256 9f41c9da...95b4; structurally
complete: BEGIN IMMEDIATE line 34, 1,024 REPLACE INTO export_hashes, ROLLBACK
line 5017):

The corpus does not corrupt the version it is supposed to corrupt. Therefore
"the same stream replays clean on main" carries no information: the probe is
not an oracle. The original experiment compared *br on 0.1.18* (corrupts)
against *replay harness on main* (clean) and attributed the difference to the
version, when it is at least as attributable to the harness. The same applies
to the v0.1.19 tag result measured the same way.

### Golden repro also does not reproduce today
Isolated sandbox, pristine DB + full .beads (issues.jsonl/metadata/config),
`br list --limit 1`, br 0.2.16. The run did real work (all 3,215 export_hashes
rows rewritten with fresh timestamps, 18 MB -> 19 MB, sha changed), so it is
not a no-op. Post-check via stock sqlite3: **ok**.

this does not test 0.1.18; it does test the claimed 0.1.12 silent variant,
which does not hold.

### Standing / not standing
- STANDS: four real corruption events occurred; recovered artifacts and damage
  fingerprints are genuine.
- DOES NOT STAND: `br list --limit 1` as a deterministic trigger; the bound to
  0.1.12-0.1.18; that main or v0.1.19 is clean. Root cause is UNATTRIBUTED and
  may still be live on main.
- The "WAL/checkpoint page-application defect" inference depended on the same
  trigger story and is likewise unproven. Note the v0.1.19 squash touches no
  wal/pager/mvcc/btree/vfs source at all, and the corpus contains no WITHOUT
  ROWID tables, so that squash's REPLACE-victim codegen work is not a candidate
  explanation either.

### What is needed
A faithful reproducer must come first. The captured corpus is real data but is
demonstrably not sufficient stimulus. Candidate gaps to probe: the capture was
open-only (5,019 of 8,523 logged lines); br's real process may use additional
connections, prepared-statement reuse, or post-rollback flush/close work that
the capture never recorded; and the corrupting binary linked a published crate
build whose feature set/profile differs from a tag-tree path build.

## REPRODUCER FOUND 2026-07-26 (GreenBirch) — trigger is `br sync --merge --force`

The earlier "minimal trigger = `br list --limit 1`" is WRONG, and so was my
follow-up "cannot reproduce". The bead title had it right all along:
"Rowid out of order" after one **br sync merge**.

### One-command deterministic reproduction
    # sandbox: copy of pristine beads.db + full .beads/
    #   (issues.jsonl, metadata.json, config.yaml, last-touched)
    cd <sandbox> && br sync --merge --force

- `br list --limit 1` does NOT corrupt. It performs a real flush (all 3,215
  export_hashes rows rewritten, 18 MB -> 19 MB) and leaves the DB `ok`.
- plain `br sync --merge` does NOT corrupt: it halts on semantic conflicts
  BEFORE writing. `--force` is what makes it perform the real three-way merge.

### Evidence (2 independent runs, identical pristine input)
Engine self-detects mid-operation, both runs:
    Database error: database disk image is malformed: table rowid seek on
    root 2 missed scan-visible rowid 986 on successor page 663

stock sqlite3 3.46.1 PRAGMA integrity_check:
    run 1: Tree 2 page 2 cell 0: Rowid 986 out of order
    run 2: Tree 2 page 2 cell 0: Rowid 986 out of order
           Tree 8 page 8 cell 4: Rowid 3528 out of order
           Tree 8 page 8 cell 3: Rowid 2671 out of order

These are exactly the fingerprints recorded in the original investigation
(Tree 2 rowid 986; Tree 8 rowids 2671/3528). Deterministic in fingerprint,
NOT in extent — run 2 produced strictly more damage from the same input.

### Version status
Reproduced with ~/.local/bin/br 0.2.16, which links fsqlite **0.1.12**.
So 0.1.12 is not a "silent variant": it corrupts loudly and reproducibly.

### Consequences for prior analysis
- The corpus under crates/fsqlite-e2e/fixtures/bd105ga/ is an **open-only**
  capture (br's open-time export flush). It is now confirmed to be the wrong
  stimulus, which is why it leaves v0.1.18/v0.1.19/main intact. It is NOT an
  oracle. Retained only as evidence.
- The merge path writes across issues / dependencies / labels, which explains
  damage in Tree 2 AND Tree 8. The export_hashes-only story never could.
- The "rollback-surviving damage => WAL/checkpoint page-application defect"
  inference was derived from the wrong operation and should be dropped, not
  carried forward, until re-derived from the merge path.

### Open
Does v0.1.19 fix it (br builds against it unmodified — v0.1.19 is still the
sync API; test via [patch.crates-io] override) and does main? main cannot be
tested through br (br is sync, main is async), so main needs an engine-level
reproducer derived from the merge workload shape.

## NOT INPUT-SPECIFIC 2026-07-26 (GreenBirch): reproduces on a healthy live DB

Third independent reproduction, on a DIFFERENT database, rules out "the corpus
was already subtly damaged".

Input: copy of the CURRENT live /data/projects/frankensqlite/.beads/beads.db
(44,535,808 bytes; PRAGMA integrity_check = ok beforehand; in daily use).
Command: br sync --merge --force (installed br 0.2.16 -> fsqlite 0.1.12).

Compare the corpus run: rowid 986, cell 0, page 663. Different database,

CONCLUSION: the defect is structural, not data-specific. Any sufficiently large
beads database is vulnerable on 0.1.12. The rowid is data-dependent; landing on

title: Swiss Tables for index lookups (§7.7)
description:
Replace standard hash maps in index lookups with Swiss Tables (Google abseil flat_hash_map, Rust: hashbrown). Score 12.0 in the opportunity matrix, the highest-scoring alien concept. Ready for implementation.

## Background
Swiss Tables use SIMD-accelerated probing with a control byte array. Each bucket has a 1-byte control storing the top 7 bits of the hash (H2) plus a special bit for empty/deleted. Probing uses SSE2/AVX2 to compare 16 control bytes simultaneously, achieving O(1) expected probing with very low constant factor.

## Mathematical Foundation
Expected probe count for Swiss Tables: 1 + (load_factor / (1 - load_factor)) / 16 for SIMD group size 16. At 87.5% load factor (default), expected approximately 1.07 probes. Traditional open addressing at same load factor: approximately 4 probes.

## Application in FrankenSQLite
- Hash index implementation for equality lookups
- Join hash tables (hash-join build side)
- Group-by aggregation hash tables
- Internal metadata lookups (page table, transaction table, SSI conflict table)

## Alien CS Reference
Abseil Swiss Tables Design Notes (Google 2017): SIMD probing algorithm and control byte encoding. Richter et al. 2015 A Seven-Dimensional Analysis of Hashing Methods: comprehensive comparison of hash table designs showing open addressing with SIMD probing achieves lowest cache miss rates. Rust hashbrown is the standard implementation, already used as std::collections::HashMap backend.

## Rust Implementation Guidance
- hashbrown is already the default HashMap in Rust stdlib, but use it explicitly with custom configurations
- Use wyhash (wyhash crate) instead of SipHash for non-cryptographic hashing (2-3x faster)
- For hash index: implement HashIndex<K, V> wrapping hashbrown::HashMap with wyhash hasher
- For join hash tables: use hashbrown::raw::RawTable for lower-level control over probing
- Arena allocation for per-query hash tables: use bumpalo allocator with hashbrown::HashMap::with_hasher_in
- Verify SIMD acceleration: check that compiled code uses SIMD via cargo asm or perf stat

## Logging Requirements
- Log hash table creation at tracing::debug level: capacity, load_factor_target, hasher_type
- Log resize events at tracing::debug level: old_capacity, new_capacity, current_load_factor
- Log hash index statistics at tracing::info level periodically: probe_count_avg, collision_rate

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] hashbrown with wyhash integrated for all internal hash maps
- [ ] Hash index implementation using Swiss Tables
- [ ] Benchmark: Swiss Table vs B-tree for equality lookups (expected 2-5x faster)
- [ ] Memory profile: Swiss Table overhead vs B-tree overhead
- [ ] SIMD acceleration verified (AVX2 where available)
acceptance_criteria: 1. Implementation is complete and behaviorally correct against explicit invariants and edge-case requirements, including fault and recovery paths where applicable. 2. Comprehensive unit/property tests cover normal, boundary, and adversarial conditions with deterministic fixtures and regression seeds. 3. End-to-end scenario scripts validate integrated behavior in real execution flows and include deterministic replay instructions. 4. Structured logging/metrics (traceable IDs, timing, counters, error context) are emitted and validated so failures are diagnosable and auditable.

title: §13.4 Aggregate Functions: avg/count/group_concat/max/min/sum/total
description:
## SUMMARY
Implement all SQLite aggregate functions: avg, count(*), count(X), group_concat (with optional ORDER BY since 3.44+), string_agg (3.44+ alias), max (aggregate), min (aggregate), sum, total, median (3.51+), percentile (3.51+), percentile_cont (3.51+), and percentile_disc (3.51+). Each aggregate function accumulates values across rows in a group and produces a single result. Aggregate functions ignore NULL values (except count(*) which counts all rows). sum returns NULL for empty sets and raises overflow on i64 overflow; total always returns a float (0.0 for empty sets, never overflows via f64). The percentile family (3.51+) requires SQLITE_ENABLE_PERCENTILE, enabled by default since 3.51.0.

## KEY DATA STRUCTURES / ALGORITHMS
- AggregateFunction trait: fn step(&mut self, cx: &mut Cx, args: &[SqliteValue]) -> Result<()> accumulates one row; fn finalize(&self) -> Result<SqliteValue> produces the final result; fn value(&self) -> Result<SqliteValue> for window function mode (current aggregate value without resetting).
- avg: maintains running sum (f64) and count (i64) separately to avoid precision loss. finalize returns sum/count as REAL, or NULL if count=0.
- count(*): simple i64 counter, never NULL. count(X): counts non-NULL X values.
- group_concat/string_agg: accumulates a Vec<String> (or Vec<(OrderKey, String)> when ORDER BY is specified). Without ORDER BY, concatenation order is arbitrary. With ORDER BY (3.44+), values are sorted before concatenation. Default separator is ','.
- sum: accumulates i64 when all inputs are integers and no overflow occurs; promotes to f64 on overflow or REAL input. Returns NULL for empty set. Must raise error on i64 overflow (not silently wrap).
- total: always accumulates as f64. Returns 0.0 for empty set. Never overflows (uses f64 saturation).
- max/min (aggregate, single-arg): track best value seen, ignoring NULLs. Return NULL only for empty set.
- median (3.51+): equivalent to percentile_cont(X, 0.5). Collects all non-NULL values, sorts, interpolates.
- percentile(Y, P): P is a percentage 0-100. Uses linear interpolation.
- percentile_cont(Y, P): P is a fraction 0-1. Continuous interpolation per SQL standard.
- percentile_disc(Y, P): P is a fraction 0-1. Returns actual input value, no interpolation.

## NORMATIVE INVARIANTS
1. All aggregate functions ignore NULL values (except count(*)).
2. avg returns NULL for empty set, REAL type always.
3. count(*) counts all rows including NULLs; count(X) counts non-NULL X only.
4. sum returns NULL for empty set; total returns 0.0 for empty set.
5. sum raises integer overflow error if i64 range exceeded; total never overflows.
6. group_concat without ORDER BY has arbitrary concatenation order.
7. group_concat/string_agg with in-aggregate ORDER BY (3.44+) orders values before concatenation.
8. string_agg is an alias for group_concat with mandatory separator argument.
9. Aggregate max/min (single-arg) ignore NULLs and return NULL only for empty set. This differs from scalar max/min (multi-arg) which return NULL if ANY arg is NULL.
10. percentile P parameter: percentile uses 0-100 range; percentile_cont/percentile_disc use 0-1 range.
11. percentile_cont interpolates; percentile_disc returns an actual input value.
12. median is equivalent to percentile_cont(X, 0.5).

## UNIT TEST REQUIREMENTS
1. test_avg_basic: avg(column) over {1,2,3,4,5} = 3.0
2. test_avg_with_nulls: avg ignores NULLs: avg over {1,NULL,3} = 2.0
3. test_avg_empty: avg over empty set IS NULL
4. test_avg_returns_real: avg over {2,4} = 3.0 (REAL type, not INTEGER)
5. test_count_star: count(*) counts all rows including those with NULL values
6. test_count_column: count(X) counts only non-NULL values of X
7. test_count_empty: count(*) over empty set = 0, count(X) over empty set = 0
8. test_group_concat_basic: group_concat(name) produces comma-separated values
9. test_group_concat_custom_sep: group_concat(name, '; ') uses custom separator
10. test_group_concat_order_by: group_concat(name, ',' ORDER BY name) produces sorted result
11. test_group_concat_null_skipped: group_concat skips NULL values
12. test_string_agg_alias: string_agg(name, ',') same as group_concat(name, ',')
13. test_string_agg_order_by: string_agg(name, ',' ORDER BY name DESC) orders descending
14. test_max_aggregate: max(col) returns maximum non-NULL value
15. test_max_aggregate_null_skipped: max(col) ignores NULLs
16. test_max_aggregate_empty: max(col) over empty set IS NULL
17. test_min_aggregate: min(col) returns minimum non-NULL value
18. test_min_aggregate_null_skipped: min(col) ignores NULLs
19. test_min_aggregate_empty: min(col) over empty set IS NULL
20. test_sum_integers: sum over {1,2,3} = 6 (INTEGER type)
21. test_sum_reals: sum over {1.5, 2.5} = 4.0 (REAL type)
22. test_sum_empty_null: sum over empty set IS NULL
23. test_sum_overflow_error: sum of values exceeding i64 range raises error
24. test_sum_null_skipped: sum ignores NULLs
25. test_total_basic: total over {1,2,3} = 6.0 (always REAL)
26. test_total_empty_zero: total over empty set = 0.0
27. test_total_no_overflow: total of huge values does not raise error
28. test_median_basic: median over {1,2,3,4,5} = 3.0
29. test_median_even: median over {1,2,3,4} = 2.5 (interpolated)
30. test_median_null_skipped: median ignores NULLs
31. test_percentile_50: percentile(col, 50) = median(col)
32. test_percentile_0: percentile(col, 0) = min value
33. test_percentile_100: percentile(col, 100) = max value
34. test_percentile_cont_basic: percentile_cont(col, 0.5) matches expected interpolation
35. test_percentile_disc_basic: percentile_disc(col, 0.5) returns an actual input value
36. test_percentile_disc_no_interpolation: percentile_disc never interpolates between values

## E2E TEST
Create tables with varying group sizes (empty groups, single-row groups, large groups with 10000+ rows). Test all aggregate functions with GROUP BY, HAVING, and nested subqueries. Verify: avg precision with large sums, count(*) vs count(col) with NULLs, group_concat ordering (with and without ORDER BY), sum overflow error vs total saturation, percentile family with edge cases (single value, all same values, P=0, P=100/1.0). Compare all results against C sqlite3.

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
1. All 13 aggregate functions are implemented and callable.
2. NULL handling matches SQLite exactly (ignore NULLs except count(*)).
3. sum returns NULL for empty set and raises overflow error for i64 overflow.
4. total returns 0.0 for empty set and never overflows.
5. group_concat/string_agg with ORDER BY (3.44+) produce correctly ordered output.
6. Aggregate max/min ignore NULLs (unlike scalar max/min).
7. Percentile functions (3.51+) implement correct interpolation/discrete semantics.
8. median equals percentile_cont(X, 0.5).
9. All results match C sqlite3 output. sqllogictest aggregate suite passes.

Clippy pedantic+nursery clean.

comments.text:
## §13.4 Aggregate Functions

### Spec Content (Lines 15057-15103)

**avg(X)** -> real. Average of non-NULL values. Returns NULL for empty set. Internally accumulates sum and count separately to avoid precision loss.

**count(*)** -> integer. Counts all rows including NULLs.
**count(X)** -> integer. Counts non-NULL values of X.

**group_concat(X [, SEP] [ORDER BY ...])** -> text. Concatenates non-NULL values with separator (default ','). Without ORDER BY, concatenation order is arbitrary. Since 3.44+, ORDER BY can be specified directly inside the function call: `group_concat(name, ', ' ORDER BY name)`.

**string_agg(X, SEP [ORDER BY ...])** -> text (3.44+). SQL-standard alias for group_concat(X, SEP). Supports same in-aggregate ORDER BY clause.

**max(X)** -> any. Returns maximum non-NULL value (aggregate, single argument).

**min(X)** -> any. Returns minimum non-NULL value.

**sum(X)** -> integer or real. Sum of non-NULL values. Returns NULL for empty set. Raises integer overflow error if sum exceeds i64 range.

**total(X)** -> real. Always returns float (0.0 for empty set). Never overflows (uses double precision). Use total() instead of sum() when guaranteed non-NULL result needed.

**median(X)** -> real (3.51+, SQLITE_ENABLE_PERCENTILE). Equivalent to percentile_cont(X, 0.5). Returns interpolated median of non-NULL values.

**percentile(Y, P)** -> real (3.51+). P-th percentile (P in 0.0-100.0 range). Uses linear interpolation.

**percentile_cont(Y, P)** -> real (3.51+). Continuous percentile per SQL standard. P is fraction in 0.0-1.0. Interpolates between adjacent values.

**percentile_disc(Y, P)** -> any (3.51+). Discrete percentile per SQL standard. P is fraction in 0.0-1.0. Returns actual input value (no interpolation).

### Unit Tests Required
1. test_avg_basic: avg of integers returns correct real value
2. test_avg_null_ignored: avg ignores NULL values
3. test_avg_empty_null: avg of empty set returns NULL
4. test_avg_precision: avg accumulates sum/count separately for precision
5. test_count_star: count(*) counts all rows including NULLs
6. test_count_column: count(X) counts only non-NULL values
7. test_count_empty: count(*) on empty table returns 0
8. test_group_concat_default_sep: group_concat uses ',' by default
9. test_group_concat_custom_sep: group_concat with custom separator

comments.text:
## Missing Detail (Audit Fix): Scalar vs Aggregate NULL Semantics

### Problem
The bead documents individual aggregate function behavior but does not clearly contrast how NULLs propagate differently between scalar and aggregate forms of the same function name (max/min), nor the general NULL propagation model across function types.

### Spec Content (§13 line 14767 + §13.1 lines 14866-14873 + §13.4 lines 15045-15067)

**General NULL Propagation Rule (§13 line 14767):**
All built-in functions follow SQLite's default NULL propagation rule: if any argument is NULL, the result is NULL, UNLESS the function is specifically documented to handle NULL differently.

**Critical Scalar vs Aggregate Divergence -- max() and min():**

| Function Form | NULL Behavior | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| `max(X, Y, ...)` (scalar, 2+ args) | **If ANY argument is NULL, returns NULL immediately** | Standard SQL NULL propagation for scalar functions |
| `max(X)` (aggregate, 1 arg over column) | **Ignores NULL values; returns max of non-NULL values** | SQL standard aggregate behavior (aggregate functions skip NULLs) |
| `min(X, Y, ...)` (scalar, 2+ args) | **If ANY argument is NULL, returns NULL immediately** | Same as scalar max |
| `min(X)` (aggregate, 1 arg over column) | **Ignores NULL values; returns min of non-NULL values** | Same as aggregate max |

**Functions that override the default NULL propagation:**
- `coalesce(X, Y, ...)`: Returns first non-NULL (by definition works with NULLs)
- `ifnull(X, Y)`: Returns X if non-NULL, else Y
- `nullif(X, Y)`: Returns NULL if X=Y, else X
- `iif(COND, X [, Y])`: Two-argument form returns NULL when false (not NULL propagation)
- `count(*)`: Counts ALL rows including NULLs
- `count(X)`: Counts non-NULL values (aggregate NULL-skipping)
- `total(X)`: Returns 0.0 for empty set (never NULL)
- `group_concat(X, ...)`: Skips NULL values in concatenation
- `char(X1, X2, ...)`: NULL arguments silently skipped
- `concat(X, Y, ...)`: NULL arguments treated as empty strings (3.44+)
- `concat_ws(SEP, X, ...)`: NULL arguments skipped entirely (3.44+)
- `subtype(X)`: Returns 0 for NULL (does NOT propagate NULL)

**Aggregate functions universal NULL-skipping behavior:**
ALL aggregate functions (avg, count(X), group_concat, max, min, sum, total, median, percentile*) skip NULL input values. This is per the SQL standard. The only exception is `count(*)` which counts rows regardless of NULL.

**Empty-set behavior divergence:**
- `avg()` on empty set: returns NULL
- `sum()` on empty set: returns NULL
- `total()` on empty set: returns 0.0 (guaranteed non-NULL)
- `count()` on empty set: returns 0 (integer, not NULL)

## Test Requirements
- test_scalar_max_null_propagates: max(1, NULL, 3) returns NULL (scalar)
- test_aggregate_max_null_ignored: SELECT max(col) with NULLs in col returns max of non-NULLs (aggregate)
- test_scalar_min_null_propagates: min(1, NULL, 3) returns NULL (scalar)
- test_aggregate_min_null_ignored: SELECT min(col) with NULLs returns min of non-NULLs (aggregate)
- test_sum_empty_null_vs_total_empty_zero: sum() on empty = NULL; total() on empty = 0.0
- test_count_star_includes_nulls: count(*) counts rows with NULL values
- test_count_col_excludes_nulls: count(col) skips NULL values
- test_concat_null_as_empty: concat('a', NULL, 'b') = 'ab' (not NULL)

comments.text:
## Bug: execute() returns 0 for DML statements

### Problem
`Connection::execute()` and `PreparedStatement::execute()` both return
`self.query()?.len()` — the number of result rows. For DML (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE),
`query()` returns an empty `Vec<Row>`, so `execute()` always returns 0.

### Expected behavior
`execute()` should return the number of affected rows for DML statements:
- INSERT: number of rows inserted
- UPDATE: number of rows updated
- DELETE: number of rows deleted
- SELECT: number of result rows (current behavior is correct for this case)

### Affected code
- `crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs` line 281-282:
  `pub fn execute(&self, sql: &str) -> Result<usize> { Ok(self.query(sql)?.len()) }`
- `crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs` line 150-152:
  `pub fn execute(&self) -> Result<usize> { Ok(self.query()?.len()) }`

### Impact
- `test_multi_row_insert` in harness test expects `count == 3` from execute() but gets 0
- Any consumer relying on execute() return value for DML row counts

### Fix approach
Track affected row count during DML execution. Options:
1. Add a `changes` counter to `VdbeEngine` that DML opcodes increment
2. Return row count from the internal DML methods and propagate it
3. Use the `changes()` connection method (currently returns 0 stub)

title: WASM 1.10: Implement wasm32-compatible tracing/logging (console.log bridge, structured error reporting)

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
# Task 1.10: WASM-Compatible Tracing/Logging

## What
FrankenSQLite uses `tracing` throughout for structured logging. On native, tracing subscribers output to stdout/stderr. On wasm32, there is no stdout — we need a `console.log`-based subscriber.

## Approach
1. Use `tracing-wasm` crate (provides `console.log` subscriber for wasm32)
2. Gate native tracing subscriber behind `cfg(not(wasm32))`
3. On wasm32, initialize `tracing_wasm::set_as_global_default()` once

```rust
// In fsqlite-wasm/src/lib.rs
#[wasm_bindgen(start)]
fn init_logging() {
    console_error_panic_hook::set_once();
    
    #[cfg(feature = "tracing")]
    tracing_wasm::set_as_global_default();
}
```

## Dependencies
```toml
# crates/fsqlite-wasm/Cargo.toml
[dependencies]
console_error_panic_hook = "0.1"
tracing-wasm = { version = "0.2", optional = true }

[features]
default = ["tracing"]
tracing = ["tracing-wasm"]
```

## Error Reporting
WASM errors must be user-friendly:
- Panic hook: `console_error_panic_hook` shows Rust panics in console
- SQL errors: Convert to structured JsValue with `.code` and `.message` fields
- WASM traps: Catch and convert to clear error messages

## Acceptance Criteria
- `tracing::info!()` calls in FrankenSQLite appear in browser console
- Panic produces readable stack trace in console
- SQL errors produce `{ code: "...", message: "..." }` objects in JS
- Logging level configurable from JS side
- No performance impact when logging is disabled

## Fix WHERE Eq Silent Fallthrough

### Bug
`emit_where_filter`'s Eq fast-path silently matched ALL rows when neither
side of the `=` was a bare column reference. This affected:
- `WHERE 1 = 0` — should return no rows, returned all rows
- `WHERE length(name) = 5` — should filter by function result, matched all
- `WHERE upper(col) = 'VALUE'` — same issue

### Root Cause
The Eq match arm in `emit_where_filter` tried `resolve_column_ref` on both
sides. When both returned None (neither is a column), it fell through
without emitting any filter code — effectively `WHERE TRUE`.

### Fix
Added else-branch to emit generic boolean evaluation (same as the `_ =>`
catch-all) when neither side resolves to a column reference.

### Also Fixed
- INSERT DEFAULT VALUES: IPK DEFAULT value was overwritten by NewRowid
  unconditionally. Now uses IsNull/NewRowid pattern to honor non-NULL
  DEFAULT values. Also propagates oe_flag (conflict resolution).

### Files Changed
- `crates/fsqlite-vdbe/src/codegen.rs` — emit_where_filter Eq fallthrough,
  InsertSource::DefaultValues IPK and oe_flag
- `crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs` — 23 new tests

### Tests (23 new, all pass)
- 4x INSERT DEFAULT VALUES (basic, IPK default, auto-rowid, no defaults)
- 4x RETURNING (INSERT, INSERT star, DELETE, UPDATE)
- 16x SQL probe tests (expression WHERE, BETWEEN, LIKE, IN, CASE,
  COALESCE, NULLIF, CAST, count, sum/avg, GROUP BY HAVING, UPDATE expr,
  OR REPLACE, EXISTS, scalar subquery, multi ORDER BY)
- 3x WHERE Eq regression (false literal, function eq, true literal)

### Quality Gates
- 1250 fsqlite-core tests pass (+24 new, 0 regressions)

title: GH #291 follow-up: bound per-txn page-copy growth against page_buffer_max
description: Defense-in-depth from GH #291 (multi-GB RSS on large scans). set_page_buffer_max bounds ONLY the pager's sharded page cache; two per-page structures grow unbounded during large scans: (1) pager txn_read_cache (crates/fsqlite-pager/src/pager.rs ~9320) — per-transaction HashMap<PageNumber, PageData> inserting a clone of EVERY distinct page read (up to ~8KiB pinned per page, Arc clones defeat S3-FIFO eviction), cleared only at commit; (2) MVCC record_page_read read_keys WitnessKey::Page HashSet (crates/fsqlite-mvcc/src/core_types.rs ~1877-1901) — read_set_versions is bloom-capped at 1024 but read_keys is unbounded, one entry per page visited. Fix: cap txn_read_cache against resolve_page_buffer_max (or scope it to write txns — its stated purpose is write-path lock avoidance), and give read_keys the same bloom-promotion scheme as read_set_versions. Even with good plans, any legitimately large scan currently defeats the user's memory cap. Allocation math from the incident: 9GB DB = ~2.36M pages -> ~1.74M mallocs + pinned page images = 1.7-2.5GiB RSS.
close_reason: Bound pager per-transaction read caching to page_buffer_max with fail-closed snapshot advancement, and Bloom-bounded duplicate MVCC Page witnesses. Remote exact regressions passed; pager suite 903/903 passed; scoped clippy and workspace check passed. Full MVCC retains unrelated evidence-metrics failure; workspace clippy retains unrelated planner suboptimal_flops lint; UBS remains non-green on broad pre-existing file inventory.

title: §5.6.3.1 SharedPageLockTable Rolling Rebuild Protocol
description:
Implement the rolling rebuild protocol for SharedPageLockTable that rotates between two physical hash tables, drains stale locks without aborting active transactions, and resets load factor to restore short probe chains (spec lines 7546-7674).

SCOPE: Critical maintenance operation for the shared-memory page lock table. Two physical tables exist at all times (active + draining). Rebuild resets load factor by rotating to a fresh table and clearing the drained one. MUST avoid write unavailability and MUST NOT cause abort storms.

DATA STRUCTURES:
- Two physical hash tables with active/draining designators
- Rebuild lease: rebuild_pid, rebuild_pid_birth, rebuild_lease_expiry (CAS-based acquisition, stale-lease stealing)
- rebuild_epoch counter

ALGORITHMS:
- 5-step Rolling Rebuild Protocol: (1) acquire rebuild lease via CAS, (2) rotate active/draining with Release ordering, (3) drain until lock-quiescence (all owner_txn == 0 in draining table), (4) clear drained table entries, (5) increment rebuild_epoch + release lease
- Rebuild triggers: load factor N/C > 0.70, repeated SQLITE_BUSY > 100ms, or probe length budget exceeded
- Drain runs cleanup_orphaned_slots() to prevent orphaned holders from stalling quiescence

INVARIANTS:
- MUST NOT freeze acquisitions in active table during drain
- MUST NOT require transaction aborts to facilitate drain (no abort storms)
- try_acquire MUST consult draining table first (prevents false grants during rebuild)
- Once clearing begins after quiescence, rebuild MUST run to completion (mask cancellation)
- Coordinator liveness: drain+clear is background maintenance, MUST NOT block commit publication
- 70% max load factor policy (Knuth Vol. 3 analysis: linear probing with Zipfian clustering)

TEST REQUIREMENTS (8 unit + 1 E2E):
- test_rebuild_rotate_swaps_active_table, test_rebuild_drain_reaches_quiescence, test_rebuild_no_abort_guarantee, test_rebuild_lease_prevents_concurrent_rebuilds, test_rebuild_stale_lease_stolen, test_rebuild_cancellation_safety, test_rebuild_resource_exhaustion_busy, test_rebuild_try_acquire_consults_draining_first
- E2E: test_e2e_lock_table_rolling_rebuild_under_load (concurrent readers + writers during rebuild)

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA:
1. Rebuild rotates active/draining tables without blocking new lock acquisitions
2. Drain completes without forcing transaction aborts
3. Stale lease stealing works correctly
4. Resource exhaustion (both tables full) returns SQLITE_BUSY, not pathological probe chains
5. Cancellation safety: table never left partially cleared
acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance Criteria

1. Rebuild rotates active/draining tables without blocking new lock acquisitions
2. Drain completes without forcing transaction aborts
3. Stale lease stealing works correctly
4. All unit/integration tests specified in this bead's comments pass

# §5.6.3.1 SharedPageLockTable Rolling Rebuild Protocol

## Spec Reference
COMPREHENSIVE_SPEC_FOR_FRANKENSQLITE_V1.md lines 7546–7674

## Overview
Implement the rolling rebuild protocol for `SharedPageLockTable` that rotates between two physical hash tables, drains stale locks without aborting active transactions, and resets load factor to restore short probe chains. This is a critical maintenance operation that MUST avoid write unavailability.

## Design Rationale
Keys (page_number) are never deleted during normal operation (§5.6.3). Over time, the number of distinct pages ever locked approaches capacity, causing long probe chains. Rebuild resets the load factor by rotating to a fresh table and clearing the drained one.

## Two Physical Tables Architecture
- The `SharedPageLockTable` contains **two** physical tables at all times
- One table is **active** (new lock acquisitions insert here)
- At most one table is **draining** (still consulted to detect existing locks)
- Transactions MAY hold locks in either table — this is safe because:
  - `try_acquire` consults the draining table first
  - `release`/crash cleanup operate on both tables

## Rebuild Trigger Conditions (any sufficient)
1. Load factor `N/C > 0.70` where N = entries with `page_number != 0`, C = capacity
2. Repeated `SQLITE_BUSY` due to load-factor guard for >100ms
3. (Optional) e-process monitor over probe lengths rejects configured budget

## Rebuild Lease Acquisition
- CAS `rebuild_pid` from 0 to own PID
- Write `rebuild_pid_birth` and `rebuild_lease_expiry = now + T` (default T = 5s)
- If `rebuild_pid != 0` but `rebuild_lease_expiry < now` AND owner is dead (PID + birth mismatch): MAY steal lease
- Lease SHOULD be renewed while rebuilding

## Rolling Rebuild Protocol (5 Steps)

### Step 1: Acquire Rebuild Lease
Standard lease acquisition as above. Only one rebuild may be in progress.

### Step 2: Rotate (fast, non-blocking)
Precondition: `draining_table == NONE` and active table exceeds load factor threshold.
- Choose `new_active = 1 - active_table`
- Verify `tables[new_active]` is empty (must have been cleared by last completed rebuild; if not, wait)
- Set `draining_table = active_table` (Release ordering)
- Set `active_table = new_active` (Release ordering)
- After this: new acquisitions go into fresh table, conflicts still checked against draining table

### Step 3: Drain (no abort storms — CRITICAL)
While `draining_table != NONE`, periodically check lock-quiescence:
- **Lock-quiescence barrier:** `forall entry in draining.entries: entry.owner_txn == 0`
- **MUST NOT** freeze acquisitions in the active table
- **MUST NOT** require other transactions to abort to facilitate drain
- Normal `release()` calls drive the draining table to quiescence naturally
- Read-only transactions MUST NOT block rebuild (they don't touch lock table)
- **Coordinator liveness rule:** If rebuilder is also commit sequencer, MUST treat drain+clear as background maintenance, MUST NOT block commit publication waiting for quiescence. MAY poll between commit batches or when commit queue is empty.
- During drain, SHOULD run `cleanup_orphaned_slots()` to prevent orphaned holders from stalling quiescence

### Step 4: Clear Drained Table
Once lock-quiescent:
- Clear all entries: `page_number = 0`, `owner_txn = 0`
- Safe because `owner_txn == 0` everywhere means clearing keys cannot cause false negatives
- Set `draining_table = NONE` (Release ordering)

### Step 5: Increment rebuild_epoch + Release Lease
- Increment `rebuild_epoch`
- Release lease: `rebuild_pid = 0`

## Resource Exhaustion Behavior
If `draining_table != NONE` AND active table also beyond load factor threshold:
- New acquisitions requiring a **new** key MAY fail with `SQLITE_BUSY`
- This is a capacity-budget signal: either increase table capacity (config) or reduce concurrent working set

## Cancellation Safety
**Once drain observes lock-quiescence and clearing begins, the rebuild MUST run to completion** (mask cancellation). The lease must be released and the table must not be left partially cleared.

## Load Factor Analysis (Knuth Vol. 3)

### Linear Probing Expected Probe Lengths
- Successful search: `0.5 * (1 + 1/(1 - α))`
- Unsuccessful search (insert): `0.5 * (1 + (1/(1 - α))^2)`

### Zipfian Clustering Impact
| Load factor | Unsuccessful probes (linear) | Unsuccessful probes (Zipfian s=1) |
|-------------|-----------------------------|------------------------------------|
| 0.25        | 1.39                        | ~2.0                               |
| 0.50        | 2.50                        | ~5.0                               |
| 0.75        | 8.50                        | ~20.0                              |
| 0.90        | 50.50                       | ~100+                              |

### 70% Load Factor Policy
- Maximum load factor: 0.70
- With C = 1,048,576 (V1 default): allows up to 734,003 distinct page numbers
- Beyond 70%: new acquisitions return SQLITE_BUSY rather than degrading to pathological probe chains

### Robin Hood Hashing Alternative
If Zipfian clustering proves problematic: Robin Hood hashing bounds variance of probe lengths (max probe length difference O(log log C)) while maintaining same shared-memory-friendly fixed-size layout.

## Unit Test Specifications

### Test 1: `test_rebuild_rotate_swaps_active_table`
Create a SharedPageLockTable with table 0 active and load factor > 0.70. Trigger rebuild. Verify active_table becomes 1, draining_table becomes 0. Verify new acquisitions go to table 1.

### Test 2: `test_rebuild_drain_reaches_quiescence`
Populate draining table with entries whose owner_txn != 0. Release all locks. Verify drain phase detects lock-quiescence (all owner_txn == 0). Verify table is cleared and draining_table set to NONE.

### Test 3: `test_rebuild_no_abort_guarantee`
Start rebuild while active transactions hold page locks. Verify NO transaction is forcefully aborted. Verify transactions can still commit/abort normally. Verify drain completes only after natural release.

### Test 4: `test_rebuild_lease_prevents_concurrent_rebuilds`
Attempt two concurrent rebuilds. Verify only one acquires the lease (CAS contention). Second attempt gets rebuild_pid != 0 and backs off.

### Test 5: `test_rebuild_stale_lease_stolen`
Set rebuild_pid to a dead process with expired lease. Attempt rebuild from a new process. Verify lease is stolen successfully and rebuild proceeds.

### Test 6: `test_rebuild_cancellation_safety`
Start rebuild. After quiescence detected but during clearing, simulate cancellation. Verify clearing completes to the end — table is not left partially cleared, lease is released.

### Test 7: `test_rebuild_resource_exhaustion_busy`
Set draining_table != NONE. Fill active table past 70% load factor. Attempt new key acquisition. Verify SQLITE_BUSY returned (not pathological probe chain).

### Test 8: `test_rebuild_try_acquire_consults_draining_first`
During drain phase, insert conflicting lock into draining table. Attempt try_acquire for same page in active table. Verify conflict detected (SQLITE_BUSY), not a false grant.

title: §6.3-6.4 ARC REPLACE + REQUEST Algorithms (Full Pseudocode)
description:
Implements §6.3-6.4 of the FrankenSQLite spec: the full ARC REPLACE and REQUEST algorithms with complete pseudocode for the MVCC-aware buffer pool.

SUMMARY: Defines the two core ARC subroutines — REPLACE (victim selection between T1 and T2) and REQUEST (cache lookup, miss handling, ghost hit processing). Includes the async singleflight protocol for concurrent page loading, cancellation safety, and the critical safety valve for all-pinned scenarios. This is the algorithmic heart of the buffer pool.

KEY DATA STRUCTURES AND ALGORITHMS:
- REPLACE subroutine: Selects victim using adaptive parameter p and B2 tie-breaking. prefer_t1 = |T1| > 0 AND (|T1| > p OR (|T1| == p AND target_key IN B2)). Pinned pages skipped via rotate_front_to_back. Safety valve: rotations_t1 >= |T1| AND rotations_t2 >= |T2| triggers capacity_overflow (temporary growth, no deadlock).
- REQUEST subroutine — 4 cases: Case I (T1 hit): promote to T2. Case I (T2 hit): refresh MRU. Case II (B1 ghost hit): p += max(1, |B2|/|B1|), REPLACE, fetch, insert T2. Case III (B2 ghost hit): p -= max(1, |B1|/|B2|), REPLACE, fetch, insert T2. Case IV (complete miss): manage L1/L2 sizes, trim ghosts, REPLACE, fetch, insert T1.
- Async Singleflight Protocol: CacheEntry = Ready(Arc<CachedPage>) | Loading{done: watch::Receiver}. REQUEST_ASYNC: lock, check entry; Ready -> promote+pin; Loading -> clone receiver, unlock, await; Missing -> install Loading placeholder, unlock, fetch, install result, wake waiters.
- Complexity: O(1) amortized per operation. Ghost list overhead ~160KB for 2000-entry cache.

NORMATIVE INVARIANTS:
- parking_lot::Mutex guard MUST NOT be held across I/O or .await
- REPLACE prefer_t1 is a hint: if preferred list exhausted (all pinned), MUST fall back to other list for liveness
- Preferred list exhaustion MUST fall back to other list (CRITICAL for liveness)
- Safety valve: all pages pinned triggers capacity_overflow += 1 rather than deadlock
- Cancellation safety: loader cancelled after placeholder MUST resolve done latch (send Err(Cancelled)) and remove placeholder
- Case IV L1 invariant: if |T1| < capacity, evict LRU of T1 directly without adding to B1 (violates L1 <= capacity)

UNIT TEST REQUIREMENTS:
1. test_replace_prefers_t1_when_over_p: |T1| > p triggers eviction from T1
2. test_replace_b2_tiebreaker: |T1| == p AND target in B2 triggers T1 eviction
3. test_replace_skips_pinned: Pinned pages rotated not evicted
4. test_replace_overflow_safety_valve: All pinned triggers capacity overflow (no deadlock)
5. test_replace_fallback: Preferred list exhausted falls back to other list
6. test_request_t1_to_t2_promotion: Hit in T1 moves entry to T2
7. test_request_t2_refresh: Hit in T2 refreshes MRU position
8. test_request_b1_ghost_increases_p: Ghost hit in B1 increases p
9. test_request_b2_ghost_decreases_p: Ghost hit in B2 decreases p
10. test_request_miss_inserts_t1: Complete miss inserts into T1
11. test_request_ghost_trim: L1 reaching capacity triggers B1 front trimming

E2E TEST: test_e2e_arc_cache_behavior_under_mixed_workload — wire ARC into pager, run mixed workload (scan + point-lookups + hot-set), verify p adapts and ARC achieves better hit rate than pure LRU.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA:
- REPLACE correctly selects victims based on p, B2 tie-breaking, and pinned-page skipping
- REQUEST correctly handles all 4 cases with proper p adjustments and list transitions
- Async singleflight prevents duplicate fetches for the same page
- Cancellation safety verified: cancelled loaders clean up placeholders
- Safety valve prevents deadlock under all-pinned scenario
- O(1) amortized complexity verified via benchmark (no O(n) scans)

REQUEST handles all 4 cases (T1 hit, T2 hit, B1 ghost, B2 ghost, miss) with correct p adjustment. Scan resistance confirmed. Implementation in crates/fsqlite-pager/src/arc_cache.rs.

## Merged from P2 bead bd-2v3d (§6.3-6.4 Full ARC Algorithm)

## §6.3 REPLACE Subroutine

Selects victim for eviction. Chooses between T1 and T2 based on adaptive parameter p and tie-breaking when target_key found in B2.

**Full Algorithm:**
- Track rotations_t1 and rotations_t2 separately
- Safety valve: if rotations_t1 >= |T1| AND rotations_t2 >= |T2|, all pages pinned — allow temporary capacity_overflow rather than deadlock
- CRITICAL: pinned/failing preferred list MUST NOT prevent eviction from other list
- prefer_t1 = |T1| > 0 AND (|T1| > p OR (|T1| == p AND target_key IN B2))
- prefer_t1 is a hint: if preferred list exhausted (all pinned), MUST fall back to other list for liveness
- TRY_T1: evict LRU of T1, skip pinned via rotate_front_to_back, add evicted key to B1
- TRY_T2: evict LRU of T2, skip pinned, add evicted key to B2

**Async integration (normative):** parking_lot::Mutex guard MUST NOT be held across I/O or .await. REPLACE itself does no I/O (pure), but REQUEST must drop mutex before fetch.

## §6.4 REQUEST Subroutine

**Case I — Cache hit in T1:** Remove from T1, push_back to T2 (promote to frequency list), increment ref_count.
**Case I — Cache hit in T2:** Move to back of T2 (refresh MRU), increment ref_count.

**Case II — Ghost hit in B1:** Evidence T1 too small. p += max(1, |B2|/|B1|), clamped to capacity. Call REPLACE. Remove from B1. Fetch from storage. Insert into T2 (second lifetime access).

**Case III — Ghost hit in B2:** Evidence T2 too small. p -= max(1, |B1|/|B2|), floor at 0. Call REPLACE. Remove from B2. Fetch from storage. Insert into T2.

**Case IV — Complete miss:** L1=|T1|+|B1|, L2=|T2|+|B2|. If L1==capacity: pop_front B1 if |T1|<capacity else evict LRU of T1 directly (do NOT add to B1 — would violate L1<=capacity invariant; evicted key is simply discarded). Else if L1<capacity AND L1+L2>=capacity: pop B2 if L1+L2>=2*capacity, then REPLACE. Insert into T1 (new pages always enter T1).

**Async Singleflight Protocol (normative):**
CacheEntry = Ready(Arc<CachedPage>) | Loading { done: watch::Receiver }
LoadStatus = Pending | Ok | Err(Arc<Error>)

REQUEST_ASYNC pattern: lock mutex, check entry. Ready -> promote+pin, return. Loading -> clone receiver, unlock, await changed(), re-loop. Missing -> install Loading placeholder, unlock, fetch_from_storage_async(cx) outside mutex, lock, install result, wake waiters via tx.send.

**Cancellation safety:** Loader cancelled after placeholder MUST resolve done latch (send Err(Cancelled)) and remove placeholder so waiters don't block forever.

**Complexity:** O(1) amortized per operation. Ghost list overhead: ~160KB for 2000-entry cache (16B/CacheKey + ~24B container, 2x2000 entries).

### §6.4.1 Optional p-Update as Online Learning (Research Note)
OCO-style controller: p_{t+1} = clamp(p_t + eta_t * s_t, 0, capacity), s_t = +1 for B1 hit, -1 for B2 hit. Diminishing eta yields no-regret in abstract model. BUT ARC/CAR properties rely on canonical update — any alternative MUST be treated as harness experiment until proven.
