title: Understand and Verify RaptorQ Decoding Pipeline (§3.2.4)
description:
Ensure deep understanding and verification of the 6-step RaptorQ decoding process with inactivation decoding.

SPEC REFERENCE: §3.2.4 (Decoding Step by Step)

THE 6 DECODING STEPS:

STEP 1: COLLECT RECEIVED SYMBOLS
Collect N encoding symbols with their ISIs. N >= K_prime and ideally N is close to K_prime.
- Some may be source symbols (ISI < K_prime)
- Others may be repair symbols (ISI >= K_prime)
- Receiver does NOT need to know which symbols were lost -- it only needs N symbols, ANY N symbols

STEP 2: BUILD THE DECODING MATRIX A_prime (N x L)
Construct N x L matrix A_prime where row i corresponds to received symbol with ISI X_i:

```
For each received symbol with ISI X_i:
    If X_i < K_prime (source symbol):
        Row i = row S+H+X_i of the original constraint matrix A
    Else (repair symbol):
        Row i = LT encoding vector for ISI X_i
        (computed from Tuple(K_prime, X_i), same as during encoding)
```

Prepend the S LDPC constraint rows and H HDPC constraint rows:
```
A_extended (S+H+N rows x L columns):
    Rows 0..S-1:       LDPC constraints
    Rows S..S+H-1:     HDPC constraints
    Rows S+H..S+H+N-1: received symbol constraints

D_extended:
    D[0..S-1]       = zero symbols
    D[S..S+H-1]     = zero symbols
    D[S+H..S+H+N-1] = received symbol data
```

System is overdetermined (S+H+N >= L when N >= K_prime), need to find C[0..L-1] satisfying at least L of the S+H+N equations.

STEP 3: INACTIVATION DECODING (TWO PHASES)
This is the heart of RaptorQ decoding. Direct Gaussian elimination on L x L matrix over GF(256) costs O(L^3). Inactivation decoding exploits sparse structure for near-linear average-case performance.

PHASE 1 -- PEELING (O(K) average case):
Iteratively process rows with exactly one unknown symbol (one non-zero entry in remaining unresolved columns):

```
peeling():
    resolved = {}   // set of resolved symbol indices
    while exists row r with exactly 1 unresolved column c:
        // Row r: a_{r,c} * C[c] = D[r] - sum(a_{r,j} * C[j] for j in resolved)
        // Since a_{r,c} is the only unresolved coefficient:
        C[c] = (D[r] XOR sum(a_{r,j} * C[j] for resolved j)) * inverse(a_{r,c})
        resolved.add(c)
        // Remove column c from all other rows (update their right-hand sides)
```

Because LDPC and LT rows are sparse, peeling resolves the MAJORITY of intermediate symbols. For a well-received block (N slightly above K_prime), peeling typically resolves 90-95% of symbols in O(K) total operations (each row touches only ~d columns where d is the LT degree, average degree is O(log K)).

Peeling also identifies INACTIVE symbols: those that cannot be resolved by peeling because they appear in multiple unresolved rows. Inactive count typically O(sqrt(K_prime)) to O(log(K_prime)), thanks to careful code design.

PHASE 2 -- GAUSSIAN ELIMINATION ON INACTIVE SUBSYSTEM:
After peeling, a small dense subsystem of I inactive symbols remains. I ~ O(sqrt(K_prime)), typically < 50 for K_prime < 10000.

```
gaussian_solve(inactive_matrix, inactive_rhs):
    // inactive_matrix is approximately I x I where I ~ O(sqrt(K_prime))
    // Standard GF(256) Gaussian elimination with nonzero pivot selection
    // NOTE: "partial pivoting" not needed over exact fields -- no rounding error
    for col in 0..I:
        // Find pivot row
        pivot_row = find_row_with_nonzero_entry_in_column(col)
        if pivot_row is None:
            return DECODING_FAILURE
        swap_rows(col, pivot_row)
        // Eliminate column from all other rows
        pivot_val = inactive_matrix[col][col]
        for row in 0..I:
            if row != col and inactive_matrix[row][col] != 0:
                factor = mul(inactive_matrix[row][col], inverse(pivot_val))
                // Row operation: row[row] -= factor * row[col]
                for j in col..I:
                    inactive_matrix[row][j] ^= mul(factor, inactive_matrix[col][j])
                inactive_rhs[row] = symbol_addmul(inactive_rhs[row], factor, inactive_rhs[col])
    // Back-substitute to get inactive symbol values
    for col in (0..I).rev():
        C[inactive[col]] = symbol_mul(inverse(inactive_matrix[col][col]), inactive_rhs[col])
```

Cost: O(I^2 * T) for symbol operations + O(I^3) for matrix operations. Since I is small (typically < 50 for K_prime < 10000), this is negligible compared to Phase 1.

STEP 4: RECOVER ALL INTERMEDIATE SYMBOLS
After Phase 2, all inactive symbols are known. "Reverse peel" through Phase 1 resolutions in reverse order to recover all intermediate symbols.

STEP 5: RECONSTRUCT SOURCE SYMBOLS
With all intermediate symbols C[0..L-1] known:
```
for i in 0..K_prime:
    C_prime[i] = LTEnc(K_prime, C[0..L-1], i)
    // Since code is systematic, just picks right linear combination
```

For source symbols that were received directly, the reconstructed value SHOULD match exactly (serves as verification check).

STEP 6: STRIP PADDING
Discard (K_prime - K) padding symbols to recover original K source symbols C_prime[0], ..., C_prime[K-1].

DECODING FAILURE BEHAVIOR (Normative):
1. Correctness MUST NOT depend on decoding succeeding with exactly K symbols
2. Durability/replication code MUST be able to obtain more symbols (local repair store and/or peers) and retry decode
3. For durability-critical objects, the writer MUST persist an explicit overhead policy (e.g., "store K+r repair symbols") in the object metadata so readers know what to request

VERIFICATION DISCIPLINE (Alien-Artifact):
Do NOT hard-code or assume numerical failure probabilities. Instead, continuously validate the OBSERVED failure rate envelope as a function of (K, r, symbol_size) using lab tests and anytime-valid monitoring (e-process/e-values) so regressions are caught even under optional stopping.

V1 DEFAULT POLICY:
Persist enough symbols for decoder to collect K+2 without coordination. This pushes P_fail < 10^-7.

VERIFICATION TEST CASES:
1. Decode with exactly K symbols: verify ~99% success over 1000 trials (P_fail < 0.02)
2. Decode with K+1 symbols: verify ~99.99% success (P_fail < 0.001)
3. Decode with K+2 symbols: verify ~99.99999% success (zero failures over 1000 trials)
4. Decode failure: verify failure is handled gracefully (no panic, returns error, retry possible)
5. Decode proof: verify decode failure produces explainable artifact with replay verification
6. Verify peeling resolves > 80% of symbols for K > 100
7. Verify inactive subsystem size I < sqrt(K_prime) for K > 100
8. Verify received source symbols match reconstructed values (integrity check)
9. Verify padding stripped correctly: K=5, K_prime=6, decoded output has exactly 5 symbols

E2E TESTS:
- For K in {5, 50, 500, 5000}:
  a. Encode K source symbols (page-sized)
  b. Lose random subset, keep K+2 symbols
  c. Decode, verify all K symbols recovered exactly
- Stress test: K=56403 (max), verify decode completes in reasonable time
- Mixed ISIs: decode from combination of source + repair symbols in random order

CRATE: Integration tests in fsqlite-harness
ACCEPTANCE: Decode tests pass for all K ranges. Failure handled gracefully. Decode proof produced on failure. Performance within expected bounds.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Decoding pipeline matches the spec and is verified against `asupersync::raptorq` (stage sequence, erasure handling, and explicit failure signaling when <K symbols).
- [ ] Unit tests listed in the §3.2.4 section of the §3 testing-requirements comment for **bd-1hi.4** are implemented and pass (including the stated performance target for a representative K/T).
- [ ] E2E encode/decode pipeline test passes under symbol loss/erasures and is deterministic across runs.
- [ ] Logging requirements implemented: stage progress at DEBUG, success/failure at INFO, near-threshold at WARN, unrecoverable failures at ERROR with minimal reproducer context.

title: Implement RaptorQ Source Block Partitioning for Large Databases (§3.1)
description:
E2E Test:
- test_e2e_bd_1hi_6_compliance: concrete E2E identifier for structure lint compliance.

Implement source block partitioning for databases larger than a single RaptorQ source block.

CONSTRAINTS (from §3.1 and §3.4.3):
- RFC 6330 supports up to K_max = 56,403 source symbols per source block
- With T = page_size = 4096 bytes, one source block covers up to 56,403 pages = ~220 MiB (231 MB) of database content
- Larger databases MUST be partitioned into multiple source blocks
- RFC 6330 bounds Source Block Number (SBN) to 8 bits, so SBN_max = 255

SOURCE BLOCK PARTITIONING ALGORITHM (from §3.4.3, per RFC 6330 §4.4.1):

```
partition_source_blocks(P: u32, page_size: u32) -> Vec<SourceBlock>:
    K_max = 56403
    T = page_size    // symbol size = page size

    if P <= K_max:
        // Single source block covers the entire database
        return [SourceBlock { index: 0, start_page: 1, num_pages: P }]

    // Multiple source blocks needed
    // Partition P pages into Z blocks as evenly as possible
    Z = ceil(P / K_max)
    // RFC 6330 partitioning: Z_L blocks of K_L symbols, Z_S blocks of K_S symbols
    K_L = ceil(P / Z)    // larger block size
    K_S = floor(P / Z)   // smaller block size
    Z_L = P - K_S * Z    // number of larger blocks
    Z_S = Z - Z_L        // number of smaller blocks

    blocks = []
    offset = 1    // page numbers are 1-based
    for i in 0..Z_L:
        blocks.append(SourceBlock { index: i, start_page: offset, num_pages: K_L })
        offset += K_L
    for i in Z_L..(Z_L + Z_S):
        blocks.append(SourceBlock { index: i, start_page: offset, num_pages: K_S })
        offset += K_S

    assert(offset == P + 1)
    return blocks
```

WORKED EXAMPLE (from spec):
A 1GB database with 4096-byte pages has P = 262,144 pages.
```
Z = ceil(262144 / 56403) = 5 source blocks
K_L = ceil(262144 / 5) = 52429
K_S = floor(262144 / 5) = 52428
Z_L = 262144 - 52428 * 5 = 4 blocks of 52429 pages
Z_S = 5 - 4 = 1 block of 52428 pages

Source blocks:
    Block 0: pages 1-52429      (52,429 pages, ~205 MB)
    Block 1: pages 52430-104858 (52,429 pages, ~205 MB)
    Block 2: pages 104859-157287 (52,429 pages, ~205 MB)
    Block 3: pages 157288-209716 (52,429 pages, ~205 MB)
    Block 4: pages 209717-262144 (52,428 pages, ~205 MB)
```

DATA STRUCTURES:

```rust
struct SourceBlock {
    index: u8,           // 0-based block index (SBN). MUST fit in u8 (max 255)
    start_page: u32,     // 1-based first page number in this block
    num_pages: u32,      // K = number of source symbols in this block
}
```

INVARIANTS (normative):
- Each block MUST have num_pages <= K_max = 56,403
- Blocks MUST be contiguous and non-overlapping
- Block indices MUST be sequential starting from 0
- Total pages across all blocks MUST equal database page count P
- SBN fits in u8, so total blocks Z MUST be <= 256
- For each block, K_prime (from systematic index table lookup) >= num_pages

EDGE CASES:
- Single page database: 1 block, 1 symbol, K_prime from Table 2 lookup
- Empty database (P=0): no blocks (degenerate case)
- P exactly equals K_max: single block, no padding needed (if K_max is in Table 2)
- Last block may have fewer pages than others (K_S < K_L), requiring different K_prime lookup and zero-padding to K_prime

REPLICATION SHARDING NOTE (from §3.4.2):
For replication, if K_source > 56,403, the sender MUST shard the transfer into multiple independent changeset objects (each with its own changeset_bytes and changeset_id) such that each shard satisfies K_source <= 56,403. Multi-block (SBN>0) changesets are NOT used in V1.

- prop_bd_1hi_6_structure_compliance: concrete property identifier for structure lint compliance.

- Two blocks: P=56404 (just over K_max), verify 2 blocks with correct sizes

- Maximum blocks: P=56403*256, verify 256 blocks (SBN boundary)
- Overflow: P > 56403*256 must be handled (error or multi-level sharding)

- test_e2e_bd_1hi_6_compliance: concrete E2E identifier for structure lint compliance.

title: Implement RaptorQ Failure Probability Monitoring (§3.1.1)
description:
Implement runtime monitoring of RaptorQ decode failure probability using e-processes (anytime-valid monitoring).

SPEC REFERENCES: §3.1.1 (Operational Guidance), §3.2.4 (Decoding Failure Behavior), §4.3 (E-Process Framework)

FAILURE PROBABILITY RULES OF THUMB (RFC 6330 Annex B simulation data):
- Decoding with exactly K received symbols: ~99% success (P_fail < 0.01)
- Decoding with K+1 symbols: P_fail < 10^-4
- Decoding with K+2 symbols: P_fail < 10^-7

V1 DEFAULT POLICY: Aim to persist/replicate enough symbols that a decoder can almost always collect K+2 symbols without coordination. This eliminates the need for "just one more symbol" negotiation loops in the common case.

CAUTION ON FAILURE PROBABILITY CLAIMS (from §3.1):
The exact failure probability depends on K, the symbol size, and implementation quality. The figures above are from RFC 6330 Annex B simulation data. Do NOT cite "0.01%" (10^-4) for exactly-K decoding; that overstates the guarantee by ~100x. Our V1 policy (K+2 symbols) is specifically chosen to push well past this ambiguity.

NORMATIVE DECODING FAILURE BEHAVIOR (from §3.2.4):
1. Correctness MUST NOT depend on decoding succeeding with exactly K symbols
2. Durability/replication code MUST be able to obtain more symbols (local repair store and/or peers) and retry decode
3. For durability-critical objects, the writer MUST persist an explicit overhead policy (e.g., "store K+r repair symbols") in the object metadata so readers know what to request

ALIEN-ARTIFACT DISCIPLINE (from §3.2.4):
We do NOT hard-code or assume numerical failure probabilities. Instead, we continuously validate the OBSERVED failure rate envelope as a function of (K, r, symbol_size) using:
- Lab tests with known ground truth
- Anytime-valid monitoring (e-process/e-values) in production
- Regressions caught even under optional stopping (the key property of e-processes vs fixed-sample tests)

E-PROCESS MONITORING IMPLEMENTATION:

Data collection:
```
struct DecodeAttempt {
    k_source: u32,           // K (number of source symbols)
    symbols_received: u32,   // total symbols available for decode
    overhead: u32,           // symbols_received - k_source
    symbol_size: u32,        // T (bytes per symbol)
    success: bool,           // did decode succeed?
    decode_time_us: u64,     // for performance monitoring
    object_type: ObjectType, // WAL group, snapshot block, ECS object, etc.
}
```

E-process for failure rate monitoring:
```
struct FailureRateMonitor {
    // Bucket by (K-range, overhead) for granular monitoring
    // E.g., K in [1,10], [11,100], [101,1000], [1001,10000], [10001,56403]
    // Overhead: 0, 1, 2, 3+
    buckets: HashMap<(KRange, u32), EProcessState>,
}

struct EProcessState {
    e_value: f64,           // Running e-value (product martingale)
    total_attempts: u64,
    total_failures: u64,
    null_rate: f64,         // H0: P_fail <= null_rate (theoretical bound)
    alert_threshold: f64,   // Reject H0 if e_value > threshold (e.g., 20)
}

fn update(state: &mut EProcessState, success: bool) {
    // Betting e-process: e_{n+1} = e_n * (1 + lambda * (X_n - null_rate))
    // where X_n = 1 if failure, 0 if success
    // lambda chosen to maximize expected log-growth under alternative
    let x = if success { 0.0 } else { 1.0 };
    let lambda = 0.5; // Conservative bet size
    state.e_value *= 1.0 + lambda * (x - state.null_rate);
    state.total_attempts += 1;
    if !success { state.total_failures += 1; }
}
```

Null hypotheses (theoretical bounds from RFC 6330 Annex B):
- Overhead 0 (exactly K): H0: P_fail <= 0.02 (conservative, spec says ~0.01)
- Overhead 1 (K+1): H0: P_fail <= 0.001 (conservative, spec says ~10^-4)
- Overhead 2 (K+2): H0: P_fail <= 10^-5 (conservative, spec says ~10^-7)

Alert conditions:
- e_value exceeds threshold: something is wrong (implementation bug, hardware issue, etc.)
- Observed failure rate significantly above theoretical bound
- Log alert, trigger diagnostic decode proof collection

INTEGRATION WITH ADAPTIVE REDUNDANCY (§3.5.12):
The failure rate monitor feeds into the adaptive redundancy autopilot. If observed failure rates are higher than expected for a given K range, the autopilot MAY increase the repair symbol count to compensate.

title: Implement Tuple Generator and Systematic Index Table Integration (§3.2.5)
description:
Verify and integrate the Tuple generator and systematic index table from asupersync (RFC 6330 §5.3.5.4).

SPEC REFERENCE: §3.2.5 (The Tuple Generator and Systematic Index Table)

TUPLE FUNCTION DEFINITION:
The Tuple function maps an ISI (Internal Symbol ID) to a 6-tuple (d, a, b, d1, a1, b1) that determines which intermediate symbols participate in generating that encoding symbol. This function is DETERMINISTIC and depends ONLY on K_prime and the ISI.

```
Tuple(K_prime, ISI) -> (d, a, b, d1, a1, b1)
    d  = LT degree (number of intermediate symbols XORed)
    a  = LT stride parameter (step between selected intermediate symbols)
    b  = LT start position (first intermediate symbol index)
    d1 = permanent inactivation degree
    a1 = permanent inactivation stride
    b1 = permanent inactivation start
```

The 6-tuple determines the encoding vector for each symbol:
- Positions b, (b+a) mod W, (b+2a) mod W, ..., (b+(d-1)*a) mod W (LT component)
- Plus permanent inactivation entries from d1, a1, b1 in columns W..K_prime-1

SYSTEMATIC INDEX TABLE (RFC 6330 Table 2):
Precomputed table of supported K_prime values (up to K_max = 56,403). For each K_prime, stores:
- J(K_prime): the systematic index, chosen so first K_prime encoding symbols (ISIs 0..K_prime-1) correspond exactly to K_prime source symbols
- S(K_prime): number of LDPC symbols
- H(K_prime): number of HDPC symbols
- W(K_prime): LT generator modulus parameter
- L = K_prime + S + H: total number of intermediate symbols

The systematic property is ENGINEERED: J(K_prime) is selected so the encoding matrix has an embedded identity for the source symbols. This means:
- For ISI X < K_prime: the encoding symbol IS the source symbol (zero encoding overhead)
- For ISI X >= K_prime: the encoding symbol is a repair symbol (computed via LTEnc)

RAND FUNCTION:
The Tuple function uses the Rand function (RFC 6330 §5.3.5.1) which combines K_prime, ISI, and an iteration counter to pseudorandomly but deterministically select the LT degree and positions.

```
Rand(y, i, m) -> u32:
    // RFC 6330 §5.3.5.1
    // y: ISI, i: iteration, m: modulus
    x0 = (y + i) mod 2^8
    x1 = (floor(y / 2^8) + i) mod 2^8
    x2 = (floor(y / 2^16) + i) mod 2^8
    x3 = (floor(y / 2^24) + i) mod 2^8
    return (V0[x0] ^ V1[x1] ^ V2[x2] ^ V3[x3]) mod m
```

Where V0, V1, V2, V3 are the four 256-entry random tables defined in RFC 6330 §5.5.

DEGREE DISTRIBUTION:
The LT degree d is selected from the "RaptorQ degree distribution" (RFC 6330 §5.3.5.4). This is a carefully tuned soliton-like distribution optimized for inactivation decoding. The distribution ensures:
- Most encoding symbols have small degree (fast peeling in Phase 1)
- A few encoding symbols have large degree (algebraic coverage for Phase 2)
- The balance is tuned so the inactive subsystem size I is minimized (I ~ O(sqrt(K_prime)))

LT ENCODING (from §3.2.3):
```
LTEnc(K_prime, C[0..L-1], X):
    (d, a, b, d1, a1, b1) = Tuple(K_prime, X)
    result = C[b]
    for j in 1..d:
        b = (b + a) mod W
        result = result XOR C[b]
    // Permanent inactivation component
    while b1 >= L:
        b1 = (b1 + a1) mod P1
    result = result XOR C[b1]
    for j in 1..d1:
        b1 = (b1 + a1) mod P1
        while b1 >= L:
            b1 = (b1 + a1) mod P1
        result = result XOR C[b1]
    return result
```

LT ROWS IN CONSTRAINT MATRIX (from §3.2.3):
Row S+H+i corresponds to source symbol C_prime[i]. Each LT row is generated by the Tuple function:
```
(d, a, b, d1, a1, b1) = Tuple(K_prime, i)
Row S+H+i has 1s at positions:
    b                          (always)
    (b + a) mod W              (if d >= 2)
    (b + 2*a) mod W            (if d >= 3)
    ...
    (b + (d-1)*a) mod W        (if degree is d)
Plus "permanent inactivation" entries from d1, a1, b1 in columns W..K_prime-1
```

IMPLEMENTATION NOTES:
FrankenSQLite uses asupersync implementation, NOT re-implementing RFC 6330. This bead is about:
1. Verification that asupersync Tuple output matches RFC 6330
2. Understanding for correct integration and debugging
3. Verifying the systematic property holds

FrankenSQLite relies on asupersync for these derivations; do NOT substitute ad-hoc formulas.

VERIFICATION TEST CASES:
- For K=5 (K_prime=6): verify Tuple output for ISIs 0..5 produces identity encoding (systematic property)
- For K=10 (K_prime=10): verify Tuple output for ISIs 10..14 (repair symbols) produces non-trivial combinations
- For K=100 (K_prime=101): verify systematic property and spot-check repair symbol tuples
- For K=1000: verify systematic property at scale
- Verify Rand function output against RFC 6330 V0-V3 tables
- Verify degree distribution histogram matches RFC 6330 §5.3.5.4 probabilities (statistical test over many ISIs)
- Verify J(K_prime) values from Table 2 produce systematic codes (the key correctness property)
- Cross-check: encode K_prime source symbols, verify first K_prime encoding symbols are identity

E2E TEST:
- For representative K values (5, 50, 500, 5000, 56403): create encoder, verify systematic property, generate repair symbols, decode from mix of source+repair, verify round-trip correctness.

CRATE: fsqlite-harness (verification tests)
ACCEPTANCE: Tuple function verified against RFC 6330 for representative K_prime values. Systematic property confirmed for all tested K values. Rand function matches RFC 6330 tables. Degree distribution statistically matches specification.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Tuple generator implementation matches RFC 6330 exactly (byte-for-byte behavior for (K, ISI) inputs) and is deterministic.
- [ ] Systematic index table is loaded/accessible for the supported K range and provides O(1) lookup.
- [ ] Unit tests listed in the §3.2.5 section of the §3 testing-requirements comment for **bd-1hi.8** are implemented and pass.
- [ ] E2E encode/decode pipeline test covers tuple generation + systematic index usage end-to-end.

title: Implement Self-Healing WAL: .wal-fec Sidecar Format (§3.4.1)
description:
Implement the .wal-fec sidecar file format for RaptorQ-coded WAL durability.

SPEC REFERENCE: §3.4.1 (Self-Healing WAL: Erasure-Coded Durability)

PROBLEM STATEMENT:
SQLite WAL recovery is conservative: if any WAL frame that should be replayable is corrupted (checksum mismatch), recovery truncates at the first invalid frame. This most often discards an in-flight tail transaction after crash, but can also discard committed history when corruption occurs within frames that were previously durable (media errors, latent sector corruption, device bugs).

SOLUTION:
Each WAL commit group is RaptorQ-encoded. Source symbols in .wal (standard frames), repair symbols in .wal-fec sidecar.

```
WAL Commit (N pages):
  Source symbols:   [Page1_data | Page2_data | ... | PageN_data]
  Repair symbols:   R additional symbols (PRAGMA raptorq_repair_symbols)
  Written to disk:
    - .wal: N standard SQLite WAL frames (source symbols)
    - .wal-fec: R repair symbols + group metadata (sidecar)
```

OBJECT MODEL:
Each committed SQLite WAL transaction (set of frames up to commit frame with db_size \!= 0) is treated as a compat ECS object:
- Object type: CompatWalCommitGroup
- Source symbols (K): ordered page images from .wal frames (NOT duplicated into .wal-fec)
- Repair symbols (R): PRAGMA raptorq_repair_symbols repair symbols, stored in .wal-fec

GROUP ID:
```
group_id := (wal_salt1, wal_salt2, end_frame_no)
```

.WAL-FEC FILE FORMAT:
.wal-fec is an append-only sequence of records, one per commit group:
1. A WalFecGroupMeta record (variable length; length-prefixed)
2. R ECS SymbolRecords (§3.5.2) for ESIs K..K+R-1

DATA STRUCTURE -- WalFecGroupMeta:
```
WalFecGroupMeta := {
    magic              : [u8; 8],    // "FSQLWFEC"
    version            : u32,        // 1
    wal_salt1          : u32,
    wal_salt2          : u32,
    start_frame_no     : u32,        // inclusive, 1-based frame numbering within the WAL
    end_frame_no       : u32,        // inclusive; commit frame
    db_size_pages      : u32,        // commit frame db_size (pages) after this commit
    page_size          : u32,
    k_source           : u32,        // K
    r_repair           : u32,        // R
    oti                : OTI,        // decoding params (symbol size, block partitioning)
    object_id          : [u8; 16],   // ObjectId of CompatWalCommitGroup (content-addressed)
    page_numbers       : Vec<u32>,   // length = K; maps ISI 0..K-1 -> Pgno (frame order; duplicates permitted)
    source_page_xxh3_128: Vec<[u8; 16]>,  // length = K; xxh3_128(page_data) for ISI i
    checksum           : u64,        // xxh3_64 of all preceding fields
}
```

INVARIANTS (normative):
- k_source == end_frame_no - start_frame_no + 1
- page_numbers.len() == k_source
- source_page_xxh3_128.len() == k_source
- end_frame_no is the group commit frame (corresponding WAL frame has db_size \!= 0 when fully intact)
- db_size_pages MUST equal the commit frame db_size field

WHY source_page_xxh3_128 EXISTS (critical design rationale):
SQLite WAL checksums are CUMULATIVE (§7.5). Each frame checksum depends on the previous frame checksum, forming a chain. Once this chain breaks at frame i (checksum mismatch), frames i+1 onward CANNOT be validated via the WAL format alone, even if their bytes are perfectly intact. The source_page_xxh3_128 array provides INDEPENDENT per-source validation, enabling:
- Random-access validation of individual source frames regardless of chain state
- Safe feeding of surviving source frames into RaptorQ decoder
- Detection of stale/corrupt source data before decode

WRITE ORDERING AND SEMANTICS (normative):
- DURABLE (SQLite semantics): commit is durable once .wal frames for the group (including commit frame) are written and fsync-d and wal-index (foo.db-shm) is updated (§5.6.7 step 2)
- REPAIRABLE (FrankenSQLite enhancement): commit group becomes repairable ONLY after its .wal-fec WalFecGroupMeta + R repair SymbolRecords are appended and fsync-d

WORKED EXAMPLE: COMMIT OF 5 PAGES WITH 2 REPAIR SYMBOLS
Transaction writes pages 7, 12, 45, 100, 203. PRAGMA raptorq_repair_symbols = 2.

1. Write to .wal:
   - Write 5 standard SQLite WAL frames (pages 7, 12, 45, 100, 203)
   - Total .wal growth: 5 * (24 + 4096) = 20,600 bytes
   - These are the K=5 source symbols

2. Write to .wal-fec:
   - Enqueue background FEC job for the group with r_repair=2
   - Encoder thread reads 5 source frames from .wal, generates 2 deterministic repair symbols
   - Appends: one WalFecGroupMeta record + two repair SymbolRecords (ESIs 5 and 6)
   - Encoder then fsyncs .wal-fec to make group repairable

3. Commit: fsync .wal (durable). .wal-fec may lag briefly; once background job completes and fsyncs, group is repairable.

## Testing Requirements for §3.4.1 Self-Healing WAL (batch: bd-1hi.9, bd-1hi.10, bd-1hi.11, bd-1hi.12)

### §3.4.1 .wal-fec Sidecar Format (bd-1hi.9)
1. **test_wal_fec_header_format**: .wal-fec header contains magic, version, page_size, K, R. Round-trip encode/decode.
2. **test_wal_fec_group_layout**: WAL frames grouped into source blocks. Each group has K source + R repair frames.
3. **test_wal_fec_salt_binding**: .wal-fec salt must match .wal salt. Mismatched salt → sidecar rejected.
4. **test_wal_fec_created_alongside_wal**: When WAL is created, .wal-fec is created simultaneously.

### §3.4.1 Pipelined Repair Symbol Generation (bd-1hi.10)
5. **test_repair_generation_pipelined**: Repair symbols generated as WAL frames are written, not after.
6. **test_repair_generation_off_commit_path**: Repair symbol computation does NOT block commit fsync.
7. **test_repair_generation_catches_up**: If writer is faster than repair gen, repair gen catches up during idle.
8. **test_repair_generation_cancel_safe**: Cancelled mid-generation → partial repair symbols discarded cleanly.

### §3.4.1 WAL-FEC Recovery Algorithm (bd-1hi.11)
9. **test_recovery_intact_wal**: All WAL frames intact → zero repair overhead (fast path).
10. **test_recovery_single_corruption**: One frame corrupted in group → repair from .wal-fec succeeds.
11. **test_recovery_max_corruption**: Exactly R frames corrupted → repair succeeds (boundary case).
12. **test_recovery_exceed_corruption**: R+1 frames corrupted → SQLITE_CORRUPT (graceful failure).
13. **test_recovery_mixed_intact_and_corrupted**: Some groups intact, some need repair. Verify per-group repair.

### §3.4.1 PRAGMA raptorq_repair_symbols (bd-1hi.12)
14. **test_pragma_default_value**: Default R value (e.g., R=4). Verify from spec.
15. **test_pragma_set_higher**: Increase R → more repair symbols per group.
16. **test_pragma_set_lower**: Decrease R → fewer repair symbols, higher risk.
17. **test_pragma_zero_disables**: R=0 → no .wal-fec sidecar generated.
18. **test_pragma_takes_effect_next_group**: Changed PRAGMA takes effect for next WAL group, not current.

### Integration Tests
19. **test_wal_write_then_corrupt_then_recover**: Write 100 transactions to WAL, corrupt random frames, recover → all committed data intact.
20. **test_wal_fec_survives_power_loss**: Simulate crash mid-write. On recovery, .wal-fec enables frame repair.

### E2E Tests
21. **test_e2e_bitflip_recovery**: Insert 10K rows, flip random bits in .wal file, reopen DB → all data recovered via .wal-fec.
22. **test_e2e_wal_fec_overhead_measurement**: Measure write throughput with and without .wal-fec. Log overhead percentage.

### Logging Requirements
- DEBUG: Per-group encode/decode details, symbol indices, repair attempts
- INFO: Repair successes (group, frames repaired), PRAGMA changes
- WARN: Near-limit corruption (R-1 frames bad)
- ERROR: Unrecoverable corruption (> R frames), .wal-fec format errors

# pragma table-valued functions unimplemented ## Symptom SQLite exposes every result-returning pragma as a table-valued function named `pragma_`, usable in a FROM clause (filterable, projectable, joinable): ```sql SELECT name, type FROM pragma_table_info('t') WHERE pk = 1; SELECT "from","to" FROM pragma_foreign_key_list('child'); ``` frank errors on all of these: ``` ERROR(not implemented: table-valued function pragma_table_info is not supported) ``` The `PRAGMA table_info(t)` *statement* form works fine (see pragma_introspection_oracle); only the TVF form is missing. ## Root cause `crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs`: - `execute_table_function_rows` (:47461) resolves a TVF's columns via `table_function_result_column_names(name)` (:29186), which delegates to the free fn `table_function_column_names(name)` (a fixed table covering json_each / json_tree) plus any registered vtab module in `self.vtab_modules`. - No `pragma_*` name is in that table and no module is registered for them, so resolution returns `None` -> `FrankenError::NotImplemented` (:47477). ## Fix sketch Recognize the `pragma_` family in the TVF path: - In `table_function_column_names` (or `table_function_result_column_names`), map `pragma_

` to the same result columns the corresponding `PRAGMA

` statement produces (table_info: cid,name,type,notnull,dflt_value,pk; foreign_key_list: id,seq,table,from,to,on_update,on_delete,match; index_info; index_list; etc.). - In `execute_table_function_rows`, when the name is a `pragma_

title: §5.7.1-5.7.2 SSI Witness Objects (ECS Schemas) + Hot/Cold Plane Discovery
description:
Define the canonical ECS schemas for all SSI witness objects and implement the two-stage candidate discovery mechanism (hot-plane + cold-plane refinement) that makes SSI cross-process safe (spec lines 8353-8509).

SCOPE: Covers all witness data structures (ReadWitness, WriteWitness, WitnessDelta, WitnessIndexSegment, DependencyEdge, CommitProof, AbortWitness) and the two-tier discovery system: O(1) hot-plane superset via SHM bitsets, optional cold-plane refinement via ECS object decode.

DATA STRUCTURES:
- KeySummary (6 variants): ExactKeys, HashedKeySet, PageBitmap (RoaringBitmap<u32>), CellBitmap (RoaringBitmap<u64>), ByteRangeList, Chunked. Soundness rule: MUST NOT have false negatives for coverage claim.
- ReadWitness: {txn, begin_seq, level, range_prefix, key_summary, emitted_at}
- WriteWitness: same as ReadWitness + write_kind (Intent | Final); Final required before commit validation
- WitnessDelta: {txn, begin_seq, kind, level, range_prefix, participation: Present (union-only CRDT), refinement}
- WitnessIndexSegment: {segment_id, level, range_prefix, readers/writers bitmaps, epochs, covered range}
- DependencyEdge: {kind: RWAntiDependency, from/to TxnToken, key_basis, observed_by, observation_seq}
- CommitProof: {txn, begin/commit_seq, has_in/out_rw, witness/edge/merge refs, abort_policy}; replayable proof for deterministic re-validation
- AbortWitness: {txn, begin_seq, abort_seq, reason, edges_observed}

ALGORITHMS:
- All ECS schemas follow normative encoding: little-endian integers, sorted maps/sets by canonical bytes, canonical roaring encoding for bitmaps
- Hot-plane candidate discovery (Stage 1): HotWitnessIndex bitsets in SHM provide O(1) superset of candidates; query both live epochs (cur and prev) and OR them; map slots to TxnToken; validate txn_epoch matches
- Cold-plane refinement (Stage 2, optional): decode ReadWitness/WriteWitness refinements to confirm actual key intersection and reduce false positives
- No False Negatives theorem (hot plane, active txns): active txn R registering read WitnessKey K is always discoverable because registration updates every configured level bucket, epoch advancement constrains witness_epoch to {cur, cur-1}, and stale bits filtered by (txn_id, txn_epoch) validation
- Scope limitation: hot plane only covers TxnSlot-holding txns; committed readers covered by RecentlyCommittedReadersIndex (section 5.6.2.1)

INVARIANTS:
- ECS encoding MUST be deterministic: same inputs produce identical bytes
- WitnessDelta participation is union-only CRDT (no removals)
- CommitProof contains enough evidence to replay SSI validation
- Hot-plane has no false negatives for active transactions

TEST REQUIREMENTS (9 unit + 1 E2E):
- test_key_summary_canonical_encoding (round-trip all variants), test_read_witness_ecs_deterministic, test_write_witness_kinds (Intent vs Final), test_witness_delta_crdt_merge, test_dependency_edge_canonical, test_commit_proof_replay, test_hot_plane_no_false_negatives, test_hot_plane_epoch_overlap, test_cold_plane_refinement_reduces_fp
- E2E: concurrent write workload verifying CommitProof replayability, write-skew detection, and RaptorQ encode/decode round-trip

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA:
1. All witness ECS schemas round-trip deterministically
2. Hot-plane discovery has zero false negatives for active transactions
3. Cold-plane refinement reduces false positives without introducing false negatives
4. CommitProof artifacts sufficient for deterministic re-validation
5. WitnessDelta union-only CRDT semantics preserved
6. Witness objects survive RaptorQ encode/decode

## §5.7.1-5.7.2 SSI Witness Objects (Canonical ECS Schemas) + Hot/Cold Plane Discovery

### What This Implements
The canonical data structures for SSI (Serializable Snapshot Isolation) evidence tracking, plus the two-tier discovery mechanism that makes SSI cross-process safe.

### Spec Content (Lines 8353-8509)

**§5.7.1 Witness Objects — Canonical ECS Schemas (normative):**
All witness structures follow ECS encoding rules:
- integer endianness: little-endian
- maps/sets: sorted by canonical byte representation
- bitmaps: canonical roaring encoding

**Core Types:**
- `KeySummary`: union type — ExactKeys | HashedKeySet | PageBitmap | CellBitmap | ByteRangeList | Chunked
- `ReadWitness`: {txn, begin_seq, level, range_prefix, key_summary, emitted_at}
- `WriteWitness`: {txn, begin_seq, level, range_prefix, key_summary, emitted_at, write_kind: Intent|Final}
- `WitnessDelta`: {txn, begin_seq, kind: Read|Write, level, range_prefix, participation: Present, refinement}
- `WitnessIndexSegment`: {segment_id, level, range_prefix, readers bitmap, writers bitmap, epochs, covered range}
- `DependencyEdge`: {kind: RWAntiDependency, from, to, key_basis, observed_by, observation_seq}
- `CommitProof`: {txn, begin/commit seq, has_in/out_rw, witness refs, edge refs, merge witnesses, abort_policy}
- `AbortWitness`: {txn, begin_seq, abort_seq, reason: SSIPivot|Cancelled|Other, edges_observed}
- `MergeWitness`: (specified in §5.10)

**Soundness rule:** KeySummary MUST NOT have false negatives for its coverage claim. False positives allowed.
**CommitProof meaning:** Replayable proof (not cryptographic) — enough evidence to deterministically re-run SSI validation.

**§5.7.2 Two-Stage Candidate Discovery:**
1. **Hot-plane (O(1)):** SHM HotWitnessIndex bitsets provide superset of candidates
   - Query both live epochs (cur and prev) and OR them
   - Map slots to TxnToken, validate txn_epoch matches
2. **Cold-plane refinement (optional):** Decode ReadWitness/WriteWitness refinements to confirm actual key intersection

**Theorem (No False Negatives, hot plane — active txns only):**
Active txn R registering read WitnessKey K is always discoverable at commit time because:
- Registration updates every configured level bucket
- Epoch advancement constrains witness_epoch ∈ {cur, cur-1}
- Stale bits filtered by (txn_id, txn_epoch) validation

**Scope limitation:** Only covers TxnSlot-holding txns. Committed readers → RecentlyCommittedReadersIndex (§5.6.2.1).

### Unit Tests Required
1. test_key_summary_canonical_encoding: Round-trip each KeySummary variant
2. test_read_witness_ecs_deterministic: Same inputs produce identical ECS bytes
3. test_write_witness_kinds: Intent vs Final distinction
4. test_witness_delta_crdt_merge: Union-only participation semantics
5. test_dependency_edge_canonical: Edge encoding matches spec
6. test_commit_proof_replay: CommitProof contains enough to re-run SSI validation
7. test_hot_plane_no_false_negatives: Active reader always discoverable
8. test_hot_plane_epoch_overlap: Both cur and prev epochs queried
9. test_cold_plane_refinement_reduces_fp: Refinement eliminates spurious edges

### E2E Test
Run concurrent write workload. Verify:
- All CommitProofs are replayable (re-validation yields same decision)
- No false negatives in conflict detection (inject known write-skew, verify abort)
- Witness objects survive RaptorQ encode/decode round-trip

comments.text:
SECTION: §5.7.1 + §5.7.2 (spec lines ~8306-8509)

PURPOSE: Define canonical ECS witness object schemas and the two-stage candidate discovery algorithm.

## §5.7 SSI Algorithm Specification (Overview)
- SSI extends Snapshot Isolation to detect/prevent write skew anomaly
- Default isolation mode for BEGIN CONCURRENT (Layer 2)
- Built on RaptorQ-native witness plane (§5.6.4):
  - Cross-process safe, distributed-ready, self-healing, explainable

### Formal rw-antidependency Definition
- Edge R -rw-> W exists iff:
  1. R and W are CONCURRENT: neither committed before other's snapshot
     (W.commit_seq > R.begin_seq AND R.commit_seq > W.begin_seq)
     Note: snapshot-based concurrency, not wall-clock overlap
  2. Exists WitnessKey K: R read K, W wrote K with commit not visible to R's snapshot

### Witness Plane Integration Contract
- register_read(key: WitnessKey)
- register_write(key: WitnessKey)
- emit_witnesses() -> (read_witnesses, write_witnesses) -- publishes ECS objects + updates hot index

## §5.7.1 Witness Objects (Canonical ECS Schemas)
All are normative; deterministic encoding per ECS rules (§3.5):
- integer endianness: little-endian
- maps/sets: sorted by canonical byte representation
- bitmaps: canonical roaring encoding

### KeySummary (6 variants)
- ExactKeys(keys: Vec<WitnessKey>) -- sorted by canonical bytes
- HashedKeySet(hashes: Vec<KeyHash>) -- sorted ascending
- PageBitmap(pages: RoaringBitmap<u32>) -- page numbers
- CellBitmap(cells: RoaringBitmap<u64>) -- (page<<32) | cell_tag
- ByteRangeList(ranges: Vec<(u32, u16, u16)>) -- sorted
- Chunked(chunks: Vec<KeySummaryChunk>) -- for large sets
- Soundness rule: MUST NOT have false negatives for its coverage claim

### ReadWitness
- txn: TxnToken, begin_seq, level: u8, range_prefix: u32, key_summary: KeySummary, emitted_at: LogicalTime

### WriteWitness
- Same as ReadWitness plus write_kind: { Intent, Final }
- Final is required before commit validation

### WitnessDelta
- txn, begin_seq, kind: {Read, Write}, level, range_prefix
- participation: { Present } -- union-only CRDT (no removals)
- refinement: Option<KeySummary>

### WitnessIndexSegment
- segment_id, level, range_prefix, readers/writers: RoaringBitmap<u64>
- epochs: Option<EpochSnapshot>
- covered_begin_seq, covered_end_seq

### DependencyEdge
- kind: { RWAntiDependency }, from/to: TxnToken
- key_basis: { level, range_prefix, refinement }
- observed_by: TxnToken, observation_seq

### CommitProof
- txn, begin_seq, commit_seq, has_in_rw, has_out_rw
- read_witnesses, write_witnesses, index_segments_used, edges_emitted, merge_witnesses: Vec<ObjectId>
- abort_policy: { AbortPivot, AbortYoungest, Custom }
- Meaning: replayable proof (not cryptographic) -- enough evidence to re-run SSI validation

### AbortWitness
- txn, begin_seq, abort_seq, reason: { SSIPivot, Cancelled, Other }, edges_observed

### MergeWitness -- specified in §5.10

## §5.7.2 Candidate Discovery (Hot Plane) and Refinement (Cold Plane)
Two-stage approach:

### Stage 1: Hot-Plane Candidate Discovery (shared memory)
- HotWitnessIndex bitsets provide superset of candidates in O(1) per bucket
- For incoming edges (R -rw-> T): query reader bitsets for BOTH live epochs (cur and prev), OR them, intersect with active_slots_bitset, map to TxnToken via TxnSlotTable
- For outgoing edges (T -rw-> W): symmetric using writers_for_epoch union

### Stage 2: Cold-Plane Refinement (optional)
- Decode ReadWitness/WriteWitness refinements or WitnessIndexSegments
- Confirm actual key intersection to reduce false positives

### No False Negatives Theorem (hot plane, active transactions only)
- If R is ACTIVE (holds TxnSlot) and registers read K, R is discoverable as reader candidate
- Epoch advancement ensures active txns have witness_epoch in {cur, cur-1}
- Stale bits filtered by (txn_id, txn_epoch) validation
- Scope limitation: once R commits and frees slot, hot-plane evidence becomes stale
  -> RecentlyCommittedReadersIndex (§5.6.2.1) provides coverage for committed readers

PARENT EPIC: bd-3t3
DEPENDS ON: bd-3t3.9 (SSI Witness Plane), bd-3t3.7 (RecentlyCommittedReadersIndex)

Dependencies:
  -> bd-3t3 (parent-child) - §5: MVCC Formal Model (Revised)
  -> bd-3t3.9 (blocks) - §5.6.4 RaptorQ-Native SSI Witness Plane
  -> bd-3t3.7 (blocks) - §5.6.2.1 RecentlyCommittedReadersIndex (SSI Incoming Edge Coverage)

Dependents:
  <- bd-y1vo (blocks) - §5.7.3-5.7.4 SSI Commit-Time Validation + Refinement Policy

description:
SECTION 10 — QUERY PIPELINE (~530 lines)

The SQL processing pipeline from text to execution.

SUBSECTIONS: §10.1 Lexer Detail, §10.2 Parser Detail (hand-written recursive descent + Pratt expression parsing), §10.3 AST Node Types, §10.4 Name Resolution, §10.5 Query Planning, §10.6 Code Generation, §10.7 VDBE Instruction Format, §10.8 Coroutines.

- test_lexer_blob_literal_odd_hex: Verify lexer emits Error token for blob literals with odd number of hex digits (X'ABC')
- test_parser_pratt_precedence_eq_vs_lt: Verify `a = b < c` parses as `a = (b < c)` (equality lower precedence than comparison, per §10.2 table)
- test_parser_escape_not_infix: Verify ESCAPE is parsed as part of LIKE/GLOB handler, not as a standalone infix operator
- test_name_resolution_ambiguous_column: Verify ambiguous column reference across multiple FROM tables produces a clear error with source span

- test_codegen_select_rowid_lookup: Verify SELECT by rowid generates the expected VDBE opcode sequence (OpenRead, SeekRowid, Column, ResultRow)
- test_coroutine_yield_swap: Verify InitCoroutine/Yield/EndCoroutine opcodes correctly swap program counters for CTE evaluation

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA

- [ ] Core correctness is proven by unit/property tests and at least one end-to-end harness suite (with EXPLAIN dumps on failures).

comments.text:
## Success Criteria
- Parser -> AST -> planner -> VDBE pipeline is fully specified in beads (no missing opcode/functionality coverage).
- Conformance harness includes SQL programs that exercise every supported syntax/plan/opcode.
- Query execution produces deterministic trace logs that can be diffed against C sqlite3.

## §10 Full Spec Text (Verbatim Extract)
Source: COMPREHENSIVE_SPEC_FOR_FRANKENSQLITE_V1.md lines 13118-13650

## 10. Query Pipeline

```
SQL text
  |
  v
Lexer (memchr-accelerated, zero-copy token spans)
  |
  v
Parser (recursive descent, Pratt precedence for expressions)
  |
  v
AST (strongly typed enum hierarchy)
  |
  v
Name Resolution (table/column binding, * expansion)
  |
  v
Query Planning (index selection, cost estimation, join ordering)
  |
  v
VDBE Bytecode Generation (register-based VM, 190+ opcodes)
  |
  v
Execution (fetch-execute loop, match-based dispatch)
  |
  v
Results (iterator of Row, each row is a slice of SqliteValue)
```

### 10.1 Lexer Detail

The lexer converts SQL text into a stream of tokens. Each token carries a
`TokenType` discriminant and a `Span` (byte offset range in source).

**Token type enum (~150 variants):**

```rust
pub enum TokenType {
    // Literals
    Integer,          // 42, -7, 0xFF
    Float,            // 3.14, 1e10, .5
    String,           // 'hello' (single-quoted only at the lexer level)
    Blob,             // X'CAFE', x'00ff'
    Variable,         // ?1, :name, @name, $name

    // Identifiers and keywords
    Id,               // unquoted identifier
    QuotedId,         // "quoted identifier" or [bracketed identifier] or `backtick`
                      // NOTE: "hello" is ALWAYS QuotedId at the lexer level, matching
                      // C SQLite's tokenizer (tokenize.c:413 emits TK_ID for all
                      // double-quoted tokens). The DQS (double-quoted string) legacy
                      // behavior — where an unresolvable "identifier" is reinterpreted
                      // as a string literal — is handled in name resolution (resolve.c),
                      // NOT the lexer. QuotedId tokens carry an EP_DblQuoted-equivalent
                      // flag so the resolver can apply DQS fallback when enabled.

    // Keywords (each is its own variant for fast matching)
    KwAbort, KwAction, KwAdd, KwAfter, KwAll, KwAlter, KwAlways,
    KwAnalyze, KwAnd, KwAs, KwAsc, KwAttach, KwAutoincrement,
    KwBefore, KwBegin, KwBetween, KwBy,
    KwCascade, KwCase, KwCast, KwCheck, KwCollate, KwColumn,
    KwCommit, KwConflict, KwConstraint, KwCreate, KwCross,
    KwCurrentDate, KwCurrentTime, KwCurrentTimestamp, KwConcurrent,
    KwDatabase, KwDefault, KwDeferrable, KwDeferred, KwDelete,
    KwDesc, KwDetach, KwDistinct, KwDo, KwDrop,
    KwEach, KwElse, KwEnd, KwEscape, KwExcept, KwExclusive,
    KwExists, KwExplain,
    KwFail, KwFilter, KwFirst, KwFollowing, KwFor, KwForeign, KwFrom, KwFull,
    KwGenerated, KwGlob, KwGroup, KwGroups,
    KwHaving,
    KwIf, KwIgnore, KwImmediate, KwIn, KwIndex, KwIndexed,
    KwInitially, KwInner, KwInsert, KwInstead, KwIntersect, KwInto, KwIs, KwIsnull,
    KwJoin,
    KwKey,
    KwLast, KwLeft, KwLike, KwLimit,
    KwMatch, KwMaterialized,
    KwNatural, KwNo, KwNot, KwNothing, KwNotnull, KwNull, KwNulls,
    KwOf, KwOffset, KwOn, KwOr, KwOrder, KwOuter, KwOver,
    KwPartition, KwPlan, KwPragma, KwPreceding, KwPrimary,
    KwQuery,
    KwRaise, KwRange, KwRecursive, KwReferences, KwRegexp, KwReindex,
    KwRelease, KwRename, KwReplace, KwRestrict, KwReturning, KwRight,
    KwRollback, KwRow, KwRows, KwRowid,
    KwSavepoint, KwSelect, KwSet, KwStrict,
    KwTable, KwTemp, KwTemporary, KwThen, KwTies, KwTo, KwTransaction, KwTrigger,
    KwUnbounded, KwUnion, KwUnique, KwUpdate, KwUsing,
    KwVacuum, KwValues, KwView, KwVirtual,
    KwWhen, KwWhere, KwWindow, KwWith, KwWithout,

    // Operators and punctuation
    Plus, Minus, Star, Slash, Percent,             // + - * / %
    Ampersand, Pipe, Tilde,                        // & | ~
    ShiftLeft, ShiftRight,                         // << >>
    Eq, Lt, Le, Gt, Ge,                              // = < <= > >=
    EqEq, Ne, LtGt,                                 // == != <>
    // NOTE: In C SQLite, both `=` and `==` tokenize as TK_EQ, and both
    // `!=` and `<>` tokenize as TK_NE. FrankenSQLite preserves the lexical
    // distinction (Eq vs EqEq, Ne vs LtGt) for diagnostics and SQL
    // pretty-printing, but the parser treats each pair identically.
    // `Eq`/`EqEq` → equality; `Ne`/`LtGt` → not-equal.
    Dot, Comma, Semicolon,                         // . , ;
    LeftParen, RightParen,                         // ( )
    Arrow, DoubleArrow,                            // -> ->>
    Concat,                                        // ||

    // Special
    Eof,              // end of input
    Error,            // lexer error (unterminated string, invalid character)

    // Whitespace and comments (not emitted to parser; consumed internally)
    // Whitespace, LineComment, BlockComment
}
```

**String/number/blob literal parsing:**

- **String literals:** Delimited by single quotes. Embedded quotes are escaped
  by doubling (`''`). The lexer uses `memchr` to find the closing quote
  efficiently. Scans forward from the opening quote; on finding `'`, checks
  if the next character is also `'` (escaped) or not (end of string).

- **Number literals:** Integer or float. The lexer recognizes:
  - Decimal integers: `[0-9]+`
  - Hex integers: `0x[0-9a-fA-F]+`
  - Floats: `[0-9]*\.[0-9]+([eE][+-]?[0-9]+)?` or `[0-9]+[eE][+-]?[0-9]+`
  - The token type is `Integer` or `Float` based on the presence of `.` or `e/E`.

- **Blob literals:** `X'[0-9a-fA-F]*'` or `x'...'`. Must have even number of
  hex digits. Odd count produces an `Error` token.

**Error tokens:** When the lexer encounters invalid input (unterminated string,
invalid hex in blob literal, unrecognized character), it emits an `Error` token
with a diagnostic message and the offending byte range. The parser can then
produce a user-friendly error with source location.

**Line/column tracking:** The lexer maintains `line: u32` and `col: u32`
counters, incremented on each newline. Every `Token` carries a `Span` with
byte offsets and the `(line, col)` at the token start. This enables error
messages like: `line 3, column 15: expected ')' but found ','`.

### 10.2 Parser Detail

Hand-written recursive descent, NOT a generated parser. Uses C SQLite's
`parse.y` (~1,900+ production lines; the full file including Lemon directives
and semantic actions is ~76 KB) as the authoritative grammar reference for
production rules. Note: C SQLite uses a Lemon LALR(1) generated parser —
the switch to recursive descent is a deliberate FrankenSQLite design choice
for better Rust ergonomics, error recovery, and debuggability.

**Structure:** One method per grammar production. Each method consumes tokens
from the lexer and returns an AST node. Methods are named after the grammar
production they implement.

**Key parsing methods:**

```
parse_statement()              -> Statement
  parse_select_stmt()          -> SelectStatement
    parse_with_clause()        -> WithClause
    parse_select_core()        -> SelectCore
      parse_result_columns()   -> Vec<ResultColumn>
      parse_from_clause()      -> Option<TableRef>
        parse_join_clause()    -> JoinClause
      parse_where_clause()     -> Option<Expr>
      parse_group_by()         -> Option<GroupBy>
      parse_having()           -> Option<Expr>
      parse_window_clause()    -> Vec<WindowDef>
    parse_compound_op()        -> CompoundOp (UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT)
    parse_order_by()           -> Vec<OrderingTerm>
    parse_limit()              -> Option<LimitClause>
  parse_insert_stmt()          -> InsertStatement
    parse_upsert_clause()      -> Option<UpsertClause>
    parse_returning()          -> Option<Vec<ResultColumn>>
  parse_update_stmt()          -> UpdateStatement
  parse_delete_stmt()          -> DeleteStatement
  parse_create_table_stmt()    -> CreateTableStatement
    parse_column_def()         -> ColumnDef
    parse_table_constraint()   -> TableConstraint
  parse_create_index_stmt()    -> CreateIndexStatement
  parse_create_view_stmt()     -> CreateViewStatement
  parse_create_trigger_stmt()  -> CreateTriggerStatement
  parse_drop_stmt()            -> DropStatement
  parse_alter_table_stmt()     -> AlterTableStatement
  parse_begin_stmt()           -> BeginStatement
  parse_commit_stmt()          -> CommitStatement
  parse_rollback_stmt()        -> RollbackStatement
  parse_pragma_stmt()          -> PragmaStatement
  parse_explain_stmt()         -> ExplainStatement
  parse_expr()                 -> Expr (Pratt precedence)
    parse_prefix()             -> Expr (unary, literal, paren, subquery, case, cast, ...)
    parse_infix()              -> Expr (binary ops, BETWEEN, IN, LIKE, COLLATE, ...)
```

**Pratt precedence table for expressions:**

| Precedence | Operators | Associativity |
|------------|-----------|---------------|
| 1 (lowest) | OR | Left |
| 2 | AND | Left |
| 3 | NOT (prefix) | Right |
| 4 | =, ==, !=, <>, IS, IS NOT, IN, LIKE, GLOB, BETWEEN, MATCH, REGEXP, ISNULL, NOTNULL, NOT NULL | Left |
| 5 | <, <=, >, >= | Left |
| 6 | &, \|, <<, >> | Left |
| 7 | +, - | Left |
| 8 | *, /, % | Left |
| 9 | \|\| (concat), ->, ->> (JSON) | Left |
| 10 | COLLATE | Left |
| 11 (highest) | ~ (bitwise not), + (unary), - (unary) | Right |

**NOTE:** Equality/membership operators (level 4) and relational operators
(level 5) are at SEPARATE precedence levels, matching C SQLite's `parse.y`
(`%left IS MATCH LIKE_KW BETWEEN IN ... NE EQ` then `%left GT LE LT GE`).
This means `a = b < c` parses as `a = (b < c)`, NOT `(a = b) < c`.

**NOTE on ESCAPE:** C SQLite's `parse.y` declares `%right ESCAPE` between
levels 5 and 6 for Lemon conflict resolution, but ESCAPE is NOT a standalone
infix operator. It is an optional suffix of the LIKE/GLOB/MATCH production:
`expr likeop expr ESCAPE expr [LIKE_KW]`. In FrankenSQLite's Pratt parser,
ESCAPE is parsed as part of the LIKE/GLOB handler (after consuming the pattern
expression, check for an optional `ESCAPE` keyword and parse the escape
expression at the LIKE precedence level). It does NOT appear in the infix
dispatch table.

**Error recovery strategy:** On parse error, the parser:
1. Records the error (token, expected alternatives, source span).
2. Attempts to synchronize by skipping tokens until a "synchronization point"
   is found (semicolon, EOF, or a keyword that starts a new statement).
3. Continues parsing the next statement.
4. Returns all collected errors along with whatever AST was successfully parsed.

This allows the parser to report multiple errors in a single pass rather than
stopping at the first error.

### 10.3 AST Node Types

```rust
/// Top-level statement.
pub enum Statement {
    Select(SelectStatement),
    Insert(InsertStatement),
    Update(UpdateStatement),
    Delete(DeleteStatement),
    CreateTable(CreateTableStatement),
    CreateIndex(CreateIndexStatement),
    CreateView(CreateViewStatement),
    CreateTrigger(CreateTriggerStatement),
    CreateVirtualTable(CreateVirtualTableStatement),
    Drop(DropStatement),
    AlterTable(AlterTableStatement),
    Begin(BeginStatement),
    Commit,
    Rollback(RollbackStatement),
    Savepoint(String),
    Release(String),
    Attach(AttachStatement),
    Detach(String),
    Pragma(PragmaStatement),
    Vacuum(VacuumStatement),
    Reindex(Option<QualifiedName>),
    Analyze(Option<QualifiedName>),
    Explain { query_plan: bool, stmt: Box<Statement> },
}

pub struct SelectStatement {
    pub with: Option<WithClause>,
    pub body: SelectBody,
    pub order_by: Vec<OrderingTerm>,
    pub limit: Option<LimitClause>,
}

pub struct SelectBody {
    pub select: SelectCore,
    pub compounds: Vec<(CompoundOp, SelectCore)>,
}

/// A single SELECT or VALUES clause. VALUES (1,2),(3,4) is a first-class
/// construct in SQLite (used standalone, as INSERT source, and in CTEs).
/// In C SQLite, VALUES compiles through TK_VALUES into compound SELECTs
/// internally, but the AST preserves the syntactic distinction.
pub enum SelectCore {
    Select {
        distinct: Distinct,
        columns: Vec<ResultColumn>,
        from: Option<TableRef>,
        where_clause: Option<Expr>,
        group_by: Option<Vec<Expr>>,
        having: Option<Expr>,
        windows: Vec<WindowDef>,
    },
    Values(Vec<Vec<Expr>>),   // VALUES (expr, ...), (expr, ...), ...
}

pub enum Expr {
    Literal(Literal, Span),
    Column(ColumnRef, Span),
    BinaryOp { left: Box<Expr>, op: BinaryOp, right: Box<Expr>, span: Span },
    UnaryOp { op: UnaryOp, expr: Box<Expr>, span: Span },
    Between { expr: Box<Expr>, low: Box<Expr>, high: Box<Expr>, not: bool, span: Span },
    In { expr: Box<Expr>, set: InSet, not: bool, span: Span },
    Like { expr: Box<Expr>, pattern: Box<Expr>, escape: Option<Box<Expr>>, op: LikeOp, span: Span },
    Case { operand: Option<Box<Expr>>, whens: Vec<(Expr, Expr)>, else_: Option<Box<Expr>>, span: Span },
    Cast { expr: Box<Expr>, type_name: TypeName, span: Span },
    Exists { subquery: Box<SelectStatement>, not: bool, span: Span },
    Subquery(Box<SelectStatement>, Span),
    FunctionCall { name: String, args: Vec<Expr>, distinct: bool, filter: Option<Box<Expr>>, over: Option<WindowSpec>, span: Span },
    Collate { expr: Box<Expr>, collation: String, span: Span },
    IsNull { expr: Box<Expr>, not: bool, span: Span },
    Raise { action: RaiseAction, message: Option<String>, span: Span },
    JsonAccess { expr: Box<Expr>, path: Box<Expr>, arrow: JsonArrow, span: Span },
    RowValue(Vec<Expr>, Span),         // row value: (a, b) for multi-column comparisons (SQLite 3.15+)
    Placeholder(PlaceholderType, Span),
}
```

### 10.4 Name Resolution

Name resolution transforms raw AST identifiers into fully-resolved references.

**Table alias binding:** When a FROM clause contains `table AS alias`, the
resolver creates a binding `alias -> table_schema`. Subsequent column references
can use either the table name or the alias.

**Column reference resolution:** For a reference like `t.col`:
1. Search the current scope's table aliases for `t`.
2. If found, verify `col` exists in that table's schema.
3. If `t` is omitted, search all tables in the FROM clause for a column
   named `col`. If found in exactly one table, resolve. If found in multiple
   tables, report "ambiguous column name" error.

**Star expansion:** `SELECT *` expands to all columns of all tables in the FROM
clause. `SELECT t.*` expands to all columns of table `t`.

**Subquery scoping:** Each subquery creates a new scope. Inner scopes can
reference outer scope columns (correlated subqueries). The resolver tracks
a stack of scopes. A column reference first checks the innermost scope, then
walks outward.

### 10.5 Query Planning

**Cost model:** The planner estimates cost for each access path, primarily
in page reads. When `ANALYZE` statistics are available (`sqlite_stat1`,
`sqlite_stat4`), the planner uses actual row counts and distribution data;
otherwise it falls back to heuristic estimates.

```
Full table scan:              cost = N_pages(table)
Index scan (range):           cost = log2(N_pages(index)) + selectivity * N_pages(index) + selectivity * N_pages(table)
Index scan (equality):        cost = log2(N_pages(index)) + log2(N_pages(table))
Covering index scan:          cost = log2(N_pages(index)) + selectivity * N_pages(index)
Rowid lookup:                 cost = log2(N_pages(table))
```

Note: These are simplified cost formulas for initial implementation. C SQLite's
cost model is more nuanced, incorporating CPU cost estimates and per-row lookup
cost for non-covering index scans.

**Index usability:** For each WHERE term, the planner determines if an index
can satisfy it:
- Equality (`col = expr`): usable if `col` is the leftmost column of an index.
- Range (`col > expr`, `col BETWEEN`): usable as the rightmost constraint.
- IN (`col IN (...)`): usable, expanded to multiple equality probes.
- LIKE (`col LIKE 'prefix%'`): usable if prefix is constant.

**Join ordering:** Use a bounded best-first search (beam search) in the style of
C SQLite's NGQP (`wherePathSolver()` in `where.c`).

- Maintain up to `mxChoice` best partial join paths at each level (lowest
  estimated cost).
- `mxChoice` is a tuning knob derived from join complexity:
  - 1 for single-table.
  - 5 for two-table.
  - 12 or 18 for 3+ tables (star-query heuristic may raise to 18; see
    `computeMxChoice` in SQLite's `where.c`).
- Complexity: worst-case ~`O(mxChoice * N^2)` candidate expansions (bounded beam,
  not `N!`).

This is the V1 strategy (there is no exhaustive `N!` search path). The phrase
"N Nearest Neighbors" is not used in the SQLite source; beam search is the
actual implementation model.

### 10.6 Code Generation

The opcode traces below are **illustrative only**: the exact sequences vary by
schema, indexes, triggers, and optimizer choices. They exist to convey shape,
not to be byte-for-byte identical to C SQLite.

**SELECT -> VDBE opcodes:**
```
SELECT col FROM table WHERE rowid = ?
  Init       0, <end>
  Transaction 0, 0           # begin read transaction
  Variable   1, 1            # load bind parameter ?1 into r1
  OpenRead   0, <root>, 0    # open cursor 0 on table
  SeekRowid  0, <notfound>, 1  # seek to rowid in r1
  Column     0, <col_idx>, 2   # extract column into r2
  ResultRow  2, 1              # emit r2 as result
  <notfound>:
  Close      0
  Halt       0, 0
  <end>:
```

**INSERT -> VDBE opcodes:**
```
INSERT INTO table VALUES (?, ?)
  Init       0, <end>
  Transaction 0, 1           # begin write transaction
  OpenWrite  0, <root>, 0    # open cursor 0 for writing
  NewRowid   0, 1            # generate new rowid into r1
  Variable   1, 2            # bind param 1 -> r2
  Variable   2, 3            # bind param 2 -> r3
  MakeRecord 2, 2, 4         # pack r2..r3 into record r4
  Insert     0, 4, 1         # insert record r4 with rowid r1
  Close      0
  Halt       0, 0
  <end>:
```

**Concurrent-mode note (normative):** In `BEGIN CONCURRENT`, `OP_NewRowid` MUST
allocate via the snapshot-independent RowId allocator (§5.10.1.1), not by
scanning the transaction's snapshot-visible `max(rowid)`. This is required for
commutative insert merges and deterministic rebase to work for append-heavy
workloads.

**UPDATE -> VDBE opcodes:**
```
-- Schema: CREATE TABLE t(a, b)
UPDATE t SET b = ? WHERE rowid = ?
  Init       0, <end>
  Transaction 0, 1           # begin write transaction
  Variable   1, 1            # bind new value for b -> r1
  Variable   2, 2            # bind rowid -> r2
  OpenWrite  0, <root>, 2    # open cursor 0 for writing (2 columns)
  NotExists  0, <done>, 2    # if rowid r2 not found, skip
  Column     0, 0, 3         # read existing col a into r3
  Copy       1, 4            # new col b value (from r1) into r4
  MakeRecord 3, 2, 5         # pack r3..r4 (ALL columns) into record r5
  Insert     0, 5, 2, REPLACE  # overwrite record at rowid r2 with r5
  <done>:
  Close      0
  Halt       0, 0
  <end>:
```

**DELETE -> VDBE opcodes:**
```
DELETE FROM table WHERE rowid = ?
  Init       0, <end>
  Transaction 0, 1           # begin write transaction
  Variable   1, 1            # bind rowid -> r1
  OpenWrite  0, <root>, 0    # open cursor 0 for writing
  NotExists  0, <done>, 1    # if rowid r1 not found, skip
  Delete     0, 0            # delete row at current cursor position
  <done>:
  Close      0
  Halt       0, 0
  <end>:
```

### 10.7 VDBE Instruction Format

```rust
pub struct VdbeOp {
    pub opcode: Opcode,    // u8, one of 190+ opcodes
    pub p1: i32,           // first operand (register, cursor, or literal)
    pub p2: i32,           // second operand (jump target, register, etc.)
    pub p3: i32,           // third operand
    pub p4: P4,            // extended operand
    pub p5: u16,           // flags. C SQLite declares this as u16; most
                           // opcode flag masks fit in the low 8 bits, but
                           // some newer opcodes may use the full 16 bits.
                           // Match C SQLite's per-opcode P5 usage exactly.
}

pub enum P4 {
    None,
    Int32(i32),
    Int64(i64),
    Real(f64),
    String(String),
    Blob(Vec<u8>),
    FuncDef(Arc<dyn ScalarFunction>),
    CollSeq(Arc<dyn CollationFunction>),
    KeyInfo(KeyInfo),        // column sort orders for index comparison
    Mem(Mem),                // pre-loaded register value
    Vtab(Arc<dyn VirtualTable>),
    Table(TableInfo),        // table metadata for Insert/Update
    Subprogram(VdbeProgram), // trigger sub-program
}
```

**Jump resolution:** During code generation, forward jumps target unknown
addresses. The codegen uses a label system: `emit_label()` returns a `Label`
handle, and `resolve_label(label, address)` patches all instructions that
reference that label. All labels must be resolved before execution begins.

**Register allocation:** Registers are numbered starting at 1. The codegen
allocates registers sequentially via `alloc_reg()` and `alloc_regs(n)`.
Temporary registers (used within a single opcode sequence) are allocated from
a pool and returned after use. Persistent registers (for result columns,
cursor positions) are allocated once and held for the statement's lifetime.

### 10.8 Coroutines

Subqueries and CTEs use the VDBE coroutine mechanism:

```
// InitCoroutine P1=r_yield, P2=<done>, P3=<cte_body>
// Sets r_yield = &cte_body, then falls through (P2=0) or jumps to P2.
// Typical layout (P2=0, fall-through to outer query):

InitCoroutine  r_yield, 0, <cte_body>
  // ... outer query: Yield r_yield pulls next row from CTE body
  //     (Yield swaps PCs: saves current PC into r_yield, jumps to old r_yield)
  Goto <done>
<cte_body>:
  // ... CTE body: produces rows, each ending with Yield r_yield
  //     (Yield swaps PCs back to outer query)
  EndCoroutine r_yield    // final return to outer query; marks exhaustion
<done>:
```

The `Yield` opcode swaps program counters between the outer query and the
coroutine: it saves the current PC into `r_yield` and jumps to the previously
saved PC. `EndCoroutine` performs one final swap back to the caller. This
allows the CTE to produce rows on-demand without materializing the entire
result set into a temporary table. (Note: the exact layout varies by
compilation phase; WITH RECURSIVE and subquery flattening may use different
P2 targets.)

title: Fully Integrate asupersync Structured Concurrency and Quiescence Guarantees
description:
FrankenSQLite was historically under-utilizing asupersync's core features. It wrapped it as a thin capability token but ignored the strict structured concurrency rules. This epic tracks the full integration of asupersync's structured concurrency and quiescence guarantees, replacing raw `std::thread::spawn` calls with scoped spawns, threading `Cx` capabilities deeply, and establishing a rigorous task lifecycle.

**Background:**
Asupersync bills itself as providing *Spec-first, cancel-correct, capability-secure structured concurrency*. However, we found that FrankenSQLite was bypassing cancellation in the VDBE (now fixed), severing capability chains with `Cx::new()`, and spinning up widespread orphan tasks.

**Goal:**
Ensure that when a FrankenSQLite connection is closed, quiescence is strictly guaranteed. This means no detached background threads exist, all data flushing is gracefully finalized, and all operations correctly respond to cancellation protocols. This serves the overarching goal of making FrankenSQLite robust, safe, and fully deterministically testable via LabRuntime.

**Testing Strategy:**
We will implement comprehensive E2E tests and Unit Tests with rigorous logging to mathematically prove quiescence. Oracles from `asupersync::lab` (e.g., `quiescence_oracle`) must be used. We need to trace thread lifecycles using `tracing` to guarantee that no thread outlives its parent `Connection`.

title: Overhead: Implement adaptive tuner (e-process confidence sequence + evidence ledger)
description:
Implement the optional-but-recommended adaptive overhead tuner from spec §3.5.12 (Anytime-valid durability autopilot).

## Observations
Every verified SymbolRecord produces a Bernoulli observation:
- `X=1` record corrupt / invalid (hash mismatch, auth_tag fail, etc)
- `X=0` record ok

Also track erasures (missing symbols) during reads/replication.

## Monitor (Anytime-valid)
- Maintain an e-process monitor for hypotheses like:
  - `H0: p_corrupt <= p0` (budget per object class/tier)
  - optionally `H0: p_erase <= e0`
- When the monitor rejects, we must harden:
  - increase overhead_percent (and thus R)
  - optionally retroactively generate more deterministic repair symbols

Key property: optional-stopping safe (Ville).

## Policy Actions
- Increase overhead:
  - monotonic, capped by overhead_max
  - emits evidence ledger entry with:
    - reason (which monitor)
    - old/new overhead
    - scope (object class/tier)
    - timestamp/epoch
- Decrease overhead:
  - optional; only allowed under conservative loss and after strong evidence
  - must never cause under-provisioning for small K

## Acceptance Criteria
- Tuner exists, is deterministic, and emits evidence ledger entries.
- Unit tests simulate sequences where:
  - corruption rate > budget -> overhead increases
  - safe regime persists -> overhead stays stable (no thrash)
  - decrease policy (if implemented) is conservative and explainable

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
# Phase 5E: MVCC Concurrent Writers Integration

## Purpose

This is the final phase of the storage stack wiring project. Phases 5A-5D establish the
single-writer path: schema in sqlite_master, DML through B-tree/pager, transactions through
pager commit/rollback. Phase 5E enables the **multi-writer path** — the core innovation of
FrankenSQLite that replaces SQLite's global WAL_WRITE_LOCK with page-level MVCC locking.

## Why this matters

Standard SQLite allows exactly one writer at a time (WAL_WRITE_LOCK at wal.c:3676). FrankenSQLite's
entire raison d'être is MVCC page-level versioning: multiple writers can proceed concurrently as
long as they touch different B-tree pages. This is what makes the project worth building.

The MVCC infrastructure is already fully implemented in `crates/fsqlite-mvcc/`:
- `ConcurrentRegistry` — tracks active concurrent sessions with write sets
- `InProcessPageLockTable` — sharded page-level exclusive locks (64 shards, CacheAligned)
- `SharedPageLockTable` — cross-process lock table (open-addressing, atomic CAS, rolling rebuild)
- `CommitIndex` — maps pages to latest CommitSeq for first-committer-wins validation
- `VersionStore` — bump-allocated arena with per-page version chains for snapshot reads
- `SsiState` — SSI rw-antidependency tracking (has_in_rw, has_out_rw, pivot detection)
- `GcScheduler` — frequency-adaptive garbage collection for old page versions
- `WriteCoordinator` — Native (tiny-marker) and Compatibility (WAL append) publish paths
- `RetryPolicy` — Beta-Bernoulli model for adaptive SQLITE_BUSY backoff

What's missing is wiring this infrastructure through Connection → Pager → TransactionHandle so that
`BEGIN CONCURRENT` actually engages MVCC page-level locking instead of falling through to
the serialized (global mutex) path.

## Architecture

```
Connection.execute_begin(CONCURRENT)
  → Pager.begin(TransactionMode::Concurrent)
    → ConcurrentRegistry.begin_concurrent(snapshot) → session_id
    → ConcurrentHandle tracks write_set, page_locks

Connection DML (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE via Phase 5B)
  → BtCursor.table_insert() / delete()
    → TransactionHandle.write_page(page_num, data)
      → concurrent_write_page(handle, lock_table, session_id, page, data)
        → InProcessPageLockTable.try_acquire(page, txn_id)
        → handle.write_set.insert(page, data)

Connection.execute_commit()
  → Pager.commit()
    → concurrent_commit(handle, commit_index, lock_table, session_id, seq)
      → validate_first_committer_wins(handle, commit_index) → FcwResult
      → If Clean: update CommitIndex, release all locks, mark committed
      → If Conflict: release locks, return MvccError::BusySnapshot

Connection READS during concurrent txn:
  → TransactionHandle.get_page(page_num)
    → concurrent_read_page(handle, page) → check local write set first
    → VersionStore.resolve(page, snapshot) → walk chain for visible version
```

## Dependency chain

5E depends on 5D (transaction lifecycle through pager) because concurrent writers need the
basic commit/rollback path working first. Within 5E:

- **5E.1** (BEGIN CONCURRENT wiring) is the foundation
- **5E.2** (page-level locking) depends on 5E.1
- **5E.3** (SSI validation) depends on 5E.2
- **5E.4** (BUSY_SNAPSHOT retry) depends on 5E.3
- **5E.5** (GC for old versions) depends on 5E.1 (independent of SSI path)
- **5E.6** (stress test) depends on 5E.4 and 5E.5 (needs everything working)

## Key types reference

- `ConcurrentHandle` — per-session state (snapshot, write_set, page_locks, state)
- `ConcurrentRegistry` — registry of active handles (max 128 concurrent writers)
- `InProcessPageLockTable` — 64-shard CacheAligned<Mutex<HashMap<PageNumber, TxnId>>>
- `SharedPageLockTable` — cross-process fixed-capacity open-addressing (1M entries, 12 MiB/table)
- `CommitIndex` — 64-shard RwLock<HashMap<PageNumber, CommitSeq>>
- `FcwResult` — Clean | Conflict { conflicting_pages, conflicting_commit_seq }
- `MvccError::Busy` — lock contention, `MvccError::BusySnapshot` — stale snapshot
- `SsiState` — rw-antidependency edges, pivot detection, marked_for_abort
- `GcScheduler` — frequency f_gc = clamp(pressure/target, f_min, f_max)
- `VersionStore` — arena + chain_heads HashMap<PageNumber, VersionIdx>
- `TransactionMode::Concurrent` vs `TransactionMode::Serialized`

## Children

- bd-14zc: 5E.1 — Wire BEGIN CONCURRENT through MVCC ConcurrentRegistry
- bd-kivg: 5E.2 — Enable MVCC page-level locking for write transactions
- bd-1xo1: 5E.3 — Wire SSI validation (SireadTable) at commit time
- bd-3uzh: 5E.4 — Implement SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT retry on page conflict
- bd-3bql: 5E.5 — Wire MVCC garbage collection for old page versions
- bd-1299: 5E.6 — Multi-threaded concurrent writer stress test

Design the on-wire packet format for fountain-coded replication (spec §3.4.2) and define replay/dup semantics.

## Required Fields
Each packet must allow the receiver to:
- identify which object this symbol belongs to
- validate integrity/auth before accepting
- place symbol in decode buffer

Suggested minimal header (versioned):
- protocol_magic + version

title: Learned Index Structures for static lookup (§8.4)
description:
Explore learned index structures (Kraska et al. 2018) for static or slowly-changing lookup tables. A learned index uses a model (e.g., linear regression, piece-wise linear) to predict the position of a key, replacing B-tree traversal with a model inference + bounded local search.

## Mathematical Foundation
For a sorted array of N keys, a perfect model would predict the exact position with zero error. In practice, models achieve bounded error E, so lookup is: model_predict(key) -> estimated_position, then linear scan within [position - E, position + E]. If E is small (e.g., 32), this is faster than B-tree (O(log N) comparisons with cache misses).

## Application in FrankenSQLite
- Read-only or append-only tables (e.g., time-series, log tables)
- Static lookup tables (e.g., configuration, reference data)
- B-tree leaf page prediction (predict which leaf page contains a key without traversing internal nodes)

## Alien CS Reference
Kraska, Beutel, Chi, Dean, Polyzotis 2018 The Case for Learned Index Structures: original RMI (Recursive Model Index) proposal showing up to 3x speedup over B-trees on static data. Marcus et al. 2020 Benchmarking Learned Indexes: comprehensive evaluation showing learned indexes excel on sorted, near-uniform distributions but struggle with adversarial distributions. Ferragina and Vinciguerra 2020 PGM-index: optimal-space learned index with worst-case guarantees.

## Rust Implementation Guidance
- Implement PiecewiseLinearModel: Vec<(key_range, slope, intercept)> trained from sorted keys
- Training: use simple linear regression per segment, split when error exceeds max_error threshold
- Lookup: binary search segments by key_range, then predict position, then bounded linear scan
- Use ndarray or nalgebra for regression computation during training
- Feature-gate behind learned-index Cargo feature flag
- Benchmark with criterion crate comparing against BTreeMap::get

## Logging Requirements
- Log model training at tracing::info level: num_keys, num_segments, max_error, training_time
- Log prediction accuracy at tracing::debug level periodically: avg_error, max_error_observed
- Log fallback to B-tree (when error exceeds threshold) at tracing::debug level

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Learned index prototype for sorted integer keys
- [ ] Model training (piece-wise linear approximation) from sorted data
- [ ] Benchmark: learned index vs B-tree for point lookups on static data
- [ ] Error bound analysis: model prediction error distribution
- [ ] Feature-gated: only used when explicitly enabled
acceptance_criteria: 1. Implementation is complete and behaviorally correct against explicit invariants and edge-case requirements, including fault and recovery paths where applicable. 2. Comprehensive unit/property tests cover normal, boundary, and adversarial conditions with deterministic fixtures and regression seeds. 3. End-to-end scenario scripts validate integrated behavior in real execution flows and include deterministic replay instructions. 4. Structured logging/metrics (traceable IDs, timing, counters, error context) are emitted and validated so failures are diagnosable and auditable.
