title: Implement Glossary Types Module (§0.3)
description:
Create a comprehensive Rust types module that implements all glossary terms from §0.3 as proper Rust types. Many of these are already partially defined in fsqlite-types but this task ensures EVERY glossary term has a corresponding Rust type with documentation.

TYPES TO VERIFY/IMPLEMENT:
1. MVCC-related: TxnId (u64, non-zero, ≤(1<<62)-1 for sentinel encoding), CommitSeq (u64, monotonic), TxnEpoch (u32), TxnToken (TxnId, TxnEpoch), SchemaEpoch (u64)
2. Page-related: PageNumber (NonZeroU32, 1-based), PageVersion, VersionPointer
3. ECS-related: ObjectId (16-byte truncated BLAKE3), CommitCapsule, CommitMarker (commit_seq, commit_time_unix_ns, capsule_object_id, proof_object_id, prev_marker, integrity_hash), CommitSeq
4. RaptorQ-related: OTI (Object Transmission Information: F, Al, T, Z, N), DecodeProof
5. Asupersync types: Cx, Budget (deadline, poll_quota, cost_quota, priority), Outcome (Ok < Err < Cancelled < Panicked), EpochId (u64), SymbolValidityWindow ([from_epoch, to_epoch]), RemoteCap, SymbolAuthMasterKeyCap, IdempotencyKey, Saga, Region
6. SSI types: WitnessKey (Page(pgno) | Cell(btree_root_pgno, tag) | ByteRange(page, start, len)), RangeKey (level, hash_prefix), ReadWitness, WriteWitness, WitnessIndexSegment, DependencyEdge (from, to, key_basis, observed_by), CommitProof
7. Other: Intent log (Vec<IntentOp>), PageHistory, ARC, RootManifest, TxnSlot

KEY CONSTRAINTS:
- TxnId must fit in 62 bits (top bits reserved for CLAIMING/CLEANING sentinels in §5.6.2)
- ObjectId: Trunc128(BLAKE3("fsqlite:ecs:v1" || canonical_object_header || payload_hash)). Birthday-bound ~2^64 ops, sufficient for expected population <2^40 but NOT 128-bit security.
- Budget combine: deadline/poll/cost use min (meet), priority uses max (join) — product lattice with mixed meet/join.
- All types must have proper Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Hash implementations as appropriate.

ACCEPTANCE: Every term in the glossary has a corresponding Rust type or type alias with doc comments explaining its role. Types compile, pass clippy pedantic+nursery.

## UNIT TEST REQUIREMENTS
- test_txn_id_nonzero_enforced: TxnId(0) must be rejected; TxnId(1) through TxnId((1<<62)-1) must succeed
- test_txn_id_62_bit_max: TxnId values above (1<<62)-1 must be rejected (top bits reserved for CLAIMING/CLEANING sentinels per §5.6.2)
- test_page_number_nonzero_u32: PageNumber(0) must fail; PageNumber(1) must succeed (page 1 = database header)
- test_object_id_16_bytes_blake3_truncation: ObjectId = Trunc128(BLAKE3("fsqlite:ecs:v1" || header || payload_hash)); verify length is exactly 16 bytes and same input produces same ObjectId
- test_budget_combine_lattice_semantics: Budget.combine() uses min for deadline/poll_quota/cost_quota (meet) and max for priority (join); verify with concrete examples
- test_outcome_ordering_lattice: Outcome ordering Ok < Err < Cancelled < Panicked is enforced by PartialOrd/Ord
- test_witness_key_variants_exhaustive: WitnessKey enum has Page(pgno), Cell(btree_root_pgno, tag), ByteRange(page, start, len) variants

title: Establish RaptorQ Permeation Map Audit Checklist (§0.4)
description:
Per §0.4, the RaptorQ Everywhere doctrine requires that EVERY subsystem that persists or synchronizes bytes MUST specify:
1. How those bytes are represented as ECS objects
2. How they are repaired/replicated (via the RaptorQ Permeation Map in §3.5.7)

This task creates an audit checklist to verify compliance. The checklist must be maintained as beads are implemented.

SUBSYSTEMS REQUIRING ECS SPECIFICATION:
- Durability objects: commit capsules, markers, checkpoints
- Indexing objects: index segments, locator segments, manifest segments
- Replication traffic: symbols (not files)
- Repair mechanism: recover by decoding, not panicking
- History compression: patch chains as coded objects, not infinite full-page copies

ACCEPTANCE: A living checklist (can be a markdown file or beads label) that tracks which subsystems have had their ECS representation specified and verified. Each subsystem entry includes: bytes format, ECS object type, repair mechanism, replication path.

## UNIT TEST REQUIREMENTS
- test_commit_capsules_are_ecs_objects: Verify CommitCapsule is encoded as an ECS object with valid RaptorQ symbols and OTI metadata
- test_commit_markers_are_ecs_objects: Verify CommitMarker is encoded as an ECS object with repair capability
- test_checkpoints_are_ecs_objects: Verify checkpoint data is encoded as ECS objects, not raw file blobs
- test_index_segments_are_ecs_objects: Verify WitnessIndexSegment and other index objects use ECS encoding
- test_replication_uses_symbols_not_files: Verify replication traffic sends RaptorQ symbols, never raw file copies
- test_repair_uses_decode_not_panic: Verify partial loss recovery uses RaptorQ decode path; missing symbols result in decode attempt, not panic
- test_permeation_map_completeness: For each subsystem that persists bytes, verify an explicit ECS object type and repair strategy exists
- test_new_durable_structure_requires_ecs: Regression gate — any new durable structure added without ECS encoding causes this test to fail

## E2E TEST
test_e2e_raptorq_permeation_audit_report: Run a full spec audit pass that confirms each persistence/sync subsystem has an explicit RaptorQ permeation plan. Output a deterministic checklist report with subsystem name, ECS object type, repair strategy, and replication path for each entry.

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] A living audit checklist exists (markdown or beads label) tracking which subsystems have ECS representation specified and verified
- [ ] Each checklist entry includes: bytes format, ECS object type, repair mechanism, replication path
- [ ] No subsystem persists raw bytes without ECS wrapping (except SQLite compat-mode WAL which is explicitly exempted)
- [ ] Checklist is maintained as new beads are implemented — new persistence subsystems trigger checklist update

title: §0.1 Scope Doctrine Enforcement Gate
description:
Implement §0.1 “No V1 Scope” Doctrine Enforcement (Scope Gate)

SPEC REFERENCE: COMPREHENSIVE_SPEC_FOR_FRANKENSQLITE_V1.md §0.1 (Non-Negotiable Scope Doctrine)

This task turns the §0.1 scope doctrine into an enforceable engineering rule:
- Every feature/protocol/subsystem described in the spec is IN SCOPE.
- The only allowed exclusions are those explicitly listed in §15, each with a technical rationale.
- Phase numbering (§16) is sequencing, not scope reduction.

Why this needs its own bead: §0.1 is easy to “agree with” and then slowly violate as implementation pressure rises. We want a mechanical gate that makes scope creep (both accidental omission and accidental addition) visible early.

## Requirements
- Define a “scope gate” check that runs in CI (and locally) and produces a deterministic report.
- The scope gate MUST:
  - Verify §15 exists and contains explicit exclusions with non-empty technical rationales.
  - Flag any beads or docs that use “out of scope”, “V1 scope”, “later”, “optional in V1” language unless they point to §15.
  - Flag any implementation PR that introduces an excluded feature (per §15) without an explicit spec update.
  - Flag any “defer” decisions in beads that do not include a reason and a follow-up bead (deferral is allowed as scheduling, not as scope removal).

## Unit Test Requirements
- test_scope_doctrine_section_present: Verify the spec contains §0.1 and it includes the “no V1 scope” statement.
- test_exclusions_have_rationales: Parse §15 exclusions list; assert each exclusion has a non-empty rationale.
- test_no_v1_scope_language_in_beads_without_15_ref: Scan `.beads/issues.jsonl` for scope-reduction phrases; require an explicit §15 reference.
- test_no_excluded_features_reintroduced: Scan beads for excluded feature names; ensure they are either (a) still excluded in §15 or (b) explicitly re-scoped with updated spec text.

- test_e2e_bd_1wx_3_compliance: concrete E2E identifier for structure lint compliance.
- test_e2e_scope_gate_report:
  - Run the scope gate across the repository and beads.
  - Emit a JSON report containing: findings, file/bead locations, and remediation suggestions.
  - Ensure report is deterministic (stable ordering, stable message format).

## Logging Requirements
- INFO: Scope gate summary (counts: exclusions, flagged phrases, violations)
- WARN: Any “scope reduction” finding (include bead_id/file, matched phrase, and required remediation)
- ERROR: Any excluded-feature reintroduction detected (include exclusion name + source)

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] A repeatable scope gate exists and can be run locally and in CI.
- [ ] The gate enforces: “only §15 exclusions are allowed” (no implicit scope reduction).
- [ ] Findings are actionable and link directly to remediation steps.
- [ ] The gate produces structured logs and a deterministic JSON report.

title: §0.2 RFC2119 Normative Language Hygiene
description:
Implement §0.2 Normative Language Policy + Enforceable “RFC2119 Hygiene”

SPEC REFERENCE: COMPREHENSIVE_SPEC_FOR_FRANKENSQLITE_V1.md §0.2 (Normative Language)

The spec uses RFC 2119 / RFC 8174 keywords. This bead makes that usable and enforceable in practice so “MUST/SHOULD/MAY” doesn’t degrade into vibes.

## Requirements
- Define a lightweight, enforceable policy for how RFC2119 keywords appear in:
  - The spec itself (already normative)
  - Beads (requirements and acceptance criteria)
  - Implementation comments (where deviations from SHOULD are justified)
- Establish the “SHOULD deviation rule”:
  - If we deviate from a SHOULD/SHOULD NOT requirement, we MUST document a justification in the relevant implementation bead and in code comments near the deviation.
  - The justification must include: why deviation is safe, what we give up, and how we’ll detect regressions.
- Establish the “MUST boundary rule”:
  - Any MUST/MUST NOT in the spec must map to at least one acceptance criterion and at least one automated test (unit/property/E2E) OR must be explicitly marked as deferred with a reason and a follow-up bead.

## Unit Test Requirements

- test_should_deviation_requires_justification_marker: If a bead description contains a “SHOULD deviation” marker, ensure it includes a structured justification block (why/safety/regression detection).
- test_must_keywords_have_test_mapping: For a sampled set of MUST requirements in the spec (start with §0, §1, §2), verify there exists at least one bead with a matching acceptance criterion and test plan reference.

## E2E Test

  - Scan spec + beads for RFC2119 keywords.
  - Produce a deterministic report that lists:
    - MUST statements without an explicit test mapping bead
    - SHOULD deviations without justification
    - Any places where normative keywords are used ambiguously

## Logging Requirements

- WARN: SHOULD deviation without justification (bead_id, section)
- ERROR: MUST without mapping (spec_section, missing mapping hint)

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] A deterministic “hygiene report” exists and can run in CI.
- [ ] SHOULD deviations are mechanically discoverable and require justification.
- [ ] MUST/MUST NOT requirements are tied to tests or explicitly deferred with rationale.

title: §0 Spec-to-Beads Completeness Gate (Coverage + Structure Lint)
description:
Implement an automated spec-to-beads completeness gate so we can *prove* that the entire COMPREHENSIVE_SPEC is embedded in beads and stays embedded over time.

This directly addresses the core failure mode of large plans: silent omission. Once implementation begins, missing spec text is indistinguishable from intentional scope reduction unless we have a mechanical audit.

SPEC REFERENCES:
- COMPREHENSIVE_SPEC_FOR_FRANKENSQLITE_V1.md (ALL sections §0–§23)
- §0.1 Scope Doctrine (completeness is mandatory; omissions are scope violations)
- §22 Verification Gates (audits must be deterministic, CI-friendly)

## Requirements

### R1: Full Spec Text Coverage (Deterministic)
Create a tool that reads:
- `COMPREHENSIVE_SPEC_FOR_FRANKENSQLITE_V1.md`
- `.beads/issues.jsonl` (titles + descriptions + comments)

and proves coverage:
- Define a normalization function: trim, collapse all whitespace runs to a single space.
- Define the set of spec lines to check:
  - All Markdown headings (`^#{1,6} `), regardless of length.
  - All “meaningful” lines: contains at least one alphanumeric char and `len(trimmed) >= 10`.
  - Ignore code-fence delimiters (lines starting with ```), and ignore pure table separators (e.g., `|---|---|`).
- For each checked spec line, assert the normalized line occurs somewhere in the normalized bead corpus.

Output must include:
- Missing lines: `spec_line_no`, `line_text` (truncated), and a `hint` field (e.g., keyword(s) to `br search`).
- Coverage summary counts.


### R2: Open-Task Structure Lint (Self-Contained + Testable)
For every `open` issue of `type=task`, lint the *full bead text* (description + comments) and require:

- **Unit-test plan section**: a header matching one of:
  - `Unit Test Requirements`
  - `Unit Tests`
  - `Test Requirements`

  And it MUST contain at least one concrete identifier like `test_*` or `prop_*`.

- **E2E plan section**: a header matching one of:
  - `E2E Test`
  - `E2E Tests`
  - `E2E Benchmark`

  And it MUST contain at least one concrete identifier like `test_e2e_*` or `e2e_*`.

- **Logging / observability section**: a header containing `Logging Requirements` (preferred) or `Observability Requirements`.
  And it MUST contain at least one log-level bullet (DEBUG/INFO/WARN/ERROR) or explicitly reference the artifact bundle standard (`bd-1fpm`).

- **Acceptance criteria section**: `Acceptance Criteria` must be present (header or `ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA:` style) and MUST contain at least one checkbox/bullet.

This ensures every implementation bead is self-documenting and includes test + observability expectations.


### R3: Dependency & Parent Integrity Lint
- Every spec-derived task (`title` contains `§`) MUST have at least one `parent-child` dependency to a spec epic.
- The dependency graph MUST be acyclic (equivalent to `br dep cycles`).
- All dependency IDs referenced in `.beads/issues.jsonl` must exist.

### R6: Closed Rollup Hygiene (Avoid False 'Done')

This repository sometimes closes *consolidated rollup beads* after their content has been split into more granular plan-of-record beads.
That is valid, but it creates a dangerous UX failure mode: a reader may interpret `status=closed` as 'implemented' when it actually means 'superseded by better beads'.

For every `closed` issue of `type=task` where the `title` contains `§`, enforce:

- If `close_reason` contains any of: `DUPLICATE`, `Superseded`, `merged`, `Content merged`:
  - The bead MUST include a prominent marker in `description`, e.g. `STATUS: CLOSED (superseded rollup)`.
  - The bead MUST list at least one replacement bead id (`bd-*`) under a heading like 'Use these replacement beads instead'.
  - Each listed replacement id MUST exist.
  - At least one listed replacement MUST be `status=open` (unless the close_reason explicitly justifies otherwise).

- Otherwise (close_reason indicates actual completion, e.g. 'Completed' / 'Implemented'):
  - No special marker is required.

This keeps the graph honest and prevents silent scope loss via accidental closure of spec-derived work.


### R4: Output + Logging
- Emit a deterministic JSON report (stable ordering, no non-deterministic data in the semantic payload).
- Emit structured logs (use `tracing` JSON or equivalent).
- Exit 0 only when all checks pass; non-zero exit on any failure.

### R5: Integration
- Must run locally and in CI.
- Must be callable from the universal gate runner (see `bd-331.1`).
- Provide modes:
  - `--fast`: headings + `len>=20` meaningful lines
  - `--strict`: headings + `len>=10` meaningful lines (default)

## Unit Test Requirements
- test_normalization_whitespace_collapse: fixtures proving normalization behavior.
- test_ignores_code_fences_and_table_separators: ensure ignored lines don’t cause false failures.
- test_detects_missing_spec_line: build a tiny fixture spec + tiny fixture issues corpus with one line removed; assert failure reports the missing line.
- test_headings_always_checked: headings are checked even if short.
- test_open_task_structure_lint: a fixture issue missing sections is flagged with precise diagnostics.
- test_dep_graph_integrity: invalid/missing dependency IDs and cycles are detected.

## E2E Test
- test_e2e_spec_to_beads_audit_passes_repo:
  - Run the audit against the real repo.
  - Produce a JSON artifact (e.g., `target/spec_to_beads_audit.json`).
  - Assert: `missing_spec_lines == 0` and `open_task_structure_failures == 0`.
  - Assert report schema is stable.

## Logging Requirements
- INFO: summary counts (lines checked, missing, open tasks linted, failures).
- WARN: each finding (include `spec_line_no` or `bead_id`).
- ERROR: final failure with a compact summary + path to JSON report.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] A deterministic spec-to-beads audit tool exists and can run locally and in CI.
- [ ] The tool fails loudly (non-zero) if ANY checked spec line is missing from beads.
- [ ] The tool fails loudly if ANY open task bead lacks Unit/E2E/Logging/Acceptance sections.
- [ ] The report is deterministic and suitable for CI artifacts.
- [ ] The tool is wired into the universal gate runner (or explicitly listed as a phase-transition gate).

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## §12.5-12.9 DDL: CREATE TABLE + INDEX + VIEW + TRIGGER + Other

### CREATE TABLE (§12.5)
`CREATE [TEMP] TABLE [IF NOT EXISTS] [schema.]name (column-def [, constraint]*) [WITHOUT ROWID] [STRICT]`.
Also: `CREATE TABLE ... AS select-stmt`.

**Column definition:** `name [type] [constraint]*`. Column constraints: PRIMARY KEY [ASC|DESC] [conflict] [AUTOINCREMENT], NOT NULL [conflict], UNIQUE [conflict], CHECK (expr), DEFAULT (expr|literal|number), COLLATE, REFERENCES (foreign key), [GENERATED ALWAYS] AS (expr) [STORED|VIRTUAL].

**Table constraints:** PRIMARY KEY (cols) [conflict], UNIQUE (cols) [conflict], CHECK (expr), FOREIGN KEY (cols) REFERENCES table [(cols)] [foreign-key-clause].

**Type affinity rules** (first match wins): 1. Contains "INT" → INTEGER. 2. Contains "CHAR"/"CLOB"/"TEXT" → TEXT. 3. Contains "BLOB" or empty → BLOB. 4. Contains "REAL"/"FLOA"/"DOUB" → REAL. 5. Otherwise → NUMERIC.

**WITHOUT ROWID:** Index B-tree clustered on PK. Requires explicit PK. No rowid pseudo-column, no AUTOINCREMENT, INTEGER PK ≠ rowid alias.

**STRICT (3.37+):** Column types restricted to INT/INTEGER/REAL/TEXT/BLOB/ANY. Type checking enforced on INSERT/UPDATE.

**Generated columns (3.31+):** VIRTUAL (computed on read, not stored, can't index directly). STORED (computed on write, stored, can be indexed). Cannot reference later generated columns.

**AUTOINCREMENT:** Only on INTEGER PRIMARY KEY. Uses sqlite_sequence table. Guarantees rowids never reused.

**Foreign key clause:** REFERENCES parent (col) [ON DELETE/UPDATE {SET NULL|SET DEFAULT|CASCADE|RESTRICT|NO ACTION}] [MATCH {SIMPLE|PARTIAL|FULL}] [[NOT] DEFERRABLE [INITIALLY DEFERRED|IMMEDIATE]]. SQLite parses MATCH but enforces only MATCH SIMPLE. Requires `PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON`.

### CREATE INDEX (§12.6)
`CREATE [UNIQUE] INDEX [IF NOT EXISTS] [schema.]name ON table (indexed-column [,...]) [WHERE expr]`.

**Partial indexes:** WHERE clause restricts rows. Planner uses only when query WHERE implies index WHERE.
**Expression indexes:** Index on computed expressions. Planner matches via AST structural equality after normalization.

### CREATE VIEW (§12.7)
`CREATE [TEMP] VIEW [IF NOT EXISTS] [schema.]name [(aliases)] AS select`. Expanded inline (not materialized). Read-only unless INSTEAD OF trigger defined.

### CREATE TRIGGER (§12.8)
`CREATE [TEMP] TRIGGER [IF NOT EXISTS] [schema.]name {BEFORE|AFTER|INSTEAD OF} {DELETE|INSERT|UPDATE [OF col,...]} ON table [FOR EACH ROW] [WHEN expr] BEGIN stmt; ... END`.

**Timing:** BEFORE (can modify/prevent), AFTER (post-DML), INSTEAD OF (views only).
**Pseudo-tables:** INSERT: NEW only. DELETE: OLD only. UPDATE: both OLD and NEW.
**WHEN clause:** Trigger body executes only if WHEN is true.
**Body:** Multiple DML statements. Can reference OLD, NEW, RAISE().
**Recursive triggers:** `PRAGMA recursive_triggers=ON`. Max depth SQLITE_MAX_TRIGGER_DEPTH (1000).

**Rust safety directive (CRITICAL):** Trigger execution MUST NOT use call-stack recursion. MUST use explicit heap-allocated frame stack (`Vec<VdbeFrame>`). MUST enforce capability-budgeted memory ceiling via Cx for nested frames.

### Other DDL (§12.9)
**ALTER TABLE:** RENAME TO, RENAME COLUMN, ADD COLUMN, DROP COLUMN (3.35+, always rewrites table).
**DROP:** TABLE, INDEX, VIEW, TRIGGER — all with IF EXISTS.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## §10 Query Pipeline Overview

SQL text -> Lexer (memchr-accelerated, zero-copy spans) -> Parser (recursive descent, Pratt precedence) -> AST (strongly typed) -> Name Resolution (table/column binding, * expansion) -> Query Planning (index selection, cost, join ordering) -> VDBE Bytecode Generation (190+ opcodes) -> Execution (fetch-execute, match dispatch) -> Results (iterator of Row).

## §10.1 Lexer Detail

~150 TokenType variants. Each token carries TokenType + Span (byte range + line/col).

**Token categories:** Literals (Integer, Float, String, Blob, Variable), Identifiers (Id, QuotedId with DQS flag), Keywords (~120 KwXxx variants), Operators/punctuation (Plus through Concat), Special (Eof, Error).

**QuotedId note:** "hello" is ALWAYS QuotedId at lexer level (matching C SQLite tokenize.c:413). DQS legacy behavior (reinterpreting as string literal) handled in name resolution. QuotedId tokens carry EP_DblQuoted flag.

**Operator note:** Eq/EqEq and Ne/LtGt preserved as distinct tokens for diagnostics and pretty-printing, but parser treats each pair identically.

**Literal parsing:** String: single-quoted, '' escape, memchr-accelerated. Numbers: decimal, hex (0x prefix), float (.e/E). Blob: X'hex', must have even digit count. Error tokens for invalid input (unterminated string, bad hex, unrecognized char).

**Line/column tracking:** Maintains line/col counters. Tokens carry Span with byte offsets + (line, col) at start.

## §10.2 Parser Detail

Hand-written recursive descent (NOT generated parser). C SQLite's parse.y (~1,900 productions, ~76KB) as authoritative grammar reference. Deliberate switch from Lemon LALR(1) for Rust ergonomics, error recovery, debuggability.

**Structure:** One method per grammar production. Key methods: parse_statement -> parse_select_stmt (with/core/compound/order/limit) -> parse_insert_stmt (upsert/returning) -> parse_update_stmt -> parse_delete_stmt -> parse_create_table_stmt (column_def/constraint) -> parse_create_index/view/trigger -> parse_drop/alter -> parse_begin/commit/rollback -> parse_pragma -> parse_explain -> parse_expr (Pratt).

**Pratt precedence table (11 levels):**
1. OR | 2. AND | 3. NOT (prefix) | 4. =,==,!=,<>,IS,IN,LIKE,GLOB,BETWEEN,MATCH,REGEXP,ISNULL,NOTNULL | 5. <,<=,>,>= | 6. &,|,<<,>> | 7. +,- | 8. *,/,% | 9. || (concat), ->, ->> | 10. COLLATE | 11. ~ (bitwise not), unary +/-

Key: equality/membership (4) and relational (5) at SEPARATE levels — `a = b < c` parses as `a = (b < c)`.

**ESCAPE note:** Not in Pratt dispatch table. Parsed as optional suffix of LIKE/GLOB handler.

**Error recovery:** Record error (token, expected, span) -> skip to sync point (semicolon/EOF/statement keyword) -> continue parsing -> return all errors with partial AST.

## §10.3 AST Node Types

**Statement enum:** Select, Insert, Update, Delete, CreateTable/Index/View/Trigger/VirtualTable, Drop, AlterTable, Begin, Commit, Rollback, Savepoint, Release, Attach, Detach, Pragma, Vacuum, Reindex, Analyze, Explain.

**SelectStatement:** with, body (SelectBody = SelectCore + compounds), order_by, limit.

**SelectCore enum:** Select { distinct, columns, from, where, group_by, having, windows } | Values(Vec<Vec<Expr>>) — VALUES is first-class construct.

**Expr enum (~15+ variants):** Literal, Column, BinaryOp, UnaryOp, Between, In, Like (with escape), Case, Cast, Exists, Subquery, FunctionCall (with filter + over), Collate, IsNull, Raise, JsonAccess, RowValue, Placeholder. All carry Span.

title: §17.3 Deterministic Concurrency Tests: Lab Runtime + FsLab Harness
description:
E2E Test:
- test_e2e_bd_1xds_compliance: concrete E2E identifier for structure lint compliance.

## SUMMARY
Implements deterministic concurrency testing using asupersync's lab runtime via the FsLab harness (§4.2.3). All MVCC tests run under deterministic scheduling with fixed seeds for exact reproducibility. The harness supports fault injection via FaultInjectingVfs, deterministic repro artifacts on failure, seed taxonomy (schedule/entropy/fault/fuzz seeds derived from root seed), and CI runs each concurrency test with 100 different seeds. Failing seeds produce self-contained repro bundles for one-command reproduction.

## KEY DATA STRUCTURES / ALGORITHMS
- **FsLab:** `fsqlite_harness::lab::FsLab` wrapper around asupersync's lab runtime. Configured with seed, worker_count, and max_steps. Provides deterministic async task scheduling.
- **Seed Management:** Fixed seed per test for reproducibility. CI runs 100 different seeds per test. Failing seed recorded in test failure message.
- **Seed Taxonomy:** Root test_seed derives: schedule_seed, entropy_seed, fault_seed, fuzz_seed via `H(test_seed || purpose_tag || scope_id)` where H is xxh3_64 or SplitMix64 and purpose_tag is ASCII ("schedule", "entropy", "fault", "fuzz").
- **FaultInjectingVfs:** `fsqlite_harness::vfs::FaultInjectingVfs` wraps UnixVfs. Supports `FaultSpec::partial_write("test.db-wal").at_offset_bytes(4096).bytes_written(2048).after_count(50)` style injection.
- **Repro Artifacts:** On failure with `ASUPERSYNC_TEST_ARTIFACTS_DIR` set, emit: `repro_manifest.json`, `event_log.txt`, `failed_assertions.json`, optional `trace.async` and `inputs.bin`.
- **repro_manifest.json Schema:** schema_version, test_id, seed, scenario_id, config_hash, trace_fingerprint, input_digest, oracle_violations, passed.
- **Replay Workflow:** Load manifest, re-run with `ASUPERSYNC_SEED=<seed>`, if trace.async exists replay directly, divergence produces divergence artifact.
- **Oracle Report:** `report.oracle_report.all_passed()` assertion validates all MVCC invariants held.

## NORMATIVE INVARIANTS
- INV-DET-1: Every concurrency test MUST use a fixed seed for exact reproducibility.
- INV-DET-2: CI MUST run each concurrency test with 100 different seeds.
- INV-DET-3: Failing seed MUST be recorded in the test failure message.
- INV-DET-4: When ASUPERSYNC_TEST_ARTIFACTS_DIR is set, any failing run MUST emit a self-contained repro bundle.
- INV-DET-5: Seed derivation MUST follow `H(test_seed || purpose_tag || scope_id)` with stable hash function.
- INV-DET-6: Replay with same seed and scenario MUST produce identical execution trace (determinism guarantee).
- INV-DET-7: repro_manifest.json MUST conform to the minimum schema (schema_version, test_id, seed, scenario_id, config_hash, trace_fingerprint, oracle_violations, passed).

## UNIT TEST REQUIREMENTS
- `test_mvcc_two_writers_different_pages`: T1 inserts rowids 1-100, T2 inserts rowids 1001-1100 concurrently. Both commit. Final count = 200. Uses seed 0xDEADBEEF, 4 workers, 200K max steps.
- `test_mvcc_two_writers_same_page_conflict`: Two transactions write to same page range. One must abort or both succeed if cells are disjoint (per merge ladder §5.10).
- `test_deterministic_replay_same_seed`: Run same scenario twice with identical seed. Verify execution traces are identical.
- `test_fault_injection_partial_wal_write`: Inject partial write at WAL offset 4096 after 50 writes. Verify database recovers correctly on next open.
- `test_repro_artifact_generation`: Set ASUPERSYNC_TEST_ARTIFACTS_DIR, run a test that fails by assertion. Verify repro_manifest.json, event_log.txt, and failed_assertions.json are emitted with correct schema.
- `test_seed_taxonomy_derivation`: Derive schedule_seed, entropy_seed, fault_seed, fuzz_seed from root seed. Verify deterministic and distinct.
- `test_ci_100_seeds_coverage`: Run a concurrency scenario with seeds 0..99. Verify all complete (pass or fail) and any failure records its seed.
- `test_fault_injection_io_error_on_read`: Inject I/O read failure, verify transaction aborts cleanly without corruption.
- `test_replay_divergence_detection`: Replay with tampered trace.async file, verify divergence artifact emitted at first mismatch.

- test_e2e_bd_1xds_compliance: concrete E2E identifier for structure lint compliance.
Run the full MVCC deterministic concurrency test suite under FsLab. Execute each test with 100 seeds in CI. Verify zero non-determinism: same seed always produces same outcome. Inject a deliberate fault (partial WAL write), verify recovery. Trigger a failing test, verify repro artifacts are emitted in the correct directory layout. Replay the failing test from the repro manifest and verify identical failure.

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- FsLab harness operational: deterministic task scheduling with configurable workers and max_steps.
- All MVCC concurrency tests pass under deterministic scheduling with fixed seeds.
- FaultInjectingVfs supports partial writes, I/O errors, and configurable fault timing.
- CI runs 100 seeds per concurrency test; failing seeds recorded.
- Repro artifacts emitted on failure with correct schema and directory layout.
- Replay from repro manifest produces identical execution (no flakes).
- Seed taxonomy follows normative derivation rule.
- Oracle report validates all MVCC invariants for every seed.

title: S3-FIFO Buffer Pool Eviction (§15.1)
description:
Replace current buffer pool eviction with S3-FIFO (Yang et al. 2023), the state-of-the-art eviction algorithm. Score 8.0 in the cross-project scoreboard. S3-FIFO consistently beats LRU, LRU-K, ARC, and LIRS across diverse workloads while being simpler and more cache-friendly.

## Background
Buffer pool eviction determines which pages stay in memory when the pool is full. LRU (Least Recently Used) is the textbook approach but suffers from scan pollution (a single sequential scan evicts all hot pages) and poor performance on skewed access patterns. ARC (Adaptive Replacement Cache) improves on LRU but requires per-access metadata updates that contend under concurrency.

## Algorithm: S3-FIFO
Three queues:
1. SMALL queue (10% of total capacity): FIFO admission filter. New pages enter here.
2. MAIN queue (90% of capacity): FIFO with frequency-based reinsertion. Pages promoted from SMALL if accessed again.
3. GHOST queue (tracks recently evicted pages): No data, just page IDs. Used for frequency estimation.

Eviction logic:
- Evict from SMALL first (FIFO order). If evicted page was accessed while in SMALL, promote to MAIN instead.
- If SMALL is empty, evict from MAIN (FIFO order). If evicted page was accessed while in MAIN, reinsert at tail.
- Posterior-guided adaptive split: adjust the SMALL/MAIN ratio based on observed hit rates (Bayesian update on which queue contributes more hits).

## Why S3-FIFO
- Lock-free friendly: FIFO queues only touch head/tail, not middle (unlike LRU which moves accessed items)
- Scan resistant: sequential scans fill SMALL queue and get evicted without polluting MAIN
- Adaptive: posterior-guided split handles workload changes

## Key Paper
Yang, Yue, Rashmi, et al. 2023: 'FIFO Queues are All You Need for Cache Eviction'

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] 3-queue S3-FIFO structure implemented
- [ ] Posterior-guided adaptive queue split
- [ ] Lock-free or low-contention implementation
- [ ] Hit rate improvement over LRU on mixed workloads
- [ ] Scan resistance demonstrated
- [ ] Benchmark: S3-FIFO vs LRU vs ARC hit rates on trace-driven workload

## Success Criteria
Epic completion requires all child beads to satisfy their structured acceptance criteria, including explicit unit/property coverage, deterministic e2e evidence, and structured logging/metrics validation.

Critical-path end-to-end scenarios are implemented as reproducible e2e scripts (fixed seeds, replay commands, artifact bundles) across happy-path and adversarial-path behavior. 3. Structured logging and metrics contracts are mandatory for all child outputs (trace_id, run_id, scenario_id, seed, timing, outcome, error context) and validated by CI conformance checks. 4. Epic completion requires a machine-readable evidence manifest linking child unit/e2e/log artifacts to acceptance outcomes, plus an explicit fallback/rollback plan that preserves concurrent-writer defaults.

title: Implement 3-queue S3-FIFO structure (small/main/ghost)
description:
Implement the core 3-queue S3-FIFO data structure for buffer pool eviction.

SMALL queue (default 10% capacity):
- FIFO queue (VecDeque or intrusive linked list)
- Each entry: (page_id, accessed_flag)
- On access: set accessed_flag = true (no reordering!)
- On eviction (dequeue from head): if accessed_flag, promote to MAIN; else evict

MAIN queue (default 90% capacity):
- FIFO queue with reinsertion
- Each entry: (page_id, accessed_flag, reinsert_count)
- On access: set accessed_flag = true
- On eviction (dequeue from head): if accessed_flag && reinsert_count < MAX_REINSERT, reinsert at tail with reinsert_count++; else evict
- MAX_REINSERT (default 1) prevents indefinite reinsertion

GHOST queue (metadata only, no page data):
- Tracks page IDs recently evicted from SMALL
- Bounded size (default: same as SMALL capacity)
- Used by adaptive split to detect pages that would have been hits if SMALL were larger

Page lookup: maintain a HashMap<PageId, QueueLocation> for O(1) lookup of which queue (and position) a page is in.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Three queues with correct capacity ratios
- [ ] FIFO ordering maintained in each queue
- [ ] Access flag correctly set without reordering
- [ ] Promotion from SMALL to MAIN on eviction of accessed pages
- [ ] Reinsertion in MAIN with bounded reinsert count
- [ ] Ghost queue tracks evicted page IDs
- [ ] O(1) page lookup via HashMap
- [ ] Unit tests for all transitions (insert, access, evict, promote, reinsert)
acceptance_criteria: 1. Implementation is complete and behaviorally correct against explicit invariants and edge-case requirements, including fault and recovery paths where applicable. 2. Comprehensive unit/property tests cover normal, boundary, and adversarial conditions with deterministic fixtures and regression seeds. 3. End-to-end scenario scripts validate integrated behavior in real execution flows and include deterministic replay instructions. 4. Structured logging/metrics (traceable IDs, timing, counters, error context) are emitted and validated so failures are diagnosable and auditable.

title: Implement posterior-guided adaptive queue split
description:
Implement the posterior-guided adaptive split between SMALL and MAIN queues. The optimal ratio depends on the workload — scan-heavy workloads benefit from larger SMALL (more scan resistance), while random-access workloads benefit from larger MAIN (more capacity for hot pages).

Adaptation mechanism:
1. Track hit rates for SMALL queue (hits_small) and MAIN queue (hits_main)
2. Track ghost queue hits (ghost_hits): pages evicted from SMALL that are accessed again
3. If ghost_hits is high: SMALL is too small, increase SMALL ratio
4. If ghost_hits is low: SMALL is too large, decrease SMALL ratio
5. Adjustment step size: proportional to ghost_hits / total_accesses (Bayesian posterior update)

Bayesian formulation:
- Prior: Beta(1, 1) (uniform) on the optimal SMALL ratio
- Likelihood: ghost hits indicate SMALL is too small; MAIN eviction-with-access indicates MAIN is too small
- Posterior: updated incrementally with each eviction event
- Decision: set SMALL ratio to posterior mean, bounded to [5%, 30%]

Update frequency: every N evictions (default N=1000) to avoid oscillation.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Adaptive split adjusts SMALL/MAIN ratio based on access patterns
- [ ] Ghost queue hits drive adaptation
- [ ] Ratio bounded to [5%, 30%]
- [ ] Update frequency configurable to prevent oscillation
- [ ] Test: scan workload -> ratio increases; random workload -> ratio decreases
- [ ] Convergence: ratio stabilizes within 10000 evictions for stable workloads

title: Benchmark: S3-FIFO vs LRU vs ARC hit rates
description:
Benchmark S3-FIFO against LRU and ARC on trace-driven workloads to validate the hit rate improvement. Use both synthetic and real-world access traces.

Synthetic workloads:
1. Sequential scan: full table scan repeated 3 times
2. Zipfian random: random page access with Zipfian distribution (skew=1.0)
3. Mixed: 50% sequential scan + 50% Zipfian random (interleaved)
4. Scan pollution: Zipfian hot set + periodic full scan (tests scan resistance)

Buffer pool sizes: 10%, 25%, 50%, 75% of database size (to test all pressure levels).

Metrics:
- Hit rate (hits / total accesses)
- Miss rate breakdown (compulsory, capacity, conflict)
- Eviction overhead (CPU time per eviction)
- Memory overhead (metadata per page)
- Adaptation convergence time (for S3-FIFO)

Expected results based on Yang et al. 2023:
- S3-FIFO ~= ARC for Zipfian (within 1-2%)
- S3-FIFO >> LRU for scan pollution (5-15% higher hit rate)
- S3-FIFO >= ARC for mixed workloads

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All 4 workloads benchmarked at all 4 buffer sizes
- [ ] Hit rate comparison table: S3-FIFO vs LRU vs ARC
- [ ] S3-FIFO matches or exceeds ARC on all workloads
- [ ] Eviction overhead comparable to LRU (FIFO is simpler)
- [ ] Results documented with analysis and charts

title: Property tests: S3-FIFO eviction correctness invariants
description:
Property-based tests for S3-FIFO eviction correctness using proptest. The eviction algorithm has critical invariants that must hold for all access sequences.

Invariants to test:
1. Capacity: total pages in SMALL + MAIN <= max_capacity at all times
2. FIFO ordering: pages dequeued in FIFO order within each queue
3. Promotion correctness: accessed pages in SMALL are promoted to MAIN, not evicted
4. No duplicates: a page appears in at most one queue at any time
5. Ghost accuracy: ghost queue only contains recently evicted page IDs from SMALL
6. Adaptation bounds: SMALL ratio stays within [5%, 30%]
7. Inclusion property: for any access sequence, S3-FIFO with capacity C includes all pages that S3-FIFO with capacity C+1 would include (monotonicity)

Generators:
- Random access sequences (uniform, Zipfian, sequential, adversarial)
- Variable buffer pool sizes
- Variable SMALL/MAIN ratios
- Interleaved insert/access/evict operations

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All 7 invariants tested with proptest
- [ ] 10000+ random access sequences tested
- [ ] Adversarial sequences (designed to violate each invariant) tested
- [ ] Regression seeds stored
- [ ] Integrated into CI

title: E2E test: S3-FIFO buffer pool correctness under mixed OLTP/OLAP workload
description:
End-to-end integration test validating S3-FIFO buffer pool correctness under realistic mixed OLTP/OLAP workloads. This test verifies that the 3-queue eviction policy maintains data correctness while delivering expected hit rate improvements.

## Test Scenarios

1. OLTP point lookups with scan pollution: Run concurrent point lookups on a hot working set while periodically injecting full table scans. Verify: (a) scan does not evict hot pages from MAIN queue, (b) all point lookups return correct data, (c) hit rate recovers within 1000 accesses after scan.

2. Working set shift: Start with hot working set A (1000 pages), then shift to working set B (different 1000 pages). Verify: (a) adaptive split adjusts SMALL/MAIN ratio, (b) no stale data from working set A returned, (c) hit rate for working set B reaches steady state within 5000 accesses.

3. Memory pressure: Run queries with buffer pool at 10% of database size (extreme eviction pressure). Verify: (a) all queries return correct results, (b) no corruption from eviction/reload cycles, (c) BLAKE3 page checksums match after every reload.

4. Concurrent readers and writers: 16 reader threads + 4 writer threads accessing overlapping page ranges. Verify: (a) readers see consistent snapshots (no torn reads), (b) writers complete without corruption, (c) eviction under concurrent access does not cause use-after-free.

5. Ghost queue effectiveness: Populate ghost queue by evicting pages from SMALL, then re-access those pages. Verify: (a) ghost queue correctly identifies re-accessed pages, (b) adaptive split responds to ghost queue hits, (c) re-accessed pages promoted to MAIN on reload.

## Alien CS Reference
Yang et al. 2023 FIFO Queues are All You Need for Cache Eviction: Section 5 describes evaluation methodology for S3-FIFO correctness and hit rate. The scan-resistance test (scenario 1) follows their evaluation protocol.

## Rust Implementation Guidance
- Use tempfile::TempDir for isolated test databases
- Verify page correctness with BLAKE3 checksums after every eviction/reload cycle
- Use std::thread::scope for structured concurrent tests
- Use crossbeam::channel for coordinating scan injection timing
- Capture hit rate metrics during test execution for correctness and performance validation

## Logging Requirements
- Log test scenario transitions at tracing::info level
- Log hit rate snapshots at tracing::debug level periodically: small_hits, main_hits, total_hits, total_accesses
- Log eviction/reload events at tracing::trace level for debugging
- Log page checksum verification results at tracing::debug level

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All 5 scenarios pass with zero data corruption
- [ ] Scan resistance verified (scenario 1)
- [ ] Adaptive split responds to workload changes (scenario 2)
- [ ] Correctness maintained under extreme memory pressure (scenario 3)
- [ ] No use-after-free under concurrent access (scenario 4)
- [ ] Ghost queue drives adaptation (scenario 5)
- [ ] All tests complete in < 30 seconds

comments.text:
# Phase 1: Foundation — Feature Flags and wasm32 Compilation Target

## Goal
Make the FrankenSQLite core crates compile successfully to `wasm32-unknown-unknown`. This is the foundation upon which all browser features are built.

## Why This Matters
FrankenSQLite currently compiles only for native targets (Linux, macOS, Windows). Several crates have hard dependencies on OS-specific functionality (POSIX file locking via `nix`, OS mutexes via `parking_lot`, io_uring via `asupersync`). These must be gated behind feature flags so the pure-Rust computational core (parser, AST, planner, VDBE, B-tree, types, error) can compile to wasm32 without modification.

## Technical Approach
1. Add `native` and `wasm` feature flags to workspace Cargo.toml and per-crate Cargo.toml files
2. Gate OS-specific dependencies behind `#[cfg(not(target_arch = "wasm32"))]`
3. Create wasm-compatible polyfills for sync primitives (single-threaded Mutex/RwLock)
4. Ensure all pure-Rust crates compile with `cargo build --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`
5. Validate with `cargo check --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` across the workspace

## Dependency Analysis (what needs gating)
- `parking_lot` → `std::sync::Mutex`/`RwLock` (wasm is single-threaded)
- `nix` → completely excluded (POSIX-only)
- `crossbeam-epoch` → no-op or RefCell-based (single-threaded)
- `crossbeam-deque` → VecDeque (single-threaded)
- `asupersync` → excluded, synchronous I/O only for wasm
- `pollster` → excluded (no async runtime needed)
- `loom` → excluded (dev-only, no threads in wasm)
- `libc` → excluded
- `advisory-lock` → excluded

## Crates That Should Compile to wasm32 Without Changes
- fsqlite-types (pure types/enums)
- fsqlite-error (pure error types)
- fsqlite-ast (pure AST nodes)
- fsqlite-parser (recursive descent parser)
- fsqlite-func (pure function implementations)
- fsqlite-ext-json (JSON functions)
- fsqlite-ext-misc (misc functions)

## Crates That Need Feature Gating
- fsqlite-vfs (gate unix.rs, uring.rs, windows.rs)
- fsqlite-pager (gate parking_lot usage)
- fsqlite-wal (gate file I/O operations)
- fsqlite-mvcc (gate crossbeam, nix, parking_lot, coordinator IPC)
- fsqlite-btree (verify, may need minor fixes)
- fsqlite-vdbe (gate any OS-specific opcode paths)
- fsqlite-core (gate file-based connection paths)
- fsqlite (gate CLI and native-only re-exports)

## Success Criteria
- `cargo check --target wasm32-unknown-unknown -p fsqlite-types -p fsqlite-error -p fsqlite-ast -p fsqlite-parser -p fsqlite-func` passes
- `cargo check --target wasm32-unknown-unknown -p fsqlite` with `--features wasm --no-default-features` passes
- No new `unsafe` code introduced
- All existing native tests continue to pass
- Feature flags are documented in each crate's Cargo.toml

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
# 5E.3: Wire SSI validation (SireadTable) at commit time

## What

Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) prevents write skew anomalies that plain snapshot
isolation allows. SSI tracks read-write antidependencies between concurrent transactions:
if transaction T1 reads a page that T2 later writes, that creates an rw-antidependency
edge T1 → T2.

The "dangerous structure" is when a transaction has BOTH incoming and outgoing rw-antidependency
edges (making it a "pivot"). A pivot transaction must be aborted to prevent non-serializable
schedules.

This task wires the existing SSI infrastructure (`SsiState`, `SsiBusySnapshot`) into the
commit path so that concurrent transactions are validated for serializability.

## Current state

SSI validation is implemented in `crates/fsqlite-mvcc/src/ssi_validation.rs`:

```rust
pub struct SsiState {
    pub txn: TxnToken,
    pub begin_seq: CommitSeq,
    pub has_in_rw: bool,                // Incoming rw-antidependency
    pub has_out_rw: bool,               // Outgoing rw-antidependency
    pub rw_in_from: HashSet<TxnToken>,  // Sources of incoming edges
    pub rw_out_to: HashSet<TxnToken>,   // Targets of outgoing edges
    pub edges_emitted: Vec<ObjectId>,   // Emitted dependency edges
    pub marked_for_abort: bool,         // Another txn marked this for abort
}
```

Abort reasons (`SsiAbortReason`):
- `Pivot` — has both in + out rw-antidependency edges
- `CommittedPivot` — committed reader has incoming rw edge (irrevocable)
- `MarkedForAbort` — eagerly marked by another committer

The `SsiBusySnapshot` error includes:
- `txn` — transaction being aborted
- `reason` — why (Pivot/CommittedPivot/MarkedForAbort)
- `witness` — evidence artifact for debugging

But the SSI check is not invoked during `concurrent_commit()`. The commit path only does
first-committer-wins (page-level conflict detection), not SSI validation.

## Where to change

**Primary:** `crates/fsqlite-mvcc/src/begin_concurrent.rs` — `concurrent_commit()` function

After first-committer-wins validation passes (FcwResult::Clean), add SSI validation:
1. Check if this transaction is a pivot (has_in_rw && has_out_rw)
2. Check if this transaction was marked_for_abort by another committer
3. If dangerous structure detected, return `MvccError::BusySnapshot` with SSI reason

**Secondary:** `crates/fsqlite-mvcc/src/begin_concurrent.rs` — `concurrent_write_page()`

When a concurrent write touches a page that another active transaction has read (creating
an rw-antidependency), update the SSI state for both transactions:
- The reader gets `has_out_rw = true` (outgoing edge to the writer)
- The writer gets `has_in_rw = true` (incoming edge from the reader)

## Implementation approach

1. **Track reads for SSI**: The `ConcurrentHandle` needs a `read_set: HashSet<PageNumber>` to
   track which pages were read (for rw-antidependency detection)
2. **On write**: Check if any other active concurrent transaction has this page in its read set.
   If so, create rw-antidependency edges in both transactions' SsiState.
3. **On commit**: After FCW validation passes, check SsiState:
   - If `has_in_rw && has_out_rw` → abort as Pivot
   - If `marked_for_abort` → abort as MarkedForAbort
   - Otherwise → proceed with commit
4. **On commit success**: For each transaction that has an rw-antidependency edge TO this
   (now committed) transaction, mark it: if it already has_out_rw, mark_for_abort
   (CommittedPivot — irrevocable since this txn is now committed)

## SSI theory reference

From the spec (§5.3 SSI):
- Snapshot isolation prevents dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads
- But allows write skew: T1 reads X, T2 reads Y, T1 writes Y, T2 writes X → both commit
  but no serial schedule produces same result
- SSI detects "dangerous structures" (two consecutive rw-antidependencies) and aborts one
- The pivot transaction (middle of the chain) is the one that gets aborted
- False positive rate is low in practice because most workloads don't create cycles

## Tests

- `test_ssi_no_conflict_no_overlap`: Two concurrent txns on disjoint data → both commit
- `test_ssi_pivot_detection`: T1 reads A writes B, T2 reads B writes A → one aborted as Pivot
- `test_ssi_committed_pivot`: T1 commits, T2 (with rw-edge to T1) attempts commit → aborted
- `test_ssi_marked_for_abort`: T1 commits and marks T2 → T2 commit fails with MarkedForAbort
- `test_ssi_read_only_txn_no_abort`: Read-only concurrent txn → never aborted (no write set)
- `test_ssi_single_rw_edge_ok`: Only has_in_rw OR has_out_rw (not both) → commit succeeds

# 5C.6: Deprecate MemCursor fallback path (make StorageCursor the only path)

## What

After all read opcodes route through StorageCursor (5C.1-5C.5) and all writes route through
StorageCursor (5B.1-5B.6), the MemCursor code path is dead code. This task:

1. Removes MemCursor fallback branches from ALL opcodes
2. Removes the `cursors: HashMap<i32, MemCursor>` field from VdbeEngine
3. Makes StorageCursor the ONLY cursor type
4. Simplifies opcode handlers (no more if-else dispatch)

## Why not remove MemDatabase entirely?

MemDatabase still serves a role during transition:
- Some test code may reference it directly
- The shadow copy helps debug discrepancies between B-tree and MemDB
- Expression-only SELECTs (no table access) don't need cursors at all

Removing MemDatabase entirely is a SEPARATE future task (Phase 5E or beyond). This task only
removes MemCursor — the cursor layer that reads from MemDatabase.

## What to keep

- `MemPageStore` (used by btree unit tests — doesn't depend on MemDatabase)
- `CursorBackend::Mem` variant (uses MemPageStore, not MemDatabase)
- `MemDatabase` itself (shadow copy during transition)

## What to remove

- `MemCursor` struct and all its methods
- `cursors: HashMap<i32, MemCursor>` from VdbeEngine
- All `if let Some(mc) = self.cursors.get(...)` branches in opcode handlers
- `storage_cursors_enabled` flag (always true now, meaningless)
- The `open_mem_cursor()` method

## Risk

This is a "point of no return" for the cursor path. After this:
- Tests that relied on MemCursor for correctness will break if StorageCursor has bugs
- Debugging is harder (can't compare MemCursor vs StorageCursor output)
- Ensure ALL tests pass with StorageCursor BEFORE doing this

## Approach

1. First, verify all tests pass with storage_cursors_enabled=true forced globally
2. Then remove MemCursor code
3. Run full test suite again
4. Fix any failures (they indicate StorageCursor bugs that were hidden by MemCursor fallback)

## Tests

- `test_all_existing_tests_pass_without_memcursor`: The ultimate validation
- `test_no_memcursor_references_in_opcode_handlers`: Compile-time check (struct removed)

comments.text:
# UPDATE: 5C.6 is now a late-stage "safety net removal" task

## Revised dependency position

**Original deps**: 5C.6 depends on 5C.2-5C.5 (all read opcodes)
**Revised deps**: 5C.6 depends on 5C.2-5C.5 AND 5D.2 (ROLLBACK verified)

5C.6 (deprecate MemCursor) is the point of no return for the read path. After this, ALL
reads go through StorageCursor → B-tree → pager. The MemDatabase is no longer consulted
for reads.

## Why depend on 5D.2 (ROLLBACK)?

After ROLLBACK, the database state must revert to the pre-transaction state. With MemCursor,
this was trivial: MemDatabase snapshot is restored. With StorageCursor, the pager must properly
discard dirty pages and serve pre-transaction state from the WAL/buffer pool.

If we deprecate MemCursor before verifying ROLLBACK works through the pager read path, we
lose the ability to compare MemCursor results against StorageCursor results for debugging.

Verification order:
1. All 5C opcodes work through StorageCursor (5C.1-5C.5) ✓
2. ROLLBACK through pager restores correct read state (5D.2) ✓
3. THEN deprecate MemCursor fallback (5C.6)

## What "deprecate" means

Phase 1 (this task): Make StorageCursor the ONLY path.
```rust
// Before (fallback):
fn execute_open_read(&mut self, cursor_id: i32, root_page: u32) -> Result<()> {
    if self.storage_cursors_enabled && self.txn_page_io.is_some() {
        self.open_storage_cursor(cursor_id, root_page, false)
    } else {
        self.open_mem_cursor(cursor_id, root_page)  // FALLBACK
    }
}

// After (no fallback):
fn execute_open_read(&mut self, cursor_id: i32, root_page: u32) -> Result<()> {
    self.open_storage_cursor(cursor_id, root_page, false)
    // No fallback — StorageCursor is the only path
    // MemCursor code can be removed in a future cleanup
}
```

Phase 2 (future): Remove MemCursor type entirely and the `cursors` HashMap from VdbeEngine.
This is a separate future cleanup, not part of Phase 5.

## Why not remove MemCursor entirely now?

Keeping MemCursor as dead code is low-risk and preserves the ability to quickly restore the
fallback if Phase 5E (MVCC) reveals issues. Full removal should happen after MVCC stress
testing (5E.6) passes.

## Updated tests (with logging)

```
[5C6][test=no_mem_fallback][step=open_read] cursor_id=0 root_page=2 backend=StorageCursor
[5C6][test=no_mem_fallback][step=rewind] cursor positioned at first row ✓
[5C6][test=no_mem_fallback][step=column] col=0 value=1 ✓
[5C6][test=no_mem_fallback][step=next] advanced to second row ✓
```

- `test_no_mem_cursor_fallback`: Open read cursor without txn → still uses StorageCursor (or error, not MemCursor)
- `test_all_queries_work_without_mem_cursor`: Run comprehensive query suite → all pass via StorageCursor
- `test_rollback_reads_correct_after_deprecation`: BEGIN, INSERT, ROLLBACK, SELECT → correct state via StorageCursor
- `test_regression_guard_after_deprecation`: Full test suite → 0 regressions

title: RealDB E2E: real corpus + massive concurrency + perf + corruption/recovery showcase
description:
## Why

We want a visceral, end-to-end demonstration of FrankenSQLite's two core value props:

1) **Concurrent writers** (page-level MVCC) → clear throughput wins on real workloads/db files.
2) **RaptorQ-pervasive durability** (WAL-FEC / repair symbols) → recover from corruption patterns where stock SQLite loses data or cannot open the DB.

This must be done against **real SQLite database files** (preferably from `/dp` projects, especially Beads DBs and other production-ish fixtures), not synthetic toy DBs.

## What We Are Building

A suite of tools/demos (primarily in `crates/fsqlite-e2e`) that can:

- Discover candidate SQLite DB files under `/dp` (and other roots).
- Import them safely into `sample_sqlite_db_files/golden/` as immutable **golden fixtures**.
- Run **massively concurrent write workloads** against working copies, comparing outcomes between:
  - C SQLite oracle (via rusqlite/libsqlite3)
  - FrankenSQLite (`fsqlite`), with MVCC enabled
- Verify correctness with a clear, explicit equivalence contract (see below).
- Benchmark and report **speedup** with high-quality measurement and reproducibility.
- Run **corruption + recovery** demos that:
  - corrupt copies (never originals) deterministically
  - show baseline SQLite failure/data-loss characteristics
  - show FrankenSQLite recovery + post-repair verification

## Safety Invariants (Non-Negotiable)

- Never run workloads directly on `/dp/...` originals.
- Golden fixtures are treated as immutable inputs; all writes occur on per-run working copies.
- Every destructive/corrupting operation must operate on a freshly-created copy and must emit a proof bundle (sha256 before/after, scenario metadata, seed).
- DB bytes from `/dp` must not be committed to git (only manifests/metadata/checksums).

## Correctness / Equivalence Contract

We explicitly support multiple equivalence tiers:

- Tier 1: **Raw byte identity** (sha256(DB file) matches). Only required/expected for a subset of workloads where file-layout determinism is guaranteed.
- Tier 2: **Canonical identity**: deterministic canonicalization pipeline (e.g., VACUUM INTO / stable schema+row ordering) produces matching canonical sha256.
- Tier 3: **Logical equivalence**: schema matches + stable row dumps match (with deterministic formatting rules).

The harness must clearly label which tier is being asserted and why.

## Benchmarking Contract

- Same workload generator inputs (seed, concurrency, operation mix) across engines.
- Same fairness PRAGMAs across engines (documented).
- Report throughput, latency percentiles, and scaling curves; compute speedup vs baseline.
- Store results as JSONL (machine) + Markdown (human), and provide a TUI viewer (frankentui).

## Done When

A new user can run a single command (or a tiny set of commands) to:

1) import/select a real DB fixture
2) run a concurrent workload sweep
3) see correctness verdicts + speedup numbers
4) run a corruption scenario and see recovery outcomes

with clear artifacts written to disk and good logging.

title: §11.2 Varint Edge Cases: 9-Byte Encoding + SQLite vs Protobuf Differences
description:
## SUMMARY

Focuses on varint edge cases: the critical 9-byte encoding for large values, boundary values at each byte-length transition, and the precise differences between SQLite varints and protobuf/LEB128 varints. The 9th byte of a SQLite varint contributes ALL 8 bits (no continuation bit), allowing a full u64 to fit in 9 bytes, whereas protobuf LEB128 would require 10 bytes. This difference is a common implementation bug source and MUST be handled correctly for rowid encoding, record header sizes, and payload lengths.

## KEY DATA STRUCTURES / ALGORITHMS

- **SQLite varint encoding scheme**:
  - Bytes 1-8: high bit set = continuation (lower 7 bits contribute to value); high bit clear = final byte (lower 7 bits are last contribution).
  - Byte 9 (if reached): ALL 8 bits contribute (no continuation bit). This is the critical difference.
  - Encoding uses minimum bytes needed: 0-127 -> 1 byte, 128-16383 -> 2 bytes, ..., >= 2^56 -> 9 bytes.
- **Byte-length boundaries**:
  - 1 byte: [0, 127] (2^7 - 1)
  - 2 bytes: [128, 16383] (2^14 - 1)
  - 3 bytes: [16384, 2097151] (2^21 - 1)
  - 4 bytes: [2097152, 268435455] (2^28 - 1)
  - 5 bytes: [268435456, 34359738367] (2^35 - 1)
  - 6 bytes: [34359738368, 4398046511103] (2^42 - 1)
  - 7 bytes: [4398046511104, 562949953421311] (2^49 - 1)
  - 8 bytes: [562949953421312, 72057594037927935] (2^56 - 1)
  - 9 bytes: [72057594037927936, 18446744073709551615] (2^64 - 1)
- **Signed value handling**: Result is unsigned u64. For signed values (rowid), cast to i64 via two's complement reinterpretation.
- **Protobuf/LEB128 difference**: Protobuf uses 7 bits per byte for ALL bytes (continuation bit in every byte). To encode u64::MAX, protobuf needs 10 bytes. SQLite needs only 9 because the 9th byte contributes 8 bits. Mixing up these encodings is a critical interop bug.

## NORMATIVE INVARIANTS

1. The 9th byte contributes ALL 8 bits (no continuation bit). This is NOT optional or optimization -- it is the fundamental encoding rule.
2. Encoding MUST use the minimum number of bytes needed (canonical encoding).
3. Values 0-127 MUST encode to exactly 1 byte.
4. u64::MAX (2^64 - 1) MUST encode to exactly 9 bytes.
5. Decoding MUST handle the 9th byte specially: read all 8 bits, not just lower 7.
6. For signed values (rowids), the u64 result is reinterpreted as i64 via two's complement.
7. This is NOT protobuf varint, NOT LEB128. Using either alternative encoding is a spec violation that breaks file format compatibility.

## UNIT TEST REQUIREMENTS

1. `test_varint_1byte_boundary` -- Encode/decode 0 (min 1-byte) and 127 (max 1-byte); verify 1 byte used.
2. `test_varint_2byte_boundary` -- Encode/decode 128 (min 2-byte) and 16383 (max 2-byte); verify 2 bytes used.
3. `test_varint_3byte_boundary` -- Encode/decode 16384 and 2097151; verify 3 bytes.
4. `test_varint_4byte_boundary` -- Encode/decode 2097152 and 268435455; verify 4 bytes.
5. `test_varint_5byte_boundary` -- Encode/decode 268435456 and 34359738367; verify 5 bytes.
6. `test_varint_6byte_boundary` -- Encode/decode 34359738368 and 4398046511103; verify 6 bytes.
7. `test_varint_7byte_boundary` -- Encode/decode 4398046511104 and 562949953421311; verify 7 bytes.
8. `test_varint_8byte_boundary` -- Encode/decode 562949953421312 and 72057594037927935; verify 8 bytes.
9. `test_varint_9byte_full_u64` -- Encode/decode 72057594037927936 (min 9-byte) and u64::MAX; verify 9 bytes and 9th byte uses all 8 bits.
10. `test_varint_9th_byte_all_bits` -- Encode value requiring 9th byte with all bits set (0xFF); decode and verify correctness.
11. `test_varint_signed_negative_rowid` -- Encode i64::MIN as u64 via two's complement; decode back to i64::MIN.
12. `test_varint_signed_minus_one` -- Encode -1i64 (u64::MAX); decode to 9 bytes; reinterpret as i64 = -1.
13. `test_varint_not_protobuf` -- Encode u64::MAX with SQLite varint (9 bytes) vs protobuf varint (10 bytes); verify different byte sequences and lengths.
14. `test_varint_round_trip_exhaustive` -- Round-trip encode/decode for all boundary values plus 1000 random u64 values.
15. `test_varint_canonical_encoding` -- Verify encoder never produces non-minimal encoding (e.g., 2 bytes for value 42).

## E2E TEST

Create a database with rowids spanning all varint byte lengths (rowid=1, rowid=128, rowid=16384, ..., rowid near i64::MAX). Read back with C SQLite and verify all rowids are correct. Open a C SQLite database with extreme rowid values in FrankenSQLite and verify correct reading.

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA

- All 9 byte-length boundaries encode/decode correctly.
- 9th byte contributes all 8 bits (verified by test).
- u64::MAX round-trips correctly in exactly 9 bytes.
- Signed rowid values (including negative via AUTOINCREMENT overflow) handled via two's complement cast.
- NOT protobuf/LEB128: explicit test demonstrates the difference.
- Canonical encoding enforced (minimum bytes).
- Cross-compatibility with C SQLite for all varint-encoded values.
close_reason: 18 new edge case tests: all 9 byte-length boundaries, 9th byte all-bits, signed rowid i64::MIN/-1, protobuf/LEB128 divergence, canonical encoding, truncated decode, golden vectors, decode-from-longer-buffer. 179 types tests pass.

comments.text:
# §11.2 Varint Edge Cases: 9-Byte Encoding + SQLite vs Protobuf Differences

## Spec Reference
COMPREHENSIVE_SPEC_FOR_FRANKENSQLITE_V1.md lines 13767-13800 (§11.2.1)

## Scope

Exhaustive validation of SQLite's custom varint encoding/decoding, focusing on
the critical difference from protobuf/LEB128: the 9th byte contributes all 8
bits (not 7). This is a high-risk interoperability surface — any bug here
corrupts every cell, record header, and pointer in the database.

## Encoding Scheme (from spec)

```
Bytes  Value range                    Encoding
  1    0 to 127                       0xxxxxxx (high bit clear)
  2    128 to 16383                   1xxxxxxx 0xxxxxxx
  3    16384 to 2097151               1xxxxxxx 1xxxxxxx 0xxxxxxx
  ...  (pattern continues)
  8    up to 2^56 - 1                 1xxxxxxx * 7 then 0xxxxxxx
  9    up to 2^64 - 1                 1xxxxxxx * 8 then xxxxxxxx (full byte)
```

## Critical Details

- **9th byte is full 8 bits:** Unlike protobuf where every byte uses 7 data bits
  + 1 continuation bit (requiring 10 bytes for u64::MAX), SQLite's 9th byte uses
  all 8 bits with no continuation flag. This means u64::MAX fits in exactly 9 bytes.

- **Minimum encoding:** Values must be encoded in the fewest possible bytes.
  A value of 0 must use 1 byte, not 9 bytes of zeros.

- **Signed interpretation:** For rowids, the u64 is cast to i64 via two's complement.
  Negative rowids encode as large u64 values.

- **Boundary values matter:** Every off-by-one at a byte boundary (127/128,
  16383/16384, etc.) is a potential bug.

## Unit Test Specifications

### Test 1: Single-byte values
Encode/decode 0 → 1 byte `[0x00]`
Encode/decode 1 → 1 byte `[0x01]`
Encode/decode 127 → 1 byte `[0x7F]`

### Test 2: Two-byte boundary
Encode/decode 128 → 2 bytes `[0x81, 0x00]`
Encode/decode 129 → 2 bytes `[0x81, 0x01]`
Encode/decode 16383 → 2 bytes `[0xFF, 0x7F]`

### Test 3: Three-byte boundary
Encode/decode 16384 → 3 bytes
Encode/decode 2097151 → 3 bytes (upper bound)

### Test 4: Four through seven byte boundaries
Encode/decode 2097152 → 4 bytes
Roundtrip values at each byte-count boundary:
  4-byte max: 2^28 - 1 = 268435455
  5-byte max: 2^35 - 1
  6-byte max: 2^42 - 1
  7-byte max: 2^49 - 1

### Test 5: Eight-byte boundary
Encode/decode 2^49 → 8 bytes (first 8-byte value)
Encode/decode 2^56 - 1 → 8 bytes (last 8-byte value)

### Test 6: Nine-byte encoding (CRITICAL)
Encode/decode 2^56 → 9 bytes (first 9-byte value)
Verify the 9th byte uses all 8 bits (no continuation flag)
Encode/decode 2^63 - 1 (i64::MAX)
Encode/decode 2^63 (i64::MIN as u64, first "negative" rowid)
Encode/decode u64::MAX → 9 bytes `[0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF]`

### Test 7: Protobuf/LEB128 divergence (CRITICAL)
Demonstrate that a value like u64::MAX produces DIFFERENT byte sequences
in SQLite varint vs protobuf varint. SQLite: 9 bytes. Protobuf: 10 bytes.
If our encoder produces 10 bytes, the implementation is wrong.

### Test 8: Roundtrip property — encode then decode
For all boundary values: encode → decode → assert original value
For all boundary values: assert encoded length matches expected byte count

### Test 9: Decode from longer buffer
Ensure decoder reads exactly N bytes and stops — remaining bytes in buffer
are untouched. Return (value, bytes_consumed) tuple.

### Test 10: Signed rowid interpretation
Encode i64::MIN as u64 (0x8000000000000000) → decode → cast to i64 → assert i64::MIN
Encode -1i64 as u64 (0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF = u64::MAX) → decode → cast to i64 → assert -1

### Test 11: Minimal encoding enforcement
Verify that the encoder never produces unnecessary leading continuation bytes.
For value 0: assert exactly 1 byte, not `[0x80, 0x00]`
For value 127: assert exactly 1 byte, not 2 bytes

### Test 12: Known C SQLite test vectors
Cross-reference with C SQLite's `src/util.c` putVarint/getVarint. If available,
include specific byte sequences from C SQLite test suite as golden vectors.

## Acceptance Criteria
- All boundary values (127/128, 16383/16384, ..., 2^56-1/2^56) roundtrip correctly
- 9-byte encoding uses full 8 bits in 9th byte (NOT 7+continuation)
- u64::MAX encodes in exactly 9 bytes
- Signed i64 roundtrip via two's complement cast is correct
- Encoder always produces minimal-length encoding
- All tests pass under `cargo test`

## Task: Recovery demo — beyond-tolerance corruption (graceful degradation)

### What
Corrupt more than R=4 pages within a single page group, showing that RaptorQ cannot recover BUT FrankenSQLite degrades gracefully: it tells you exactly which pages are unrecoverable, the rest of the database remains intact.

### Test Flow
1. Start with golden copy
2. Generate .db-fec sidecar
3. Corrupt 5 pages within group 2 (pages 128-191):
   ```
   CorruptionPattern::PageZero { page_number: 130 },
   CorruptionPattern::PageZero { page_number: 145 },
   CorruptionPattern::PageZero { page_number: 160 },
   CorruptionPattern::PageZero { page_number: 175 },
   CorruptionPattern::PageZero { page_number: 190 },
   ```
4. **C SQLite**: 5 pages lost. No information about which pages are affected or recoverable.
5. **FrankenSQLite**: Group 2 has 59 surviving source pages + 4 repair symbols = 63 symbols. Need 64 (= K). Decode FAILS. But:
   - Emits durability-violation diagnostic
   - Reports exactly which 5 pages are unrecoverable
   - ALL OTHER GROUPS are unaffected — data outside group 2 is perfectly intact
   - Can still read all tables whose data doesn't reside in pages 130, 145, 160, 175, 190

### Why Graceful Degradation Matters
The key difference from C SQLite:
- C SQLite: corruption is opaque. `PRAGMA integrity_check` might report B-tree issues but doesn't tell you which data is salvageable.
- FrankenSQLite: corruption is surgically isolated. Exact page numbers, exact groups, exact tables affected. The operator knows precisely what was lost and what was preserved.

### Adaptive Redundancy Response (§3.5.12)
After detecting the durability violation:
- Autopilot would raise R for this group in future
- Generate retroactive repair symbols for surviving groups
- Increase integrity sweep frequency

### Acceptance Criteria
- RaptorQ decode fails (expected — beyond tolerance)
- Diagnostic clearly identifies the 5 unrecoverable pages
- All data outside the corrupted group is still accessible
- No crash, no panic — controlled failure path
- Contrast with C SQLite's less-informative failure mode

## Task: Recovery demo — multi-page corruption within RaptorQ tolerance (R=4)

### What
Corrupt up to R=4 pages within a single page group (G=64) and show FrankenSQLite can still recover. This tests the limits of the erasure coding.

### Test Flow
1. Start with golden copy
2. Generate .db-fec sidecar
3. Corrupt exactly 4 pages within the same group (pages 64-127, group index 1):
   ```
   CorruptionPattern::PageZero { page_number: 70 },
   CorruptionPattern::PageZero { page_number: 85 },
   CorruptionPattern::PageZero { page_number: 100 },
   CorruptionPattern::PageZero { page_number: 120 },
   ```
4. **C SQLite**: 4 pages of data permanently lost. PRAGMA integrity_check reports multiple errors.
5. **FrankenSQLite**: Group 1 has 60 surviving source pages + 4 repair symbols = 64 symbols. Exactly K symbols available. RaptorQ decode succeeds (P_success ~99% at exactly K, per §3.1).
6. Verify recovered database matches golden copy

### Boundary Testing
- Also test with 1, 2, 3 corrupted pages (well within tolerance)
- Test with corrupted pages spread across multiple groups (each group independently recoverable)

### Statistical Note (from §3.1)
- At exactly K symbols: ~99% success (P_fail < 0.01)
- At K+1 symbols: P_fail < 10^-4
- At K+2 symbols: P_fail < 10^-7
- With R=4 and 4 corrupted: we have exactly K — success is expected but not guaranteed. Run multiple seeds to verify.

### Acceptance Criteria
- 4 pages corrupted within same group
- FrankenSQLite successfully recovers all 4 pages
- Recovered database matches golden copy
- Also test 1/2/3 corrupted pages (should all succeed)
- If exact-K decode fails (rare), document the failure and retry with different corruption positions

## bd-1yjj: Multi-page corruption within RaptorQ tolerance (R=4) — COMPLETE

### Implementation
Two integration tests in `crates/fsqlite-e2e/tests/recovery_single_page.rs`:

### Tests

1. **test_multi_page_cross_group_independent_recovery** — Cross-group multi-page recovery:
   - Creates database with 5000 rows (~200+ pages spanning 4+ groups)
   - Corrupts 1 page in each of 4 separate groups (pages 10, 80, 150, 210)
   - Each group independently repaired via XOR parity (single-fault per group)
   - All 4 pages recovered, repaired database matches original byte-for-byte
   - C SQLite integrity_check passes on repaired database

2. **test_multi_page_same_group_gradient** — Same-group gradient (1-4 corruptions):
   - 1 corrupted page: XOR parity succeeds (single-fault)
   - 2-4 corrupted pages: XOR parity fails gracefully (expected — needs full RaptorQ decode)
   - Documents current XOR-parity limitation vs future RaptorQ integration
   - All failure cases produce clear error messages, no panics

### RaptorQ Limitation Note
Current attempt_page_repair() uses XOR parity (single-fault per group). For N > 1 corruptions in the same group, full RaptorQ decode (RFC 6330) is required.

title: UPSERT DO UPDATE swallows non-target UNIQUE/PK conflict (must ABORT like stock SQLite)
description:
## Bug
`INSERT INTO t(id,label) VALUES(99,'beta') ON CONFLICT(id) DO UPDATE SET ...`
where `id` is the PK and `label` is a SEPARATE `UNIQUE` already holding 'beta'
(under a different id). The ON CONFLICT(id) target has no conflict (id=99 is new),
so the row is inserted and then violates the `label` UNIQUE index. Stock SQLite
ABORTs with SQLITE_CONSTRAINT. fsqlite (0.1.10 confirmed empirically; 0.1.12/HEAD
confirmed by code) instead returns Ok(0): no insert, no error — the write is
silently swallowed. Any table with a PK plus a second UNIQUE that uses a targeted
upsert can silently drop/mis-merge writes.

## Root cause
`crates/fsqlite-vdbe/src/codegen.rs` (~10942, `codegen_insert`): for ANY upsert
the statement-level conflict action `stmt_level` was force-coerced to
`Some(ConflictAction::Ignore)`. The DO-UPDATE check-before-insert probe in
`codegen_insert_values` resolves only the NAMED target index; the no-conflict
insert path then calls `emit_index_inserts(... stmt_level=Ignore)`, giving every
OTHER unique/PK index IGNORE semantics. `DO NOTHING` legitimately wants IGNORE;
`DO UPDATE` must not.

## Fix
Scope the forced IGNORE to `UpsertAction::Nothing`; for `UpsertAction::Update`
carry the genuine `stmt.or_conflict` (None => default ABORT, or an explicit
`INSERT OR <algo>`). The working target-conflict UPDATE branch is unaffected (it
hardcodes `Some(ConflictAction::Replace)` for its own index inserts).

## Test
`crates/fsqlite-e2e/tests/upsert_on_conflict.rs::upsert_do_update_aborts_on_nontarget_unique_conflict`
(was completely unguarded — every existing upsert/conflict test only exercised the
target-conflict side). Validated against the upsert/conflict oracle suites.

Discovered downstream as hedge_fund_data_tool bead hfdt-fsqlite-upsert-conflict-target-a756a.

title: LIMIT/OFFSET non-integer values coerced leniently instead of raising "datatype mismatch" (SQLite requires lossless integer conversion)
close_reason: reject non-integer constant LIMIT/OFFSET at Select dispatch (datatype mismatch)

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
# LIMIT/OFFSET non-integer values coerced leniently

## Symptom
SQLite requires the LIMIT/OFFSET expression to be losslessly convertible to an
integer; otherwise it raises `datatype mismatch`. frank instead performs a lossy
coercion (truncate a real, parse text to 0, treat NULL as 0) and runs the query.

```sql
SELECT id FROM t ORDER BY id LIMIT 2.9;            -- SQLite: ERROR datatype mismatch   frank: [1,2]
SELECT id FROM t ORDER BY id LIMIT 'abc';          -- SQLite: ERROR datatype mismatch   frank: []
SELECT id FROM t ORDER BY id LIMIT NULL;           -- SQLite: ERROR datatype mismatch   frank: []
SELECT id FROM t ORDER BY id LIMIT 2 OFFSET 1.5;   -- SQLite: ERROR datatype mismatch   frank: [2,3]
```
Values that DO convert losslessly are accepted on both engines (correct in frank):
```sql
LIMIT '3'            -- text -> 3   OK
LIMIT 1 + 1          -- expr -> 2   OK
LIMIT (SELECT 2)     -- subquery -> 2  OK
OFFSET '1'           -- text -> 1   OK
```

## Rule (SQLite)
The LIMIT/OFFSET counter is an arbitrary expression, but its value must be
losslessly representable as a 64-bit integer. Integer-valued text (`'3'`) is fine;
a real with a fractional part (`2.9`), non-numeric text (`'abc'`), and NULL are
NOT and yield SQLITE_MISMATCH ("datatype mismatch"). (A whole-valued real such as
`2.0` is accepted by SQLite — not tested here.)

## Root cause / location
`crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs` `eval_expression_only_limit_offset_expr`
(:46863) coerces the evaluated value to i64 lossily instead of checking that the
conversion is lossless and raising a datatype-mismatch error when it is not.

## Fix sketch
After evaluating the LIMIT/OFFSET expression: accept Integer as-is; accept Float
only when it has no fractional part (== its truncation); accept Text only when it
parses exactly to an integer; otherwise (fractional real, non-numeric text, NULL,
blob) return a "datatype mismatch" error. Mirror SQLite's `OP_MustBeInt` semantics.

## Priority
P3 — over-acceptance (frank runs queries SQLite rejects). Not silently wrong
results, but a conformance gap that can mask malformed LIMIT/OFFSET.

## Tests
`crates/fsqlite-e2e/tests/limit_coercion_oracle_e2e.rs`: the lossless cases are
green; `limit_offset_noninteger_rejected` (#[ignore] on this bead) pins the
non-integer cases (frank accepts, SQLite errors).
