title: FTS5-S4.7 User-visible command-channel and fts5vocab parity
description:
Implement the user-visible FTS5 command-channel and introspection surface that sits above the maintenance primitives. This bead exists so “full support” is explicit about the command paths real users touch, not just the underlying storage operations.

Deliverables:
- special INSERT command-channel support and parity/fencing for stock FTS5 control commands,
- user-visible tuning/configuration surfaces such as rank and merge-related controls where stock FTS5 exposes them,
- `fts5vocab` row/col/instance support or an explicitly justified staged fence.
design:
Separate this work from the lower-level maintenance machinery so the storage primitives stay clean and the user-visible command surface is tested as an API in its own right. Drive the command matrix from the vendored SQLite behavior study and be explicit about how each command maps to persisted config, pending-state flushes, merge scheduling, or integrity routines.

This bead should also own precise diagnostics: invalid or unsupported commands must fail clearly, not silently noop. Replayable e2e scripts with structured logs should exercise every command family and record both effect and on-disk state transitions.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The stock FTS5 control-command matrix is explicit and implemented or deliberately fenced with rationale, including optimize/rebuild/integrity-check/merge plus merge-tuning and control surfaces such as automerge, crisismerge, usermerge, deletemerge, secure-delete, delete, delete-all, pgsz, rank, and insttoken where applicable.
2. `fts5vocab` row/col/instance behavior is implemented or explicitly fenced with a documented compatibility boundary.
3. Unit tests and replayable e2e scripts cover each command family with structured logs, golden outputs, and useful failure diagnostics, including tokenizer/locale-sensitive `fts5vocab` and command cases once S4.8 parity exists.
4. Invalid command sequences and unsupported combinations produce deterministic, documented behavior instead of silent compatibility holes.
5. This bead is scoped to command-channel and vocab behavior; core tokenizer/locale semantics are owned by S4.8, but this bead must validate the command/introspection surfaces against those final token semantics instead of assuming them.
notes: Code investigation showed the current Rust implementation only handles a very narrow control-command subset, so this surface should not remain hidden inside a broad maintenance bead. Making it explicit helps future implementers and downstream users understand what “full FTS5 support” actually means.

title: FTS5-S4.8 Tokenizer, locale, and token-semantics parity
description:
Implement the user-visible tokenizer, locale, and token-semantics parity surface. This bead exists so multilingual search behavior, tokenizer options, locale-tagged values, synonym/co-located token behavior, and token-data semantics are explicit deliverables instead of accidental side effects of lower-level config work.

Deliverables:
- built-in tokenizer parity for the supported tokenizer set and option matrix,
- locale-tagged value support and locale-sensitive SQL surfaces such as `fts5_locale()` / `fts5_get_locale()` where they are part of stock FTS5 behavior,
- parity for token-semantics features that materially affect users: query/document/aux tokenization differences, `tokendata=1`, synonym/co-located tokens, and detail-mode restrictions that affect phrase/snippet/highlight behavior,
- multilingual and tokenizer-stress unit/integration/e2e scenarios with detailed logs and golden outputs.
design:
Drive the work from the vendored tokenizer and locale behavior, not from the current simplified Rust tokenizer implementations. Be explicit about unicode61 option handling (`remove_diacritics`, `categories`, `tokenchars`, `separators`), porter wrapping semantics, trigram behavior, locale-tagged text encoding/decoding, and how tokenization differs across document/query/prefix/aux contexts.

This bead should also make the product boundary obvious: either custom tokenizer behavior is genuinely supported through S2.5 and exercised here, or the compatibility fence is explicit and tested. Users should not need to reverse-engineer whether multilingual or custom tokenizer behavior is “probably fine”.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Supported tokenizer behaviors and options match stock SQLite closely enough for differential fixtures and real consumer expectations.
2. Locale-tagged values and locale-sensitive FTS5 SQL surfaces are implemented or explicitly fenced with documented rationale.
3. Token-semantics behaviors that affect search results or aux functions, including query/document/aux mode differences, `tokendata=1`, and synonym/co-located token handling, are tested explicitly.
4. Multilingual and tokenizer-stress unit/integration/e2e suites with structured logs and golden artifacts make tokenizer regressions easy to reproduce.
notes: Vendored references include `ext/fts5/fts5.h`, `fts5_config.c`, `fts5_main.c`, `fts5_aux.c`, `fts5_tokenize.c`, and tests such as `fts5tokenizer.test` and `fts5locale.test`. This bead is about the search semantics users feel directly, not just internal configuration plumbing.

title: FTS5-S5 MVCC, Contention, and Extreme Performance
description: This phase protects FrankenSQLite's core value proposition while making shadow-backed FTS5 fast. It covers MVCC/savepoints, hot-page contention mitigation, bounded-memory reopen/query behavior, and the observability/benchmark loop needed to make optimization decisions with evidence instead of intuition.
design: The work is intentionally separated between correctness-preserving transaction semantics, contention control, memory/IO efficiency, and instrumentation/benchmarking. That keeps performance changes honest: first prove semantics, then attack the real bottlenecks revealed by measurement.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Shadow-backed FTS5 preserves concurrent-writer defaults and correct savepoint/rollback semantics.
2. Hot-page contention risks are measured and actively mitigated rather than hand-waved.
3. Reopen and query behavior are bounded-memory and benchmarked against explicit targets.
4. Optimization work is backed by dedicated telemetry and repeatable benches.
notes: This phase should be run with `extreme-software-optimization` discipline: baseline first, one lever at a time, verify no semantic drift, and prefer algorithmic wins over micro-tuning. It also has to respect the project's “never regress to serialized locking” rule from AGENTS.md.

title: FTS5-S5.1 Preserve MVCC/savepoint semantics for shadow-backed FTS5 writes without global writer serialization
description:
Define and implement the MVCC/savepoint semantics for shadow-backed FTS5 writes. The backend must integrate with FrankenSQLite transactions without introducing a hidden global writer lock, while still giving the module enough structure to manage pending token state, flush boundaries, and rollback.

Deliverables:
- explicit begin/sync/commit/rollback/savepoint behavior for shadow-backed FTS5,
- tests for nested savepoints and failure cleanup,
- a clear statement of what state lives in connection-local pending buffers vs pager-visible shadow tables.
design: Use the module lifecycle hooks and writer pipeline to keep transaction boundaries explicit. Make savepoint semantics first-class instead of retrofitting them after DML works. This is also the place to decide which pending-state structures are transaction-local and how they interact with pager visibility and reload.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Shadow-backed FTS5 obeys explicit transaction and savepoint semantics without global serialization.
2. Tests cover commit, rollback, rollback-to-savepoint, nested savepoints, and failure cleanup.
3. Pending state vs persisted state boundaries are clearly defined and exercised.
4. Concurrency stress e2e scripts with structured logs demonstrate that this work preserves the AGENTS.md concurrent-writer default and does not reintroduce file-level write serialization.
notes: This bead is the semantic backbone for DML and maintenance commands. It should be reviewed specifically against the project's non-negotiable requirement that concurrent-writer mode remain on by default and not be undermined by FTS5 implementation shortcuts.
close_reason: Done: FTS5 update decode failures now preserve existing rows with transaction/savepoint proof coverage

title: FTS5-S5.2 Design and validate hot-page contention mitigation for structure-record and idx-page updates
description:
Design and validate contention mitigation for the shadow-backed FTS5 hot spots, especially structure-record updates and `%_idx`/segment publication pages. The objective is not just “make it work”; it is “make it compatible with FrankenSQLite's multi-writer story under realistic write concurrency”.

Deliverables:
- a measured hotspot profile for FTS5 write conflicts,
- concrete mitigation strategies such as append-friendly segment publication, deferred metadata writes, batching, or structured page-patch publication where justified,
- acceptance benchmarks that prove conflict behavior improved instead of merely moving around.
design:
Start from measurements, not guesses. Use the baseline harness and dedicated counters to identify the real hot pages and update patterns. Then evaluate mitigation strategies one by one with explicit semantic proof.

If structured page-patch publication is considered for the structure record or related metadata, the design must explain why the patch is commutative/safe on SQLite-structured pages and how it respects MVCC visibility.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The real FTS5 write-hot spots are identified with evidence.
2. At least one concrete mitigation strategy is implemented and benchmarked against the baseline.
3. The mitigation preserves correctness and concurrent-writer invariants.
4. Conflict-rate and throughput improvements are captured in repeatable benches, structured logs, and deterministic replay scripts so regressions can be re-run without guesswork.
notes:
This is where the plan should be clever, not magical. Avoid cargo-cult lock-free tricks. Prefer strategies grounded in the actual `%_data`/`%_idx` update patterns and the project's structured page-merge philosophy.

Expected proof artifacts include conflict heatmaps, page-hotspot traces, and before/after benchmark bundles keyed to identical corpora and seeds.
close_reason: Done: added deterministic FTS5 shadow-write hotspot profile plus tests for append-only segment publication and idx-page hot writes

title: FTS5-S5.3 Make reopen/query memory-bounded with lazy hydration, scratch arenas, and batched page access
description:
Make reopen and query execution bounded-memory and IO-efficient. The shadow-backed backend should not replace one compatibility gap with a slower, more memory-hungry implementation that rehydrates large amounts of state on open or query.

Deliverables:
- lazy hydration rules for config/structure/content/docsize/segment state,
- scratch-buffer and iterator memory-reuse strategy,
- explicit reopen/query memory and IO targets validated by benchmark evidence,
- replayable no-mock e2e scripts and benchmark manifests for large-corpus and consumer-like reopen/query workloads with detailed structured logs.
design:
Favor tiny always-hot metadata caches plus lazy readers over broad caches that duplicate the on-disk truth. Reuse scratch buffers and iterator state aggressively where that does not complicate correctness.

This bead should also consider page read batching/prefetch opportunities, but only where evidence shows real wins.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Reopen does not whole-hydrate FTS table contents or indexes.
2. Query execution uses bounded-memory iterators and measured scratch reuse across the real shadow-backed MATCH/aux path.
3. Benchmarks and replayable no-mock e2e scripts demonstrate acceptable reopen/query RSS and IO behavior relative to the baseline, including large-corpus and tokenizer/locale-sensitive cases.
4. Structured logs and manifests make memory/IO regressions reproducible rather than anecdotal.
5. The optimization path does not change query semantics or maintenance correctness.
notes: This bead is where the project cashes in on the “shadow-backed but still fast” promise. Keep the implementation understandable enough that later corruption and integrity work can still reason about reader state.

title: FTS5-S5.4 Add FTS5-specific observability, benchmark suites, and profile-driven optimization loop
description:
Add the FTS5-specific observability, benchmark suites, and optimization loop that will keep this subsystem honest over time. This includes structured metrics for pending bytes, flush counts, merge debt, segment counts, query phases, contention, and memory behavior.

Deliverables:
- targeted metrics/logging and, where appropriate, PRAGMA or virtual-table exposure,
- benches/scripts for the important read/write/maintenance/conflict regimes,
- the manifest/logging plumbing needed to make proof artifacts uniform across unit, integration, e2e, and downstream cutover runs,
- a repeatable profile-driven optimization workflow for future work.
design:
Instrument the subsystem where decisions are made: pending accumulation, flush, merge, reopen, query iteration, aux-function content fetches, and conflict points. Keep the metrics cheap enough for regular use and structured enough for longitudinal comparison.

This bead should make it easy to prove that future optimizations help and to catch regressions before downstream projects rediscover them the hard way.
acceptance_criteria:
1. FTS5-specific metrics and logs exist for write, read, maintenance, contention, and memory behavior.
2. Benchmarks/scripts cover the main operating regimes and are easy to rerun.
3. Artifact manifests and structured logs are consistent with the proof-artifact contract so later debugging and downstream rehearsal are cheap.
4. The optimization workflow is explicit enough that future tuning changes can be evidence-driven.
5. Observability overhead is measured and acceptable.
notes: This bead complements S1.3 by making measurement part of the final subsystem rather than just a one-off planning artifact. Prefer metrics that correlate directly with design decisions: segment counts, merge debt, pending bytes, conflict retries, and lazy-fetch hit rates.

title: FTS5-S6 Verification, Migration, and Cutover
description: This phase closes the loop: differential validation, fuzz/recovery hardening, migration away from the legacy materialized path, downstream cutover rehearsal, and the operator/developer playbook for adoption. It is where the subsystem becomes shippable rather than merely impressive in a branch.
design: The work is split between differential correctness, destructive/edge-case validation, internal migration/cutover, real-consumer rehearsal, and documentation/downstream rollout. That separation matters because a subsystem can be feature-complete and still be operationally unsafe or too ambiguous for downstream adoption.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The shadow-backed backend is validated against stock SQLite with differential fixtures, destructive tests, replayable proof artifacts, and an operator-grade validation entrypoint.
2. The legacy materialized positive-rootpage path is migrated or retired in a controlled way.
3. Recovery/migration/documentation surfaces are good enough that downstream consumers can remove their rusqlite FTS retention with confidence.
4. At least one real consumer-repo cutover rehearsal has been run and its results are captured.
5. The final graph includes the proof artifacts and triage tooling needed for long-term maintenance, not just implementation code.
notes: This phase is where the project proves that the new backend is not just more compatible but also more maintainable. It should leave behind explicit fixtures, scripts, and operational guidance so future regressions are easier to catch.

title: FTS5-S6.1 Build differential conformance corpus against stock SQLite across all content modes
description:
Build the differential conformance corpus against stock SQLite across all relevant content modes and lifecycle shapes. This corpus is the main defense against “close enough” implementations that only work on happy-path test cases.

Deliverables:
- stock SQLite-generated fixture databases and expected outputs,
- differential tests for create/open/query/write/maintenance/command-channel/lifecycle behavior,
- explicit coverage for stored, external-content, and contentless/contentless-delete tables plus prefix/detail variations,
- golden manifests and structured trace bundles so every corpus scenario is replayable.
design: Keep the corpus composable: small targeted fixtures for specific invariants plus larger end-to-end fixtures for realistic behavior. Reuse the same fixtures across unit/integration/e2e where possible so evidence accumulates instead of fragmenting.
acceptance_criteria:
1. There is a durable stock-SQLite differential corpus covering the intended FTS5 surface.
2. Differential tests catch behavioral drift in query results, maintenance effects, command-channel behavior, tokenizer/locale semantics, auxiliary-function extension-context semantics, and lifecycle semantics.
3. Fixtures cover the major content modes, key option combinations, multilingual/tokenizer-sensitive cases, and locale-tagged values where supported.
4. Corpus scenarios emit structured logs and golden manifests that make failures easy to reproduce and compare over time.
5. The corpus is easy to extend when new parity gaps are found.
notes: This bead should include real on-disk databases created by stock SQLite, not just statement-level comparisons. It is the main validation bridge between the vendored code study and the final Rust implementation.

title: FTS5-S6.2 Add fuzz/property/corruption/recovery suites for segment codecs and shadow-table invariants
description:
Add fuzz/property/corruption/recovery suites for the shadow-backed backend. This includes codecs, structure records, segment readers, maintenance flows, and database-open behavior under malformed or partially damaged shadow tables.

Deliverables:
- fuzz/property tests for codecs and iterators,
- corruption/recovery scenarios for missing or inconsistent shadow tables,
- crash/reopen and integrity-check validation for destructive cases,
- deterministic mutation seeds and structured failure logs so corruption cases can be replayed exactly,
- tokenizer/locale/tokendata-sensitive corruption variants so destructive testing covers the richer real-world database shapes introduced by full parity.
design:
Build the destructive tests on the same primitives used by the real implementation so the results are meaningful. Prefer targeted generators and mutation strategies over blind randomization when the file format has rich structure.

This bead should also define which failures are recoverable, which require rebuild, and which must be hard corruption errors.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Codec, iterator, and metadata logic are covered by fuzz/property tests.
2. Corruption/recovery scenarios are explicit and exercised on real databases.
3. Integrity-check and reopen behavior under damage is tested and diagnosable.
4. Deterministic mutation seeds, manifests, and structured crash/recovery logs make destructive failures replayable.
5. The destructive corpus includes tokenizer/locale/tokendata-sensitive variants so recovery behavior is not only proven on generic ASCII/simple-tokenizer cases.
6. The subsystem has a clear corruption taxonomy rather than ad hoc error handling.
notes: Use this bead to pressure-test the assumptions made in S3 and S4. The more the reader/writer/integrity logic shares code paths, the more valuable these tests become.

title: FTS5-S6.3 Migrate or rebuild current materialized positive-rootpage FTS5 tables and retire placeholder logic
description:
Migrate or rebuild current FrankenSQLite-created materialized positive-rootpage FTS5 tables and retire the placeholder logic that exists only because shadow-backed FTS5 was not yet first-class. This bead is the cutover line from “new backend exists” to “new backend is the engine's canonical path”.

Deliverables:
- a migration/rebuild strategy for legacy materialized FTS5 tables,
- retirement or fencing of the legacy placeholder/materialized code paths,
- upgrade and reopen rehearsal scripts with structured logs for existing FrankenSQLite databases,
- before/after manifests that prove tokenizer, locale, tokendata, content-mode, and user-visible query semantics survive migration or are rebuilt deterministically.
design: Prefer explicit migration or rebuild over silently preserving a permanent dual-backend world. If a temporary bridge is needed for compatibility, give it narrow scope, clear diagnostics, and an end state where the shadow-backed backend is canonical.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Existing FrankenSQLite materialized FTS5 tables have a defined migration or rebuild path.
2. The engine's canonical FTS5 backend after cutover is the shadow-backed one.
3. Legacy placeholder/materialized logic is removed or explicitly fenced to migration-only scenarios.
4. Upgrade tests and replayable migration/reopen scripts prove existing databases can reach the new backend safely.
5. Migration validation covers tokenizer/locale/tokendata/content-mode preservation or deterministic rebuild semantics, with before/after manifests and structured logs.
6. The cutover story includes explicit rollback/fallback guidance for failed upgrades instead of leaving operators to improvise.
notes: This bead should pay down the current split in `connection.rs` around materialized live vtabs vs legacy rootpage=0 placeholders. It is also the place to decide what happens to old on-disk FrankenSQLite FTS5 data when users upgrade.

title: FTS5-S6.4 Finalize operator/developer docs and downstream cutover playbook
description:
Finalize the operator/developer documentation and downstream cutover playbook for removing rusqlite FTS retention. This includes architecture notes, migration instructions, validation steps, known failure modes, and what downstream maintainers should measure when they switch.

Deliverables:
- documentation for the new backend and its operational model,
- a downstream migration checklist/playbook that incorporates the real cutover rehearsal,
- explicit verification steps for removing rusqlite-based FTS fallback/repair paths,
- links or references to the proof artifacts, logs, and benchmark bundles that justify the guidance.
design:
The documentation should assume the reader is trying to cut over a real project, not admire the architecture. Be concrete about database shapes, migration/rebuild steps, integrity checks, expected performance signatures, rollback options, and how to interpret the structured logs produced by the verification beads.

This is a finalization bead: it should absorb the lessons from the real downstream rehearsal instead of freezing the docs before a consumer has actually tried them.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Operators and downstream developers have a clear playbook for adopting the shadow-backed backend.
2. The docs explain migration, validation, observability, tokenizer/locale behavior, and failure diagnosis concretely.
3. Downstream projects can remove rusqlite FTS retention using the provided checklist, validation driver, and evidence bundle.
4. Documentation is aligned with the final implemented subsystem, validation artifacts, operator-grade validation entrypoint, and real downstream rehearsal results.
notes: This bead should explicitly address the cross-project motivation that triggered this planning session: downstream projects want to eliminate dual-driver retention caused by the shadow-table gap. Make the path to that outcome operationally obvious.

title: FTS5-S6.5 Real downstream cutover rehearsal on consumer repos
description:
Execute a real downstream cutover rehearsal on consumer repos so the program ends with verified adoption evidence instead of only internal tests and documentation. Start with `/dp/coding_agent_session_search`, which is the motivating real-world consumer for this planning session, and expand to additional consumers if needed.

Deliverables:
- a branch-level rehearsal that removes or bypasses rusqlite FTS retention/repair paths in at least one real consumer,
- deterministic validation runs using the new proof-artifact contract, including unit/integration/e2e scripts, benchmarks, and structured logs,
- a blocker ledger that feeds back into FrankenSQLite beads or the downstream cutover playbook.
design:
Treat this as an engineering rehearsal, not a marketing demo. The downstream repo should run using the same documented migration and validation steps an actual adopter would follow. Capture exact database fixtures, command traces, benchmark deltas, and any gaps that still force a fallback to rusqlite or a manual rebuild path.

If the first consumer still exposes compatibility gaps, those deltas should become explicit follow-up work rather than hand-waved caveats in the docs.
acceptance_criteria:
1. At least one real consumer repository completes a branch-level cutover rehearsal using the shadow-backed backend as the intended primary FTS5 path.
2. The rehearsal produces deterministic proof artifacts: unit/integration/e2e outputs, structured logs, benchmark summaries, reopen/query memory-IO summaries, and a precise blocker ledger.
3. The rehearsal exercises migration or rebuild of realistic databases where applicable, including tokenizer/locale-sensitive cases rather than only trivial fixtures.
4. The rehearsal runs through the operator-grade validation driver and captures the resulting artifact index/scorecard.
5. Any gaps discovered during rehearsal are translated into explicit bead or documentation updates rather than buried in tribal knowledge.
6. The project has real adoption evidence, not just synthetic parity claims, before declaring downstream cutover readiness.
notes: This bead exists to make the plan more user-serving. A subsystem can look complete in isolation and still fail the moment a real consumer removes its fallback paths. The rehearsal is the shortest route to discovering that honestly.

title: FTS5-S6.6 Operator-grade validation driver, artifact index, and failure-triage pack
description:
Build the operator-grade validation driver, artifact index, and failure-triage pack for the shadow-backed FTS5 program. This bead exists because the plan already defines many unit/integration/e2e/differential/migration/cutover proofs, but a real user still needs a concrete entrypoint that runs the right subsets, gathers the structured logs, and tells them what failed.

Deliverables:
- a unified validation driver with local, CI, and downstream-cutover modes,
- an artifact index/scorecard that points to logs, manifests, goldens, benchmark summaries, memory-IO summaries, and migration outputs,
- concise failure-triage summaries that map failing checks to likely subsystem domains and exact replay commands,
- end-to-end scripts that prove the driver works against real backend runs instead of only mocked or partial workflows.
design:
This is not a replacement for the underlying tests; it is the operator-facing composition layer that makes them usable. The driver should consume the proof-artifact contract, the observability outputs, and the differential/migration suites rather than inventing parallel formats.

Design for three audiences explicitly:
- implementers who need a fast smoke vs full-proof split,
- CI/release workflows that need deterministic pass/fail bundles,
- downstream adopters who need a cutover-grade checklist and artifact pack after they run the suite.

Keep the outputs detailed but navigable. A bundle full of raw logs without an index or replay hints is not user-serving.
acceptance_criteria:
1. There is a single documented validation entrypoint with modes appropriate for local development, CI/release gating, and downstream cutover rehearsal.
2. Running the driver produces an artifact index/scorecard that links unit/integration/e2e/differential/migration/benchmark outputs, structured logs, manifests, and replay commands.
3. Failure-triage summaries make it easy to distinguish semantic, migration, corruption, performance, and observability regressions without reading raw logs first.
4. The driver is exercised by replayable e2e scripts against real backend runs, with detailed structured logging and deterministic manifests.
5. Downstream rehearsal and final docs use this same driver instead of bespoke one-off command lists.
notes: This bead is the user-facing culmination of S1.4, S5.4, and the S6 verification work. It should leave future maintainers and downstream adopters with a practical “run this, inspect this bundle, follow these replay commands” workflow instead of forcing them to reconstruct the validation matrix manually.

title: WAL-FEC: Pipelined background FEC job (durable vs repairable semantics)
description:
Implement the default required pipelining for repair symbol generation.

Spec rules (normative):
- Commit is durable once .wal frames are written+fsync and wal-index updated.
- Commit becomes repairable only after WalFecGroupMeta + R SymbolRecords are appended to .wal-fec and fsync.
- Encoding MUST NOT happen inside WAL write critical section.

Implementation:
- After commit durability, enqueue background job:
  - read source frames from .wal
  - deterministically generate repair symbols
  - append meta+symbols to .wal-fec
  - fsync .wal-fec

Optional:
- Synchronous mode MAY wait for .wal-fec fsync before ack commit; off by default.

Done when:
- concurrency/ordering is correct and tested.
close_reason: Pipelined background FEC job implemented via WalFecRepairPipeline in wal_fec.rs. Encoding outside WAL write critical section, background thread reads source frames, generates repair symbols, appends to .wal-fec, fsyncs. Async pipeline tests pass.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Commit is durable once .wal frames written+fsync and wal-index updated.
- [ ] Commit becomes repairable after WalFecGroupMeta + R SymbolRecords appended to .wal-fec and fsync.
- [ ] FEC encoding does NOT happen inside WAL write critical section.
- [ ] Background job reads source frames, generates repair symbols, appends to .wal-fec, fsyncs.
- [ ] Ordering: commits become repairable in commit order.
- [ ] Optional synchronous mode waits for .wal-fec fsync before ack.
- [ ] Concurrency is correct under concurrent writers and readers.

## Unit Test Requirements
- test_pipeline_commit_durable_before_repairable: Commit visible before FEC completes.
- test_pipeline_encoding_outside_critical_section: WAL lock not held during encode.
- test_pipeline_ordering: Multiple commits become repairable in order.
- test_pipeline_sync_mode: Synchronous mode blocks until .wal-fec fsynced.
- test_pipeline_concurrent_writers: Two concurrent writers produce correct FEC.

## E2E Test
- test_e2e_fec_pipeline: Write multiple commits, verify repairable status progression.

## Logging Requirements
- DEBUG: emit job enqueue, encode start/end, and fsync timing.
- INFO: emit commit durable and repairable state transitions.
- WARN: emit pipeline backpressure or slow encode.
- ERROR: emit .wal-fec write failures with reproducible context.

title: Overhead: Implement PRAGMA raptorq_overhead (defaults, persistence, per-object policy)
description:
Implement `PRAGMA raptorq_overhead` as specified.

## Semantics
- `PRAGMA raptorq_overhead = <percent>` sets the default multiplicative overhead policy.
- The value is used by budgeting to derive `R` from `K_source`:
  - `R = max(slack_decode, ceil(K_source * overhead_percent / 100))` with `slack_decode=2`.

## Persistence / Scope
- Define whether the setting is:
  - connection-local (default SQLite style), and/or
  - persisted into database metadata for replication determinism.

If persisted, it MUST be versioned and included in any object metadata required for deterministic decoding/proofs.

## Interaction With Object Types
- Provide a mechanism to override overhead per object class (markers vs pages vs index segments), even if V1 exposes only a global PRAGMA.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Setting is parsed/validated (bounds, rounding rules) and stored deterministically.
- Budgeting API exposes the effective overhead used for each object (for evidence/proofs).
- Unit tests cover:
  - bounds clamping
  - rounding behavior
  - small-K behavior (no under-provisioning)
close_reason: Implemented PRAGMA raptorq_overhead policy state: deterministic parse/clamp/rounding, optional versioned persisted metadata scope, per-object overrides, and policy_controller unit coverage for bounds/rounding/small-K/exposure.

title: WASM 1.3b: Gate OS-specific deps in fsqlite-observability (parking_lot, std::time::Instant)

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
# Task 1.3b: Gate OS-Specific Deps in fsqlite-observability

## Why This Task Exists (Found During Deep Audit)
The original WASM bead plan missed fsqlite-observability entirely. However, codebase inspection reveals:
- `fsqlite-observability/src/lib.rs` line 22: `use parking_lot::Mutex;`
- `fsqlite-observability/src/lib.rs` line 19: `use std::time::{Duration, Instant};`
- fsqlite-observability is a dependency of: **fsqlite-vfs**, **fsqlite-mvcc**, **fsqlite-core**

Without gating this crate, ALL downstream crates will fail to compile on wasm32.

## Current Dependencies (from Cargo.toml)
```toml
[dependencies]
fsqlite-types = { workspace = true }
parking_lot = { workspace = true }
serde = { workspace = true, features = ["derive"] }
tracing = { workspace = true }
```

## Changes Required
1. **Replace `parking_lot::Mutex`** with the sync polyfill from task 1.2:
   ```rust
   use fsqlite_types::sync::Mutex;
   ```
2. **Gate `std::time::Instant`** behind cfg:
   ```rust
   #[cfg(not(target_arch = "wasm32"))]
   ```

title: Leapfrog Triejoin Implementation (§8.1)
description:
Implement worst-case optimal Leapfrog Triejoin for multi-way joins. Traditional pairwise hash/merge joins can be EXPONENTIALLY worse than optimal for 3+ relation joins — the AGM (Atserias-Grohe-Marx) bound proves this gap exists. Leapfrog Triejoin matches the AGM bound, making it the theoretically optimal algorithm for multi-way joins.

## Mathematical Foundation
The AGM bound (Ngo-Porat-Re-Rudra 2012) establishes that for a conjunctive query Q over relations R1...Rk, the maximum output size is bounded by the product of relation sizes raised to fractional edge cover weights. Traditional pairwise joins can produce intermediate results exponentially larger than this bound. Leapfrog avoids this by computing all joins simultaneously via sorted trie iteration.

## Key Papers
- Ngo, Porat, Re, Rudra 2012: 'Worst-case optimal join algorithms' (AGM bound proof)
- Veldhuizen 2014: 'Leapfrog Triejoin: A Simple, Worst-Case Optimal Join Algorithm'

## Implementation Plan
Store relations as sorted tries where each column = one trie level. Core operation: leapfrog_join(iterators) advances in round-robin 'leapfrog' pattern using galloping/binary search. When the current iterator's key < max(all iterator keys), it seeks forward to max. When all iterators agree on a key, emit a match and advance.

## Expected Impact
10-100x speedup on complex analytics queries with 3+ tables. Verified applicable to TPC-H Q2 (5-way join), Q7 (4-way), Q9 (6-way). Feature-gated behind 'leapfrog_join' Cargo feature flag.

## Isomorphism Proof Requirement
Both Leapfrog and hash-join produce identical output sets. Hash-join sorts post-hoc; Leapfrog output is inherently sorted via galloping seek. Golden checksums must match between both join strategies.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Trie-based relation storage format designed and implemented
- [ ] Core leapfrog_join with galloping seek passes correctness tests
- [ ] Query planner routes 3+ table joins through Leapfrog when feature-gated
- [ ] TPC-H Q2/Q7/Q9 produce correct results via Leapfrog
- [ ] Performance benchmarks show measurable improvement over pairwise hash-join
- [ ] Property-based tests verify output equivalence with hash-join for arbitrary inputs
- [ ] Golden output checksums captured and gated in CI

## Connection to Other Features
- Depends on vectorized execution for maximum throughput (morsel-driven parallelism)
- SSI conflict detection must correctly track read-sets for Leapfrog scans
- EBR version chain GC ensures trie iterators don't hold stale version references

title: Design trie-based relation storage format for Leapfrog
description:
Design the sorted trie data structure that underpins Leapfrog Triejoin. Each relation is stored as a trie where each column in the join key forms one level. The trie must support efficient: (1) open() — position at first entry, (2) seek(key) — galloping binary search to key or next, (3) next() — advance to next entry at current level, (4) atEnd() — check exhaustion. Memory layout should be cache-friendly (B+ tree style nodes, not pointer-heavy). Consider arena allocation for trie nodes to avoid fragmentation. Must integrate with the existing page-based storage through the buffer pool. Design doc should specify: node format, fan-out, compression (prefix truncation), and iterator invalidation semantics under MVCC.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Design document with node format, memory layout, and iterator API
- [ ] Prototype trie construction from sorted input
- [ ] Benchmark: trie construction overhead vs hash-table construction
- [ ] MVCC compatibility analysis (how trie iterators interact with version chains)

title: Implement core leapfrog_join with galloping seek
description:
Implement the core Leapfrog Triejoin algorithm per Veldhuizen 2014. The algorithm maintains k sorted iterators (one per relation in the join). At each level of the trie:

1. Sort iterators by current key
2. Let max_key = max of all current keys
3. For each iterator in round-robin order: seek to max_key using galloping search
4. If seek lands exactly on max_key for all iterators: MATCH — descend to next trie level
5. If any seek overshoots: update max_key and continue

Galloping search (exponential search + binary search) achieves O(log(gap)) seek time where gap is the distance between current position and target. This is crucial for skipping large ranges of non-matching keys efficiently.

The implementation must handle:
- Variable-arity joins (2 to N relations)
- NULL handling per SQL semantics (NULLs never match in equi-joins)
- Composite join keys (multi-column)
- Early termination when any iterator exhausts

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] leapfrog_join(iterators) produces correct sorted output for 2-way joins
- [ ] Correct for 3-way, 4-way, 5-way, 6-way joins
- [ ] Galloping seek achieves O(log n) per seek operation
- [ ] NULL values correctly excluded from join matches
- [ ] Composite join keys work correctly
- [ ] Unit tests with known-answer vectors

title: Golden output checksums for Leapfrog join results
description:
Capture and gate golden output checksums for all Leapfrog join results to ensure correctness across refactors. For each TPC-H query (Q2, Q7, Q9) at SF1:

1. Run query with pairwise hash-join, capture sorted output, compute BLAKE3 checksum
2. Run same query with Leapfrog Triejoin, capture sorted output, compute BLAKE3 checksum
3. Assert checksums match (isomorphism proof)
4. Store checksums as golden artifacts in CI

This is the isomorphism proof: both algorithms produce identical sorted output. Hash-join sorts post-hoc; Leapfrog is inherently sorted via galloping seek. The checksums serve as a regression gate — any change to either join algorithm must preserve output equivalence.

comments.text:
## §14.4-14.7 R*-Tree + Session + ICU + Miscellaneous Extensions

### R*-Tree (§14.4, `fsqlite-ext-rtree`)
Efficient spatial indexing (Beckmann et al., SIGMOD 1990). SQLite uses R*-tree variant (not original Guttman 1984).

`CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE idx USING rtree(id, minX, maxX, minY, maxY)`. 1-5 dimensions (2-10 coordinate columns). 32-bit floats default; `rtree_i32` for integers.

**Queries:** Range queries (bounding box constraints). Custom geometry callbacks implementing `RtreeGeometry: Send+Sync` with `query_func(bbox) → Include|Exclude|PartiallyContained`. Tree descent prunes Exclude branches.

**Geopoly extension:** Built on R*-tree. geopoly_overlap, within, area, blob, json, svg, bbox, contains_point, group_bbox, regular, ccw, xform. Polygons: 4-byte header + pairs of f32 coordinates.

### Session (§14.5, `fsqlite-ext-session`)
Records changes as changesets/patchsets for cross-database application.

**Changeset format:** Per table: 'T' byte, column count, PK flags, table name. Per row: operation byte (INSERT=18, DELETE=9, UPDATE=23). DELETE: old values. INSERT: new values. UPDATE: old+new values (undefined for unchanged non-PK). Values: type byte (0=undefined, 1=integer, 2=real, 3=text, 4=blob, 5=null) + data (varint-length-prefixed for text/blob, 8B BE for int/real).

**Conflict resolution:** ConflictAction enum (OmitChange, Replace, Abort). ConflictType enum (Data, NotFound, Conflict, Constraint, ForeignKey).

**Patchsets:** More compact: omits old values for UPDATE (only new+PK). Cannot detect conflicts as precisely.

### ICU (§14.6, `fsqlite-ext-icu`)
Unicode-aware string operations.

**Collation:** `icu_load_collation('de_DE', 'german')` creates collation from ICU locale. Uses `ucol_strcoll`.
**Case folding:** icu_upper/icu_lower(X, LOCALE) — locale-aware (vs ASCII-only built-in).
**FTS tokenizer:** `tokenize='icu zh_CN'` for language-aware word breaking via `UBreakIterator`. Critical for CJK.

### Miscellaneous (§14.7, `fsqlite-ext-misc`)
**generate_series(START,STOP [,STEP]):** Virtual table. Columns: value, start, stop, step.
**dbstat:** B-tree page usage stats (name, path, pageno, pagetype, ncell, payload, unused, mx_payload). aggregate hidden column.
**dbpage:** Direct page read/write. `SELECT data FROM dbpage WHERE pgno=1`.
**csv:** Virtual table for CSV files. filename, header, columns options.
**decimal:** Arbitrary-precision. decimal(), decimal_add/sub/mul, decimal_sum, decimal_cmp. String representation avoids float precision loss.
**uuid:** uuid() v4, uuid_str(X) blob→string, uuid_blob(X) string→16-byte blob.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## §14.5.1-§14.5.3 Full Spec Extract + Test/Logging Requirements (Session Extension)

This comment exists because the earlier bead summary for Session covered the concepts but did not explicitly include the numbered sub-subsections §14.5.1..§14.5.3.

### Session (`fsqlite-ext-session`)

The Session extension records changes to a database and represents them
as changesets or patchsets that can be applied to other databases.

#### §14.5.1 Changeset Format

A changeset is a binary blob with the following layout:
```
For each modified table:
  'T' byte (0x54)
  Number of columns (varint)
  For each column: 0x00 (not part of PK) or 0x01 (part of PK)
  Table name (nul-terminated string)

  For each changed row:
    Operation byte: SQLITE_INSERT (18), SQLITE_DELETE (9), SQLITE_UPDATE (23)

    For DELETE:
      Old values: one value per column (serial-type encoded)

    For INSERT:
      New values: one value per column (serial-type encoded)

    For UPDATE:
      Old values: one per column (undefined for non-PK columns that didn't change)
      New values: one per column (undefined for columns that didn't change)
```

Each value is encoded as: a single type byte (0x00=undefined, 0x01=integer,
0x02=real, 0x03=text, 0x04=blob, 0x05=null) followed by the value data
(varint-length-prefixed for text and blob, 8-byte big-endian for integer
and real).

#### §14.5.2 Conflict Resolution

When applying a changeset, conflicts are resolved via a callback:
```rust
pub enum ConflictAction {
    OmitChange,     // skip this change
    Replace,        // overwrite conflicting row
    Abort,          // abort the entire apply operation
}

pub enum ConflictType {
    Data,           // row exists but values differ from expected
    NotFound,       // row to update/delete does not exist
    Conflict,       // unique constraint violation
    Constraint,     // other constraint violation
    ForeignKey,     // foreign key constraint
}
```

#### §14.5.3 Patchset Differences

A patchset is a more compact format that omits the old values for UPDATE
operations (only stores new values and PK). Patchsets cannot detect
conflicts as precisely as changesets (cannot verify that the old row matched)
but are significantly smaller for tables with many columns.

### Additional FrankenSQLite Requirements (Bead-local)

1. Unit tests MUST cover:
   - changeset encode/decode round-trip for INSERT/DELETE/UPDATE
   - correct handling of undefined old/new values in UPDATE rows
   - value encoding for each type byte, including NULL and BLOB lengths
   - conflict callback invocation for each ConflictType, with each ConflictAction
2. E2E tests MUST cover:
   - generate changeset from DB-A, apply to DB-B, then verify DB-A == DB-B for the affected tables
   - negative tests: apply changeset where DB-B has diverged to force Data/NotFound/Conflict/Constraint/ForeignKey
   - patchset vs changeset behavioral difference: changeset detects mismatch where patchset cannot
3. Logging MUST include:
   - per apply: table name, op counts by kind, and whether conflicts occurred
   - on conflict: ConflictType, chosen ConflictAction, and a compact diff of expected vs found values

comments.text:
## Task: Recovery demo — stale sidecar detection via db_gen_digest mismatch

### What
Demonstrate the safety guard against using an outdated .db-fec sidecar with a modified database. This prevents silent data corruption from mismatched repair symbols.

### Background (§3.4.6)
The .db-fec sidecar header includes `db_gen_digest`:
```
db_gen_digest = BLAKE3(change_counter || page_count || freelist_count || schema_cookie)
```
When the database is modified (INSERT, DELETE, schema change), these values change. If someone tries to use an old .db-fec file with a modified database, the digest won't match, and FrankenSQLite rejects the sidecar.

### Why This Matters
Without this guard, using a stale sidecar could:
- Reconstruct pages from the OLD version of the database
- Mix old repair symbols with new source pages
- Produce silently corrupted data that passes basic checks but contains wrong values

### Test Flow
1. Start with golden copy
2. Generate .db-fec sidecar (this captures the current db_gen_digest)
3. Modify the database: INSERT 100 new rows
4. Now the database has different change_counter and page_count
5. Corrupt a page in the modified database
6. Attempt recovery using the OLD .db-fec sidecar
7. **Expected**: FrankenSQLite detects db_gen_digest mismatch, REFUSES to use stale sidecar, reports error clearly
8. Regenerate .db-fec sidecar from the modified database
9. Attempt recovery again
10. **Expected**: Recovery succeeds with fresh sidecar

### Acceptance Criteria
- Stale sidecar correctly rejected with clear error message
- Error includes both expected and actual db_gen_digest values
- Fresh sidecar generation works after database modification
- Recovery succeeds with fresh sidecar
- No silent data corruption possible via stale sidecar path

## §23 Full Spec Text (Verbatim Extract)
Source: COMPREHENSIVE_SPEC_FOR_FRANKENSQLITE_V1.md lines 18038-18179

## 23. Summary: What Makes FrankenSQLite Alien

FrankenSQLite is not an incremental improvement on SQLite. It is a
ground-up reimagination of what an embedded database engine can be when
built on near-optimal erasure coding, formal verification, and modern
language guarantees.

**1. MVCC with Serializable Concurrent Writers (In-Process and Cross-Process).**
The single biggest limitation of SQLite -- the WAL_WRITE_LOCK that serializes
all writers -- is replaced with page-level MVCC versioning and Serializable
Snapshot Isolation (SSI). Applications choose their isolation level: Serialized
mode for exact backward compatibility, Concurrent mode for true multi-writer
parallelism with full SERIALIZABLE guarantees (not merely Snapshot Isolation).
The conservative Page-SSI rule prevents write skew by default; safe write
merging (intent replay + structured page patch merge) and deterministic rebase reduce conflict rates on hot
pages without row-level MVCC metadata. Cross-process MVCC uses a shared-memory
coordination region with lease-based crash cleanup. The layered approach means
zero risk for existing applications and serializable concurrency for
applications that opt in.

**2. RaptorQ-Pervasive Architecture with ECS Substrate.** Fountain codes are
not bolted on as an afterthought. They are woven into every layer: the WAL
uses RaptorQ repair symbols for self-healing durability that survives torn
writes without double-write journaling. The replication protocol is
fountain-coded for bandwidth-optimal, UDP-based, multicast-capable data
transfer over lossy networks. Version chains use XOR delta encoding (stored as ECS objects, erasure-coded
for durability) for near-optimal compression. Conflict resolution uses semantic write merging (intent
replay + structured page patches keyed by stable identifiers); XOR/`GF(256)` is an encoding for patch/history
objects, not a merge correctness criterion. The Erasure-Coded
Stream (ECS) substrate provides content-addressed, self-describing,
deterministic object storage with BLAKE3 ObjectIds and self-healing repair
symbols. The result: data loss becomes a mathematical near-impossibility
rather than a failure mode to mitigate.

**3. Asupersync Deep Integration.** Every operation threads a Cx capability
context for type-safe cancellation and deadline propagation. The lab reactor
enables fully deterministic concurrency testing with reproducible scheduling
and precise fault injection. E-processes provide anytime-valid statistical
invariant monitoring based on Ville's inequality. Mazurkiewicz traces
systematically enumerate all non-equivalent interleavings of concurrent
transactions for exhaustive verification. Conformal calibration provides
distribution-free confidence intervals for benchmark regression detection.
Sheaf-theoretic consistency checking formally verifies that MVCC snapshot
views are globally consistent.

**4. Safe Rust, No Compromises.** `unsafe_code = "forbid"` at workspace
level. Clippy pedantic and nursery lints at deny level. If it compiles,
it is free of undefined behavior, data races, and use-after-free. The
entire database engine -- including the B-tree, VDBE, MVCC system, and
all extensions -- is memory-safe by construction.

**5. Full Compatibility.** FrankenSQLite reads and writes standard SQLite
database files. It targets **100% behavioral parity** against golden-file
tests comparing output with C sqlite3 for the supported surface. Any
intentional divergence MUST be explicitly documented and annotated in the
harness with rationale. The SQL dialect, type affinity system, VDBE
instruction set, file format, and WAL format all match SQLite 3.52.0. It aims
to be a near-drop-in replacement for the sqlite3 CLI and library, targeting
**100% parity** while deliberately omitting deprecated
or security-sensitive features (loadable extensions, shared-cache mode, legacy
schema formats 1-3; see §15).

**6. Formal Verification Depth.** The MVCC system is specified with formal
invariants (INV-1 through INV-7), safety proofs (deadlock freedom, snapshot
isolation, serializable mode, first-committer-wins, GC safety), SSI
correctness argument (conservative rw-antidependency rule prevents cycles),
and a probabilistic conflict model validated empirically. The testing strategy
combines property-based testing, deterministic concurrency testing, systematic
interleaving exploration, anytime-valid statistical monitoring, grammar-based
fuzzing, and conformance testing against the reference implementation starting
from Phase 1 (not deferred to Phase 9). An explicit crash model, risk
register, and operating mode duality (Compatibility vs Native) ensure the
system is both innovative and verifiable. This is not aspirational -- these
tools exist in asupersync and are integrated into the test infrastructure.
The monitoring stack is layered: BOCPD detects workload regime shifts (Section
4.8), e-processes detect invariant violations within any regime (Section 4.3),
and conformal calibration provides distribution-free performance bounds
(Section 4.7). SSI abort decisions are grounded in decision-theoretic expected
loss minimization with explicit asymmetric loss matrices (Section 5.7).

**7. Information-Theoretic Guarantees (Alien-Artifact Formal Theorems).**
FrankenSQLite's durability and repair contracts are not heuristic. They rest
on provable information-theoretic foundations:

**Theorem (Durability Bound).** For an ECS object encoded as K source symbols
with R repair symbols, and a local corruption model where each symbol is
independently corrupted with probability p, the probability that the object
is unrecoverable is:

```
P(loss) <= sum_{i=R+1}^{K+R} C(K+R, i) * p^i * (1-p)^(K+R-i)
```

This bound holds for any `p`. FrankenSQLite treats `p` as a budgeted and
monitored parameter (§3.5.12): e-processes provide anytime-valid guardrails,
and the system maintains living estimates of `p` (Bayesian posterior for
explainability plus a conservative `p_upper` for decisions).

When the engine reports a "durability bound" as a guarantee, it MUST plug
`p_upper` (not a point estimate) into the theorem, so the bound is conservative
under optional stopping.

Plugging in a representative design point (R ≈ 0.2K, p = 10^-4), this tail
probability is extremely small for moderate K. Concrete orders of magnitude
(using the leading term of the binomial tail):
- K=4, R=1 (n=5): P(loss) ≈ C(5,2) p^2 ≈ 1e-7
- K=16, R=4 (n=20): P(loss) ≈ C(20,5) p^5 ≈ 1.6e-16

Small-K objects are dominated by integer rounding and additive decode slack;
the engine clamps symbol policies per §3.5.3.

**Theorem (Repair Completeness).** For any ECS object, if the local symbol
store retains at least K valid symbols (out of K+R stored), the original
object bytes are recoverable exactly. The `DecodeProof` artifact witnesses
the reconstruction: it records the specific symbol subset used and the
decoder's intermediate state, constituting a mathematical certificate of
correct repair.

**Monitoring via e-processes + living bounds:** The failure probability envelope
is not merely a design-time calculation. At runtime:
- e-process monitors track whether symbol corruption exceeds the configured
  budget under optional stopping (§3.5.12),
- and the system SHOULD export a "living durability estimate" per object class:
  `(p_posterior, p_upper, P_loss(p_upper))` for the current epoch/regime.

If evidence indicates `p` drifted above budget (media degradation, firmware
bugs, correlated failures), the e-process alarm fires *before* data loss
becomes possible, and the redundancy autopilot hardens by publishing additional
repair symbols (§3.5.12.3).

FrankenSQLite demonstrates that embedded databases need not sacrifice
concurrency for simplicity, durability for performance, or safety for speed.
By building on near-optimal erasure coding (RaptorQ), formal
verification techniques (e-processes, Mazurkiewicz traces, sheaf theory),
and the memory safety guarantees of Rust, it sets a new standard for what
an embedded database engine can achieve.

Round 16 audit: harden TxnSlot TAG_CLAIMING safety by requiring early `pid/pid_birth/lease_expiry` publication (before snapshot capture) and forbidding reclaim of live claimers (prevents resumed-claimer shared-memory scribbles); fix `check_serialized_writer_exclusion()` to retry on CAS failure so stale-token cleanup cannot return Ok while a new serialized writer installs a fresh token (prevents Concurrent writers from slipping past the indicator); make coordinator IPC payload set-ordering canonical (ObjectId arrays sorted/deduped; conflict page arrays sorted; spill_pages sorted by pgno). Round 15 audit: coordinator IPC wire framing tightened (len bounds, kind mapping, permit binding); response payloads made fully canonical with explicit variant tags; BEGIN TxnId allocation corrected to read `SharedMemoryLayout.next_txn_id` in pseudocode. Round 14 audit: define cross-process coordinator IPC transport via asupersync Unix domain sockets + SCM_RIGHTS fd passing; specify cancel-safe reserve/submit framing + wire payload schemas; define coordinator-owned per-table RowId allocator + `ROWID_RESERVE`; formal model `PageData` switched to page-aligned `PageBuf` (no Vec-alignment contradiction); `SpillLoc` integrity hash clarified as `xxh3_64`; lock-table rebuild liveness rule strengthened to forbid blocking commit sequencing. title: §17.2 Property-Based Tests: proptest Strategies for B-Tree, MVCC, Record Format
description:
E2E Test:
- test_e2e_bd_2sm1_compliance: concrete E2E identifier for structure lint compliance.

## SUMMARY
Defines property-based testing strategy using proptest for B-tree invariants, parser round-trip, record format round-trip, and MVCC linearizability. Property tests generate thousands of random operation sequences and verify that structural invariants hold across all generated inputs. The proptest strategies cover the four critical subsystems: B-tree order maintenance, SQL parser AST fidelity, record format encoding stability, and MVCC snapshot isolation correctness under concurrent workloads via FsLab deterministic scheduling.

## KEY DATA STRUCTURES / ALGORITHMS
- **B-tree proptest strategy:** Generate `vec(btree_op(), 0..10000)` where btree_op is Insert(k,v) or Delete(k). Execute against both BTree and reference BTreeMap. Verify cursor iteration matches reference exactly (order + contents).
- **Parser round-trip strategy:** Generate `arbitrary_select()` SQL strings. Parse to AST, emit back to SQL string, re-parse. Assert AST equality (`ast1 == ast2`).
- **Record format round-trip strategy:** Generate `vec(arbitrary_sqlite_value(), 0..100)`. Encode via `encode_record()`, decode via `decode_record()`. Assert value-level equality.
- **MVCC linearizability strategy:** Generate `vec(arbitrary_txn_ops(), 2..16)` transaction operation sequences with a random seed. Execute concurrently under FsLab deterministic lab scheduling with 4 workers and max 200K steps. Verify: every committed transaction's reads are consistent with its snapshot; every aborted transaction had a real conflict.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## SQL Lexer + Parser: Token Types, Grammar, Error Recovery

### Spec Content (Lines 13148-13350, sections 10.1-10.2)

**10.1 Lexer Detail (lines 13148-13231)**

The lexer converts SQL text into a stream of tokens. Each token carries a `TokenType` discriminant and a `Span` (byte offset range in source).

**TokenType enum (~150 variants)** organized into categories:

**Literals:**
- `Integer` -- `42`, `-7`, `0xFF`
- `Float` -- `3.14`, `1e10`, `.5`
- `String` -- `'hello'` (single-quoted only at lexer level)
- `Blob` -- `X'CAFE'`, `x'00ff'`
- `Variable` -- `?1`, `:name`, `@name`, `$name`

**Identifiers and keywords:**
- `Id` -- unquoted identifier
- `QuotedId` -- `"quoted identifier"`, `[bracketed identifier]`, `` `backtick` ``
  - CRITICAL: `"hello"` is ALWAYS `QuotedId` at lexer level (matches C SQLite tokenize.c:413 which emits TK_ID for all double-quoted tokens)
  - DQS (double-quoted string) legacy behavior is handled in NAME RESOLUTION, NOT the lexer
  - QuotedId tokens carry an EP_DblQuoted-equivalent flag for DQS fallback

**Keywords:** Each keyword is its own variant for fast matching (KwSelect, KwFrom, KwWhere, KwInsert, KwCreate, KwTable, etc. -- roughly 120+ keyword variants listed in spec). Notable: `KwConcurrent` is included for `BEGIN CONCURRENT`.

**Operators and punctuation:**
- Arithmetic: Plus, Minus, Star, Slash, Percent
- Bitwise: Ampersand, Pipe, Tilde, ShiftLeft, ShiftRight
- Comparison: Eq, Lt, Le, Gt, Ge, EqEq, Ne, LtGt
  - NOTE: FrankenSQLite preserves lexical distinction (Eq vs EqEq, Ne vs LtGt) for diagnostics/pretty-printing, but parser treats each pair identically
- Punctuation: Dot, Comma, Semicolon, LeftParen, RightParen
- Special: Arrow (->), DoubleArrow (->>), Concat (||)
- End: Eof, Error

**String/number/blob literal parsing:**
- Strings: single-quote delimited, `''` for embedded quotes, `memchr` for closing quote
- Numbers: decimal `[0-9]+`, hex `0x[0-9a-fA-F]+`, float patterns with `.` or `e/E`
- Blobs: `X'...'` or `x'...'`, must have even number of hex digits (odd count = Error token)

**Error tokens:** Invalid input (unterminated string, invalid hex, unrecognized char) emits `Error` token with diagnostic message and offending byte range.

**Line/column tracking:** Lexer maintains `line: u32` and `col: u32` counters. Every Token carries a `Span` with byte offsets and `(line, col)` at token start. Enables error messages like `line 3, column 15: expected ')' but found ','`.

**10.2 Parser Detail (lines 13259-13350)**

Hand-written recursive descent (NOT generated). Uses C SQLite's `parse.y` (~1,900+ production lines, ~76 KB) as authoritative grammar reference. Switch from Lemon LALR(1) to recursive descent is deliberate for better Rust ergonomics, error recovery, and debuggability.

**Structure:** One method per grammar production. Each method consumes tokens and returns an AST node.

**Key parsing methods** (31 methods listed in spec):
- `parse_statement() -> Statement` (top-level dispatcher)
- `parse_select_stmt()` with sub-parsers: `parse_with_clause`, `parse_select_core`, `parse_result_columns`, `parse_from_clause`, `parse_join_clause`, `parse_where_clause`, `parse_group_by`, `parse_having`, `parse_window_clause`, `parse_compound_op`, `parse_order_by`, `parse_limit`
- DML: `parse_insert_stmt` (with `parse_upsert_clause`, `parse_returning`), `parse_update_stmt`, `parse_delete_stmt`
- DDL: `parse_create_table_stmt` (with `parse_column_def`, `parse_table_constraint`), `parse_create_index_stmt`, `parse_create_view_stmt`, `parse_create_trigger_stmt`, `parse_drop_stmt`, `parse_alter_table_stmt`
- Transaction: `parse_begin_stmt`, `parse_commit_stmt`, `parse_rollback_stmt`
- Other: `parse_pragma_stmt`, `parse_explain_stmt`
- Expressions: `parse_expr` (Pratt precedence), `parse_prefix`, `parse_infix`

**Pratt precedence table** (11 levels):
| Level | Operators | Assoc |
|-------|-----------|-------|
| 1 (lowest) | OR | Left |
| 2 | AND | Left |
| 3 | NOT (prefix) | Right |
| 4 | =, ==, !=, <>, IS, IS NOT, IN, LIKE, GLOB, BETWEEN, MATCH, REGEXP, ISNULL, NOTNULL, NOT NULL | Left |
| 5 | <, <=, >, >= | Left |
| 6 | &, \|, <<, >> | Left |
| 7 | +, - | Left |
| 8 | *, /, % | Left |
| 9 | \|\| (concat), ->, ->> (JSON) | Left |
| 10 | COLLATE | Left |
| 11 (highest) | ~ (bitwise not), + (unary), - (unary) | Right |

CRITICAL: Levels 4 and 5 are SEPARATE, matching C SQLite's parse.y. `a = b < c` parses as `a = (b < c)`, NOT `(a = b) < c`.

ESCAPE note: Not a standalone infix operator. Parsed as optional suffix of LIKE/GLOB/MATCH production. Does NOT appear in infix dispatch table.

**Error recovery strategy** (lines 13342-13350):
1. Record the error (token, expected alternatives, source span)
2. Synchronize by skipping tokens until semicolon, EOF, or statement-starting keyword
3. Continue parsing next statement
4. Return all collected errors + whatever AST was successfully parsed
This allows reporting multiple errors in a single pass.

### Unit Tests Required

1. **test_lex_integer_literals**: Verify lexing of `42`, `-7`, `0xFF`, `0x00`, `0`, max i64 value. Check token type is `Integer` and span is correct.
2. **test_lex_float_literals**: Verify `3.14`, `1e10`, `.5`, `1.0e-3`, `0.0`. Check `Float` token type.
3. **test_lex_string_literals**: Verify `'hello'`, `'it''s'` (embedded quote), `''` (empty string). Verify memchr-based scanning handles escaped quotes.
4. **test_lex_blob_literals**: Verify `X'CAFE'`, `x'00ff'`, `X''` (empty blob). Verify odd hex digit count produces `Error` token.
5. **test_lex_variables**: Verify `?1`, `:name`, `@param`, `$var`, `?` (anonymous).
6. **test_lex_quoted_identifiers**: Verify `"table_name"`, `[column]`, `` `backtick` ``. Verify double-quoted strings produce `QuotedId` (NOT `String`).
7. **test_lex_dqs_flag**: Verify QuotedId tokens from double-quotes carry the EP_DblQuoted-equivalent flag.
8. **test_lex_keywords**: Verify `SELECT`, `FROM`, `WHERE`, `INSERT`, `CREATE`, `TABLE`, `CONCURRENT` lex as their specific keyword variants. Verify case-insensitivity (`select` == `SELECT`).
9. **test_lex_operators**: Verify all operator tokens: `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%`, `&`, `|`, `~`, `<<`, `>>`, `=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `==`, `!=`, `<>`, `||`, `->`, `->>`.
10. **test_lex_eq_vs_eqeq**: Verify `=` produces `Eq` and `==` produces `EqEq` (lexical distinction preserved).
11. **test_lex_ne_vs_ltgt**: Verify `!=` produces `Ne` and `<>` produces `LtGt`.
12. **test_lex_error_unterminated_string**: Verify `'hello` (no closing quote) produces `Error` token with diagnostic.
13. **test_lex_line_column_tracking**: Verify tokens across multiple lines have correct `(line, col)` in their spans.
14. **test_lex_whitespace_and_comments_skipped**: Verify whitespace, `-- line comment`, and `/* block comment */` are consumed internally and not emitted to parser.
15. **test_parse_simple_select**: Parse `SELECT a, b FROM t WHERE a > 1` and verify AST structure.
16. **test_parse_precedence_eq_vs_lt**: Parse `a = b < c` and verify it parses as `a = (b < c)` per the Pratt table.
17. **test_parse_precedence_and_or**: Parse `a OR b AND c` and verify it parses as `a OR (b AND c)`.
18. **test_parse_like_with_escape**: Parse `col LIKE '%x%' ESCAPE '\'` and verify ESCAPE is captured as part of the LIKE node, not as a separate infix operator.
19. **test_parse_insert_with_upsert**: Parse `INSERT INTO t VALUES (1) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` and verify UpsertClause is present.
20. **test_parse_create_table_with_constraints**: Parse a CREATE TABLE with PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, CHECK, FOREIGN KEY constraints and verify all constraint types in AST.
21. **test_parse_error_recovery_multiple_errors**: Parse `SELECT; INSERT INTO; SELECT 1` and verify parser recovers after each error, returns multiple error diagnostics, and successfully parses the final `SELECT 1`.
22. **test_parse_cte_recursive**: Parse `WITH RECURSIVE cte(n) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n+1 FROM cte WHERE n < 10) SELECT * FROM cte` and verify WithClause with recursive flag.
23. **test_parse_window_function**: Parse `SELECT row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY a ORDER BY b)` and verify WindowSpec in FunctionCall node.
24. **test_parse_begin_concurrent**: Parse `BEGIN CONCURRENT` and verify the BeginStatement has the concurrent flag.

### E2E Tests

**test_e2e_lex_parse_roundtrip**: Take a complex SQL statement (multi-table join with subquery, CTE, window function, UPSERT), lex it, parse the token stream into AST, and verify the AST can be pretty-printed back to semantically equivalent SQL.

**test_e2e_error_recovery_batch**: Parse a batch of statements where some are invalid: `SELECT 1; SELEC syntax_error; SELECT 2; INSERT INTO; SELECT 3`. Verify: 3 valid ASTs are produced, 2 error diagnostics are collected, each error has correct line/column.

**test_e2e_parser_stress_deeply_nested**: Parse a deeply nested expression like `((((a + b) * c) - d) / e)` (50+ levels) and verify the parser handles it without stack overflow and produces correct AST.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
# Phase 8: Advanced Features — CRDT Sync, Offline-First, Server Replication

## Goal
Enable advanced use cases that leverage FrankenSQLite's unique position as a Rust-native, MVCC-enabled browser database:
1. **CRDT extension**: Conflict-free replicated data types for multi-device sync
2. **Offline-first**: Service Worker integration for PWA support
3. **Server sync**: Bidirectional replication between browser (WASM) and server (native) FrankenSQLite instances
4. **Edge compute**: Run FrankenSQLite in Cloudflare Workers, Deno Deploy, etc.

## Why This Matters
FrankenSQLite is the ONLY project that can run the SAME database engine natively on servers and in the browser. This means:
- Changeset replication uses the same binary format on both ends
- MVCC visibility rules are identical — no translation layer needed
- Conflict resolution happens at the page level — same algorithm everywhere
- The session extension (fsqlite-ext-session) already generates changesets

## Phase 8 is long-term vision. It builds on all previous phases and represents the full realization of FrankenSQLite as a universal database engine.

title: Upgrade Pager Cache from ARC to S3-FIFO (Alien Graveyard Protocol)
description:
# Background
The fsqlite-pager currently uses an ARC (Adaptive Replacement Cache). An ARC requires a state mutation (moving a node to the MRU position of the T2 list) on *every single cache hit*. This introduces significant lock contention on the critical path of `get_page`, degrading performance under highly concurrent MVCC read workloads.

# Rationale (Alien Graveyard primitive)
S3-FIFO (SOSP 2023) outperforms ARC while eliminating the need to reorder elements on a cache hit. S3-FIFO merely requires flipping an 'accessed' bit, which can be done atomically without taking an exclusive lock. This mathematically elegant, low-overhead adaptive logic maps perfectly to our goals for high-performance concurrent MVCC reads.

# Objectives
1. Swap `ArcCache` with `S3Fifo` in `fsqlite-pager`.
2. Make cache hits lock-free (using atomic access bits) to remove the global cache bottleneck.
3. Preserve existing behavior (isomorphism) while drastically reducing P99 latencies under contention.

title: LeanStore / Pointer Swizzling (§15.3)
description:
Buffer manager hot-path optimization via pointer swizzling per the LeanStore design (Leis et al. 2018). Score 4.5 in the opportunity matrix. Expected 2-5x page access speedup by eliminating page-table indirection on the hot path.

## Background
Traditional buffer managers maintain a page table: a hash map from (file_id, page_id) to buffer frame pointer. Every page access requires a page table lookup, which involves: hash computation, hash table probe (potentially multiple cache misses for chaining), and a pin/unpin protocol. For hot-path operations (B-tree traversal), this overhead is significant — up to 30% of total execution time.

## Pointer Swizzling
Instead of storing page IDs in B-tree internal nodes, store direct pointers to buffer frames. When a page is loaded into the buffer pool:
1. 'Swizzle' all page ID references in the parent page to point directly to the buffer frame
2. Subsequent accesses through the parent skip the page table entirely — just follow the pointer
3. When a page is evicted, 'unswizzle' the pointer back to the original page ID

The key insight: most B-tree traversals follow hot paths where pages are already in the buffer pool. Swizzling makes these hot paths pointer-chase-fast (single memory access) instead of hash-table-probe-fast (multiple memory accesses).

## Key Paper
Leis, Haubenschild, Kemper, Neumann 2018: 'LeanStore: In-Memory Data Management Beyond Main Memory'

## Implementation Challenges
- Swizzle/unswizzle must be atomic with respect to concurrent readers
- Eviction must unswizzle before freeing the buffer frame
- Need a mechanism to distinguish swizzled pointers from page IDs (tag bit or separate flag)
- Root pages must always be swizzled (never evicted)
- Recovery must handle pages that were swizzled at crash time
- Page cooling/heating state machine controls eviction candidacy

## Integration Points
- S3-FIFO (bd-1xfri): Buffer pool eviction policy determines which pages to evict; swizzle state machine handles the swizzle/unswizzle lifecycle around eviction
- EBR (bd-2y306): Epoch-based reclamation protects swizzled pointer dereference during concurrent unswizzle operations
- Vectorized scan (bd-14vp7.2): Scans can skip page table entirely for swizzled pages, feeding batches faster

## Expected Impact
- 2-5x speedup for B-tree point lookups (eliminate page table overhead)
- Reduced cache pollution (page table entries no longer in cache)
- Benefit compounds with deeper B-trees (more levels = more page table lookups eliminated)

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Pointer swizzling protocol designed with concurrency safety analysis
- [ ] SwizzlePtr type with tag-bit encoding and atomic CAS
- [ ] Swizzle on page load, unswizzle on eviction
- [ ] Atomic swizzle/unswizzle with concurrent readers (EBR-protected)
- [ ] Page cooling/heating state machine (HOT/COOLING/COLD)
- [ ] Eviction correctly unswizzles before freeing
- [ ] Root pages pinned and always swizzled
- [ ] B-tree traversal transparently handles swizzled/unswizzled pointers
- [ ] Benchmark: B-tree point lookup speedup with swizzling (target 2-5x)
- [ ] Miri clean: no use-after-free

## Success Criteria
Epic completion requires all child beads to satisfy their structured acceptance criteria, including explicit unit/property coverage, deterministic e2e evidence, and structured logging/metrics validation.

title: Design pointer swizzle/unswizzle protocol for B-tree pages
description:
Design the pointer swizzling protocol for B-tree internal page references following LeanStore (Leis et al. 2018). This is the foundational design task for the LeanStore epic.

## Design Requirements

1. Pointer representation: Define a tagged pointer type SwizzlePtr that can hold either a PageId (unswizzled, on-disk reference) or a *const BufferFrame (swizzled, in-memory direct pointer). Use the lowest bit as a tag (swizzled=1, unswizzled=0) since buffer frames are aligned.

2. Swizzle operation: When a page is loaded into the buffer pool, scan the parent page child pointers and replace any PageId matching the loaded page with a swizzled pointer to its buffer frame. Must be atomic with respect to concurrent readers (use AtomicU64 with compare_exchange).

3. Unswizzle operation: When a page is evicted from the buffer pool, scan all parent pages that reference the evicted page and replace swizzled pointers with the original PageId. Must prevent concurrent readers from following a dangling pointer during unswizzle. Use epoch-based protection (integrate with EBR from bd-2y306).

4. Root pinning: Root pages of each B-tree must always be swizzled (never evicted). Maintain a pinned set.

5. Cooling/heating states: Pages transition through HOT (swizzled, frequently accessed), COOLING (swizzled, candidate for eviction), COLD (unswizzled, evicted or never loaded).

6. Recovery: On crash, all in-memory swizzled pointers are lost. Recovery loads pages on demand (all start as unswizzled) and progressively re-swizzles as pages are accessed.

## Alien CS Reference
Leis, Haubenschild, Kemper, Neumann 2018 LeanStore In-Memory Data Management Beyond Main Memory: Sections 3.1-3.3 detail the swizzle protocol, cooling state machine, and unswizzle-under-concurrency guarantee. Graefe 2011 Modern B-Tree Techniques: Section 4.5 discusses buffer pool bypass via pointer swizzling in the context of B-tree optimizations.

## Rust Implementation Guidance
- Define SwizzlePtr as repr(transparent) wrapper around AtomicU64 for zero-cost abstraction
- Tag bit encoding: bit 0 = swizzled flag; upper 63 bits = PageId or frame pointer (both naturally aligned)
- Use Ordering::AcqRel for CAS operations on SwizzlePtr
- Design document should be a Markdown file in docs/design/ with diagrams (Mermaid state machine diagram for cooling states)
- Prototype the SwizzlePtr type in btree/swizzle.rs with comprehensive unit tests

## Logging Requirements
- Log swizzle/unswizzle events at tracing::trace level (high frequency, trace only)
- Log state transitions (HOT->COOLING->COLD) at tracing::debug level
- Log root page pinning decisions at tracing::info level
- Log design document location and review status

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Design document with node format, memory layout, and iterator API
- [ ] Concurrency safety analysis (how readers are protected during unswizzle)
- [ ] Integration points with buffer pool and EBR documented
- [ ] Recovery protocol specified
- [ ] Prototype SwizzlePtr type with tag-bit encoding
- [ ] Mermaid state machine diagram for cooling states
acceptance_criteria: 1. Design artifact defines state machine/data model, explicit invariants, failure modes, and deterministic fallback behavior with clear ownership boundaries. 2. Unit tests validate schema/state-transition invariants derived directly from the design specification. 3. A pilot end-to-end scenario proves the design contract in integrated execution and emits replayable artifacts. 4. Logging contract for the design specifies required structured fields and automated conformance checks to catch drift early.
