title: Implement SwizzlePtr and B-tree swizzle/unswizzle operations
description:
Implement the core pointer swizzling mechanism for B-tree internal pages per the LeanStore design (Leis et al. 2018).

## Implementation

1. SwizzlePtr type (in btree/swizzle.rs): Tagged pointer using AtomicU64. Bit 0 = swizzled flag. Unswizzled: PageId in upper 63 bits. Swizzled: *const BufferFrame in upper 63 bits (aligned, so bit 0 is free). Methods: is_swizzled(), as_page_id(), as_frame_ptr(), swizzle(frame_ptr), unswizzle() -> PageId.

2. Swizzle on page load: When BufferPool::fix_page(page_id) loads a page into a frame, CAS the parent child pointer from unswizzled PageId to swizzled *const BufferFrame. If CAS fails (concurrent swizzle), retry or accept (idempotent).

3. Unswizzle on eviction: When BufferPool::evict_page(frame) evicts a page, pin the current EBR epoch (prevent concurrent readers from using the frame after free), CAS the parent child pointer from swizzled to unswizzled, defer frame deallocation until epoch advances (EBR safety).

4. B-tree traversal integration: BTree::search(key) handles both pointer types. Swizzled: follow pointer directly (fast path, no page table lookup). Unswizzled: call BufferPool::fix_page(page_id) (slow path, triggers swizzle).

5. Optimistic traversal: Use optimistic latch coupling (read version counter, traverse, validate) to avoid acquiring latches on internal nodes. Only the leaf node needs a latch for modification.

## Alien CS Reference
Leis et al. 2018 LeanStore: Section 3.2 details the SwizzlePtr implementation with atomic CAS protocol. Levandoski et al. 2013 BW-Tree: alternative approach using mapping table indirection (SwizzlePtr eliminates this indirection for better cache behavior). The optimistic latch coupling follows Leis et al. 2016 The ART of Practical Synchronization.

## Rust Implementation Guidance
- SwizzlePtr must be Send + Sync (uses AtomicU64 internally)
- No raw pointer dereference without epoch protection: wrap in unsafe block with safety comment referencing crossbeam::epoch::Guard lifetime
- Use crossbeam-epoch::Guard to protect frame pointer dereference
- Implement Debug for SwizzlePtr showing swizzle state and contained value
- cfg(test) with Miri to detect use-after-free: #[cfg(miri)] tests with reduced iteration counts
- Unit test: swizzle/unswizzle roundtrip preserves PageId using proptest for random PageIds

## Logging Requirements
- Log swizzle operations at tracing::trace level: page_id, frame_ptr, CAS result
- Log unswizzle operations at tracing::trace level: page_id, old_frame_ptr
- Log CAS failures (contention) at tracing::debug level with retry count
- Log epoch-deferred deallocations at tracing::debug level

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] SwizzlePtr type with tag-bit encoding and atomic operations
- [ ] Swizzle on page load with CAS
- [ ] Unswizzle on eviction with EBR protection
- [ ] B-tree traversal handles both swizzled/unswizzled pointers

title: Implement page cooling/heating state machine with eviction integration
description:
Implement the page cooling/heating state machine from LeanStore that integrates pointer swizzling with buffer pool eviction (S3-FIFO from bd-1xfri).

## State Machine

Pages transition through three states:
1. HOT: Swizzled, actively accessed. Cannot be evicted.
2. COOLING: Swizzled but not recently accessed. Candidate for eviction. A background thread periodically moves HOT pages with low access frequency to COOLING.
3. COLD: Unswizzled, either evicted or never loaded. On-disk only.

Transitions: COLD -> HOT (page loaded via fix_page, swizzled into parent). HOT -> COOLING (background cooling thread marks low-frequency pages). COOLING -> HOT (page accessed again while in COOLING, re-heated). COOLING -> COLD (page evicted by S3-FIFO, unswizzled from parent).

## Cooling Thread
Background thread runs every COOLING_INTERVAL (default 100ms). Scans buffer pool frames, checks access counters. Pages with access_count < COOLING_THRESHOLD since last scan: transition HOT -> COOLING. Access counter uses AtomicU32 with Relaxed ordering (approximate is fine).

## Integration with S3-FIFO
S3-FIFO manages eviction ordering (which pages to evict). Swizzle state machine manages swizzle/unswizzle lifecycle. When S3-FIFO selects a page for eviction: if HOT skip (should not happen if cooling is working); if COOLING unswizzle then evict; if COLD already evicted.

## Root Pinning
Root pages of each B-tree index are permanently pinned in HOT state. Maintained in a PinnedSet: HashSet<PageId> checked during cooling scan.

## Alien CS Reference
Leis et al. 2018 LeanStore: Section 3.3 describes the cooling/heating state machine and background cooling thread. The state machine design follows the principle of separating eviction policy (S3-FIFO) from eviction mechanism (swizzle state transitions). Stoica and Ailamaki 2013: background page management in modern buffer pools.

## Rust Implementation Guidance
- Define enum PageThermalState { Hot, Cooling, Cold } with AtomicU8 storage for lock-free state transitions
- Background cooling thread: use std::thread::spawn with crossbeam::channel for shutdown signaling
- Access counter: AtomicU32 per buffer frame, incremented on access with Relaxed ordering
- PinnedSet: use dashmap::DashSet<PageId> for concurrent access from cooling thread and fix_page
- State transition: use compare_exchange on AtomicU8 to prevent TOCTOU races
- Integration test: use loom crate for model-checking concurrent state transitions (optional, high value)

## Logging Requirements
- Log state transitions at tracing::debug level: page_id, from_state, to_state, access_count
- Log cooling thread scan summary at tracing::info level: pages_scanned, pages_cooled, pages_reheated
- Log root page pinning at tracing::info level: page_id, btree_name
- Log eviction-state mismatch (evicting HOT page) at tracing::warn level

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] State machine with HOT/COOLING/COLD transitions
- [ ] Background cooling thread with configurable interval and threshold
- [ ] Root page pinning
- [ ] Integration with S3-FIFO eviction decisions
- [ ] Access counter tracking with atomic operations
- [ ] Unit test: page lifecycle through all state transitions
- [ ] Stress test: concurrent access + cooling + eviction without crashes

title: Benchmark: swizzled vs unswizzled B-tree point lookup throughput
description:
Benchmark the performance impact of pointer swizzling on B-tree point lookups to validate the expected 2-5x speedup from LeanStore-style buffer management.

## Workloads

1. Sequential point lookups: Look up N keys sequentially (tests cache-friendly traversal). N = 100K, 1M, 10M lookups. B-tree sizes: 10K, 100K, 1M, 10M rows.

2. Random point lookups: Look up N random keys (tests cache-unfriendly traversal). Same N and B-tree sizes. Uniform random and Zipfian distributions.

3. Mixed read-write: 90% point lookups + 10% inserts (tests swizzle/unswizzle churn). 32 concurrent threads. Measure impact of unswizzle overhead on read throughput.

4. Deep B-tree: Create an artificially deep B-tree (small page size, many levels). Tests the compounding benefit of swizzling (more levels = more page table lookups eliminated). Depths: 3, 5, 7, 10 levels.

## Metrics per workload
Throughput (lookups/second), latency (p50, p95, p99), CPU cycles per lookup (perf stat), L1/L2/L3 cache miss rates (perf stat), page table lookup count (counted via instrumented buffer pool), swizzle hit rate (percent of child pointer dereferences that were swizzled).

## Alien CS Reference
Leis et al. 2018 LeanStore: Section 5 presents benchmark methodology and expected speedup ranges for pointer swizzling. Their results show 2-5x for in-memory workloads. Haubenschild et al. 2020 Rethinking Logging, Checkpoints, and Recovery for High-Performance Storage Engines: extends LeanStore benchmarks with recovery-aware measurements.

## Rust Implementation Guidance
- Use criterion crate for statistical benchmarking with warmup and iteration control
- Use perf-event crate or perf stat subprocess for hardware counter collection
- Generate Zipfian keys with rand_distr::Zipf distribution
- Deep B-tree: set page_size to 256 bytes to force deeper trees without huge data
- Instrument buffer pool with conditional compilation: #[cfg(feature = benchmark-counters)] for page table lookup counting
- Output results as JSON for CI regression detection and chart generation

## Logging Requirements
- Log benchmark configuration at tracing::info level: workload type, N, B-tree size, thread count
- Log per-workload results at tracing::info level: throughput, p50/p95/p99 latency, swizzle hit rate
- Log cache miss rates at tracing::info level when perf counters available
- Log comparison summary (swizzled vs unswizzled speedup) at tracing::info level

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All 4 workloads benchmarked
- [ ] Speedup chart: swizzled vs unswizzled per workload
- [ ] Cache miss rate comparison
- [ ] Swizzle hit rate documented
- [ ] CI integration for regression detection on SF1
- [ ] Results documented in benchmark report

title: Property tests: SwizzlePtr and cooling state machine invariants
description:
Property-based tests for LeanStore pointer swizzling correctness using proptest. The swizzle/unswizzle protocol has critical safety invariants that must hold under all concurrent access patterns.

## Invariants to Test

1. Roundtrip correctness: For any PageId, swizzle(page_id, frame_ptr) followed by unswizzle() must return the original PageId. Test with proptest over random PageIds and frame pointers.

2. No dangling pointers: After unswizzle, no reader can follow a swizzled pointer to a freed buffer frame. Verify by tracking frame dereferences under EBR epoch protection and asserting no access after unswizzle + epoch advance.

3. Tag-bit integrity: SwizzlePtr tag bit correctly distinguishes swizzled from unswizzled state. For any AtomicU64 value, is_swizzled() and as_page_id()/as_frame_ptr() are consistent.

4. Concurrent swizzle safety: Multiple threads swizzling/unswizzling the same parent page pointer must not lose updates (CAS-based protocol ensures no lost writes).

5. Cooling state machine transitions: State transitions follow the allowed paths (COLD->HOT, HOT->COOLING, COOLING->HOT, COOLING->COLD). No illegal transitions (e.g., COLD->COOLING, HOT->COLD directly).

6. Root pinning invariant: Root pages must never transition out of HOT state. Verify under sustained cooling thread pressure.

7. Access counter monotonicity: Access counter per frame is monotonically increasing within a cooling interval (reset to zero on cooling scan is acceptable).

## Alien CS Reference
Leis et al. 2018 LeanStore: Section 3.3 specifies the cooling state machine invariants. The concurrent swizzle safety properties follow from the CAS-based protocol described in Section 3.2.

## Rust Implementation Guidance
- Use proptest for roundtrip and tag-bit invariant tests
- Use loom crate for model-checking concurrent swizzle/unswizzle (exhaustive state exploration)
- Use Miri for focused use-after-free detection on concurrent access scenarios
- Store proptest regression seeds in proptest-regressions/
- For state machine testing: implement a state machine model and use proptest to generate random operation sequences

## Logging Requirements
- Log property test case summaries at tracing::debug level
- Log invariant violations with full context at tracing::error level
- Log loom model-checking progress at tracing::info level

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All 7 invariants tested with proptest
- [ ] 10000+ random test cases per invariant
- [ ] Loom model-checking for concurrent swizzle/unswizzle (bounded thread count)
- [ ] Miri clean for use-after-free scenarios
- [ ] Regression seeds stored in version control
- [ ] Integrated into CI test suite

comments.text:
## §6.3 REPLACE Subroutine

Selects victim for eviction. Chooses between T1 and T2 based on adaptive parameter p and tie-breaking when target_key found in B2.

**Full Algorithm:**
- Track rotations_t1 and rotations_t2 separately
- Safety valve: if rotations_t1 >= |T1| AND rotations_t2 >= |T2|, all pages pinned — allow temporary capacity_overflow rather than deadlock
- CRITICAL: pinned/failing preferred list MUST NOT prevent eviction from other list
- prefer_t1 = |T1| > 0 AND (|T1| > p OR (|T1| == p AND target_key IN B2))
- prefer_t1 is a hint: if preferred list exhausted (all pinned), MUST fall back to other list for liveness
- TRY_T1: evict LRU of T1, skip pinned via rotate_front_to_back, add evicted key to B1
- TRY_T2: evict LRU of T2, skip pinned, add evicted key to B2

**Async integration (normative):** parking_lot::Mutex guard MUST NOT be held across I/O or .await. REPLACE itself does no I/O (pure), but REQUEST must drop mutex before fetch.

## §6.4 REQUEST Subroutine

**Case I — Cache hit in T1:** Remove from T1, push_back to T2 (promote to frequency list), increment ref_count.
**Case I — Cache hit in T2:** Move to back of T2 (refresh MRU), increment ref_count.

**Case II — Ghost hit in B1:** Evidence T1 too small. p += max(1, |B2|/|B1|), clamped to capacity. Call REPLACE. Remove from B1. Fetch from storage. Insert into T2 (second lifetime access).

**Case III — Ghost hit in B2:** Evidence T2 too small. p -= max(1, |B1|/|B2|), floor at 0. Call REPLACE. Remove from B2. Fetch from storage. Insert into T2.

**Case IV — Complete miss:** L1=|T1|+|B1|, L2=|T2|+|B2|. If L1==capacity: pop_front B1 if |T1|<capacity else evict LRU of T1 directly (do NOT add to B1 — would violate L1<=capacity invariant; evicted key is simply discarded). Else if L1<capacity AND L1+L2>=capacity: pop B2 if L1+L2>=2*capacity, then REPLACE. Insert into T1 (new pages always enter T1).

**Async Singleflight Protocol (normative):**
CacheEntry = Ready(Arc<CachedPage>) | Loading { done: watch::Receiver }
LoadStatus = Pending | Ok | Err(Arc<Error>)

REQUEST_ASYNC pattern: lock mutex, check entry. Ready -> promote+pin, return. Loading -> clone receiver, unlock, await changed(), re-loop. Missing -> install Loading placeholder, unlock, fetch_from_storage_async(cx) outside mutex, lock, install result, wake waiters via tx.send.

**Cancellation safety:** Loader cancelled after placeholder MUST resolve done latch (send Err(Cancelled)) and remove placeholder so waiters don't block forever.

**Complexity:** O(1) amortized per operation. Ghost list overhead: ~160KB for 2000-entry cache (16B/CacheKey + ~24B container, 2x2000 entries).

### §6.4.1 Optional p-Update as Online Learning (Research Note)
OCO-style controller: p_{t+1} = clamp(p_t + eta_t * s_t, 0, capacity), s_t = +1 for B1 hit, -1 for B2 hit. Diminishing eta yields no-regret in abstract model. BUT ARC/CAR properties rely on canonical update — any alternative MUST be treated as harness experiment until proven.

title: Spec evolution viz: page fails to load (createDataPacket undefined)
description:
## Summary
Fix `visualization_of_the_evolution_of_the_frankensqlite_specs_document_from_inception.html` failing to load due to a JS `ReferenceError`: `createDataPacket` is referenced but not defined.

This is a hard correctness bug: optional "lab effects" must never prevent the viz from rendering. No feature loss.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Open `visualization_of_the_evolution_of_the_frankensqlite_specs_document_from_inception.html` in a browser.
2. Observe the page fails to fully initialize due to an uncaught exception.

## Expected
- Page renders the visualization.
- Optional effects run when enabled, and never crash the page.

## Actual
- Uncaught exception: `ReferenceError: createDataPacket is not defined`.
- Observed call site: `startLabEffects()` around line ~892.

## Root Cause
`startLabEffects()` references `createDataPacket()` but the function is not defined anywhere in the page.

## Fix Requirements (No Feature Loss)
1. Implement `createDataPacket()` as a small, safe helper that creates a transient packet element and animates it.
2. Wrap effect dispatch in a `try/catch` boundary. If an effect fails, disable that effect for the remainder of the session and log once (no spam).
3. Respect `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` (disable lab effects by default).
4. Add deterministic self-test hook: `?selftest=1` (or `#selftest`) that:
   - calls `createDataPacket()` once,
   - verifies it did not throw,
   - writes `SPEC_VIZ_SELFTEST_PASS` or `SPEC_VIZ_SELFTEST_FAIL` into the DOM,
   - emits one-line JSON console logs.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Viz page loads with zero uncaught exceptions in a clean browser profile.
- Lab effects still function (packet animation occurs) when motion is allowed.
- With reduced motion enabled, lab effects are disabled and the page still renders.
- Self-test mode renders `SPEC_VIZ_SELFTEST_PASS` in the DOM on success.

## Test Plan
### E2E smoke script (no Node toolchain)
1. `python3 -m http.server` in repo root.
2. `chromium --headless --dump-dom "http://127.0.0.1:8000/visualization_of_the_evolution_of_the_frankensqlite_specs_document_from_inception.html?selftest=1"`.
3. `grep -q SPEC_VIZ_SELFTEST_PASS` on dumped DOM.
4. On failure, capture dumped DOM + console logs as artifacts.

## Logging Requirements
- INFO (once): `{ "event": "spec_viz_effect_disabled", "effect": "createDataPacket", "reason": "exception" }`
- DEBUG: `{ "event": "spec_viz_create_data_packet", "duration_ms": N }`
- INFO (selftest): `{ "event": "spec_viz_selftest", "result": "pass"|"fail", "error": "..." }`
close_reason: Implemented createDataPacket() + effect try/catch disable-once logging; respects prefers-reduced-motion; added ?selftest=1/#selftest DOM marker + JSON console log. Also switched DB fetch to XHR arraybuffer for iOS Safari reliability + header validation.

title: HTM Guard Implementation
description:
**Goal:** Implement the HTM fast-path in `FlatCombiner`.
**Implementation:**
- Use Rust's `core::arch::x86_64::{_xbegin, _xend, _xabort}` (or ARM equivalents where available).
- Wrap the accumulator modification logic in the HTM transaction.
- If `_xbegin()` returns `_XBEGIN_STARTED`, perform the combination and `_xend()`. 
- If it fails, fall back to the existing `try_lock()` and spin mechanism.
**Testing & Logging:**
- Unit Tests: Verify correct fallback if `_xbegin` fails immediately (mocked).
- E2E Tests: Script `tests/e2e_htm_benchmark.sh` proving the 30-50ns latency reduction in uncontended workloads.
- Logging: `tracing::info` logging CPU feature detection (TSX/LSE) on initialization.
**Success Criteria:** Uncontended operations bypass the OS mutex/spin-loop entirely, saving 30-50ns per operation.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
# 5D.3: Wire SAVEPOINT/RELEASE/ROLLBACK TO through pager savepoint API

## What

Savepoints provide nested rollback points within a transaction. The TransactionHandle trait
already has `rollback_to_savepoint()`. This task wires the SQL SAVEPOINT/RELEASE/ROLLBACK TO
statements through the pager's savepoint API.

## SQL semantics

```sql
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1);
SAVEPOINT sp1;
INSERT INTO t VALUES (2);
ROLLBACK TO sp1;        -- undoes row 2, keeps row 1
INSERT INTO t VALUES (3);
RELEASE sp1;            -- collapses sp1 into parent
COMMIT;                 -- t contains (1, 3)
```

## Where to change

**Primary:** `crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs` — savepoint handlers

## Implementation

The pager tracks savepoints as a stack of "journal marks" — positions in the WAL or journal
that can be rolled back to. The pager API:

- `txn.savepoint(name)` → push a savepoint (record current WAL position)
- `txn.release_savepoint(name)` → pop savepoint (no rollback, just remove marker)
- `txn.rollback_to_savepoint(name)` → undo pages written since savepoint

For MemDatabase shadow during transition, we maintain parallel savepoint snapshots.

## Tests

- `test_savepoint_rollback`: CREATE, SP, INSERT, ROLLBACK TO, verify undone
- `test_savepoint_release`: SP, INSERT, RELEASE, COMMIT → data committed
- `test_nested_savepoints`: SP1, INSERT, SP2, INSERT, ROLLBACK TO SP2, verify only SP2 undone
- `test_savepoint_outside_txn`: SAVEPOINT without BEGIN creates implicit transaction (SQLite behavior)

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## Support Non-Column Expressions in GROUP BY Codegen

### Problem
`GROUP BY` with non-column expressions (e.g. `LENGTH(name)`, `val % 2`, `a + b`)
failed with `CodegenError::Unsupported("non-column GROUP BY expression")`.
SQLite supports arbitrary expressions in GROUP BY.

### Root Cause
`parse_group_by_output()` called `resolve_column_index()` on each GROUP BY expression
and failed if it wasn't a simple column reference. The sorter scan also only used
`Opcode::Column` to read values.

### Fix
Added `GroupByKey` enum with `Column(usize)` and `Expression(Expr)` variants.

**parse_group_by_output**: Try column resolution first, fall back to `Expression(expr.clone())`.

**codegen_select_group_by_aggregate Pass 1**: For `GroupByKey::Expression`, use
`emit_expr()` with a `ScanCtx` instead of `Opcode::Column`. This evaluates the
expression for each row during the sorter scan phase.

**Result column matching**: Match result columns to GROUP BY keys by structural
equality (`Expr::PartialEq`) for expression-based keys.

**emit_having_filter/emit_having_expr**: Updated parameter type from `&[usize]`
to `&[GroupByKey]` and adjusted column reference resolution.

### Files Changed
- `crates/fsqlite-vdbe/src/codegen.rs` — Added `GroupByKey` enum, updated
  `parse_group_by_output`, `codegen_select_group_by_aggregate`,
  `emit_having_filter`, `emit_having_expr`

### Tests (5 existing tests now pass)
- `test_group_by_arithmetic_expression` (a + b)
- `test_group_by_expression_with_duplicate_keys` (val % 2)
- `test_group_by_function_expression` (LENGTH(name))
- `test_group_by_expression_with_having` (val % 3 with HAVING)
- `test_group_by_expression_with_aggregate_sum` (a % 2 with SUM)

### Quality Gates
- 1204 fsqlite-core tests pass (0 regressions)
- Clippy clean, fmt clean

title: §14.3 FTS3/FTS4 Extension: Legacy Full-Text Search Compatibility
description:
E2E Test:
- test_e2e_bd_2xl9_compliance: concrete E2E identifier for structure lint compliance.

## SUMMARY
Implement the FTS3/FTS4 extension (crate: fsqlite-ext-fts3) providing legacy full-text search compatibility. FTS3 and FTS4 share an implementation crate because FTS4 is a backward-compatible extension of FTS3. Key differences from FTS5: B-tree-based segment structure (not LSM-like), explicit AND in query syntax (not implicit), column-level MATCH (not table-level), and FTS4-specific features including matchinfo(), offsets(), content= tables, and compress/uncompress support. matchinfo(X, FORMAT) returns a blob of 32-bit unsigned integers with match statistics controlled by format string (p/c/n/a/l/s/x). offsets(X) returns byte offset text listing all match positions.

## KEY DATA STRUCTURES / ALGORITHMS
- FTS3/4 inverted index uses B-tree-based segments (unlike FTS5's LSM-like segments).
- Query syntax: AND is explicit (not implicit like FTS5), OR, NOT (unary NOT IS allowed in FTS3/4 unlike FTS5).
- MATCH operates at column level: WHERE column MATCH 'query' (vs FTS5's table-level match).
- matchinfo(X, FORMAT): returns blob of packed 32-bit unsigned integers. Format characters: p=number of matchable phrases, c=number of user-defined columns, n=total rows, a=average tokens per column per row, l=current row length per column, s=longest common subsequence, x=3 values per phrase/column (hits in this row, hits in all rows, rows with hits).
- offsets(X): returns text "col_num term_num byte_offset byte_length ..." for all matches.
- FTS4 content= tables: external content references, same concept as FTS5 but different implementation.
- FTS4 compress/uncompress: custom compression functions for stored content (e.g., zlib). Specified at table creation: compress=func_name, uncompress=func_name.

## NORMATIVE INVARIANTS
1. FTS3/4 uses column-level MATCH (WHERE col MATCH 'q'), not table-level MATCH like FTS5.
2. AND is explicit in FTS3/4 query syntax.
3. Unary NOT IS allowed in FTS3/4 (unlike FTS5 where NOT is binary-only).
4. matchinfo format string characters: p, c, n, a, l, s, x each produce specific statistics.
5. matchinfo returns a blob of 32-bit unsigned integers (little-endian on most platforms).
6. offsets returns space-separated integers: col_num, term_num, byte_offset, byte_length repeated.
7. compress/uncompress functions (FTS4 only) must be registered before table creation.
8. FTS4 is backward-compatible with FTS3 (any FTS3 table works as FTS4).

## UNIT TEST REQUIREMENTS
1. test_fts3_create: CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE USING fts3 succeeds
2. test_fts4_create: CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE USING fts4 succeeds
3. test_fts3_insert_match: INSERT and column MATCH query finds document
4. test_fts3_explicit_and: 'word1 AND word2' matches documents with both words
5. test_fts3_or: 'word1 OR word2' matches documents with either
6. test_fts3_unary_not: 'NOT word1' is valid (unlike FTS5)
7. test_fts3_binary_not: 'word1 NOT word2' matches docs with word1 but not word2
8. test_fts3_phrase: '"exact phrase"' matches consecutive tokens
9. test_fts3_column_match: WHERE col1 MATCH 'query' restricts to col1
10. test_fts4_matchinfo_p: matchinfo(X, 'p') returns phrase count
11. test_fts4_matchinfo_c: matchinfo(X, 'c') returns column count
12. test_fts4_matchinfo_n: matchinfo(X, 'n') returns row count
13. test_fts4_matchinfo_x: matchinfo(X, 'x') returns per-phrase/column hit stats
14. test_fts4_matchinfo_full: matchinfo(X, 'pcnalsx') returns all statistics
15. test_fts4_offsets: offsets(X) returns correct byte positions
16. test_fts4_content_table: content= references external table
17. test_fts4_compress: compress/uncompress custom functions work
18. test_fts3_fts4_compat: FTS3 table readable as FTS4
19. test_fts3_near: NEAR query works
20. test_fts4_matchinfo_blob_format: blob contains packed 32-bit unsigned integers

- test_e2e_bd_2xl9_compliance: concrete E2E identifier for structure lint compliance.
Create FTS3 and FTS4 tables with multiple columns. Insert a corpus of documents. Test all query types (explicit AND, OR, NOT, phrase, NEAR, column match). Verify matchinfo returns correct statistics for all format characters. Verify offsets returns correct byte positions. Test FTS4 content= external tables and compress/uncompress. Verify backward compatibility (FTS3 tables readable by FTS4 code). Compare all results against C sqlite3.

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
1. FTS3 and FTS4 virtual tables can be created and queried.
2. Column-level MATCH works correctly.
3. Query syntax differences from FTS5 are correctly implemented (explicit AND, unary NOT allowed).
4. matchinfo returns correct blob with all format characters (p/c/n/a/l/s/x).
5. offsets returns correct match positions.
6. FTS4 content= and compress/uncompress work.
7. FTS3/FTS4 backward compatibility is maintained.
8. Extension is independently feature-gated.
9. All results match C sqlite3 FTS3/4.

## §14.3 FTS3/FTS4 Extension

### Spec Content (Lines 15488-15516)

FTS3 and FTS4 are predecessors to FTS5, sharing an implementation crate (`crates/fsqlite-ext-fts3`) because FTS4 is a backward-compatible extension of FTS3.

**Key differences from FTS5:**
- FTS3/4 uses a different segment structure (B-tree based, not LSM-like)
- Query syntax differs: AND is explicit, not implicit
- FTS4 adds matchinfo(), offsets(), content= tables, compress=/uncompress=

**matchinfo(X, FORMAT)** returns a blob of 32-bit unsigned integers. FORMAT string:
- 'p': Number of matchable phrases
- 'c': Number of user-defined columns
- 'n': Number of rows in FTS table

- 'l': Length of current row in tokens per column

**compress/uncompress (FTS4 only):** Custom compression for stored content:

title: §5.6.2.2 TxnSlot Crash Recovery: cleanup_orphaned_slots Algorithm
description:
Implement the cleanup_orphaned_slots() algorithm that reclaims TxnSlots left behind by crashed processes, handling three slot states (TAG_CLEANING, TAG_CLAIMING, real TxnId) with distinct reclamation logic (spec lines 7091-7238).

SCOPE: Correctness-critical shared-memory maintenance routine. Scans all TxnSlots and reclaims orphaned entries using CAS-based state transitions, process liveness checks, and tiered timeouts.

DATA STRUCTURES:
- TxnSlot fields: txn_id (atomic, sentinel-tagged), pid, pid_birth, lease_expiry, claiming_timestamp, cleanup_txn_id, and state/mode/commit_seq/begin_seq/snapshot/witness fields
- TAG_CLEANING sentinel: preserves original TxnId payload for retryable lock release
- TAG_CLAIMING sentinel: Phase 1 of acquire, claimer may be dead

ALGORITHMS:
- State machine with three branches per slot iteration (single Acquire load of txn_id per iteration):
  (1) TAG_CLEANING: seed claiming_timestamp if zero; if timeout exceeded, extract orphan_txn_id, release page locks, clear all fields with txn_id=0 last (Release ordering)
  (2) TAG_CLAIMING: seed timestamp if zero; check process_alive(pid, birth); if alive SKIP UNCONDITIONALLY; select timeout (5s if pid known, 30s if pid zero); CAS to CLEANING, clear fields
  (3) Real TxnId: check lease_expiry < now + process dead; write cleanup_txn_id before sentinel; CAS to CLEANING; release page locks; clear fields
- Field-clearing discipline: all paths clear same fields in same order, txn_id=0 LAST with Release ordering

INVARIANTS:
- CRITICAL: An alive claimer MUST NEVER be reclaimed (process_alive check is unconditional skip)
- Single-read-per-iteration rule: snapshot txn_id ONCE per slot to avoid sentinel mis-handling
- claiming_timestamp MUST be cleared after Phase 3 (Publish) to prevent stale-timestamp race (spec review fix)
- CAS ensures only one concurrent cleaner transitions a slot to CLEANING
- Lock release via release_page_locks_for() is idempotent

TEST REQUIREMENTS (10 unit + 1 additional + 1 E2E):
- test_cleanup_skips_free_slots, test_cleanup_reclaims_expired_dead_process, test_cleanup_skips_alive_process_even_expired_lease, test_cleanup_claiming_no_pid_uses_30s_timeout, test_cleanup_claiming_with_pid_uses_5s_timeout, test_cleanup_claiming_alive_process_never_reclaimed, test_cleanup_cleaning_stuck_slot_reclaimed, test_cleanup_concurrent_cas_contention, test_cleanup_field_clearing_order, test_cleanup_cleaning_preserves_payload_for_lock_release
- test_claiming_timestamp_cleared_after_publish (spec review addition)
- E2E: test_e2e_orphaned_txnslot_cleanup_after_crash

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA:
1. Alive processes are NEVER reclaimed regardless of elapsed time or lease expiry
2. Dead processes reclaimed after appropriate timeout (5s with pid, 30s without)
3. Concurrent cleaners resolved via CAS with no double-free or double lock release
4. Field clearing order is strict: txn_id=0 is always the last store
5. claiming_timestamp cleared after successful publish (Phase 3) to prevent stale-timestamp race

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
# §5.6.2.2 TxnSlot Crash Recovery: cleanup_orphaned_slots Algorithm

## Spec Reference
COMPREHENSIVE_SPEC_FOR_FRANKENSQLITE_V1.md lines 7091–7238

## Overview
Implement the `cleanup_orphaned_slots()` algorithm that reclaims TxnSlots left behind by crashed processes. This is a correctness-critical shared-memory maintenance routine that must handle three slot states (TAG_CLEANING, TAG_CLAIMING, real TxnId) with distinct reclamation logic.

## Key Invariants

### CRITICAL SAFETY RULE
**An alive claimer MUST NEVER be reclaimed.** If a process has published `pid`/`pid_birth` (non-zero) and `process_alive(pid, birth)` returns true, the cleaner MUST skip that slot unconditionally. Violating this allows the resumed claimer to scribble over a slot that has been freed and re-claimed by another process — shared-memory corruption.

### Single-Read-per-Iteration Rule
`tid = slot.txn_id.load(Acquire)` — snapshot txn_id ONCE per slot iteration. Branching on multiple unsynchronized reads can mis-handle sentinels and free a slot while another cleaner is still releasing locks.

## Timeout Constants
- `CLAIMING_TIMEOUT_SECS = 5` — used when pid/pid_birth are published (non-zero) but process is dead
- `CLAIMING_TIMEOUT_NO_PID_SECS = 30` — used when pid/pid_birth are still zero (conservative; claimer may have crashed before publishing identity)

## State Machine Handling

### 1. TAG_CLEANING slots (another cleaner's sentinel)
- If `claiming_timestamp == 0`: seed it via CAS(0, now), continue (let original cleaner finish)
- If elapsed > CLAIMING_TIMEOUT_SECS: the cleaner crashed mid-reset
  - Extract `orphan_txn_id = decode_payload(tid)` — TAG_CLEANING payload preserves original TxnId for retryable lock release
  - If orphan_txn_id != 0: call `release_page_locks_for(orphan_txn_id)`
  - Clear ALL fields in strict order, `txn_id = 0` LAST with Release ordering

### 2. TAG_CLAIMING slots (Phase 1 of acquire, claimer may be dead)
- If `claiming_timestamp == 0`: seed via CAS(0, now), continue
- Load pid/pid_birth with Acquire ordering
- If pid != 0 && birth != 0 && process_alive(pid, birth): **skip unconditionally** (CRITICAL rule)
- Otherwise, select timeout:
  - pid == 0 || birth == 0 → CLAIMING_TIMEOUT_NO_PID_SECS (30s)
  - else → CLAIMING_TIMEOUT_SECS (5s)
- If elapsed > timeout:
  - CAS txn_id from CLAIMING(tok) → CLEANING(tok) — sentinel transition
  - Stamp `claiming_timestamp = now` so other cleaners don't immediately treat as stuck
  - Clear stale snapshot/epoch fields (begin_seq, witness_epoch) per §5.6.5, §5.6.4.8
  - Clear ALL fields, `txn_id = 0` LAST with Release ordering

### 3. Real TxnId (active transaction)
- Check `lease_expiry < now`
- If expired: check `process_alive(slot.pid, slot.pid_birth)` (PID reuse defense via pid_birth)
- If process dead:
  - Write `cleanup_txn_id = old_txn_id` BEFORE sentinel overwrite (crash-safety)
  - CAS txn_id → CLEANING(old_txn_id). If CAS fails, another cleaner won — skip
  - Stamp `claiming_timestamp = now`
  - Call `release_page_locks_for(old_txn_id)`
  - Clear ALL fields, `txn_id = 0` LAST with Release ordering

## Field-Clearing Discipline
Every reclamation path clears the same set of fields in the same order:
```
state = Free, mode = Serialized, commit_seq = 0, begin_seq = 0,
snapshot_high = 0, witness_epoch = 0, has_in_rw = false, has_out_rw = false,
marked_for_abort = false, write_set_pages = 0, pid = 0, pid_birth = 0,
lease_expiry = 0, cleanup_txn_id = 0, claiming_timestamp = 0,
txn_id = 0  // LAST — Release ordering
```
`txn_id = 0` is always the final store because it is the sentinel that marks the slot as free. Any reader that observes txn_id == 0 must see all other fields already cleared (Release/Acquire pairing).

## Crash Scenarios to Handle
1. **Pre-Phase-2 crash**: Claimer CAS'd CLAIMING but crashed before writing pid/pid_birth → pid/birth are zero or stale from prior occupant → use 30s timeout
2. **Pre-Phase-3 crash**: Claimer wrote pid/pid_birth but crashed before writing lease_expiry → process_alive check resolves it
3. **Stale pid_birth**: PID recycled to new process but pid_birth differs → process_alive returns false → safe to reclaim
4. **Cleaner crash mid-CLEANING**: TAG_CLEANING persists beyond timeout → re-enter cleanup, re-release locks (idempotent)
5. **Concurrent cleaners**: Two cleaners see same orphaned slot → CAS ensures only one transitions to CLEANING

## Unit Test Specifications

### Test 1: `test_cleanup_skips_free_slots`
Create a slot array with txn_id == 0 (free). Run cleanup_orphaned_slots(). Verify no state changes, no panics.

### Test 2: `test_cleanup_reclaims_expired_dead_process`
Create a slot with real TxnId, expired lease, pid pointing to a dead process. Run cleanup. Verify: slot freed (txn_id == 0), all fields zeroed, page locks released.

### Test 3: `test_cleanup_skips_alive_process_even_expired_lease`
Create a slot with real TxnId, expired lease, but pid/pid_birth matching the current test process (alive). Run cleanup. Verify slot is NOT reclaimed (txn_id unchanged).

### Test 4: `test_cleanup_claiming_no_pid_uses_30s_timeout`
Create a slot with TAG_CLAIMING, claiming_timestamp = now - 10s, pid = 0, pid_birth = 0. Run cleanup. Verify slot is NOT reclaimed (10s < 30s threshold). Then set claiming_timestamp = now - 31s. Run cleanup. Verify slot IS reclaimed.

### Test 5: `test_cleanup_claiming_with_pid_uses_5s_timeout`
Create a slot with TAG_CLAIMING, pid/pid_birth set to a dead process, claiming_timestamp = now - 3s. Run cleanup. Verify NOT reclaimed (3s < 5s). Set claiming_timestamp = now - 6s. Verify IS reclaimed.

### Test 6: `test_cleanup_claiming_alive_process_never_reclaimed`
Create a slot with TAG_CLAIMING, pid/pid_birth set to current process (alive), claiming_timestamp = now - 60s. Run cleanup. Verify slot is NEVER reclaimed regardless of elapsed time. This is the CRITICAL safety invariant.

### Test 7: `test_cleanup_cleaning_stuck_slot_reclaimed`
Create a slot with TAG_CLEANING(original_txn_id), claiming_timestamp = now - 6s. Run cleanup. Verify: release_page_locks_for(original_txn_id) called, slot freed.

### Test 8: `test_cleanup_concurrent_cas_contention`
Spawn two cleaner threads targeting the same orphaned slot. Use a barrier to synchronize. Verify exactly one cleaner succeeds the CAS (transitions to CLEANING), the other skips. No double-free, no double lock release.

### Test 9: `test_cleanup_field_clearing_order`
Use a mock atomic slot where stores are recorded in order. Run cleanup on an orphaned slot. Verify `txn_id = 0` is the LAST store, and all other fields are cleared before it.

### Test 10: `test_cleanup_cleaning_preserves_payload_for_lock_release`
Create a slot that transitions from real TxnId X to CLEANING(X). Verify decode_payload(CLEANING(X)) == X, and release_page_locks_for is called with the correct original TxnId.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## Critical Spec Fix: claiming_timestamp MUST be cleared after Phase 3 (Publish)

This is a correctness-critical race identified during spec review (see `spec_review_findings.md`).

### Problem
`cleanup_orphaned_slots()` uses `claiming_timestamp` to decide whether a `TXN_ID_CLEANING` sentinel is "stuck" (cleaner crashed) and can be taken over.

If the acquire protocol sets `claiming_timestamp` during Phase 1 (CLAIMING) but does **not** clear it after Phase 3 (PUBLISH), then a long-lived transaction can leave a stale, old timestamp in the slot.

When a cleaner later CAS's `txn_id` to `TXN_ID_CLEANING`, there is a window where another cleaner can observe:
- `txn_id == TXN_ID_CLEANING`
- `claiming_timestamp == <very old value from the prior txn>`

and incorrectly conclude the current cleaner is stuck, forcibly taking over cleanup while the first cleaner is still operating. This is shared-memory corruption risk.

### Normative Fix (Required)
On the successful transition from `TXN_ID_CLAIMING` to the real `TxnId` (Phase 3: Publish), the owner MUST clear `claiming_timestamp`:
- after the publish CAS succeeds, store `claiming_timestamp = 0` with `Release` ordering.

This ensures any later transition to CLEANING cannot inherit a stale timestamp.

### Additional Unit Test (Add)
- `test_claiming_timestamp_cleared_after_publish`:
  - simulate acquire Phase 1/3: set CLAIMING + claiming_timestamp, then publish real TxnId
  - verify claiming_timestamp is 0 after publish
  - transition to CLEANING and ensure other cleaners observing CLEANING + claiming_timestamp==0 do NOT steal cleanup (they seed timestamp via CAS and continue)

title: EBR for Version Chain GC (§14.10)
description:
Implement Epoch-Based Reclamation (EBR) for MVCC version chain garbage collection. Score 8.0 in the opportunity matrix. Currently version chains grow unbounded — every update creates a new version that is never reclaimed, leading to memory exhaustion under write-heavy workloads.

## Background
In page-level MVCC, each page can have multiple versions forming a chain: current -> v_n -> v_(n-1) -> ... -> v_1. Old versions are only needed by active transactions that started before the version was superseded. Once all such transactions complete, the old version can be safely freed.

## Mathematical Foundation
EBR divides time into epochs. Each thread 'pins' an epoch when entering a critical section. A version created in epoch E can be freed once all threads have advanced past epoch E. The key invariant: no thread can observe a version after it has been freed.

Formally: version V created at epoch E_create is safe to free when global_min_epoch > E_create, where global_min_epoch = min(pinned_epoch[t] for all active threads t).

## Implementation Plan
1. Use crossbeam-epoch as the foundation (battle-tested Rust EBR implementation)
2. Each MVCC transaction pins an epoch on begin, unpins on commit/abort
3. When a version is superseded (new version written), the old version is 'retired' — placed in a thread-local retirement list tagged with current epoch
4. Periodically, attempt to advance the global epoch and free retired versions from epochs that are now safe
5. Chain-length controls: if a version chain exceeds MAX_CHAIN_LENGTH (configurable, default 64), force GC by blocking new versions until old ones are freed

## Why This Matters
Without EBR, FrankenSQLite's MVCC will consume unbounded memory under write-heavy workloads, making it impractical for production use. EBR is the standard solution used by all modern MVCC databases (PostgreSQL uses a different but related approach with xmin/xmax horizons).

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] crossbeam-epoch integrated for version chain lifecycle
- [ ] Versions correctly freed after all observing transactions complete
- [ ] Chain-length bounds prevent unbounded memory growth
- [ ] No use-after-free (Miri clean, AddressSanitizer clean)
- [ ] Benchmark: memory usage bounded under sustained write workload
- [ ] Tail latency impact of epoch advance measured and tuned

## Success Criteria
Epic completion requires all child beads to satisfy their structured acceptance criteria, including explicit unit/property coverage, deterministic e2e evidence, and structured logging/metrics validation.

title: Integrate crossbeam-epoch for version chain GC
description:
Integrate crossbeam-epoch into the MVCC version chain lifecycle. This is the foundational task — all version chain memory management flows through EBR after this.

Implementation steps:
1. Add crossbeam-epoch dependency to the mvcc crate
2. Create a VersionGuard type that pins an epoch on creation (transaction begin) and unpins on drop (transaction end)
3. When a page version is superseded by a newer version, call Guard::defer_destroy() to retire the old version
4. The old version's memory is freed only after all Guards that could observe it have been dropped
5. Hook into transaction begin/commit/abort paths to manage Guard lifecycle
6. Handle long-running read transactions: they hold epoch pins that block GC. Implement a 'stale reader' detection mechanism that warns when a reader is pinning an epoch for too long.

Key design decisions:
- Use crossbeam-epoch's Guard for pinning (not raw epoch manipulation)
- Thread-local retirement lists for amortized overhead
- Batch collection: collect freed versions in batches to amortize overhead

title: Implement chain-length controls and bounds
description:
Implement chain-length controls to prevent unbounded version chain growth. Without bounds, a hot page updated millions of times would have a million-entry version chain, consuming excessive memory and slowing lookups.

Controls:
1. MAX_CHAIN_LENGTH (configurable, default 64): maximum number of versions in a chain
2. When chain length reaches MAX_CHAIN_LENGTH: trigger eager GC — scan the chain and free any versions that are safe to free (no active readers)
3. If chain is still at MAX after eager GC: backpressure — block the writing transaction until a version is freed (reader completes)
4. CHAIN_LENGTH_WARNING (default 32): emit a structured log warning when chain exceeds this threshold, indicating potential GC pressure

Version chain lookup optimization:
- Short-circuit: when looking up a version for a transaction at epoch E, stop scanning the chain once versions are older than E (cannot be visible)
- Cache the 'horizon epoch' (oldest active transaction's epoch) to enable fast pruning

Monitoring:
- Expose metrics: max_chain_length_observed, avg_chain_length, gc_freed_count, gc_blocked_count
- These feed into the MVCC observability dashboard

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] MAX_CHAIN_LENGTH enforced with eager GC
- [ ] Backpressure when chain cannot be shortened
- [ ] Chain-length warning at configurable threshold
- [ ] Lookup optimization with horizon epoch
- [ ] Metrics exposed for monitoring
- [ ] Stress test: 10000 updates to same page, verify chain bounded

title: Tune epoch advance frequency for tail latency
description:
Tune the epoch advance frequency to balance GC throughput against tail latency. Epoch advance is a global synchronization point — advancing too frequently adds overhead, too infrequently wastes memory.

Tuning dimensions:
1. Epoch advance interval: time-based (default 100ms) or operation-count-based (default 1000 operations)
2. Collection batch size: how many retired versions to process per collection cycle
3. Background vs inline collection: collect in background thread vs inline during transaction operations

Measurements:
- GC pause duration at p50, p95, p99
- Memory reclamation latency (time from version retirement to actual free)
- Impact on transaction commit latency (should be < 1% at p50, < 5% at p99)
- Memory overhead vs advance frequency (plot the tradeoff curve)

Expected tradeoff: faster epoch advance -> lower memory usage, higher synchronization overhead. Find the Pareto-optimal point for typical workloads (OLTP: many small transactions; OLAP: few long transactions; mixed).

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Configurable epoch advance interval (time and operation-count)
- [ ] Background collection thread option
- [ ] GC pause p99 < 1ms for typical workloads
- [ ] Memory reclamation latency documented
- [ ] Tradeoff curve documented for different advance frequencies
- [ ] Default settings work well for mixed OLTP/OLAP workloads

title: Property tests: EBR version chain invariants under concurrent access
description:
Property-based tests for EBR version chain garbage collection correctness using proptest. EBR has critical safety invariants that must hold under all concurrent access patterns.

## Invariants to Test

1. No use-after-free: A version that is still observable by any active transaction must never be freed. Formally: if any Guard G pinned at epoch E_pin exists, and version V was created at epoch E_create where E_create >= E_pin, then V must not be freed.

2. Eventual reclamation: Once all transactions that could observe a version have completed, the version must eventually be freed (no memory leaks). Test by running write-heavy workload with short-lived transactions and verifying memory plateaus.

3. Monotonic epoch advance: The global epoch counter must be monotonically increasing. No epoch regression.

4. Chain-length bound: Version chain length must never exceed MAX_CHAIN_LENGTH + 1 (the +1 is for the in-flight write that triggers eager GC).

5. Thread-local retirement correctness: Versions retired on thread T retirement list are eventually freed, even if thread T terminates.

6. Stale reader detection: A reader that pins an epoch for longer than STALE_READER_THRESHOLD triggers a warning (not an error, just observability).

## Alien CS Reference
Fraser 2004 Practical Lock-Freedom: epoch-based reclamation formalized with safety proofs. Brown 2015 Reclaiming Memory for Lock-Free Data Structures: comparative analysis of EBR vs hazard pointers vs reference counting, showing EBR achieves lowest overhead for epoch-aligned workloads. crossbeam-epoch implements the three-epoch protocol from Keir Fraser thesis.

## Rust Implementation Guidance
- Use proptest for random transaction schedule generation
- Use crossbeam::epoch::Guard lifetime tracking to verify no use-after-free
- Integrate Miri (#[cfg(miri)]) for focused hot-page scenarios (Miri is slow, limit scope)
- Use std::sync::atomic::AtomicUsize for allocation/deallocation counting to detect leaks
- For thread lifecycle tests: use std::thread::scope for structured concurrency (avoids detached threads)
- Store proptest regression seeds in proptest-regressions/ directory

## Logging Requirements
- Log epoch advances with old/new epoch values at tracing::debug level
- Log GC collection cycles: versions_freed, versions_pending at tracing::debug level
- Log stale reader warnings with reader_epoch, current_epoch, duration at tracing::warn level
- Log invariant violations (if detected in property tests) at tracing::error level with full context

## Test Generators
- Random transaction schedules: begin/read/write/commit/abort sequences
- Variable transaction lifetimes: short (1 op), medium (10 ops), long (1000 ops)
- Variable write rates: from 1 writer to 100 concurrent writers
- Hot-page scenarios: all writes targeting same page
- Thread lifecycle: spawn and terminate threads during test

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All 6 invariants tested with proptest
- [ ] 10000+ random schedules tested per invariant
- [ ] Miri clean for hot-page scenario
- [ ] Regression seeds stored
- [ ] Integrated into CI test suite
- [ ] No memory leaks detected (track allocation/deallocation counts)

title: Unit tests: EBR VersionGuard lifecycle and eager GC trigger
description:
Focused unit tests for the EBR VersionGuard lifecycle, eager GC triggering, and chain-length enforcement. These complement the property tests (bd-2y306.5) with deterministic, targeted scenarios.

## Test Categories

1. VersionGuard lifecycle: Create a VersionGuard (pin epoch), perform reads and writes, drop VersionGuard (unpin). Verify: (a) epoch is pinned during guard lifetime, (b) epoch is unpinned on drop, (c) nested guards work correctly.

2. Version retirement: Create a version, supersede it with a new version, verify the old version is placed in the retirement list. Then advance epoch and verify the old version is freed.

3. Eager GC trigger: Create MAX_CHAIN_LENGTH versions on a single page, verify that eager GC is triggered on the next write. Verify chain length is reduced after GC.

4. Backpressure: Create MAX_CHAIN_LENGTH versions with active readers holding all versions, attempt another write. Verify the writer is blocked (backpressure) until a reader drops its guard.

5. Stale reader detection: Create a VersionGuard, hold it for longer than STALE_READER_THRESHOLD, verify a warning is emitted. Verify the stale reader does not prevent GC of versions created after it.

6. Transaction abort cleanup: Begin a transaction, create versions, abort. Verify all versions created by the aborted transaction are retired immediately.

7. Concurrent version creation: Multiple threads create versions on the same page simultaneously. Verify all versions are correctly linked in the chain and no version is lost.

## Alien CS Reference
crossbeam-epoch documentation and implementation: three-epoch protocol ensures no use-after-free with deferred destruction. The eager GC trigger and chain-length bound are FrankenSQLite extensions beyond standard EBR.

## Rust Implementation Guidance
- Use #[test] with direct crossbeam::epoch::pin() calls for lifecycle tests
- For backpressure test: use std::thread::spawn with barrier for synchronization, then verify writer blocks
- For stale reader: use std::thread::sleep(STALE_READER_THRESHOLD + margin) and capture tracing output
- Use tracing-test crate to assert on emitted log events (e.g., verify stale reader warning)
- Each test should be deterministic and complete in < 1 second

## Logging Requirements
- Log epoch pin/unpin at tracing::trace level for lifecycle verification
- Log GC trigger at tracing::debug level: chain_length, max_chain_length, versions_freed
- Log backpressure events at tracing::warn level: blocked_writer_thread, blocking_reader_epoch
- Log stale reader warnings at tracing::warn level: reader_epoch, current_epoch, hold_duration

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All 7 test categories implemented and passing
- [ ] Deterministic tests (no timing-dependent flakiness)
- [ ] Miri clean for lifecycle and retirement tests
- [ ] Backpressure correctly blocks writer and unblocks on reader drop
- [ ] Stale reader warning verified via tracing-test
- [ ] Concurrent version creation verified with 8+ threads
- [ ] All tests complete in < 5 seconds total

title: PRAGMA case_sensitive_like silently ignored: LIKE stays ASCII-case-insensitive even when set ON
close_reason: PRAGMA case_sensitive_like wired into all LIKE eval paths via per-statement thread-local; 5/5 oracle e2e green, regression+clippy+fmt clean

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
# PRAGMA case_sensitive_like silently ignored

## Symptom
`PRAGMA case_sensitive_like = ON` is accepted (no error) but has **no effect**:
LIKE remains ASCII-case-insensitive afterwards. SQLite makes LIKE byte-exact
(case-sensitive) when this pragma is ON.

## Minimal repro (vs rusqlite / real SQLite)
```sql
PRAGMA case_sensitive_like = ON;
SELECT 'A' LIKE 'a';   -- SQLite: 0   frank: 1  (WRONG)
SELECT 'apple' LIKE 'APPLE';  -- SQLite: 0   frank: 1  (WRONG)
```
In a filter:
```sql
CREATE TABLE t(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1,'apple'),(2,'Apple'),(3,'APPLE');
PRAGMA case_sensitive_like = ON;
SELECT id FROM t WHERE name LIKE 'apple';  -- SQLite: [1]   frank: [1,2,3]  (WRONG)
```

GLOB (always case-sensitive) and the *default* LIKE behavior (ASCII fold, non-ASCII
never folded) are both correct in frank — only the pragma toggle is unwired.

## Root cause
1. `crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs` pragma dispatch has **no arm** for
   `case_sensitive_like`; the only references to the name are in `#[cfg(test)]`
   functions. Unknown pragmas are silently no-op'd, so the setting is dropped.
2. `crates/fsqlite-func/src/builtins.rs:1817` — `like_match(pattern, string, escape)`
   calls `sql_like(...)` with no case-sensitivity parameter; it is hardwired to
   ASCII-fold. Even if the flag were stored on the connection, the matcher has no
   way to honor it.

## Fix sketch (multi-layer)
- Add a per-connection `case_sensitive_like: Cell<bool>` (default `false`) to
  `Connection`.
- Recognize `PRAGMA case_sensitive_like = ON|OFF|1|0|true|false` in connection.rs
  pragma dispatch and set the flag.
- Thread the flag into the LIKE path: `sql_like`/`like_match` need a
  `case_sensitive: bool` argument. Because LIKE compiles to either the global
  `like()` scalar or an inline comparison, the flag must be bound at compile time
  per-connection (e.g. via codegen reading the connection setting, or registering
  a connection-scoped LIKE). GLOB is unaffected and must stay case-sensitive.

## Tests
`crates/fsqlite-e2e/tests/case_sensitive_like_pragma_oracle_e2e.rs`:
- PASS: `like_default_is_ascii_case_insensitive`, `glob_unaffected_by_case_sensitive_like`
- IGNORED on this bead: `like_case_sensitive_pragma_on`, `like_pragma_toggles_back_off`,
  `like_pragma_in_where_filter`

Exact sites:

1) fsqlite-types/src/value.rs: add case_sensitive-aware matching WITHOUT breaking ~30 existing test callers — keep sql_like(p,t,esc)=sql_like_with_case(p,t,esc,false) wrapper; add sql_like_with_case + sql_like_fast_path_matches_with_case(kind,lit,text,cs). Thread cs into sql_like_inner + the ascii_ci_* helpers (when cs: exact byte/char compare; else current eq_ignore_ascii_case). value.rs:1171 sql_like, :1220 sql_like_fast_path_matches, :1262 matcher-struct method, :1305 sql_like_inner, :1371-1431 ascii_ci_*.

2) fsqlite-vdbe/src/engine.rs: add field pub case_sensitive_like: bool (near :480) + init=false in ALL constructors (~:6145) + setter set_case_sensitive_like (near :7613, mirror set_column_defaults_by_root_page). Two LIKE read sites: (a) Opcode::LikeConstFast :11790-11826 (3 arms call sql_like_fast_path_matches) -> pass self.case_sensitive_like to the _with_case variant; NOTE p5 is ALREADY the NOT flag, do NOT reuse it. ## Session 53 — Fix #79: KBN Compensated Summation + 25 Conformance Oracle Tests

### Bug Fix #79: Kahan-Babuska-Neumaier Summation Precision

**Problem:** `SUM(s.qty * p.price)` over three-table JOINs produced `209.82000000000002` instead of `209.82`. The accumulated floating-point error from naive summation was visible in the output.

**Root cause:** FrankenSQLite used simple Kahan summation while C SQLite uses the more precise Kahan-Babuska-Neumaier (KBN) algorithm with magnitude-aware error term selection (func.c:1871-1883).

**Fix applied to ALL float accumulation paths:**
1. `agg_builtins.rs` — `kahan_add()` now uses KBN algorithm; SUM/AVG/total finalize adds compensation term
2. `connection.rs` — `compute_aggregate()` fallback GROUP BY path uses new `kbn_step()` helper
3. `vectorized_agg.rs` — Accumulator struct gains `sum_err` field, update/finalize use KBN
4. `window_builtins.rs` — WindowSumFunc step/inverse/value use KBN
5. `value.rs` — SumAccumulator gains `float_err` field, accumulate/finish use KBN

### New Conformance Oracle Tests (25 tests, separate integration test file)
Added `crates/fsqlite-core/tests/conformance_oracle_ext.rs` to avoid concurrent edit conflicts on connection.rs:
- hex/bitwise/CAST/boolean expressions
- total()/COUNT(DISTINCT)/SUM edges
- LIKE/ESCAPE/GLOB patterns
- abs()/typeof()/scalar min-max/zeroblob/unicode/char/hex/instr
- EXCEPT/INTERSECT compound chaining
- UPDATE self-referencing CASE expressions

- Savepoint nesting with ROLLBACK/RELEASE
- DEFAULT clause expressions
- String function edge cases (substr, replace, trim, printf)
- Numeric edges (overflow, division by zero, modulo, unary minus)
- Complex WHERE (nested AND/OR, BETWEEN, IN subquery, EXISTS correlation)
- ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN + post-alter INSERT
- Subquery patterns (correlated, scalar, derived, EXISTS, NOT EXISTS)

- CASE expression variants (simple, searched, nested, aggregate, ORDER BY)
- Index queries (point lookup, range, composite, LIKE prefix, MIN/MAX)

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## Completion Evidence for bd-2yqp6.4.3

### Deliverable: D3: Align transaction/savepoint/pragma semantics with oracle

### What Was Implemented

#### 1. PRAGMA foreign_keys ignored inside transactions (sqlite3 pragma.c behavior)

SQLite silently ignores `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON/OFF` when a transaction is active. FrankenSQLite was applying the change unconditionally. Added a guard in `execute_pragma()` that checks `in_transaction` before allowing `apply_connection_pragma` to modify the `foreign_keys` flag. When inside a transaction, the setter returns the current value without modification.

#### 2. PRAGMA table_list reports "view" for views (sqlite3 table_list output)

`PRAGMA table_list` only iterated `self.schema` (tables) and hardcoded "table" as the type. Views are stored separately in `self.views`. Added a second pass that appends view entries with type="view", ncol from the view's column list, and strict=0.

#### 3. ROLLBACK outside transaction error verified correct

Investigated SQLite's vdbe.c:4055-4057 AutoCommit opcode: ROLLBACK outside a transaction returns "cannot rollback - no transaction is active" (SQLITE_ERROR). FrankenSQLite already had this behavior. A previous session incorrectly changed it to a no-op (return Ok(())); that was reverted and the correct error behavior restored.

### Tests (2 new, all passing)

1. `test_pragma_table_list_reports_view_type` — CREATE TABLE + CREATE VIEW, verifies table_list returns "table" for tables and "view" for views
2. `test_pragma_foreign_keys_ignored_inside_transaction` — Verifies foreign_keys=ON outside txn works, SET inside txn is silently ignored, value persists correctly after COMMIT, and can be changed again outside txn

### Validation

- `cargo test -p fsqlite-core --lib` => 1543 passed, 0 failed, 2 ignored
- `cargo clippy -p fsqlite -p fsqlite-core --all-targets -- -D warnings` => PASS (exit 0)
- `cargo fmt --all --check` => PASS

### Files Changed

1. **`crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs`**:
   - `execute_rollback()`: Restored correct error on ROLLBACK outside transaction (reverted incorrect no-op change)
   - `execute_pragma()`: Added guard to skip `PRAGMA foreign_keys = X` inside active transaction
   - PRAGMA `table_list` handler: Added view entries with type="view" from `self.views`
   - Added 2 new tests in `pager_routing_tests` module

title: G9: Certify MemDatabase fallback transparency and denial evidence
description:
## Background and reason

The parity-cert program already requires the declared runtime path to use real Pager/WAL/MVCC/B-Tree storage, and D4 is currently wiring strict rejection for MemDatabase fallback in certifying mode. That is necessary but not sufficient for final certification: future fallback entrypoints can still be added, helper-local materialization paths can regress, and evidence consumers need a machine-checkable way to prove that no parity run silently used the in-memory compatibility image.

This G9 feature turns fallback transparency into an explicit certification surface. It does not remove MemDatabase from all compatibility paths by itself. Instead, it makes every fallback decision observable, classifies which decisions are allowed outside certification, forces strict denial in certifying scopes, and gives G3/G5/G8 a replayable proof pack that can answer: which backend produced this parity result, which fallback boundaries were reachable, which were denied, and what exact command reproduces the first failure.

## Scope

- Inventory every connection/VDBE/harness path that can route through MemDatabase or connection-level compatibility execution.
- Define a structured fallback-decision event schema with trace_id, run_id, scenario_id, statement fingerprint, statement kind, backend identity, fallback reason, certifying mode, strictness, decision outcome, and first-failure diagnostic fields.
- Build deterministic e2e scenarios that intentionally try to trigger view/CTE/sqlite_schema/temp-table/materialized helper fallback under parity-cert mode and verify strict denial or documented non-cert compatibility routing.
- Integrate the proof pack into the machine-readable certificate path so final parity evidence cannot be generated without fresh fallback-transparency artifacts.
- Provide operator-facing remediation text that points from a fallback failure to the exact statement shape and subsystem that needs Pager/VDBE cutover work.

## Acceptance criteria

1. A complete fallback-boundary inventory exists and is linked to concrete source touchpoints, statement shapes, and certification policy decisions.
2. Structured fallback decision telemetry is emitted or validated by tests with the required identifiers and denial/allowance fields.
3. Deterministic e2e replay scripts run under parity-cert strict mode and prove helper-local fallback bypasses fail closed rather than silently producing parity evidence from MemDatabase.
4. G3 certificate generation depends on the fallback-transparency artifact bundle and records artifact paths/hashes in the manifest.
5. The proof pack includes unit tests, e2e tests, log-schema validation, first-failure diagnostics, and one-command replay instructions.

title: G9.1: Inventory and classify every MemDatabase fallback boundary
description:
## Goal

Build the canonical fallback-boundary inventory for parity certification. Future agents must not need to grep session logs to understand which statement shapes still depend on MemDatabase or connection-level compatibility execution.

## Required work

- Audit `crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs`, VDBE execution boundaries, extension hooks, and e2e parity harnesses for every path that can use MemDatabase, materialized compatibility execution, or helper-local fallback.
- Classify each boundary as one of: real-backend only, certifying-mode denied, non-cert compatibility allowed, pending Pager/VDBE cutover, or intentionally in-memory-only.
- For each boundary record statement kind, trigger condition, decision reason, expected backend identity, first failure diagnostic, and the bead that should own full cutover if one already exists.
- Explicitly include view materialization, sqlite_schema virtualization, CTE and DML-with-CTE materialization, temp-table materialization, INSERT ... SELECT, aggregate/window/JOIN fallback, extension virtual tables, and time-travel snapshot routes.

## Acceptance criteria

1. The inventory is machine-readable or directly consumable by later tests and certificate generation.
2. Every row names source touchpoints and the certifying-mode policy.
3. The inventory distinguishes compatibility fallback allowed outside certification from fallback denied inside parity-cert strict mode.
4. Unit or static validation catches missing policy fields for any inventory row.
5. Evidence notes include the exact audit commands and source line ranges inspected.

title: G9.2: Emit and validate structured fallback-decision telemetry
description:
## Goal

Make fallback decisions inspectable by machines and useful to humans. A parity run should never leave reviewers guessing whether a result came from real Pager/WAL/MVCC/B-Tree storage or from MemDatabase compatibility execution.

## Required work

- Define the fallback-decision event schema with at minimum: trace_id, run_id, scenario_id, statement_fingerprint, statement_kind, backend_identity, fallback_boundary, decision_reason, certifying_mode, strict_mode, decision_outcome, source_touchpoint, and first_failure_diag.
- Emit or surface the event consistently from fallback decision points and strict-denial paths.
- Add schema validation tests that fail when required fields are missing, empty, or inconsistent with backend identity.
- Ensure non-cert compatibility fallback can still be diagnosed without weakening parity-cert strictness.

## Acceptance criteria

1. Structured fallback events carry all required identifiers and are stable enough for CI/log-schema validation.
2. Strict-denial events are distinguishable from allowed non-cert fallback events.
3. Tests cover successful real-backend execution, denied certifying fallback, and allowed non-cert compatibility fallback.
4. First-failure diagnostics name the statement shape and boundary that caused rejection.
5. The event contract is documented inside the bead notes or a linked machine-readable schema artifact.

- `allowed_compatibility_fallback` for non-cert compatibility execution that is observable but cannot certify parity.
- `real_backend_dispatch` for positive native Pager/WAL/MVCC/B-Tree or VDBE storage-cursor dispatch.

title: G9.3: Build deterministic fallback-denial e2e replay suite
description:
## Goal

Provide a one-command replay suite that tries to force fallback under certifying mode and proves the runtime fails closed with actionable diagnostics.

## Required work

- Add deterministic e2e scenarios with fixed seeds and artifact bundle capture for view materialization, sqlite_schema virtualization, ordinary CTEs, DELETE/UPDATE/INSERT with CTEs, materialized temp tables, aggregate/window/JOIN fallback, and extension or virtual table boundaries where relevant.
- Run the suite on file-backed storage with parity-cert strict mode enabled and assert that any fallback attempt is rejected before MemDatabase execution can produce certifying evidence.
- Include non-cert control cases to prove compatibility fallback remains explainable where it is intentionally still allowed.
- Emit trace/log artifacts with backend identity and fallback-decision events from G9.2.

## Acceptance criteria

1. The suite has a stable replay command and writes artifacts under a deterministic path.
2. Every scenario records backend identity, statement shape, fallback boundary, decision outcome, and first-failure diagnostic.
3. Certifying-mode fallback attempts fail closed and cannot be mistaken for successful real-backend parity.
4. Control cases prove non-cert fallback behavior is observable without creating certification evidence.
5. The suite is runnable through `rch exec --` for all cargo-heavy commands.
close_reason: Completed deterministic fallback-denial replay matrix, verifier script, inventory ID corrections, and full validation gates.

comments.text:
## G9.3 deterministic replay-suite matrix handoff (2026-06-05, MistyDesert)

This is a Beads-only handoff from the G9.1 inventory draft and the G9.2 telemetry handoff. G9.3 should not start by rediscovering fallback boundaries; it should turn the inventory row families into deterministic replay scenarios with strict-denial and non-cert control expectations.

Replay artifact contract:
- Stable logical artifact key: `fallback_denial_replay.v1`.
- Each scenario artifact should include: `trace_id`, `run_id`, `scenario_id`, `seed`, `statement_sql`, `statement_fingerprint`, `statement_kind`, `backend_identity`, `fallback_boundary`, `boundary_id`, `decision_reason`, `certifying_mode`, `strict_mode`, `decision_outcome`, `source_touchpoint`, `first_failure_diag`, `inventory_row_id`, `telemetry_event_id`, `replay_command`, and `artifact_hash`.
- File-backed strict runs should record `backend_identity=<backend_kind>:parity_cert_strict` for real-backend successes and `decision_outcome=denied` or `vdbe_mempage_fallback_rejected` for denied fallback attempts.
- Non-cert controls should use a separate scenario id suffix, should never be included as certifying evidence, and should record `decision_outcome=allowed_compatibility_fallback` or `vdbe_mempage_fallback_allowed` only with `certifying_mode=false`.

Suggested deterministic scenario matrix:
1. `view_materialization_strict_denied`
   - inventory family: `conn.select.view_materialization`.
   - statement shape: create base table, create view, then `SELECT` from the view shape known to route through materialization.
   - strict expected outcome: denial before helper-local MemDatabase materialization; diagnostic names view materialization and source touchpoint.
   - non-cert control: allowed compatibility fallback with full event fields.

2. `sqlite_schema_virtual_materialization_strict_denied`
   - inventory family: `conn.select.sqlite_schema_virtual_materialization`.
   - statement shape: query `sqlite_schema`/schema virtual materialization route on file-backed storage.
   - strict expected outcome: denial with boundary distinct from ordinary view materialization; diagnostic mentions sqlite_schema virtualization/root-page collision boundary where applicable.

3. `select_cte_materialization_strict_denied`
   - inventory family: `conn.select.with_clause_materialization`.
   - statement shape: ordinary `WITH`/CTE `SELECT` that currently reaches helper materialization or VDBE unsupported boundary.
   - strict expected outcome: denied before CTE temp data enters MemDatabase; diagnostic names CTE/WITH statement shape.

4. `dml_cte_materialization_strict_denied`
   - inventory family: `conn.dml.with_clause_materialization.update_delete` plus `conn.insert.with_clause_materialization`.
   - statement shapes: `INSERT ... WITH`, `UPDATE ... WITH`, and `DELETE ... WITH` on file-backed storage.
   - strict expected outcome: denied before helper-local materialization; statement_kind must distinguish INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE even if reason strings share a family.

5. `insert_select_replay_strict_denied`
   - inventory family: `conn.insert_select.row_by_row_replay`.
   - statement shape: `INSERT INTO dst SELECT ... FROM src` that would use bounded materialization or streaming replay.
   - strict expected outcome: denied before row-by-row MemDatabase replay; artifact also records a related `real_backend_refresh` event if refresh occurs only as state synchronization.

6. `insert_values_trigger_fk_replay_strict_denied`
   - inventory family: `conn.insert_values.trigger_fk_replay` / `conn.insert_values.morsel_dispatch`.
   - statement shape: multi-row INSERT with trigger or FK work that currently uses row replay/morsel dispatch.
   - strict expected outcome: denied unless implementation proves a real-backend row-stream path; for G9.3 initial suite, treat as denial/control evidence.

7. `materialized_temp_table_execution_strict_denied`
   - inventory family: `conn.materialized_temp_table_execution`.
   - statement shape: attached-schema or temp-table route that invokes materialized temp table execution.
   - strict expected outcome: helper guard fails closed before temporarily disabling fallback rejection.

8. `aggregate_window_join_fallback_strict_denied`
   - inventory families: `conn.select.aggregate_window_fallbacks` and `conn.select.join_subquery_live_vtab_fallbacks`.
   - statement shapes: GROUP BY/JOIN fallback, window function fallback, correlated subquery fallback, and live-vtab fallback where applicable.
   - strict expected outcome: fallback attempts denied; native-positive variants should be separate `real_backend_dispatch` controls, not mixed into fallback-denial cases.

9. `vdbe_open_storage_cursor_mempage_rejected`
   - inventory family: `vdbe.open_storage_cursor.mempage_fallback`.
   - statement shape: file-backed VDBE read path that can force the MemPageStore decision surface or a synthetic harness fixture if direct SQL cannot reach it deterministically.
   - strict expected outcome: `decision_outcome=vdbe_mempage_fallback_rejected`, exact reason among `no_pager_transaction`, `pager_read_failed_mem_fallback`, `txn_page_invalid_mem_fallback`, or `parity_cert_rejection`.

10. `time_travel_snapshot_classification_control`
   - inventory family: `conn.select.time_travel_snapshot`.
   - statement shape: historical snapshot/time-travel query if still present in the user-visible surface.
   - expected outcome: either explicit `intentional_time_travel_snapshot` with cert exclusion, or `pending_classification` failure. Do not silently count this as real-backend parity evidence.

Implementation gates:
- G9.3 should fail fast if G9.2 events are absent for any scenario that reaches a fallback decision.
- Every strict scenario must prove MemDatabase did not produce certifying results. A generic SQL error is not enough unless it carries the structured fallback event and first-failure diagnostic.
- At least one positive real-backend dispatch scenario should be included so the suite proves the event path distinguishes native success from denied fallback.
- At least one non-cert control should prove compatibility fallback remains observable without weakening strict parity-cert.
- The replay command should be a single, copyable `rch exec -- ... cargo ...` command for cargo-heavy execution, preferably with a dedicated `CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/data/tmp/...` to avoid shared lock contention.

Closeout requirements for G9.3:
- Final notes must list the exact scenario ids implemented, the inventory rows covered, the artifact directory, artifact hashes, first-failure examples, and the `rch exec --` validation command.
- G9.4 should not gate certificates on this suite until the artifact schema includes hashes and enough backend-identity summary data for manifest validation.

title: G9.4: Gate parity certificates on fallback-transparency artifacts
description:
## Goal

Wire fallback-transparency evidence into final certificate generation so certification cannot proceed when the fallback proof pack is missing, stale, or contradictory.

## Required work

- Extend the G3 machine-readable certificate manifest inputs to require the G9 inventory, fallback-decision schema validation result, e2e replay bundle, artifact hashes, and backend-identity summary.
- Add gate logic that rejects certificate generation when a certifying scenario records an allowed MemDatabase fallback or lacks fallback-decision evidence for a covered boundary.
- Ensure the gate distinguishes missing evidence, stale artifacts, strict-denial failures, and true real-backend success.
- Preserve one-command parity verification ergonomics by making the missing/failing G9 evidence path obvious to users.

## Acceptance criteria

1. G3 cannot generate a final parity certificate without fresh G9 artifact references and hashes.
2. Any certifying-mode MemDatabase fallback is a hard gate failure unless explicitly documented as a non-cert control case.
3. Gate output contains actionable first-failure diagnostics and the replay command from G9.3.
4. CI or local verification can validate the manifest/schema contract deterministically.
