title: Track I: Autocommit Transaction Bypass — Eliminate 31x Autocommit Gap

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## Problem
Autocommit 10K rows = 10K separate begin/commit cycles = 31.52x slower than C SQLite. Each cycle: allocate TransactionHandle, acquire locks, publish snapshot, commit, release. Total overhead: ~30 µs per row vs C SQLite's ~1.3 µs.

## Solution: Retained Transaction with Implicit Auto-Flush
Instead of begin/commit per statement, maintain a retained write transaction across autocommit statements. Flush (publish) changes only when:
1. A read would require seeing the just-written data
2. 64 statements have accumulated (configurable)
3. The connection goes idle

This matches C SQLite's internal behavior: it batches autocommit writes into journal pages and only fsyncs at actual commit boundaries.

## Expected Impact: Reduce autocommit overhead from 31.52x to ~4x (matching single-txn performance)
The remaining 4x gap is the per-row INSERT cost addressed by Tracks F, G, H.

## Safety
The retained transaction is invisible to the user. ACID semantics are preserved because:
- Each statement is atomic (rollback on error restores the retained txn state)
- The flush-on-read ensures read-after-write consistency
- Connection close always flushes

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## Interaction with Track F (Lock-Free Page Cache)
The retained autocommit transaction holds pages dirty across multiple statements. With Track F's flat page array, dirty pages are simply marked in the array (no DashMap update needed). This is a POSITIVE interaction — both optimizations compose well.

However: if the retained txn accumulates >64K dirty pages, the flat array may need expansion. Add a check: if dirty_page_count > flat_array_capacity, flush the retained txn early.

## Interaction with Track J (MemDB Mirror Elimination)
With lazy MemDB tracking (Track J), the retained txn can skip MemDB sync for ALL accumulated statements, not just one. This AMPLIFIES Track J's benefit — instead of saving 0.10 µs per statement, we save 0.10 µs × N statements between flushes.

However: the lazy dirty tracking must persist across retained txn boundaries. Dirty flags should only clear on actual flush, not on internal autocommit-to-retained promotion.

## Interaction with Track G (BTREE_APPEND)
The retained txn means the B-tree cursor state persists across autocommit statements. This means the append fast path (G1) can maintain its rightmost_leaf cache across multiple statements — a BIG win for sequential autocommit INSERT workloads.

## Testing: The TI test suite MUST include multi-optimization interaction tests:
- test_retained_txn_with_flat_page_array — I1 + F1 combined
- test_retained_txn_with_lazy_memdb — I1 + J1 combined
- test_retained_txn_with_append_fastpath — I1 + G1 combined

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## Verification finding 2026-06-28 (Opus 4.8): NOT closeable — retained-autocommit bypass does NOT engage for ad-hoc autocommit in the default concurrent mode.

Ran the full Track I acceptance suite + engagement probes. All PASS, but the engagement metrics expose the gap:

- crates/fsqlite-e2e/tests/bd_iuvw4_track_i_autocommit.rs (5/5 pass): AUTOCOMMIT-10K => flushes=0, reuses=0; INTERLEAVED-100 => flushes=0, parks=0, read_after_write_flushes=0; RETAINED-100 => parks=0, reuses=0, flushes=0. Throughput: fsqlite 111.5 rows/s vs C SQLite (rusqlite) 334.7 rows/s on autocommit-10K — ~3x SLOWER, NOT the targeted ~4x.
- crates/fsqlite-core/tests/sequential_autocommit_increment_probe.rs (3/3 pass; durability ok).

ROOT CAUSE (precise): the retained-autocommit park gate at connection.rs:36782-36787 requires `!is_concurrent_txn && concurrent_plan.is_none()`. `is_concurrent_txn = self.concurrent_txn.get()` (connection.rs:36695). Ad-hoc `execute("INSERT ...")` autocommit writes in the default (always-on) concurrent mode run as CONCURRENT txns (concurrent_txn=true, concurrent_plan=Some), so BOTH gates fail => the txn is never parked => the bypass never engages => full begin/commit per statement.

WHERE IT DOES ENGAGE (verified via prepared_hit_rate_proof.rs:483/487, parks>=ROWS-1): the PREPARED direct-insert fast lane (prepared_insert_fast_lane_hits==ROWS) which sets concurrent_txn=false; and the private :memory: autocommit fast path (memory_autocommit_fast_path_begins).

CONCLUSION: Track I is implemented + ACID-correct + engaged ONLY for the prepared-direct and private-:memory: autocommit lanes. It is DISABLED for the realistic ad-hoc autocommit path under the always-on concurrent mode (the project default). The bead's own e2e assertion (`flush_count <= INSERT_COUNT`) passes trivially with flush_count=0 — it does NOT gate the perf goal, so a green suite does NOT prove the bead is done. Closing now would be a FALSE close. Sub-beads bd-otbu1 (I1 retained txn) and bd-iuvw4 (TI tests) remain correctly closed; only this capstone's default-path engagement is unmet.

REMAINING WORK (deep; out of scope for a read-only verify pass, and concurrency-correctness-sensitive):
- Option A: route simple single-statement ad-hoc autocommit INSERTs onto a non-concurrent direct lane like prepared inserts. RISK: making ad-hoc autocommit non-concurrent could serialize cross-connection autocommit writers — must NOT regress the concurrent-writer invariant (AGENTS.md).
- Option B: design a safe way to park a concurrent (SSI) txn across autocommit statements without holding page write-locks / blocking other writers across the batch window.
Both overlap connection.rs work in progress (bd-2yqp6.4.4 "wire default runtime path") — coordinate before editing the autocommit/commit dispatch. Reverting bd-3klej to open with this finding rather than rubber-stamp-closing.

SECTION 21 — RISK REGISTER, OPEN QUESTIONS, AND FUTURE WORK (~213 lines)

SUBSECTIONS: §21.0 Risk Register (8 risks with mitigations: R1-R8), §21.1 Open Questions (with how we answer them), §21.2 Cross-Process MVCC (implementation notes), §21.3 Write-Ahead-Log Multiplexing, §21.4 Distributed Consensus Integration, §21.5 GPU-Accelerated RaptorQ Encoding, §21.6 Persistent Memory (PMEM) VFS, §21.7 Vectorized VDBE Execution, §21.8 Column-Store Hybrid for Analytical Queries, §21.9 Erasure-Coded Page Storage (implementation notes), §21.10 Time Travel Queries and Tiered Symbol Storage.

## UNIT TEST REQUIREMENTS
- test_risk_r1_ssi_abort_rate_measurable: Verify SSI abort rate instrumentation exists and produces measurable counters (conflicts_detected, conflicts_aborted) per §18.6
- test_risk_r2_raptorq_cpu_budget: Verify RaptorQ encode/decode operations respect a configurable CPU budget and do not monopolize the event loop
- test_risk_r3_gc_horizon_bounds_growth: Verify MVCC GC horizon advances when the oldest active snapshot closes, pruning version chains per Theorem 5
- test_risk_r5_cross_process_lease_cleanup: Verify TxnSlot lease-based cleanup correctly reclaims slots from crashed processes without blocking active transactions
- test_open_question_q2_witness_key_granularity: Verify SSI witness keys start at page granularity and abort rate is observable for future refinement decisions
- test_open_question_q6_blink_fallback: Verify the system handles hot-page split contention gracefully (retry or queue) without deadlock or starvation

## E2E TEST
test_e2e_risk_mitigations.rs: Run a stress test that exercises each high-risk scenario (R1: high-contention SSI workload, R3: long-running reader preventing GC, R5: simulated process crash during MVCC) and verify all mitigations activate correctly (abort rates within budget, GC completes after reader closes, lease cleanup recovers slots).

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA

- [ ] Each risk has at least one validation strategy (test, harness scenario, or measurement) and a clear close condition.

## Success Criteria

- High-risk items have explicit detection signals (tests/monitors) and a concrete mitigation plan.

## §21 Full Spec Text (Verbatim Extract)
Source: COMPREHENSIVE_SPEC_FOR_FRANKENSQLITE_V1.md lines 17739-17952

## 21. Risk Register, Open Questions, and Future Work

### 21.0 Risk Register (With Mitigations)

**R1. SSI abort rate too high (Page-SSI is conservative).**
Mitigations:
- Refine witness keys from page → (page, range/cell tag) to reduce false positives.
- Add safe snapshot optimizations for read-only transactions.
- Intent-level rebase (Section 5.10.2) turns page conflicts into merges,
  reducing effective conflict rate by 30-60%.
- PostgreSQL's measured false positive rate is ~0.5% at row granularity; our
  page granularity will be higher, but merge compensation helps.

**R2. RaptorQ overhead dominates CPU.**
Mitigations:
- Choose symbol sizing policy based on object type (capsules: small symbols
  for fast commit; checkpoints: large symbols for throughput).
- Cache decoded objects aggressively (ARC cache).
- Profile and tune encoder/decoder hot paths (one lever per change, per
  the Extreme Optimization methodology).

**R3. Append-only storage grows without bound.**
Mitigations:
- Checkpoint, GC, and compaction are first-class (Section 5.5 for MVCC GC/version chain trimming, Section 7.13 for ECS compaction, Section 7.9 for the crash contract).
- Enforce budgets for MVCC history, SSI witness plane, symbol caches.
- Safe GC horizon = min(active `begin_seq`) (Theorem 4) bounds version chain length (Theorem 5).

**R4. Bootstrapping chicken-and-egg (need index to find symbols, need symbols
to decode index).**
Mitigations:
- Symbol records are self-describing (header + OTI).
- One tiny mutable root pointer per database.
- Rebuild-from-scan is always possible as a fallback.

**R5. Multi-process MVCC coordination is complex.**
Mitigations:
- Shared-memory coordination protocol specified (Section 5.6.1).
- Lease-based TxnSlot cleanup handles process crashes without blocking.
- Both in-process and cross-process MVCC are validated in Phase 6.
- Explicit tests for multi-process behaviors required before shipping.

**R6. File format compatibility vs "do it right".**
Mitigations:
- Compatibility Mode (Section 7.10) treats SQLite `.db/.wal` as the standard
  format for conformance.
- Native Mode is the innovation layer.
- Conformance harness validates observable behavior, not byte-identical layout.

**R7. Mergeable writes become a correctness minefield.**
Mitigations:
- Strict merge ladder (Section 5.10.4): only take merges we can justify.
- Proptest invariants + DPOR tests (Section 5.10.5).
- Start with deterministic rebase replay for a small op subset (inserts/updates
  on leaf pages), grow coverage guided by conflict benchmarks.

**R8. Distributed mode correctness is hard.**
Mitigations:
- Symbol-native replication uses "leader commit clock" as the default mode.
- Use sheaf checks + TLA+ export for bounded model checking.
- Replication protocol is ECS-native: ObjectId set reconciliation + anti-entropy.
- Implementation phased: single-node first, then multi-node (Phase 9).

### 21.1 Open Questions (With How We Answer Them)

**Q1. Multi-process writers:** What is the performance envelope for cross-process
concurrent writes?
*Answer plan:* Implement shared-memory coordination (Section 5.6.1); benchmark
contention vs in-process baseline; tune TxnSlot count and lease intervals.

**Q2. How far do we go with range/cell refinement for SSI witness keys?**
*Answer plan:* Start page-only; collect abort witnesses; refine only when
abort rate is proven unacceptable by benchmark.

**Q3. Symbol sizing policy per object type (capsule vs checkpoint vs index).**
*Answer plan:* Benchmark encode/decode throughput vs object sizes; pick
defaults; expose PRAGMA overrides for experiments.

**Q4. Where to checkpoint for compatibility `.db` without bottlenecking writes?**
*Answer plan:* Background checkpoint with ECS chunks; measure; keep export
optional.

**Q5. Which B-tree operations can be replayed deterministically for rebase merge?**
*Answer plan:* Implement inserts/updates on leaf pages first; grow coverage
guided by conflict benchmarks.

**Q6. Do we need B-link style concurrency for hot-page split/merge contention?**
*Answer plan:* Benchmark workloads that hammer the same index/table. If
internal-page conflicts dominate, add an internal "structure modification"
protocol (ephemeral metadata, not file format changes) inspired by B-link
trees: optimistic descent + right-sibling guidance + deterministic retry.

### 21.2 Cross-Process MVCC (Implementation Notes)

Cross-process MVCC is specified in Section 5.6.1. Implementation notes:
- Phase 6 validates both in-process and cross-process MVCC correctness
  (the Phase 6 gates in §22 explicitly test multi-process lease expiry
  and TxnSlot reuse; Phase 7 is "Advanced Query Planner", not cross-process)
- Key challenge: benchmarking the mmap-based TxnSlot array vs in-process atomics
- Lease-based cleanup must be stress-tested under process crash scenarios

### 21.3 Write-Ahead-Log Multiplexing

For very high write throughput (>100K TPS), a single WAL file becomes the
bottleneck (sequential append to one file). WAL multiplexing shards WAL
frames across multiple files:
- WAL file selected by `hash(page_number) % num_wal_files`
- Each WAL file has its own checkpoint state
- Commit requires atomic append to all WAL files touched by the transaction
  (2PC across WAL files; crash recovery replays prepared-but-uncommitted
  entries using a global commit marker in the primary WAL)
- Potential improvement in sustained write throughput on NVMe SSDs
  with high queue depth (actual speedup depends on workload page
  distribution and device parallelism; requires benchmarking)

### 21.4 Distributed Consensus Integration

For multi-node deployments, integrate Raft or Paxos for replicated state:
- WAL entries as the replicated log
- Leader handles all writes, followers handle reads (read replicas)
- Snapshot shipping (Section 3.4.3) for new follower initialization
- RaptorQ-coded replication (Section 3.4.2) for steady-state log shipping
- Challenge: linearizable reads require either reading from leader or
  implementing read leases

### 21.5 GPU-Accelerated RaptorQ Encoding

For bulk operations (full database backup, large changeset replication),
RaptorQ encoding is CPU-bound. GPU acceleration via compute shaders:
- GF(256) arithmetic maps well to SIMD/GPU (each symbol byte independent)
- Matrix multiplication for intermediate symbol generation is embarrassingly
  parallel
- Expected speedup: 10-50x for large source blocks (K > 10,000)
- Framework: wgpu for cross-platform GPU compute

### 21.6 Persistent Memory (PMEM) VFS

CXL-attached persistent memory (and legacy Intel Optane DCPMM) enable
byte-addressable persistent storage. A PMEM VFS would:
- Memory-map the database file directly to PMEM
- Eliminate the WAL entirely (copy-on-write page updates with 8-byte
  atomic pointer swings for crash consistency)
- Use `clflush`/`clwb` instructions for cache line persistence
- MVCC version chains stored directly in PMEM with epoch-based reclamation
- Expected latency reduction: 10-100x for small transactions (eliminate
  WAL write + fsync)

### 21.7 Vectorized VDBE Execution

Current VDBE processes one row at a time (Volcano model). Vectorized
execution processes batches of rows through each operator:
- Column-at-a-time processing enables SIMD utilization
- Better CPU cache behavior (fewer instruction cache misses)
- Applicable to full table scans, aggregations, and nested-loop joins
- Expected speedup: 2-5x for analytical queries, negligible for point lookups
- Challenge: must maintain row-at-a-time semantics for triggers and
  RETURNING clause

### 21.8 Column-Store Hybrid for Analytical Queries

For mixed OLTP/OLAP workloads, a column-store representation alongside
the row-store B-tree:
- Column groups stored in separate B-trees per column
- Automatic materialization of frequently-scanned columns
- RLE and dictionary compression for low-cardinality columns
- Query planner selects row-store or column-store based on query pattern
- Challenge: maintaining consistency between row-store and column-store
  under concurrent writes

### 21.9 Erasure-Coded Page Storage (Implementation Notes)

Section 3.4.6 specifies erasure-coded page storage and the required correctness
constraints for Compatibility mode mutability. Implementation notes:
- Modified page allocation: allocate G pages as a group
- Repair page storage: in the ECS object store (Native mode) or in a
  `foo.db-fec` sidecar file (Compatibility mode)
- Read path: attempt source page first, fall back to erasure recovery
- Group size selection: benchmark G=32, G=64, G=128 to find the optimal
  balance of space overhead vs recovery capability per workload

Additional notes:
- **Checkpoint-only writer:** In Compatibility mode, `.db-fec` is maintained only
  by checkpoint (never by transaction writers) to avoid group-level write
  contention and repair-symbol races.
- **WAL truncation ordering:** `RESTART/TRUNCATE` checkpoints must not discard
  WAL history unless `.db-fec` has been updated and `fsync`'d for affected page
  groups (Section 3.4.6). If `.db-fec` is behind, degrade to a non-truncating
  checkpoint mode.

### 21.10 Time Travel Queries and Tiered Symbol Storage (Implementation Notes)

Native mode's source of truth is an immutable commit stream (`CommitCapsule` +
`CommitMarker`). The canonical spec already includes:
- Time travel queries (§12.17: `FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF ...` including a `COMMITSEQ` form), and
- Tiered symbol storage (§3.5.11: L1/L2/L3 with fetch-on-demand under capability).

The remaining work is operational: explicit retention policy, predictable
latency control, and failure-mode hardening (idempotency + sagas; §4.19).

- **Retention policy:** Time travel is only meaningful within a configured
  history window. GC/compaction MUST remain free to drop old history unless a
  retention policy pins it.
- **Addressing:** The stable history coordinate is `commit_seq`. Timestamp-based
  APIs require persisting `commit_time` metadata per commit and an index to map
  time → `commit_seq` (under `LabRuntime`, this uses deterministic virtual time).
- **SQL surface:** FrankenSQLite supports `FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF` (§12.17) as
  the primary interface, plus `... AS OF COMMITSEQ <n>` as a stable coordinate
  that avoids timestamp ambiguity.
- **Tiered SymbolStore:** `SymbolStore` SHOULD remain pluggable with an optional
  cold backend (object storage). Remote fetch MUST require an explicit capability
  (`RemoteCap`; §4.19.1) and MUST be paired with caching and prefetching so query
  latency remains predictable.

- test_bd_3kp_1_unit_compliance_gate: concrete unit identifier for structure lint compliance.
- prop_bd_3kp_1_structure_compliance: concrete property identifier for structure lint compliance.

E2E Test:
- test_e2e_bd_3kp_1_compliance: concrete E2E identifier for structure lint compliance.

SECTION 21.1 — OPEN QUESTIONS WITH ANSWER PLANS (Q1–Q6)

Each open question represents a design decision that must be resolved empirically (via benchmarking, prototyping, or analysis) before the affected implementation phase can proceed. This bead tracks all six questions, their context, implications, answer plans, decision criteria, and verification requirements.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Q1. MULTI-PROCESS WRITERS: PERFORMANCE ENVELOPE
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Question: What is the performance envelope for cross-process concurrent writes?

Context: Section 5.6.1 specifies shared-memory coordination for multi-process MVCC. The TxnSlot array is mmap'd, with lease-based cleanup for crashed processes. The question is whether cross-process coordination overhead (mmap atomics, lease expiry polling, TxnSlot contention) is acceptable compared to the in-process baseline.

Implications for implementation:
- If cross-process overhead is >3x in-process, may need to redesign coordination (e.g., dedicated coordinator process, or restrict to single-writer-multi-reader for cross-process).
- Affects Phase 6 scope: multi-process MVCC validation gates depend on acceptable performance.
- TxnSlot count and lease intervals are tunable parameters that affect both performance and crash recovery latency.

Potential answers/approaches:
1. Implement Section 5.6.1 as specified; benchmark contention curves (1-16 writer processes, varying TxnSlot counts).
2. Compare mmap-based atomics vs Unix domain socket-based coordination vs shared-memory futex.
3. Tune lease intervals: shorter leases = faster crash recovery but higher overhead; longer leases = less overhead but slower recovery.

Decision needed before: Phase 6 (MVCC & SSI). The cross-process MVCC test gates in Phase 6 (§22) explicitly require multi-process lease expiry and TxnSlot reuse testing.

Answer plan (from spec): Implement shared-memory coordination (Section 5.6.1); benchmark contention vs in-process baseline; tune TxnSlot count and lease intervals.

- test_bd_3kp_1_unit_compliance_gate: concrete unit identifier for structure lint compliance.
- prop_bd_3kp_1_structure_compliance: concrete property identifier for structure lint compliance.
- Benchmark harness: measure TPS for 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 writer processes vs same count of in-process writer threads.
- Latency distribution comparison (P50, P99, P999) for cross-process vs in-process.
- Crash recovery test: kill writer process mid-transaction, verify lease expiry reclaims TxnSlot within configured interval.
- Verify no TxnEpoch validation failures after lease expiry + TxnSlot reuse (Phase 6 gate).

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Q2. SSI WITNESS KEY REFINEMENT: PAGE vs RANGE/CELL
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Question: How far do we go with range/cell refinement for SSI witness keys?

Context: Page-SSI (R1) is conservative — it tracks read/write witnesses at page granularity, which causes false positives when two transactions touch different rows on the same page. Refining to range or cell granularity reduces false positives but increases witness tracking overhead (more witness keys, larger witness index segments).

Implications for implementation:
- Page-only witnesses are simpler but cause higher abort rates (R1 mitigation).
- Cell-level witnesses approach PostgreSQL's row-level granularity (~0.5% false positive rate) but require B-tree cell-level tracking.
- Range witnesses are a middle ground: track key ranges within a page.
- Witness index segments grow with key count; ECS encoding overhead scales accordingly.

Potential answers/approaches:
1. Start page-only (simplest, most conservative).
2. Collect abort witness statistics in production-like benchmarks.
3. Refine to range/cell ONLY when abort rate is proven unacceptable by benchmark.
4. Measure: false positive rate at page granularity vs cell granularity; witness index segment size impact; SSI validation CPU cost.

Decision needed before: Phase 6 (MVCC & SSI). Initial implementation uses page-only; refinement decision based on Phase 6 benchmark data.

Answer plan (from spec): Start page-only; collect abort witnesses; refine only when abort rate is proven unacceptable by benchmark.

Test requirements:
- Abort rate benchmark: run OLTP workloads (TPC-C style) with page-only witnesses; measure abort rate.
- If abort rate > 5% (configurable threshold), implement range/cell refinement and re-benchmark.
- Verify SSI correctness (no write skew escapes) at all granularity levels via Mazurkiewicz trace exploration.
- Witness index segment size regression test: ensure segment size does not exceed budget at chosen granularity.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Q3. SYMBOL SIZING POLICY PER OBJECT TYPE
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Question: What is the optimal symbol sizing policy per object type (capsule vs checkpoint vs index)?

Context: RaptorQ encoding performance and overhead depend heavily on symbol size. Small symbols mean faster encoding but more symbols per object (higher metadata overhead). Large symbols mean fewer symbols but slower encoding per symbol. Different object types have different size profiles and latency requirements:
- CommitCapsules: small (typically <1KB), latency-critical (on commit path).
- CheckpointChunks: large (potentially MBs), throughput-critical (background operation).
- IndexSegments: medium, latency-sensitive for reads.

Implications for implementation:
- Symbol size directly affects R2 (RaptorQ overhead dominates CPU).
- Wrong sizing for capsules could add unacceptable latency to the commit path.
- Wrong sizing for checkpoints could make background operations too slow.
- PRAGMA overrides allow runtime experimentation.

Potential answers/approaches:
1. Capsules: small symbols (e.g., 64-256 bytes) for fast commit-path encoding.
2. Checkpoints: large symbols (e.g., 4KB-16KB) for throughput.
3. Index segments: medium symbols (e.g., 512-2048 bytes) balancing latency and throughput.
4. Benchmark encode/decode throughput vs object sizes systematically.
5. Expose PRAGMA overrides: PRAGMA fsqlite.symbol_size_capsule, PRAGMA fsqlite.symbol_size_checkpoint, etc.

Decision needed before: Phase 5 (File Format & WAL), where ECS encoding is first used in the commit path.

Answer plan (from spec): Benchmark encode/decode throughput vs object sizes; pick defaults; expose PRAGMA overrides for experiments.

Test requirements:
- Benchmark matrix: symbol sizes {64, 128, 256, 512, 1K, 2K, 4K, 8K, 16K} x object types {capsule, checkpoint, index}.
- Measure: encode throughput (MB/s), decode throughput (MB/s), commit latency impact, metadata overhead ratio.
- Verify chosen defaults via end-to-end benchmark: commit latency within 2x of no-ECS baseline.
- PRAGMA override test: verify runtime symbol size changes take effect on next encode.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Q4. COMPATIBILITY CHECKPOINT WITHOUT BOTTLENECKING WRITES
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Question: Where to checkpoint for compatibility `.db` without bottlenecking writes?

Context: Compatibility Mode (Section 7.10) maintains a standard SQLite `.db` file for interoperability. Checkpointing (copying WAL pages to the database file) can block writers in standard SQLite. With ECS-backed storage, checkpointing could use background ECS chunk operations instead of blocking the WAL.

Implications for implementation:
- Blocking checkpoints degrade write throughput.
- Background checkpoints require careful crash consistency (Section 7.9 crash contract).
- The `.db-fec` sidecar file (§21.9) adds checkpoint ordering constraints.
- Export to `.db` could be optional (not needed if only Native mode is used).

Potential answers/approaches:
1. Background checkpoint with ECS chunks: checkpoint runs as a background task that reads committed pages from ECS and writes to `.db`.
2. Measure checkpoint throughput and writer blocking time.
3. Keep export optional: only checkpoint to `.db` when PRAGMA compatibility_export=ON.
4. Use incremental checkpointing: checkpoint a few pages at a time to amortize I/O.

Decision needed before: Phase 5 (File Format & WAL), where Compatibility Mode is implemented.

Answer plan (from spec): Background checkpoint with ECS chunks; measure; keep export optional.

Test requirements:
- Benchmark: concurrent write throughput with vs without active checkpoint.
- Verify crash consistency: crash during checkpoint does not corrupt `.db` or WAL.
- Verify `.db` is valid SQLite database readable by C sqlite3 after checkpoint.
- Measure checkpoint lag: time from commit to availability in `.db`.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Q5. DETERMINISTIC REBASE: WHICH B-TREE OPERATIONS?
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Question: Which B-tree operations can be replayed deterministically for rebase merge?

Context: Intent-level rebase (Section 5.10.2) turns page-level conflicts into logical merges by replaying operations. Not all B-tree operations are deterministic under concurrent modification — page splits, merges, and defragmentation can produce different results depending on page layout.

Implications for implementation:
- Deterministic replay is critical for correctness (R7: mergeable writes correctness minefield).
- Non-deterministic operations must be excluded from rebase or handled with explicit conflict detection.
- The merge ladder (Section 5.10.4) defines which merges are safe.
- Starting small reduces risk; growing coverage increases merge success rate.

Potential answers/approaches:
1. Start with inserts/updates on leaf pages only (simplest, most deterministic).
2. Exclude: page splits, page merges, overflow page operations, defragmentation.
3. Grow coverage guided by conflict benchmarks: measure how many conflicts are resolved vs rejected.
4. For each new operation type, add proptest + DPOR tests (Section 5.10.5) before enabling.

Decision needed before: Phase 6 (MVCC & SSI), specifically the rebase merge gates in §22 (1,000 merge attempts with distinct-key inserts, zero false rejections).

Answer plan (from spec): Implement inserts/updates on leaf pages first; grow coverage guided by conflict benchmarks.

Test requirements:
- Proptest: 1,000 merge attempts with distinct-key inserts on same page, zero false rejections (Phase 6 gate).
- Structured merge safety: 1,000 merge attempts with commuting, cell-key-disjoint operations, no lost updates (Phase 6 gate).
- Negative test: B-tree lost-update counterexample (cell move/defrag vs update at old offset) must never be accepted (Phase 6 gate).
- DPOR test: verify all non-equivalent orderings for 3-transaction merge scenarios.
- Coverage expansion benchmark: for each new operation type, measure conflict resolution rate improvement.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Q6. B-LINK STYLE CONCURRENCY FOR HOT-PAGE SPLITS
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Question: Do we need B-link style concurrency for hot-page split/merge contention?

Context: When many transactions target the same index/table, B-tree internal pages experience high split/merge contention. B-link trees add right-sibling pointers and allow optimistic descent, which reduces the lock held during structural modifications.

Implications for implementation:
- If internal-page conflicts dominate the abort rate, B-link concurrency is needed.
- B-link modifications are ephemeral metadata (not file format changes) — they affect the in-memory tree structure only.
- Adds complexity to B-tree cursor implementation.
- Only needed if benchmarks show internal-page split/merge contention is a bottleneck.

Potential answers/approaches:
1. Benchmark workloads that hammer the same index/table (e.g., auto-increment inserts on right-edge pages).
2. Measure: fraction of aborts caused by internal-page structural modification operations.
3. If internal-page conflicts dominate, add: optimistic descent + right-sibling guidance + deterministic retry.
4. Protocol is inspired by B-link trees: ephemeral metadata only, no file format changes.

Decision needed before: Phase 6 (MVCC & SSI), but only if Phase 6 benchmarks show the problem. Could be deferred to a later optimization pass.

Answer plan (from spec): Benchmark workloads that hammer the same index/table. If internal-page conflicts dominate, add an internal "structure modification" protocol (ephemeral metadata, not file format changes) inspired by B-link trees: optimistic descent + right-sibling guidance + deterministic retry.

Test requirements:
- Benchmark: high-contention index workload (100+ concurrent writers inserting into same index).
- Measure: abort rate breakdown by cause (leaf conflict vs internal-page structural modification).
- If B-link protocol added: verify correctness with proptest (random concurrent inserts + deletes + splits + merges).
- Verify no lost pages after crash recovery with B-link metadata (ephemeral metadata must not corrupt persistent state).

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
CROSS-CUTTING CONCERNS
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
- All questions require benchmark infrastructure (Phase 2-3 test harness).
- Decisions should be recorded as ADRs (Architecture Decision Records) when resolved.
- Each resolved question should update this bead with the decision, rationale, and pointer to implementation bead.
- Questions Q1, Q2, Q5, Q6 cluster around Phase 6; Q3, Q4 cluster around Phase 5.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA:
- Each question has a documented decision with empirical evidence (benchmark data or analysis).
- Each decision has corresponding test gates that verify the chosen approach works.
- No question is left unresolved past its decision deadline phase.

Scoped gates pass; full workspace gates currently blocked by concurrent edits in bd-26be and mvcc formatting/clippy deltas.

## Logging Requirements (Meta)

- Maintain a decision register as an append-only log (human-readable + diff-friendly).
- Each decision entry MUST include: `decision_id`, `date`, `status` (proposed|accepted|rejected), `context`, `options_considered`, `decision`, `rationale`, and links to the affected beads/tests.
- Decisions that affect correctness (MVCC/SSI, file format, recovery) MUST link to the specific conformance or deterministic test that guards the decision.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## Unit Tests (Meta)

Even though this is a planning bead, we still need testable invariants for the decision register so it stays correct and usable.

- `test_decision_register_entry_schema`: parse a decision entry and assert required fields exist: `decision_id`, `date`, `status`, `context`, `options_considered`, `decision`, `rationale`, `links`.
- `test_decision_register_links_resolve`: each referenced bead/test link resolves (bead IDs exist; referenced test names exist once implemented).
- `test_decision_register_append_only`: ensure tooling enforces append-only semantics (no in-place mutation without explicit revision markers).

These tests should log `trace_id` and the `decision_id` for any failure so it is easy to debug.

Generate a decision-register report and verify:
- every open question (Q1..Q6) has a current status and an explicit owner bead if it blocks implementation

The report should be reproducible and diff-friendly (stable ordering).

title: §21.0 Risk Register R1–R8: Mitigations & Monitoring
description:
Unit Test Requirements:
- test_bd_3kp_2_unit_compliance_gate: concrete unit identifier for structure lint compliance.
- prop_bd_3kp_2_structure_compliance: concrete property identifier for structure lint compliance.

E2E Test:
- test_e2e_bd_3kp_2_compliance: concrete E2E identifier for structure lint compliance.

SECTION 21.0 — RISK REGISTER WITH MITIGATIONS (R1–R8)

Each risk represents a known technical hazard that could impair correctness, performance, or project viability. This bead tracks all eight risks with their full description, likelihood, impact, mitigation strategies, monitoring approaches, trigger conditions, and test requirements.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
R1. SSI ABORT RATE TOO HIGH (PAGE-SSI IS CONSERVATIVE)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
Description: Page-level SSI witnesses track read/write sets at page granularity. When two transactions touch different rows on the same page, SSI may falsely detect a conflict and abort one transaction. At scale, this false positive rate could make Serializable isolation impractical for OLTP workloads.

Likelihood: MEDIUM-HIGH. Page granularity is coarser than PostgreSQL's row-level (~0.5% false positive rate). Hot pages with many rows will see elevated false positives.

Impact: HIGH. Excessive abort rates degrade throughput, increase retry load, and may force users to drop to Snapshot Isolation (losing serializability guarantees).

Mitigation strategies (from spec):
1. Refine witness keys from page → (page, range/cell tag) to reduce false positives (Q2 decision).
2. Add safe snapshot optimizations for read-only transactions (read-only txns never cause write skew).
3. Intent-level rebase (Section 5.10.2) turns page conflicts into merges, reducing effective conflict rate by 30-60%.
4. PostgreSQL's measured false positive rate is ~0.5% at row granularity; our page granularity will be higher, but merge compensation helps.

Monitoring approach:
- E-process monitor: track abort rate per transaction type (read-only vs read-write).
- Witness statistics: count false positives (aborts where re-execution would succeed).
- Abort witness collection: for each abort, record the witness key(s) that triggered it.
- Dashboard metric: abort_rate_pct, false_positive_rate_pct, merge_compensation_rate_pct.

Trigger conditions for escalation:
- Abort rate > 5% for OLTP workloads → escalate to range/cell refinement.
- False positive rate > 2% → investigate merge compensation effectiveness.
- Merge compensation < 20% of conflicts resolved → review merge ladder (§5.10.4).

- test_bd_3kp_2_unit_compliance_gate: concrete unit identifier for structure lint compliance.
- prop_bd_3kp_2_structure_compliance: concrete property identifier for structure lint compliance.
- SSI correctness: write skew patterns produce abort under default serializable mode (Phase 6 gate).
- SSI no false negatives: no write skew anomaly escapes detection in 3-transaction Mazurkiewicz trace exploration (Phase 6 gate).
- Abort rate benchmark: OLTP workload (TPC-C style), measure abort rate at page granularity.
- Merge compensation benchmark: measure conflict resolution rate with intent-level rebase enabled vs disabled.
- Stress test: 100 concurrent writers, 100 operations each, all committed rows present, no phantom rows (Phase 6 gate).

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
R2. RAPTORQ OVERHEAD DOMINATES CPU
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
Description: RaptorQ fountain coding (used for ECS object encoding, replication, and erasure-coded storage) could consume excessive CPU on the commit path. If encoding latency exceeds the time saved by other optimizations, the ECS architecture becomes a net negative.

Likelihood: MEDIUM. GF(256) arithmetic is inherently expensive. Small objects (capsules) encode quickly; large objects (checkpoints) may dominate CPU.

Impact: HIGH. Commit-path latency directly affects transaction throughput. If encoding is on the critical path, single-writer TPS could fall far below the 3x-of-C-SQLite target.

Mitigation strategies (from spec):
1. Choose symbol sizing policy based on object type (Q3 decision): capsules use small symbols for fast commit; checkpoints use large symbols for throughput.
2. Cache decoded objects aggressively (ARC cache) to avoid redundant decoding.
3. Profile and tune encoder/decoder hot paths (one lever per change, per the Extreme Optimization methodology from §17).

Monitoring approach:
- CPU profiling: measure encode/decode time as fraction of total commit time.
- Per-object-type encode latency: capsule_encode_us, checkpoint_encode_us, index_encode_us.
- ARC cache hit rate: if high, encoding is amortized; if low, encoding dominates.
- Benchmark regression: conformal prediction (§17.8) for encode throughput.

Trigger conditions for escalation:
- Encode time > 30% of commit latency → profile hot paths, review symbol sizing.
- Single-writer TPS < 1/3 of C SQLite → investigate whether RaptorQ is the bottleneck.
- ARC cache hit rate < 80% → increase cache budget or review access patterns.

Test requirements:
- Benchmark: encode/decode throughput for each object type at various symbol sizes (Q3 test matrix).
- Commit latency test: measure end-to-end commit time with ECS encoding vs without (direct write).
- Phase 9 gate: single-writer within 3x of C SQLite.
- Regression gate: no regression compared to Phase 8 (conformal upper bound, alpha=0.01).
- Profile test: verify no single encode/decode call exceeds 10ms for capsule-sized objects.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
R3. APPEND-ONLY STORAGE GROWS WITHOUT BOUND
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
Description: The ECS object store is append-only (immutable objects). Without effective garbage collection, storage grows monotonically. MVCC version chains, SSI witness plane objects, and symbol caches all contribute to growth.

Likelihood: HIGH. Append-only is inherent to the architecture. Growth is guaranteed; the question is whether GC keeps up.

Impact: MEDIUM-HIGH. Unbounded growth exhausts disk, degrades read performance (more objects to scan), and increases backup/replication time.

Mitigation strategies (from spec):
1. Checkpoint, GC, and compaction are first-class operations (Section 5.5 for MVCC GC/version chain trimming, Section 7.13 for ECS compaction, Section 7.9 for the crash contract).
2. Enforce budgets for MVCC history, SSI witness plane, symbol caches.
3. Safe GC horizon = min(active begin_seq) (Theorem 4) bounds version chain length (Theorem 5).

Monitoring approach:
- Storage metrics: total_objects, total_bytes, objects_per_commit, gc_freed_bytes_per_cycle.
- MVCC chain length: max_chain_length, avg_chain_length (should be bounded by Theorem 5).
- GC lag: time since last GC cycle, objects pending GC.
- Budget enforcement: witness_plane_bytes, symbol_cache_bytes vs configured budgets.

Trigger conditions for escalation:
- Storage growth rate > 2x steady-state expectation → review GC frequency.
- Max chain length > 100 versions → investigate long-running transactions holding GC horizon.
- GC freed < 50% of objects created in last cycle → GC is falling behind.

Test requirements:
- GC memory bound test: memory usage under sustained load stays within 2x of minimum theoretical (active transactions * pages per transaction * page size) (Phase 6 gate).
- Crash model test: 100 crash-recovery scenarios validating self-healing durability contract (Section 7.9) (Phase 6 gate).
- Storage growth test: run sustained write workload for 1 hour, verify storage stabilizes (GC keeps up).
- Budget enforcement test: verify that exceeding configured budget triggers GC or rejects new allocations.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
R4. BOOTSTRAPPING CHICKEN-AND-EGG
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
Description: Need an index to find symbols, but need symbols to decode the index. The ECS architecture creates a circular dependency at startup: the object locator index is itself stored as ECS objects, but you need the index to find those objects.

Likelihood: LOW. The architecture has explicit mitigations.

Impact: HIGH if triggered. A corrupted or missing root pointer means the entire database is inaccessible.

Mitigation strategies (from spec):
1. Symbol records are self-describing (header + OTI — Object Transmission Information).
2. One tiny mutable root pointer per database (the only mutable state).
3. Rebuild-from-scan is always possible as a fallback (scan all symbol records, reconstruct index).

Monitoring approach:
- Root pointer integrity: checksum validation on every open.
- Startup time monitoring: if rebuild-from-scan is triggered, log it as anomalous.
- Symbol record header validation: verify OTI consistency on decode.

Trigger conditions for escalation:
- Root pointer checksum failure → trigger rebuild-from-scan.
- Rebuild-from-scan takes > 30 seconds → investigate why index was lost.
- Repeated root pointer corruption → investigate write path for root pointer.

Test requirements:
- Bootstrap test: create database, corrupt root pointer, verify rebuild-from-scan recovers all data.
- Round-trip test: encode index as ECS objects, decode from self-describing symbol records.
- Startup test: verify database opens correctly after clean shutdown, crash, and root pointer corruption.
- Performance test: measure rebuild-from-scan time for databases of various sizes (1MB, 100MB, 1GB).

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
R5. MULTI-PROCESS MVCC COORDINATION IS COMPLEX
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
Description: Cross-process MVCC requires shared-memory coordination (mmap'd TxnSlot array), lease-based cleanup for crashed processes, and careful atomics. The complexity creates risk of subtle correctness bugs (stale state, race conditions, ABA problems).

Likelihood: MEDIUM. Shared-memory coordination is well-understood but error-prone. Lease-based cleanup adds temporal complexity.

Impact: HIGH. MVCC bugs cause data corruption, lost updates, or phantom reads — all catastrophic for a database.

Mitigation strategies (from spec):
1. Shared-memory coordination protocol fully specified (Section 5.6.1).
2. Lease-based TxnSlot cleanup handles process crashes without blocking.
3. Both in-process and cross-process MVCC are validated in Phase 6.
4. Explicit tests for multi-process behaviors required before shipping.

Monitoring approach:
- TxnSlot usage: active_slots, expired_leases_reclaimed, lease_expiry_events.
- Multi-process coordination: shm_contention_events, atomic_retry_count.
- Correctness monitors: E-process invariants INV-1 through INV-7.

Trigger conditions for escalation:
- Any E-process invariant violation → stop and investigate.
- Lease expiry reclamation fails → potential ABA problem in TxnSlot reuse.
- TxnEpoch validation failure after lease expiry → stale hot-index bits binding to new TxnToken.

Test requirements:
- MVCC stress test: 100 concurrent writers, 100 operations each, all committed rows present, no phantom rows (Phase 6 gate).
- Multi-process lease expiry + TxnSlot reuse: verify TxnEpoch validation holds (Phase 6 gate).
- E-process monitors: INV-1 through INV-7, zero violations over 1M operations (Phase 6 gate).
- Crash model: kill writer processes at random points, verify lease expiry reclaims correctly.
- ABA test: rapidly reuse TxnSlots after lease expiry, verify no stale state leaks.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
R6. FILE FORMAT COMPATIBILITY VS "DO IT RIGHT"
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
Description: FrankenSQLite has two modes: Compatibility Mode (standard SQLite .db/.wal format for interoperability) and Native Mode (ECS-backed for full features). Maintaining both creates ongoing engineering burden and the risk of subtle behavioral differences.

Likelihood: MEDIUM. Dual-mode architectures are inherently complex.

Impact: MEDIUM. Users may encounter unexpected behavior differences between modes. Conformance testing burden is doubled.

Mitigation strategies (from spec):
1. Compatibility Mode (Section 7.10) treats SQLite .db/.wal as the standard format for conformance.
2. Native Mode is the innovation layer.
3. Conformance harness validates observable behavior, not byte-identical layout.

Monitoring approach:
- Conformance test pass rate: Compat mode vs Native mode vs C SQLite.
- Behavioral divergence log: any query that produces different results between modes.
- Engineering effort tracking: time spent on Compat mode maintenance vs Native mode development.

Trigger conditions for escalation:
- Conformance pass rate < 99% for Compat mode → prioritize conformance fixes.
- Behavioral divergence found → classify as bug or intentional divergence with documentation.
- Compat mode maintenance > 30% of engineering effort → consider deprecation timeline.

Test requirements:
- File format test: database created by FrankenSQLite readable by C sqlite3 (Phase 5 gate).
- File format test: database created by C sqlite3 readable by FrankenSQLite (Phase 5 gate).
- Phase 9 gate: 100% parity target across 1,000+ golden files (intentional divergences documented).
- Mode switching test: convert database between Compat and Native modes, verify data integrity.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
R7. MERGEABLE WRITES BECOME A CORRECTNESS MINEFIELD
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
Description: Intent-level rebase and structured merge (Section 5.10) allow some page-level conflicts to be automatically resolved. However, incorrect merge logic can cause lost updates, phantom rows, or corrupted B-tree structure — bugs that may not manifest until specific workload patterns trigger them.

Likelihood: MEDIUM-HIGH. Merge correctness is notoriously difficult. The space of possible merge scenarios is combinatorially large.

Impact: CRITICAL. Lost updates or corrupted B-tree structure are catastrophic — silent data corruption is the worst possible database bug.

Mitigation strategies (from spec):
1. Strict merge ladder (Section 5.10.4): only take merges we can justify with formal reasoning.
2. Proptest invariants + DPOR tests (Section 5.10.5) explore the merge state space.
3. Start with deterministic rebase replay for a small op subset (inserts/updates on leaf pages), grow coverage guided by conflict benchmarks.

Monitoring approach:
- Merge statistics: merges_attempted, merges_succeeded, merges_rejected, merges_failed.
- Correctness checks: post-merge B-tree integrity verification (key ordering, page count, overflow chain consistency).
- DPOR coverage: percentage of non-equivalent orderings explored for N-transaction scenarios.

Trigger conditions for escalation:
- Any post-merge B-tree integrity check failure → disable merge, investigate.
- Merge success rate < 50% → review whether merge ladder is too aggressive or too conservative.
- DPOR finds a counterexample → fix merge logic before re-enabling.

Test requirements:
- Rebase merge: 1,000 merge attempts with distinct-key inserts on same page, zero false rejections (Phase 6 gate).
- Structured merge safety: 1,000 merge attempts with commuting, cell-key-disjoint operations on the same page, no lost updates (Phase 6 gate).
- Negative test: B-tree lost-update counterexample (cell move/defrag vs update at old offset) must never be accepted (Phase 6 gate).
- Proptest: random merge scenarios with B-tree integrity invariants (key ordering, no duplicate keys, valid page structure).
- DPOR: exhaustive exploration of 3-transaction merge scenarios.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
R8. DISTRIBUTED MODE CORRECTNESS IS HARD
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
Description: Multi-node replication with ECS-native symbol-level replication, anti-entropy, quorum durability, and authenticated symbols is inherently complex. Distributed systems have failure modes (network partitions, split brain, Byzantine faults) that are absent in single-node operation.

Likelihood: HIGH. Distributed consensus is a known-hard problem. Even well-tested systems have subtle bugs.

Impact: HIGH. Replication bugs can cause data divergence between nodes, lost commits, or inconsistent reads.

Mitigation strategies (from spec):
1. Symbol-native replication uses "leader commit clock" as the default mode (simpler than multi-writer).
2. Use sheaf checks + TLA+ export for bounded model checking.
3. Replication protocol is ECS-native: ObjectId set reconciliation + anti-entropy.
4. Implementation phased: single-node first, then multi-node (Phase 9).

Monitoring approach:
- Replication lag: time from leader commit to follower visibility.
- Anti-entropy convergence: cycles_to_convergence, missing_objects_after_sync.
- Sheaf check results: anomalies_detected, false_positives.
- Quorum durability: quorum_ack_latency, quorum_failures.

Trigger conditions for escalation:
- Anti-entropy fails to converge within 2x expected time → investigate missing symbols.
- Sheaf check detects anomaly → halt replication, investigate.
- Quorum durability failure → potential data loss, escalate immediately.
- TLA+ model checker finds counterexample → fix protocol before deploying.

Test requirements:
- Phase 9 gate: database replicates correctly under 10% packet loss within 1.2x of no-loss time.
- Anti-entropy convergence test: introduce missing objects, verify convergence.
- Authenticated symbols: verify unauthenticated symbols are rejected.
- Sheaf check: verify anomalies are detected for known-bad replication scenarios.
- TLA+ model: bounded model checking for leader-follower replication protocol.
- Quorum durability: verify commit fails if quorum is not reached.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
CROSS-CUTTING RISK MANAGEMENT
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
Automated verification (risk register hygiene):
1. test_risks_have_unique_ids: R1..R8 unique; no renumbering without explicit note.
2. test_each_high_priority_risk_has_signal: For each risk with an empirical component (abort rate, overhead, growth), ensure a detection signal exists (benchmark/test/e-process).
3. test_each_risk_has_mitigation_pointer: Link each risk to at least one mitigation bead.

E2E review script (planned): e2e/risk_register_report.sh — emits summary table, missing signal/mitigation lists, JSONL per risk.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA:
- Every risk has at least one mitigation strategy with a corresponding test.
- Every risk has a monitoring approach and trigger conditions.
- Risk register is reviewed and updated at each phase boundary.
- No HIGH-impact risk enters a phase without at least one mitigation validated by tests.

title: §21.2–21.10 Future Work Items (9 Subsections)
description:
SECTIONS 21.2–21.10 — FUTURE WORK ITEMS (ALL 9 SUBSECTIONS)

Each future work item represents a capability or optimization that is explicitly deferred from V1 but has been specified to the level of implementation notes. This bead tracks all 9 items with their description, rationale for deferral, dependencies on current V1 work, rough scope, and prerequisites for starting.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
§21.2 CROSS-PROCESS MVCC (IMPLEMENTATION NOTES)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
What it is: Implementation notes for cross-process MVCC as specified in Section 5.6.1. This covers the mmap-based TxnSlot array, lease-based cleanup, and benchmark comparison of cross-process vs in-process coordination.

Why it's deferred: Cross-process MVCC is specified and validated in Phase 6, but the implementation notes here capture additional operational concerns (benchmark methodology, lease tuning) that extend beyond Phase 6 scope.

Dependencies on current work:
- Section 5.6.1: shared-memory coordination protocol (must be implemented first).
- Phase 6: MVCC & SSI validation gates (must pass first).
- Q1 (multi-process writer performance envelope) must be answered.

Rough scope: 2-3 weeks. Primarily benchmarking and tuning, not new implementation.

What needs to be true before starting:
- Phase 6 complete with passing MVCC gates.
- In-process MVCC stable and performant.
- Benchmark infrastructure for multi-process scenarios available.

Key implementation notes from spec:
- Phase 6 validates both in-process and cross-process MVCC correctness.
- Phase 6 gates (§22) explicitly test multi-process lease expiry and TxnSlot reuse; Phase 7 is "Advanced Query Planner", not cross-process.
- Key challenge: benchmarking the mmap-based TxnSlot array vs in-process atomics.
- Lease-based cleanup must be stress-tested under process crash scenarios.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
§21.3 WRITE-AHEAD-LOG MULTIPLEXING
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
What it is: For very high write throughput (>100K TPS), a single WAL file becomes the bottleneck (sequential append to one file). WAL multiplexing shards WAL frames across multiple files to exploit NVMe SSD parallelism.

Why it's deferred: V1 targets correctness and reasonable performance (within 3x of C SQLite). WAL multiplexing is an optimization for extreme throughput scenarios that adds significant complexity (2PC across WAL files, crash recovery for multi-WAL).

Dependencies on current work:
- Phase 5: File Format & WAL must be complete and stable.
- Single-WAL crash recovery must be rock-solid before multiplexing.
- WAL checkpoint logic must be modular enough to handle per-file checkpoint state.

Rough scope: 4-6 weeks. New WAL file management, 2PC commit protocol, multi-WAL crash recovery, benchmarking on NVMe SSDs.

What needs to be true before starting:
- Single-WAL implementation passes all Phase 5 gates (100 crash-recovery scenarios, zero data loss).
- Benchmark evidence that single WAL is the bottleneck (not RaptorQ, not MVCC, not B-tree).
- NVMe SSD test infrastructure with high queue depth available.

Key implementation details from spec:
- WAL file selected by hash(page_number) % num_wal_files.
- Each WAL file has its own checkpoint state.
- Commit requires atomic append to all WAL files touched by the transaction (2PC across WAL files).
- Crash recovery: replay prepared-but-uncommitted entries using a global commit marker in the primary WAL.
- Potential improvement in sustained write throughput on NVMe SSDs with high queue depth (actual speedup depends on workload page distribution and device parallelism; requires benchmarking).

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
§21.4 DISTRIBUTED CONSENSUS INTEGRATION
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
What it is: Integration of Raft or Paxos for multi-node replicated state, enabling true distributed database operation with leader-based writes and read replicas.

Why it's deferred: V1 focuses on single-node correctness. Distributed consensus is complex (R8) and requires the single-node implementation to be stable before adding replication. Phase 9 gates include replication under packet loss, but the consensus protocol itself is future work beyond the leader-commit-clock default.

Dependencies on current work:
- Phase 9: ECS-native replication with leader commit clock (the simpler default).
- Section 3.4.2: RaptorQ-coded replication for steady-state log shipping.
- Section 3.4.3: Snapshot shipping for new follower initialization.
- R8 mitigations must be validated (sheaf checks, TLA+ export).

Rough scope: 8-12 weeks. Raft/Paxos implementation, WAL-as-replicated-log integration, linearizable read implementation, snapshot shipping, extensive distributed testing.

What needs to be true before starting:
- Phase 9 complete with leader-commit-clock replication passing all gates.
- Anti-entropy convergence proven correct under packet loss.
- TLA+ model for leader-follower protocol has no counterexamples.
- Benchmark shows leader-commit-clock is insufficient for target use cases.

Key implementation details from spec:
- WAL entries as the replicated log.
- Leader handles all writes, followers handle reads (read replicas).
- Snapshot shipping (Section 3.4.3) for new follower initialization.
- RaptorQ-coded replication (Section 3.4.2) for steady-state log shipping.
- Challenge: linearizable reads require either reading from leader or implementing read leases.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
§21.5 GPU-ACCELERATED RAPTORQ ENCODING
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
What it is: GPU acceleration of RaptorQ encoding via compute shaders for bulk operations (full database backup, large changeset replication) where encoding is CPU-bound.

Why it's deferred: V1 uses CPU-based RaptorQ encoding. GPU acceleration is an optimization for bulk operations that requires GPU compute infrastructure (wgpu), which adds a significant dependency and platform-specific complexity.

Dependencies on current work:
- Phase 5: RaptorQ encoding/decoding must be working and profiled.
- R2 mitigations (symbol sizing, ARC cache) must be implemented first — GPU acceleration is the last resort if CPU optimizations are insufficient.
- Q3 (symbol sizing policy) must be resolved.

Rough scope: 6-8 weeks. wgpu integration, GF(256) compute shader implementation, matrix multiplication kernel, host-device data transfer optimization, benchmarking across GPU vendors.

What needs to be true before starting:
- CPU-based encoding is profiled and optimized (R2 mitigations applied).
- Benchmark evidence that encoding is still the bottleneck for bulk operations after CPU optimization.
- wgpu is mature enough for production use on target platforms.
- Source blocks large enough to benefit (K > 10,000) are common in actual workloads.

Key implementation details from spec:
- GF(256) arithmetic maps well to SIMD/GPU (each symbol byte independent).
- Matrix multiplication for intermediate symbol generation is embarrassingly parallel.
- Expected speedup: 10-50x for large source blocks (K > 10,000).
- Framework: wgpu for cross-platform GPU compute.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
§21.6 PERSISTENT MEMORY (PMEM) VFS
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
What it is: A VFS implementation for CXL-attached persistent memory (and legacy Intel Optane DCPMM) that eliminates the WAL entirely by using byte-addressable persistent storage with copy-on-write page updates.

Why it's deferred: PMEM hardware is not widely deployed. The VFS is a specialized optimization for specific hardware platforms. V1 targets general-purpose storage (SSD/HDD with standard file I/O).

Dependencies on current work:
- Phase 2: VFS trait abstraction must be general enough to support PMEM semantics.
- Phase 5: WAL implementation must be modular (PMEM VFS eliminates WAL).
- MVCC version chains (Phase 6) must support direct PMEM storage with epoch-based reclamation.

Rough scope: 6-8 weeks. PMEM VFS implementation, clflush/clwb integration, copy-on-write page management, epoch-based reclamation, PMEM-specific crash consistency testing.

What needs to be true before starting:
- VFS trait is stable and supports the operations needed for PMEM (memory-mapping, cache line flush).
- PMEM test hardware is available (CXL or Optane DCPMM).
- V1 is stable on standard storage — PMEM VFS is an incremental addition.
- Epoch-based reclamation design is validated for MVCC version chains.

Key implementation details from spec:
- Memory-map the database file directly to PMEM.
- Eliminate the WAL entirely (copy-on-write page updates with 8-byte atomic pointer swings for crash consistency).
- Use clflush/clwb instructions for cache line persistence.
- MVCC version chains stored directly in PMEM with epoch-based reclamation.
- Expected latency reduction: 10-100x for small transactions (eliminate WAL write + fsync).

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
§21.7 VECTORIZED VDBE EXECUTION
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
What it is: Replacing the current Volcano-model (row-at-a-time) VDBE execution with vectorized (batch-of-rows) execution for improved CPU utilization on analytical queries.

Why it's deferred: V1 targets correctness and SQLite compatibility. The Volcano model is simpler to implement correctly and matches C SQLite's execution model. Vectorized execution is an optimization for analytical workloads.

Dependencies on current work:
- Phase 4: VDBE implementation must be complete and correct (row-at-a-time).
- Phase 7: Query planner must be able to select between row-at-a-time and vectorized execution.
- Trigger and RETURNING clause semantics must be preserved (row-at-a-time fallback required).

Rough scope: 8-12 weeks. Vectorized operator implementations (scan, filter, aggregate, join), SIMD integration, batch memory management, fallback to row-at-a-time for triggers/RETURNING.

What needs to be true before starting:
- Phase 7 complete with all query planner gates passing.
- Benchmark evidence that analytical query performance is insufficient with Volcano model.
- SIMD abstraction layer available (portable across x86-64 and AArch64).
- Trigger and RETURNING clause behavior fully tested in row-at-a-time mode.

Key implementation details from spec:
- Column-at-a-time processing enables SIMD utilization.
- Better CPU cache behavior (fewer instruction cache misses).
- Applicable to full table scans, aggregations, and nested-loop joins.
- Expected speedup: 2-5x for analytical queries, negligible for point lookups.
- Challenge: must maintain row-at-a-time semantics for triggers and RETURNING clause.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
§21.8 COLUMN-STORE HYBRID FOR ANALYTICAL QUERIES
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
What it is: A column-store representation alongside the row-store B-tree for mixed OLTP/OLAP workloads, enabling the query planner to select the optimal storage format per query.

Why it's deferred: V1 uses row-store B-tree exclusively (matching C SQLite). Column-store adds significant complexity in maintaining consistency between two storage formats under concurrent writes.

Dependencies on current work:
- Phase 3: B-tree implementation must be complete.
- Phase 7: Query planner must support cost-based optimization to choose between row-store and column-store.
- §21.7 (Vectorized VDBE) would maximize column-store benefit but is not strictly required.

Rough scope: 10-14 weeks. Column group storage, automatic materialization, RLE and dictionary compression, query planner integration, consistency protocol for dual-store updates.

What needs to be true before starting:
- Row-store B-tree is stable and performant.
- Query planner can estimate costs for different access paths.
- Workload analysis shows significant OLAP query patterns that would benefit.
- Consistency protocol designed and formally verified (dual-store updates under concurrent writes are the main challenge).

Key implementation details from spec:
- Column groups stored in separate B-trees per column.
- Automatic materialization of frequently-scanned columns.
- RLE and dictionary compression for low-cardinality columns.
- Query planner selects row-store or column-store based on query pattern.
- Challenge: maintaining consistency between row-store and column-store under concurrent writes.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
§21.9 ERASURE-CODED PAGE STORAGE (IMPLEMENTATION NOTES)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
What it is: Implementation notes for erasure-coded page storage as specified in Section 3.4.6. This covers modified page allocation (group allocation), repair page storage, read path with erasure recovery fallback, and group size selection.

Why it's deferred: The spec (Section 3.4.6) defines the correctness constraints, but the implementation details (group size selection, checkpoint-only writer policy, WAL truncation ordering) require benchmarking and tuning that is beyond V1 scope.

Dependencies on current work:
- Section 3.4.6: Erasure-coded page storage specification (normative).
- Phase 5: File format and WAL implementation.
- RaptorQ encoding (Phase 5) must be working for page-level erasure coding.
- Compatibility Mode checkpoint logic must support .db-fec sidecar.

Rough scope: 4-6 weeks. Group allocation, .db-fec sidecar file management, erasure recovery read path, group size benchmarking (G=32, 64, 128), checkpoint-only writer enforcement.

What needs to be true before starting:
- Phase 5 complete with standard page storage working.
- RaptorQ encoding profiled and optimized (R2 mitigations applied).
- Checkpoint logic stable and modular.
- Benchmark infrastructure for measuring space overhead vs recovery capability.

Key implementation details from spec:
- Modified page allocation: allocate G pages as a group.
- Repair page storage: in the ECS object store (Native mode) or in a foo.db-fec sidecar file (Compatibility mode).
- Read path: attempt source page first, fall back to erasure recovery.
- Group size selection: benchmark G=32, G=64, G=128 to find optimal balance.
- Checkpoint-only writer: In Compatibility mode, .db-fec is maintained only by checkpoint (never by transaction writers) to avoid group-level write contention and repair-symbol races.
- WAL truncation ordering: RESTART/TRUNCATE checkpoints must not discard WAL history unless .db-fec has been updated and fsync'd for affected page groups (Section 3.4.6). If .db-fec is behind, degrade to non-truncating checkpoint mode.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
§21.10 TIME TRAVEL QUERIES AND TIERED SYMBOL STORAGE
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
What it is: Implementation notes for time travel queries (FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF) and tiered symbol storage (L1/L2/L3 with fetch-on-demand). The canonical spec already includes these features (§12.17 and §3.5.11); the remaining work is operational.

Why it's deferred: The features are specified but the operational aspects (retention policy, latency control, failure-mode hardening with idempotency + sagas per §4.19) require production experience to tune correctly.

Dependencies on current work:
- §12.17: Time travel queries (FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF) — SQL surface specified.
- §3.5.11: Tiered symbol storage (L1/L2/L3) — architecture specified.
- §4.19: Idempotency + sagas for failure-mode hardening.
- Phase 5+: ECS object store with immutable commit stream (CommitCapsule + CommitMarker).

Rough scope: 6-8 weeks. Retention policy implementation, commit_time metadata persistence, time-to-commit_seq index, tiered SymbolStore with cold backend, RemoteCap enforcement, caching/prefetching for predictable latency.

What needs to be true before starting:
- ECS object store stable with immutable commit stream.
- GC/compaction respects retention policy (can pin old history).
- LabRuntime supports deterministic virtual time for testing.
- Object storage backend available for cold tier (S3-compatible or similar).

Key implementation details from spec:
- Retention policy: Time travel is only meaningful within a configured history window. GC/compaction MUST remain free to drop old history unless a retention policy pins it.
- Addressing: The stable history coordinate is commit_seq. Timestamp-based APIs require persisting commit_time metadata per commit and an index to map time to commit_seq (under LabRuntime, this uses deterministic virtual time).
- SQL surface: FrankenSQLite supports FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF (§12.17) as the primary interface, plus ... AS OF COMMITSEQ <n> as a stable coordinate that avoids timestamp ambiguity.
- Tiered SymbolStore: SymbolStore SHOULD remain pluggable with an optional cold backend (object storage). Remote fetch MUST require an explicit capability (RemoteCap; §4.19.1) and MUST be paired with caching and prefetching so query latency remains predictable.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
CROSS-CUTTING CONCERNS
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
- All 9 future work items depend on V1 being complete and stable.
- Items §21.2-§21.3 are closest to V1 (extensions of Phase 5-6 work).
- Items §21.4-§21.6 require external infrastructure (distributed systems, GPU, PMEM hardware).
- Items §21.7-§21.8 are query execution optimizations (post-Phase 7).
- Items §21.9-§21.10 are storage layer enhancements (post-Phase 5).
- Prioritization should be driven by user workload analysis and benchmark evidence.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA:
- Each future work item has a clear description of what it is and why it's deferred.
- Each item has documented dependencies on V1 work.
- Each item has prerequisites that must be true before starting.
- No future work item is started before its prerequisites are met.
- Scope estimates are updated as V1 implementation provides better data.

comments.text:
## Task: Collect top-20 beads.db files from /dp via sqlite3 .backup

### What
Copy the 20 largest beads.db files from /dp projects into `sample_sqlite_db_files/golden/` using SQLite's `.backup` command for consistency.

### Why .backup instead of cp
Some databases have active WAL/SHM files (8 identified). A raw `cp` could capture a torn state. The `.backup` command performs a consistent snapshot regardless of WAL state.

### Source databases (top 20 by size)
1. flywheel_connectors (17 MB)
2. flywheel_gateway (13 MB)
3. asupersync (12 MB)
4. jeffreys-skills.md (11 MB)
5. meta_skill (9.6 MB)
6. frankensqlite (9.5 MB)
7. destructive_command_guard (9.4 MB)
8. remote_compilation_helper (9.3 MB)
9. brenner_bot (8.3 MB)
10. jeffreysprompts_premium (8 MB)
11. frankentui (7.7 MB)
12. coding_agent_session_search (7.7 MB)
13. agentic_coding_flywheel_setup (7.6 MB)
14. flywheel_private (7 MB)
15. ntm (6.8 MB)
16. repo_updater (4.4 MB)
17. beads_rust (3.9 MB — use the .backup file if available)
18. process_triage (3 MB)
19. dp-level beads (2.8 MB)
20. mcp_agent_mail (1.4 MB)

### Method
```bash
for db in <source_list>; do
    name=$(basename $(dirname $(dirname $db)))
    sqlite3 "$db" ".backup 'sample_sqlite_db_files/golden/${name}.db'"
done
```

### Naming Convention
Files named after their project: `flywheel_connectors.db`, `asupersync.db`, etc.

### Acceptance Criteria
- 20 database files in golden/
- Each created via .backup (not raw cp)
- Total corpus ~170+ MB of real-world data
- No WAL/SHM files alongside golden copies (backup produces clean database)

# PARITY-B5: Comprehensive unit tests for INSERT + IPK codegen paths

## Context

The existing IPK test coverage is asymmetric: SELECT paths have tests
(`test_codegen_select_ipk_column_uses_rowid_opcode`, `test_codegen_select_star_uses_rowid_for_ipk_column`
at codegen.rs:4179+) but INSERT paths have ZERO codegen-level tests for IPK handling.

This bead covers writing comprehensive unit tests at TWO levels:
1. **Codegen-level tests** in `crates/fsqlite-vdbe/src/codegen.rs` (opcode verification)
2. **Connection-level tests** in `crates/fsqlite/src/lib.rs` and `crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs`

## Test Matrix

### Level 1: Codegen Opcode Verification (in codegen.rs #[cfg(test)])

These verify the BYTECODE is correct (not execution results):

| Test | Verifies |
|------|----------|
| `test_codegen_insert_values_ipk_uses_value_as_rowid` | No NewRowid when IPK value is non-NULL literal |
| `test_codegen_insert_values_ipk_null_uses_newrowid` | NewRowid emitted when IPK value is NULL |
| `test_codegen_insert_values_no_ipk_uses_newrowid` | NewRowid emitted for tables WITHOUT IPK |
| `test_codegen_insert_select_ipk_uses_value_as_rowid` | INSERT SELECT routes IPK from source |
| `test_codegen_insert_values_multi_row_ipk` | Each row independently routes IPK |

### Level 2: Connection-Level End-to-End (in lib.rs or connection.rs #[cfg(test)])

These verify CORRECT RESULTS through the full stack:

| Test | SQL | Expected Result |
|------|-----|-----------------|
| `test_insert_ipk_explicit_value` | `INSERT VALUES (42, 'x'); SELECT id` | 42 |
| `test_insert_ipk_null_autoincrement` | `INSERT VALUES (NULL, 'x'); SELECT id` | auto (>0) |
| `test_insert_ipk_multiple_rows` | `INSERT VALUES (10,'a'),(20,'b'),(30,'c'); SELECT id ORDER BY id` | [10, 20, 30] |
| `test_insert_ipk_column_list_reorder` | `INSERT INTO t(name,id) VALUES('x',42); SELECT id` | 42 |
| `test_insert_ipk_column_list_omitted` | `INSERT INTO t(name) VALUES('x'); SELECT id` | auto |
| `test_insert_ipk_zero_value` | `INSERT VALUES (0, 'x'); SELECT id` | 0 |
| `test_insert_ipk_negative_value` | `INSERT VALUES (-5, 'x'); SELECT id` | -5 |
| `test_insert_ipk_max_i64` | `INSERT VALUES (9223372036854775807, 'x'); SELECT id` | i64::MAX |
| `test_insert_select_preserves_ipk` | `INSERT INTO t2 SELECT * FROM t; SELECT id FROM t2` | same ids |
| `test_insert_ipk_returning_id` | `INSERT VALUES (42, 'x') RETURNING id` | 42 |
| `test_insert_ipk_returning_star` | `INSERT VALUES (42, 'x') RETURNING *` | [42, 'x'] |
| `test_insert_ipk_returning_rowid` | `INSERT VALUES (42, 'x') RETURNING rowid` | 42 |
| `test_insert_ipk_delete_reinsert` | `INSERT (1,'a'); DELETE WHERE id=1; INSERT (1,'b'); SELECT id` | 1 |
| `test_insert_ipk_duplicate_fails` | `INSERT (1,'a'); INSERT (1,'b')` | PK violation error |

### Level 3: Interaction Tests

| Test | Verifies |
|------|----------|
| `test_insert_ipk_with_rollback` | After ROLLBACK, IPK rows are gone |
| `test_insert_ipk_with_savepoint` | Savepoint + rollback to + re-insert |
| `test_insert_ipk_group_by` | GROUP BY on IPK column with correct values |
| `test_insert_ipk_order_by` | ORDER BY on IPK column |
| `test_insert_ipk_where_filter` | WHERE id = 42 finds the row |
| `test_insert_ipk_in_predicate` | WHERE id IN (1,2,3) finds correct rows |

## Where to Add Tests

- Codegen-level: `crates/fsqlite-vdbe/src/codegen.rs` at the end of the existing `#[cfg(test)]`
  module (after line 4216 where the SELECT IPK tests live)
- Connection-level: `crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs` in the existing test module
  (where `test_group_by_rowid_alias_variants` lives)
- Public API level: `crates/fsqlite/src/lib.rs` in the existing test module
  (near `probe_insert_returning_rowid`)

## Acceptance Criteria

- All tests in the matrix above are implemented and passing
- No test uses `#[ignore]` (all must be live)
- Tests cover all three INSERT paths: VALUES, SELECT, DEFAULT VALUES
- Tests cover NULL, explicit value, column list, multi-row, and edge cases
- cargo clippy passes (no new warnings)

## Dependencies

Blocked by B1 (bd-13b8), B2 (bd-1kwn), B3 (bd-hhcs), B4 (bd-1kqz) — all fixes must land first.
