comments.text:
FIX LOCATION PINNED (merge approach, user-chosen). The merge must re-read the durable freelist UNDER the flusher's cross-connection write serialization, then patch the batch frames. Why it is deep:
- Group commit: first writer to arrive becomes the FLUSHER and writes ALL accumulated batches in one consolidated I/O (group_commit.rs:16-22). The leak is two flushers (connection A FLUSHING while B enters a new FILLING->FLUSHING) overlapping: B's erasure-guard gate-read (pager.rs:20478) happens BEFORE B's flusher write, so it misses A's concurrently-completing frees. The per-Arc physical_lock_window (20317) does NOT serialize flushers cross-connection.
- The write serialization is inside prepare_persisted_epoch (pager.rs:1937) -> the ParallelWalDurabilityRequest / durability combiner. input.batches is IMMUTABLE there.
- FrameSubmission.page_data is PRE-checksum (checksums computed at append, group_commit.rs:1724), so patching a page-1 frame + injecting a trunk FrameSubmission is mechanically safe IF done before the consolidated write.

MERGE IMPLEMENTATION PLAN (prepend-trunk, no re-serialization of the existing chain, no double-grant):
1. Under the flusher's write serialization (inside/just-before the consolidated write in prepare_persisted_epoch's combiner path), for the freelist-publishing batch: re-read the fresh durable page-1 freelist via read_page_at_appended_tail (now truly current, post-peer-flush).
2. missing = fresh_current (<= committed_db_size) - batch.published_durable_freelist - batch.consumed_freelist_pages - {pages in batch.frames}. Exclude page 1.
3. If missing empty: no-op. If missing fits one trunk (len-1 <= max_leaf_entries): pick trunk=missing[0], build trunk bytes {next=old_first_trunk, count=len-1, leaves=missing[1..]}, INJECT FrameSubmission{trunk, bytes, db_size_if_commit:0} before the commit frame, PATCH page-1 frame [32..36]=trunk [36..40]=old_total+len, extend published_durable_freelist. If it overflows one trunk (rare): fall back to BusySnapshot refuse (retry) for that batch.

RISK: this is the consolidated-flush path (project core). Requires making the batch mutable at the fresh-read point, careful ordering vs the combiner, and correct handling of multi-batch flush groups (only the publishing batch(es) merge; multi-publication already refuses at 9437). VALIDATION: churn_acceptance_corruption_family FSQLITE_CHURN_SCALE=large, 0 fails / >=20 runs, AND the full pager+e2e concurrency suites (no new deadlock/livelock). This is a focused, careful multi-hour effort with a slow validation loop; NOT a safe rushed one-turn patch.

comments.text:
ROOT CAUSE DECISIVELY PINNED (redirects the whole investigation): the dominant "page N never used" leak is an ALLOCATION-leak, NOT a free-leak.

EVIDENCE: inspected the leaked pages' CONTENT in a captured leak DB (/data/tmp/.tmp5kMGgI page-22 family): pages 22,23,24,25 are ALL ZEROED (type_byte=0, non_zero_bytes=0, all-zero 4096B). Stock oracle agrees "never used". Zeroed => the page was NEVER written and NEVER freed — db_size (page_count) grew to include it and it orphaned. RH4FREEGHOST=0 across runs confirms the free path (#2 stale-index) is OUT; page invisible to all freelist probes confirms it was never freed.

MECHANISM (code-confirmed) = bd-vnxjd ABANDONED-EOF-RESERVATION pool CLEARED AT CHECKPOINT WITHOUT FOLDING:
- A CONCURRENT/WAL txn allocates pages from EOF (db_size grows in its view), then abandons them (rollback / unused allocation). restore_uncommitted_allocations_for_clean_commit (pager.rs:18920-18940) parks them in inner.abandoned_eof_reservations, deferring the fold to "the next WAL commit".
- The commit fold (pager.rs:22592-22652) only folds pool pages <= committed_db_size (frameless => reclaim into pending_free_pages -> durable freelist). Pool pages ABOVE committed_db_size stay in the (per-connection) pool for a later commit.
- THE HOLE: the checkpoint clears the pool unconditionally — MaintenanceActivityGuard::drop (pager.rs:13024, also 13129, 25274): `inner.checkpoint_active = false; inner.abandoned_eof_reservations.clear();`. Any pool page not yet folded (the connection's TAIL, or a page a peer grew db_size past while the owning connection never committed again) is DISCARDED. The checkpointed db_size includes it but the freelist does not -> zeroed "never used". The bd-vnxjd "next commit folds it" assumption fails when there is no next commit before checkpoint/close.

FIX DIRECTION (deep, checkpoint/db_size path — design carefully, do NOT rush like the reverted merge): before the checkpoint clears the pool, FOLD its <=db_size frameless pages into the durable freelist (symmetric to the commit fold, but the clear is in a SYNC Drop guard so the fold must happen in the async checkpoint op before completion); OR refine the bd-vnxjd db_size floor so db_size never advances past an abandoned-but-unwritten page that is not covered by a peer's committed frame. VALIDATION: churn 0-fail/>=20 runs (the leaked pages must reach the freelist; keep the alloc-leak-detecting KEEP_DB inspection in the harness). RH4FREEGHOST probe (238fe6cdd) is now known to target the WRONG (free) path — it correctly RULED OUT the free hypothesis; leave it (inert) or remove in the fix.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
FIX LANDED fe99bf9b9 (checkpoint fold, VALIDATION RUNNING brsx45xvn 24 runs). This is the ALLOC-LEAK fix at the RIGHT layer (not the reverted publication-path merge).

Mechanism (recap): "page N never used" = zeroed page <= db_size, neither in a b-tree nor on the freelist (verified: pages 22-25 all-zero in the captured leak DB). Abandoned-EOF reservations parked in the per-connection pool, checkpoint clears the pool without folding the tail -> orphaned holes.

FIX: SimplePager::fold_zero_holes_into_durable_freelist, called in checkpoint() after wal.checkpoint applies frames, under the exclusive maintenance fence, before the guard Drop clears the pool. Scans pages 2..=db_size of the checkpointed main image; any page that is entirely zero AND not already on the durable freelist is prepended as a new freelist trunk (chained if > one trunk's leaves), page-1 head/count patched, synced FULL, and reflected in inner.freelist via return_pages_to_freelist.

SAFE BY CONSTRUCTION (addresses the merge-revert lesson): a live b-tree/overflow page is never all-zero, so ONLY provable allocation holes are folded -> can NEVER free a live page (no double-grant); worst case a hole is missed (no regression). Cross-connection COMPLETE (scans durable content, not a per-connection pool -> catches holes any connection abandoned). Best-effort: a repair error logs + leaves holes for the next checkpoint (does not fail the checkpoint). Compiles clean (fsqlite-pager 9.89s).

PERF NOTE: the scan is O(db_size) reads per checkpoint. Acceptable for the churn (infrequent checkpoints). Follow-up optimization if a benchmark flags it: gate the scan (e.g., only when db_size > freelist+high-water, or track a suspected-hole high-water), or bound the range. title: unixepoch(X,'subsec') drops fractional seconds: returns truncated integer instead of real
close_reason: Fixed (commit pending): strftime %F + unixepoch subsec fractional. Tests un-ignored & passing; fmt+clippy clean.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
# unixepoch(X,'subsec') drops fractional seconds

## Symptom
With the `'subsec'` modifier, `unixepoch()` should return a REAL with the
fractional seconds; frank returns a truncated INTEGER.
```sql
SELECT unixepoch('2023-06-15 12:30:45.500', 'subsec');
-- SQLite: 1686832245.5   frank: 1686832245   (WRONG)
SELECT unixepoch('2023-06-15 12:30:45');   -- both 1686832245 (OK, no subsec)
```
`datetime(..., 'subsec')`, `time(..., 'subsec')`, and `strftime('%f', ...)` all
keep fractional seconds correctly in frank — only `unixepoch` ignores the flag.

## Root cause
`crates/fsqlite-func/src/datetime.rs`: `apply_modifiers` (:550) tracks a `subsec`
bool (the flag is a no-op on the JDN, set at :555/:487). The `datetime`/`time`
formatters consult that flag, but the `unixepoch` builtin returns
`Integer(seconds)` unconditionally and never widens to `Float(seconds)` when
`subsec` is set. Thread the flag into the unixepoch result: when subsec is on,
return `Float` with the fractional part (3 decimal places, as SQLite does).

title: N1: Cranelift IR lowering for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE VDBE programs
acceptance_criteria: Cranelift IR lowering compiles INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE VDBE programs; differential test proves identical results and side effects vs the interpreter on the DML conformance corpus; fallback to interpreter on unsupported opcodes.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## What
Translate VDBE programs for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE into Cranelift IR. Each opcode becomes one or more Cranelift instructions:
- Integer/String8/Null → immediate loads
- MakeRecord → inline serialization code (no function call)
- Insert → direct call to B-tree insert API
- SeekRowid → direct call to cursor seek
- Comparison → native cmp + branch

## Where
- New file: crates/fsqlite-vdbe/src/jit.rs
- Integration: crates/fsqlite-vdbe/src/engine.rs — before execute loop, check if JIT version exists
- Crate dep: cranelift-codegen, cranelift-frontend, cranelift-module

## Scope: Only INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE with no subqueries, no triggers, no RETURNING
Complex queries remain interpreted. This covers the hot path that matters most.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. JIT-compiled INSERT matches interpreted INSERT results (proptest)
2. INSERT benchmark: ≥ 15% faster for repeated prepared statements
3. JIT compilation time: < 1 ms per statement (amortized over 3+ executions)
4. No unsafe code in JIT bridge (Cranelift manages the native code)

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: TRIAGE 2026-06-29 (Opus 4.8): a DIFFERENT JIT already exists — crates/fsqlite-vdbe/src/jit.rs is a TEMPLATE-FUSION JIT (compiles recognized VDBE patterns into specialized closures/templates that skip the interpreter dispatch loop; NOT runtime machine-code gen) and is engaged via engine.rs JitCacheEntry/JitRuntimeState. There is NO cranelift dependency. So this bead's 'Cranelift IR lowering' (real machine-code JIT for DML programs) is FROM-SCRATCH: add the cranelift dep, lower INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE VDBE opcodes to Cranelift IR, JIT-compile + cache, fall back to the interpreter/template-JIT for unsupported shapes. description: Follow-up to bd-p0xje (multi-table UPDATE...FROM JOIN/comma DONE in this session). codegen_update_from now supports N named-table FROM sources (JOIN/comma, INNER/CROSS), but a FROM source that is a SUBQUERY or TABLE-FUNCTION still errors ('UPDATE ... title: GH #236 PRAGMA reverse_unordered_selects: readback + actually reverse unordered scans
description:
GH issue https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/frankensqlite/issues/236 — verified OPEN, zero implementation (`rg reverse_unordered_selects crates/` returns nothing).

## Oracle behavior (sqlite3 3.46.1)
- `PRAGMA reverse_unordered_selects=ON;` emits **no rows** (needs `PragmaOutput::NoRows` from bd-ji5oe).
- Bare `PRAGMA reverse_unordered_selects;` returns one integer row, 0 or 1. Default 0.
- Semantics: when enabled, any scan whose row order is not constrained by the query (no ORDER BY, no index-imposed order the planner is relying on) is walked in the opposite direction. It is a *test* knob, deliberately designed to shake out queries that accidentally depend on unspecified order — so it must affect real scan direction, not just readback.

## Two-part fix
1. **Readback** (cheap): `reverse_unordered_selects: bool` on `ConnectionPragmaState` + `apply_bool_toggle`-shaped handler in crates/fsqlite-vdbe/src/lib.rs. Assignment must emit no rows.
2. **Effect** (the real work): thread the flag into the planner/codegen so a full-table or full-index scan with no ordering requirement emits a reverse cursor walk (Last/Prev instead of Rewind/Next). This is the part that makes the GH validation ('records baseline scan order, enables the pragma, compares readback AND resulting sequence with SQLite') actually pass.

Do NOT close #236 on readback alone — the issue title explicitly says 'has no effect and no readback' and the reporter's test compares the row sequence.

title: EPIC: Matrix dominance program — fused transaction entry, immutable metadata publication, and per-core parallel WAL
description:
## Goal
Drive FrankenSQLite toward decisive benchmark superiority over legacy SQLite across the canonical matrix by attacking the three structural bottlenecks that the latest local evidence says still dominate the engine:
1. duplicated prepared-DML transaction-boundary work,
2. expensive hot-metadata publication and refresh choreography,
3. centralized-ish WAL durability/publication behavior that still limits multi-writer scaling.

This epic is a program overlay, not a duplicate architecture track. It ties together the already-existing `db300`, `track6`, and `3wop3` beads into one explicit performance strategy with measurable before/after gates.

## Why This Exists
The most recent local weak-cell evidence says the engine is still bleeding time in control-plane work rather than row execution. In the current `release-perf` artifact for `commutative_inserts_disjoint_keys / c1 / single-writer`, `boundary_coordination` is about `40.10ms` while `body_execution_time` is about `2.25ms`. The same artifact family still shows `prepared_schema_refreshes = 50` and `pager_publication_refreshes = 52`, which strongly suggests that the common prepared DML lane is re-paying freshness/publication costs that should be fused into one transaction-entry proof.

The direct transaction API alone was not enough. A pager begin fast-path plus commit-side fingerprint bookkeeping helped, but only modestly. That means the next gains require architecture work, not cosmetic micro-optimizations.

1. Pillar A is encoded as detailed beads covering measurement, design, implementation, invalidation or fallback rules, relevant compatibility reruns for prepared DML, and matrix verification for the fused prepared-DML entry path.
2. Pillar B is encoded as detailed beads covering metadata-class inventory, primitive selection, immutable publication implementation, reclamation or retry rules, operator-visible diagnostics, relevant compatibility reruns for metadata-bound reads, and topology or interference evidence.
3. Pillar C is encoded as detailed beads covering parallel WAL design, per-core append staging, durability or publication handoff, recovery or checkpoint semantics, WAL-compatibility reruns, and failure-injection plus matrix verification.
4. Each pillar names the exact baseline comparator it is trying to beat, the relevant conformance or API surfaces that must remain intact, and the verification artifacts required to claim success.
5. The final scorecard states not just which cells improved, but also whether any user-visible semantics, compatibility surfaces, fallback behavior, or diagnosability got worse.
6. The performance-program subgraph added for this epic remains acyclic and self-contained enough that a future agent can execute the program without reopening this conversation, even if unrelated legacy cycles still exist elsewhere in the repository.

Future-self intent:
- This is the explicit answer to the question "what are we missing for magnificent gains?"
- The answer is not one more parser tweak. The answer is that the common path still spends too much time proving the same truth multiple times and too much of the concurrency substrate still publishes truth too expensively.
- Use this epic to keep the work honest: if a proposed optimization does not reduce boundary cost, metadata read cost, or WAL publication cost on the canonical matrix, it is probably not the next best use of time.

title: Track P: Software Prefetching + Cache-Line Optimization — Hide Memory Latency in B-tree Descent

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## Problem (from extreme-software-optimization ADVANCED.md)
B-tree descent is a pointer-chasing pattern: load page → find child pointer → load next page. Each page load that misses L1/L2 cache costs ~50 ns (L3) to ~100 ns (DRAM). With 3 levels, that's 150-300 ns of stall time where the CPU does nothing.

## Solution: Software Prefetch Hints
While processing the current interior node (binary search), issue a prefetch hint for the likely child page. By the time binary search completes and we need the child page, it's already in L1/L2 cache.

## How
1. After loading an interior page, before binary search: estimate likely child page
2. For sequential insert (rightmost): prefetch rightmost child (100% prediction accuracy)
3. For random insert: prefetch BOTH children at the midpoint (50% hit rate, still saves 25 ns average)
4. Use _mm_prefetch(ptr, _MM_HINT_T0) for L1 prefetch

## Alien Graveyard Reference: §7.16 Masstree (prefetch-aware node layout)

## Expected Impact: -0.05 to -0.15 µs per INSERT (hides L3/DRAM latency for page loads)

## Additional: Cache-Line-Aligned B-tree Nodes
Ensure B-tree node headers and cell pointer arrays are aligned to 64-byte cache line boundaries. This prevents false sharing and ensures the hot search region fits in 1-2 cache lines.

title: PERF-P0: correlated EXISTS subquery is ~26,000x slower than C SQLite at 10k rows (~427ms/exec) — naive nested re-execution, unmasked by the bd-czzlp cache-defeat fix
description:
Receipt (2026-07-27, WildFrog): comprehensive-bench --quick --filter subquery, debug profile, rch worker hz1 (diagnostic-only provenance, but the magnitude is 5 orders — not noise). Parameter-varying EXISTS row (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM products p WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM categories c WHERE c.id = p.category_id AND c.id <= ?1), threshold varied per iteration to defeat the retained result cache):

  rows=100:    C=20.0us  F=14.76ms  (~740x)
  rows=1000:   C=16.3us  F=155.68ms (~9,500x)
  rows=10000:  C=16.1us  F=4.27s over 10 iters = ~427ms/exec (~26,000x)

Scaling is ~linear in (products x categories) => per-outer-row re-execution of the inner subquery as a full scan of categories: no early-termination on first match, no INTEGER PRIMARY KEY probe (c.id = p.category_id is a rowid lookup C SQLite serves in O(1)). C SQLite additionally rewrites the whole shape into an index-assisted skip; F appears to run a naive O(N*M) nested loop, possibly through the interpreted compatibility path.

Same section's other rows are HEALTHY (scalar subquery + CTE+JOIN are F-faster: 48.6us vs 84.6us at 10k; 92.7us vs 330us CTE), so this is subquery-execution-specific, not general read regression. The IN (subquery) sibling is bd-2dgf5 (~89x, planner full-scan, in_progress) — related but distinct shape: EXISTS here is CORRELATED (references outer p.category_id), so the fix likely needs (a) rowid/PK probe for c.id = p.category_id, (b) EXISTS early-termination, and/or (c) decorrelation to semi-join. Check EXPLAIN on both engines first; note bd-jyyae (CLOSED) fixed EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN lying about SEARCH vs SCAN, so EXPLAIN output is now trustworthy for this.

History: this was invisible before the parameter-varying rewrite of the EXISTS row (the constant-threshold shape hit the retained autocommit count/sum cache after warmup and reported ~70ns 'wins'). First honest measurement of this shape in the matrix.
close_reason: FIXED at fa85adfc. Root cause was ROUTING, not execution: two connection.rs gates sent the parameterized shape to the per-outer-row nested-statement fallback solely because the subquery contained ?1 — Gate A (exists_subquery_supported_by_vdbe :72633 blanket placeholder rejection under frankensim-kl17o, firing before its own semijoin-shape check) and Gate B (select_correlated_exists_where_requires_fallback, whose only escape required an integer-literal rowid bound via select_rowid_upper_bound_exclusive :7797). The fallback = clone subquery AST + substitute outer value + full execute_statement per outer row (~43us x 10k = ~427ms/exec). The compiled CountIndexEqRun semijoin already handled placeholders natively (Opcode::Variable, rebound per execution). Fix: shape-scoped carve-outs at both gates via the existing correlated_exists_matches_count_semijoin_shape predicate; known-bad multi-correlated-term family stays on fallback; kl17o stands for everything else. RECEIPTS: new test (compiled program with CountIndexEqRun+Variable, correct across 4 rebinds, aggregate + non-aggregate); 242-test adjacency battery green (1 solo-green load-flake in an unrelated copy-profile test); clippy --lib -D warnings green; paired same-host pre/post bench: EXISTS rows 14.76ms/155.68ms/~427ms-per-exec -> 366.9us/461.1us/190.1us at 100/1k/10k (artifacts exists-semijoin-fix-20260728T0230Z-hz1 + subq-oracle-receipt-20260727T2345Z-hz1, both in-repo). Scaling inversion eliminated; residual ~9-22x is debug-profile + per-sample bridge entry, not algorithmic. Remaining siblings: IN-subquery ~600x at 10k = bd-2dgf5; general recursive CTE ~33x visible in the same receipt.

comments.text:
# PARITY-C1: Verify WHERE/ORDER/GROUP on IPK columns after INSERT fix

## Context

After PARITY-B fixes INSERT IPK handling, this task verifies that query operations on IPK
columns work correctly. The hypothesis is that these operations already work and the test
failures were caused by wrong INSERT values, not wrong query codegen.

## Verification Steps

1. Re-run `test_group_by_rowid_alias_variants` (the currently failing test in fsqlite-core)
2. If it passes: this task is done (close with "verified — INSERT fix resolved GROUP BY")
3. If it fails: investigate GROUP BY codegen for IPK-specific issues and create follow-up tasks

## Additional Verification Matrix

Run these queries after inserting rows with explicit IPK values:

```sql
CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, cat TEXT, val INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (10, 'a', 1), (20, 'a', 2), (30, 'b', 3);

-- WHERE on IPK
SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = 20;            -- should return (20, 'a', 2)
SELECT * FROM t WHERE id > 15;            -- should return (20, 'a', 2), (30, 'b', 3)
SELECT * FROM t WHERE id IN (10, 30);     -- should return (10, 'a', 1), (30, 'b', 3)
SELECT * FROM t WHERE id BETWEEN 10 AND 25; -- should return (10, 'a', 1), (20, 'a', 2)

-- ORDER BY on IPK
SELECT * FROM t ORDER BY id ASC;          -- 10, 20, 30
SELECT * FROM t ORDER BY id DESC;         -- 30, 20, 10

-- GROUP BY on IPK
SELECT id, COUNT(*) FROM t GROUP BY id;   -- (10,1), (20,1), (30,1)

-- Aggregate with IPK in expression
SELECT MAX(id), MIN(id) FROM t;           -- 30, 10
SELECT id + 1 FROM t;                     -- 11, 21, 31

-- IPK in subquery
SELECT * FROM t WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM t WHERE val > 1);  -- (20,'a',2), (30,'b',3)
```

## If Tests Fail After INSERT Fix

If any of the above fail, investigate:
1. `emit_expr` for column references — does it dispatch to Rowid for IPK?
2. `emit_where_clause` — does it resolve IPK correctly in predicates?
3. `codegen_order_by` — does sort key extraction use Rowid for IPK?
4. `codegen_group_by` — does grouping key extraction use Rowid for IPK?

Create targeted fix beads for each failing path.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `test_group_by_rowid_alias_variants` passes
- All verification queries above return correct results
- No regressions in existing WHERE/ORDER/GROUP tests

## Dependencies

Blocked by B1 (bd-13b8) and B5 (bd-3l6e) — INSERT fixes and tests must land first.

title: RCH-BLOCKER: remote release-perf builds exit 0 but return no binary (2 files/524 bytes), leaving a stale artifact in place — silent stale-bench hazard
description:
Reproduced twice this session on two different workers.

RUN 1: RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1 rch exec -- cargo build --profile release-perf -p fsqlite-e2e --bin comprehensive-bench
  -> [RCH] remote hz2 (532.3s), exit 0
  -> 'Custom CARGO_TARGET_DIR artifacts retrieved: 2 files, 590 bytes'
  -> no binary locally

RUN 2 (with the campaign-prescribed env handling): RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1 env -u CARGO_TARGET_DIR rch exec -- cargo build --profile release-perf -p fsqlite-e2e --bin comprehensive-bench
  -> [RCH] remote vmi1153651 (1740.7s = 29 min), exit 0
  -> 'Custom CARGO_TARGET_DIR artifacts retrieved: 2 files, 524 bytes'
  -> still no binary locally

The remote compiles into an opaque per-worker pool dir (.rch-target-<worker>-pool-<hash>) and the retrieval step brings back only a couple of small files, never the executable.

WHY THIS IS P1 AND NOT JUST SLOW: the ONLY local comprehensive-bench is /data/tmp/cargo-target/release-perf/comprehensive-bench dated 2026-07-23 16:40 - two days stale. A build that exits 0 and silently leaves a stale binary in place is worse than a build that fails: any agent that runs the bench next times a 2-day-old binary and attributes the result to today's source. The campaign's own section 2.1 names this exact hazard ('rch compiles into an opaque per-worker pool target dir you cannot predict') and prescribes a self-reporting ELF SHA-256 as line 1 of bench output. That mitigation detects the problem; it does not fix the retrieval.

NOTE: CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/data/tmp/cargo-target is set in the shell environment (not in .cargo/config.toml, which sets only LIBSQLITE3_FLAGS). 'env -u' on the rch process did NOT change the outcome, so the custom-target-dir retrieval path is not simply an env leak.

IMPACT: blocks every profile-first measurement in the perf campaign for this repo - you cannot profile-attribute a frame without a binary built from current source. Surfaced per campaign section 0 ('a degraded rch slot means SURFACE THE BLOCKER - never silently fall back to local cargo').

WORKAROUND (not applied - drains /data and the campaign forbids silent local fallback): local cargo build --profile release-perf.

Related: bd-he3ua (the measurement this blocked), bd-gcndj.

comments.author: AmberFortress
comments.text: Independent HARNESS-lane reproduction on 2026-07-25. First, a strict-remote rowid_eq_aggregate_bench launch exited 0 but emitted the legacy rows= output with no bench_elf_sha256 first line, proving that the launched artifact did not contain the current harness source; that timing was invalidated immediately. Second, RCH_WORKER=hz2 RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1 env -u CARGO_TARGET_DIR rch exec -- cargo bench --config profile.release-perf.lto=false --config profile.release-perf.codegen-units=16 --profile release-perf -j3 -p fsqlite-e2e --bench pipeline_stage_bench --features bench-internals -- --ledger-resurrection failed before launch because the worker compiled stale crates/fsqlite-pager/src/encrypt.rs text using XNonce::try_from at line 357, while both local HEAD b52a3236 and the synchronized working tree use XNonce::from_slice and hash 3b54f5ca13551b921814f366848c81116e0f563a781425fe357ae3266b174548. No benchmark ELF identity line was emitted, so no candidate result was admitted. This independently confirms both stale-executable launch and stale-remote-source hazards; the self-reporting ELF line correctly turned the first into an obvious invalid run. No local Cargo fallback was used.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
ROOT CAUSE FOUND 2026-07-25 (YellowCardinal), plus a third reproduction and an escalation.

ESCALATION: you cannot opt out by running cargo locally. The Claude Code PreToolUse hook in ~/.claude/settings.json runs 'rch' on EVERY Bash call, so a plain 'cargo build --profile release-perf' is transparently offloaded. Third repro: exit 0 after 1440.2s on vmi1153651, 'Artifacts retrieved 2 files, 590 bytes', binary still dated 2026-07-23. The operator believes they ran a local build; they did not.

ROOT CAUSE (from rch's own log line, transfer.rs:1028):
  'Rewriting CARGO_TARGET_DIR for remote execution (worker-scoped path): /data/tmp/cargo-target -> /data/projects/frankensqlite/.rch-target-<worker>-pool-<hash>'

RCH rewrites CARGO_TARGET_DIR to a worker-scoped pool path INSIDE the repo directory for the build, then syncs the repo directory back. But the local CARGO_TARGET_DIR here is /data/tmp/cargo-target - OUTSIDE the repo tree. So build outputs land in the synced pool dir remotely but the reverse mapping to an out-of-tree custom target dir does not deliver the executable; only 2 files / ~590 bytes come back. This is why 'rch doctor' is 28/28 green: no worker is unhealthy, the artifact mapping is just wrong for out-of-tree CARGO_TARGET_DIR.

NOTE: 'env -u CARGO_TARGET_DIR rch exec -- ...' (the campaign-prescribed form) does NOT fix it - the log still reports 'Custom CARGO_TARGET_DIR'. The Bash tool re-sources a shell snapshot that exports CARGO_TARGET_DIR, so the unset does not reach the hook.

ALSO: env-prefix syntax breaks under the hook. 'RCH_MIN_LOCAL_TIME_MS=... cargo build' is passed to the remote shell verbatim and fails with 'sh: 1: RCH_MIN_LOCAL_TIME_MS=999999999: not found', exit 127.

CANDIDATE FIXES (for the rch owner):
1. Point CARGO_TARGET_DIR INSIDE the repo (CARGO_TARGET_DIR=<repo>/target) so the pool-dir sync-back lands somewhere the retrieval maps. Testing now.
2. RCH_ENV_ALLOWLIST=CARGO_TARGET_DIR - rch's help documents this var with CARGO_TARGET_DIR as the literal example, suggesting it is meant to be forwarded rather than rewritten.
3. Make retrieval detect out-of-tree CARGO_TARGET_DIR and copy the built artifacts to it explicitly, or FAIL LOUDLY instead of exiting 0 with 590 bytes.

Fix 3 matters most regardless of 1/2: a build that exits 0 having delivered no binary, leaving a stale one in place, is the worst possible failure mode for a benchmarking fleet.

INDEPENDENT CONFIRMATION: AmberFortress (cod lane) hit the same thing from the bench side - 'The first RCH bench launch proved stale (legacy output, no self-reported SHA), so it is invalid'. Two agents, two code paths, same defect.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
WORKAROUND CONFIRMED + hypothesis proven 2026-07-25 (YellowCardinal).

Setting CARGO_TARGET_DIR to an IN-REPO path fixes it completely:

  CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/data/projects/frankensqlite/target cargo build --profile release-perf -p fsqlite-e2e --bin comprehensive-bench

  -> Finished release-perf profile in 7m01s
  -> target/release-perf/comprehensive-bench, 19 MB, timestamped 8 seconds after the build
  -> sha256 f033faa14db6b3eb7945ebe873e660cbeb4ce947f8cc2c027f7edb358831cff4

Compare the SAME command with the machine default CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/data/tmp/cargo-target (out of tree): exit 0, 'Artifacts retrieved: 2 files, 590 bytes', no binary, stale Jul 23 artifact left in place. Three reproductions of the failure, one clean success. The variable is in-tree vs out-of-tree, exactly as the transfer.rs:1028 rewrite line implies.

ROOT CAUSE (restated precisely): rch rewrites CARGO_TARGET_DIR to a worker-scoped pool dir INSIDE the repo, builds there, and syncs the repo directory back. When the local CARGO_TARGET_DIR is inside the repo the sync delivers the artifacts. When it is outside the repo, the artifacts are stranded remotely and only ~590 bytes of metadata return - with exit 0.

FLEET ACTION: every repo whose agents export an out-of-tree CARGO_TARGET_DIR is silently benching stale binaries. Note frankenfs uses an in-repo target dir (/data/projects/frankenfs/target) and is therefore NOT affected - which is why this has gone unnoticed fleet-wide despite heavy use.

RECOMMENDED FIXES, in priority order:
1. Make retrieval FAIL LOUDLY (non-zero exit) when the expected binary is not delivered. A build that exits 0 having produced no artifact is the worst possible failure mode for a benchmarking fleet; everything else here is secondary.
2. Copy artifacts from the pool dir to an out-of-tree CARGO_TARGET_DIR explicitly on retrieval.
3. Until 1/2 ship: agents should set CARGO_TARGET_DIR to an in-repo path for any build whose binary they intend to run. Confirmed working above.

Note that 'env -u CARGO_TARGET_DIR' (the campaign-prescribed form) does NOT work around this - the Bash tool re-sources a shell snapshot that re-exports the variable, so the unset never reaches the hook.

comments.text:
WORKAROUND IS UNRELIABLE, NOT A FIX — 2026-07-25 23:50 (YellowCardinal). Downgrade the earlier 'in-repo CARGO_TARGET_DIR fixes it' note.

FOURTH OCCURRENCE, and this one had the workaround applied:
  CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/data/projects/frankensqlite/target cargo build --profile release-perf -p fsqlite-e2e --bin comprehensive-bench
  -> [RCH] remote ovh-a (411.5s), exit 0
  -> target/release-perf/comprehensive-bench still timestamped 22:04:18, sha256 f033faa1... = BYTE-IDENTICAL to the pre-change binary built hours earlier.

The source change (hoisting Runtime construction out of the timed closure, commit 5bb3c6af) was NOT in the delivered binary. cargo check on the same source succeeded, so the code compiles; the artifact simply never came back.

WHAT CHANGED vs the successful case: the earlier successful in-repo build ran on vmi1153651/hz2. This failure ran on ovh-a. Same command, same in-repo CARGO_TARGET_DIR, different worker, different outcome. So retrieval is WORKER-DEPENDENT and INTERMITTENT, which is worse than a deterministic failure - an agent who validates the workaround once will trust it thereafter.

REVISED GUIDANCE: pointing CARGO_TARGET_DIR inside the repo is NOT a reliable workaround. The only safe practice is to VERIFY THE BINARY AFTER EVERY BUILD, before every measurement:
  stat -c '%y' <binary>   and/or   sha256sum <binary>
and refuse to measure if the timestamp predates the source edit. That freshness gate is what caught this: I was about to measure a hoist fix using the pre-hoist binary and would have reported the old code's numbers as the new code's.

This elevates the campaign's section 2.1 self-reporting ELF SHA from 'good practice' to 'the only defense'. A hash printed by the binary itself is the sole way to know which ELF ran, because the build system reports success either way.

Escalating priority: this is not a slow-build annoyance, it is a silent-wrong-answer generator that has now fired 4 times in one session on 3 different workers.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
# CREATE TABLE/VIEW cross-kind name conflict not rejected

## Symptom
SQLite uses a single schema namespace for tables and views, so a new VIEW cannot
take an existing table's name and a new TABLE cannot take an existing view's
name. frank accepts the cross-kind cases.
```sql
CREATE TABLE t (a);
CREATE VIEW t AS SELECT 1;
-- SQLite: ERROR table t already exists
-- frank:  OK   (WRONG)

CREATE TABLE u (a);
CREATE VIEW w AS SELECT a FROM u;
CREATE TABLE w (a);
-- SQLite: ERROR view w already exists
-- frank:  OK   (WRONG)
```

## What is already correct
- same-kind duplicates ARE rejected: `CREATE TABLE t; CREATE TABLE t` -> error;
  `CREATE VIEW v; CREATE VIEW v` -> error.
- `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`/`CREATE VIEW IF NOT EXISTS` on the existing
  same-kind name -> no error (correct).

## Root cause
The duplicate-name check during CREATE TABLE / CREATE VIEW only consults the
*same-kind* namespace (tables when creating a table, views when creating a view)
rather than the unified schema namespace. See the CREATE TABLE / CREATE VIEW
handlers in `crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs`.

## Fix sketch
Look up the proposed name in the unified schema (tables + views + indexes when
relevant; SQLite also reserves index names in the same namespace and rejects
e.g. CREATE TABLE with an existing index name). If the name is taken by ANY
schema object, raise the appropriate
"<existing-kind> <name> already exists" error (preserving SQLite's wording).
`IF NOT EXISTS` should silence the error only when the SAME-kind object already
exists; a cross-kind name clash should still error even with IF NOT EXISTS in
SQLite.

## Priority
P3 — over-acceptance with serious downstream confusion (a view shadowing a real
table, or vice versa, breaks normal name resolution). Part of the recurring
validate-then-reject class.

## Tests
`crates/fsqlite-e2e/tests/create_duplicate_name_oracle_e2e.rs`: IF NOT EXISTS
and same-kind duplicate rejection green; `create_duplicate_cross_kind_rejected`
#[ignore]'d on this bead.

title: §11.10-11.12 WAL Index (SHM) + sqlite_master Table + Encoding
description:
## SUMMARY

Covers WAL-index (SHM) structure, sqlite_master table schema, and database text encoding. The WAL-index uses shared memory mapped into 32KB segments with a 136-byte header (duplicated for lock-free reads), checkpoint info (nBackfill, 5 reader marks, 8 lock slots), and hash table segments for frame-to-page mapping. The sqlite_master table (rooted at page 1) stores schema objects (tables, indexes, views, triggers) with type/name/tbl_name/rootpage/sql columns. Text encoding (UTF-8/UTF-16le/UTF-16be) is set at database creation and affects all text storage and comparison.

## KEY DATA STRUCTURES / ALGORITHMS

- **WAL-index header (136 bytes)**:
  - [0..48]: WalIndexHdr first copy: iVersion(u32)=3007000, unused(u32), iChange(u32), isInit(u8), bigEndCksum(u8), szPage(u16), mxFrame(u32), nPage(u32), aFrameCksum[2](u32), aSalt[2](u32), aCksum[2](u32).
  - [48..96]: WalIndexHdr second copy (lock-free reads: reader reads both, uses only if they match).
  - [96..136]: WalCkptInfo (40 bytes): nBackfill(u32) at 96, aReadMark[5](u32) at 100-119, aLock[8](u8) at 120-127, nBackfillAttempted(u32) at 128, notUsed0(u32) at 132.
- **Reader marks (aReadMark[5])**: 5 u32 values at offsets 100-119. Each records WAL frame count at reader begin time, preventing checkpoint from overwriting frames needed by active readers.
- **WAL-index lock slots (aLock[8])**: aLock[0]=WAL_WRITE_LOCK (byte 120), aLock[1]=WAL_CKPT_LOCK (byte 121), aLock[2]=WAL_RECOVER_LOCK (byte 122), aLock[3..7]=WAL_READ_LOCK(0..4) (bytes 123-127). These are lockable file regions; their byte values are not the coordination mechanism -- OS-level locks on these offsets provide correctness.
- **Hash table segments (32KB each)**: Page-number array u32[4096] at [0..16384) + hash table u16[8192] at [16384..32768). First segment: 4062 usable entries (136-byte header overlaps first 34 slots).
- **sqlite_master schema**: `CREATE TABLE sqlite_master (type TEXT, name TEXT, tbl_name TEXT, rootpage INT, sql TEXT)`. Types: 'table', 'index', 'view', 'trigger'. Root is page 1. sql is NULL for auto-indexes. temp database uses sqlite_temp_master.
- **Text encoding**: UTF-8(1), UTF-16le(2), UTF-16be(3) at header offset 56. Set at creation, immutable afterward. BINARY collation uses memcmp on raw bytes. NOCASE operates on Unicode code points regardless of encoding.

## NORMATIVE INVARIANTS

1. WAL-index iVersion MUST be 3007000; mismatch is an error.
2. WalIndexHdr is duplicated; reader MUST read both copies and use only if they match (lock-free consistency).
3. Reader marks prevent checkpoint from overwriting frames still needed by active readers.
4. Lock slot byte values are NOT the coordination mechanism -- OS-level fcntl locks on these byte offsets provide correctness.
5. sqlite_master is always rooted at page 1.
6. sqlite_master.sql is NULL for automatically created indexes (e.g., UNIQUE constraint indexes).
7. On database creation, page 1 is a table leaf page with zero sqlite_master rows.
8. Text encoding is set once at creation and CANNOT be changed afterward (except via VACUUM INTO).
9. BINARY collation uses memcmp on raw bytes; for UTF-8 this produces correct Unicode code point ordering.
10. SHM fields are native byte order (not big-endian).

## UNIT TEST REQUIREMENTS

1. `test_wal_index_header_layout` -- Verify WalIndexHdr fields at correct byte offsets (iVersion at 0, szPage at 14, mxFrame at 16, etc.).
2. `test_wal_index_header_duplication` -- Write header copy 1, copy 2; verify reader accepts matching copies, rejects mismatched.
3. `test_wal_ckpt_info_layout` -- nBackfill at offset 96, aReadMark[5] at 100-119, aLock[8] at 120-127, nBackfillAttempted at 128.
4. `test_reader_marks_prevent_checkpoint_overwrite` -- Set reader mark to frame N; checkpoint MUST NOT overwrite frames <= N.
5. `test_lock_slot_mapping` -- aLock[0]=WRITE_LOCK, aLock[1]=CKPT_LOCK, aLock[2]=RECOVER_LOCK, aLock[3..7]=READ_LOCK(0..4).
6. `test_sqlite_master_schema` -- sqlite_master has exactly 5 columns: type, name, tbl_name, rootpage, sql.
7. `test_sqlite_master_page1_root` -- sqlite_master is always rooted at page 1.
8. `test_sqlite_master_types` -- Valid type values are 'table', 'index', 'view', 'trigger'.
9. `test_sqlite_master_auto_index_null_sql` -- Auto-created indexes have sql=NULL in sqlite_master.
10. `test_encoding_utf8_default` -- New database defaults to text encoding 1 (UTF-8).
11. `test_encoding_utf16le` -- Database with encoding=2 stores text as UTF-16LE; memcmp ordering differs from UTF-8.
12. `test_encoding_immutable` -- Attempting to change encoding after creation fails.
13. `test_binary_collation_memcmp` -- BINARY collation compares raw bytes via memcmp.
14. `test_nocase_collation_unicode` -- NOCASE collation operates on Unicode code points regardless of encoding.

## E2E TEST

Create a database in FrankenSQLite, populate with tables/indexes/views/triggers, verify sqlite_master contains correct rows. Open in C SQLite and verify all schema objects are visible. Test multi-process WAL-index sharing: one process writes, another reads via shared SHM; verify reader marks prevent stale reads.

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA

- WAL-index header layout byte-for-byte compatible with C SQLite SHM format.
- Dual-copy header mechanism provides lock-free read consistency.
- Reader marks correctly prevent checkpoint from overwriting active reader frames.
- sqlite_master schema matches C SQLite exactly with all 5 columns.
- Text encoding set at creation and immutable; UTF-8/UTF-16le/UTF-16be all supported.
- Multi-process SHM interop with C SQLite verified.
close_reason: done

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## WAL Index (SHM) + sqlite_master Table + Encoding

### Spec Content (Lines 13979-14069, sections 11.10-11.12)

**11.10 WAL Index / wal-index / SHM (lines 13979-14035)**

**Byte order:** Unlike the main database file and WAL file (big-endian), all WAL-index (SHM) header fields are stored in **native byte order** of the host machine (except salt values copied verbatim from WAL header). SHM is not involved in crash recovery and does not need to be portable across architectures.

**Header (136 bytes):**
```
[0..48]:   WalIndexHdr (first copy):
             iVersion(u32) = 3007000 (MUST match)
             unused(u32)
             iChange(u32)
             isInit(u8)
             bigEndCksum(u8)
             szPage(u16)
             mxFrame(u32)
             nPage(u32)
             aFrameCksum[2](u32)
             aSalt[2](u32)
             aCksum[2](u32)

[48..96]:  WalIndexHdr (second copy)
           Lock-free reads: reader reads both copies, uses them only if they match.

[96..136]: WalCkptInfo (40 bytes total):
             nBackfill(u32) at offset 96
             aReadMark[5](u32) at offsets 100-119 (5 reader marks, 20 bytes)
             aLock[8](u8) at offsets 120-127 (8 SHM lock slots, 1 byte each)
             nBackfillAttempted(u32) at offset 128
             notUsed0(u32) at offset 132
```

**Hash table segments (32 KB each):**
- Physical layout: page-number array (`u32[4096]`) at bytes `[0..16384)` and hash table (`ht_slot[8192]`, u16) at bytes `[16384..32768)` in ALL segments.
- First segment: 136-byte header overlaps first 34 u32 page-number slots, leaving 4062 usable entries (wal.c compile-time assert).
  - `[0..136)`: Header
  - `[136..16384)`: Page number array: 4062 entries x 4 bytes
  - `[16384..32768)`: Hash table: 8192 slots x 2 bytes
- Subsequent segments: full 4096 entries (32 KB region).
  - `[0..16384)`: Page number array: 4096 entries x 4 bytes
  - `[16384..32768)`: Hash table: 8192 slots x 2 bytes

**Hash function:** `(page_number * 383) & 8191`, linear probing.
- NOT simple modulo. Prime multiplier 383 (`HASHTABLE_HASH_1` in C SQLite) provides better distribution for sequential page numbers.
- Using `page_number % 8192` would produce a working but INCOMPATIBLE wal-index when sharing SHM files with C SQLite in multi-process mode.

**Reader marks (offsets 100-119):** 5 reader marks (u32 each, 20 bytes total). Each records the WAL frame count at the time a reader began. Prevents checkpoint from overwriting frames still needed by active readers.

**WAL-index lock slot mapping (required for Hybrid SHM interop):**
- `aLock[0]` (byte 120) = `WAL_WRITE_LOCK` (exclusive; writer exclusion)
- `aLock[1]` (byte 121) = `WAL_CKPT_LOCK`
- `aLock[2]` (byte 122) = `WAL_RECOVER_LOCK`
- `aLock[3 + i]` (bytes 123..127) = `WAL_READ_LOCK(i)` for `i in 0..4`

These bytes are lockable file regions. Their values are not used as a coordination protocol; correctness depends on OS-level locks taken on these byte offsets.

**11.11 sqlite_master Table (lines 14037-14056)**

Every database contains a `sqlite_master` table (page 1 root) with this schema:
```sql
CREATE TABLE sqlite_master (
    type TEXT,      -- 'table', 'index', 'view', 'trigger'
    name TEXT,      -- object name
    tbl_name TEXT,  -- associated table name (for indexes/triggers)
    rootpage INT,   -- root B-tree page number (0 for views/triggers)
    sql TEXT        -- CREATE statement text (NULL for auto-indexes)
);
```

For the temp database, the equivalent is `sqlite_temp_master`.

On database creation, FrankenSQLite creates page 1 as a table leaf page containing zero rows in sqlite_master. First `CREATE TABLE` inserts a row with the CREATE statement text.

**11.12 Encoding (lines 14057-14069)**

**Default:** UTF-8 (text encoding = 1 at header offset 56).

**UTF-16 alternatives:** UTF-16le (2) and UTF-16be (3) supported. Encoding is set at database creation and cannot be changed afterward. When UTF-16 is used, all text in the database is UTF-16 encoded, and text comparisons use UTF-16 collation.

**Encoding affects comparison:**
- BINARY collation uses `memcmp` on raw bytes. For UTF-8, this produces correct Unicode code point ordering. For UTF-16, byte-order matters (LE vs BE).
- NOCASE collation always operates on Unicode code points regardless of encoding.

### Unit Tests Required

1. **test_wal_index_header_size**: Verify total header is 136 bytes (48 + 48 + 40).
2. **test_wal_index_hdr_copy_match**: Create WalIndexHdr, write both copies at offsets 0..48 and 48..96. Read both, verify they match.
3. **test_wal_index_hdr_iversion**: Verify iVersion field is 3007000.
4. **test_wal_index_native_byte_order**: On current platform, write header fields in native byte order. Read them back, verify they decode correctly without byte-swapping.
5. **test_wal_index_ckpt_info_layout**: Verify WalCkptInfo fields at correct offsets: nBackfill(96), aReadMark(100-119), aLock(120-127), nBackfillAttempted(128), notUsed0(132).
6. **test_wal_index_hash_function**: Verify `(page_number * 383) & 8191` for page numbers 1, 2, 100, 4096. Verify it is NOT `page_number % 8192`.
7. **test_wal_index_hash_distribution**: Hash 1000 sequential page numbers, verify distribution across 8192 slots is reasonably uniform (no excessive clustering).
8. **test_wal_index_hash_linear_probing**: Insert page numbers that hash to the same slot, verify linear probing finds the correct entries.
9. **test_wal_index_first_segment_capacity**: Verify first segment has 4062 usable entries (136 / 4 = 34 slots consumed by header; 4096 - 34 = 4062).
10. **test_wal_index_subsequent_segment_capacity**: Verify subsequent segments have 4096 entries.
11. **test_wal_index_segment_physical_layout**: Verify page-number array at bytes 0..16384 and hash table at bytes 16384..32768 in a 32KB segment.
12. **test_wal_index_reader_marks**: Set 5 reader marks at offsets 100-119 with different WAL frame counts. Read them back, verify correct values.
13. **test_wal_index_lock_slots**: Verify lock slot mapping: byte 120=WRITE, 121=CKPT, 122=RECOVER, 123-127=READ(0..4).
14. **test_sqlite_master_schema**: Verify the sqlite_master table has exactly 5 columns: type(TEXT), name(TEXT), tbl_name(TEXT), rootpage(INT), sql(TEXT).
15. **test_sqlite_master_type_values**: Verify valid type values are 'table', 'index', 'view', 'trigger'.
16. **test_sqlite_master_page1_root**: Verify sqlite_master is rooted on page 1.
17. **test_sqlite_master_empty_on_create**: Create a new database, verify sqlite_master on page 1 has zero rows (table leaf page with 0 cells).
18. **test_encoding_utf8_default**: Create database, verify header offset 56 = 1 (UTF-8).
19. **test_encoding_utf16le**: Create database with UTF-16le, verify header offset 56 = 2.
20. **test_encoding_binary_collation_utf8**: Verify BINARY collation on UTF-8 text produces correct Unicode code point ordering via memcmp.
21. **test_encoding_nocase_utf8_vs_utf16**: Verify NOCASE collation produces identical ordering results for the same strings regardless of UTF-8 vs UTF-16 encoding.

### E2E Tests

**test_e2e_wal_index_multi_reader**: Open a database in WAL mode, start 5 readers at different points (setting different reader marks). Verify reader marks prevent checkpoint from overwriting frames needed by active readers. After all readers close, verify checkpoint can proceed.

**test_e2e_sqlite_master_schema_tracking**: Create several tables, indexes, views, and a trigger. Read sqlite_master. Verify each object has a correct row with type, name, tbl_name, rootpage, and sql fields. Drop a table, verify its rows are removed from sqlite_master.

**test_e2e_wal_index_hash_lookup**: Write 5000 frames to WAL (spanning multiple hash segments). Look up various page numbers via the hash table. Verify all lookups return the correct latest frame for each page.

**test_e2e_encoding_utf16_database**: Create a database with UTF-16le encoding, insert text with international characters, read it back and verify the data is stored as UTF-16le in the database file and comparisons work correctly.

title: G2.1: fault matrix for batched append and publish paths
description:
## Goal
Build the authoritative fault matrix for batched append and publish paths so every later WAL batching, publication, and recovery bead is grounded in an explicit failure model rather than scattered intuition.

## Why This Matters
The new parallel WAL program changes where ordering, durability, and visibility truth are established. That means append, publish, checkpoint, reset, and restart failure points must be enumerated before implementation and proof beads can claim correctness. This bead is the canonical catalog of those failure points and the expected observable outcomes.

## Scope
Cover fault points and expected outcomes for at least:
- local frame staging before durable publication,
- ordered durability or combiner entry,
- commit-certificate assignment or equivalent ordering record publication,
- visibility metadata publication,
- checkpoint overlap,
- truncate or reset,
- restart and recovery after abnormal termination,
- stale-lane cleanup and replay continuity.

For each case, define:
- injected fault point,
- preconditions,
- expected durability and visibility outcome,
- allowed fallback or safe-mode behavior,
- required logs and artifact fields,
- verification surface that exercises the case.

## Required Verification and Logging
- Deterministic fault-table tests for the matrix rows themselves.
- Integration or fault-injection scenarios that exercise append, publication, checkpoint, reset, and restart transitions.
- A named operator entrypoint such as `scripts/verify_g2_1_fault_matrix.sh` that replays the matrix and writes artifact manifests.
- Structured logs exposing at minimum `trace_id`, `scenario_id`, `fault_point`, `wal_lane_id`, `commit_certificate`, `publication_generation`, `expected_outcome`, `observed_outcome`, and first-failure diagnostics.

## Acceptance Criteria
- The matrix covers the append-to-publication path comprehensively enough that later proof beads can reference it mechanically.
- Every row names the required observable outcome, not just the injected fault.
- The matrix is reusable by recovery, checkpoint, and performance-proof beads.
- Logging and replay requirements are explicit enough that another agent can diagnose a failure without reopening this design debate.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The bead defines a replayable fault matrix spanning append staging, ordered durability, publication, checkpoint overlap, reset, restart, and stale-lane cleanup.
2. Each matrix row names preconditions, injected fault point, expected durability and visibility outcome, allowed fallback, and required evidence.
3. `scripts/verify_g2_1_fault_matrix.sh` or an equivalent named entrypoint is specified for replaying the matrix and collecting artifacts.
4. Structured logs expose fault point, lane identity, commit certificate context, publication generation, expected versus observed outcome, and first-failure diagnostics.
5. The matrix is self-contained enough to serve as a prerequisite for later recovery and failure-injection proof beads.
notes:
Program intent:
- this bead is the canonical failure-model companion to the parallel WAL work
- later WAL proof beads should cite this matrix rather than inventing ad hoc fault cases

title: V3.1: JIT template — closure compiler for simple sequential INSERT
description:
## What
Implement the first JIT template: compile `INSERT INTO t(cols...) VALUES (?1, ?2, ...)` with autoincrement rowid to a native Rust closure that bypasses the VDBE interpreter.

## Pattern to match
The opcode sequence for a simple prepared INSERT:
```
Init → Transaction → OpenWrite(cursor, root, N) → [SetSnapshot] →
NewRowid(cursor, r_rowid) → [Variable ?1 → r1, Variable ?2 → r2, ...] →
MakeRecord(r_start, N, r_record) → Insert(cursor, r_record, r_rowid) →
[IdxInsert for each index] → Close → Halt
```

## Generated closure signature
```rust
fn compiled_insert(
    txn: &RefCell<TransactionKind>,
    root_page: PageNumber,
    page_size: PageSize,
    params: &[SqliteValue],
    last_alloc_rowid: &mut i64,
    autoincrement_max: i64,
) -> Result<(usize, i64)>  // (affected_rows, last_insert_rowid)
```

## What the closure does
1. Allocate rowid: `last_alloc_rowid.max(autoincrement_max) + 1`
2. Serialize record: call `serialize_record_iter_into` directly from params slice
3. Open/reuse BtCursor on root_page (cursor can be a closure capture)
4. `table_insert_prechecked_absent` with append mode
5. Return (1, new_rowid)

No register file, no opcode dispatch, no bounds checking, no metrics branches.

## Files
- `crates/fsqlite-vdbe/src/jit.rs` (NEW) — template matcher + closure generator
- `crates/fsqlite-vdbe/src/engine.rs` — wire into maybe_trigger_jit
- `crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs` — dispatch to closure when available

## Estimated impact
~1µs dispatch overhead eliminated per row.
At 10K rows: ~10ms saved.

## Verification  
- Unit test: compile and execute a simple INSERT via closure, compare output to interpreter
- Conformance: no regressions
- Benchmark: section 1 tiny_1col improvement

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
# bd-9e3xf cache-miss classification rerun (2026-04-24)

Re-ran `audit_cell_slot_cache_hit_rate_write_vs_read` after shipping the
CellRef-parse skip family plus the inline-capacity / image-token rework
(7 commits listed in the shipment ledger below). All numbers from
MemPageStore, 10 000 rows, 35-byte payload, release build.

## Shipment ledger since baseline (5392c91e)

| commit | lever | measured speedup (microbench) |
|---|---|---|
| 4fe87d5c | CellSlotCache MRU fast-path lookup | audit-only, no microbench |
| 4b061dcc | child_page_at → read_interior_child_inline | 5.41x (28.04 → 5.19 ns) |
| 385591f8 | replace_separator left-child → read_interior_child_inline | 5.50x (28.10 → 5.11 ns) |
| 1be6ee30 | CachedCellSlots inline 8 → 16 + image_token key swap | structural |
| b35f091c | predecessor_idx rowid-only → parse_leaf_table_rowid | 2.01x (6.47 → 3.22 ns) |
| 145bfe36 | quick_balance_divider rowid-only → parse_leaf_table_rowid | 2.01x (same helper) |
| de40c3df | balance_nonroot child_page_number → read_interior_left_child | 5.41x (same pattern) |

## Cache-miss classification — before vs after

All six audit scenarios, counters read from `cell_slot_cache_counter_snapshot`:

| scenario                    | h_before | h_after | c_before | c_after | i_before | i_after | s_before | s_after |
|-----------------------------|---------:|--------:|---------:|--------:|---------:|--------:|---------:|--------:|
| monotonic_append            |        0 |       0 |        1 |       1 |        0 |       0 |        0 |       0 |
| random_insert               |        0 |       0 |        4 |       4 |        8 |       8 |        0 |       0 |
| read_heavy_after_append     |        0 |       0 |        0 |       0 |        0 |       0 |        0 |       0 |
| reverse_seek_preloaded      |        0 |       0 |        0 |       0 |        0 |       0 |        0 |       0 |
| delete_all_after_append     |       98 |      98 |        2 |       2 |    9 998 |   9 998 |        0 |       0 |
| index_random_insert         |   64 416 |       0 |    6 366 |   7 439 |    5 747 |  20 869 |   54 739 | 102 960 |

Legend: h = hits, c = miss_cold, i = miss_invalidated, s = miss_slot. "before" =
`5392c91e` (bd-9e3xf baseline); "after" = current HEAD post-`de40c3df`.

## Interpretation

1. **`index_random_insert` went from 49.07 % hit rate to 0 %.** This is *not* a
   regression for production — it's an artefact of `1be6ee30`'s switch from
   `xxh3_64(page_bytes)` to `PageData::image_token` as the cache key. `MemPageStore`
   allocates a fresh `Vec` (and therefore a fresh `image_token`) on every
   `read_page_data`, so successive descents see new tokens even when the bytes
   are identical — every cache lookup misses. The production pager caches
   `PageData` instances via the pager page-cache and returns `Clone()` on read,
   which preserves the token; the 49 % hit-rate the original audit measured
   should carry over to real workloads.

2. **`MISS_SLOT` ceased to dominate `index_random_insert` — `MISS_INVALIDATED`
   and `MISS_SLOT` now split the traffic.** Before: 54 739 / 76 852 misses
   (71 %) were `MISS_SLOT`. After: 102 960 / 131 268 (78 %). Total call count
   is unchanged (131 268) — the 64 416 `hits` got redistributed across the
   three miss buckets, mostly into `MISS_SLOT` (+48 221) and `MISS_INVALIDATED`
   (+15 122). The `CachedCellSlots 8 → 16` widen still stands as the right
   fix for the `MISS_SLOT`-dominant pattern; it just stops paying the heap
   spill on the 9th slot even in the zero-hit regime.

3. **`delete_all_after_append` is unchanged at 99 % `MISS_INVALIDATED`, 10 098
   total calls.** This is fundamental and expected: every delete writes the
   leaf, bumping the page `image_token`, so the cache cannot help the
   predecessor/separator lookups. The right fix is to skip the cache entirely
   for those callers — which is exactly what commits `b35f091c` (predecessor)
   + `145bfe36` (quick_balance divider) + `de40c3df` (balance_nonroot
   left_child) + `385591f8` (replace_separator) + `4b061dcc` (child_page_at)
   ship. These 5 commits don't change the audit's MemPageStore call-count
   because `index_random_insert` exercises `binary_search_index_*` (which
   still go through `parse_cell_at`), not the skipped callers. But they pay
   off on the DELETE / split rebalance hot paths that hit the same
   `MISS_INVALIDATED` regime.

## What this leaves on the table

- **`binary_search_index_leaf` / `binary_search_index_interior`** are the two
  remaining `parse_cell_at` callers that genuinely need the full parse
  (they call `read_cell_payload` using `cell.payload_offset`,
  `cell.local_size`, `cell.overflow_page`). No skip lever available.

- **Production-pager audit**: the MemPageStore rerun is enough to confirm
  that the shipped skips don't introduce a cache-behaviour regression, but
  it can't validate cross-descent hit rate under a pager that preserves
  `image_token`. A production-pager rerun of the same bench would resolve
  whether the 49 % hit rate carries over. Out of scope for this summary.

## Artefact

- `current.txt`: raw `audit_cell_slot_cache_hit_rate_write_vs_read` output
  captured at HEAD `de40c3df`.
- `baseline.md` / `5392c91e-snapshot`: already captured in the bd-9e3xf
  bead comment and commit message.

Run the audit:

```
CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/tmp/rch_target_cc3_btree_local cargo test \
    -p fsqlite-btree --release --lib \
    audit_cell_slot_cache_hit_rate_write_vs_read -- --ignored --nocapture
```

title: Wire bd-97kjm namespace quiesce()/guard_generation() into pool/connection drop + quarantine paths (connection.rs/pager) for end-to-end lsof-clean

Then the bd-2pmu6 end-to-end acceptance holds: pool drop -> lsof-clean (no retained fd in /proc/self/fd), quarantine/rename -> no writes to the old inode. comments.author: NobleCedar
comments.text:
NobleCedar 2026-08-11 read-only analysis (no builds run).

FINDING A - latent DELETE-mode conflict-check asymmetry (NOT the producer of the clean-DB run; recorded so it is not re-derived).
Concurrent page allocation is purely connection-local: allocate_page picks inner.next_page under a PER-CONNECTION Arc<Mutex<PagerInner>> (pager.rs:20369, 20464-20477), no file lock, no shared claim. BEGIN recomputes next_page = db_size+1 (pager.rs:8258) under a SHARED lock only (pager.rs:14063 -> LockLevel::Shared), which is compatible with the RESERVED lock a WAL committer holds, so N connections routinely derive the SAME next_page. Collision safety is deferred entirely to commit.
There is no read set in pager.rs; validation is write-set vs pages-committed-since-snapshot. A newly allocated page DOES enter write_pages_sorted when first written (pager.rs:20229 -> 8681) so it IS a conflict candidate (pager.rs:17356); never-having-been-read only costs it a hash baseline, which the primary WAL validator ignores (fsqlite-core/src/wal_adapter.rs:1777).
WAL mode is covered (frame scan wal_adapter.rs:1773; cross-batch epoch scan pager.rs:9195; generation-change fail-closed wal_adapter.rs:2246).
DELETE mode sets cross_process_conflict_pages = Vec::new() (pager.rs:20923, 21634). Its only defense is the EXCLUSIVE-lock check in commit_journal (pager.rs:17850-17930), which has an ASYMMETRY: committed_db_size is read from ONLY page-1 header bytes 28..32 (pager.rs:17862), while original_db_size = inner.db_size (pager.rs:11779), which refresh_committed_state sets to header.page_count.max(file_derived).max(1) (pager.rs:8220 - the max() added for GH#49 crash-between-grow-and-header-update). Whenever the file is longer than the header page_count at our BEGIN, original_db_size is inflated above any peer header value, so 'if committed_db_size > original_db_size' (pager.rs:17864) is false and the entire range conflict scan is SKIPPED. Rollbacks leaving the file extended make this reachable. UNPROVEN without a firing repro; do NOT touch the allocator on this basis alone. Worth a targeted probe.

FINDING B - retained autocommit, a separate real hazard for the implicit-autocommit half.
autocommit_retain_enabled defaults TRUE for file-backed connections (connection.rs:11951). After an autocommit write the txn is PARKED UNCOMMITTED and Ok(()) returned to the caller (connection.rs:43593-43609), then reused by the next write (connection.rs:41419-41439). Both park and reuse force concurrent_txn=false and concurrent_session_id=None (connection.rs:43602, 41432), deliberately excluding the batch from concurrent conflict handling. Matches 'corruption with writer_errors=0' for the implicit-autocommit scenarios. It does NOT explain the explicit-BEGIN failure: can_retain_autocommit_batch requires !is_concurrent_txn (connection.rs:43577).

STATUS vs the 2026-08-11 clean-DB run: with integrity ok, row_count 100, balance_sum 100000, durable balances matched, the 0-row credit is NOT b-tree damage, so neither Finding A nor B produces it. Producer is a transient in-transaction rowid-seek or affected-count path under concurrent peers; that trace is in progress.

title: Track L: Pointer Swizzling — Eliminate Buffer Manager Hash Lookup Entirely

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## Problem (from alien-graveyard §15.3)
Even with a flat page array (Track F), we still do pointer indirection: load page number → index into array → get page data. C SQLite stores raw memory pointers directly in B-tree node child slots. We should do the same.

## Solution: LeanStore-Style Pointer Swizzling
Tag the high bit of every page pointer: bit63=1 means "this is a raw memory address", bit63=0 means "this is a page ID needing lookup." On first access, CAS the parent's child pointer from page-ID to raw memory pointer. ALL subsequent accesses are direct memory dereferences — zero indirection, zero lookup, zero atomic operations.

## How It Works
1. B-tree node stores child pointers as u64
2. First access: load page via pager, get memory address
3. CAS parent's child slot: page_id → (memory_addr | 0x8000_0000_0000_0000)
4. Next access: check high bit → already swizzled → direct dereference
5. On eviction: un-swizzle by CAS back to page_id

## Alien Graveyard Reference: §15.3 (LeanStore), also used by Umbra DB

## Expected Impact: -0.08 to -0.15 µs per B-tree level traversed
For a 3-level tree: -0.24 to -0.45 µs total — this ALONE nearly closes the gap.

## Why This Is Different From Track F
Track F replaces DashMap with flat array (still indexed by page number).
Track L eliminates the index lookup entirely — parent nodes store raw pointers to child pages.
They compose: F provides the backing array, L makes traversal zero-cost.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## SAFETY: Pointer Swizzling Requires Controlled Unsafe
Pointer swizzling inherently requires dereferencing raw pointers (the swizzled memory address). This means:
1. The swizzle/un-swizzle code MUST live in fsqlite-vfs or fsqlite-pager (crates that already override workspace unsafe policy for mmap/shm)
2. The B-tree cursor code in fsqlite-btree must NOT contain unsafe — it calls a safe abstraction that handles the swizzled pointer internally
3. The safe abstraction: `fn read_page(&self, pgno_or_ptr: u64) -> &PageData` checks the tag bit and either indexes the flat array or dereferences the swizzled pointer — all within one unsafe block in the pager crate
4. ALL unsafe blocks must have SAFETY comments explaining the invariant (pointer is valid because page is epoch-pinned)

## Alternative: If the unsafe surface is too risky, implement pointer swizzling as a page-number-to-index cache instead (safe, ~80% of the benefit):
- Cache: HashMap<PageNumber, usize> where usize is the index into the flat page array
- Lookup: check cache first (2 ns), then fall back to pager (50 ns)
- This avoids ALL raw pointer manipulation while still eliminating most of the lookup cost

title: Benchmark ARC vs S3-FIFO page-cache eviction and decide the default policy
close_reason: Decided: KEEP S3-FIFO as the default page-cache eviction policy. Real-policy hit-rate benchmark through the live ShardedPageCache (new test bench_real_eviction_policies_hot_cold_scan_hit_rate) on a hot-set+cold-scan workload: arbitrary=19.92%, s3fifo=24.88%, arc=24.88%, s3fifo_adaptive=24.88% (ideal=25%). ARC and S3FifoAdaptive match S3-FIFO exactly (all give near-ideal scan resistance) — neither beats the default, so flipping the hot-path default would add reconstruction/bandit cost for zero hit-rate gain (unjustified per AGENTS.md). Only flip pager.rs default with a real-policy hit-rate artifact showing a clear win (AGENTS.md: no unbacked perf claims; negative-results ledger lists page-cache tuning as strict). comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: DECISION 2026-06-29 (Opus 4.8): KEEP S3-FIFO as the default. Real-policy hit-rate comparison through the live ShardedPageCache (new test bench_real_eviction_policies_hot_cold_scan_hit_rate, page_cache.rs) on a deterministic hot-set(8) + cold-scan(24/round x200) workload, max_buffers=64. title: ORDER BY text returns insertion order instead of sorted order when index-assisted scan is used with MemDatabase
close_reason: Fixed: index-seek path bypassed ORDER BY sorter. Added stmt.order_by.is_empty() guard to index_eq dispatch in codegen.rs

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## Root Cause Analysis

`resolve_order_by_index_plan()` in codegen.rs finds a matching index for ORDER BY and bypasses the sorter, using `codegen_select_index_ordered_scan` instead. This works correctly with pager-backed StorageCursor (real B-tree indexes maintain sorted order) but fails with MemDatabase (MemCursor) because MemDatabase indexes don't iterate in key-sorted order — they iterate in insertion order.

### Affected Tests (4 tests, all :memory: databases)
- `test_conformance_index_with_queries_s84`: idx_iwq_name index
- `test_conformance_multi_index_queries`: product name index  
- `test_conformance_update_with_correlated_in_s502`: post-UPDATE ORDER BY
- `test_conformance_schema_introspection_s134`: sqlite_master text ordering

### Reproduction
```sql
CREATE TABLE t(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, cat TEXT);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_name ON t(name);
INSERT INTO t VALUES(1,'gamma','A'),(2,'alpha','A'),(3,'epsilon','A');
-- Returns ['gamma','alpha','epsilon'] (insertion order) instead of ['alpha','epsilon','gamma']
SELECT name FROM t WHERE cat = 'A' ORDER BY name;
```

### Fix Options
1. **Disable index-assisted ORDER BY for MemDatabase**: Check if the backend is MemDatabase and fall back to sorter path
2. **Make MemDatabase indexes maintain sorted order**: Use BTreeMap instead of Vec for index storage
3. **Fix MemCursor index iteration**: Ensure index iteration follows key order

Option 1 is the safest minimal fix. Option 2 is the correct long-term fix.

### Key Code Locations
- `codegen.rs:8680` — `resolve_order_by_index_plan()`
- `codegen.rs:1497` — index plan dispatch
- `codegen.rs:2139` — `codegen_select_index_ordered_scan()`
- `engine.rs:91` — `MemTable` struct (rows stored in insertion order)

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## Refined Analysis (Session 70)

The ORDER BY text regression is NOT caused by index-assisted scan optimization. Even after disabling index-assisted ORDER BY (via `index_ordered_scan_reliable = false`), the bug persists.

### Reproduction
```sql
CREATE TABLE t(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, cat TEXT);
CREATE INDEX idx ON t(name);
INSERT INTO t VALUES(1,'Gadget','A'),(2,'Bolt','A'),(3,'Alpha','B'),(4,'Zebra','A');
-- Returns ['Gadget','Bolt','Zebra'] (wrong) instead of ['Bolt','Gadget','Zebra']
SELECT name FROM t WHERE cat = 'A' ORDER BY name;
```

### Key Finding
- Simple `SELECT name FROM t ORDER BY name` WORKS (sorter produces correct order)
- `SELECT name FROM t WHERE cat = 'A' ORDER BY name` FAILS when there's an index on `name`
- Without the index, the query passes
- The sorter is being invoked (confirmed by disabling index optimization) but still produces wrong order

### Hypothesis
The presence of the index changes the WHERE filter execution path, possibly causing the VDBE to use the index cursor for the WHERE scan, which returns rows in index key order for `name` but the sorter doesn't re-sort because it thinks the data is already sorted. Or the sorter receives rows with swapped sort key values.

This needs deeper VDBE trace analysis to pinpoint exactly what bytecodes are being emitted and executed.

title: EMERGENT-5-2 HIGH: FK cascade DELETE in morsel-parallel INSERT lane + SSI abort in sibling lane → cascade orphans violate FK constraint at commit
close_reason: PREMISE NOT CURRENTLY APPLICABLE (structurally impossible in the current engine; reopen when parallel morsel execution lands). The bead posits 'FK cascade DELETE in a morsel-parallel INSERT lane + SSI abort in a sibling lane'. But morsel-driven INSERT dispatch (connection.rs:24164) is gated on !self.fk_enforcement_enabled() (FK tables NEVER use morsel dispatch — they fall back to row-by-row, connection.rs:24150-24158) AND execute_morsel_insert uses MorselScheduler::new(1, MORSEL_INSERT_SIZE) i.e. worker_count=1 SEQUENTIAL execution (the comment at 24162 states parallel execution is future work). So there are neither morsel-parallel lanes for FK INSERTs nor sibling lanes that could SSI-abort. The realistic concern — connection-level concurrent FK CASCADE + child INSERT contention — is covered by bd_9sf3q_fk_cascade_parallel F1-F5 (passes 5/5: concurrent insert+cascade, multi-level cascade, same-parent SSI contention, SET NULL, rapid parent delete/reinsert; foreign_key_check stays empty). FUTURE GUARD: if parallel morsel execution (worker_count>1) is implemented and/or morsel dispatch is extended past the FK exclusion, the FK-cascade + SSI-abort-in-sibling-lane interaction must be re-evaluated before shipping.
