comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
# ORDER BY / GROUP BY out-of-range integer ordinal not rejected

## Symptom
A bare integer in ORDER BY / GROUP BY is a 1-based reference to an output column.
SQLite validates the ordinal range; frank only honors in-range ordinals and
silently treats an out-of-range integer as a constant expression (so ORDER BY
becomes a no-op and GROUP BY collapses to a single group).

```sql
CREATE TABLE t (a INTEGER, b INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (3,1),(1,2),(2,3);

SELECT a, b FROM t ORDER BY 3;
-- SQLite: ERROR 1st ORDER BY term out of range - should be between 1 and 2
-- frank:  OK -> [(3,1),(1,2),(2,3)]  (unordered; treated 3 as a constant)

SELECT a, b FROM t ORDER BY 0;   -- SQLite: ERROR (1-based)   frank: OK (no-op)
SELECT a, b FROM t ORDER BY -1;  -- SQLite: ERROR             frank: OK (no-op)
SELECT a FROM t GROUP BY 2;      -- SQLite: ERROR 1st GROUP BY term out of range - should be between 1 and 1
                                 -- frank:  OK -> [3]         (treated 2 as a constant -> one group)
```
In-range ordinals are correct in frank:
```sql
SELECT a, b FROM t ORDER BY 1;   -- OK on both (by a)
SELECT a, b FROM t ORDER BY 2;   -- OK on both (by b)
SELECT b FROM t GROUP BY 1;      -- OK on both
```

## Root cause
The ORDER BY / GROUP BY ordinal resolution honors a bare integer in
`[1, ncol]` as a column reference but, when the integer is out of range (or 0 /
negative), falls through to evaluating it as a constant expression rather than
raising an error. SQLite always treats a bare integer ORDER BY/GROUP BY term as
an ordinal and range-checks it.

## Fix sketch
When an ORDER BY / GROUP BY term is a bare integer literal, treat it as a 1-based
ordinal unconditionally and validate `1 <= n <= ncol`; otherwise raise
"Nth ORDER BY term out of range - should be between 1 and <ncol>" (and the
GROUP BY variant). Do NOT fall back to constant-expression evaluation for an
out-of-range bare integer. (Note: a non-literal integer expression, e.g. `0+3`,
is NOT an ordinal — only a bare literal is, matching SQLite.)

## Priority
P3 — over-acceptance (frank runs queries SQLite rejects, with surprising no-op /
single-group results). Same class as bd-tp6ia (ORDER BY after VALUES compound)
and bd-1zc9p (non-integer LIMIT coercion).

## Tests
`crates/fsqlite-e2e/tests/orderby_ordinal_range_oracle_e2e.rs`: in-range ordinals
green (`ordinal_in_range_sorts_and_groups`); `ordinal_out_of_range_rejected` is
#[ignore]'d on this bead.

title: BENCH-P2: mt-mvcc-bench FSQLITE_RETRY_TIMEOUT=5s fixed wall-clock budget makes 64+ writer arms unmeasurable — scale with threads x rows
description: First 64-writer attempt (artifact highwriter-baseline-20260728T0510Z-superserver) aborted: '[fsqlite t0] INSERT 0 exhausted retry budget after 1 retries: database is busy'. Mechanism: FsqliteRetryBudget::next_wait (mt_mvcc_bench.rs:454) gives up when started.elapsed() >= FSQLITE_RETRY_TIMEOUT (5s const, :94). At 64 writers x 1000-row txns with p95 txn latency already 2.3s at 32 writers, a txn can sit >5s in queue before its first meaningful retry — the budget measures wall-clock convoy time, not retry effort. title: Open .fsqlite read-only at a historical root_page with cross-process page-pin/refcount registry
description: Implement FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF COMMITSEQ N for file-backed databases: locate the historical root_page from .fsqlite-history, register a page-pin in shm so background reapers cannot reuse pages reachable from that root, and open a read-only snapshot at that root.
design: Plumb FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF COMMITSEQ N end-to-end: (1) parser already accepts the syntax (verify); (2) planner emits a HistoricalRead op that carries N; (3) at open-historical-snapshot time, locate the .fsqlite-history record for N (via sparse-index bisect from bd-hsi34), extract root_page; (4) page-pin/refcount: register a historical reader against the root_page so any background page-reaper or VACUUM operation cannot reuse pages reachable from this root while the reader is alive — maintain a pin registry keyed by (commit_seq, refcount, expiry_lease) in shm so multi-process readers coordinate; (5) open a read-only connection (Cx::new_read_only_cx) that swaps in the historical root_page in place of the live root for all page-table lookups; (6) reuse the existing in-memory snapshot ring machinery from #23 — the only difference is the root_page binding source. Index visibility: if an index page was freed/reused since commit_seq N, the historical reader sees the old contents via pinning. fcntl: SQLITE_FCNTL_DATA_VERSION returns the historical commit_seq (not the live one) for the duration of the snapshot. SQLITE_FCNTL_CKPT_DONE is unaffected.
acceptance_criteria: (1) Issue #82's exact repro (insert+update+commit+commit, then AS OF COMMITSEQ 1/2/3 before AND after close+reopen) returns the correct historical values; rusqlite oracle on a manually-constructed equivalent agrees on the row content. (2) Concurrent page reaper during a historical read: harness opens a snapshot at commit_seq N, immediately runs VACUUM in another process; the snapshot continues to read historical values until close. (3) Index visibility: if a non-unique index is rebuilt between the historical commit and now, the historical reader sees the OLD index entries, not the new ones. (4) SQLITE_FCNTL_DATA_VERSION returns the historical commit_seq from within the snapshot connection. (5) Pin registry stress: 100 concurrent historical readers across 8 processes, each on a different commit_seq, no page-reuse collisions, all readers close cleanly. (6) Pin registry crash recovery: if a holder dies, the reaper from bd-wekio sweeps the dead pin entry within lease/2.
notes: Pin registry shares semantics with bd-wekio (sweeper) and bd-lyrja (process_alive). Both are now explicit blockers; historical page retention and open must extend an already-retained set and fail closed when absent.

title: §12.17 Time Travel Queries (Native Mode Extension: AS OF COMMIT)
description:
E2E Test:
- test_e2e_bd_cfj0_compliance: concrete E2E identifier for structure lint compliance.

## SUMMARY

Implements Time Travel Queries (S12.17), a FrankenSQLite Native Mode extension that enables reading historical database state via the immutable commit stream (capsules + markers). Syntax uses FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF with either a timestamp string (converted to commit sequence via binary search of marker space) or COMMITSEQ N (direct commit sequence reference). A synthetic read-only snapshot S is created with S.high = target_commit_seq and the query executes using normal MVCC resolution rules: resolve(P, S) returns the newest committed version with version.commit_seq <= S.high. Time travel is strictly read-only; INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DDL in a time-travel context MUST fail with SQLITE_ERROR. If retention policy has pruned the requested state, the query fails with 'history not retained'. With tiered storage, older capsules may be fetched on demand from remote storage under Cx budgets.

## KEY DATA STRUCTURES / ALGORITHMS

- **Commit Sequence Resolution**: For timestamp-based queries, binary-search commit sequence space using random-access marker reads (S3.5.4.1) to find greatest marker with marker.commit_time_unix_ns <= target_time_unix_ns.
- **Synthetic Read-Only Snapshot**: Create snapshot S with S.high = target_commit_seq. No write capability.
- **MVCC Resolution**: resolve(P, S) returns newest committed version with version.commit_seq <= S.high, using standard S3.6/S5 resolution rules.
- **Timestamp Parsing**: SQLite-compatible datetime rules (same inputs accepted by unixepoch()) converted to target_time_unix_ns.
- **Tiered Storage Fetch**: Older capsules/index segments in remote storage fetched on demand under Cx capability budgets with decode/repair as usual (S3.5.11).
- **Retention Policy Check**: Before executing time-travel query, verify requested commit sequence is within retention bounds.

## NORMATIVE INVARIANTS

1. FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF COMMITSEQ N MUST use exact commit sequence N.
2. FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF timestamp MUST convert to commit sequence via binary search of markers.
3. Time travel queries MUST be read-only; INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DDL in time-travel context MUST fail with SQLITE_ERROR.
4. Synthetic snapshot MUST use S.high = target_commit_seq for MVCC resolution.
5. resolve(P, S) MUST return newest committed version with version.commit_seq <= S.high.
6. Pruned historical state MUST fail with explicit 'history not retained' error.
7. Tiered storage fetches MUST respect Cx capability budgets.
8. Time-travel queries MUST see a consistent snapshot at the target commit.
9. Multiple tables in the same time-travel query MUST all resolve against the same target commit sequence.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## §12.17 Time Travel Queries (Native Mode: AS OF COMMIT)

### Spec Content (Lines 14717-14761)

Native mode persists an immutable commit stream (capsules + markers). This enables time travel queries that evaluate reads against a historical commit sequence.

**Syntax (extension):**
```sql
SELECT ... FROM my_table FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF '2023-10-27 10:00:00';
SELECT ... FROM my_table FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF COMMITSEQ 1234567;
```

**Semantics (normative):**
1. Determine target_commit_seq:
   - If `AS OF COMMITSEQ N`, then `target_commit_seq := N`.
   - Otherwise parse the time-string using SQLite-compatible datetime rules (same inputs accepted by unixepoch(...)) and convert to target_time_unix_ns. Binary-search commit sequence space using random-access marker reads (§3.5.4.1) for greatest marker with `marker.commit_time_unix_ns <= target_time_unix_ns`, set `target_commit_seq := marker.commit_seq`.
2. Create a synthetic read-only snapshot S with `S.high = target_commit_seq`.
3. Execute query using normal MVCC resolution rules: `resolve(P, S)` returns newest committed version with `version.commit_seq <= S.high` (§3.6, §5).

**Restrictions (V1):**
- Time travel is read-only. Any attempt to execute INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DDL in a time-travel context MUST fail with SQLITE_ERROR (or more specific SQLite-compatible error code).

**Retention and tiered storage:**
- If retention policy has pruned the requested historical state, time travel MUST fail with explicit error "history not retained".
- With tiered storage enabled (§3.5.11), older capsules/index segments MAY reside only in remote storage; engine MUST fetch on demand under Cx budgets and decode/repair as usual.

### Unit Tests Required
1. test_time_travel_as_of_timestamp: FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF 'datetime' returns data at that point in time
2. test_time_travel_as_of_commitseq: FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF COMMITSEQ N uses exact commit sequence
3. test_time_travel_timestamp_to_commitseq_resolution: Timestamp is converted to correct commit sequence via binary search
4. test_time_travel_read_only: INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE in time-travel context fails with SQLITE_ERROR

6. test_time_travel_snapshot_isolation: Time-travel query sees consistent snapshot at target commit
7. test_time_travel_mvcc_resolution: resolve(P, S) returns newest committed version with commit_seq <= S.high
8. test_time_travel_pruned_history: Request for pruned history fails with "history not retained" error
9. test_time_travel_tiered_storage_fetch: Older capsules in remote storage are fetched on demand
10. test_time_travel_cx_budget_enforcement: Remote fetches respect Cx capability budget

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
`col IN (<literal list>)` does not coerce the list literals to the comparison
affinity of `col`, so an INTEGER column tested against text literals matches
nothing. (Same class as the BETWEEN-affinity bug bd-36kv6, different operator.)

Repro (FrankenSQLite vs rusqlite, both `:memory:`):
```sql
CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, i INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1,5),(2,10),(3,20),(4,100);
SELECT id FROM t WHERE i IN ('10','100') ORDER BY id;
```
frank => [] (empty)
csql  => [2, 4]

The plain comparison `i = '10'` and the range `i > '5'` already apply INTEGER
affinity correctly (those pass); only the IN-list path drops the coercion. Each
IN-list element should be compared using comparison_affinity(aff(col),
aff(element)) — i.e. a text literal acquires the INTEGER column's affinity.

Fix location: the IN-list lowering/eval (and the index-seek IN path) in
fsqlite-vdbe / fsqlite-core must apply the LHS column's affinity to each list
value, mirroring the binary `=`/range comparison path. Reproduces with an index
on the column present.

crates/fsqlite-e2e/tests/index_features_oracle_e2e.rs::index_in_list_affinity

acceptance_criteria:

comments.text:
## Goal
The previous-session Tier-B plan (deferred in 2026-04-19) called for a "focused prepared-statement-lifecycle rewrite" to collapse per-statement ceremony. W5-4 shipped a narrow fix (concurrent-handle cache) but NOT the full rewrite. Do the full rewrite now.

## Why this moves the needle
The 100-rows UPDATE-10 scenario is still ~12x slower than C SQLite (was 354x pre-QF-fix, 12x now). The residual is per-statement ceremony: compile-cache lookup, plan-cache probe, direct-simple gate, cursor construction, concurrent-mode probe, Cx checkpoint, page probe. Each layer is <1% self-time, but sum to ~8-10% on single-row UPDATE scenarios.

## Design sketch
- Unify compile-cache + plan-cache into one CompiledStatement with lazy materialization
- Cache the "fast-path eligibility" decision on CompiledStatement (eligibility doesn't change unless schema changes — invalidate on DDL)
- Pre-compute concurrent-mode branch at CompiledStatement creation time (avoid per-call probe)
- Peel the execute_prepared_with_params_after_background_status wrapper when bound_params are empty
- Batch multiple UPDATEs inside a single VDBE invocation for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE LOOPS from prepared statements

## Target paths
- `crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs` — most of this lives here
- `crates/fsqlite-vdbe/src/prepared.rs` (if exists) or equivalent PreparedStatement struct

## Measurement
- Target scenario: update-100-rows-update-10 (was 12.09x)
- Goal: ≤4x
- Also measure single-row INSERT ceremony (was ~4.24% self-time for `execute_prepared_direct_simple_insert`)
- Goal: ≤1.5%

## Correctness
- All conformance oracle suites stay green
- Concurrent-mode default stays true at all 4 key sites (AGENTS.md critical rule)
- Property test: prepared statement semantics identical to interpreter path

## Dependencies
- W5-6 hotspot table identifies exact ceremony frames to peel

## Non-goals
- NOT a total Connection API rewrite
- NOT touching asupersync runtime integration

title: printf/format: alt-form-2 (!) ignores explicit precision on %f; comma (,) thousands-grouping flag unimplemented — both diverge from stock
description:
Oracle-probe-found scalar divergences in fsqlite-func FormatFunc printf (crates/fsqlite-func/src/builtins.rs), vs sqlite3 3.46.1:

1. printf('%!5.2f', 3.14159): frank rendered '3.14159' (Rust shortest round-trip, ignoring the explicit precision); stock applies precision then strips trailing zeros -> ' 3.14'. The '!' (alternate-form-2) flag on %f must format at the requested precision FIRST, then strip trailing fractional zeros (keeping >=1 digit; '.0' forced at precision 0), width/sign applied last. '%!.0f' 5.5 -> '6.0'; '%!f' 5.0 -> '5.0'.

2. printf('%,d', 1234567): frank emitted the spec verbatim ('%,d') because ',' was not a recognized flag; stock groups the integer digits into thousands -> '1,234,567'. The ',' flag applies to %d/%i/%u and the integer part of %f, and is accepted-but-inert for %e/%g/%x/%o. Zero-pad pads raw digits BEFORE grouping ('%,08d' 1234 -> '00,001,234'); space-pad AFTER ('%,10d' -> ' 1,234,567').

Found via a broad scalar-function divergence probe (frank vs rusqlite over 115 exprs). Leaf-crate fix, no connection.rs dependency.
close_reason: Fixed in 798edcd67 (main+master). printf %f alt-form-2 (!) now applies explicit precision then strips trailing zeros (%!5.2f 3.14159 -> ' 3.14', %!.0f 5.5 -> '6.0'), preserving %!f 0.1 -> '0.1' (#176). Comma (,) thousands-grouping implemented for %d/%i/%u + %f integer part, inert for %e/%g/%x/%o; zero-pad groups after padding raw digits (%,08d 1234 -> '00,001,234'). 2 new oracle unit tests (28 cases) vs sqlite3 3.46.1; fsqlite-func --lib 443 passed/0 failed, clippy+fmt clean, ubs no new defects. Removed now-dead format_float_f. Found via broad scalar divergence probe.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## BUG: json_group_array / json_group_object aggregates not registered (implemented but unexposed)

Oracle parity vs rusqlite. t(id PK, g, k, v) = (1,a,x,10),(2,a,y,20),(3,b,z,30).
```sql
SELECT json_group_array(v) FROM t;
  -- frank: ERROR("no such function: JSON_GROUP_ARRAY/1")   csql: '[10,20,30]'
SELECT json_group_object(k, v) FROM t;
  -- frank: ERROR("no such function: JSON_GROUP_OBJECT/2")  csql: '{"x":10,"y":20,"z":30}'
SELECT g, json_group_object(k, v) FROM t GROUP BY g;
  -- frank: (a,NULL),(b,NULL)   csql: (a,'{"x":10,"y":20}'),(b,'{"z":30}')
```
Note the two manifestations: the whole-table aggregate ERRORS "no such function",
but the GROUP BY form SILENTLY returns NULL for the column (worse — a silent
wrong result). Both stem from the same root.

### Root cause
The functions are implemented in crates/fsqlite-ext-json/src/lib.rs
(`json_group_array`, `json_group_object`, and jsonb variants) but are NEVER
registered into any function registry — `register_json_scalars`
(fsqlite-ext-json/src/lib.rs:2908) registers only the scalar JSON funcs, and
there is no `register_json_aggregates` call wiring json_group_array/object into
the aggregate registry that connection.rs builds (connection.rs:2873 calls
register_json_scalars). So the SQL names resolve to "no such function".

### Fix
Register `json_group_array` and `json_group_object` (and their jsonb variants) as
aggregate functions in the registry that connection.rs populates, alongside the
scalar JSON registration. Also: the GROUP BY path should error on an unknown

INDEPENDENT RE-VERIFICATION at HEAD — reader deadlock FIXED. batch_pending.

ROOT CAUSE (original): concurrent_readers_consistency used a fallible post-open Barrier. When one reader Connection::open returned BusyRecovery, that reader never reached the Barrier, so the successful peers waited there FOREVER, preventing close and stranding the test (deadlock).

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
# JOIN USING with a column not present in both tables accepted

## Symptom
A `USING (col)` join requires `col` to exist in BOTH joined tables; SQLite rejects
it at prepare time otherwise. frank accepts the query and returns an empty result.
```sql
CREATE TABLE a (id INTEGER, x TEXT);
CREATE TABLE b (id INTEGER, y TEXT);

SELECT * FROM a JOIN b USING (nope);
-- SQLite: ERROR cannot join using column nope - column not present in both tables
-- frank:  OK -> []   (WRONG: over-accepts, yields empty rows)

SELECT * FROM a JOIN b USING (x);   -- x is only in a
-- SQLite: ERROR cannot join using column x - column not present in both tables
-- frank:  OK -> []
```
The valid case is correct on both:
```sql
SELECT * FROM a JOIN b USING (id);  -- OK, coalesced join on id
```
And NATURAL JOIN with no common columns correctly degrades to a cross join in frank.

## Root cause
The USING-clause resolution does not verify that each named column is present in
BOTH sides of the join; an unresolved USING column silently yields a join
condition that matches nothing (empty result) instead of raising an error. See
the JOIN/USING handling in `crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs` (and/or the
planner's join-column resolution).

## Fix sketch
When resolving a `USING (c1, c2, ...)` list, require every `ci` to appear in the
column set of BOTH joined relations; otherwise raise "cannot join using column
<ci> - column not present in both tables". (NATURAL JOIN auto-derives the common
set and needs no such error — and is already correct.)

## Priority
P3 — over-acceptance with a silently-wrong (empty) result. Part of the recurring
validate-then-reject class (bd-tp6ia / bd-1zc9p / bd-c9v0f / bd-1sgq2 / bd-z8pzx /
bd-bkbe6).

## Tests
`crates/fsqlite-e2e/tests/join_using_natural_edge_oracle_e2e.rs`: valid USING(id)
and NATURAL-no-common cross join green; `join_using_nonexistent_column_rejected`
#[ignore]'d on this bead.

title: BENCH-P0: comprehensive-bench subquery/CTE rows measure cache hits and discard fsqlite results (unvalidated, asymmetric)
description:
## Two measurement-integrity defects in comprehensive_bench.rs (cc_fsq, 2026-07-09)

### 1. The FrankenSQLite side discards its result; the C SQLite side does not.
crates/fsqlite-e2e/src/bin/comprehensive_bench.rs, "Subquery & CTE" section:

  // C SQLite - extracts the value, forcing full execution + column decode
  let _: i64 = stmt.query_row([], |r| r.get(0)).unwrap();

  // FrankenSQLite - discards the Row
  let _ = fs_stmt.query_row();

Consequences:
(a) The fsqlite side is never checked for correctness. A wrong COUNT would be
    reported as a speed win. No assertion compares the two engines' answers.
(b) Asymmetric work: C SQLite pays an i64 column extraction that fsqlite does
    not. Every row in this section inherits that bias.

Fix: bind both sides to the same value extraction and assert equality against
the C SQLite answer before recording a timing.

### 2. Repeated-identical-query loops reward a result cache that C SQLite lacks.
`measure()` prepares once, warms up, then re-executes the SAME statement
against a static in-memory DB. FrankenSQLite has a retained autocommit
count/sum cache (see `retained_autocommit_count_star_sum_row_in_txn` and the
`retained_autocommit_count_sum_cache_row` tests in connection.rs), so after
warmup it returns a cached row in ~70 ns while C SQLite re-executes in ~5.1 us.

The reported "72.43x faster" for "10000 rows / IN subquery" is therefore
"cache hit vs real execution". Measured against the same query with a fresh
prepare on a real DB file, fsqlite is ~89x SLOWER (see bd-2dgf5).

Similarly "Recursive CTE (1..1000 SUM)" reports 27.61x faster because a narrow
pattern matcher (`recursive_cte_integer_series_sum_plan`) recognizes exactly
`WITH RECURSIVE cnt(x) AS (SELECT a UNION ALL SELECT x+s FROM cnt WHERE x < b)
SELECT SUM(x) FROM cnt` and replaces the engine with a native integer loop.
Any deviation (COUNT instead of SUM, a second carried column, an outer WHERE)
falls back to the general path. The matcher requires: exactly 1 column, no FROM
and no WHERE in the base case, exactly one UNION ALL, recursive core selecting
only `x+step` with `WHERE x < bound`.

The 2026-05-05 ledger entry measured the GENERAL recursive-CTE path at
1.16x-1.24x SLOWER than C SQLite. The benchmark row does not exercise it.

Fix: vary parameters between iterations (defeats the result cache), and add at
least one recursive-CTE row that does NOT match the integer-series-sum matcher,
so the general frontier loop is actually measured.

### Why this matters
AGENTS.md "Documentation Invariants for Performance Claims" forbids describing
a workload as "N x faster" unless the cited benchmark measures that workload
shape. Any README/CHANGELOG claim sourced from these rows needs re-derivation.

title: Remove test-only Asupersync contexts from production RaptorQ/FEC paths
description:
## Background & Why This Exists
`crates/fsqlite-core/src/raptorq_codec.rs` currently constructs `AsCx::for_testing()` inside the production `AsupersyncCodec::encode()` and `decode()` paths. That is a real integration smell.

It means the production codec path is bypassing the caller's actual Asupersync / FrankenSQLite context:
- no inherited deadline or budget,
- no inherited trace identity,
- no real cancellation linkage back to the connection / worker region,
- and no guarantee that codec behavior matches the runtime semantics the rest of the engine is trying to standardize.

This is especially relevant because WAL FEC / repair work is exactly the kind of background workload where Asupersync's context propagation, cancellation, and structured shutdown semantics are supposed to matter.

## Scope
Focus on the production RaptorQ / WAL-FEC paths, especially:
- `crates/fsqlite-core/src/raptorq_codec.rs`
- any callers that currently treat codec work as detached from the connection / worker `Cx`
- the WAL / FEC background flow under `bd-d1tdm`

## Implementation Tasks
1. Replace `AsCx::for_testing()` in production codec encode/decode with a context derived from the real FrankenSQLite `Cx` / native Asupersync bridge.
2. Make the codec path inherit caller or worker budgets, deadlines, and cancellation, rather than silently manufacturing a fresh test context.
3. Ensure background WAL-FEC workers pass a region-owned / task-owned context into codec work so shutdown and poisoning semantics remain coherent.
4. Emit tracing fields that prove the codec work is attached to the same request / connection lineage as the invoking operation.
5. Preserve test ergonomics by keeping `for_testing()` only in tests or explicit test-only helpers, not in production execution paths.

## Testing & Verification
- Unit: cancel a parent context during large encode/decode work and verify the codec path aborts or yields according to the chosen shutdown contract.
- Unit: verify trace / budget propagation from the invoking connection or worker into codec spans.
- Unit: grep-style policy test ensuring `AsCx::for_testing()` is absent from production codec paths.
- E2E: run WAL-FEC repair under load, cancel or close the owning connection/region, and verify work is either drained or cancelled according to policy with no orphan background activity.
- Regression: existing codec correctness tests must still pass byte-for-byte.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Production codec work no longer uses `AsCx::for_testing()`.
2. Codec execution is attached to real caller/worker context, including cancellation and tracing lineage.
3. WAL-FEC background work remains correct and does not regress concurrent-writer behavior.
4. Tests make the policy explicit so the project cannot silently drift back to test-only contexts on production paths.

## Notes For Future Implementation
- This bead is deliberately narrow: it is about making the existing codec / FEC path obey real Asupersync context semantics.
- It should reuse the canonical `Cx` foundation (`bd-28z4i.2`, `bd-19vic`) rather than inventing a third context-propagation mechanism.

title: §12.10 BEGIN CONCURRENT + Cross-Database Two-Phase Commit
description:
E2E Test:
- test_e2e_bd_d2m7_compliance: concrete E2E identifier for structure lint compliance.

## SUMMARY

Implements the BEGIN CONCURRENT transaction mode (S12.10) and cross-database two-phase commit (S12.11) as FrankenSQLite extensions. BEGIN CONCURRENT enters MVCC concurrent writer mode with Snapshot Isolation where multiple transactions can write simultaneously to different pages. Page-level conflict detection uses first-committer-wins: if two CONCURRENT transactions modify the same page, the second committer gets SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT. Cross-database atomic WAL transactions use a two-phase commit protocol across attached database WAL files, overcoming standard SQLite's limitation of WAL-mode atomicity only within a single database. The 2PC protocol uses a global commit marker, with crash recovery semantics ensuring either all databases commit or none do.

## KEY DATA STRUCTURES / ALGORITHMS

- **MVCC Snapshot**: On BEGIN CONCURRENT, a read snapshot is established. No global write mutex is acquired; page locks replace it.
- **Page-Level Conflict Detection**: At commit time, check if any page in the write set was modified by another committed transaction since the snapshot was taken. Conflict returns SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT.
- **First-Committer-Wins Rule**: The transaction that commits first succeeds. Conflicting transactions must retry.
- **Two-Phase Commit Protocol**: Phase 1 (Prepare): Write WAL frames to all involved databases, fsync, but do not update WAL-index. Phase 2 (Commit): Write global commit marker, then update each database's WAL-index to make frames visible.
- **Global Commit Marker**: Records participating databases and prepare state in the primary WAL or dedicated coordinator file.
- **Crash Recovery**: Before Phase 1 complete: no effect. After Phase 1 but before Phase 2 marker: roll forward on recovery. During Phase 2: complete remaining WAL-index updates on recovery. Phase 1 failure on any DB: roll back all.
- **Savepoint Integration**: Savepoints within CONCURRENT transactions work normally; ROLLBACK TO reverts to savepoint but keeps CONCURRENT snapshot active.

## NORMATIVE INVARIANTS

1. BEGIN CONCURRENT MUST establish a snapshot and enter MVCC concurrent writer mode without acquiring global write mutex.
2. Multiple concurrent writers MUST be able to hold active transactions simultaneously.
3. Page-level conflict detection: same-page modification by two CONCURRENT transactions MUST result in SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT for the second committer.
4. First-committer-wins: the transaction that commits first succeeds.
5. SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT MUST be distinguishable from SQLITE_BUSY for application retry logic.
6. Cross-database WAL transactions MUST be atomic via two-phase commit.
7. Phase 1 MUST write WAL frames to all databases and fsync before Phase 2.
8. Phase 2 MUST make all frames visible atomically via WAL-index updates.
9. Crash after Phase 1 (all prepared) but before Phase 2 marker MUST roll forward on recovery.
10. Failure during Phase 1 on any database MUST roll back all databases.
11. 2PC MUST handle up to 12 total databases (main + temp + 10 attached via SQLITE_MAX_ATTACHED).
12. Savepoints within CONCURRENT transactions MUST preserve the CONCURRENT snapshot on ROLLBACK TO.
13. Cannot DETACH a database with active transactions.

## UNIT TEST REQUIREMENTS

1. test_begin_concurrent_multiple_writers -- Two connections both BEGIN CONCURRENT; insert into different pages; both commit successfully
2. test_begin_concurrent_page_conflict_busy_snapshot -- Two connections same snapshot; one commits page X; other updates same page X and gets SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT
3. test_begin_concurrent_first_committer_wins -- Three concurrent txns: T1 writes page 5, T2 writes page 5, T3 writes page 10; T2 commits first (ok), T1 gets BUSY_SNAPSHOT, T3 succeeds
4. test_cross_database_two_phase_commit -- ATTACH two databases; INSERT into both; COMMIT; verify both visible; simulate crash after Phase 1 and verify atomicity
5. test_savepoint_within_concurrent -- BEGIN CONCURRENT; INSERT A; SAVEPOINT sp1; INSERT B; ROLLBACK TO sp1; INSERT C; COMMIT; verify A and C visible, B not
6. test_attach_detach_limit -- Attach 10 databases (max); 11th fails; detach one; attach succeeds
7. test_cross_db_2pc_both_committed -- ATTACH aux DB, INSERT into both, COMMIT; verify both show inserts
8. test_cross_db_2pc_crash_after_prepare -- Simulate crash after Phase 1; on recovery, transaction fully committed or fully rolled back
9. test_cross_db_2pc_one_db_fails_prepare -- Simulate disk-full on one DB during prepare; all DBs rolled back
10. test_cross_db_2pc_crash_during_phase2 -- Simulate crash during WAL-index updates; on recovery, complete the commit
11. test_cross_db_2pc_max_attached -- Transaction spanning main + 10 attached databases commits atomically
12. test_cross_db_2pc_wal_mode_required -- Verify 2PC works in WAL mode

- test_e2e_bd_d2m7_compliance: concrete E2E identifier for structure lint compliance.

ATTACH a second database. Perform writes to both under BEGIN CONCURRENT. Inject a failure between prepare and commit phases. Verify: either both DBs reflect the transaction or neither does (atomic 2PC). Test multiple concurrent writers with page-level conflict detection. Verify SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT is returned on conflict. This is partially a FrankenSQLite-only test (CONCURRENT mode), with standard transaction features compared against C sqlite3.

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA

- All 12 unit tests pass.
- BEGIN CONCURRENT allows multiple simultaneous writers without global write mutex.
- Page-level conflict detection correctly identifies same-page conflicts and returns SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT.
- Cross-database 2PC ensures atomicity across all attached WAL databases.
- Crash recovery correctly handles all failure points (before Phase 1, between phases, during Phase 2).
- Savepoints within CONCURRENT transactions preserve snapshot correctly.
- SQLITE_MAX_ATTACHED limit of 10 is enforced.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
# §12.10 BEGIN CONCURRENT + Cross-Database Two-Phase Commit

## Scope

This bead covers the transaction control extensions specified in §12.10 and §12.11: the BEGIN CONCURRENT mode (MVCC concurrent writer entry point) and the requirement for cross-database atomic transactions via two-phase commit across attached WAL files.

## Spec References

- §12.10: "CONCURRENT: FrankenSQLite extension. Enters MVCC concurrent writer mode with Snapshot Isolation. Multiple CONCURRENT transactions can write simultaneously to different pages. Conflict on the same page results in SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT for the second committer."
- §12.10: Savepoints form a stack with RELEASE/ROLLBACK TO semantics
- §12.11: "Maximum 10 attached databases by default (SQLITE_MAX_ATTACHED)"
- §12.11: "Cross-database transactions are atomic only in rollback journal mode (not WAL mode in standard SQLite; FrankenSQLite MUST support cross-database atomic WAL transactions via two-phase commit across attached database WAL files)."
- §2.4 Layer 2: "BEGIN CONCURRENT: New non-standard syntax (matching SQLite's experimental BEGIN CONCURRENT branch). Uses page-level MVCC with SSI"
- §5.4: Global write mutex for Serialized mode; Concurrent mode uses page locks instead

## Requirements

### BEGIN CONCURRENT Mode
1. Parse and accept `BEGIN CONCURRENT [TRANSACTION]` syntax
2. On BEGIN CONCURRENT: establish a snapshot, enter MVCC concurrent writer mode (no global write mutex acquisition)
3. Multiple concurrent writers MUST be able to hold active transactions simultaneously
4. Page-level conflict detection: if two CONCURRENT transactions modify the same page, the second committer gets SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT
5. First-committer-wins rule: the transaction that commits first succeeds; the other must retry

### SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT Handling
6. When a CONCURRENT writer attempts to commit and finds a page conflict, return SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT (not SQLITE_BUSY)
7. The application-level retry loop can distinguish SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT from SQLITE_BUSY and decide whether to retry or abort

### Savepoint Interaction with CONCURRENT
8. Savepoints within a CONCURRENT transaction work normally (stack semantics)
9. ROLLBACK TO within CONCURRENT reverts to savepoint but keeps the CONCURRENT snapshot active
10. RELEASE within CONCURRENT commits savepoint work into the transaction's write set

### Cross-Database Two-Phase Commit
11. When a transaction spans multiple ATTACHed databases (all in WAL mode), COMMIT MUST be atomic across all databases
12. Implement two-phase commit protocol: Phase 1 (prepare) writes WAL frames to all involved databases; Phase 2 (commit) makes all visible atomically
13. If any database fails during Phase 1, roll back all databases
14. SQLITE_MAX_ATTACHED = 10: maximum number of attached databases (configurable)

### ATTACH/DETACH Constraints
15. ATTACH adds a new schema namespace; DETACH removes it
16. Cannot DETACH a database with active transactions
17. The main database is always named "main", temp is always "temp"

## Unit Test Specifications

### Test 1: `test_begin_concurrent_multiple_writers`
Open two connections. Both execute BEGIN CONCURRENT. Conn1 inserts into table A (page X). Conn2 inserts into table B (page Y, different page). Both COMMIT successfully -- no conflict because different pages.

### Test 2: `test_begin_concurrent_page_conflict_busy_snapshot`
Open two connections. Both execute BEGIN CONCURRENT with the same snapshot. Conn1 updates row on page X, commits. Conn2 updates different row on same page X, attempts commit. Verify Conn2 gets SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT.

### Test 3: `test_begin_concurrent_first_committer_wins`
Three concurrent transactions all reading the same snapshot. T1 writes page 5, T2 writes page 5, T3 writes page 10. T2 commits first (succeeds). T1 commits second (SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT on page 5). T3 commits third (succeeds, no conflict on page 10).

### Test 4: `test_cross_database_two_phase_commit`
ATTACH two databases. Begin transaction. INSERT into main.t1 and aux.t2. COMMIT. Verify both inserts are visible. Then begin another transaction, INSERT into both, simulate crash after Phase 1 prepare on main but before Phase 2 on aux. On recovery, verify either both or neither are committed (atomicity).

### Test 5: `test_savepoint_within_concurrent`
BEGIN CONCURRENT. INSERT row A. SAVEPOINT sp1. INSERT row B. ROLLBACK TO sp1. INSERT row C. COMMIT. Verify rows A and C are visible but B is not.

### Test 6: `test_attach_detach_limit`
Attach 10 databases (the maximum). Attempt to attach an 11th. Verify it fails with appropriate error. Detach one, then attach succeeds.

comments.text:
## Missing Detail (Audit Fix): Cross-Database Two-Phase Commit Protocol Detail

### Problem
The bead covers the high-level requirement for cross-database 2PC but lacks the protocol mechanics -- the specific phases, failure modes, and how this differs from standard SQLite.

### Spec Content (§12.11 lines 14617-14623 + §18 WAL Multiplexing lines 17847-17851)

**Standard SQLite limitation:** Cross-database transactions are atomic ONLY in rollback journal mode in standard SQLite. In WAL mode, standard SQLite does NOT guarantee atomicity across attached databases -- each database has its own WAL file, and a crash between writing one WAL and the other leaves databases inconsistent.

**FrankenSQLite requirement (normative):** FrankenSQLite MUST support cross-database atomic WAL transactions via two-phase commit across attached database WAL files.

**Two-Phase Commit Protocol for Cross-Database WAL Transactions:**

**Phase 1 -- Prepare:**
1. For each attached database touched by the transaction, prepare WAL frames (dirty pages serialized into WAL frame format)
2. Write WAL frames to each database's WAL file BUT do not update the WAL-index to make them visible
3. Ensure all frames are fsynced to stable storage
4. A global commit marker (in the primary WAL or a dedicated coordinator file) records which databases are participating and their prepare state

**Phase 2 -- Commit (make visible):**
1. Write the global commit marker indicating all databases are prepared
2. Update each database's WAL-index to make the new frames visible to readers
3. If all WAL-index updates succeed, the transaction is committed

**Crash Recovery Semantics:**
- Crash before Phase 1 completes: No WAL frames visible, no effect (automatic rollback)
- Crash after Phase 1 (all prepared) but before Phase 2 marker: On recovery, roll forward -- the prepared frames exist in all WAL files; write the commit marker and complete Phase 2
- Crash during Phase 2 (partial visibility): On recovery, detect the commit marker and complete any remaining WAL-index updates
- If any database fails during Phase 1 (e.g., disk full on one WAL): Roll back all databases -- discard uncommitted WAL frames from all involved databases

**WAL Multiplexing interaction (§18):** When WAL multiplexing is enabled (WAL frames sharded across multiple files), commit requires atomic append to all WAL files touched by the transaction. 2PC across WAL files uses a global commit marker in the primary WAL. Crash recovery replays prepared-but-uncommitted entries using this global commit marker.

**Constraint:** Maximum 10 attached databases by default (`SQLITE_MAX_ATTACHED`). The 2PC protocol must handle up to 12 total databases (main + temp + 10 attached).

## Test Requirements
- test_cross_db_2pc_both_committed: ATTACH aux DB, INSERT into both, COMMIT; verify both databases show the inserts
- test_cross_db_2pc_crash_after_prepare: Simulate crash after Phase 1 prepare on all databases; on recovery, transaction either fully committed or fully rolled back
- test_cross_db_2pc_one_db_fails_prepare: Simulate disk-full on one database during prepare; all databases rolled back
- test_cross_db_2pc_crash_during_phase2: Simulate crash during WAL-index updates; on recovery, complete the commit
- test_cross_db_2pc_max_attached: Transaction spanning main + 10 attached databases commits atomically
- test_cross_db_2pc_wal_mode_required: Verify 2PC works in WAL mode (not just rollback journal mode)

acceptance_criteria:
Acceptance Criteria:

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## Goal
Kill avg-ratio as the primary performance score. The 2.74x → 2.59x Wave-5 result hid significant wins and was demotivating precisely because the metric was wrong. Emit a richer scorecard.

## Why this matters
- avg-ratio is mean-of-ratios; mean is highly sensitive to tail outliers (the 12x max-ratio scenarios drag it up artificially)
- median-ratio tells the "typical case" story (currently 1.30x — fsqlite within 30% of C on half of scenarios)
- per-category weighted ratios (read / write / concurrent / mixed) tell the real-world story
- geomean-of-ratios is the mathematically correct "typical speedup" aggregator for ratio data
- P90 ratio tells the "tail performance" story — how bad is it in the worst cases we still lose on

## Design sketch
Update the comprehensive-bench summary emitter to output JSON with:
```json
{
  "avg_ratio": 2.59,               // keep for continuity but no longer primary
  "geomean_ratio": 1.47,           // correct aggregator for ratio data
  "median_ratio": 1.30,
  "p90_ratio": 5.2,                // 90th percentile ratio
  "p99_ratio": 10.1,
  "per_category": {
    "read_single": {"geomean": 0.95, "median": 0.91, "n": 40},
    "read_aggregate": {"geomean": 1.1, "median": 1.0, "n": 20},
    "write_single": {"geomean": 4.2, "median": 3.8, "n": 30},
    "write_bulk": {"geomean": 2.5, "median": 2.1, "n": 15},
    "concurrent_writers": {"geomean": 0.65, "median": 0.60, "n": 15}
  },
  "per_category_weighted": {        // weighted by realistic-workload weights
    "score": 1.52,                  // THIS is the new primary number
    "weights": {"read_single": 0.35, "write_single": 0.30, ...}
  }
}
```

## Target paths
- `crates/fsqlite-e2e/src/comprehensive_bench.rs` (emitter)
- `crates/fsqlite-e2e/src/bench_summary.rs` (schema — may need to create)
- Update bd-m4tju (W5-11 regression gate) to gate on new primary metric, not avg_ratio

## Measurement
- Re-run current scoreboard with richer schema
- Publish BEFORE and AFTER comparison: the avg-ratio says 2.59x; the geomean + per-category weighted score reveals the true picture

## Correctness
- Backward-compatible: the avg_ratio field stays in the JSON for anyone tooling against it
- Per-category tagging requires adding a category label to each of the 120 scenarios

## Dependencies
- None. This can ship independently of W5-6/W5-8.

## Non-goals
- Not changing the scenario set (keep all 120)
- Not changing the run infrastructure

title: Epic: many-core write-path reclamation to leapfrog legacy SQLite
description:
## Context
FrankenSQLite is still materially behind legacy SQLite on real Beads databases even after removing several catastrophic self-inflicted costs. The current honest repo-harness baseline remains roughly: c1 disjoint SQLite 7528.8 ops/s vs FrankenSQLite MVCC 1145.6 and forced single-writer 1156.9; c4 mixed_read_write SQLite 2769.5 vs MVCC 424.2 vs single-writer 130.9; c8 mixed_read_write SQLite 965.3 vs MVCC 620.1 vs single-writer 80.8. MVCC already retries less than SQLite under contention, so the remaining gap is primarily per-successful-transaction cost, synchronization, and hot-path waste rather than just conflict rate.

## Program Shape
This epic turns that diagnosis into an explicit many-core performance program for Threadripper/Xeon-class machines. The program is organized around measurement, synchronization removal, batched publish, VDBE and decode reduction, many-core architecture, optional async compile, single-writer cleanup, and correctness or rollout gates. The graph is intentionally self-contained so future execution can proceed from Beads alone.

## Success Criteria
- The graph covers the full optimization program and its verification obligations.
- Dependency edges remain honest and acyclic.
- Every implementation path can be understood from the beads themselves without reopening earlier planning discussions.
- The final scorecard can distinguish real wins from benchmark noise or one-profile lab wins.
design:
- Preserve the core product invariant: concurrent-writer mode stays ON by default. Nothing in this epic may regress FrankenSQLite back into a file-level single-writer design.
- Treat evidence as a first-class artifact. Every major optimization needs comparable before/after numbers on the same real Beads fixtures, workload matrix, retry policy, and build profile.
- Prefer per-core private work, bounded publish, and lock-free or sharded publication over global synchronization. Many-core scale will not come from one giant shared critical section.
- Optimize both MVCC mode and forced single-writer mode honestly. MVCC is the flagship path, but the comparison path must not be pathologically worse because of avoidable overhead.
- Require tests, crash/fault validation, and a final scorecard that distinguishes real wins from benchmark noise.
acceptance_criteria:
- The Beads graph covers measurement, synchronization removal, WAL/pager rewrite, VDBE/decode work, many-core architecture, optional async pre-JIT, single-writer cleanup, and correctness/rollout gates.
- Every implementation bead includes concrete acceptance criteria that mention validation or benchmark evidence, not just code changes.
- Dependency edges reflect real blockers and remain acyclic.
- Future work can infer the motivation, constraints, and target outcomes from the beads themselves without consulting the earlier markdown discussion.
- This bead set explicitly includes comprehensive unit-test, end-to-end, and structured-logging obligations rather than treating verification as implied follow-up work.

title: A3: automate perf, strace, hyperfine, and allocation artifact capture
description:
## Goal
Automate collection of the primary evidence artifacts for the hot benchmark cells: wall-clock benchmarks, sampled and off-CPU profiles, syscall summaries, allocation-oriented profiles, and topology-aware hardware-counter captures such as topdown, cache-to-cache/HITM, scheduler wakeup, and migration evidence when the host supports them. The purpose is to stop re-deriving ad hoc command lines every time a new hotspot investigation starts and to make cache, NUMA, and synchronization diagnosis first-class rather than afterthoughts.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. There is a repeatable workflow for `hyperfine`/`perf`/`strace`/heap-oriented collection on the canonical matrix, plus topology-aware `perf stat`/topdown and `perf c2c`/HITM or best-available equivalents on supported hosts.
2. Artifact names encode fixture, workload, concurrency, mode, date, and build profile.
3. Artifact manifests capture exact command lines, source revision, Beads data hash, tool versions, fixture identifier, kernel version, and placement policy for each run.
4. At least one representative hot cell is captured end-to-end through the automated flow in both profiler-safe and full-validation forms, including one cache-or-NUMA-focused evidence pack and one off-CPU-or-scheduler-focused evidence pack.
5. The workflow records when a requested counter set is unavailable and what fallback metric or trace was used instead.
6. The scripts, harness changes, or reports in this bead emit structured logs and artifact manifests rich enough to reproduce results without reconstructing the workflow by hand.

title: A4: define the performance scorecard and regression thresholds
description:
## Goal
Define the scorecard that this program will use to decide whether an optimization is real: throughput, retries, wall time, CPU utilization, IPC, futex share, p50/p95/p99 end-to-end latency, commit-latency markers, placement-profile stability, and any mode-specific indicators that matter. Without this, the project will keep drifting between numbers that are not directly comparable.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. The scorecard lists every primary metric and its collection source.
2. Thresholds or target directions are explicit for throughput, retry pressure, blocking indicators, and `p50/p95/p99` end-to-end plus commit-latency markers.
3. The scorecard also defines how to treat placement-profile stability, including what counts as a transferable win versus a profile-specific lab result.
4. Where a claimed improvement relies on cache, NUMA, or scheduler behavior, the corresponding supporting indicators are named explicitly on the scorecard.
5. The scorecard is usable by later rollout and reporting beads without additional interpretation work.
6. The scripts, harness changes, or reports in this bead emit structured logs and artifact manifests rich enough to reproduce results without reconstructing the workflow by hand.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The scorecard lists every primary metric and its collection source.
2. Thresholds or target directions are explicit for throughput, retry pressure, blocking indicators, and `p50/p95/p99` end-to-end plus commit-latency markers.
3. The scorecard also defines how to treat placement-profile stability, including what counts as a transferable win versus a profile-specific lab result.
4. Where a claimed improvement relies on cache, NUMA, or scheduler behavior, the corresponding supporting indicators are named explicitly on the scorecard.
5. The scorecard is usable by later rollout and reporting beads without additional interpretation work.
6. The scripts, harness changes, or reports in this bead emit structured logs and artifact manifests rich enough to reproduce results without reconstructing the workflow by hand.
notes: Current evidence strongly suggests that CPU utilization and futex share belong on the scorecard alongside raw ops/s, because the project is underutilizing many-core hardware even when retry counts are acceptable. Users also care whether the win survives outside one carefully pinned benchmark profile.

title: A5: classify hot cells by dominant bound type (sync, CPU, cache/memory, or I/O)
description:
## Goal
Classify each canonical hot benchmark cell by dominant bound type and microarchitectural signature so the optimization program stops conflating lock contention, cache-line ping-pong, remote NUMA access, TLB or branch waste, allocator churn, and durable I/O. This bead is the explicit answer to the question "what is spending cycles and wall time on 32-64 core machines?" rather than a generic hotspot label.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Each canonical hot cell is classified by dominant bound type with supporting counters and trace evidence.
- The output decomposes `queueing + synchronization + retries + service + allocator/cache + durable I/O` and records the dominant microarchitectural signature (`HITM/false-sharing`, `remote NUMA`, `LLC/TLB miss`, `branch/uop`, or `syscall/durability`).
- Ambiguous or mixed-bound cells are called out explicitly with confidence notes instead of forced into a false category.
- The resulting classification is detailed enough to steer share-nothing lane design, false-sharing elimination, residual-lock strategy, and durability-lane work.
- The scripts, harness changes, or reports in this bead emit structured logs and artifact manifests rich enough to reproduce results without reconstructing the workflow by hand.

title: A6: capture hardware topology, affinity, NUMA/SMT state, and placement policy
description:
## Goal
Capture the hardware-topology and placement contract for this optimization campaign so results can be interpreted correctly on high-end Threadripper and Xeon-class machines. This includes socket, node, CCD/CCX/LLC topology where discoverable, SMT sibling relationships, preferred-core and boost behavior, memory topology, pinning policy, memory-placement policy, and any runtime environment details that materially affect write-path scaling.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Artifact bundles record CPU model, stepping, and microcode or firmware revision where accessible; socket or NUMA topology; CCD/CCX/LLC domains where discoverable; SMT state; memory topology or NUMA distances; kernel version; governor or EPP/energy-policy state; boost/C-state state; huge-page or THP state; relevant scheduler or IRQ placement settings; and the benchmark placement profile.
2. The benchmark methodology states when pinning, SMT spreading or packing, NUMA-local allocation, interleave, automatic NUMA balancing, IRQ pinning, compile/helper-lane placement, or other placement strategies are used or intentionally avoided.
3. Future many-core measurements can be reproduced on comparable hardware without rediscovering the environment contract.
4. The scripts, harness changes, or reports in this bead emit structured logs and artifact manifests rich enough to reproduce results without reconstructing the workflow by hand.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Artifact bundles record CPU model, stepping, and microcode or firmware revision where accessible; socket or NUMA topology; CCD/CCX/LLC domains where discoverable; SMT state; memory topology or NUMA distances; kernel version; governor or EPP/energy-policy state; boost/C-state state; huge-page or THP state; relevant scheduler or IRQ placement settings; and the benchmark placement profile.
2. The benchmark methodology states when pinning, SMT spreading or packing, NUMA-local allocation, interleave, automatic NUMA balancing, IRQ pinning, compile/helper-lane placement, or other placement strategies are used or intentionally avoided.

4. The scripts, harness changes, or reports in this bead emit structured logs and artifact manifests rich enough to reproduce results without reconstructing the workflow by hand.
notes: This bead exists because 32+ core machines can mislead badly when affinity, NUMA placement, SMT sibling use, or boost policy are left implicit. The environment contract must be explicit before the project can claim many-core insights confidently.

title: A7: refresh authoritative c1 and persistent 16t evidence around the actual 2026-03-23 failures
description:
## Goal
Refresh the authoritative evidence surface around the two failures that matter most right now: the `c1` fixed-tax problem and the persistent 8t/16t commit-path collapse.

Why this bead exists now:
- The latest canonical matrix shows MVCC and forced single-writer are almost identical at `c1`, so the first-order problem there is core engine service time rather than MVCC conflict logic.
- The persistent writer benchmark still falls off a cliff by 16 threads, so the many-writer story needs its own evidence lane.
- The repo already has useful counters and older artifacts, but future work needs a current, authoritative pack focused on the exact failing cells rather than relying on older mixed hot-cell captures.

This bead is the measurement anchor for the current overlay. It should produce the evidence packs and classification needed by the low-tax, commit-collapse, advanced-decision, and final-scorecard lanes.

comments.author: codex
comments.text:
## Intent of A7

`A7` is the evidence-refresh lane. It exists because the 2026-03-23 results changed the story: the project is not looking at one generic “performance gap,” but at a split failure signature with one low-concurrency disease and one many-writer tail-collapse disease.

The deliverables in this lane should leave behind authoritative artifact packs for the exact red cells, not just rerun logs. At minimum the packs should carry:
- benchmark command lines, toolchain/build profile, machine context, and fixture identity,
- throughput plus p50/p95/p99/max latency where applicable,
- top CPU and allocation profiles for the worst `c1` cells,
- phase-attribution and wake-path evidence for persistent `8t` and `16t`,
- an explicit classification of each red cell into service, queueing, synchronization, allocation, or mixed causes.

## Why this track is first

The previous local matrix makes two facts too strong to ignore:
- `c1` MVCC and single-writer are nearly identical, so low-concurrency underperformance is not primarily a page-conflict or multi-writer story.
- Persistent `16t` collapses far harder than `8t`, which is typical of a convoy or publication pathology, not just “a bit more work.”

This lane therefore exists to freeze the real before-state and prevent the project from optimizing against folklore. It follows the extreme-software-optimization rule: baseline first, profile first, and re-profile after each shift because the dominant bottleneck will move.

## Reading the child beads

- `A7.1` owns authoritative `c1` hot-path packs.
- `A7.2` owns authoritative persistent `8t/16t` phase packs.
- `A7.3` converts raw evidence into causal classification.
- `A7.4` freezes provenance and scorecard conventions so later reruns remain comparable.

A future agent should treat this lane as the ground truth source for the rest of the overlay. If these packs are weak, every downstream conclusion is weak.

| Workload | SQLite | MVCC | Single-writer | MVCC/SQLite | SW/SQLite | MVCC/SW |

comments.text:
## A7.1 Script Review (pane 6 — roaming reviewer)

### Defect 1: Hot-profile always targets commutative_inserts_disjoint_keys (line 114)

The script hardcodes `--preset "commutative_inserts_disjoint_keys"` for the hot-profile step. The bead says "worst c1 cells" — but the worst c1 cell may be `hot_page_contention` (c1 = 0.633x) or `mixed_read_write` (c1 = 3.519x is actually a win). The measured worst is `commutative_inserts_disjoint_keys` (c1 = 0.205x), so the hardcoding happens to be correct for the current data. But the script should either:
- (a) Parse the JSONL output from the bench run to find the actual worst cell, or
- (b) Profile ALL three workloads (not just commutative) since c1 hot profiles are cheap (~30s each).

**Recommendation:** Profile all three. The cost is minimal and eliminates the fixed-workload assumption.

### Defect 2: Hot-profile output goes to stdout log only (line 118)

The `hot-profile` subcommand's output is captured via `tee` to a `.log` file, but the bead says "full hot-profile bundle." If `hot-profile` produces structured artifacts (flamegraph SVGs, opcode histograms, etc.), those go to `$HP_DIR` via `--output-dir`. But the `--pretty` flag suggests the primary output is human-readable stdout. The script should verify that `$HP_DIR` actually contains machine-readable artifacts, not just pretty-printed text.

**Check needed:** Does `realdb-e2e hot-profile --output-dir` produce structured files? If not, the hot-profile step is capturing logs, not artifacts.

### Defect 3: No SQLite baseline comparison in the output

The script captures SQLite control, MVCC, and single-writer runs separately, but doesn't compute ratios. The bead says "enough hot-path detail that later beads can attribute the fixed-tax problem." The raw JSONL files are useful but downstream consumers (bd-db300.4.5, D5 track) need pre-computed ratios to triage.

**Recommendation:** Add a summary step that reads all three JSONL files per fixture and computes `fsqlite_mvcc / sqlite3` and `fsqlite_single / sqlite3` ratios. Output as `$OUTPUT_DIR/summaries/ratios.json`.

### Non-defect observation: Script structure is correct

- All three canonical fixtures are run (frankensqlite, frankentui, frankensearch)
- All three workloads per fixture
- Both MVCC and single-writer modes
- Build metadata captured
- Profile is release-perf

## A7.2 Authoritativeness Review

### Current state

The A7.2 capture script (`capture_persistent_phase_pack.sh`) has the right structure but falls back to manual instructions when `realdb-e2e bench --threads` doesn't work. This means A7.2 evidence is NOT yet automatically capturable.

### Is A7.2 output authoritative enough for C8.3/C8.8?

**For C8.3 (convoy audit):** YES, if the output includes:
- Wake-reason snapshot (`notify/timeout/flusher_takeover/failed_epoch/busy_retry` counts)
- Phase-B histogram percentiles (p50/p95/p99/max)
- `consolidator_lock_wait` histogram percentiles
- `is_lock_topology_limited()` verdict
- Thread count in provenance

These are all available via `GLOBAL_CONSOLIDATION_METRICS.snapshot()`. The script must call this after the benchmark and serialize it to JSON.

**For C8.8 (rerun after commit-path steps):** YES, if the output is **machine-comparable** — same JSON schema, same field names, same units. The current script outputs YAML provenance + ad-hoc JSON. It should output a single canonical JSON bundle with a fixed schema.

### What's missing for authoritativeness

1. **Structured JSON output of `ConsolidationMetricsSnapshot`** — not just log parsing. The benchmark binary should serialize the snapshot directly.
2. **Thread-count parametrization** — `realdb-e2e bench --threads N` must work, not fall back to manual capture.
3. **Machine-readable schema** — a fixed JSON envelope: `{ "bead_id", "thread_count", "provenance": {...}, "consolidation_metrics": {...}, "throughput": {...}, "latency_percentiles": {...} }`.
4. **Baseline comparison** — same workload run against C SQLite at the same thread count for ratio computation.

### Verdict

A7.2 is NOT yet authoritative. It's a correct scaffold. To become authoritative it needs items 1-3 above, which require `realdb-e2e` CLI work (thread-count flag + JSON metrics dump). Item 4 is a nice-to-have — C8.3 can use standalone FrankenSQLite numbers for the convoy audit.

- FrankenSQLite 8t: latency-derived throughput varies widely (p50 ranges 429-1478us across samples)

| p99 | 660-3000us | 15,500-47,500us (20-50x worse) |

FrankenSQLite p50 is 2-4x worse than SQLite. p99 is catastrophically worse (20-50x). But max is actually better — SQLite max hits 2-6 SECONDS while FrankenSQLite max stays under 410ms. This suggests SQLite has rare multi-second stalls (likely WAL checkpoint interference) while FrankenSQLite has consistently high tail latency (convoy-shaped).

**Lock topology (representative sample 23):**
- `flusher_lock_wait_fraction`: 1003 basis points (10.03%) — barely over the "I/O-limited" vs "lock-topology-limited" boundary
- `lock_topology_limited`: false (but barely — 50.15% lock wait)
- `flusher_commits`: 6385, `waiter_commits`: 2826 — 69% flusher, 31% waiter

**Wake reasons (zero timeouts — good):**
- notify: 2826 (100% of waiter wakes)
- timeout: 0 (condvar notifications not being lost)
- flusher_takeover: 125 (~4.4% of waiter wakes)
- failed_epoch: 0
- busy_retry: 30

**Phase histogram headlines:**
- `waiter_epoch_wait`: p50=59us, **p99=1129us** — this is the convoy tail. Waiters spend up to 1.1ms waiting for the flusher.
- `wal_append`: p50=29us, p99=66us — WAL I/O itself is fast and stable.
- `arrival_wait`: p50=20us, p99=25us — flusher batch assembly is quick.
- `consolidator_lock_wait`: p50=0, p99=0 — no consolidator lock contention.
- `wal_backend_lock_wait`: p50=0, p99=0 — no WAL backend lock contention at 8t.
- `full_commit`: p50=66us, p99=179us — full commit time is reasonable.

### C8.3 implications

At 8t:
1. **No timeout-shaped convoy.** Zero timeout wakes confirms `notify_all` is working.
2. **Waiter epoch wait IS the tail.** p99=1129us vs `wal_append` p99=66us. Waiters are paying ~17x the actual I/O cost waiting for the flusher to finish.
3. **Lock topology is borderline.** lock_wait_fraction=10.03% is on the edge. At 16t this will likely tip over.
4. **Flusher takeover is non-negligible.** 4.4% of wakes result in takeover — suggests some flusher contention or vacancy windows.
5. **The herd wakeup convoy from the C8.3 prep note is NOT the primary issue at 8t.** The `consolidator_lock_wait` is 0 — no thundering herd visible at this concurrency. The issue is pure flusher serialization: one flusher does WAL I/O while 7 waiters park.

## A7.2 16t Pack Partial Review (pane 6 — read-only)

### Pack status: 8/10 FrankenSQLite samples captured, run still in progress (no Criterion "Analyzing" line yet). SQLite 16t complete (11 samples).

### 16t findings — the tail collapse is now mechanically visible

**Latency (FrankenSQLite 16t, 8 samples):**
- p50: 8,500-11,300us (8.5-11.3ms)
- p99: 1,592,000-1,807,000us (1.59-1.81 SECONDS)
- p99/p50 ratio: **~180x** — catastrophic tail amplification

**Compare to 8t:**
- 8t p50: 430-1,480us → 16t p50: 8,500-11,300us — **~10x worse**
- 8t p99: 15,500-47,500us → 16t p99: 1,592,000-1,808,000us — **~50x worse**

**Wake reasons — timeout convoy CONFIRMED at 16t:**
- notify: ~13,600-14,300 per sample
- **timeout: 3,300-4,600 per sample (20-25% of all wakes)**
- flusher_takeover: 940-1,460 per sample
- busy_retry: 145-229 per sample

At 8t, timeout was ZERO. At 16t, **20-25% of wakes are timeouts**. This confirms the C8.3 convoy hypothesis: the 200ms condvar timeout is firing routinely, not as a safety net. Waiters are timing out because the flusher is too slow (wal_append p99 = 1,012,837us ≈ 1 second).

**Phase histogram — wal_append is the bottleneck:**
- `wal_append`: p50=2,338us, **p99=1,012,837us** (1 second!)
- `waiter_epoch_wait`: p50=5,899us, **p99=1,122,033us** — tracks wal_append tail exactly
- `consolidator_lock_wait`: p50=0, p99=0 — NOT the bottleneck
- `wal_backend_lock_wait`: p50=0, p99=0 — NOT the bottleneck
- `lock_topology_limited`: False (lock_frac=1bp)

**Root cause at 16t is NOT lock convoy — it's WAL I/O collapse.**
The `wal_append` p99 hits 1 second at 16t (vs 66us at 8t — **15,000x worse**). This is likely filesystem/IO scheduler saturation: 16 concurrent writers producing 16x the WAL frame volume, hitting IO queue depth limits or fsync coalescing breakdowns.

The C8.3 herd-wakeup convoy is a secondary effect: waiters time out because the flusher takes 1+ second on WAL I/O, not because of condvar thundering herd.

### Flusher/waiter ratio
- flusher_commits: 3,700-5,500 (~25%)
- waiter_commits: 13,600-14,300 (~75%)
- At 8t: 69% flusher, 31% waiter. At 16t: 25% flusher, 75% waiter. More waiters = more timeout exposure.

comments.text:
## A7.2 final evidence correction and close rationale

The pack is now complete and authoritative enough to unblock the next commit-path work.

Artifacts:
- `artifacts/persistent_phase_pack_20260323_222108/8t`
- `artifacts/persistent_phase_pack_20260323_222108/16t`
- `artifacts/persistent_phase_pack_20260323_222108/provenance/environment.yaml`
- `artifacts/persistent_phase_pack_20260323_222108/rerun.sh`

Corrected headline verdict:
- `8t`: FrankenSQLite loses badly at about `0.66x` SQLite.
- `16t`: FrankenSQLite technically wins at about `1.66x` SQLite, but only because SQLite collapses even harder under retry tail; this is not a healthy result.

What the completed pack proves:
1. The persistent benchmark failure is split by regime, not one generic "commit path slow" story.
2. At `8t`, the measured loss is **not** explained by MVCC conflicts, consolidator lock convoy, or WAL backend lock wait. The main measured tail is waiter/epoch delay while append remains relatively small.
3. At `16t`, the first-order measured service explosion is append-side time inside the WAL append bucket itself: `wal_append` p99 is in the ~`0.84s` to `0.93s` range, average flusher append is ~`25ms` to `30ms`, and `phase_B` average is ~`66ms` to `71ms`.
4. At `16t`, waiter publication and timeout recovery are still real amplifiers: timeout wakes rise into the thousands per sample and flusher takeovers rise sharply. But the explicit lock-wait counters remain near zero, so the evidence does **not** support lock-topology convoy as the primary measured cause.

Implication for sequencing:
- `C8.6` append-side service-time reduction should move ahead of any ambitious publication rewrite.
- `C8.4` remains justified as the second-stage fix because timeout/takeover amplification is real at `16t`, but it is not the best first cut.

Residual caveat:
- The `16t` "win" is against a catastrophically degraded SQLite comparator. It should not be read as success; it only means the capture is now sufficient to guide causality and implementation order.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## A7.3 Dominant-Cost Classification — Red Cell Decomposition

### Evidence basis
- **c1**: A7.1 pack (commutative_inserts at 0.56x, hot_page at 1.12x, mixed at 6.7x)
- **8t persistent**: A7.2 pack (FrankenSQLite 1.23 Kelem/s vs SQLite 1.85 = 0.66x)
- **16t persistent**: A7.2 pack (FrankenSQLite 78 elem/s vs SQLite 47 = 1.66x)

---

### Cell 1: c1 commutative_inserts_disjoint_keys (0.56x)

**Dominant bucket: SERVICE (parse→compile→execute ceremony)**

Evidence:
- MVCC/single-writer ratio = 0.924x → MVCC adds <8% overhead
- parse=3759 SQL bytes per iteration, row_materialization=2363ns
- mvcc_page_lock_wait = 0ns (zero contention at c1)
- The fixed cost is the per-statement lifecycle: parse → plan → compile → VDBE dispatch → pager begin/commit

Decomposition:
| Bucket | Share | Evidence |
|--------|-------|----------|
| Service (parse/compile/execute) | ~70% | Hot-path profile: parse bytes dominate; MVCC/SW nearly identical |
| Allocator churn (VDBE engine, decode buffers) | ~20% | cached_vdbe_engine reuse already deployed; residual row materialization |
| Synchronization | ~5% | Mutex on pager begin/commit even at c1 (no contention but ceremony cost) |
| I/O | ~3% | MemoryVfs — no disk, but WAL frame assembly still runs |
| Queueing | ~0% | Single writer, no queue |
| Retries | ~0% | Zero conflicts |

**Next lever: D5.2 (fused prepared-DML entry)**. The ceremony cost is the per-statement begin→commit wrapper, not any single phase. Fusing the prepared statement path to skip redundant pager lifecycle steps is the highest-EV intervention.

---

### Cell 2: 8t persistent disjoint writers (0.66x)

**Dominant bucket: QUEUEING (group-commit waiter epoch wait) + SERVICE (WAL append)**

Evidence (steady state, typical iteration):
- phase_B avg: 94-107µs (total commit path)
- Flusher: arrival_wait=15µs, wal_append=30µs, exclusive_lock=3µs
- Waiter: epoch_wait=108-137µs (waiting for flusher to complete their batch)
- Flusher/waiter ratio: ~6400/2900 = 2.2:1
- Wake reasons: notify=2900, takeover=~120, busy_retry=~25

Spike iteration (last measurement):
- wal_append spiked 30→102µs (3.4x), phase_B spiked 100→748µs (7.5x)
- busy_retry spiked 25→241 (10x)
- This single spike dominates the Criterion mean

Decomposition:
| Bucket | Share | Evidence |
|--------|-------|----------|
| Queueing (waiter epoch_wait) | ~45% | 2900 waiters × 120µs = 348ms queued per iteration; flusher serializes all |
| Service (WAL append) | ~25% | 30µs avg × 6400 flushers = 192ms; spikes to 102µs = 653ms |
| Synchronization (consolidator lock + exclusive) | ~15% | consolidator_lock_wait ~0µs avg but exclusive_lock=3µs × 6400 = 19ms |
| Retries (busy_retry) | ~10% | 25-241 retries with exponential backoff; dominates spike iterations |
| I/O (wal_sync) | ~0% | wal_sync=0µs (MemoryVfs backend, no fsync) |
| Allocator | ~5% | Batch assembly churn (frame scratch buffers) |

**Key insight: the loss at 8t is NOT the flusher being slow. It's the waiter queue.**
At 8 threads, ~2900 commits wait 120µs each for a flusher that takes 48µs of real work.
The 2.5x amplification (120/48) is pure queueing overhead — waiters block on a condvar
while the flusher processes other writers' batches.

**Next lever: C8.6 (reduce flusher-side batch assembly churn)** addresses the flusher
service time, shrinking the queueing tail proportionally. However, the bigger structural
issue is the single-flusher bottleneck — C8.4 (parallel WAL commit paths) would
eliminate the queueing bucket entirely.

**Recommended priority: C8.6 first (low risk, 10-20% improvement by shrinking flusher
service time), then C8.4 if 8t is still red after C8.6.**

---

### Cell 3: 16t persistent disjoint writers (1.66x WIN, but both engines collapsed)

**Dominant bucket: SERVICE (WAL append monopoly) + QUEUEING (waiter convoy)**

Evidence:
- wal_append avg: **25,812µs** (26ms!) per flusher commit
- waiter epoch_wait avg: **67,664µs** (68ms!)
- phase_B avg: **70,949µs** (71ms!)
- Flusher/waiter ratio: 4200/13700 = 1:3.3 (most threads are waiters)
- wal_append p99: **842,617µs** (843ms!) — WAL append tail is nearly 1 second
- phase_b p99: **1,036,445µs** (1s!)
- Wake reasons: notify=13582, **timeout=3939** (22%), takeover=1296, busy_retry=285
- **Conflicts: 189-343 per iteration** — actual page conflicts emerging at 16t

Decomposition:
| Bucket | Share | Evidence |
|--------|-------|----------|
| Service (WAL append) | ~35% | 26ms avg × 4200 flushers; single flusher monopolizes WAL for entire batch |
| Queueing (waiter epoch_wait convoy) | ~40% | 68ms avg × 13700 waiters; 22% wake by timeout not notify |
| Retries (busy + conflicts) | ~10% | 285 busy_retry + 189-343 conflicts per iteration |
| Synchronization (timeout-wakeup convoy) | ~10% | 3939 timeout wakes (22%) indicate condvar missed notifications or convoy |
| I/O | ~0% | MemoryVfs |
| Allocator | ~5% | Batch assembly for 16-writer batches |

**Key insight: 16t is a waiter convoy.** The single flusher takes 26ms to process a
16-writer batch through WAL append. During that 26ms, all other threads are parked on
the condvar. 22% of wakes are TIMEOUTS, not notifications — this means the condvar
notification is being lost or the flusher is taking longer than the 200ms timeout in
some cases. The takeover count (1296) shows waiters are frequently taking over a
stalled flusher.

**FrankenSQLite wins 1.66x only because C SQLite is worse**: C SQLite at 16t hits
550 SQLITE_BUSY retries per iteration with p99=1s and max=247s. Both engines have
collapsed; FrankenSQLite's group-commit convoy is less bad than C SQLite's BUSY-retry
cascade.

---

### Summary: Priority Sequencing

| Priority | Bead | Target | Expected impact | Rationale |
|----------|------|--------|----------------|-----------|
| **1** | **C8.6** | 8t: reduce flusher batch assembly | 10-20% 8t throughput | Shrinks flusher service time → proportional waiter queue reduction. Low risk. |
| **2** | **D5.2** | c1: fused prepared-DML entry | 30-50% c1 throughput | Eliminates per-statement ceremony for the dominant c1 cost. Structural fix. |
| **3** | **C8.4** | 8t/16t: parallel WAL commit | 2-4x 16t, 1.5-2x 8t | Eliminates single-flusher bottleneck entirely. High risk, high reward. |
| 4 | C8.3 | 16t: condvar/timeout convoy audit | 10-15% 16t | Fixes the 22% timeout-wake problem. Lower EV than C8.4 but independent. |
| 5 | C8.5 | 8t: evidence-gated arrival-wait policy | 5-10% 8t | Replace fixed 20µs heuristic. Low EV unless flusher service time drops first. |

**Explicit sequencing recommendation:**
C8.6 → D5.2 → C8.4. Do C8.6 first because it's the narrowest win with the
least risk. D5.2 is independent (different code surface) and can run in parallel.
C8.4 is the structural fix for the single-flusher bottleneck but carries the most
implementation risk.

**Do NOT prioritize C8.5 (arrival-wait heuristic) until C8.6 lands.** The arrival
wait is 15µs at 8t — it's not the dominant cost. Changing the heuristic before
reducing the flusher service time risks making the spike behavior worse.

---

### Closure assessment

This bead is **closure-ready**. The classification covers all three red-cell regimes
with measured decomposition, names the dominant bucket for each, and recommends
concrete priority sequencing. The residual gap is:
- No c1 flamegraph-level attribution within the parse/compile ceremony (would
  require perf or samply capture, not available from counter data alone)
- 16t data was captured under load 135 (noisy for absolute numbers but the
  proportional decomposition holds because all phases are affected equally)

Until the phase-pack script grows 2t/4t capture, 2t/4t may come from the dated local logs in artifacts/perf/YYYY-MM-DD-local/, but 8t/16t must come from a same-pack capture.

### 4. Required reporting fields
Any future scorecard or closeout derived from these packs must report, at minimum:
- exact artifact root(s)
- git commit and dirty-state provenance
- machine/load provenance
- comparator engines present
- per-critical-cell ratios, not only aggregates
- for persistent 8t/16t fsqlite rows: phase timing / wake-reason evidence or an explicit statement that it is missing

### 5. Allowed aggregate views
These are secondary only:
- geometric means
- medians
- per-fixture rolled summaries

These are never allowed to hide red cells. The report must always surface the critical cells first:
- c1 low-concurrency red cells
- persistent 8t comparator loss
- persistent 16t collapse state, even if the SQLite ratio is numerically >1.0

### 6. Invalid-pack and invalid-report rules
A pack or report is invalid if any of the following holds:
- missing provenance root or per-lane provenance files
- persistent 8t or 16t includes only one engine in the same-pack comparator story
- throughput claims are taken from samples.jsonl alone without Criterion stdout context
- the report omits c1 cells while citing only c4/c8 or global geomeans

title: Track J: revised baseline engine tax reduction with arenas, caches, and data-motion cuts
description:
## Goal
Close the broad per-operation efficiency gap versus SQLite even when contention is not the dominant problem.

## Background
The matrix proves that MVCC-only thinking is insufficient. FrankenSQLite is also too slow at `c1`, on mixed rows with low retry pressure, and in forced single-writer mode. That means the engine still burns too much work in parser/planner reuse, decode/materialization, page staging, ownership transitions, and transient allocation/copy churn.

## Scope
This track covers:
- baseline truthing for cache-hit and hot-path reuse rates
- arenas/lookaside storage and reusable page buffers
- prepared-statement, plan, and decode caches
- PageData ownership and data-motion reduction
- VDBE fast paths, reusable frames, and safe read-path improvements
- build/profile hygiene for honest perf binaries
- explicit verification across c1, mixed, and single-writer rows with structured logs

## Guardrails
- baseline work must improve both MVCC and single-writer when it touches shared code
- avoid giant mixed-scope patches; each child bead should target one measured waste family
- keep correctness and invalidation semantics explicit whenever reuse is introduced

## Acceptance Criteria
Success means:
- the track covers memory reuse, plan reuse, decode reuse, PageData/data-motion cleanup, VDBE fast paths, and perf-binary hygiene
- the track explicitly carries verification obligations for unit tests, e2e scripts, structured logging, and benchmark attribution
- the track is self-contained enough that future agents can use it without reopening the original revised-plan markdown

It exists because the matrix shows a separate baseline-efficiency deficit that would still matter even if the concurrent-writer story were perfect.

- Track J is parallel to Track I by design; it is not allowed to hide behind structural work, and structural work is not allowed to use baseline-tax progress as an excuse to leave convoy pathologies unresolved
