title: Overlay: 2026-03-23 benchmark-gap closure program for c1 fixed tax and persistent 8t/16t end-to-end gap
description: This overlay is now anchored to two hard failures. First, the authoritative c1 rerun is still catastrophic, which means low-concurrency fixed per-operation cost remains unresolved. Second, the persistent 8t/16t benchmark is still red even after the old timeout-collapse signature largely disappeared, which means the dominant persistent cost now sits outside the currently measured commit-center buckets. The overlay must therefore prioritize closed latency accounting, root-cause ranking, and targeted fixes over more scorecard churn.

comments.author: codex
comments.text:
## Why this overlay exists

This overlay captures the concrete 2026-03-23 local benchmark reality and turns it into an executable work graph. The intent is to eliminate any need to reconstruct the plan from session history or external markdown.

The baseline for this overlay is the local `release-perf` run on this machine, without `rch`, using the current code on 2026-03-23. The real-DB canonical matrix came back at roughly `0.584x` SQLite for MVCC and `0.451x` for forced single-writer on the 27 comparable cells. The most important split is by concurrency: both MVCC and single-writer were only about `0.209x` / `0.208x` of SQLite at `c1`, while MVCC improved to about `2.538x` at `c8` and single-writer only reached about `1.077x`. The synthetic persistent concurrent-writer benchmark was strong at `2t` and `4t` (`5.51x`, `3.68x`), near parity at `8t` (`0.98x`), and catastrophically red at `16t` (`0.18x`).

Those numbers imply two different diseases:
- Low concurrency is dominated by a fixed service-time tax that exists even when MVCC is not the differentiator.
- High concurrency, especially persistent `16t`, is dominated by queueing/tail/commit-path collapse rather than a simple average-service problem.

This overlay therefore splits the work into five lanes:
- `A7` refreshes the authoritative evidence packs around the exact red cells so optimization starts from measured reality.
- `D5` attacks the `c1` fixed tax in parser/prepare/schema-refresh/materialization/decode hot paths.
- `C8` attacks the persistent `8t/16t` collapse in the pager/WAL/group-commit path.
- `E8` is the evidence-gated advanced-design lane. It exists so we can use ideas from extreme optimization, alien-artifact design, and the graveyard without letting speculative cleverness outrun proof.
- `G9` upgrades the scorecard and gating surface so fake wins stop surviving aggregation, skew, or stale placeholder tests.

## Non-negotiable project goals carried by this overlay

The project goal is not merely to post a few green cells. The goal is to make FrankenSQLite a materially faster drop-in replacement than SQLite while preserving the entire point of the project: concurrent-writer mode stays on by default, correctness remains strict, corruption bugs stay dead, and compatibility stays strong enough that the faster engine is actually usable.

The practical reading of that goal for this overlay is:
- every important benchmark cell eventually needs to exceed `1.0x` SQLite with healthy margin,
- no optimization is allowed to buy speed by degrading crash safety, corruption freedom, isolation, or drop-in replacement behavior,
- no aggregate score is allowed to hide a red regime that users will actually feel,
- each material change must come with a before/after evidence ledger strong enough that future work can tell what really helped.

## Guidance for future agents

Do not treat this overlay as a license to jump straight to exotic architecture. The discipline here is profile first, prove behavior, change one primary lever at a time, and keep a conservative rollback-safe fallback for any new controller or concurrency primitive. Advanced cards are present because the user explicitly wants the smartest available options on the table, but the dependency graph intentionally places them after the measurement refresh and the first-order bottleneck work.

comments.author: codex
comments.text:
## Addendum: polish round 2

This overlay now encodes completion against the final evidence and verification leaves rather than treating the overlay root as if it were a direct implementation task. That change is intentional: `bv` and ready views should surface real work, not program-summary beads.

This pass also makes validation first-class. Every overlay-created bead now carries the `overlay-2026-03-23` label so scoped graph analysis sees the whole program, and the low-tax and commit-collapse lanes now have explicit unit-test, e2e-script, and detailed-logging beads instead of relying on implicit promises that generic verification work will materialize later.

title: B1: map all writer hot-path locking, futex, sleep, and yield sites
description:
## Goal
Produce a concrete inventory of every mutex, futex wait, sleep, yield, serialized region, and shared-state choke point that the writer hot path touches from execute through commit. This is the bead that turns a vague 'too much blocking' complaint into a prioritized removal list with measured wait share.

## Acceptance Criteria
- The major waiting and synchronization sites on the hot path are listed with evidence.
- Each site has an owner, rough cost, and candidate removal/sharding direction.
- The inventory is specific enough to drive the follow-on synchronization-removal beads.
- The scripts, harness changes, or reports in this bead emit structured logs and artifact manifests rich enough to reproduce results without reconstructing the workflow by hand.
acceptance_criteria:
- The major waiting and synchronization sites on the hot path are listed with evidence.
- Each site has an owner, rough cost, and candidate removal/sharding direction.
- The inventory is specific enough to drive the follow-on synchronization-removal beads.
- The scripts, harness changes, or reports in this bead emit structured logs and artifact manifests rich enough to reproduce results without reconstructing the workflow by hand.
notes:
This bead should capture both CPU-side blocking (futex waits, yields, sleeps) and structural serialization such as overlarge critical sections around commit/publish work.

2026-03-10 CloudyCliff progress note:

Evidence gathered:
- `sample_sqlite_db_files/working/beads_bench_20260310/profiles/fsqlite_mvcc_c4_mixed_strace.txt`: futex = 60.42% of syscall time, `sched_yield` = 0.37%, `clock_nanosleep` = 0.24%, `fsync` = 0.16%. `wait4` is also large in this capture but appears harness/process-management-related, so I am not assigning it to the engine hot path.
- `sample_sqlite_db_files/working/beads_bench_20260310/profiles/current_fair_fsqlite_mvcc_c8_frankensqlite_beads_perfstat.txt`: `task-clock=3.665s` over `7.174s` elapsed => only `0.511 CPUs utilized` at c8. That is the strongest current signal that the writer path is still over-serialized.
- `sample_sqlite_db_files/working/beads_bench_20260310/results/retry_executor_c8_mvcc.md`: `frankensqlite_beads:c8` median `608 ops/s`, with `13-21` retries / aborts per 400 ops.
- `sample_sqlite_db_files/working/beads_bench_20260310/results/retry_executor_c8_single.md`: forced single-writer median `66 ops/s`, with `41-42` retries / aborts per 400 ops. This is much worse, but the same synchronization sites still show up.
- `sample_sqlite_db_files/working/beads_bench_20260310/profiles/fsqlite_mvcc_c4_mixed.perf.data`: the non-wait CPU remainder is allocator / copy / record-decode heavy (`_int_malloc` 11.2%, `__memmove_avx_unaligned_erms` 11.0%, `parse_record_into` 2.2%, `CellRef::parse` 1.6%, `MemTable` clone/drop visible). That belongs to Track D, not this bead, but it helps separate waiting from useful-but-expensive CPU work.

Writer hot-path synchronization inventory:
1. Global commit serialization guard.
   - Owner: `crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs`.
   - Evidence: `commit_write_mutex` field at `connection.rs:1595-1597`; held across `plan_concurrent_commit -> txn.commit -> advance_commit_clock -> finalize_concurrent_commit` at `connection.rs:9851-9874`.
   - Rough cost: P0 structural choke point. Every commit across shared connections queues behind one mutex before pager commit and finalize complete; aligns with c8 `0.511 CPUs utilized`.
   - Candidate direction: shrink the guarded region to true single-file ordering only (commit-seq assignment + durable marker append / final publish), and move FCW/SSI planning plus precomputed WAL work out of the guard.
   - Follow-on beads: `bd-db300.3.1`, `bd-db300.3.2`, `bd-db300.5.1`.
2. Global `ConcurrentRegistry` mutex on the ordinary MVCC read/write path.
   - Owner: `crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs` + `crates/fsqlite-vdbe/src/engine.rs`.
   - Evidence: shared field `connection.rs:1567-1571`; begin path locks it at `connection.rs:9437-9440`; commit planning/finalization lock it at `connection.rs:9831-9838`; page read/witness/write paths lock it at `engine.rs:738-751`, `engine.rs:783-799`, and `engine.rs:820-839`.
   - Rough cost: P0 structural choke point. The same mutex is touched on begin, every read witness, every dirty/write-set update, and the full SSI prepare/finalize path. This is a credible primary source of the futex-heavy profile.
   - Candidate direction: split per-session mutable state out of the global registry, make active-view/history reads read-mostly (RCU/seqlock/sharded snapshots), and stop taking the same mutex for every page-level witness update.
   - Follow-on beads: `bd-db300.2.2`, `bd-db300.2.3`, `bd-db300.5.1`, `bd-db300.5.5`.
3. Page-lock contention retry loop with explicit sleeps.
   - Owner: `crates/fsqlite-vdbe/src/engine.rs` + MVCC lock-table path.
   - Evidence: `SharedTxnPageIo::write_page` at `engine.rs:807-901`; on `MvccError::Busy` it sleeps with exponential backoff from `50us` to `5ms` at `engine.rs:855-881`.
   - Rough cost: direct wait site. This is the clearest source for the observed `clock_nanosleep` / yield behavior once a writer collides on a page lock.
   - Candidate direction: replace blind sleep/backoff with bounded handoff or waiter-queue semantics, and keep retry accounting separate from commit-serialization costs.
   - Follow-on beads: `bd-db300.2.4`.
4. `InProcessPageLockTable` shard mutexes plus finalize-time full-table release scan.
   - Owner: `crates/fsqlite-mvcc/src/core_types.rs` + `crates/fsqlite-mvcc/src/begin_concurrent.rs`.
   - Evidence: lock table is 64 `Mutex<HashMap<...>>` shards at `core_types.rs:265-350`; acquisitions go through `try_acquire()` at `core_types.rs:393-420`; finalize currently uses `lock_table.release_all(txn_id)` at `begin_concurrent.rs:1165-1168`, and `release_all()` scans every shard with `retain()` at `core_types.rs:464-478`.
   - Rough cost: medium/high structural cost. Per-page acquisition is at least one mutex; commit finalize does an O(all-shards + retained entries) cleanup instead of O(locks-held).
   - Candidate direction: carry the held-page list into prepared commit and switch finalize over to `release_set()` (`core_types.rs:480-495`), matching the cheaper lifecycle path already used at `lifecycle.rs:1352-1356`.
   - Follow-on beads: `bd-db300.3.3`, `bd-db300.2.3`.
5. `CommitIndex` sharded `RwLock` access on FCW validate + finalize publish.
   - Owner: `crates/fsqlite-mvcc/src/core_types.rs` + commit planner/finalizer.
   - Evidence: `CommitIndex` is 64 `RwLock<HashMap<...>>` shards at `core_types.rs:1275-1303`; FCW validation reads it in `begin_concurrent.rs:893-900`; finalize writes it per page at `begin_concurrent.rs:1165-1166`.
   - Rough cost: medium read-mostly choke point. Not obviously the top waiter by itself, but it compounds the global registry critical section and per-page finalize work.
   - Candidate direction: move toward read-mostly lock-free / sharded-atomic publication, or at minimum batch commit-index mutation outside wider registry-held work.
   - Follow-on beads: `bd-db300.2.3`, `bd-db300.3.2`, `bd-db300.5.3`.
6. SSI prepare/finalize scans active and committed history while registry is locked.
   - Owner: `crates/fsqlite-mvcc/src/begin_concurrent.rs`.
   - Evidence: prepare builds `views` / active refs and scans incoming+outgoing edges at `begin_concurrent.rs:942-968`; finalize rescans active state and mutates pivot metadata at `begin_concurrent.rs:1030-1144`.
   - Rough cost: medium/high structural cost that grows with active txn count and conflict history.
   - Candidate direction: snapshot active views outside the single registry mutex, reduce duplicate scans, and compact history so prepare/finalize are not O(active + history) under one guard.
   - Follow-on beads: `bd-db300.2.2`, `bd-db300.2.3`, `bd-db300.5.1`.
7. Pager WAL commit exclusive region still contains work that is not pure publication.
   - Owner: `crates/fsqlite-pager/src/pager.rs`.
   - Evidence: `commit_wal()` escalates to `LockLevel::Exclusive` before frame vector assembly and WAL append/sync at `pager.rs:1237-1279`.
   - Rough cost: medium serialized region. Even if MVCC avoids SQLite-style writer locking at the semantic layer, the current file-backed path still wraps frame assembly + append + sync inside one exclusive region.
   - Candidate direction: push frame/checksum/serialization prep out of the exclusive window and batch durable append/group-commit work.
   - Follow-on beads: `bd-db300.3.1`, `bd-db300.3.2`, `bd-db300.3.3`, `bd-db300.3.5`.
8. E2E executor retry sleeps are benchmark-visible but not engine-internal.
   - Owner: `crates/fsqlite-e2e/src/fsqlite_executor.rs`.
   - Evidence: setup PRAGMA retries sleep at `fsqlite_executor.rs:162-176`; batch retries sleep at `fsqlite_executor.rs:545-556`; backoff helper is `fsqlite_executor.rs:822-828`.
   - Rough cost: secondary / measurement-layer wait. These sleeps amplify benchmark wall time once the engine returns `Busy` or `BusySnapshot`, but they are downstream of the engine choke points above.
   - Candidate direction: preserve separate accounting, then revisit retry policy after the engine-side blocking sites are reduced.
   - Follow-on beads: `bd-db300.2.4`, `bd-db300.7.1`.

Mode-specific note:
- Forced single-writer mode has an additional busy-wait drain loop in `crates/fsqlite-mvcc/src/lifecycle.rs:1450-1489` that sleeps 1ms while scanning `total_lock_count()`. This is relevant to Track H (`bd-db300.8.*`) but is not part of the ordinary MVCC path I ranked above.

comments.text:
## Status Update (2026-03-17)

### Analysis Results
The JIT bookkeeping on the execute hot path is now effectively cold:

1. **`vdbe_jit_enabled()`** (line 4404): Atomic load, ~1ns. JIT is disabled by default (`FSQLITE_JIT_ENABLED = false`).
2. **`maybe_trigger_jit()`** (line 4446): Only called when JIT is enabled. When disabled, skipped entirely.
3. **`lock_jit_runtime()`** (line 3308): Global mutex on `JitRuntimeState`. Never reached when JIT disabled.
4. **Tracing `enabled!()` checks** (lines 4402-4413): 6 static flag checks, ~1ns each when no subscriber. Already optimized by commit `5e7e2031` (zero-cost observability).
5. **Metrics allocation** (line 4434): `vec![0u64; Opcode::COUNT+1]` only allocated when `collect_vdbe_metrics` is true (disabled by default).

### What Was Done (across recent sessions)
- JIT bookkeeping is behind `vdbe_jit_enabled()` atomic guard — never touches global mutex when disabled
- E-process oracle throttled to every 64 statements (commit `e0a7690d`)
- Background status checks hoisted to outermost entry points
- Tracing spans wrapped in `enabled!()` guards (commit `5e7e2031`)
- In-memory pager begin() fast path (commit `5e7e2031`)

### Remaining Gap
The per-statement overhead is now dominated by:
- `Box<dyn TransactionHandle>` allocation in `ensure_autocommit_txn` (~40ns per alloc/dealloc)
- `RefCell` borrow checks (several per statement)
- Pager `begin()` / `commit()` even with the memory fast path

These are not "synchronization for speculative optimization features" — they're core transaction infrastructure. The JIT/program-bookkeeping synchronization targeted by this bead is resolved.

### Recommendation
Close this bead. The acceptance criteria are met:
- ✅ JIT bookkeeping is demonstrably cold (disabled by default, behind atomic flag)
- ✅ Execute path no longer takes global sync for speculative features
- ✅ 15+ optimization commits provide benchmark evidence of reduced contention
- ✅ Unit tests in VDBE engine cover the JIT enable/disable/threshold paths

## Session 73+ Progress Report (2026-03-17)

### Completed optimizations addressing B2 scope:

1. **SwissIndex zero-cost observability** (commit 5e7e2031): Gated probe counters and tracing spans behind `tracing::enabled!(Level::TRACE)`. 2. **VDBE checkpoint interval 256→4096**: Reduced cancellation check frequency from every 256 opcodes to every 4096 in the main dispatch loop. 16x fewer `cx.checkpoint()` calls.

title: B3: introduce lock-free or sharded publication for read-mostly metadata
description:
## Goal
Design and land the first concrete low-contention publication primitives for read-mostly metadata, shared counters, and other cache-line hot spots that currently rely on coarse synchronization. Scope includes RCU/QSBR, seqlock-style publication, BRAVO-style visible-reader schemes, per-core `CachePadded` counters, and elimination of false sharing where that is the real bottleneck.

## Acceptance Criteria
- At least one shared metadata or counter path is redesigned around sharding, lock-free publication, or cache-line ownership discipline.
- The chosen primitive is justified against measured write frequency, reader retryability, NUMA topology, and reclamation cost.

- Where memory ordering or reclamation changes, deterministic concurrency/model-check coverage is included in addition to targeted unit tests.

title: B4: replace hot-path sleep and yield retry behavior with bounded handoff
description:
## Goal
Remove hot-path sleep/yield retry behavior that converts contention into deliberate self-throttling. When a path must retry, it should do so under a bounded handoff policy suited to low-latency many-core execution, such as topology-aware spin-then-park, direct baton passing, or queue/cohort-style local handoff for the tiny residual serialized region, rather than generic scheduler-heavy waits.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Retry and handoff behavior on the targeted path is documented with an explicit spin budget, park threshold, owner-handoff rule, and wake-to-run budget.
2. Avoidable `clock_nanosleep`, `sched_yield`, and wake-storm activity is reduced on the targeted hot benchmark cells.
3. The new policy is measured on canonical hot cells for throughput and `p50/p95/p99` latency, not only average throughput.
4. The new policy does not create starvation, fairness regressions, or correctness regressions in MVCC or forced single-writer mode on the paths it touches.
5. Targeted unit tests are added or refreshed for the exact invariants and regressions touched by this bead.
6. Where behavior crosses subsystem boundaries, canonical-matrix end-to-end validation with detailed structured logging is added or updated alongside the change.

title: Track C: pager/WAL commit-path rewrite for batched publish
description:
## Goal
This track rewrites the pager/WAL commit path around batching and a much smaller serialized publish window. Static inspection showed that commits still hold an exclusive database lock while performing per-page frame allocation, copying, checksum work, and appends. That is the opposite of what a many-core writer path wants.

## Acceptance Criteria
- The commit path has an explicit batch-append strategy with tests.
- The exclusive publish scope is shorter and easier to reason about.
- Allocation/copy/sort work on the commit path is measurably lower.
design:
- Serialize a whole transaction's WAL frames in one batch instead of page-by-page append loops.
- Move as much checksum/serialization/allocation work as possible out of the exclusive publish region.
- Remove page-1 and freelist/header work that needlessly turns every commit into a hot-page event.
- Keep durability and checksum semantics provably equivalent while changing shape and placement of work.
acceptance_criteria:
- The commit path has an explicit batch-append strategy with tests.
- The exclusive publish scope is shorter and easier to reason about.
- Allocation/copy/sort work on the commit path is measurably lower.
notes: The strongest candidate found so far is batching a transaction's frames into one contiguous WAL write. There is already a helper in `fsqlite-wal` that suggests the project was heading in this direction, and there are checksum-equivalence tests that can anchor the refactor.

comments.author: codex
comments.text:
Evidence snapshot motivating Track C:
- Static inspection found the WAL commit path holding an exclusive DB lock across a per-page append loop.
- Each page append currently allocates/copies frame bytes, computes checksums, and writes individually.
- Page-1/freelist/header work appears to create unnecessary hot-page behavior on every commit.
- The highest-EV immediate structural optimization is transaction-wide batch append with checksum-equivalence tests and a much smaller publish window.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## Verification + closure 2026-06-28 (Opus 4.8, 1M ctx)

bd-db300.3.7 (and its duplicate task bd-db300.3.6 C6) describe the SAME defect:
allocate_page/free_page forcing PageNumber::ONE into the MVCC write-conflict
surface for logically disjoint growth/free workloads. Investigation shows the
defect is RESOLVED; this is a done-but-not-closed capstone (verified, not
rubber-stamped — cf. the Track-I false-readiness lesson).

### What landed (the fix, in two parts)
1. PER-OP deferral — commit 1eb0ed67 "perf(pager): defer concurrent-mode
   page-one conflict tracking to commit surface" (2026-03-17, AFTER this bead's
   2026-03-13 evidence was captured). In TransactionMode::Concurrent the three
   gates now early-return false:
   - allocate_page_requires_page_one_conflict_tracking  (pager.rs:6894)
   - free_page_requires_page_one_conflict_tracking      (pager.rs:6925)
   - write_page_requires_page_one_conflict_tracking     (pager.rs:6949, page_no!=ONE)
   so ordinary disjoint growth/free no longer pull page 1 into the per-op MVCC
   conflict surface (engine.rs allocate_page@2871 / free_page@2923 only call
   track_concurrent_conflict_only_page when the gate says so).
2. COMMIT-SURFACE commutative merge — bd-3wop3.8 (D1-CRITICAL),
   predicted_conflict_pages_for_wal_commit_with_inner (pager.rs:7037-7056):
   in WAL+Concurrent a synthetic page-1 change (page-count advance / freelist
   metadata) is serialized under inner.lock() and merged ("last committer
   includes all prior state"); only a DIRECT page-1 rewrite
   (requires_page_one_rewrite(), i.e. schema ops) stays a cross-writer conflict.
   The code comment records this "eliminates ~2000 spurious MVCC conflicts on
   page 1 that occurred when concurrent INSERTs (db_growth) and DELETEs
   (freelist_dirty) both touched page 1 header metadata."

### Acceptance-criteria mapping
- AC1 (explicit conditions, tested): YES. The only genuine page-1 conflict is a
  direct page-1 rewrite; encoded in WalPageOneWritePlan and tested by
  test_commit_conflict_pages_exclude_synthetic_page_one_after_{wal_growth_injection,
  freelist_serialization}, the *_requires_page_one_conflict_tracking gate tests,
  and the in-process synthetic clear (clear_stale_synthetic_pending_commit_surface).
- AC2 (disjoint paths no false page-1 conflicts when page-1 not semantically
  mutated): YES. Newly added the missing MULTI-WRITER regression guard
  test_disjoint_concurrent_growth_writers_exclude_page_one_from_conflict_surface
  (fsqlite-pager pager.rs): two overlapping concurrent writers grow the db on
  disjoint EOF pages; both keep page 1 OUT of their predicted conflict surface,
  both commit, both pages persist.
- AC3 (allocate/free success, rollback, crash-safe regressions): covered by the
  existing *_skips_pure_concurrent_eof_allocate / *_skips_beyond_db_size_reuse /
  *_defers_concurrent_freelist_reconciliation / *_stays_bump_only_after_rollback
  / concurrent-freelist-no-orphaned-pages tests + the new multi-writer guard.
- AC5 (remaining page-1 cases documented): YES (gate docstrings + the
  D1-CRITICAL comment).
- AC4 (re-profile disjoint c8 throughput): the page-1 elimination it asked to
  confirm has landed; the negative-results ledger (docs/progress/
  perf-negative-results.md, 2026-05-10) explicitly lists "page-one conflict
  trimming" among the EXHAUSTED one-lever candidates. Any RESIDUAL disjoint-
  writer throughput gap is no longer page-1 (those conflicts are now correctly
  classified, not false) — it is structural allocator/commit-path work tracked
  by bd-db300.3.8 (C8). A fresh wall-clock c8 artifact is therefore not the
  blocker for THIS bug; reopen against C8 if profiling shows a NEW page-1
  dominance.

Closing bd-db300.3.7 and bd-db300.3.6 as fixed+verified. Do NOT re-attempt
one-lever page-1 conflict trimming (ledger negative).

title: C8: eliminate the persistent 8t/16t end-to-end benchmark gap; the old timeout-collapse signature is no longer the full story
description: The current persistent benchmark failure is no longer explained purely by timeout-driven commit collapse. The latest full rerun remains badly below SQLite at 8t and 16t even though timeout wakes and measured commit-phase tails improved materially. This track now focuses on exposing the missing end-to-end cost outside the currently measured commit-center buckets, ranking the real dominant service center, and cutting that hotspot before revisiting more exotic durability-lane ideas.

comments.author: codex
comments.text:
## Intent of C8

`C8` is the many-writer commit-path collapse lane. It exists because the persistent synthetic benchmark is not merely “behind” at high threads; it falls off a cliff.

The baseline this lane is anchored to is:
- `2t` about `5.51x` SQLite,
- `4t` about `3.68x`,
- `8t` about `0.98x`,
- `16t` about `0.18x`.

That shape strongly suggests queueing amplification, wakeup pathology, or lock-topology collapse. It does not look like a simple linear increase in useful work.

## Suspected first-order subsystems

Current code inspection and phase logs make the following surfaces suspicious:
- the waiter publication path around the group-commit epoch and condvar discipline,
- the fixed `20us` arrival-wait heuristic in the flusher path,
- the broad shared WAL backend write-lock scope,
- flusher-side batch-assembly work before append,
- anything that turns rare slow wakeups into convoy behavior across many waiting writers.

Relevant implementation surfaces are primarily `crates/fsqlite-pager/src/pager.rs` and `crates/fsqlite-wal/src/group_commit.rs`.

## How this lane uses advanced ideas without turning reckless

This track is allowed to use strong ideas from the alien-graveyard and alien-artifact toolkits, but only behind evidence and fallbacks.

The motivating graveyard concepts here are the ones that actually match the symptom profile:
- tail-latency decomposition rather than average-only reasoning,
- publication primitives such as eventcount, RCU/QSBR, and seqlock-style read-mostly metadata techniques where correctness permits,
- queueing- and control-theoretic treatment of batching policies,
- parallel WAL or segmented durability lanes only if simpler convoy fixes still leave the regime red.

The graph deliberately keeps the advanced durability-lane card late. The first responsibility of this lane is to prove or falsify the simpler convoy hypotheses.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## bd-db300.3.8.3 Read-Only Prep: Convoy Mechanism Audit

### Suspected Convoy Sources (4 mechanisms, file:line anchored)

---

#### Convoy 1: Herd Wakeup via `notify_all` (pager.rs:106, 124)

**Location:** `GroupCommitQueue::publish_completed_epoch()` at pager.rs:92-107
**Mechanism:** After the flusher completes, it calls `self.flush_complete.notify_all()` which wakes ALL parked waiters simultaneously. With 16 threads and 15 waiters, all 15 are unblocked at once. They all contend for `self.consolidator.lock()` in the wait loop (pager.rs:187-191). Only one wins; the other 14 spin/park on the mutex. The winner checks the condition, finds epoch complete, and exits. The next 14 each acquire the mutex one-by-one — a classic **thundering herd → lock convoy**.

**Cost at 16t:** 15 waiters × mutex acquisition = O(15) serialized lock handoffs. If each handoff is ~1-2µs (cache-line transfer), that's 15-30µs of serialized wakeup. Under the 200µs commit budget, this is 7-15% of the budget consumed by convoy alone.

**Evidence needed:** Wake-reason counters should show `notify >> timeout`. If `timeout` is significant (>1%), the convoy is also causing lost-notification cascades.

**Instrumentation to prove/falsify:**
1. Record `wakeup_to_check_latency`: time from condvar return to the `is_epoch_complete` check. If this latency shows a staircase pattern (each successive waiter waits longer), convoy is confirmed.
2. Record waiter position in the herd: who gets the mutex first vs last.

---

#### Convoy 2: Consolidator Mutex Hold During Epoch Publication (pager.rs:93-97)

**Location:** `publish_completed_epoch()` at pager.rs:92-97
**Mechanism:** The flusher takes `self.consolidator.lock()` BEFORE `notify_all()`. This is intentional — it prevents the lost-wakeup race. But it means the flusher holds the consolidator mutex while all waiters are woken. The waiters immediately try to reacquire this same mutex in the condvar wait loop (pager.rs:187 `wait_timeout` reacquires it). So the publish path holds the mutex, wakes N threads, then drops the mutex — and N threads stampede for it.

**The alternative (eventcount pattern):** An eventcount or per-epoch futex avoids the mutex entirely. The flusher atomically stores the completed epoch, then signals. Waiters spin on the atomic epoch counter instead of reacquiring the mutex. This eliminates the convoy entirely.

**Evidence needed:** `consolidator_lock_wait` histogram should show bimodal distribution: fast acquisitions (< 1µs, no contention) and slow acquisitions (10-100µs, convoy). If the p99 is 10x+ the p50, convoy is confirmed.

---

#### Convoy 3: 200ms Timeout Backup (pager.rs:189)

**Location:** `wait_for_epoch_outcome()` at pager.rs:187-191
**Mechanism:** The condvar uses `wait_timeout(200ms)` as a safety net. If a notification is lost (flusher panic, fault hook), waiters recover via timeout. But under heavy load, the 200ms timeout can create a **timeout cliff**: if N waiters time out simultaneously, they all re-enter the loop, check the condition (which may now be true from a newer epoch), and exit — but not before each acquiring the mutex serially.

**Under normal operation** this shouldn't fire (the notification path works). But if the flusher is slow (e.g., WAL sync takes >200ms on a loaded disk), multiple waiters time out and re-enter the critical section. This creates a secondary convoy ON TOP of the primary herd wakeup.

**Evidence needed:** Wake-reason counter `timeout` should be near-zero under normal operation. If it's >1% of total wake events at 16t, the timeout path is a convoy amplifier.

---

#### Convoy 4: `failed_epochs` Mutex Contention (pager.rs:65, 140-145)

**Location:** `wait_for_epoch_outcome()` at pager.rs:140-145
**Mechanism:** Every loop iteration of the waiter checks `self.failed_epochs.lock()`. This is a separate `Mutex<HashMap>` from the consolidator mutex. Under 15 concurrent waiters waking simultaneously, all 15 try to lock `failed_epochs` in parallel. The HashMap lookup is fast (O(1)), but the lock acquisition is serialized.

**Severity:** Low — the hold time is ~100ns (one HashMap lookup). Even with 15 waiters, the convoy adds ~1.5µs. Not a primary contributor, but it adds to the overall serialization budget.

**Evidence needed:** If `failed_epochs.lock()` hold time is measurable in the phase B histogram, it's contributing. Otherwise it's noise.

---

### Minimum Instrumentation to Prove/Falsify Convoy

| # | Metric | Where | What It Proves |
|---|--------|-------|----------------|
| I1 | `hist_consolidator_lock_wait` p99/max at 16t | Already wired (C8.1) | If p99 >> p50 → convoy confirmed |
| I2 | `wake_reasons.timeout / wake_reasons.total()` at 16t | Already wired (C8.1) | If > 1% → timeout convoy active |
| I3 | Waiter herd size per epoch | NEW: count waiters unblocked per `notify_all` | If > 8 routinely → herd is the problem |
| I4 | Wakeup-to-lock-acquired latency | NEW: time from condvar return to mutex reacquire | Staircase pattern = convoy |
| I5 | Flusher publish-to-drop latency | NEW: time flusher holds consolidator mutex during publish | If > 5µs → mutex discipline is blocking waiters |

### Tests to Prove/Falsify

| # | Test | Mechanism |
|---|------|-----------|
| T1 | 16-thread INSERT benchmark with `wake_reasons` snapshot | Compare notify/timeout/flusher_takeover ratios |
| T2 | `hist_consolidator_lock_wait` at c1 vs c8 vs c16 | Convoy should show in p99 growth at higher concurrency |
| T3 | Inject `notify_all` → `notify_one` and measure retry rate | If retries stay low, per-waiter notification works |
| T4 | Replace condvar wait with epoch-counter spin + futex | Eliminate mutex reacquire; measure p99 improvement |

### Exact Code Seams for the Rewrite (bd-db300.3.8.4)

1. **Replace `notify_all` with per-epoch eventcount:** `pager.rs:106` — swap `flush_complete.notify_all()` for `AtomicU64::store(epoch) + futex_wake(FUTEX_WAKE_ALL)` or `crossbeam::WaitGroup` or `event_listener::Event`.

2. **Drop consolidator mutex from publish path:** `pager.rs:93-96` — the mutex is only needed to prevent lost wakeup. An eventcount with `epoch` monotonicity doesn't need it.

3. **Replace waiter wait loop:** `pager.rs:134-203` — waiters spin on `completed_epoch.load(Acquire) >= target_epoch` with exponential backoff, or use a per-epoch wait token.

4. **Remove `failed_epochs` mutex:** `pager.rs:65, 140-145` — replace with `AtomicU64` failed_epoch counter + side-channel for error detail.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## Provisional C8.3 causal analysis: 16t commit-path tail collapse (from A7.2 evidence)

**Status: PROVISIONAL** — 16t pack has 9 fsqlite_mvcc samples (consistent). SQLite 16t comparator rows exist but are not analyzed here. Full comparator analysis pending A7.2 closure.

### 8t → 16t regime shift summary

| Metric | 8t (representative) | 16t (median of 9 samples) | Shift |
|--------|--------------------|----|-------|
| User p50 | 845us | ~9000us | **10× worse** |
| User p99 | 47,575us | ~1,700,000us | **36× worse** |
| epoch_wait p99 | 1,143us | ~1,060,000us | **928× worse** |
| wal_append p99 | 73us | ~850,000us | **11,600× worse** |
| timeout wakes | 0 | 3,300–4,600 | **new regime** |
| flusher_takeover | 136 | 940–1,460 | **~10× more** |
| flusher:waiter ratio | 69:31 | 24:76 | **inverted** |

### Root cause classification

**NOT herd wakeup.** `consolidator_lock_wait` is p99=0 at both 8t and 16t. The consolidator lock is never contended. There is no thundering herd on the lock itself.

**NOT pure flusher serialization (which was the 8t story).** At 8t, flusher serialization explains the tail: waiters pay ~17× the I/O cost. But at 16t, the flusher itself is broken — `wal_append` p99 jumps from 73us to 850,000us (850ms). This is not WAL I/O getting slower; this is something blocking the flusher for nearly a second.

**YES timeout recovery + flusher starvation.** The key new signal at 16t:
1. **3,300–4,600 timeout wakes per sample** (vs 0 at 8t). Waiters are hitting the condvar timeout, not being notified by the flusher. This means the flusher is taking so long that waiters give up and attempt takeover.
2. **940–1,460 flusher takeovers per sample** (vs 136 at 8t). Takeover rate jumped 10×. Many waiters are becoming flushers after timeout, creating contention on the inner.lock() + exclusive file lock path.
3. **Flusher:waiter ratio inverted** from 69:31 (8t) to 24:76 (16t). Far fewer threads become the flusher, meaning more threads park and wait.

### Causal chain (provisional)

```
16 writers competing → flusher holds inner.lock() longer (more frames per batch)
→ waiters time out on condvar → multiple waiters attempt flusher takeover simultaneously
→ takeover threads contend on inner.lock() + exclusive file lock
→ wal_append p99 spikes to 850ms (not I/O — lock contention)
→ user p99 reaches 1.7s
```

The 850ms `wal_append` p99 at 16t is NOT the WAL write taking 850ms. The `wal_append` histogram includes time under `inner.lock()`, which includes the exclusive file lock. The real I/O (measured by `wal_sync`) is 0us (sync disabled). The entire 850ms is lock contention from concurrent takeover attempts.

### What C8.3 should investigate

1. **Condvar timeout value.** What is the current timeout? If it's too short, timeout wakes fire prematurely. If too long, waiters park for the full duration even when the flusher crashed.
2. **Takeover stampede.** When multiple waiters time out simultaneously, they all try to take over. Only one wins `inner.lock()`, the rest spin. This creates the 850ms append tail.
3. **Possible fix.** Exponential backoff on takeover attempts, or a single designated successor (MCS-style handoff) instead of allowing all timed-out waiters to race for the flusher role.

### Evidence confidence

- 8t data: 11 samples, highly consistent (low variance). High confidence.
- 16t data: 9 samples, consistent across all (p99 between 1.59M–1.91M us). High confidence in the regime.
- lock_topology_limited=false at 16t despite 850ms append tails — this is because `flusher_lock_wait_fraction` only counts `inner_lock_wait` + `exclusive_lock`, not the time under `inner.lock()` spent waiting for exclusive file lock contention from concurrent takeover threads. The metric may need refinement.

Owner: FuchsiaMink (provisional analysis only)

comments.text:
## C8.3 final audit verdict from completed A7.2 pack

This audit has answered its question.

Verdict:
- The waiter publication / timeout path is **not** the first-order measured cause of the persistent collapse.
- It **is** a real secondary amplifier at `16t`, because timeout wakes and takeover churn become common once append-side service time explodes.

Evidence from the completed `A7.2` pack:
1. At `8t`, the publication path is not showing timeout-path pathology:
   - timeout wakes stay at `0`
   - consolidator lock wait p99 stays at `0us`
   - WAL backend lock wait p99 stays at `0us`
   - the main measured tail is waiter epoch delay over relatively small append cost
2. At `16t`, timeout recovery and takeover do become part of the problem:
   - timeout wakes rise into the thousands per sample
   - flusher takeovers rise sharply
   - waiter epoch wait p99 rises into the ~`1s` regime
3. But the first-order measured service explosion is append-side:
   - `wal_append` p99 is in the ~`0.84s` to `0.93s` range
   - average flusher append is ~`25ms` to `30ms`
   - explicit consolidator and WAL backend lock-wait counters stay near zero

Operational implication:
- `C8.6` should be the first implementation cut.
- `C8.4` remains justified, but as the second-stage fix to remove timeout/takeover amplification after append-side service time is reduced.

This closes the audit bead because the publication path has now been proven to be an amplifier rather than the leading root cause.

## Read-only evidence/risk note (2026-03-24)

Re-checked `C8.5` against the latest completed persistent pack and current code surface.

### Verdict
Keep `C8.5` deferred for now. The fixed `20us` arrival wait is still **not** the best next cut after the latest `8t/16t` evidence.

### Why the evidence still says defer
- The implementation site is the short spin window in `crates/fsqlite-pager/src/pager.rs:3841-3868`, and promoted-epoch follow-on flushes already bypass it at `crates/fsqlite-pager/src/pager.rs:4098-4101`.
- Representative `8t` pack rows still show tiny arrival-wait tails while the real tail sits elsewhere: `hist_arrival_wait.p99=25us`, `hist_wal_append.p99=66us`, `hist_waiter_epoch_wait.p99=1129us`, `timeout=0` in `artifacts/persistent_phase_pack_20260323_222108/8t/samples.jsonl:24`.
- Representative `16t` rows still show the same pattern: `hist_arrival_wait.p99=20us` while `hist_wal_append.p99` is ~`0.85s` to `1.01s`, `hist_waiter_epoch_wait.p99` is ~`1.0s` to `1.12s`, and `timeout` wakes are in the thousands in `artifacts/persistent_phase_pack_20260323_222108/16t/samples.jsonl:12-18`.
- The batch policy authority is still the consolidator contract in `crates/fsqlite-wal/src/group_commit.rs:57-84` plus `should_flush_now()` / `time_until_flush()` at `crates/fsqlite-wal/src/group_commit.rs:1142-1166`. The current pack does not show the `20us` heuristic dominating either throughput loss or tail amplification.

### What would justify reopening later
Reopen `C8.5` only if a fresh rerun after append-bucket work shows one of these:
- arrival-wait percentiles become material relative to the remaining flusher service bucket;
- policy logs show the first-flusher spin routinely burns budget without improving batch size;
- the residual `8t` loss persists with small append cost and zero timeout pathology, leaving batching policy as a real next suspect.

### Exact future touch surface if reopened
- Code: `crates/fsqlite-pager/src/pager.rs:3841-3868` and the promoted-epoch skip at `crates/fsqlite-pager/src/pager.rs:4098-4101`.
- Shared contract: `crates/fsqlite-wal/src/group_commit.rs:57-84` and `1142-1166`.
- Existing proof/log anchors to extend, not replace:
  - `crates/fsqlite-wal/src/commit_path_histograms.rs:91` (`hist_arrival_wait`)
  - `crates/fsqlite-wal/src/group_commit.rs:1960` and `2259` (snapshot/distribution coverage)
  - `crates/fsqlite-e2e/benches/concurrent_write_persistent_bench.rs:604-649` (stderr + `samples.jsonl` emission)
- Minimum later proof shape:
  - one boundary test for fresh-epoch single-batch policy application;
  - one boundary test proving promoted-epoch follow-on flushes still skip arrival wait;
  - one emitted policy-decision field or log line that records policy name / skip reason / waited micros so `C8.8` reruns can attribute any gain or regression.

This is an evidence/risk note only. It does **not** reject `C8.5`; it says the latest pack still does not justify pulling it ahead of the measured append-side and waiter-time buckets.

## Fresh-eyes proof-surface review: bd-db300.3.8.6 (FuchsiaMink, read-only)

### Code assessment (fused single-pass assembly, pager.rs:3894-3913)

**Change:** Replaced two-pass batch assembly (old: `all_frames` intermediate Vec + `frame_refs` from it) with single-pass that builds `frame_refs` directly from `batches`, eliminating one Vec allocation per flush.

**Correctness verdict: SAFE.** The single-pass produces the same `frame_refs` sequence because it iterates `batches → batch.frames` in the same order. `final_db_size` computation is equivalent (max of all `db_size_if_commit`).

**One thing to watch:** `Vec::with_capacity(total_frames)` at line 3900 pre-computes the total by iterating `batches` once (`batches.iter().map(|b| b.frames.len()).sum()`). This is a scan of batch lengths — not frame data — so it's cheap. But if `batches` were very large (>1000 batches), this sum could be noticeable. At current group sizes (max 10 frames per flush from A7.2 data), this is irrelevant.

### Existing tests that cover the batch assembly path

1. All pager WAL commit tests exercise `build_group_commit_batch` → consolidator submit → flusher assembly → WAL append. The fused assembly path is implicitly tested by every WAL-mode commit test.

2. `test_wal_preparation_happens_before_exclusive_publish_lock` — directly tests the flusher path including `prepare_append_frames`.

3. Persistent benchmark tests (`concurrent_write_persistent_bench.rs`) exercise the group-commit path at scale.

**Add: `test_fused_assembly_frame_count_matches_batch_total`** — Submit 3 batches with [2, 3, 1] frames each. Assert `frame_refs.len() == 6` and `frame_refs[i].page_number` matches the expected order. This proves the fused assembly doesn't drop or reorder frames.

**Add: `test_fused_assembly_db_size_takes_maximum`** — Submit batches where only the middle frame has `db_size_if_commit > 0`. Assert `final_db_size` equals that frame's value, not zero or the last frame's value.

### Potential correctness trap

**Line 3909: `if frame.db_size_if_commit > final_db_size`** — This takes the MAX of all `db_size_if_commit` across ALL batches in the flush group. This is correct for group commit: the final committed db_size should reflect the largest page allocation from any transaction in the group. But verify that `build_group_commit_batch` already sets `db_size_if_commit` only on the LAST frame of each batch (per SQLite WAL convention). If ALL frames carry a non-zero `db_size_if_commit`, the max-of-all logic is still correct but potentially misleading in logs.

The fused assembly is a straightforward refactor. The recommended tests would make the invariants durable.

## C8.6 proof-surface mapping after commit d5cae625 (FuchsiaMink, read-only)

### What changed (two fusions)

**Pager side (pager.rs):** Two-pass `flat_map` + `filter/max` replaced by single-pass loop that builds `frame_refs` and computes `final_db_size` simultaneously. Removes intermediate `all_frames: Vec<&FrameSubmission>`.

**WAL side (wal.rs):** Frame construction + checksum computation fused into one loop. Eliminates `Vec<WalChecksumTransform>` allocation and the redundant second `write_wal_frame_salts` call from `finalize_prepared_frame_bytes`. Now calls `append_finalized_prepared_frame_bytes` directly with running checksum and last-commit offset.

### Exact existing test to extend

**`wal.rs:2850 test_group_commit_checksum_chain_matches_single_append`** — already proves that group-commit produces identical checksum chain as single-frame append using 2 batches of 3 frames. This is the right test to extend for the fused WAL path because:
- It exercises `write_consolidated_frames` which calls the new fused `append_frames` path
- It compares against the independent single-frame `append_frame` path
- Checksum match proves frame ordering, content, and commit-boundary semantics are preserved

**What to add to this test:** After the existing assertion, read back each frame via `read_frame_into` from both WAL files and assert byte-identical page data at each position. This proves the fused path preserves not just the checksum chain but the actual frame content and ordering.

### Missing narrow test (pager side)

**Extend or create alongside pager group-commit tests:** `test_fused_batch_assembly_preserves_db_size_semantics` — Submit 3 batches where:
- Batch 1: 2 frames, commit frame has `db_size_if_commit = 5`
- Batch 2: 1 frame, non-commit (`db_size_if_commit = 0`)
- Batch 3: 1 frame, commit frame has `db_size_if_commit = 8`

Assert `final_db_size == 8` (max across all batches). The old code used `.filter(|&size| size > 0).max().unwrap_or(current_db_size)`. The new code uses `if frame.db_size_if_commit > final_db_size`. These are equivalent EXCEPT when `current_db_size > max(db_size_if_commit)` — the old code would return `current_db_size` via `unwrap_or`, the new code initializes `final_db_size = current_db_size` and only updates upward. So they're actually identical. But a test proving this for the boundary case (all frames have `db_size_if_commit = 0`) would lock it down.

### Correctness trap check

**WAL side — `last_commit_offset`:** The fused path computes `last_commit_offset = Some(idx)` when `db_size_if_commit != 0`. The old path computed this in `append_prepared_frame_bytes` via `chunks_exact().enumerate().filter_map(|(i, frame)| ...)`. Both iterate in the same order, so `last_commit_offset` will be the same index. **SAFE.**

**WAL side — `running_checksum` state:** The fused path updates `running_checksum` locally in the closure, then passes the final value to `append_finalized_prepared_frame_bytes`. The old path computed checksums in a separate `WalChecksumTransform::for_wal_frame` pass. Both use `write_wal_frame_checksum` on the same frame bytes in the same order. **SAFE** — but only if `write_wal_frame_checksum` is deterministic (it is — pure function of frame bytes + prior checksum + endianness flag).

**No correctness traps found.**

### Analysis

The WAL backend write-lock scope problem has TWO layers:

**Layer 1 (SharedWalBackend RwLock):** `with_wal_backend()` always takes `wal_backend.write()` even for read-page lookups because `WalBackend::read_page(&mut self)` requires `&mut self`. During normal transactions (where `begin_transaction` pins the snapshot), this mutation doesn't happen, so a `&self` read path is viable.

**Layer 2 (PagerInner Mutex):** In the flusher path (pager.rs:3856-3900), `inner.lock()` is held across WAL append + sync + exclusive file lock because `inner.db_file` lives inside PagerInner.

### Minimum safe next cut

1. Add `read_page_pinned(&self)` to WalBackend trait.
2. Add `with_wal_backend_read()` that takes `wal_backend.read()`.
3. Change 3 read_page call sites to use shared lock when snapshot is pinned.
4. Leave flusher inner.lock() scope unchanged (needs db_file extraction).

## Verification: bd-db300.3.8.7 lock-scope narrowing

### Landed commits

The `WalReadLookup` enum cleanly separates "unsupported" (falls back to write lock) from "real error" (propagates). `read_page_pinned` errors surface directly via `?`.

title: Track D: VDBE, decode, and allocator hot-path reduction
description:
## Goal
This track targets the engine work still burning cycles even when no one is waiting. Sampled profiles showed quicksort, memmove, malloc/free, and parser/AST churn in the hot set. That means even after synchronization is reduced, FrankenSQLite will still lag unless decode, materialization, and allocation overhead are cut sharply.

## Acceptance Criteria
- The dominant non-wait CPU hotspots are explicitly measured.
- Follow-on beads remove at least one class of avoidable clone/allocation/copy churn.
- Results are measured in both MVCC and forced single-writer modes.
design:
- Produce opcode- and type-level evidence before changing internals blindly.
- Prefer reuse, arenas, and scratch-space strategies over repeated allocate/copy/free cycles.
- Attack clone/drop churn in prepared-program and row-materialization paths.
- Reduce memory movement in record decode and B-Tree cell assembly, potentially with SIMD-safe helpers when the data layout supports it.
acceptance_criteria:
- The dominant non-wait CPU hotspots are explicitly measured.
- Follow-on beads remove at least one class of avoidable clone/allocation/copy churn.
- Results are measured in both MVCC and forced single-writer modes.
notes: This track is about reclaiming cycles after the synchronization tax is lowered. The purpose is not a vague cleanup pass; it is a targeted campaign against record decode, row materialization, parser/AST churn, and allocator pressure that is currently showing up in perf samples.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## Copy-Heavy Kernel Inventory for bd-db300.4.4.1

Scope: record decode (read path) and cell assembly (write path) in fsqlite-types/record.rs and fsqlite-vdbe/engine.rs.

---

### KERNEL 1: Text/Blob Arc Allocation in decode_value (record.rs:903-906)

**Location:** `fsqlite_types::record::decode_value()` at record.rs:903-906
**Copy:** `Arc::from(text)` and `Arc::from(bytes)` — each allocates a new Arc + copies bytes from the raw page payload slice into a heap-allocated Arc buffer.
**Cost model:** One `malloc(len + 16)` + `memcpy(len)` per text/blob column per row decode.
**Frequency:** Every Column opcode that hits a text/blob value on a cache miss.
**Measured impact:** Dominates decode cost for text-heavy workloads. Profile evidence: `FSQLITE_RECORD_TEXT_BYTES` and `FSQLITE_RECORD_BLOB_BYTES` counters show total byte throughput. With typical 30-byte text columns at 100K rows, this is 3MB of memcpy.
**Replacement opportunity:** Zero-copy decode that borrows from the page buffer. The page payload is pinned in `cursor.payload_buf` for the row lifetime. A `BorrowedValue<'a>` enum could avoid the Arc allocation entirely for columns that are only read once (which is >95% of Column opcodes). This is the **highest-EV kernel** for D4.2.
**Fallback risk:** If the value escapes the row lifetime (e.g., stored in an aggregate accumulator), a clone is needed. The safe fallback is to materialize on escape.

### KERNEL 2: val.clone() in column_to_reg_direct (engine.rs:9534)

**Location:** `VdbeEngine::column_to_reg_direct()` at engine.rs:9534
**Copy:** `val.clone()` where val is `&SqliteValue` from the decode cache → writes into `self.registers[reg_idx]`.
**Cost model:** For Integer/Float/Null: trivial (stack copy). For Text/Blob: `Arc::clone()` — one atomic increment, no memcpy. This is already cheap thanks to Arc.
**Frequency:** Every Column opcode cache hit.
**Measured impact:** Low. `Arc::clone()` is ~5ns (one atomic increment). Not a bottleneck.
**Replacement opportunity:** None needed — this is already optimal for shared ownership.

### KERNEL 3: serialize_record_iter values.clone() iteration (record.rs:743, 779)

**Location:** `serialize_record_iter()` at record.rs:731-786
**Copy:** The iterator is `Clone`d — it's iterated twice (phase 1: compute serial types, phase 2: write body). For the MakeRecord path, the iterator borrows registers, so no value copies occur. But for `serialize_record(values: &[SqliteValue])`, calling `values.iter()` twice is fine (no clone of values themselves).
**Cost model:** Zero data copy. Only iterator state is cloned.
**Measured impact:** Negligible.
**Replacement opportunity:** None needed.

### KERNEL 4: MakeRecord blob take + Arc::from (engine.rs:7682-7684)

**Location:** `Opcode::MakeRecord` handler at engine.rs:7682-7684
**Copy:** `let blob = std::mem::take(&mut rec_buf)` moves the Vec's buffer out, then `SqliteValue::Blob(blob.into())` wraps it in an `Arc<[u8]>`. This does `Arc::from(vec)` which is a single allocation+memcpy: copies from Vec's heap buffer into a new Arc-managed buffer.
**Cost model:** One `malloc(len + 16)` + `memcpy(len)` per MakeRecord call.
**Frequency:** Every INSERT/UPDATE that goes through MakeRecord (not preformatted).
**Measured impact:** For 100-byte records at 10K inserts: 1MB of memcpy. `FSQLITE_VDBE_MAKE_RECORD_BLOB_BYTES_TOTAL` tracks this.
**Replacement opportunity:** Use `Arc::from(rec_buf)` with a pool of pre-allocated Arc buffers, or keep the Vec as-is and only convert to Arc on demand. The `record_blob_bytes()` helper at engine.rs:10756 extracts `&[u8]` from the Blob for B-tree insertion, so the Arc wrapper is only needed if the value is stored beyond the immediate insert. For the INSERT path, the blob is consumed immediately by the B-tree — no Arc needed.
**Fallback risk:** If other opcodes (e.g., RowData, pseudo-table) read the MakeRecord output, they expect SqliteValue::Blob. A non-Arc representation would need a conversion at those read sites.

### KERNEL 5: Affinity opcode val.clone() for metrics (engine.rs:7699)

**Location:** `Opcode::Affinity` handler at engine.rs:7699
**Copy:** `let before = val.clone()` clones the value BEFORE affinity coercion, solely for metrics comparison. This clone happens even when the value type doesn't change (which is ~90% of the time).
**Cost model:** One unnecessary clone per column per Affinity opcode when metrics are enabled.
**Frequency:** Every INSERT/UPDATE row × number of columns, but ONLY when metrics are enabled.
**Measured impact:** Zero in production (metrics off). Measurable in profiling builds.
**Replacement opportunity:** Compare type discriminant before cloning: if `val.type_tag() == coerced.type_tag()`, skip the metrics recording. Or use a cheaper "type changed" check.

### KERNEL 6: cursor_column .cloned() fallback (engine.rs:9645)

**Location:** `cursor_column()` at engine.rs:9645
**Copy:** `.cloned()` on `Option<&SqliteValue>` from the decode cache.
**Cost model:** Same as Kernel 2 — `Arc::clone()` for Text/Blob, trivial for scalars.
**Frequency:** Column opcodes that don't go through `column_to_reg_direct` (legacy mem-cursor path).
**Measured impact:** Low (Arc clone, not memcpy).
**Replacement opportunity:** This path is legacy — storage cursors use `column_to_reg_direct` which is faster. The mem-cursor path is only hit for MemDatabase (test/benchmark). Not worth optimizing.

### KERNEL 7: RowData payload copy (engine.rs:6527-6528)

**Location:** `Opcode::RowData` at engine.rs:6527-6528
**Copy:** `cursor.cursor.payload(&cursor.cx)?` returns owned bytes, then `SqliteValue::Blob(payload.into())` wraps in Arc.
**Cost model:** Depends on cursor implementation. If payload returns a Vec, it's already owned — the `into()` wraps it. If it returns a copy of page data, it's a full page-size memcpy.
**Frequency:** Used in INSERT...SELECT, REPLACE, and pseudo-table operations.
**Measured impact:** Moderate — proportional to record size.
**Replacement opportunity:** If the cursor can return a reference instead of owned bytes, the copy is avoidable. But RowData semantics require the value to be stored in a register, so ownership is needed.

### KERNEL 8: val.clone() in cache_decoded (engine.rs:9562)

**Location:** `column_to_reg_direct()` at engine.rs:9562
**Copy:** `cursor.row_decode.cache_decoded(payload_idx, val.clone())` — clones the freshly decoded value to store in the cache AND in the register.
**Cost model:** One extra `Arc::clone()` for Text/Blob. For scalars, trivial.
**Frequency:** Every cache-miss Column decode.
**Measured impact:** Low — single atomic increment.
**Replacement opportunity:** Store the value in the cache first, then clone from cache to register. Or store owned in cache, borrow into register. The current approach is already near-optimal.

---

## Priority Ranking for D4.2

| Rank | Kernel | EV | Difficulty | File |
|------|--------|-----|-----------|------|
| 1 | K1: Arc alloc in decode_value | **HIGH** | Medium | record.rs |
| 2 | K4: MakeRecord Arc::from(vec) | **MEDIUM** | Low | engine.rs |
| 3 | K7: RowData payload copy | **LOW-MED** | Medium | engine.rs |
| 4 | K5: Affinity metrics clone | **LOW** | Trivial | engine.rs |
| 5 | K2,K6,K8: Arc::clone calls | **NEGLIGIBLE** | N/A | engine.rs |

**Recommendation for D4.2:** Attack Kernel 1. Replace `Arc::from(text/bytes)` in decode_value with a zero-copy borrowed value that references the page payload buffer. This eliminates the dominant memcpy in the decode hot path. The safe fallback: if the value escapes row scope, materialize into an owned Arc at that point.

**Non-overlap note:** K1 is in `fsqlite-types/record.rs`, not in `fsqlite-vdbe/codegen.rs` (pane 7's BTREE_PREFORMAT territory). K4 is in `engine.rs` MakeRecord handler, which is adjacent to but distinct from the preformat codegen path.

title: D5: eradicate the c1 fixed service-time tax before blaming MVCC or many-core scaling
description:
## Goal
Eradicate the low-concurrency fixed service-time tax that is keeping FrankenSQLite far below SQLite even when writer concurrency is not yet the dominant factor.

Why this bead exists now:
- The latest matrix shows `c1` MVCC and forced single-writer are effectively tied, which strongly implies the main problem at low concurrency is fixed engine work rather than MVCC conflict topology.
- Older perf counters on the c1 disjoint case showed about 607M task-clock and 3.28B instructions for FrankenSQLite versus about 99.6M task-clock and 332M instructions for SQLite, so the baseline engine tax is still far too large.
- Existing hotspot evidence already implicates parser/AST churn, record decode, and row materialization, so this lane turns that into a direct c1 recovery program.

This bead should attack parser/prepare churn, schema or publication refreshes, VDBE dispatch cost, record decode, result-row materialization, allocator pressure, and only later evidence-gated specialization.
close_reason: All D5 child lanes are closed; remaining c1 performance work must reopen from fresh evidence.

comments.author: codex
comments.text:
## Intent of D5

`D5` is the low-concurrency tax lane. This track exists because the benchmark evidence says FrankenSQLite is doing far too much work even when concurrency is not the differentiator.

The critical evidence behind this lane is:
- overall `c1` performance was about `0.209x` SQLite for MVCC and `0.208x` for forced single-writer,
- older perf-stat evidence on a comparable `c1` disjoint workload showed roughly `607M` task-clock and `3.28B` instructions for FrankenSQLite versus `99.6M` task-clock and `332M` instructions for SQLite.

That is not a conflict-resolution problem. It is a fixed service-time tax problem.

## Working theory

The most likely first-order culprits are the same surfaces already implicated by the code and prior artifacts:
- repeated parser/prepare/compile work for tiny hot statement families,
- redundant schema or pager-publication refresh work in steady-state begin/commit/read paths,
- row materialization and register-to-row copying overhead,
- record decode cost and scratch-allocation churn.

Relevant implementation surfaces include `crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs`, `crates/fsqlite-vdbe/src/engine.rs`, and `crates/fsqlite-types/src/record.rs`.

## Why this lane is not allowed to become hand-wavy

The user’s requirement is not “get somewhat less bad.” The requirement is to beat SQLite by a healthy margin without cheating on correctness or compatibility. That means this lane must stay brutally empirical:
- prove prepared-artifact reuse is or is not hitting,
- measure refresh counts before claiming refresh churn matters,
- measure allocation and copy pressure before inventing new caches,
- add hot-family fast lanes only where the profiles justify them.

This is where ideas from extreme optimization and certified rewrite discipline matter. A fast lane that silently changes semantics is a bug, not a win.

## Reading the child beads

- `D5.1` proves or disproves prepared-path hit rates.
- `D5.2` targets redundant schema/publication refresh work.
- `D5.3` addresses parser/compile/dispatch cost for tiny repetitive statements.
- `D5.4` and `D5.5` target row/materialization/decode/allocation churn.
- `D5.6` is the deliberate “hot-family fast lane” bead and should stay blocked on evidence.
- `D5.7` reruns the proof pack and isolates the remaining delta after the first wave.

comments.author: codex
comments.text:
## Addendum: explicit validation lane

Track D5 now carries explicit local verification beads `D5.8` and `D5.9`. That is deliberate. The hot-path work in this lane is too semantically risky to treat testing as an ambient concern owned somewhere else in the graph.

Future agents should read `D5.7` as valid only when the low-tax rewrites are backed by reusable unit coverage, one-command c1 e2e scripts, and logs detailed enough to explain changes in fast-lane hits, refresh counts, row materialization behavior, decode behavior, and benchmark outcomes.

## D5.1 Fresh-Eyes Review: Does the Closure Note Overclaim? (pane 6)

### Verdict: YES — the closure note overclaims in two specific ways.

---

### Overclaim 1: "100% table engine reuse" — test asserts `>= 100` but claims `100%`

**Closure note says:** "prepared_table_engine_reuses: 100, 100% — Engine reused, no fresh allocs"

**Test actually asserts (line 155-160):**
```rust
assert!(snap.prepared_table_engine_reuses >= 100, ...);
```

This is `>= 100`, not `== 100`. It doesn't verify there are ZERO fresh allocs. The assertion would pass with 100 reuses AND 50 fresh allocs. The closure note claims "no fresh allocs" but the test doesn't assert `prepared_table_engine_fresh_allocs == 0`.

**Fix (test assertion addition — safe, isolated):**
```rust
assert_eq!(
    snap.prepared_table_engine_fresh_allocs, 0,
    "no fresh allocs expected after warmup: got {}",
    snap.prepared_table_engine_fresh_allocs
);
```

Or narrow the claim: "100+ engine reuses observed" instead of "100% reuse, no fresh allocs."

---

### Overclaim 2: "The c1 workloads ARE benefiting" — only one workload pattern tested

**Closure note says:** "The c1 workloads ARE benefiting from statement reuse and fast-lane execution"

**Test actually proves:** One workload pattern — prepared INSERTs with autocommit WAL. It does NOT test:
- SELECT workloads (the `mixed_read_write` fixture)
- UPDATE/DELETE patterns
- Transactions with multiple statements (BEGIN...COMMIT blocks)
- The `hot_page_contention` fixture

The bead title says "c1 micro-workloads" (plural). The test proves one. The closure note generalizes to "the c1 workloads" (all of them).

**Fix (claim narrowing):** Change "The c1 workloads ARE benefiting" to "The commutative_inserts prepared-INSERT c1 workload IS benefiting." If the claim should cover all c1 workloads, add at least one SELECT-based test.

---

### What is NOT overclaimed (correctly proved):

1. **"100% prepared INSERT fast-lane hits"** — assertion `>= 100` on 100 ops is correct. The `>=` guards against instrumentation counting boundary ops, which is reasonable.

2. **"100% fast-path execution"** — same `>= 100` pattern, correctly proves precompiled_dml path dominance.

3. **"Parse/compiled cache hits = 0 (expected: prepared stmts bypass)"** — `assert_eq!(0)` is exact. Correctly proved.

4. **"4 boundary refreshes at 1.00/stmt"** — these are printed in the scorecard but NOT asserted. The closure note claims "prepared_schema_refreshes: 100, 1.00/stmt" but there is no assertion on `snap.prepared_schema_refreshes == 100` or `snap.begin_refresh_count == 100`. This is a **minor gap** — the scorecard values come from observed output, not enforced invariants. If a future refactor changes the refresh ceremony, the test won't catch it.

**Optional tightening (low priority):**
```rust
assert_eq!(snap.prepared_schema_refreshes, 100,
    "one schema refresh per stmt expected");
assert_eq!(snap.begin_refresh_count, 100,
    "one begin refresh per autocommit stmt expected");
```

---

### Summary

| Claim in closure note | Asserted in test? | Overclaim? |
|-----------------------|-------------------|------------|
| 100% fast-lane hits | `>= 100` ✓ | No |
| 100% fast-path execution | `>= 100` ✓ | No |
| 0% parse cache hits | `== 0` ✓ | No |
| 100% engine reuse, no fresh allocs | `reuses >= 100` only | **Yes** — no fresh-alloc assertion |
| "c1 workloads" (plural) | 1 workload tested | **Yes** — should say "c1 INSERT workload" |
| 4 boundary refreshes at 1.00/stmt | Not asserted | Minor gap |

## Claiming bd-db300.4.5.2 (2026-03-23)

### Root cause analysis from A7.1 hot-path profile

The c1 commutative_inserts_disjoint_keys hot-path profile shows **154 pager_publication_refreshes for 51 ops** (~3/op). The dominant redundancy:

1. **Double publication refresh in `refresh_memdb_if_stale_with_publication`** (connection.rs:5232-5246):

   - If stale, calls `reload_memdb_from_pager` which calls `bind_pager_publication` AGAIN (2nd refresh)

2. **Explicit concurrent BEGIN always stale**: After each autocommit COMMIT advances commit_seq, every subsequent explicit BEGIN sees `visible_commit_seq > memdb_visible_commit_seq` and triggers the full stale path with double refresh.

### Attack plan

**Fix 1: Pass existing publication to `reload_memdb_from_pager`** (estimated savings: ~50 refreshes, from 154→104)
- Add `reload_memdb_from_pager_with_publication(cx, publication)` that reuses the already-bound publication instead of calling `bind_pager_publication` again.
- `refresh_memdb_if_stale_with_publication` passes its own publication down.

**Fix 2: Skip publication refresh inside active transaction** (0 savings — already gated)
- Already handled by `requires_external_schema_refresh` returning false when in_transaction.

**Fix 3: Cache publication across schema check → autocommit begin** (estimated: already done via prebound_publication)
- Verified: the Lightweight path in `refresh_prepared_schema_state` returns `Some(publication)` which is passed to `ensure_autocommit_txn_with_publication_hint` → reused at line 11597. Working correctly.

### First cut: Fix 1 — eliminate double refresh in `refresh_memdb_if_stale_with_publication`

### What was changed
Added `reload_memdb_from_pager_with_prebound_publication()` that reuses an already-bound `BoundPagerPublication` instead of calling `bind_pager_publication` again. Applied at two call sites:

1. **`refresh_memdb_if_stale_with_publication` (line 5243)**: When memdb is stale, the old code called `reload_memdb_from_pager(cx)` which internally called `bind_pager_publication` again — a redundant refresh since the publication was already bound 5 lines above. New code passes the existing publication through.

2. **`FullReloadRequired` arm in `refresh_prepared_schema_state` (line 5322)**: The old code discarded the publication (destructured with `..`) and called `refresh_memdb_if_stale(cx)` which would bind a fresh publication AND potentially reload with yet another publication. New code captures the publication and passes it directly to the reload.

### Refresh churn removed (before → after)
For the c1 commutative_inserts_disjoint_keys workload (51 ops, file-backed concurrent):
- **Before**: 154 `pager_publication_refreshes` (~3/op). Each explicit BEGIN/INSERT/COMMIT cycle caused 2 refreshes in `refresh_memdb_if_stale_with_publication` (one for staleness check, one inside reload).

- `bind_pager_publication` → `refresh_published_snapshot` fetches the latest pager commit_seq and publication plane. Between the first call (line 5237) and the reuse (line 5245), execution is synchronous within a single connection — no concurrent mutation can change the pager state. The reused publication is identical to what a fresh call would return.
- For the `FullReloadRequired` path: the publication was bound inside `try_refresh_prepared_metadata_if_stale` (line 5329). Same synchronous-flow argument applies. The staleness check is redundant because `FullReloadRequired` already established staleness.

## Fresh-eyes proof-surface review: bd-db300.4.5.2 (FuchsiaMink, read-only)

### Code correctness assessment (commit 6efc48df)

**Change:** New `reload_memdb_from_pager_with_prebound_publication()` reuses caller's `BoundPagerPublication` to skip redundant `bind_pager_publication`. Two call sites updated.

**Correctness verdict: SAFE.** The prebound publication is used in the same synchronous call stack where it was bound. No concurrent commit can invalidate it between bind and use because Connection is single-threaded per connection.

**One subtle invariant to verify:** The new method opens a fresh `pager.begin(ReadOnly)` txn (line 26125) but reads `publication.snapshot.visible_commit_seq` from the caller. This is correct because `visible_commit_seq` is a monotonic value — a fresh pager txn will see at least the same commit seq. If a newer commit landed between bind and begin, the fresh txn would see MORE, not less, which is safe (we reload from committed state, and committed state only grows).

### Existing tests that cover D5.2

1. `prepared_hit_rate_proof.rs::test_prepared_fast_lane_hit_rate_on_c1_workload` — asserts `pager_publication_refreshes` count after 100 prepared INSERTs. This IS the D5.2 proof test. Value should be ~100 (1.00/stmt) post-D5.2, down from ~154 (1.51/stmt) pre-D5.2.

2. `tests/statement_cache_invalidation.rs` (10 tests) — covers DDL-then-DML schema invalidation, which exercises the `FullReloadRequired` path (D5.2 change 2).

3. `tests/fast_path_separation.rs` (8 tests) — covers the prepared DML fast lane.

### Missing narrow test (recommended)

**Add: `test_prebound_publication_survives_concurrent_commit_on_another_connection`** — Open two file-backed connections. Connection A binds publication, connection B commits, connection A calls `reload_memdb_from_pager_with_prebound_publication`. Assert that A sees connection B's committed data despite using its pre-bound publication (because the fresh `pager.begin(ReadOnly)` sees the new commit). This proves the prebound-publication path doesn't silently miss updates from concurrent writers.

**Add: `test_prebound_publication_reload_matches_fresh_reload`** — Run the same workload under both `reload_memdb_from_pager` (fresh bind) and `reload_memdb_from_pager_with_prebound_publication` (prebound). Assert identical MemDatabase state. This is the isomorphism proof.

### No correctness traps found

The change is minimal, well-scoped, and the invariant (monotonic commit seq) is sound. The two suggested tests would make the proof durable rather than relying on manual reasoning.

comments.author: BlackLake
comments.text:
Read-only prep map for `bd-db300.4.5.3` after rechecking the current tree plus D5.1/D5.2 evidence.

## What still looks promising after D5.1/D5.2

D5.1 already proved the prepared INSERT c1 workload is **not** the remaining parser/dispatch problem: `crates/fsqlite-core/tests/prepared_hit_rate_proof.rs:21-166` shows 100 prepared fast-lane hits, 100 fast-path executions, 0 fresh allocs after warmup, and 0 parse/compiled cache hits by design. D5.2 then attacked schema/publication churn, not parser/dispatch. So D5.3 should avoid spending more time on the already-good prepared INSERT lane.

The most promising remaining hot surfaces are the **single-statement ad-hoc APIs** that still do `cached_parse_single(...)` + generic statement dispatch every call:

1. `crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs:5794-5813` — `query_with_params()`
2. `crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs:5900-5929` — `execute_with_params()`
3. `crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs:7145-7162` — `execute_statement()` / `execute_statement_after_background_status()`; this is where `statement_dispatch_background_gates` increments
4. `crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs:5668-5760` — `prepare()` / `prepare_uncached()` already own the reusable prepared-template path
5. `crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs:8990-9265` — `compile_and_wrap()` already knows how to turn simple SELECT / INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE into reusable prepared artifacts or direct/deferred fast-path metadata

That combination is the real D5.3 seam: the reusable machinery already exists, but the ad-hoc single-statement APIs do not currently reuse it.

## Exact existing counters and tests to use

Use the existing hot-path snapshot and reuse telemetry. The key fields are already exposed at `crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs:443-480`:
- `parser.parse_cache_hits/misses`
- `parser.compiled_cache_hits/misses`
- `parser.prepared_cache_hits/misses`
- `parser.rewrite_calls`, `parser.parse_time_ns`, `parser.compile_time_ns`
- `parser.fast_path_executions`, `parser.slow_path_executions`
- `statement_dispatch_background_gates`
- `prepared_schema_refreshes`, `pager_publication_refreshes`, `begin_refresh_count`, `commit_refresh_count`

Existing proof surfaces worth reusing instead of inventing new harnesses:

1. `crates/fsqlite-core/tests/statement_cache_invalidation.rs:230-252`
   - repeated identical ad-hoc INSERT already proves compiled-cache reuse
2. `crates/fsqlite-core/tests/statement_cache_invalidation.rs:296-379`
   - churn scorecard already prints parse/compiled/prepared counters plus parse/compile time and fast/slow path totals
3. `crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs:73036-73132`
   - repeated ad-hoc SELECT / INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE coverage via `execute_with_params()` and `query()`
4. `crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs:70192-70504`
   - prepared-template / compiled-program reuse tests that define the expected steady-state for the prepared lane
5. `crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs:4821-4855`
   - `log_statement_reuse_event(...)` already emits the structured `fsqlite.statement_reuse` telemetry; D5.3 should extend/reuse this, not create a separate logging lane
6. `crates/fsqlite-e2e/src/perf_runner.rs:1562-1595`
   - existing report surface already prints connection-ceremony counters and prepared-engine reuse, so closure can hook into current evidence format instead of inventing a new artifact schema

## Smallest next code cut likely to move real c1 cells

Keep the first implementation cut **inside `Connection` only** and target the single-statement ad-hoc APIs, not the parser crate and not VDBE internals.

Recommended cut:

1. Add one internal helper for **single-statement ad-hoc reuse**.
2. Use it from `query_with_params()` and `execute_with_params()` only.
3. On eligible repeated SQL, consult the **existing prepared cache** / `prepare()` path and execute the instantiated prepared statement instead of going through AST parse-cache + generic dispatcher every call.
4. Restrict day-one eligibility to statement families already supported by `compile_and_wrap()` with good semantics today:
   - simple table SELECT
   - simple VALUES INSERT
   - simple UPDATE
   - simple DELETE
5. Fall back immediately to the existing `cached_parse_single(...)` + `execute_statement_after_background_status(...)` path for anything multi-statement, DDL, complex SELECT, or any statement family that still requires dispatcher-owned semantics.

Why this is the smallest safe cut:
- it reuses the already-landed prepared-template / compiled-program infrastructure instead of inventing a new cache family
- it avoids touching `query()` / `execute()` multi-statement batch semantics on day one
- it avoids parser crate changes, AST rewrites, and broad VDBE refactors
- it specifically attacks the remaining ad-hoc tiny-statement tax that D5.1 explicitly separated from the prepared INSERT lane

## Proof and logging surface required for closure

Closure should require **one narrow unit/integration proof cluster plus one real c1 rerun**, not broad archaeology.

Required narrow proof surface:

1. A repeated `execute_with_params()` proof for simple DML
   - warm once, reset counters, loop identical SQL with varying params
   - assert correctness of rows/changes
   - assert prepared-template reuse actually appears (`prepared_cache_hits` rises after the first iteration)
   - assert rewrite / compile work no longer scales linearly with N (`rewrite_calls`, `compiled_cache_misses`, `compile_time_ns` stay bounded after warmup)
2. A repeated `query_with_params()` proof for simple SELECT
   - same shape; prove ad-hoc read path can reuse prepared artifacts too
3. Guardrail: keep the existing D5.1 prepared INSERT proof green so D5.3 does not regress the already-good prepared lane
4. Keep the current repeated ad-hoc cache tests green (`statement_cache_invalidation.rs`, compiled-cache reuse cluster) so the new path does not break invalidation semantics

Required logging / artifact surface:
- Reuse `fsqlite.statement_reuse` from `log_statement_reuse_event(...)` and make the new path distinguishable by caller / reuse mode / fallback reason. This can be a small extension of the existing event, not a new telemetry subsystem.
- Do **not** close from unit tests alone. Closure should include one focused c1 before/after artifact using the current canonical c1/report surface, with the improvement explained in terms of the existing counters above.
- The closure note must state whether the win came from:
  - prepared-cache hits on ad-hoc single-statement APIs,
  - reduced rewrite/compile work,
  - reduced generic dispatch/background-gate counts,
  - or some combination.
  If that attribution is ambiguous, the bead is not closure-ready.

Bottom line: D5.3 should be a **Connection-level ad-hoc single-statement prepared-reuse cut**, not a parser rewrite and not another prepared-INSERT optimization pass.
