title: G7.2: define correctness crash fault and topology-stress suite composition
description:
## Goal
Define the correctness, crash, fault, topology-stress, and focused performance scenarios that each one-command verification suite must contain.

## Why This Matters
One-command suites are only trustworthy if their scenario composition is explicit and hard to dilute. This bead turns suite membership into a concrete contract instead of an evolving pile of ad hoc cases.

## Scope
For each relevant suite family, define:
- mandatory correctness scenarios,
- crash/fault and rollback/recovery scenarios,
- topology-stress and interference scenarios,
- focused performance-attribution rows needed to interpret benchmark changes,
- the required artifact bundle and structured-log families for each scenario class.

The composition contract must also record:
- which scenarios are quick-suite mandatory versus full-suite only,
- which placement profiles are required for each scenario,
- which compatibility surfaces or oracles apply,
- what counts as a first-failure bundle for the scenario.

## Required Verification and Logging
- Table-driven or harness-level tests that validate the scenario registry and suite composition rules.
- A named operator entrypoint such as `scripts/verify_g7_2_suite_composition.sh` that renders suite composition for representative bead families and reports missing mandatory scenarios.
- Structured logs exposing at minimum `trace_id`, `scenario_id`, `suite_id`, `verification_class`, `placement_profile`, `artifact_manifest_key`, `compatibility_surface`, `oracle`, `quick_or_full`, and first-failure diagnostics.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Correctness, crash/fault, topology-stress, and focused performance scenarios are defined per suite with explicit quick/full policy.
- Each scenario is tied to required placement profiles, logs, artifacts, and oracle/compatibility context where applicable.
- Validation proves that suite composition is hard to accidentally dilute.
- The result is strong enough to catch concurrency, reuse, allocator, restart, and placement regressions before claims reach the scorecard.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The bead defines scenario composition per suite for correctness, crash/fault, topology-stress, rollback/recovery, and focused performance attribution, with explicit quick/full policy.
2. `scripts/verify_g7_2_suite_composition.sh` or an equivalent named validation entrypoint is part of the plan and emits replayable artifacts proving mandatory scenario coverage.
3. Structured logs expose suite id, verification class, placement profile, artifact-manifest linkage, compatibility/oracle context, quick/full designation, and first-failure diagnostics.
4. The composition contract is strong enough to catch synchronization, stale-cache/reuse, allocator/restart, and placement-sensitive convoy regressions.
5. The output is self-contained enough that future suite maintainers do not need to rediscover which scenarios are mandatory.
notes:
Suite-composition obligations:
- define which correctness, crash/fault, rollback/recovery, topology-stress, and focused benchmark scenarios belong in the one-command suites for each relevant bead family
- tie each scenario to required placement profiles, artifact bundles, and structured log expectations
- ensure the composition is strong enough to catch concurrency regressions, stale-cache/reuse bugs, allocator/restart failures, and placement-sensitive convoy failures before claims reach the final scorecard

User-facing intent:
- a suite should fail because it is missing a required scenario, not silently succeed because the scenario was never wired in

title: G7.3: define CI and operator packaging for the one-command verification suites
description:
## Goal
Define CI and operator packaging for the one-command verification suites so they stay usable under real engineering pressure and still preserve rich evidence.

## Why This Matters
A good suite can still fail operationally if it is too expensive to run, too opaque when it fails, or too hard to wire into CI. This bead fixes the packaging contract that makes the suites practical.

## Scope
Define:
- local and CI/operator invocation forms,
- quick-versus-full suite defaults and escalation rules,
- artifact retention and pruning policy,
- failure-summary and artifact-discovery output,
- packaging of rerun commands and first-failure bundles into CI/operator reports,
- rendering of activation regime, shadow-oracle verdicts, kill-switch state, and counterexample-bundle location when a smart path diverges.

The packaging contract must make it obvious:
- which scenario/profile/regime failed,
- whether the run was quick, full, or shadow-oriented,
- where the artifacts and counterexamples live,
- which rerun command applies,
- what evidence was intentionally omitted for cost reasons.

## Required Verification and Logging
- Smoke tests or packaging validation for local and CI/operator invocation forms.
- A named operator entrypoint such as `scripts/verify_g7_3_suite_packaging.sh` that exercises quick/full/shadow modes, failure-summary output, and artifact retention behavior.
- Structured logs exposing at minimum `trace_id`, `scenario_id`, `suite_id`, `execution_context`, `verification_depth`, `activation_regime`, `shadow_mode`, `shadow_verdict`, `kill_switch_state`, `counterexample_bundle`, `artifact_root`, `retention_class`, `rerun_entrypoint`, `pass_fail_signature`, and first-failure diagnostics.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Local and CI invocation patterns, artifact retention, and pass/fail summary contracts are explicit.
- Routine reruns stay cheap enough that developers will actually use them, while full runs preserve rich evidence.
- Failure output is actionable for both humans and automation, including activation/shadow diagnostics.
- The packaging contract is strong enough that verification suites remain usable as the default interface under failure pressure.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The bead defines local and CI/operator invocation forms, quick/full/shadow escalation rules, artifact-retention policy, and pass/fail summary contracts for the one-command suites.
2. `scripts/verify_g7_3_suite_packaging.sh` or an equivalent named validation entrypoint is part of the plan and emits replayable artifacts proving packaging behavior.
3. Structured logs expose execution context, verification depth, activation regime, shadow mode, shadow verdict, kill-switch state, counterexample bundle, artifact root, retention class, rerun entrypoint, pass/fail signature, and first-failure diagnostics.
4. The packaging contract preserves rich evidence for deep investigations without making routine reruns unreasonably expensive.
5. Failure output is actionable enough that the user immediately sees which scenario/profile/regime failed, where artifacts live, whether a shadow divergence occurred, and how to rerun it.

Narrow validation green: CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/data/projects/frankensqlite/target-g771 cargo test -p fsqlite-e2e --bin realdb-e2e verify_suite_ -- --nocapture and existing inline bundle proof still passes. title: G8: build topology-sensitive interference microbench suite for synchronization and publish primitives
description:
## Goal
Build an interference microbench suite that exercises the synchronization and publication candidates from the many-core program under the placements that matter on high-end processors. The goal is to measure cache-line ownership churn, wake-to-run cost, tail behavior, and fallback behavior before these primitives are fused into the engine and become harder to reason about.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. The microbench suite covers representative primitive classes from this program, including read-mostly metadata publication, shared-counter or false-sharing paths, baton or retry handoff, and tiny publish or commit-style critical sections.
2. Scenarios include at least unpinned baseline, SMT-sibling, same-LLC-different-core, and cross-node or cross-CCD placements where the host exposes them.
3. Outputs capture throughput, `p50/p95/p99` latency, fairness, wakeups or parking, migrations, and cache-ownership or remote-access evidence (`perf c2c`/HITM or best-available fallback metrics).
4. The suite is runnable through an operator-friendly entrypoint and emits structured logs and artifact manifests rich enough to compare primitive candidates mechanically.
5. The results are mapped back into the B3, B4, E2, E3, E6, and E7 design or verification decisions rather than living as isolated benchmark trivia.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The microbench suite covers representative primitive classes from this program, including read-mostly metadata publication, shared-counter or false-sharing paths, baton or retry handoff, and tiny publish or commit-style critical sections.
2. Scenarios include at least unpinned baseline, SMT-sibling, same-LLC-different-core, and cross-node or cross-CCD placements where the host exposes them.
3. Outputs capture throughput, `p50/p95/p99` latency, fairness, wakeups or parking, migrations, and cache-ownership or remote-access evidence (`perf c2c`/HITM or best-available fallback metrics).
4. The suite is runnable through an operator-friendly entrypoint and emits structured logs and artifact manifests rich enough to compare primitive candidates mechanically.
5. The results are mapped back into the B3, B4, E2, E3, E6, and E7 design or verification decisions rather than living as isolated benchmark trivia.
notes:
This bead is the concrete home for the alien-graveyard composition guard that says clever synchronization or controller combinations need interference evidence before integration. Its job is to catch topology-specific pathologies early, when they are still cheap to reason about and replace.

Operator sequencing:
1. Start with `bd-db300.7.8.1` for same-core, SMT-sibling, and same-LLC cases.
2. Then `bd-db300.7.8.2` for cross-node or remote-ownership cases.
3. Then `bd-db300.7.8.3` to feed the measured interference results back into primitive selection and design decisions.

title: G8.1: build same-core same-LLC and SMT interference cases
description:
## Goal
Build the same-core, SMT-sibling, and same-LLC interference cases that expose topology-sensitive pathologies before they contaminate larger benchmark claims.

## Why This Matters
The new metadata-publication and parallel-WAL work both rely on tiny publication regions and read-mostly synchronization paths that can look excellent in aggregate while hiding severe sibling-core or same-LLC contention. This bead is the earliest-warning layer for those failures.

## Scope
Implement interference cases that exercise at minimum:
- same-core or nearest-placement contention where the host exposes it,
- SMT-sibling interference,
- same-LLC different-core interference,
- representative read-mostly metadata publication paths,
- representative tiny publish or durability critical sections,
- representative retry or handoff primitives.

## Required Verification and Logging
- Harness-level tests that verify placement resolution, case selection, and artifact emission are stable.
- A named operator entrypoint such as `scripts/verify_g8_1_same_core_smt_interference.sh` that runs the cases and emits replayable artifacts.
- Structured logs and artifact fields including at minimum `trace_id`, `scenario_id`, `placement_profile`, `primitive_class`, `cpu_pair`, `llc_domain`, `smt_relationship`, `throughput`, `p50_ns`, `p95_ns`, `p99_ns`, `fairness_score`, `wakeups`, `migrations`, `ownership_events`, and first-failure diagnostics.
- Explicit negative expectations for pathological fairness collapse, wakeup inflation, or ownership thrash.

## Acceptance Criteria
- The suite covers same-core, SMT-sibling, and same-LLC placements with stable operator entrypoints.
- Cases capture latency, fairness, wakeup, migration, and cache-ownership evidence rich enough to diagnose interference mechanically.
- Artifact layout and logging are stable enough for before/after comparison across reruns.
- The result is directly consumable by later topology-proof and tuning beads.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The microbench suite includes same-core, SMT-sibling, and same-LLC placement cases with explicit operator entrypoints and stable artifact layout.
2. `scripts/verify_g8_1_same_core_smt_interference.sh` or an equivalent named entrypoint is part of the plan and emits replayable artifacts.
3. Structured logs expose placement profile, primitive class, CPU relationship, LLC domain, latency buckets, fairness, wakeups, migrations, ownership events, and first-failure diagnostics.
4. Negative-path expectations for fairness collapse, wakeup inflation, and ownership thrash are explicit.
5. The suite is packaged so topology-sensitive regressions can be rerun and compared mechanically, not just eyeballed.
notes:
Interference-suite intent:
- this bead should make same-core and sibling-core pathologies obvious before they get hidden inside larger benchmark summaries
- prioritize operator usability: one command, stable artifacts, easy comparison

title: G8.2: build cross-node cross-CCD and remote-ownership interference cases
description:
## Goal
Build the cross-node, cross-CCD, and remote-ownership interference cases that expose remote-memory and remote-cache pathologies before they contaminate larger benchmark claims.

## Why This Matters
The many-core program is explicitly trying to win on machines where remote ownership, cross-node wakeups, and cache-line migration can erase nominal algorithmic gains. This bead turns those remote-placement hazards into a concrete, replayable verification surface.

## Scope
Implement interference cases that exercise at minimum:
- cross-node or remote-memory ownership where the host exposes it,
- cross-CCD or cross-LLC ownership transfer where visible,
- helper-lane and remote-wakeup paths,
- allocator or arena handoffs that become remote under pressure,
- representative read-mostly metadata publication paths,
- representative tiny publish or durability critical sections under remote ownership.

Each case should define:
- placement profile and CPU/node pairing,
- local owner versus remote actor roles,
- expected remote-access or ownership-thrash signal,
- fallback metrics when detailed topology counters are unavailable.

## Required Verification and Logging
- Harness-level tests that verify remote-placement resolution, case selection, and artifact emission are stable.
- A named operator entrypoint such as `scripts/verify_g8_2_remote_interference.sh` that runs the remote cases and emits replayable artifacts.
- Structured logs and artifact fields including at minimum `trace_id`, `scenario_id`, `placement_profile`, `primitive_class`, `local_owner_cpu`, `remote_actor_cpu`, `numa_pair`, `llc_or_ccd_pair`, `remote_access_metric`, `ownership_events`, `wakeups`, `migrations`, `throughput`, `p50_ns`, `p95_ns`, `p99_ns`, `fairness_score`, `fallback_metric_used`, and first-failure diagnostics.
- Explicit negative expectations for remote-ownership thrash, remote-wakeup inflation, unfairness, and silent metric downgrade.

## Acceptance Criteria
- The suite covers cross-node, cross-CCD, and remote-ownership cases where the host exposes them, with explicit fallback cases when it does not.
- Cases capture remote-access, migration, ownership, wakeup, latency, and fairness evidence rich enough to diagnose remote-topology pathologies mechanically.
- Artifact layout and logging are stable enough for before/after comparison across reruns.
- The result is directly consumable by G8.3, E6, D1, and final reporting beads.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The microbench suite includes cross-node, cross-CCD, and remote-ownership cases where the host exposes them, plus explicit fallback metrics when topology detail is unavailable.
2. `scripts/verify_g8_2_remote_interference.sh` or an equivalent named entrypoint is part of the plan and emits replayable artifacts.
3. Structured logs expose placement profile, primitive class, local/remote actor identity, node/domain relationship, remote-access metrics, wakeups, migrations, latency buckets, fairness, ownership events, fallback metric usage, and first-failure diagnostics.
4. Negative-path expectations for remote-ownership thrash, remote-wakeup inflation, unfairness, and silent metric downgrade are explicit.
5. The suite is packaged so remote-topology regressions can be rerun and compared mechanically, not just eyeballed.
notes:
Interference-suite intent:
- this bead should make remote-node and remote-cache pathologies obvious before they get hidden inside larger benchmark summaries
- keep fallback metrics explicit so one-node or topology-limited hosts still produce honest evidence instead of fake precision

User-facing intent:
- operators should be able to tell whether a performance win depends on locality assumptions that their machine cannot satisfy

title: G8.3: map interference results back into primitive-selection decisions
description:
## Goal
Map interference results back into primitive-selection, placement, and verification decisions so topology evidence can actually change the plan instead of becoming benchmark trivia.

## Why This Matters
The value of G8 is not the benchmark itself; it is the decision leverage. This bead converts interference evidence into kept/tuned/rejected choices, updated budgets, and new tracked work when the evidence is bad.

## Scope
For each measured primitive or tuning candidate, record:
- the relevant interference artifacts and placement profiles,
- whether the candidate is kept as-is, tuned, budget-limited, safe-mode-only, or rejected,
- which design or implementation beads are affected,
- whether a new follow-on bead or dependency change is required,
- what user-visible risk remains if the candidate is retained.

The mapping must feed back into at least:
- E2 fused-entry decisions,
- E3 metadata primitive selection,
- E6 placement and budget policy,
- D1 parallel WAL verification and matrix interpretation,
- final scorecard and next-bottleneck recommendations.

## Required Verification and Logging
- Table-driven validation that the mapping consumes the expected artifact bundles and does not silently omit measured candidates.
- A named operator entrypoint such as `scripts/verify_g8_3_interference_mapping.sh` that renders the decision map from representative artifact packs and reports missing mappings.
- Structured logs exposing at minimum `trace_id`, `scenario_id`, `primitive_class`, `placement_profile`, `interference_artifact_key`, `decision_target_bead`, `decision_outcome`, `threshold_breached`, `next_action`, and first-failure diagnostics.
- Explicit gap-conversion rules for any primitive or tuning candidate that lacks a mapped decision.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Every measured primitive or tuning candidate is mapped to a concrete decision outcome with rationale.
- Rejected or downgraded candidates remain visible so future agents do not repeat dead ends.
- Missing mappings or bad interference evidence become tracked work rather than quiet debt.
- The output is reusable by verification, design, and final-reporting beads without reinterpretation.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The bead maps every measured primitive or tuning candidate to a concrete decision outcome such as keep, tune, budget-limit, safe-mode-only, reject, or new-bead-required.
2. `scripts/verify_g8_3_interference_mapping.sh` or an equivalent named validation entrypoint is part of the plan and emits replayable artifacts proving mapping completeness.
3. Structured logs expose primitive class, placement profile, interference artifact linkage, decision target bead, decision outcome, threshold breach, next action, and first-failure diagnostics.
4. Missing mappings or bad enough evidence are converted into explicit tracked work rather than being buried in notes.
5. The result is directly consumable by E2, E3, E6, D1, G4, and other verification/reporting beads without reopening the debate.
notes:
Decision-mapping intent:
- the point of interference evidence is to change design and verification choices, not merely to produce impressive charts
- if a primitive looks clever but causes ugly locality behavior, this bead should make that rejection durable and operator-visible

User-facing intent:
- future operators should be able to see which locality assumptions are required for a claimed win and which mitigations exist when those assumptions do not hold

title: G8.4: prove controller-composition safety and timescale separation across performance policies
description:
## Goal
Prove controller-composition safety and timescale separation across the performance-program decision plane so multiple clever policies do not create oscillation, hidden coupling, or fallback storms.

## Why This Matters
The plan now has several controller-bearing seams: admission/tail guardrails, optional adaptive WAL policy, and adaptive placement/spillover policy. If these share telemetry or act on the same bottleneck at the same timescale, they can create positive feedback loops and misleading benchmark wins that collapse in production.

## Scope
Build the composition contract and proof surface for at least:
- E4 admission/tail controller,
- D1 adaptive WAL policy if present,
- E6 placement/spillover policy if present,
- any later cache or routing controller that shares signals or budget authority.

For each controller pair or triple, define:
- shared signals and authority boundaries,
- activation-regime overlap and whether the controllers are ever allowed to co-own the same regime,
- fast/slow timescale assignment,
- fallback precedence, kill-switch precedence, and budget inheritance,
- forbidden feedback loops or oscillation patterns,
- replay and microbench scenarios that can expose interference,
- the gate for rejecting a composition even if each controller looks fine in isolation.

## Required Verification and Logging
- A named validation entrypoint such as `scripts/verify_g8_4_controller_composition.sh` that runs representative composition scenarios and emits replayable artifacts.
- Interference microbench and replay cases for oscillation, fairness collapse, queue inflation, retry storms, fallback thrash, regime-overlap instability, and shadow-run divergence.
- At least one anytime-valid or sequential test gate over the replay corpus when controller interaction is statistically assessed across repeated windows.
- Structured logs exposing at minimum `trace_id`, `scenario_id`, `controller_a`, `controller_b`, `shared_signal`, `activation_regime_overlap`, `timescale_fast_ms`, `timescale_slow_ms`, `fallback_precedence`, `kill_switch_precedence`, `oscillation_metric`, `fairness_score`, `shadow_divergence`, `rejected_composition_reason`, and first-failure diagnostics.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Every controller composition in scope has an explicit timescale-separation, regime-overlap, and fallback-precedence statement.
- Interference evidence is strong enough to veto a composition that looks attractive in isolation.
- The result feeds G8.3 and G4 directly rather than leaving composition safety as a narrative warning.
- The bead is self-contained enough that future adaptive work cannot quietly skip controller-composition proof.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The bead defines a composition matrix covering shared signals, activation-regime overlap, authority boundaries, fast/slow timescales, fallback and kill-switch precedence, and rejection conditions for the relevant controller combinations.
2. `scripts/verify_g8_4_controller_composition.sh` or an equivalent named validation entrypoint is part of the plan and emits replayable artifacts proving composition coverage.
3. Structured logs expose controller pairing, shared signals, activation-regime overlap, timescale assignments, fallback/kill-switch precedence, oscillation/fairness metrics, shadow divergence, rejected-composition reason, and first-failure diagnostics.
4. Interference microbench and replay evidence are mandatory before composing controller-bearing beads in production-facing paths.
5. The output is strong enough that G8.3 and G4 can consume it mechanically and reject unsafe controller combinations.

comments.text:
# Controller-Composition Safety Proof — bd-db300.7.8.4

> Regime overlap rules, kill-switch precedence, timescale separation,
> forbidden feedback loops, and operator safety semantics for the
> performance-program decision plane.

---

## 0. Controllers In Scope

| ID | Controller | Owner bead | Signal domain | Action domain | Timescale |
|----|-----------|-----------|---------------|---------------|-----------|
| C1 | **Admission / Tail Guardrail** | bd-db300.5.4.3 (E4.3) | queue depth, wake-to-run, p95/p99 latency, retry rate, fallback rate | admit / defer / backpressure / shrink_helper_budget / force_safe_mode | **Fast**: 1-10ms decision window |
| C2 | **Adaptive WAL Policy** | D1 track | WAL frame count, sync latency, flush coalesce ratio, checkpoint pressure | per-commit-sync / batched-sync / deferred-sync / force-checkpoint | **Slow**: 100ms-1s observation window |
| C3 | **Placement / Spillover** | E6 track | LLC miss rate, remote-ownership fraction, cross-CCD wakeup rate, helper-lane utilization | pin-local / spill-to-remote / expand-helper-budget / shrink-helper-budget | **Slow**: 500ms-5s observation window |
| C4 | **SSI Abort Policy (DRO)** | bd-3t52f | abort rate, conflict topology, skew estimate, expected loss | standard-SSI / relaxed-SI / aggressive-retry / force-serializable | **Fast**: per-txn decision, 10ms EWMA |
| C5 | **HTM Guard** | bd-77l3t | abort rate (EWMA), CPU probe | available / disabled / user_disabled | **Slow**: 5s cooldown, only in flat combiner |

---

## 1. Regime Axis Definitions

Per G5.5 (regime atlas), the canonical axes are:

| Axis | Values | How measured |
|------|--------|-------------|
| **Concurrency** | c1, c2, c4, c8, c16+ | active writer count |
| **Contention geometry** | disjoint, moderate-overlap, hot-page | conflict-rate / abort-rate |
| **Read/write mix** | write-heavy, mixed, read-heavy | write-fraction over 1s window |
| **Transaction shape** | point (1-2 pages), medium (3-20), scan (20+) | avg pages-per-txn |

A **regime cell** is a 4-tuple. Controllers declare which cells they are **active** in.

---

## 2. Pairwise Composition Analysis

### 2.1 C1 × C2: Admission ↔ WAL Policy

**Shared signals:** flush latency (C1 reads it as tail evidence; C2 controls it).

**Conflict risk: HIGH.**
If C1 observes high p99 and applies backpressure while C2 simultaneously
switches from per-commit-sync to batched-sync (reducing flush frequency),
C1's backpressure starves the batch — fewer commits arrive, so the batch
never fills, sync latency stays high, C1 keeps applying backpressure.
**This is a positive feedback loop → starvation.**

**Timescale separation:** C1 is fast (1-10ms), C2 is slow (100ms-1s). ✓ Separated.
But C1's `shrink_helper_budget` action can change flush throughput within C2's
observation window, causing C2 to observe a transient it didn't cause.

**Composition rules:**
1. **C2 MUST NOT change sync policy while C1 is in `force_safe_mode`.** Safe-mode
   implies the system is already degraded; WAL policy changes add unpredictable
   latency transients. C1's kill-switch takes precedence.
2. **C1 MUST NOT use flush-latency as a direct signal when C2 is mid-transition.**
   Implementation: C2 publishes a `wal_policy_transition_epoch` counter. C1
   discounts flush-latency samples whose epoch differs from the previous sample.
3. **Forbidden combination:** C1=`backpressure` + C2=`batched-sync`. If C2 selects
   batched-sync, C1 must treat it as an implicit capacity expansion and raise its
   admit threshold proportionally to the expected batch size.

**Kill-switch precedence:** C1 > C2. Admission is the outer safety boundary.

### 2.2 C1 × C3: Admission ↔ Placement

**Shared signals:** wake-to-run latency (C1 reads it; C3 controls it via placement).

**Conflict risk: MEDIUM.**
If C3 spills work to a remote NUMA node (increasing wake-to-run), C1 may
interpret the higher latency as overload and apply backpressure. This is
a false positive — the system has MORE capacity, not less.

**Timescale separation:** C1 fast (1-10ms), C3 slow (500ms-5s). ✓ Separated.

**Composition rules:**
1. **C1 MUST distinguish local-wake-to-run from remote-wake-to-run.** If C3 is
   actively spilling, C1's wake-to-run evidence must be partitioned by locality.
   Remote wake-to-run above baseline is expected, not pathological.
2. **C3 MUST NOT expand helper budget while C1 is in `shrink_helper_budget` state.**
   These are contradictory actions on the same resource. C1 precedence wins.
3. **Forbidden combination:** C1=`force_safe_mode` + C3=`spill-to-remote`. Safe-mode
   means retreat to conservative baseline; remote spillover adds latency variance.

**Kill-switch precedence:** C1 > C3.

### 2.3 C1 × C4: Admission ↔ SSI Abort Policy

**Shared signals:** abort rate, retry rate.

**Conflict risk: MEDIUM.**
C4 may relax isolation (SI instead of SSI) to reduce aborts. C1 sees abort-rate
drop and admits more work. But the relaxation hides write-skew anomalies that
accumulate silently. This is not a feedback loop but a **correctness erosion path**.

**Timescale separation:** Both fast (per-txn). ⚠ NOT separated.

**Composition rules:**
1. **C4 MUST NOT relax isolation based on C1's admission state.** The isolation
   level is a correctness property, not a throughput knob. C4 decisions are
   independent of load.
2. **C1 MUST treat abort-rate as an input, not a control target.** C1 cannot
   instruct C4 to reduce aborts — that would be using correctness as throughput.
3. **C1 MAY use abort-rate as evidence for `defer` or `backpressure`,** since high
   aborts under contention indicate the system is above optimal concurrency.
4. **Forbidden combination:** C4=`relaxed-SI` + C1 using abort-rate as admission
   signal. If C4 is in relaxed mode, C1's abort-rate evidence is unreliable
   (artificially low) and must be discounted.

**Kill-switch precedence:** C4 correctness > C1 throughput. If C4 detects write-skew
risk and forces serializable, C1 must accept the resulting abort-rate increase.

### 2.4 C2 × C3: WAL Policy ↔ Placement

**Shared signals:** I/O bandwidth (both compete for it).

**Conflict risk: LOW.**
C2 controls sync frequency; C3 controls where computation runs. They share
I/O bandwidth indirectly but their action spaces don't directly conflict.

**Timescale separation:** Both slow (100ms-5s). ⚠ Overlapping.

**Composition rules:**
1. **C2 and C3 MUST NOT both adjust simultaneously.** One must be the "fast slow"
   (100ms) and the other the "slow slow" (1s+). Assign: C2=100ms, C3=1s.
2. **C3 placement decisions MUST account for C2's current sync mode.** If C2 is
   in per-commit-sync, I/O is already the bottleneck; C3 should avoid remote
   placement that adds I/O latency.

**Kill-switch precedence:** C2 > C3. WAL durability overrides placement optimization.

### 2.5 C2 × C4: WAL Policy ↔ SSI Abort Policy

**Shared signals:** None directly.

**Conflict risk: LOW.**
C2 affects commit latency; C4 affects commit success rate. Independent axes.

**Composition rules:**
1. No special rules needed. These controllers operate on orthogonal concerns.

**Kill-switch precedence:** C4 (correctness) > C2 (performance).

### 2.6 C3 × C4: Placement ↔ SSI Abort Policy

**Shared signals:** None directly.

**Conflict risk: LOW.**
C3 affects where work runs; C4 affects whether work succeeds.

**Composition rules:**
1. No special rules needed.

**Kill-switch precedence:** C4 (correctness) > C3 (performance).

### 2.7 C5 (HTM) interactions

C5 is narrowly scoped to the flat combiner fast-path. Its only action is
to attempt or not-attempt HTM before the combiner lock.

**Conflict with C1:** None. C5 doesn't affect admission.
**Conflict with C2:** None. C5 doesn't affect WAL.
**Conflict with C3:** LOW. If C3 places combiner threads across NUMA nodes,
HTM abort rate may spike (cache-line conflicts). C5's dynamic disable
handles this automatically. No composition rule needed beyond C5's existing
EWMA monitor.
**Conflict with C4:** None. C5 operates below the transaction level.

C5 is **composition-safe by construction** — it has no authority over shared
resources and its failure mode (fall through to lock) is the current baseline.

---

## 3. Kill-Switch Precedence Order

```
  HIGHEST PRECEDENCE
  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
  │ C4: SSI Abort Policy            │ ← correctness
  │    (write-skew prevention)      │
  ├─────────────────────────────────┤
  │ C1: Admission / Tail Guardrail  │ ← user-visible SLO
  │    (queue/latency/retry safety) │
  ├─────────────────────────────────┤
  │ C2: WAL Policy                  │ ← durability
  │    (sync mode/checkpoint)       │
  ├─────────────────────────────────┤
  │ C3: Placement / Spillover       │ ← throughput
  │    (NUMA/LLC/helper lanes)      │
  ├─────────────────────────────────┤
  │ C5: HTM Guard                   │ ← micro-optimization
  │    (combiner fast-path)         │
  └─────────────────────────────────┘
  LOWEST PRECEDENCE
```

**Semantics:** When a higher-precedence controller's kill-switch trips, all
lower-precedence controllers MUST:
1. Freeze their current state (no new transitions).
2. Revert to their conservative baseline within one observation window.
3. Remain frozen until the higher-precedence controller signals `disarmed`.

**Implementation:** Each controller publishes a `kill_switch_state: {disarmed, armed, tripped}`
in the shared policy snapshot (per G6.4). Before any transition, a controller
checks all higher-precedence kill-switches. If any is `tripped`, the transition
is rejected.

---

## 4. Timescale Separation Matrix

| Controller | Decision period | Observation window | Mandatory gap to next-faster |
|-----------|----------------|-------------------|------------------------------|
| C4 (SSI) | per-txn (~μs) | 10ms EWMA | — (fastest) |
| C1 (Admission) | 1-10ms | 10-50ms sliding | ≥10× faster than C2 |
| C5 (HTM) | per-apply (~ns) | 5s EWMA | — (self-contained) |
| C2 (WAL) | 100ms | 100ms-1s | ≥5× faster than C3 |
| C3 (Placement) | 1s | 1-5s | — (slowest) |

**Rule:** Two controllers that share a signal MUST have decision periods separated
by at least **5×**. If this cannot be guaranteed, the faster controller must
discount samples that overlap with the slower controller's transition window.

**Violation detector:** The shared policy snapshot includes each controller's
`last_transition_epoch`. At decision time, if a peer controller's
`last_transition_epoch` is within the current observation window, the sample
is marked `tainted` and excluded from the evidence vector.

---

## 5. Forbidden Feedback Loops

| # | Loop | Controllers | Mechanism | Why dangerous |
|---|------|------------|-----------|---------------|
| F1 | Starvation spiral | C1 + C2 | C1 backpressure → C2 batch underfill → latency stays high → C1 keeps backpressure | Queue drains to zero, throughput collapses |
| F2 | False-overload retreat | C1 + C3 | C3 spills remote → C1 sees high wake-to-run → C1 backpressure → C3 has less work → C3 retracts spillover → C1 admits → C3 spills again | Oscillation between expand and retreat |
| F3 | Correctness erosion | C1 + C4 | C4 relaxes to SI → aborts drop → C1 admits more → higher conflict → C4 sees write-skew → C4 re-tightens → aborts spike → C1 sheds → cycle | Violation of isolation guarantees during the relaxed window |
| F4 | Dual adjustment chaos | C2 + C3 | Both adjust at same timescale → C2 changes I/O pattern → C3 misattributes → C3 re-places → C2 re-observes | Neither converges; both chase each other's transients |

**Prevention rules:**

- **F1:** C2 MUST NOT enter batched-sync while C1.state ∈ {backpressure, force_safe_mode}.
- **F2:** C1 MUST partition wake-to-run by locality when C3.state = spill-to-remote.
- **F3:** C4 isolation level changes are NEVER influenced by C1 state. C4 is autonomous.
- **F4:** C2 and C3 have 10× timescale separation. C3 freezes during C2 transitions.

---

## 6. Activation-Regime Overlap

Each controller declares which regime cells it is allowed to be active in.
Overlap means two controllers may both be making decisions for the same workload.

| Regime cell | C1 | C2 | C3 | C4 | C5 | Overlap risk |
|------------|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| c1/disjoint/write-heavy/point | active | active | dormant | active | dormant | C1×C2×C4: 3-way. C4 independent. C1×C2 per §2.1 |
| c4/moderate/mixed/medium | active | active | active | active | active | ALL ACTIVE. Highest interference risk. |
| c8/hot-page/write-heavy/point | active | active | active | active | active | ALL ACTIVE. Same. |
| c1/disjoint/read-heavy/scan | dormant | dormant | dormant | dormant | dormant | No controllers active. Baseline. |
| c16+/disjoint/write-heavy/point | active | active | active | active | dormant | 4-way. C5 auto-disabled (high contention). |

**Rule:** In any cell where ≥3 controllers are active, the composition
must be validated via shadow-oracle (per G5.6) before becoming a default.
A divergence from the conservative oracle in any active-3+ cell triggers
the outer kill-switch (C1 force_safe_mode).

---

## 7. Unsafe Compositions — Rejection Table

These combinations MUST be statically rejected by the policy engine.
They cannot be enabled even by operator override.

| # | Composition | Why rejected |
|---|------------|-------------|
| R1 | C4=relaxed-SI + C1 using abort-rate | Abort-rate is unreliable under relaxed isolation; C1 would over-admit |
| R2 | C1=force_safe_mode + C3=spill-to-remote | Safe-mode means minimize variance; remote spillover adds variance |
| R3 | C1=backpressure + C2=batched-sync | Starvation spiral (F1) |
| R4 | C1=shrink_helper_budget + C3=expand-helper-budget | Contradictory actions on the same resource |
| R5 | C2 transition + C3 transition (within same window) | Dual-adjustment chaos (F4) |
| R6 | Any controller transition while higher-precedence kill-switch = tripped | Frozen-state invariant violation |

**Enforcement:** The shared policy snapshot includes a `validate_composition()`
function that checks these rules before any controller commits a transition.
Rejected transitions are logged with `rejected_composition_reason` and the
transition is rolled back to the previous state.

---

## 8. Replay and Interference Scenarios

Each scenario is designed to expose a specific composition failure.

| Scenario | Controllers exercised | What it tests | Pass condition |
|----------|----------------------|---------------|----------------|
| S1: Starvation probe | C1 + C2 | F1 starvation spiral | Throughput > 0 within 500ms of backpressure onset |
| S2: False-overload probe | C1 + C3 | F2 oscillation | ≤2 C3 state transitions per C1 observation window |
| S3: Correctness erosion | C1 + C4 | F3 isolation violation | Zero write-skew anomalies under any C1 state |
| S4: Dual-adjustment | C2 + C3 | F4 convergence failure | Both controllers converge within 5 observation windows |
| S5: Kill-switch cascade | C4→C1→C2→C3 | Precedence chain | All lower controllers frozen within 1 window of C4 trip |
| S6: All-active regime | C1+C2+C3+C4+C5 | c4/moderate/mixed/medium | Shadow-oracle divergence < 1% on 1000-txn workload |
| S7: Regime transition | All | Workload shifts c1→c8 mid-run | No controller oscillation during 1s transition window |
| S8: HTM abort storm | C5 + C3 | C3 remote placement triggers HTM aborts | C5 dynamic-disable within 100ms, no throughput regression vs baseline |

**Artifact:** Each scenario produces a structured log line with fields:
`trace_id, scenario_id, controller_a, controller_b, shared_signal,
activation_regime_overlap, timescale_fast_ms, timescale_slow_ms,
fallback_precedence, kill_switch_precedence, oscillation_metric,
fairness_score, shadow_divergence, rejected_composition_reason`.

---

## 9. Operator Safety Semantics

### 9.1 Default behavior (zero-config)

All controllers start in their **conservative baseline**:
- C1: admit all (no guardrails active until load > threshold)
- C2: per-commit-sync (SQLite-compatible default)
- C3: OS-default placement (no pinning)
- C4: standard SSI (full serializable)
- C5: UNAVAILABLE (Phase 1; no HTM)

No controller activates its adaptive mode without explicit evidence that
the regime benefits from it. The regime atlas (G5.5) defines the activation
frontier: which cells have enough evidence for which controller to activate.

### 9.2 Operator overrides

| PRAGMA | Controller | Effect | Precedence |
|--------|-----------|--------|-----------|
| `fsqlite_admission_mode = {auto, off, force_safe}` | C1 | Manual control | Overrides C1 adaptive; other controllers still respect C1 precedence |
| `fsqlite_wal_sync_policy = {auto, per_commit, batched}` | C2 | Manual WAL mode | Overrides C2 adaptive; checked against C1 kill-switch |
| `fsqlite_placement_mode = {auto, local_only, allow_remote}` | C3 | Manual placement | Overrides C3 adaptive |
| `fsqlite.serializable = {ON, OFF}` | C4 | Isolation level | C4 autonomous; C1 adjusts |
| `fsqlite_disable_htm = {ON, OFF}` | C5 | HTM guard | C5 autonomous |

**Rule:** Manual overrides bypass the adaptive logic but NOT the composition
rejection table. Setting C2=batched + C1=force_safe still triggers R3 rejection.
The operator sees a warning log and the rejected override is not applied.

### 9.3 Degraded-mode contract

When C1 enters `force_safe_mode`:
1. C2 reverts to per-commit-sync.
2. C3 reverts to local-only.
3. C5 reverts to disabled.
4. C4 remains autonomous (correctness is not degraded by safe-mode).
5. All transitions are logged with `control_mode=degraded`.
6. Exit from safe-mode requires C1's evidence vector to be below threshold
   for 3 consecutive observation windows (hysteresis).

---

## 10. Proof Summary

### Theorem 1: No forbidden feedback loop can persist

**Proof:** Each forbidden loop (F1-F4) has a static prevention rule that
blocks the necessary precondition. F1 is blocked because C2 cannot enter
batched-sync while C1 is in backpressure. F2 is blocked because C1
partitions wake-to-run by locality. F3 is blocked because C4 is autonomous
from C1. F4 is blocked by 10× timescale separation. ∎

### Theorem 2: Kill-switch cascade terminates in bounded time

**Proof:** There are 5 controllers in a strict total order. When the
highest active kill-switch trips, each lower controller freezes within
one observation window. The maximum cascade time is the sum of observation
windows: 10ms + 100ms + 1s + 5s ≈ 6.1s. No circular dependency exists
because the precedence order is acyclic. ∎

### Theorem 3: Composition validation is decidable and O(1)

**Proof:** The rejection table has 6 static rules. Each rule checks at most
2 controller states (current + proposed). The `validate_composition()`
function iterates the 6 rules and returns accept/reject. No dynamic
analysis or convergence check is required at decision time. ∎

### Theorem 4: Conservative baseline is always reachable

**Proof:** Every controller has a defined conservative baseline state.
The degraded-mode contract (§9.3) specifies the revert sequence.
Reverting is a single atomic state change per controller (no multi-step
protocol). The kill-switch cascade (Theorem 2) guarantees all controllers
reach their baseline within 6.1s of the highest kill-switch trip. ∎

### Theorem 5: Shadow-oracle divergence gates activation

**Proof:** Per §6, any regime cell with ≥3 active controllers requires
shadow-oracle validation before becoming a default. A divergence > 1%
triggers C1's kill-switch, which cascades to freeze all lower controllers
(Theorem 2) and revert to baselines (Theorem 4). The system cannot
persist in an unvalidated composition. ∎

---

## 11. Assumptions Ledger

| # | Assumption | If violated | Mitigation |
|---|-----------|------------|------------|
| A1 | Timescale separation holds at runtime | Controllers chase each other's transients | Tainted-sample detector (§4) discards overlapping observations |
| A2 | Kill-switch state is published atomically | Lower controllers read stale state | Use seqlock or atomic snapshot for policy struct |
| A3 | C4 is truly autonomous | C4 relaxation creates correctness risk | C4 never reads C1/C2/C3 state; enforced by API design |
| A4 | Observer overhead is negligible | Telemetry itself creates load | Budget telemetry at ≤1% of decision-period duration |
| A5 | Regime cell classification is stable within observation window | Controller acts on wrong regime | Require ≥3 consecutive consistent classifications before activation |
| A6 | Conservative baseline is correct | Baseline itself has bugs | Tested independently via existing conformance suite |

title: G9: enforce honest healthy-gain gates and causal scorecards for the 2026-03-23 overlay
description:
## Goal
Turn the 2026-03-23 overlay into an honest pass/fail framework that matches the actual standard being demanded: the critical benchmark cells should exceed SQLite by a healthy margin, and the project is not allowed to claim success by hiding a red cell behind an aggregate, a skewed fixture, or a stale placeholder gate.

Why this bead exists now:
- The latest matrix has catastrophic c1 cells and a catastrophic persistent 16-thread cell, so those must be explicit scorecard items.
- At least one aggregate was visibly distorted by a single fixture outlier, which proves the reporting rules need to get stricter.
- Older contention gates and placeholder assumptions are now out of sync with the real harnesses and current evidence.

This bead defines the anti-self-deception layer for the overlay: critical-cell visibility, no-fake-win rules, causal attribution expectations, and the final closeout record.

comments.author: codex
comments.text:
## Intent of G9

`G9` is the honesty-and-governance lane for this overlay. The technical work alone is not enough if the scorecard can still hide red regimes or let stale assumptions drive prioritization.

This lane exists because the current evidence already shows how easy it is to misread progress:
- a strong `c8` MVCC result can distract from the fact that `c1` remains disastrously slow,
- an aggregate geomean can obscure the persistent `16t` collapse,
- a single fixture outlier can distort a workload-level story,
- older contention gates can remain in the graph long after the actual harnesses and failure modes changed.

## What this lane must protect against

The project must stop awarding itself fake wins. That means the governance surface has to encode:
- explicit no-fake-win rules for outliers, skew, and aggregates,
- causal attribution packs so changes get credit only for the deltas they actually caused,
- updated regression gates that keep `c1` and persistent `16t` visible,
- reconciliation work so placeholder or outdated contention assumptions stop steering real engineering effort.

This lane is also the place where the project’s larger claims get disciplined. The project wants to be faster than SQLite, 100% correct, and a strong drop-in replacement. Those claims only remain credible if the benchmark and artifact surface makes it difficult to tell comforting stories from weak evidence.

## Reading the child beads

- `G9.1` updates the gates.
- `G9.2` defines how to read the matrix honestly.
- `G9.3` requires per-fix causal attribution.
- `G9.4` reconciles old contention assumptions with the real 2026-03-23 picture.
- `G9.5` publishes the final overlay scorecard and closeout record.

comments.author: codex
comments.text:
## Addendum: executable gate surface

The governance lane now explicitly treats the reproducible script surfaces as part of the gate definition, not just part of later verification. That is intentional. A canonical gate that cannot be run through stable entrypoints with stable logs is weaker than it looks and harder for future users to trust.

The gate surface must follow the corrected frontier: new c1 closed-ledger evidence and new persistent end-to-end evidence are mandatory prerequisites.

This bead is now explicitly downstream of `D5.9` and `C8.12`. The intent is that updated canonical gates must be wired to one-command repro entrypoints and detailed logging for the low-tax and persistent commit-collapse stories. Future agents should not satisfy this bead with a prose threshold table alone.

comments.author: codex
comments.text:
## Addendum: healthy-margin victory semantics

This bead should encode the user's real success condition, not a weak pass condition. The canonical gates should make it explicit that important benchmark cells are expected to exceed SQLite by a healthy margin, not merely flirt with parity or hide behind aggregate improvement.

At minimum the gate design here should:
- hard-fail when any critical c1 or persistent high-thread cell remains at or below `1.0x`,
- distinguish “barely above parity” from “healthy margin” so a lucky `1.01x` does not read as mission accomplished,
- keep both MVCC and forced single-writer visible where they matter for diagnosis,
- forbid an aggregate green result from masking a still-red regime that real users would feel.

title: G9.2: define no-fake-win rules for outliers, geomeans, medians, and fixture skew
description:
Define the honesty rules for reading the matrix: how to treat outliers, fixture skew, geomeans, medians, and single-cell wins that do not generalize.

This bead exists so the project stops talking itself into progress that the matrix does not actually support.
close_reason: Captured no-fake-win scorecard rules from frozen A7.4 contract and current c1/8t/16t evidence; ready for downstream gate wiring.

comments.author: codex
comments.text:
## Suggested acceptance shape

This bead should encode the anti-self-deception rules clearly enough that future reports cannot smuggle in fake wins through outliers, fixture skew, or cherry-picked aggregates. The rules should match how real users experience regressions, not just how a summary table looks.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## Draft no-fake-win scorecard rules from the frozen A7.4 contract and current c1 / 8t / 16t evidence

### Current evidence state these rules must encode
- **c1 remains red across the whole canonical matrix.** From `artifacts/perf/2026-03-23-local/canonical_mvcc.jsonl`, the 9 MVCC `c1` ratios vs `sqlite3` are all `< 1.0` with geomean `0.209`, median `0.165`, min `0.074`, max `0.771`. From `canonical_single_writer.jsonl`, the 9 single-writer `c1` ratios are also all `< 1.0` with geomean `0.208`, median `0.165`, min `0.073`, max `0.822`.
- The c1 pattern is **workload-shaped, not fixture-shaped**: commutative cells are all catastrophic (`~0.07-0.08x`), hot-page cells are all still deep red (`~0.15-0.17x`), and mixed-read-write is the least bad (`~0.74-0.82x`) but still red on every canonical fixture.
- **Persistent 8t is comparator-valid and still red.** In `artifacts/persistent_phase_pack_20260323_222108/8t/criterion_stdout.log`, Criterion reports median throughput `1.8473 Kelem/s` for `sqlite3` vs `1.2261 Kelem/s` for `fsqlite_mvcc`, so current 8t median ratio is about `0.664x`.
- **Persistent 16t is comparator-valid but only as a relative collapse win.** In `artifacts/persistent_phase_pack_20260323_222108/16t/criterion_stdout.log`, Criterion reports median throughput `47.285 elem/s` for `sqlite3` vs `77.993 elem/s` for `fsqlite_mvcc`, so current 16t median ratio is about `1.649x`. But the same log shows FrankenSQLite still running with `phase_b_p99` around `0.9-1.1s`, `wal_append_p99` around `0.8-1.0s`, and p95/p99 transaction latencies still in the collapse regime.
- The current `8t` and `16t` packs are **scorecard-valid under A7.4**: both lanes have `provenance.json`, `samples.jsonl`, and `criterion_stdout.log`; both lanes contain both engines; and the FrankenSQLite rows in `samples.jsonl` still carry non-null `phase_metrics` and `phase_timing_report`.
- The persistent `samples.jsonl` surface is **not enough by itself for throughput claims** in the current schema: its current `counter_name` surface is only `retries` / `conflicts`, so the throughput/tail story must still come from `criterion_stdout.log` plus provenance.

### No-fake-win rules
1. **Critical cells first, aggregates second.** Every scorecard must show the canonical c1 red-cell surface and the persistent `8t` + `16t` cells before any geomean, median, or rolled summary.
2. **A geomean or median may summarize, never absolve.** Any aggregate must be printed beside: `red_count/total`, `worst_cell_ratio`, and the identities of the worst c1 cell and worst persistent lane. If any critical cell is red, the aggregate cannot be used as a green headline.
3. **Single-cell wins are outliers, not program wins.** A result that improves only one fixture/workload cell may be called a `cell win` only. It must not be generalized to the whole matrix.
4. **Single-workload wins are still not c1 wins.** Because current c1 behavior clusters by workload across all three fixtures, a change that helps one workload family across fixtures may be called a `workload win`, but not a `c1 win` or `matrix win` unless the other workload families are explicitly shown and remain non-red.
5. **Fixture skew must be named, not averaged away.** If one fixture is notably better or worse than its sibling fixtures, the report must call that out explicitly and may not let per-fixture medians or geomeans hide it. Current evidence does **not** justify a fixture-skew story for c1; it is predominantly a workload-regime problem.
6. **Persistent 16t cannot hide persistent 8t.** Any 16t headline must print the 8t comparator result adjacent to it. A `16t > 1.0x` ratio is not a healthy program-level win while 8t remains red.
7. **Relative collapse wins must be labeled honestly.** When FrankenSQLite beats SQLite only because SQLite collapses harder, the label must be `relative comparator win under collapse`, not `healthy`, `fixed`, or `production-ready`. The current 16t evidence belongs in this category.
8. **Absolute throughput and tails are mandatory beside 16t ratios.** For the 16t lane, the scorecard must show absolute median throughput and the dominant tail evidence (`p95/p99`, plus preserved phase evidence for FrankenSQLite) next to the ratio. Ratio-only presentation is invalid.
9. **Causal claims require the causal surface.** The canonical c1 JSONL exports are enough for throughput scorekeeping, but not enough for causal attribution. Any explanation of *why* c1 moved must cite the matching hot-profile bundle or persistent phase/wake evidence, not just matrix aggregates.
10. **Same-pack comparator discipline stays mandatory.** Persistent comparative claims must come from the same pack and the current A7.4-required provenance/log surface. Supporting dated local logs may provide context, but they cannot replace the 8t/16t same-pack comparator of record.

### Suggested scorecard labels
- `matrix win`: all critical c1 cells required by the gate are green, persistent 8t is non-red, and 16t is not merely a collapse-relative win.
- `workload win`: one workload family improves across canonical fixtures, but the full c1 matrix is still red.
- `cell win`: one or a few isolated cells improve.
- `aggregate-only improvement`: geomean/median moves while critical red cells remain materially unresolved.
- `relative collapse win`: comparator ratio > 1.0 in a regime where absolute throughput/tails are still collapse-grade.

### Read-only evidence commands used
```bash
br show bd-db300.7.9.2 --json
br show bd-db300.1.7.4 --json
python3 - <<PY
# c1 ratio extraction from canonical_mvcc.jsonl / canonical_single_writer.jsonl
PY
python3 - <<PY
# persistent pack engine/counter inventory and phase-field presence
PY
rg -n "\\[C SQLite|\\[FrankenSQLite|Benchmarking persistent_concurrent_write_|time:|thrpt:" \
  artifacts/persistent_phase_pack_20260323_222108/8t/criterion_stdout.log \
  artifacts/persistent_phase_pack_20260323_222108/16t/criterion_stdout.log
```

title: G9.3: require per-fix causal attribution packs linking code changes to counter and phase deltas
description: Require each meaningful performance fix to carry a causal attribution pack that links the code change to the measured counter and benchmark deltas. Under the corrected frontier this means pairing the low-concurrency fixed-tax fix with its c1 closed-ledger rerun and pairing the persistent-gap fix with its 8t/16t end-to-end rerun so we do not confuse improved subphase metrics with real throughput wins.
acceptance_criteria:
Acceptance Criteria:
- The output cites the concrete benchmark artifacts, code surfaces, and failure modes that justify the decision.
- Candidate designs or gate changes include rejected alternatives and rollback constraints.
- The resulting recommendation is machine-checkable through an updated gate, scorecard, manifest, or decision record.
- Follow-up implementation beads are linked or explicitly ruled out so future agents do not reopen stale assumptions.

comments.author: codex
comments.text:
## Suggested acceptance shape

This bead should define the causal attribution pack schema in a way that aligns with the frozen provenance contract: what code change was made, what counters moved, what benchmark cells moved, what logs or artifacts support the claim, and what did not improve. It should be possible to audit a claimed win mechanically.

comments.author: codex
comments.text:
## Addendum: causal packs must include proof context

A causal attribution pack should not only say which counter moved. It should also link to the relevant verification or proof artifacts, identify the baseline comparator, record any cells or properties that did not improve, and make negative or mixed results explicit.

This is how the program avoids myth-making: every claimed win should carry enough evidence to answer both “why do we think this helped?” and “what did it not fix?”

comments.author: codex
comments.text:
Causal-pack contract tightened on the real evidence entrypoints.

What changed:
- `c1_scorecard.json` / `c1_pack_manifest.json` now carry a `causal_attribution_contract` requiring `code_change_ref`, `claim_summary`, `baseline_run_id`, `baseline_comparator`, `cells_expected_to_move`, `cells_expected_not_to_move`, and `negative_findings`.
- `persistent_scorecard.json` / `persistent_pack_manifest.json` now carry a matching causal-attribution contract for the persistent 8t/16t phase packs, plus explicit `baseline_comparator=sqlite3_same_pack` and `shadow_lineage=none` fields.
- Both pack families now expose comparator provenance as machine-readable contract data instead of leaving it implicit in prose.

Why this matters:
- A future fix claim now has an obvious place to declare what changed, what comparator it is against, what cells/counters were expected to move, and what did not improve.
- This makes the c1 and persistent packs usable as attribution-pack inputs instead of just raw result bundles.

Verification:
- `bash -n scripts/capture_c1_evidence_pack.sh scripts/capture_persistent_phase_pack.sh` -> pass
- `jq '.honest_gate_summary,.comparator_contract,.causal_attribution_contract' artifacts/bd-db300.4.5.7/bd-db300.4.5.7-c1-rerun/c1_scorecard.json` -> pass

- The contract is now present on the real capture surfaces, but there is still no separate “claim ledger” wrapper that binds a specific code diff to one of these packs. That is acceptable for now because the capture surfaces are the prerequisite truth source, but the final governance layer should add that join explicitly.

comments.text:
## G9.3 Causal Attribution Records

### Record 1: C.4 Persistent Gap Fix

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| code_change_ref | `984c5536` ("perf: eliminate redundant Mutex acquisition on concurrent commit path") |
| claim_summary | Eliminated redundant PagerInner Mutex acquisition in pending_conflict_pages() by introducing pending_conflict_pages_conservative() which returns write_pages_sorted without inner.lock(). Reduces Mutex acquisitions per concurrent commit from 3 to 2. |
| baseline_run_id | `persistent_phase_pack_c2_20260325_000003` |
| baseline_comparator | `sqlite3_same_pack` (C SQLite in same Criterion run) |
| candidate_run_id | `persistent_phase_pack_c4_20260325_004620` |
| cells_expected_to_move | 8t commit_center_avg (98→83us, -15%), 8t throughput (1.42→1.61 Kelem/s, +13.4%) |
| cells_expected_not_to_move | 16t (same structural bottleneck — concurrent_registry Mutex still dominates) |
| negative_findings | 16t throughput neutral-to-slightly-negative. Both 8t (0.74x) and 16t (0.75x) remain below parity. The commit_gap (connection-layer COMMIT wrapper) still dominates 97-99% of commit_roundtrip. Honest-gate verdict: FAIL. |

### Record 2: A.3 C1 Fixed-Tax Fix

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| code_change_ref | Uncommitted working-tree changes: `PreparedDmlEntryProof` struct + deferred-DML prebound publication threading in connection.rs. Closest committed ref: `606c3172` (bd-hjkbr.1 timing fix). |
| claim_summary | Introduced PreparedDmlEntryProof routing seam and threaded prebound publication through UPDATE/DELETE deferred-DML dispatch path, eliminating one redundant pager_publication_refresh per prepared UPDATE/DELETE on file-backed databases. Added closed c1 latency ledger instrumentation. |
| baseline_run_id | `bd-hjkbr.2-20260325T042141Z-459` |
| baseline_comparator | `sqlite3_same_pack` (C SQLite via rusqlite in same capture) |
| candidate_run_id | `bd-hjkbr.3-20260325T050156Z-459` |
| cells_expected_to_move | c1 prepared UPDATE/DELETE pager_publication_refreshes (2→1 per operation). c1 latency ledger residual (now closed, <0.1%). |
| cells_expected_not_to_move | c1 INSERT (already optimized in prior slice). Persistent 8t/16t (different code surface). |
| negative_findings | Honest-gate verdict: FAIL (18/18 comparable c1 cells below parity). The entry-proof fix eliminates one redundant refresh but does not close the fundamental c1 throughput gap to SQLite. The gap remains dominated by per-statement parse/compile/execute ceremony. |

### Fields that cannot be filled from existing artifacts

- **A.3 code_change_ref**: The PreparedDmlEntryProof + deferred-DML publication threading changes are in the working tree but not yet in a single committed ref. The closest is `606c3172` (hjkbr.1 timing) but the actual A.3 production fix spans uncommitted edits across multiple panes.

### Next concrete surface to edit (if approved)

1. `artifacts/persistent_phase_pack_c4_20260325_004620/persistent_scorecard.json` — populate the `causal_attribution_contract` fields with Record 1 values.
2. `artifacts/bd-hjkbr.3/bd-hjkbr.3-20260325T050156Z-459/c1_scorecard.json` — populate with Record 2 values (once code_change_ref is committed).
3. Optionally: a `scripts/verify_g9_3_causal_packs.sh` that runs the jq gate on both scorecards.

title: Track H: single-writer containment and honest comparison-mode cleanup
description:
## Goal
This track isolates and repairs the extra pain in forced single-writer mode without ever making it the product default. Single-writer mode is still important as a comparison path and fallback, but current c4/c8 numbers show that it is suffering from avoidable overhead on top of unavoidable serialization. Cleaning that up makes comparisons fairer and prevents shared fixes from accidentally helping only MVCC.

## Acceptance Criteria
- There is an evidence-backed explanation for why single-writer mode is still slow.
- Avoidable single-writer-only overhead is reduced.
- The final scorecard reports the mode honestly without confusing it for the project's main value proposition.
- This bead set explicitly includes comprehensive unit-test, end-to-end, and structured-logging obligations rather than treating verification as implied follow-up work.
design:
- Separate unavoidable serialization from self-inflicted waiting and duplicate work.
- Reuse the same hot-path optimizations wherever possible so improvements benefit both modes.
- Keep the purpose of the mode explicit: comparison/fallback, not the project's default operating model.
acceptance_criteria:
- There is an evidence-backed explanation for why single-writer mode is still slow.
- Avoidable single-writer-only overhead is reduced.
- The final scorecard reports the mode honestly without confusing it for the project's main value proposition.
- This bead set explicitly includes comprehensive unit-test, end-to-end, and structured-logging obligations rather than treating verification as implied follow-up work.
notes: Current corrected averages show the scale of the problem: c4 mixed_read_write SQLite 2769.5 vs MVCC 424.2 vs single-writer 130.9; c8 mixed_read_write SQLite 965.3 vs MVCC 620.1 vs single-writer 80.8. Some of this is inherent serialization, but not all of it.

comments.author: codex
comments.text: Single-writer mode exists to provide an honest reference path and fallback, not to redefine the product. The purpose of this track is to strip away avoidable overhead so comparisons against SQLite are real, while preserving the non-negotiable rule that concurrent-writer mode remains the default and the point of the project.

title: H2: remove single-writer-only wait amplification and duplicate serialized work
description:
## Goal
Remove single-writer-specific wait amplification and duplicated serialized work that makes the fallback or reference path far worse than unavoidable serialization alone would suggest. The target is not to make single-writer mode the star, but to stop it from distorting comparisons through topology-blind baton passing, generic waits, or duplicated work inside the serialized region.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. At least one avoidable single-writer-only source of waiting, wake amplification, or duplicate work is removed.
2. Hot-cell benchmarks show the mode improved on its own terms across the same placement profiles used in H1.
3. The cleanup does not change the project's MVCC-by-default behavior.
4. Targeted unit tests are added or refreshed for the exact invariants and regressions touched by this bead.
5. Where behavior crosses subsystem boundaries, canonical-matrix end-to-end validation with detailed structured logging is added or updated alongside the change.

title: Track I: revised structural convoy elimination with leases, leaf locality, and micro-publish
description:
## Goal
Eliminate the accidental shared surfaces that make logically disjoint concurrent inserts collapse.

## Background
The benchmark matrix and profiling work now support a stronger thesis than the earlier plan: FrankenSQLite should stop treating parent/internal/header/allocation state as ordinary long-lived transaction-owned pages. Shared structure must either disappear from the common path or shrink to tiny publish windows. The failed preclaim experiments matter because they falsified earlier-claim and longer-hold approaches.

## Scope
This track covers:
- the minimal truthing pass needed to stop guessing
- allocator and page-1/freelist decoupling via leases and deltas
- keeping concurrent inserts leaf-local longer
- version-gated parent micro-publish and local structural restart
- write-path tiering and restart-scope reduction
- explicit verification with targeted unit tests, e2e scripts, rich logging, and focused matrix reruns

## Guardrails
- never lengthen shared ownership without hard benchmark proof
- never regress to single-writer serialization
- preserve correctness and SQLite-file compatibility

## Acceptance Criteria
Success means:
- the track covers the full revised structural program from truthing through allocator decoupling, leaf-locality policy, micro-publish, hot-path tiering, and verification
- each child bead is self-contained enough that a future agent can implement it without reopening the original markdown plan
- the track explicitly includes unit tests, e2e checks, and structured logging obligations for every implementation phase
- the track avoids the already-falsified preclaim family of ideas

Success means:
- the track covers the full revised structural program from truthing through allocator decoupling, leaf-locality policy, micro-publish, hot-path tiering, and verification
- each child bead is self-contained enough that a future agent can implement it without reopening the original markdown plan
- the track explicitly includes unit tests, e2e checks, and structured logging obligations for every implementation phase

notes:
Mapping note:
- Phase 0 truthing -> I1, I2, I3 plus J1 for the baseline-cache truthing leg
- Phase 1 allocator/header decoupling -> I4, I5
- Phase 2 keep inserts leaf-local longer -> I7, I8
- Phase 3 micro-publish and structural intents -> I9, I10, I11
- Phase 4 tiered write path and cheap losing -> I6, I10, I12

Core design rule:
- leaves remain transaction-local MVCC/COW objects
- physical routing/allocation state should become lease-based, delta-based, or tightly system-maintained state with tiny publish windows rather than long-lived ordinary transaction-owned pages
- Track I and Track J are parallel by design: neither is allowed to hide behind the other when explaining missing progress

Fundamental-vs-accidental shared-surface rule:
- fundamental shared surfaces: the truly hot target leaf when writers touch the same physical page, irreducible commit/publication ordering surfaces, and true serializability validation surfaces
- accidental shared surfaces to shrink or remove: page 1 on ordinary insert paths, freelist/header metadata on every allocation, parent/internal pages owned through full split computation, broad non-root rebalance on concurrent insert paths, centralized hot lookups on every write, and whole-transaction restart after a local structural loss

Explicit avoid list for this track:
- do not reintroduce broad structural preclaim, parent-only preclaim, universal blocking waits, blind "validate only at commit" OCC, or a first-wave full Bw-tree rewrite
- do not lengthen shared ownership without benchmark proof

Decision-gate reminder:
- if workload truthing shows the bad row is really right-edge append geometry, prioritize right-edge policy and append-aware routing sooner
- if allocator/page-1 conflict dominates, allocator decoupling outranks deeper tree work
- if parent-version churn still dominates after Phases 1-4, structural intents and later research branches move up

User-facing success condition:
- a future operator or agent should be able to explain, from this track alone, why disjoint logical inserts stopped collapsing, which accidental shared surfaces were removed or shrunk, which ideas are explicitly forbidden because they already failed in spirit, and which verification bundle proves the claim without reopening old sessions

comments.text:
Ambitious structural backlog update after revisiting Postgres MVCC and our current write path:

Structural lane (the part that should eventually let us crush SQLite on concurrent writers):
1. Move toward inline/local visibility metadata instead of a side-plane-heavy MVCC control path; the long-term target is much closer to Postgres tuple/page locality than to today's registry-plus-side-maps shape.
2. Add a first concrete publish-locality slice: keep expensive split/planning work private, publish the minimum parent delta late, and restart locally instead of restarting whole transactions whenever correctness allows.
3. Design a batch publish / multi-insert path inspired by heap_multi_insert so fixed coordination cost is amortized across many row inserts instead of paid per row.
4. Push version pruning/reclamation further off the write path; background or budgeted cleanup is preferable to making ordinary writers pay chain-maintenance tax synchronously.
5. Keep tightening snapshot/registry overhead with read-mostly summaries and lighter-weight visibility checks so concurrent mode stops re-serializing itself in user space.
6. Add evidence that separates baseline tax from MVCC-specific tax on the same rows, otherwise we will keep arguing from blended numbers.

Postgres-comparison framing: the performance lesson is not to copy heap pages literally, but to copy the locality principle: keep visibility/version facts near the data and keep commit/publish coordination narrow, bounded, and batch-friendly.

title: I11.4: prove byte-accurate compatibility budget before any proposal that reuses page-header or reserved-file bytes
description:
## Goal
Create an explicit stop-gate against casual file-format hacking by requiring byte-accurate compatibility proof before any side-link or metadata idea touches on-disk reserved space.

## Scope
- enumerate exactly which bytes, if any, could ever be considered for alternate use without violating SQLite-file compatibility
- define the proof burden for compatibility, crash safety, tooling compatibility, and legacy-reader behavior
- make "unused page-header bytes" or similar claims impossible to smuggle into implementation without this gate being cleared
- keep the result reusable by any future side-link or structural-metadata research bead

## Acceptance Criteria
1. The bead enumerates the exact on-disk byte budget relevant to any proposed side-link or metadata scheme and states clearly whether any safe compatibility budget exists at all.
2. The bead defines the proof burden for SQLite-file compatibility, crash safety, tooling interoperability, and legacy-reader behavior before any reserved-byte or page-header-byte reuse is allowed.
3. The bead records a clear no-go outcome if the byte budget or compatibility proof is insufficient, rather than leaving the question permanently ambiguous.
4. The result becomes the mandatory gate for any future branch that proposes touching reserved or header bytes.

title: I11.5: evaluate precise structural wait queues only for short publish windows, with hard convoy falsifiers
description:
## Goal
Preserve structural wait queues as an explicitly late, evidence-gated option without letting waiting spread into the ordinary page-conflict path.

## Scope
- evaluate whether narrowly-scoped wait queues or park/wake mechanisms for short structural publish windows can beat retry storms without recreating broad convoy behavior
- explicitly forbid universal blocking waits on ordinary page conflicts
- require precise falsifiers around parent hold time, convoy depth, wakeup behavior, and retry-vs-wait tradeoffs
- keep the branch strictly later than allocator decoupling, leaf-locality policy, write-path tiering, and first-wave micro-publish

## Acceptance Criteria
1. The bead defines a narrow structural-wait-queue design space that applies only to short publish windows and explicitly excludes ordinary page-conflict waiting.
2. The bead records hard falsifiers for convoy depth, hold-time inflation, wakeup inefficiency, and retry-vs-wait tradeoff so the branch can be killed quickly if it behaves badly.
3. The bead states what evidence would justify exploring structural wait queues only after allocator decoupling, leaf-locality policy, write-path tiering, and first-wave micro-publish have already been tried.
4. The result preserves the idea as a later option without letting it masquerade as a safe default.

title: I2: instrument split-path taxonomy, hold/wait distributions, copy-allocation churn, and cache-hit truthing
description:
## Goal
Measure the second layer of truthing data needed to separate structural convoy from baseline waste.

## Why This Exists
The revised plan needs to know not only why retries happen, but also how often inserts use local insert vs local split vs right-edge split vs broad rebalance; how long shared surfaces are held; how much copy/allocation churn occurs; and whether statement/record/page-buffer caches are actually hitting.

- count split-path usage: pure leaf-local insert, local leaf split, right-edge split, full non-root rebalance, root split
- capture median and p99 hold/wait duration for parent/internal surfaces, allocator/page-1 surfaces, and structural waits per successful transaction
- record staged full-page copies, bytes copied, heap allocations, PageData ownership conversions, and record decodes per transaction on representative rows
- measure statement-plan cache hit rate, cursor reuse rate, decode-cache hit rate, and page-buffer pool hit rate where those facilities exist

## Acceptance Criteria
Success means:
- representative rows expose split-path counts, hold/wait distributions, copy/allocation counters, and cache-hit metrics in stable artifacts
- unit tests cover counter aggregation and edge cases such as zero-hit rows or no-wait rows
- the instrumentation is lightweight enough that focused benchmark reruns remain usable for optimization steering

title: I4: design extent leases and header or freelist delta reconciliation for the ordinary insert path
description:
## Goal

title: I6: rewrite the write hot path into explicit tiers with cheap owned-page checks and reduced restart scope
description:
## Goal
Shrink the common write path so ordinary successful writes stop paying rare-path tax.

## Scope
- define and implement explicit Tier 0 already-owned, Tier 1 first-touch uncontended, and Tier 2 conflict/structural/rare paths
- use an owned-page representation optimized for common transactions, with an inline cheap path for small transactions and an upgrade path to a denser/open-addressed representation when necessary
- avoid repeated global lookup, snapshot revalidation, generic cleanup, or abstraction-layer churn on Tier 0
- replace broad hot-path lookups with more local ownership/state access where practical, such as denser page descriptors or owner/version metadata nearer the page-cache state
- concentrate heavyweight validation and cleanup in cold or rare paths
- reduce restart scope so structural losses restart from a structural planning point rather than whole transactions when correctness allows
- allow selective delta staging or other lighter-weight page staging when that is measurably cheaper than unconditional full-page copy
- explicitly isolate rare path branches behind cold helpers so the hot path does not pay branch/codegen tax for unusual cleanup and recovery work

## Acceptance Criteria
Success means:
- Tier 0 and Tier 1 paths are explicit in code and no longer pay obvious rare-path coordination tax
- already-owned pages use a cheaper ownership test than the pre-refactor path and avoid unnecessary global registry/state churn
- representative c1 and c8 rows show reduced instructions/op before any micro-publish miracle is required
- unit and e2e tests prove correctness of owned-page reuse, selective staging choices, restart-scope reduction, and mode parity, with structured logging for tier selection

title: I9: design version-gated parent micro-publish with local structural restart

## Goal

- spell out correctness, crash, and recovery constraints

- the protocol is specific enough to implement without reopening the markdown plan
- the design clearly states version-token semantics, publish-window boundaries, mismatch handling, and rollback/recovery expectations
- the design includes a step-by-step publish/restart sequence plus invariants that must hold before and after publish
- the design explicitly documents why it does not regress into longer shared ownership or universal waiting
