## bd-dcjy: Fast Smoke Test — Implementation Complete

### What was implemented

Created `crates/fsqlite-e2e/src/smoke.rs` — a 30-second infrastructure verification module with 7 checks:

1. **Golden Copy Integrity** — Validates all `.db` files in `golden/` via `PRAGMA integrity_check`. Gracefully skips if directory doesn't exist (CI/fresh checkouts).
2. **FrankenSQLite Backend** — In-memory `CREATE TABLE` / `INSERT` / `SELECT` via `fsqlite::Connection`.
3. **C SQLite (rusqlite) Backend** — In-memory `CREATE TABLE` / `INSERT` / `SELECT count(*)` via `rusqlite`.
4. **Workload Generator Determinism** — Generates two OpLogs from same seed (42), verifies JSON serialization is identical.
5. **Corruption Injector** — Creates a test DB, hashes before, injects a BitFlip, hashes after, verifies change.
6. **Canonicalization Pipeline** — Runs `canonical_sha256` twice on same DB, verifies stable hash.
7. **Logging Pipeline** — Creates scoped JSON subscriber, emits a test event, verifies valid JSON output.

### Public API

- `run_smoke_tests() -> SmokeTestReport` — runs all 7 checks sequentially
- `format_smoke_report(&SmokeTestReport) -> String` — human-readable summary
- `SmokeCheckResult` / `SmokeTestReport` — serializable result types

Individual check tests + full suite structure test + serialization test. Full suite completes in ~0.15s (well under 30s target).

title: 0.3.4: bare WAL reads return Busy/BusyRecovery under concurrent writers; recovery-fence contention cascades into pool checkout failures
description:
Found gating mcp_agent_mail_rust v0.3.28 under its stress/load suites (WAL mode, busy_timeout=60000, single-writer BEGIN IMMEDIATE — FSQLITE_CONCURRENT_MODE off). Three linked behaviors, none of which the pre-registry engine lineage (local 0.3.1 line) exhibited:

1. Plain SELECTs on their own connection intermittently fail 'database is busy' while concurrent writers hold the store — WAL readers should not block on writers, and busy_timeout does not appear to be honored on this read path.
2. 'database is busy (recovery in progress)' (BusyRecovery from the WAL recovery_fence retry budget, fsqlite-wal src/recovery_fence.rs) surfaces mid-flight on reads and checkout pings under multi-connection load, implying a connection decided WAL recovery was needed during normal concurrent operation.
3. The combination cascades: sqlmodel-pool test_on_checkout pings fail against 1/2, healthy connections get discarded, and callers see 'connection validation failed' bursts lasting hundreds of ms.

Downstream absorbed this with bounded retries (mcp_agent_mail_rust commits 9a56f0d9, f9c1c607, ad855f29, 663ec548) but the engine-level question stands: why does a bare read ever see Busy in WAL single-writer mode, and why does the recovery fence get contested under normal load? Also observed once (not reproducible): a read immediately after writer-join saw N-1 of N committed rows, suggesting snapshot-refresh lag on pooled connections.
close_reason: FIXED + verified (cd525ba9f): begin_pager_txn_with_busy_timeout now retries BusyRecovery (not just Busy) within busy_timeout, so a bare WAL read no longer leaks the transient BusyRecovery raised by SimplePager::begin while the single writer's IdentityWide process-root finalization is in flight during checkpoint. NOT the recovery fence (WAL-unreachable) — the group-commit/process-root registry. Mirrors retry_busy_connection_bootstrap. One root cause covers all 3 reported behaviors (bare-Busy, BusyRecovery, pool-checkout-ping cascade). Repro bd_dhhxp_wal_reader_busy_regression.rs: 0 busy over 487616 reads; fsqlite-wal --lib 757/0; fsqlite-core --lib 3755/5 (5=bd-1v1pl baseline, 0 new). No concurrent_mode change, no new locks.

title: MemoryVfs: remove SQLite-style lock escalation (no serialized writers)
description:
## Problem

`crates/fsqlite-vfs/src/memory.rs` implemented SQLite-style file lock escalation (Shared -> Reserved -> Pending -> Exclusive) and returned Busy based on other handles.

That reintroduces file-level writer serialization, which violates FrankenSQLite's core design: concurrent writers are coordinated via MVCC at the page level, not by SQLite's file-lock protocol. In this project, MemoryVfs file locking should be a minimal stub.

## Fix

- Make `MemoryFile::lock` / `MemoryFile::unlock` minimal stubs (local bookkeeping only; no cross-handle coordination; never Busy).
- Make `check_reserved_lock` always return false for MemoryVfs.
- Update/replace any tests that assumed SQLite-style contention.

## Done When

- MemoryVfs lock/unlock no longer blocks other writers at the file level.
- `cargo check --all-targets`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`, and `cargo fmt --check` are green.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
# RAISE(FAIL) behaves like RAISE(ABORT)

## Symptom
A BEFORE-trigger `SELECT RAISE(FAIL, ...)` that fires partway through a multi-row
statement should fail the statement but KEEP the rows already changed before the
failing one. frank instead rolls those rows back (ABORT behavior).

```sql
CREATE TABLE t (x INTEGER);
CREATE TRIGGER tr BEFORE INSERT ON t WHEN NEW.x = 3
  BEGIN SELECT RAISE(FAIL, 'fail 3'); END;
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1),(2),(3),(4);   -- errors on both engines
SELECT x FROM t ORDER BY x;
-- SQLite: [1, 2]   frank: []   (WRONG: frank rolled back 1 and 2)
```
`RAISE(ABORT)` (rolls back the statement), `RAISE(ROLLBACK)` (rolls back the whole
transaction), and `RAISE(IGNORE)` (skips the row, no error) are all correct in
frank — only FAIL is wrong.

## Root cause
`crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs` `apply_trigger_raise` (:38978) handles
`RaiseAction::Abort | RaiseAction::Fail` in a SINGLE match arm (:38984), both
returning the same `Err(FrankenError::FunctionError(message))`. The caller cannot
tell ABORT from FAIL, so the statement-level rollback that ABORT requires is
applied to FAIL as well.

## SQLite semantics (the distinction to implement)
- ABORT: fail the statement and undo *all* changes made by that statement
  (the rows inserted before the failing row), but do not end the transaction.
- FAIL: fail the statement but do NOT back out changes already made by it;
  rows processed before the failing row remain.
(See SQLite ON CONFLICT docs: OE_Abort vs OE_Fail.)

## Fix sketch
Split the arm so FAIL carries a distinct signal (a dedicated error variant, or a
flag on the error / outcome) meaning "abort this statement WITHOUT rolling back
its prior row changes." The INSERT/UPDATE row loop that catches a trigger RAISE
must, on FAIL, stop and propagate the error while leaving already-applied rows in
place; on ABORT it must undo the statement's row changes (current behavior). The
existing unit test `test_trigger_raise_fail_returns_function_error`
(connection.rs:98140) only checks that an error is returned, so it does not catch
this — add a survival assertion.

## Tests
`crates/fsqlite-e2e/tests/trigger_raise_resolution_oracle_e2e.rs`:
- PASS: raise_abort_rolls_back_statement, raise_rollback_undoes_whole_transaction,
  raise_ignore_skips_row_no_error
- IGNORED on this bead: raise_fail_keeps_prior_rows

INVESTIGATION (deferred, not a clean 'split the match arm'). Root cause confirmed: apply_trigger_raise (connection.rs ~42102) collapses RaiseAction::Abort|Fail into one arm returning Err(FunctionError(msg)). But fixing FAIL requires preserving the statement's PRIOR row changes, which is transaction-atomicity work across 2 chokepoints:
1. STATEMENT SAVEPOINT: with_internal_statement_savepoint(_and_cx) (~22421/22430); the body()-Err arm at ~22504-22571 does rollback_to_savepoint (ABORT behavior). For FAIL it must release_savepoint (keep rows) instead, then propagate the error.
2. AUTOCOMMIT RESOLUTION: in autocommit mode the implicit txn is rolled back on any Err, which would still undo the kept rows. Must commit-on-FAIL — mirror the EXISTING machinery for ON CONFLICT FAIL constraint violations: commit_autocommit_on_error = preserve_prior_changes_on_constraint_violation && error_is_constraint_violation(error) (precompiled INSERT path ~18497, ~21255). preserve flag is set from insert.or_conflict==Fail (~10200) — trigger RAISE(FAIL) needs an INDEPENDENT signal.

title: BUG: DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED foreign keys not deferred — FK checked at statement time, not COMMIT (deferrable clause parsed but ignored)
close_reason: DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED FKs now deferred to COMMIT (FkDef.deferred + commit-time recheck; failed recheck leaves txn active per SQLite). 4/4 oracle tests green. commit ca28621c

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## BUG: DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED foreign keys are not deferred — checked immediately at the statement

Oracle parity vs rusqlite (foreign_keys = ON).
```sql
CREATE TABLE parent (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY);
CREATE TABLE child (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
   pid INTEGER REFERENCES parent(id) DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED);
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO child VALUES (10, 1);   -- parent 1 not present yet
  -- frank: ERROR("FOREIGN KEY constraint failed")   <-- checked immediately
  -- csql:  OK (deferred; the constraint is only checked at COMMIT)
INSERT INTO parent VALUES (1);
COMMIT;                              -- csql: commits cleanly
```
A DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED constraint must NOT be enforced at statement
time; it is checked at COMMIT, so a transaction may temporarily violate it
(insert a child before its parent, or build a self-referential tree
children-first). frank enforces it immediately, so any such transaction fails at
the first insert.

Also fails:
- self-referential deferred FK built children-first within a txn (same cause).
- the "unresolved violation should fail at COMMIT (not at the insert)" case —
  frank fails at the insert instead.

### What works
- Immediate (non-deferrable) FKs fail at the statement, matching SQLite.
- INSERT inside an explicit BEGIN does NOT panic here (the constraint error is
  raised cleanly), so this is purely the deferral being unimplemented.

### Root cause
The `Deferrable`/`DeferrableInitially` clause is parsed into the AST
(fsqlite-ast: ColumnConstraint/ForeignKey `deferrable` field) but is never
consulted by the FK enforcement logic in connection.rs — FK checks always run at
statement time. (The "deferred_*" identifiers in connection.rs are unrelated
lazy-statement caching, not constraint deferral.)

### Fix
When a FK constraint is DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED (or set deferred via
PRAGMA defer_foreign_keys / SET CONSTRAINTS), queue its check and run it at
COMMIT instead of at the statement; on COMMIT, if it still fails, error and roll
back the transaction.

### Test
crates/fsqlite-e2e/tests/deferred_fk_oracle_e2e.rs — immediate_fk_fails_at_statement
passes; the three deferred-FK scenarios are #[ignore]'d on this bead.

title: PERF-P0: FrankenSQLite-side regression ~1.9x median vs b612eb7b control (cause NOT yet attributed)
description:
STATUS: regression is REAL and severe. CAUSE IS NOT ESTABLISHED. An earlier
version of this bead asserted the async migration and WalBackend boxing as the
cause; both claims are RETRACTED as unproven. Corrected after independent
review (GPT Sol) plus my own verification.

## What is actually proven

Same host (trj, Threadripper PRO 5995WX, idle), same release-perf flags, same
comprehensive-bench --quick, control b612eb7b vs HEAD 5419dff5:

  metric                          control   HEAD      delta
  per_category_weighted(PRIMARY)  0.4004    0.8319   +107.7%
  geomean_ratio                   0.2915    0.6212   +113.1%
  p90_ratio                       1.1002    3.3170   +201.5%
  faster/comparable/slower        78/3/12   55/0/38

Across all 93 paired scenarios the median current/control timing factor was
C SQLite 1.005x vs FrankenSQLite 1.895x. That isolates the regression to the
FrankenSQLite side rather than the host. It does NOT identify which change
caused it.

The control also reproduces the recorded Jul-22 baseline artifact (0.5262 vs
0.5465 avg_ratio), so the baseline is sound.

## What is NOT proven (retracted claims)

1. 'The async migration caused it.' b612eb7b..5419dff5 spans 194 commits and
   336 files including dependency, feature, engine AND benchmark changes. The
   control is pre-async but is not an async-only control.
2. 'WalBackend/WalFuture boxing is the root cause.' Mechanism is plausible but
   there is NO allocation or CPU evidence. Note WalFuture/LocalPagerFuture are
   absent at b612eb7b but already present at the immediate pre-public-API base
   (c967eaeb/13ec577f), so they are not introduced by the public-API migration
   either. Requires heaptrack/samply evidence before any de-boxing work.
3. 'read_aggregate +139% implies a second read-path cause.' Consistent with
   per-operation bridge overhead; not independently established.

## Known benchmark-methodology defects (must fix before attributing anything)

- Only 2 warmups and 3-10 measurements; several cells exceed 5% CV.
- C and FrankenSQLite arms run sequentially, not interleaved/randomized.
- Artifact Git provenance fields are null; README cites source revision
  140e77df which is NOT a reachable git object (verified).
- ci_regression_gate status is 'rich_scorecard_schema_ready' -- it records
  thresholds but does not compute a confidence-aware pass/fail.
- The suite does not exercise the default native/linux-uring feature config.
- Benchmarks use release-perf (opt-level=3) while the SHIPPED release profile
  is opt-level='z' + lto + codegen-units=1 + panic=abort. Published binary
  performance is therefore unmeasured by this suite.
- bd-czzlp: subquery/CTE rows measure cache hits and discard fsqlite results.
- bd-jyyae: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN can report SEARCH where the VDBE emits a full
  scan, so EXPLAIN cannot confirm which path ran.

## Correct next step (Gate 0), NOT engine optimization

1. Fix benchmark asymmetries incl. the dropped fsqlite PRAGMAs (bd-fd1ra).
2. Require full provenance in every artifact (source SHA, dirty state, binary
   sha256, toolchain, feature graph, profile, runtime mode, tracing filter,
   durability mode, fallback + fast/instrumented-lane counters); fail artifact
   generation when provenance is absent.
3. Reproduce the migration boundary with c967eaeb vs 13ec577f (31fc4a3b does
   NOT compile -- 8 pager/B-tree sync-vs-Future errors), then bisect forward.
4. At HEAD run three arms in ONE binary: single top-level runtime entry for the
   whole workload; current per-operation block_on; worker-based AsyncConnection.
   Add an empty-ready-future control and regress elapsed overhead against the
   exact number of bridge calls.
5. Randomized ABBA ordering, >=20 samples, pinned CPUs, quiet host, confidence
   intervals, CPU AND allocation profiles.
6. Use mt-mvcc-bench at matched NORMAL and FULL durability for any
   concurrent-writer claim.

Do NOT change WalBackend until allocation counts and CPU samples exist for
WalFuture, LocalPagerFuture, the connection-level recursive box, runtime entry,
lock polling, and Cx creation.

Artifacts on trj: /data/tmp/fsqlite-bench-async-verify/{async-verify.json,
ctrl-preasync.json}.

comments.text:
MEASURED 2026-07-26 (SagePine): the io_uring data path is UNREACHABLE in production. Plus two corrections to this bead's own text.

=== 1. NEW MEASUREMENT: 100% unix fallback, zero uring operations ===

Probe binary: debug fsqlite-cli, self-reported ELF sha256
  8ea1d0a198e9ec474d86b9f0aee4269a20c70d687431afa699a2b3e342926e2c  (342159600 bytes, built 2026-07-26 13:36:10 -0400)
Method: 20,000-row file-backed WAL database (page_size 4096; 4.1 MB db + 4.2 MB wal) populated in one process, then read from a COLD second process (wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE) + two full scans), so every page read is a genuine miss.

PRAGMA fsqlite.io_uring_stats:
  read_samples_total   = 0
  write_samples_total  = 0
  unix_fallbacks_total = 7520

Not a ratio — an absolute. Every single I/O on the normal Connection path took the Unix fallback.

MECHANISM (code-read, consistent with the measurement): IoUringFile::{read,write,write_tracked} gate on cx.attached_native_cx() alone (uring.rs:1069/:1188/:1318). Cx::attached_native_cx() (fsqlite-types/src/cx.rs:917) reads only the attached field and never consults ambient asupersync::Cx::current(). Nothing on the Connection::open -> execute path calls set_native_cx on a connection root/op Cx — the only connection.rs sites are a background task (:73826) and a test (:97020). create_child DOES propagate it (cx.rs:1199-1202), but there is nothing to propagate. One layer up, page_cache.rs:3421-3422 already does Cx::current().or_else(|| cx.attached_native_cx()).

THIS IS INSIDE THE REGRESSION WINDOW. At control b612eb7b the read gate was just 'if self.has_uring_data_path()' with fallback only on error — no native-cx requirement. uring.rs and IoUringVfs selection both already existed at the control, so the VFS choice is not new; the always-failing gate is.

SCOPE / WHAT THIS DOES NOT SAY: this establishes that the fast path is unreachable, NOT that it accounts for the 1.895x. Two independent gates exist at HEAD — runtime.is_available() (:1065) and the native-cx gate (:1069) — and the counter does not distinguish which fired. I have applied Cx::current().or_else(..) to all three sites and am rebuilding; if read_samples_total moves off zero, the native-cx gate was the blocker, if it stays zero then runtime.is_available() is and my change is inert. Result goes in the ledger either way. No timing claim will be made from this loaded host.

=== 2. CORRECTION to 'The suite does not exercise the default native/linux-uring feature config' ===

It does, via feature unification. fsqlite-e2e declares fsqlite with default-features=false, features=[json,fts5,rtree] — but it depends on fsqlite-harness, which takes fsqlite with DEFAULT features. cargo tree -p fsqlite-e2e -e features -i fsqlite confirms both 'native' and 'linux-asupersync-uring' resolve ON for the bench build. Consequence: diagnostic-pragmas is also on (native -> diagnostic-pragmas), so PRAGMA fsqlite.io_uring_stats is available inside comprehensive-bench too, and the fallback rate can be asserted per run rather than probed separately.

=== 3. THIS BEAD IS STALE vs bd-zavyn ===

Last updated 2026-07-25 19:13, roughly 7h before bd-zavyn concluded that the comprehensive_bench INSERT regression is the harness's per-row block_on (~333 ns floor; delta flat at 660-1000 ns/row across a 10x record-width and 100x row-count range, i.e. not scaling with work) rather than the engine. The three-cohort ABBA boundary matrix independently puts the discontinuity at a0ab400a — the harness runtime-bridge commit — with DiD 2.685x [2.646, 2.724] and the following merge adding only 1.003x. Anyone reading this bead today gets a Gate 0 plan that does not know its own headline number is substantially instrument drift. Recommend the summary block be amended by its owner (RusticBasin holds Gate 0).

title: REGRESSION P0: in-txn memdb schema-cookie fast path (6889b63cb) breaks FK parent-cache invalidation — FK constraint silently bypassed
description:
REGRESSION on main, isolated-reproducible (NOT a flake). test_issue110_fk_parent_cache_invalidated_by_delete AND test_issue110_fk_parent_cache_invalidated_by_insert_or_replace (crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs ~181951/181995) FAIL: after deleting/REPLACE-deleting an FK parent row WITHIN a transaction, a subsequent child INSERT referencing the now-deleted parent WRONGLY SUCCEEDS instead of raising ForeignKeyViolation — the transaction-scoped fk_parent_validation_cache is not invalidated, so the stale 'parent exists' result is reused. (savepoint_rollback variant still passes.) This is silent FK-constraint bypass = data-integrity bug.

ATTRIBUTION (high confidence): commit 6889b63cb 'use the schema-cookie fast path on in-txn memdb refresh' flipped the per-write in-txn memdb refresh at connection.rs ~21260 from reload_memdb_from_txn_with_mode(..., allow_dirty_schema_only_fast_path=false) to =true. The 2 failing tests are :memory: + in-txn (exactly that path); they PASSED in SageBluff's bd-o01lp and bd-lryih full --lib runs earlier the same day and FAIL after 6889b63cb landed. The commit's own rationale reasons only about schema reparse + row hydration and never considers fk_parent_validation_cache; the full (false) refresh evidently reset/cleared the FK cache as a side effect that the schema-cookie fast path (true) now skips. NOT caused by bd-l3tce (054f7ab18, TVF-arg substitution — zero call path to FK cache); SageBluff initially mis-called these 2 --lib fails 'load flakes' but the ISOLATED single-threaded rerun proved them a consistent regression.

REPRO: RCH_CARGO_WRAPPER_BYPASS=1 FSQLITE_DEBUG=false cargo test -p fsqlite-core --lib test_issue110_fk_parent_cache_invalidated -- --test-threads=1  => 1 passed / 2 failed.
NEXT: confirm via revert of the false->true at ~21260; fix = schema-cookie fast path must still invalidate/rebuild fk_parent_validation_cache when a parent-mutating statement ran in-txn (or exclude that case from the fast path). CI is DISABLED (bd-gha14) so this is uncaught by automation.
close_reason: FIXED + fully verified. Landed 761919bca (main+master): reverted connection.rs:21253 allow_dirty_schema_only_fast_path true->false so the in-txn per-write memdb refresh (refresh_memdb_from_active_txn_if_dirty) takes the row-absorbing reload on a dirty mirror instead of the schema-cookie fast path that cleared memdb_requires_active_txn_reload without absorbing in-txn DML rows (6889b63cb regression). comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: ROOT CAUSE CONFIRMED (code trace, no bisect needed) — 6889b63cb IS the culprit. Mechanism: (1) in-txn DELETE parent sets memdb_requires_active_txn_reload=true (mirror dirty). (2) The per-write in-txn refresh at connection.rs:21253 now passes allow_dirty_schema_only_fast_path=true (was false). In reload_memdb_from_txn_with_mode's schema-cookie fast-path branch (83289), condition 83293 is '(!memdb_requires_active_txn_reload || allow_dirty_schema_only_fast_path)': pre-6889b63cb a DIRTY mirror was EXCLUDED from the fast path (fell to full reload that absorbed the DELETE); post-6889b63cb allow_dirty=true lets the fast path fire on a dirty mirror and at line 83323 clears memdb_requires_active_txn_reload=false WHILE LEAVING THE STALE parent row in the mirror (the fast path only refreshes schema metadata, never absorbs in-txn DML rows). (3) fk_parent_rowid_fast_lookup (58076) then sees !memdb_requires_active_txn_reload -> takes the no-refresh path (58076-58085/58092) -> reads stale mirror -> table.find_by_rowid(parent) present -> Ok(Some(true)) -> FK check wrongly passes. FIX candidates: (A) revert 21253 true->false (certain, loses 6889b63cb's schema-reparse-skip win); (B) surgical: in the fast-path branch only clear memdb_requires_active_txn_reload if it was already false (leave it set when fired via allow_dirty on a dirty mirror) so FK/row consumers still refresh — keeps the schema-reparse win. Verifying B's sufficiency via refresh_memdb_from_active_txn_if_dirty.

title: Freelist trunk-chain corruption under large-scale churn: 'freelist trunk N leaf_count 17823488 exceeds max 1022' — chain walk lands on a content page (multi-trunk serialization or torn page-1/trunk read)

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: [bd-dw8oe] CLAIMED (gh302 lane — this is my freelist-serialization surface). REPRO: FSQLITE_CHURN_SCALE=large churn_acceptance_corruption_family (32x1000 mixed insert/delete) fails ~2/2 at HEAD in ~74s: a worker's BEGIN dies with 'database disk image is malformed: freelist trunk 699 leaf_count 17823488 exceeds max 1022' (begin-refresh load_freelist_from_committed_state walking the durable chain). Default scale (16x150) never reproduces — the freelist stays under one trunk (~1022 leaves/trunk); large-scale delete churn crosses into MULTI-TRUNK chains, a shape no current keeper covered until bd-zeg99's deadlock fix let runs reach it. leaf_count=17823488 = 0x01100000: the walked page holds B-tree/content bytes, not trunk metadata — either (a) multi-trunk serialization writes a stale/wrong next-trunk pointer (serialize_freelist_to_write_set trunk chaining under trunk_count>1 is nearly untested), (b) a trunk page number is simultaneously granted as content (aliasing face), or (c) begin-refresh reads page-1 and trunk pages at INCONSISTENT visibility bounds (torn head->chain read across commits — the published-plane vs frame-resolution family from bd-o81ov). DISCRIMINATOR PLAN: (1) persist the failing db (env-gated tempdir keep) + parse page 699's actual content and the full committed chain from page 1 — content-page bytes vs stale-trunk bytes distinguishes (a/b) from (c); (2) if images are per-commit consistent, replay the WAL certificate/frame history for the chain pages (the bd-vnxjd certdump technique); (3) unit-scale repro: single connection, force freelist > 1022 entries (mass DELETE), commit, reopen, walk — pins (a) deterministically if it is serialization. Root-cause then fix at the proven layer.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: Corroborating data point from lane 6 (Claude/Fable, session 85094568), filed independently as bd-465my in the same race window (now closed as duplicate of this bead): at HEAD 705ea842b, FSQLITE_CHURN_SCALE=large churn_acceptance_corruption_family did NOT FINISH within a 580s timeout (default scale: 5.82s; linear prediction for 32k ops: ~80s). Your 74s-completion-then-oracle-red and my >580s non-finish likely unify: a trunk with garbage leaf_count 17823488 makes any subsequent freelist scan walk ~17M phantom entries, so depending on WHEN the corrupted trunk is first re-read, the run either finishes and fails integrity (yours) or spins super-linearly inside the scan (mine). Suggests the fix should include a load-time leaf_count bound check (max 1022 for 4K pages) that fails fast as corruption instead of trusting the count — that converts the silent-spin face into a deterministic red. Repro env: warm nodebug target, local build.

comments.text:
[bd-dw8oe] batch_pending — ROUND 2 RECEIPTS: mechanism fully pinned END-TO-END with commit-level forensics; four guard layers proven insufficient; RECOMMENDING STRUCTURAL CHARTER.

DEFINITIVE MECHANISM (live-WAL capture /data/tmp/.tmpnjcdHJ, DW8OE_TRACE run): commit f53867 consumes freelist page 753 (writes it as index leaf) and correctly publishes p1(head=0,count=0). NINE frames later, commit f53876 (synthetic page-1, no publication) republishes p1(head=753,count=1). MY OWN GUARDS WATCHED IT HAPPEN AND PASSED IT: trace shows PROMOTE read durable_head=753 (stale) and the append-gate compare read durable32_40=753/1 (stale) — because publish_latest_committed_snapshot's staged-batch clamp hides PEERS' appended-but-unfsynced commits (deferred sync) from a flusher refreshing mid-flush. The guards' ground truth is a lagging reader-visibility plane, not the file tail. This same lag family explains the earlier o81ov EOFGUARD committed_db regressions.

MEASURED + WITHDRAWN: relaxing the clamp to 'fsynced OR below our own staged frames' did NOT reduce the rate (large-scale 6/8 red before AND after) — withdrawn, recorded as an in-code design note (fb1a1a860). The clamp was also NOT the source of the 28 fsqlite-core lib reds seen during verification (28 fail with the relaxation fully reverted — PRE-EXISTING planner/JSON/FTS5 cluster from today's core churn; core lanes should triage — flagging separately).

Every layer validates against a plane that can lag the file, and the wholesale-republish design means ONE stale page-1 write re-poisons everything downstream.

CHARTER RECOMMENDATION (orchestrator): rework the durable-freelist protocol with a single write authority — candidates: (a) freelist head/count carried in the commit CERTIFICATE (already monotonic + gate-read, per the vnxjd db_size-floor precedent) with page-1 bytes derived at checkpoint; (b) a dedicated file-tail conflict horizon API for all append-gate guards (read frames, never planes); (c) delta-based freelist publication (add/remove lists per commit) replacing wholesale head/count republish. Evidence set for the charter: this bead + bd-o81ov + bd-vnxjd + bd-gh302 trails. title: RELEASE-GATE: cargo test --workspace --all-features is intentionally uncompilable via disabled legacy uring feature
description:
AGENTS.md mandates cargo test --workspace --all-features, but fsqlite-vfs still declares the deprecated linux-uring-fs feature and src/uring.rs unconditionally emits compile_error whenever that feature is enabled. Cargo --all-features therefore can never reach the test suite. This is a long-standing internal contradiction, not a transient test failure.

Fix by removing the disabled legacy feature/dependency and its unreachable feature-gated tests, leaving linux-asupersync-uring as the sole Linux async VFS path. Do not introduce a compatibility alias: the project explicitly rejects compatibility shims and has no users to preserve. Regenerate Cargo.lock through Cargo. Acceptance: targeted fsqlite-vfs default/native/wasm feature checks remain valid, cargo test --workspace --all-features gets past feature resolution/compilation, ordinary workspace tests remain green, and Clippy/fmt gates pass. If all-features reveals a second mutually exclusive feature family, track and resolve it rather than weakening the documented gate.

title: EPIC: C-SQLite Parity Architecture — 5 Structural Changes to Match C SQLite Single-Thread DML Speed

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## Context & Evidence

Benchmark (2026-04-01) shows FrankenSQLite 3-5x slower than C SQLite on single-thread DML despite 10 P0 optimization beads already landed. Deep analysis of C SQLite's source code (legacy_sqlite_code/sqlite/src/) reveals 5 specific architectural patterns that make C SQLite fast — patterns that FrankenSQLite's Rust abstractions currently prevent.

### The 5 Gaps (from C SQLite source analysis)

| # | C SQLite Pattern | FrankenSQLite Today | Per-Row Cost Delta | Speedup |
|---|-----------------|--------------------|--------------------|---------|
| 1 | Flat array hash, no locks (pcache1.c:1000) | 128 Mutex<HashMap> shards (page_cache.rs:532) | +35 cycles/page | 4.5x |
| 2 | MakeRecord into pre-alloc buffer (vdbe.c OP_MakeRecord) | Vec<u8> alloc per record, 3 passes (record.rs:844) | +100 cycles/row | 2-3x |
| 3 | Mem union, zero refcounting (vdbeaux.c) | SqliteValue with Arc/SmallText (value.rs) | +50 cycles/row | 1.5-2x |
| 4 | BTREE_APPEND O(1) insert (btree.c:9394) | Full seek in some paths despite G1 fix | +200 cycles/seq row | 2-5x |
| 5 | sqlite3PagerWrite 1-cycle dirty check (pager.c:6234) | Group commit Mutex+Condvar (pager.rs:38) | +100-500 cycles/row | 2-10x |

### Current Benchmark Numbers
- INSERT single txn (small 3-col): 3.34x slower than C SQLite
- INSERT autocommit 10K: 30.54x slower
- UPDATE 100K: 7.86x slower
- DELETE 100K: 5.39x slower
- Concurrent 8 writers: 6.72x FASTER (MVCC advantage — MUST NOT regress)

### Target
- INSERT single txn: ≤ 1.5x C SQLite (from 3.34x)
- INSERT autocommit: ≤ 5.0x (from 30.54x)
- UPDATE: ≤ 2.0x (from 7.86x)
- DELETE: ≤ 2.0x (from 5.39x)
- Concurrent writers: ≥ 6.0x faster (no regression)

### Strategy: 5 tracks (Q-U) implementing C-SQLite-equivalent patterns in safe Rust

Track Q: Lock-Free Flat Hash Page Cache (C SQLite pcache1.c pattern)
Track R: Zero-Alloc Record Encoding (C SQLite OP_MakeRecord pattern)
Track S: Union-Style Register File (C SQLite Mem struct pattern)
Track T: Full BTREE_APPEND Parity (C SQLite btree.c:9394 pattern)
Track U: Dirty-Page Bitmap (C SQLite sqlite3PagerWrite pattern)

title: F3: Eliminate TransactionHandle Box allocation — stack-allocate via enum dispatch
close_reason: Committed in 9abedc20: TransactionHandle enum in traits.rs (+213 lines)

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## What
Replace Box<dyn TransactionHandle> with an enum TransactionKind { Memory(MemTxnHandle), File(FileTxnHandle) }. Stack-allocated, no heap allocation per begin().

## Why
Every statement does begin() which allocates Box<dyn TransactionHandle> (~50 ns). For autocommit with 10K rows, that's 500 µs of pure allocation overhead.

## Where
- crates/fsqlite-pager/src/pager.rs: TransactionHandle trait → TransactionKind enum
- crates/fsqlite-pager/src/traits.rs: update trait bounds
- All callers in connection.rs

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Zero heap allocations in begin()/commit() for :memory: mode
2. cargo test -p fsqlite-pager passes
3. No performance regression for file-backed mode

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## Risk & Fallback
**Risk**: The TransactionKind enum may be larger than expected, causing stack pressure.
**Mitigation**: Use `std::mem::size_of::<TransactionKind>()` assertion: must be ≤ 128 bytes. If larger, use SmallBox<dyn TransactionHandle, 128> from smallbox crate instead.
**Fallback**: If enum dispatch causes too many code changes, keep Box but add a per-connection pool of 4 pre-allocated handles (reuse instead of malloc/free each time).

title: §1.3 Asupersync-Only Runtime Enforcement (No Tokio CI Gate)
description:
## SUMMARY

Establish CI-enforced verification that the FrankenSQLite workspace uses asupersync as its sole async runtime, with zero tokio/async-std/smol dependencies. Per spec §1.3: "No tokio. All async I/O uses asupersync exclusively." Asupersync provides the async runtime, RaptorQ codec, Cx capability contexts, structured concurrency (Scope + macros), lab runtime (deterministic scheduling, cancellation injection, chaos), oracles/e-process monitors, deadline monitoring, and trace/TLA export. This bead gates CI to reject any introduction of alternative async runtimes and verifies that all I/O-performing trait methods accept the `&Cx` capability parameter.

## KEY DATA STRUCTURES / ALGORITHMS

- **Cx (Capability Context)**: Asupersync's capability token (§9) threaded through all I/O-performing methods. Provides cancellation, deadline monitoring, and structured concurrency guarantees. Every VFS, pager, and MVCC trait method that performs I/O MUST accept `&Cx` as a parameter.
- **Lab Runtime**: `LabRuntime::new(seed)` — asupersync's deterministic test runtime providing reproducible scheduling, cancellation injection at await points, and chaos mode (random delays, fault injection). Used for all async tests in the workspace.
- **Dependency audit**: CI script (cargo-deny or custom) that parses `Cargo.lock` to detect direct or transitive dependencies on `tokio`, `async-std`, `smol`, or `futures-executor`. Any match fails the build with an actionable diagnostic.
- **Structured concurrency (Scope)**: Asupersync's `Scope` + macros ensure all spawned tasks are joined before the scope exits. Replaces tokio's unstructured `tokio::spawn`.

## NORMATIVE INVARIANTS

1. **INV-NO-TOKIO**: Zero workspace crates may depend on `tokio`, `async-std`, `smol`, or `futures-executor` as direct dependencies. Transitive dependencies from external crates MAY pull in tokio types but MUST NOT instantiate or use their runtime (§1.3).
2. **INV-CX-THREADING**: Every trait method that performs I/O (VFS, pager, MVCC, replication) MUST accept `&Cx` as a parameter (§9). Methods that do not perform I/O SHOULD NOT require `&Cx`.
3. **INV-LAB-DETERMINISM**: All async tests MUST be runnable under `LabRuntime` with a fixed seed, producing deterministic execution order. Non-deterministic scheduling is confined to production runtime only.
4. **INV-NO-TOKIO-MACROS**: Zero occurrences of `#[tokio::main]`, `#[tokio::test]`, `#[async_std::main]`, or equivalent macros in any workspace source file.

## UNIT TEST REQUIREMENTS

- **test_no_tokio_in_cargo_lock**: Parse `Cargo.lock` and assert that no entry has `name = "tokio"` (or `async-std`, `smol`, `futures-executor`) as a direct dependency of any workspace crate. If a transitive dep pulls tokio, verify it is behind a non-default feature gate not activated by any workspace crate.
- **test_no_tokio_macros_in_source**: Scan all `.rs` files in `crates/` for `#[tokio::main]`, `#[tokio::test]`, `#[async_std::main]`. Assert zero matches. Prevents accidental use of alternative runtime test harnesses.
- **test_cx_parameter_on_vfs_trait**: Compile-time verification (via trait bounds or a dedicated test that instantiates a mock VFS) that all VFS read/write/lock methods require `&Cx`. A missing `Cx` parameter must cause a compile error.
- **test_lab_runtime_deterministic**: Run a small async workload (3 tasks, 10 yields each) under `LabRuntime::new(42)` twice. Assert identical execution traces (task interleaving order). Confirms deterministic scheduling.
- **test_lab_cancellation_injection**: Run an async operation under LabRuntime with cancellation injection enabled. Assert the operation observes cancellation at an await point and returns a cancellation error (not a hang or panic).

## E2E TEST

- **test_e2e_no_tokio_dependency_gate**: Run the full dependency audit script as it would run in CI. Temporarily add a `tokio = "1"` dependency to a test crate's Cargo.toml, run the audit, and verify it fails with a clear diagnostic message identifying the offending crate and dependency chain. Then remove the temporary dependency and verify the audit passes.

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA

- [ ] CI script (cargo-deny rule or custom) rejects any direct tokio dependency in workspace crates, with clear error message showing the dependency chain
- [ ] All VFS, pager, and MVCC trait methods verified to accept `&Cx` parameter (compile-time enforcement)
- [ ] LabRuntime smoke test passes with deterministic seed (same seed => same execution order)
- [ ] Zero `#[tokio::main]` or `#[tokio::test]` macros anywhere in the workspace source
- [ ] Dependency audit runs in < 5 seconds and is integrated into the CI pipeline
close_reason: 6 CI gate tests: cargo metadata dep scan, macro source scan (runtime-assembled patterns to avoid self-detection), Cargo.lock scan, workspace Cargo.toml scan, VfsFile Cx parameter compile-time check, E2E summary. All pass, clippy clean, fmt clean.

title: §13.6 COLLATE Interaction: BINARY/NOCASE/RTRIM + Custom Collation Registration
description:
## SUMMARY
Implement SQLite collation interaction with built-in functions and support for custom collation registration. Three built-in collations must be provided: BINARY (memcmp byte comparison), NOCASE (ASCII case-insensitive comparison), and RTRIM (ignores trailing spaces before comparison). Functions affected by collation (min/max scalar and aggregate) must use SQLite's comparison rules respecting the active collation. Functions NOT affected by collation (instr, replace, LIKE, GLOB) implement their own byte/character and case-folding rules. Collation selection follows SQLite's precedence: explicit COLLATE clause > column schema collation > default BINARY. Custom collations are registered via the database connection API.

## KEY DATA STRUCTURES / ALGORITHMS
- Collation trait: fn compare(&self, a: &[u8], b: &[u8]) -> Ordering. Each collation is a named implementation of this trait.
- CollationRegistry: maps collation name (case-insensitive) -> Collation trait object. Pre-populated with BINARY, NOCASE, RTRIM.
- BINARY collation: delegates to memcmp (byte-by-byte comparison).
- NOCASE collation: case-insensitive for ASCII letters (A-Z folded to a-z), byte-level comparison otherwise. Does NOT handle Unicode case folding (that requires the ICU extension).
- RTRIM collation: strips trailing spaces (0x20) from both operands before BINARY comparison.
- Collation selection algorithm (when operands have different collations):
  1. Explicit COLLATE clause wins. If multiple explicit collations, leftmost wins.
  2. Column collation from schema (CREATE TABLE ... COLLATE NOCASE).
  3. Default: BINARY.
- Functions using collation: scalar min/max and aggregate min/max use the collation-aware comparison for determining minimum/maximum.
- Functions ignoring collation: instr, replace use byte/character matching; LIKE uses its own case-folding (case-insensitive for ASCII); GLOB uses its own case-sensitive matching.
- Custom collation registration API: db.create_collation("name", MyCollation::new()). Must be available before any query references the collation.

## NORMATIVE INVARIANTS
1. BINARY collation uses memcmp (byte-by-byte unsigned comparison).
2. NOCASE folds only ASCII A-Z to a-z; non-ASCII bytes are compared as-is.
3. RTRIM strips only space characters (0x20), not tabs or other whitespace.
4. Collation selection precedence: explicit COLLATE > schema COLLATE > BINARY default.
5. When multiple explicit COLLATE clauses conflict, the leftmost wins.
6. min/max (both scalar and aggregate) respect the active collation for comparisons.
7. instr, replace, LIKE, GLOB do NOT use collation; they have their own comparison rules.
8. LIKE is case-insensitive for ASCII by default (no collation involvement).
9. GLOB is always case-sensitive (no collation involvement).
10. Custom collations must be registered before use; referencing an unregistered collation is an error.
11. Collation names are case-insensitive (BINARY = binary = Binary).

## UNIT TEST REQUIREMENTS
1. test_binary_collation_basic: 'ABC' < 'abc' under BINARY (uppercase bytes are less)
2. test_binary_collation_memcmp: comparison is byte-by-byte, not character-aware
3. test_nocase_collation_equal: 'ABC' = 'abc' under NOCASE
4. test_nocase_collation_ascii_only: 'Ä' != 'ä' under NOCASE (non-ASCII not folded)
5. test_rtrim_collation_equal: 'hello' = 'hello   ' under RTRIM
6. test_rtrim_collation_tabs_not_stripped: 'hello\t' != 'hello' under RTRIM (only 0x20 stripped)
7. test_collation_selection_explicit: SELECT 'a' < 'B' COLLATE NOCASE uses NOCASE
8. test_collation_selection_leftmost: when two explicit COLLATE conflict, leftmost wins
9. test_collation_selection_schema: column defined with COLLATE NOCASE uses NOCASE by default
10. test_collation_selection_default: without any COLLATE, BINARY is used
11. test_min_respects_collation: min('ABC', 'abc') differs under BINARY vs NOCASE
12. test_max_respects_collation: max with NOCASE collation compares case-insensitively
13. test_aggregate_min_collation: SELECT min(col) with col COLLATE NOCASE
14. test_aggregate_max_collation: SELECT max(col) with col COLLATE NOCASE
15. test_instr_ignores_collation: instr always uses byte matching regardless of column collation
16. test_replace_ignores_collation: replace is byte-exact regardless of collation
17. test_like_ignores_collation: LIKE uses its own ASCII case-folding, not column collation
18. test_glob_ignores_collation: GLOB is always case-sensitive regardless of collation
19. test_order_by_collation: ORDER BY col COLLATE NOCASE sorts case-insensitively
20. test_group_by_collation: GROUP BY col COLLATE NOCASE groups 'ABC' and 'abc' together

## E2E TEST
Create tables with columns using different collations (BINARY, NOCASE, RTRIM). Insert data with mixed case, trailing spaces, and Unicode characters. Test ORDER BY, GROUP BY, DISTINCT, min/max, comparisons (=, <, >, IN, BETWEEN) under each collation. Register a custom collation and verify it works in ORDER BY, WHERE, and INDEX creation. Verify that instr/replace/LIKE/GLOB ignore collation. Compare all results against C sqlite3.

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
1. BINARY, NOCASE, RTRIM collations are built-in and produce correct comparison results.
2. Collation selection precedence (explicit > schema > default BINARY) is correctly implemented.
3. min/max respect collation; instr/replace/LIKE/GLOB do not.
4. Custom collations can be registered and used in ORDER BY, WHERE, GROUP BY, DISTINCT, and indexes.
5. Collation names are case-insensitive.

comments.text:
## §13.6 COLLATE Interaction

### Spec Content (Lines 15152-15171)

Collation affects ordering/comparison semantics, not raw string processing.

**Functions affected by collation:** min/max (scalar and aggregate) use SQLite's comparison rules and therefore respect collation.

**Functions NOT affected by collation:** instr, replace, LIKE, and GLOB do not use collation; they implement their own byte/character and/or case-folding rules.

**Collation selection rules (when operands have different collations):**
1. Explicit COLLATE clause wins (if multiple explicit collations appear, leftmost wins)
2. Column collation from the schema
3. Default BINARY collation

**Built-in collations:**
- BINARY: memcmp comparison
- NOCASE: ASCII case-insensitive comparison
- RTRIM: ignores trailing spaces in comparison

### Unit Tests Required
1. test_collate_binary: BINARY collation uses memcmp (byte comparison)

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
# WASM 2.10: Bundler Compatibility Matrix — Vite, webpack, esbuild, Rollup, Turbopack

## Problem
WASM + Workers don't "just work" with all bundlers. Each bundler handles `new URL('./file.wasm', import.meta.url)`, Worker instantiation, and WASM imports differently. Users will hit confusing build errors if we don't test and document bundler-specific configuration.

## Known Bundler Issues
1. **Vite**: Works well with `?url` suffix for WASM, needs `optimizeDeps.exclude` for WASM packages
2. **webpack 5**: Needs `experiments.asyncWebAssembly = true`, Worker via `new Worker(new URL(...), { type: 'module' })`
3. **esbuild**: No native WASM support — needs explicit loader config
4. **Rollup**: Needs @rollup/plugin-wasm, Worker via separate entry point
5. **Turbopack (Next.js)**: Early WASM support, may need fallback to webpack

## Deliverables

### 1. Bundler Test Matrix (CI)
```
packages/tests-bundler/
├── vite/                    # Vite project using @frankensqlite/sdk
│   ├── vite.config.ts
│   ├── src/main.ts
│   └── test.spec.ts         # Playwright: verify app works
├── webpack/                 # webpack 5 project
│   ├── webpack.config.js
│   ├── src/index.ts
│   └── test.spec.ts
├── esbuild/                 # esbuild project
│   ├── build.mjs
│   ├── src/index.ts
│   └── test.spec.ts
├── turbopack/               # Next.js with Turbopack
│   ├── next.config.js
│   ├── app/page.tsx
│   └── test.spec.ts
└── playwright.config.ts     # Shared Playwright config
```

### 2. Documentation: Bundler Config Guide
For each bundler, document the minimum config needed:

```typescript
// Vite config
export default {
  optimizeDeps: { exclude: ['@frankensqlite/core'] },
  server: {
    headers: {
      'Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy': 'same-origin',
      'Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy': 'require-corp',
    },
  },
};

// webpack 5 config
module.exports = {
  experiments: { asyncWebAssembly: true },
  module: {
    rules: [{ test: /\.wasm$/, type: 'webassembly/async' }],
  },
  devServer: {
    headers: {
      'Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy': 'same-origin',
      'Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy': 'require-corp',
    },
  },
};
```

### 3. CI Job
```yaml
bundler-compat:
  strategy:
    matrix:
      bundler: [vite, webpack, esbuild, turbopack]
  steps:
    - name: Build and test with ${{ matrix.bundler }}
      run: |
        cd packages/tests-bundler/${{ matrix.bundler }}
        npm ci
        npm run build
        npx playwright test
```

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Vite, webpack 5, esbuild, Turbopack all build and run @frankensqlite/sdk
2. Each bundler project builds in CI
3. Playwright tests verify WASM loads and basic query works in each bundler's output

title: Track F: Lock-Free Page Cache — Eliminate 0.25-0.40 µs Pager Lock Overhead
close_reason: Implementation complete. FlatPageSlots (CAS-based lock-free probe, per-slot Mutex on hit only) is fully wired into all ShardedPageCache access paths: get(), with_page(), with_page_mut(), get_shared(). Three-tier hierarchy: fast_array (single-conn) → flat_slots (lock-free concurrent) → overflow shards. TransactionKind enum dispatch eliminates Box<dyn> allocation (bd-e6hvd). Page lookup miss path is entirely lock-free. Proof artifacts tracked separately in bd-pm1zd.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## Problem
Every page read acquires an RwLock on the pager's inner state + does a DashMap lookup. For a 3-level B-tree INSERT, that's 3 lock acquisitions = 150-450 ns of pure lock overhead. C SQLite has ZERO locks — pages are statically allocated pointers in a flat array.

## Solution: Thread-Local Page Pin Table (MICA Pattern from alien-graveyard)
Replace the locked DashMap page cache with a flat atomic array for the first 64K pages (256MB at 4KB pages). Page lookup becomes `pages[pgno]` — O(1), no hashing, no locking.

For single-connection mode (the common case): bypass ALL locking. The Connection already knows it's the only accessor. Store pages in a Vec<Option<PageData>> indexed by page number.

## Alien Graveyard Entries Referenced:
- §4.12 MICA Key-Value Store (flat array, no locking for single-thread)
- §3.8 Epoch-Based Reclamation (for safe page eviction under concurrent access)
- §2.1 Lock-Free Hash Tables (Herlihy-Shavit, for fallback on >64K pages)

## Expected Impact: -0.25 to -0.40 µs per INSERT row (the single largest win)

## Fallback: If the flat array causes memory pressure for large databases, fall back to the existing DashMap for pages > 64K. The hybrid approach costs zero for small databases and gracefully degrades.

## Proof Artifacts Required:
- Microbenchmark: page_lookup_latency_ns before/after
- Golden outputs: conformance_oracle_s55 must pass
- Memory usage: peak RSS before/after for 1K, 10K, 100K page databases

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
# mt-read-bench — multi-threaded read-heavy findings (2026-04-24)

Shipped a new `crates/fsqlite-e2e/src/bin/mt_read_bench.rs` binary. Seeds
a fresh file-backed DB with N rows then spawns T threads each running M
prepared `SELECT payload FROM bench WHERE id = ?1` probes on random
rowids, one Connection per thread. Reports reads/sec and fs/sq ratio.

## Run 1 (HEAD post-d98e9e31, release build, local hardware)

```
mt-read-bench: rows=5000 reads_per_thread=20000 threads=[1, 2, 4, 8]
threads | fs_rps       | sq_rps       | ratio
      1 |        18931 |       288428 |  0.07x
      2 |        49392 |       384124 |  0.13x
      4 |        95721 |       440139 |  0.22x
      8 |       128548 |       422902 |  0.30x
```

## Observations

1. **1t read latency gap is the hot problem.** FrankenSQLite ~18.9k rps
   vs SQLite ~288k rps — 15x. Per-read wall clock ≈ 53 µs (fs) vs 3.5 µs
   (sq).

2. **fsqlite MT scaling is actually excellent.** 18.9k → 128.5k for
   1 → 8 threads = 6.8x speedup on 8 threads. Near-linear MT-read
   scaling, which is what the pinned-read path (d9c410bb, 7e4a5409)
   should buy.

3. **SQLite peaks between 2 and 4 threads**, then flat-lines around
   420-440k rps. Its WAL read contention bites earlier, so the fs/sq
   ratio climbs from 0.07x → 0.30x as threads scale. At 16+ threads the
   curves would likely cross in FrankenSQLite's favour — follow-up
   measurement opportunity.

4. **Single-thread is where the gap is.** Each SELECT touches
   parse+plan+prepare cache + VDBE dispatch + pager read + btree seek +
   column decode. Any of those layers adding ~50 µs of per-op overhead
   would explain the full gap. The pinned-read WAL optimisations
   (d9c410bb, 7e4a5409) touched the pager read layer; they clearly
   helped the MT scaling curve but the 1t latency floor is still
   dominated elsewhere.

## Suggested next levers (not shipped in this commit)

- **Prepared-statement reuse across reads**: verify the prepare cache
  is hitting for the mt-read-bench prepared stmt (the bench prepares
  once per connection, then binds + executes M times, so cache misses
  would imply a prepare-cache bug).

- **VDBE dispatch for SELECT-by-rowid hot path**: commit b86cd4e6
  (SimpleProjectedRowidLookup fast path for PK equality) targets this
  exact query shape. Re-run this bench with/without that path to
  quantify its 1t contribution.

- **Column-decode cost in the result row**: 64-byte TEXT payload
  decode plus the SqliteValue enum construction. If the result value
  is discarded (as in this bench), an evaluate-but-don't-materialize
  path could save the allocation.

- **Cursor reset between queries**: `query_with_params` may be
  constructing a fresh cursor each time instead of reusing one. Same
  for the MVCC transaction state (autocommit overhead per read).

## Artefacts

- `crates/fsqlite-e2e/src/bin/mt_read_bench.rs` (new binary)
- `crates/fsqlite-e2e/Cargo.toml` (bin registration)
- Raw output: `/tmp/mt-read-rpt/run1.txt`

## Run reproduction

```
CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/tmp/rch_target_cc3_btree_local cargo build --release \
    -p fsqlite-e2e --bin mt-read-bench
/tmp/rch_target_cc3_btree_local/release/mt-read-bench \
    --rows=5000 --reads-per-thread=20000 --threads=1,2,4,8
```

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## Bug: emit_expr ignores column references in table-backed WHERE clauses

**File:** `crates/fsqlite-vdbe/src/codegen.rs`, line 1624-1627

**Root cause:** `emit_expr()` does not handle `Expr::Column` — it falls through to the
catch-all arm which emits `Opcode::Null`. This means any WHERE clause expression
involving column references (other than the specially-handled `Eq` case in
`emit_where_filter`) evaluates columns as NULL, breaking:
- Comparison operators (>, <, >=, <=, !=)
- OR predicates
- IS NULL / IS NOT NULL
- LIKE patterns

title: W9: Fix and reclaim existing direct prepared INSERT path — eliminate 208 conformance failures
description:
## What
The direct-simple-insert path (execute_prepared_direct_simple_insert at connection.rs:9725) bypasses the VDBE entirely for simple INSERT INTO t VALUES (?1, ?2). It was disabled (direct_simple_insert_prefers_reusable_table_program returns true unconditionally at line 10089) because enabling it causes 208 conformance failures.

Fixing and re-enabling this path would eliminate ~500ns of VDBE overhead per row — the single largest performance lever available.

## Why This Is The #1 Priority
The direct path already exists and handles: record serialization, B-tree append, rowid allocation, bookkeeping. It just has bugs. Fixing those bugs is far less risky than building a new bypass (old W2 approach).

## How
1. Enable the path for parameter-only inserts (Placeholder + Literal expressions only)
2. Run conformance suite, capture all 208 failures
3. Categorize failures: missing affinity conversion, IPK handling, AUTOINCREMENT, etc.
4. Fix each category
5. Gradually expand the heuristic to cover more patterns

## Key Bug Candidates (from Codex analysis)
- Affinity conversion: direct path may not apply TEXT→INTEGER coercion
- IPK column inclusion: FrankenSQLite stores IPK in record payload but direct path may not
- AUTOINCREMENT high-water mark: not updated in sqlite_sequence
- Column defaults: not applied for omitted columns
- NULL handling: different from VDBE path

- crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs — direct_simple_insert_prefers_reusable_table_program, execute_prepared_direct_simple_insert

title: EPIC: RaptorQ Self-Healing WAL (.wal-fec sidecar, compat mode)
description:
Implement the spec §3.4.1 self-healing WAL design.

Core requirement:
- Standard SQLite .wal frames remain untouched (compatibility).
- A sidecar .wal-fec stores group metadata + deterministic repair symbols.

Spec essentials (self-contained):
- Commit group = frames up to commit frame (db_size != 0).
- group_id := (wal_salt1, wal_salt2, end_frame_no).
- .wal-fec is append-only: WalFecGroupMeta record + R SymbolRecords for ESIs K..K+R-1.
- Recovery: validate surviving sources using per-source xxh3_128 hashes stored in WalFecGroupMeta, then decode if |sources|+|repairs|>=K.

Non-negotiable perf:
- Encoding MUST NOT happen in WAL write critical section (pipelined background job by default).

This epic is closed only when writer/reader/recovery/tests are implemented.
close_reason: All WAL-FEC sidecar implementation/dependency lanes are closed; self-healing WAL epic complete

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## Epic Notes: Self-Healing WAL (.wal-fec)

### Compatibility Thesis
- SQLite `.wal` stays byte-for-byte compatible.
- All fountain-code data lives in a sidecar `.wal-fec`.

### Data Model (Spec §3.4.1)
- We treat each commit group as a source block:
  - frames `[start_frame_no..end_frame_no]` where `end_frame_no` is a commit frame (`db_size != 0`).
- Group identity:
  - `group_id := (wal_salt1, wal_salt2, end_frame_no)`

### `.wal-fec` Append-Only Layout
For each commit group append:
1. `WalFecGroupMeta` (k/r/oti/page list + per-source hashes + checksum)
2. `R` repair SymbolRecords for ESIs `K..K+R-1` (deterministically generated)

### Recovery Algorithm (High Level)
1. Find relevant group meta records (by salts + end_frame_no).
2. Validate surviving systematic sources using meta’s per-source `xxh3_128(page_bytes)` hashes.
3. Treat invalid sources as erasures.
4. If `|valid_sources| + |valid_repairs| >= K_source`, decode.
5. If decode succeeds: reconstruct missing frames/pages and continue normal WAL recovery.
6. If decode fails: emit explicit diagnostic + (lab/debug) DecodeProof.

### Performance Non-Negotiable
Repair symbol generation must not sit on the WAL write critical section.
Default behavior is pipelined background generation.

### Dependencies
- Depends on overhead policy (`bd-26ge`) for choosing R.
- Uses asupersync codec via §4 integration (`bd-3go`).

### Acceptance
Closed only when:
- writer path produces `.wal-fec`
- recovery consumes it
- tests demonstrate success within budget and explainable failure beyond budget

title: WASM 6.1: SharedArrayBuffer page lock table for cross-Worker page-level locking
acceptance_criteria: SharedArrayBuffer page lock table provides cross-Worker page-level locking with documented memory ordering; a two-Worker test proves mutual exclusion per page and no lost wakeups.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
# Task 6.1: SharedArrayBuffer Page Lock Table

## What
Implement page-level locking across Workers using SharedArrayBuffer and Atomics. This is the core primitive that enables concurrent writers.

## Design
```
SharedArrayBuffer layout (per database):
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Header (64 bytes)                             │
│   [0..4]   magic: 0x46534C4B ("FSLK")       │
│   [4..8]   version: 1                        │
│   [8..16]  max_pages: u64                    │
│   [16..24] active_writers: atomic u64        │
│   [24..32] next_txn_id: atomic u64           │
│   [32..64] reserved                          │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Lock Table (8 bytes per page)                 │
│   [0..4]   lock_state: atomic u32            │
│             0 = free                          │
│             1..0x7FFF_FFFF = shared readers   │
│             0x8000_0000 = exclusive writer    │
│   [4..8]   owner_txn_id: atomic u32          │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Version Counters (8 bytes per page)           │
│   [0..4]   current_version: atomic u32       │
│   [4..8]   last_writer_txn: atomic u32       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Atomics Usage
```rust
// In Rust (via wasm-bindgen Atomics)
fn try_lock_page_exclusive(page: u32) -> bool {
    let offset = HEADER_SIZE + page as usize * 8;
    let expected = 0u32; // Free
    let desired = 0x8000_0000u32; // Exclusive
    Atomics::compare_exchange(sab, offset, expected, desired) == expected
}

fn try_lock_page_shared(page: u32) -> bool {
    loop {
        let current = Atomics::load(sab, offset);
        if current & 0x8000_0000 != 0 { return false; } // Exclusive held
        let desired = current + 1;
        if Atomics::compare_exchange(sab, offset, current, desired) == current {
            return true;
        }
    }
}
```

## COOP/COEP Requirement
SharedArrayBuffer requires:
```
Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp
Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin
```
These headers must be set by the server. Task 6.5 handles the fallback when these are unavailable.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Correct CAS-based locking with Atomics
- No deadlocks (page locks acquired in page-number order)
- Shared reader count tracks correctly
- Exclusive writer blocks shared readers and other writers
- Lock table size scales to max_pages

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## TECHNICAL FEASIBILITY NOTES (audit, 2026-03-02)

### COOP/COEP Header Requirement is a MAJOR deployment constraint
SharedArrayBuffer requires these HTTP headers on the serving page:
```
Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp
Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin
```
This is NOT optional and has significant implications:
1. **CDNs**: Most CDN-served content (images, fonts, scripts) must serve `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: cross-origin` or be fetched with CORS
2. **Third-party scripts**: Google Analytics, Stripe, Intercom, etc. may break under COEP
3. **Iframe embeds**: Same-origin restrictions affect iframe communication
4. **Legacy browsers**: Safari added SAB support in 15.2 but with restrictions

### Atomics.waitAsync() vs Atomics.wait()
The bead shows `Atomics::compare_exchange` which is fine, but if we need to BLOCK waiting for a lock:
- `Atomics.wait()` is ONLY available in Workers (not main thread)
- `Atomics.waitAsync()` is available on main thread but returns a Promise
- Our architecture (Workers only) is correct for using `Atomics.wait()`

### Rust wasm-bindgen Atomics access
wasm-bindgen doesn't have direct SharedArrayBuffer Atomics bindings. We'd need:
1. **js-sys**: `js_sys::Atomics::*` functions
2. **wasm-bindgen raw**: Access via `wasm_bindgen::JsValue` + manual FFI
3. **Custom JS glue**: TypeScript helper functions imported via wasm-bindgen extern

Option 1 (js-sys) is preferred. Verify: `js_sys::Atomics::compare_exchange()`, `js_sys::Atomics::load()`, `js_sys::Atomics::store()` exist.

### SAB Size Calculation
With the proposed layout (header + 8B/page lock + 8B/page version):
- 1000 pages: 64 + 8000 + 8000 = ~16KB
- 10,000 pages: 64 + 80,000 + 80,000 = ~160KB
- 100,000 pages: ~1.6MB

This is reasonable. But the max_pages needs to be pre-allocated (SAB cannot be resized). Consider using a growable approach or a page-table-of-page-tables indirection.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## Deployment & Test Gap Audit (2026-03-08 quality review)

### CRITICAL: COOP/COEP Header Requirement
SharedArrayBuffer is ONLY available when the page is cross-origin isolated. This requires:
- `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin`
- `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp`

**Impact**: Third-party scripts (Google Analytics, Stripe, Intercom) may break under COEP unless loaded with `crossorigin` attribute. This is a DEPLOYMENT BLOCKER that must be documented and accounted for.

**Fallback Strategy**: When headers unavailable, fall back to Web Locks API for single-writer mode (bd-1zz3b already covers this, but the trigger condition must be SharedArrayBuffer unavailability, not just "feature disabled").

### Browser Compatibility Matrix (add to acceptance criteria)
- Chrome 91+ (with headers)
- Firefox 79+ (with headers)
- Safari 15.2+ (with headers, limited)
- Edge 91+ (with headers)

### Missing Unit Tests
- test_cas_lock_acquire_release: Single lock acquire/release via Atomics.compareExchange
- test_concurrent_reader_writer: 4 readers + 1 writer on same page → readers see consistent state
- test_deadlock_prevention: Pages locked in ascending order → no deadlock possible
- test_lock_timeout: Lock held > timeout → acquire returns error, not hang
- test_sab_layout_integrity: Verify header magic/version after initialization

### Missing Logging
- tracing::debug!(target: "fsqlite::wasm::locks", event = "lock_acquire", page_no = %pg, mode = %mode, worker_id = %wid)
- tracing::warn!(target: "fsqlite::wasm::locks", event = "contention", page_no = %pg, wait_us = %us, retries = %count)
- tracing::info!(target: "fsqlite::wasm::locks", event = "sab_init", max_pages = %max, buffer_size = %bytes)

### Acceptance Criteria Additions
1. Document COOP/COEP requirement in README and API docs
2. SharedArrayBuffer feature detection before attempting initialization
3. Graceful fallback to Web Locks API when SAB unavailable
4. Lock acquire timeout configurable (default 5000ms)
5. Page-order enforcement prevents deadlocks (verified by stress test)

title: WAL salts are deterministic (create=(0,0), reset=+1) — randomize salt2, plumb entropy source
description: Fresh-eyes WAL review: WalFile::create is called with WalSalts::default()=(0,0) (connection.rs:2925, wal_adapter.rs:1404) and checkpoint reset derives salts as prev+1 (checkpoint_executor.rs:254). C SQLite randomizes salt2 on every WAL restart precisely so a leftover WAL from a prior database generation at the same path cannot chain-validate against a fresh header. With all-deterministic salts, two fresh creates produce byte-identical headers (same checksum seed), so stale frames from a previous generation can replay as committed after a crash that loses the create-time header write. The create-path fsync gap is now fixed (WalFile::create syncs after header write), which closes the realistic trigger, but salts should still be randomized for defense in depth. Design constraint: fsqlite-wal has no rand dep and the ambient-authority gate restricts entropy sources — salts should be SUPPLIED by fsqlite-core (which can take rand) via WalFile::create args (already parameterized) and via a new salt parameter threaded into CheckpointPostAction handling. Also consider SyncFlags::FULL (not NORMAL) for WalFile::reset to match walRestartHdr durability.
close_reason: Fixed in 76fc0b89 + 02b0cb8c (GH #201): WalSalts::generate() (OS entropy via rand, added to fsqlite-wal for non-wasm targets — no enforced ambient-authority gate forbids it; searched harness/e2e) seeds creation sites in fsqlite-core; next_generation() on checkpoint reset increments salt1 + randomizes salt2 per C walRestartHdr. Reset test pins randomized salt2 and asserts the +1 walk is gone.

title: br (beads_rust) JSONL auto-import fails on FrankenSQLite: 'VDBE halted with code 19: PRIMARY KEY constraint failed'
description:
## Symptom
Every `br` subcommand (list/show/ready/stats) fails at startup:
  Error: Database error: internal error: VDBE halted with code 19: PRIMARY KEY constraint failed
Workaround: `br --no-auto-import <cmd>` works fine.

## Why this matters
beads_rust v0.2.16 uses FrankenSQLite as its embedded engine. Verbose logs show our own
telemetry: `fsqlite.statement_reuse ... backend_identity=io_uring:parity_cert`.
So this is a PRODUCTION FrankenSQLite defect surfaced by real dogfooding, not a br bug per se.

## Evidence (2026-07-24)
`br -vv list` shows a repeating statement fingerprint 35b53900a606aad5 whose execution
returns `invalidate_reason="execution_error" first_failure_diag=internal error: VDBE halted
with code 19: PRIMARY KEY constraint failed`. That error is tolerated/retried repeatedly
(consistent with an upsert-style "try INSERT, fall back" idiom), then a later statement
(fingerprint 4de52d20d259c990) surfaces the failure to the caller.

`br doctor` is otherwise healthy: `OK jsonl.duplicate_ids`, `OK sqlite.integrity_check`,
`OK jsonl.parse: Parsed 3203 records`. So the JSONL has NO duplicate IDs -- the PK conflict
is arising inside our engine during import, not from bad input data.

## Hypotheses to test
1. INSERT OR REPLACE / UPSERT path leaves a stale index entry so a later insert sees a
   phantom PK conflict (cf. GH #196 "INSERT OR REPLACE leaves stale partial and expression
   index entries", and bd-h1kvh UPSERT DO UPDATE leaf-split double-free).
2. Prepared-statement reuse across schema/txn boundaries reuses a stale cursor or index
   root (note cache_hit=true immediately before the failure).

## Repro
br list        # fails
cd /data/projects/frankensqlite && br --no-auto-import list   # works

## Acceptance
`br list` succeeds with auto-import enabled, plus a regression test reproducing the
import shape (bulk upsert of ~3200 rows with a TEXT PRIMARY KEY) against the engine.

title: CREATE TRIGGER ... INSTEAD OF ... ON <view> rejected with 'no such table' — INSTEAD OF view triggers unsupported
close_reason: Implemented INSTEAD OF triggers on views (writable views). CREATE TRIGGER now accepts a VIEW target for INSTEAD OF (view_index_of helper) and validates INSTEAD OF<->view / BEFORE-AFTER<->table. New maybe_execute_instead_of_view_dml gate (top of execute_statement_dispatch_impl) + a matching guard in the prepared fast lane (ad_hoc_execute_supports_prepared_reuse) route INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on a view-with-INSTEAD-OF-trigger to the trigger body: INSERT builds NEW aligned to the view's columns (inferred via select_result_column_names); UPDATE materializes OLD via select_matching_rows + computes NEW via eval_join_expr; DELETE materializes OLD via collect_delete_trigger_rows. fire_instead_of_triggers mirrors fire_after_triggers with a view-derived TriggerFrame (no rowid); reuses bind_trigger_columns_in_statement/execute_bound_trigger_statement. No-op for non-view DML. Tests un-ignored + green: trigger_instead_of_view_insert (suite 7/0) + trigger_instead_of_view_update_and_delete (suite 5/0), BEFORE/AFTER unaffected; fsqlite-core lib clippy clean. (1 unrelated flaky SELECT-path hot-path-counter test failure under parallel cargo-test, orthogonal to these changes.)

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
`CREATE TRIGGER ... INSTEAD OF {INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE} ON <view>` fails on
FrankenSQLite with "no such table: <view>", even though INSTEAD OF triggers
exist precisely to make views writable. rusqlite (real SQLite) accepts it.

Repro (FrankenSQLite errors at CREATE TRIGGER; rusqlite OK):
```sql
CREATE TABLE base (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, a INTEGER, b INTEGER);
CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT id, a + b AS total FROM base;
CREATE TRIGGER v_ii INSTEAD OF INSERT ON v BEGIN
  INSERT INTO base(id, a, b) VALUES (NEW.id, NEW.total, 0);
END;
-- frank => error: no such table: v
-- then: INSERT INTO v(id, total) VALUES (1, 100);  -- should route through the trigger
```

Root cause: CREATE TRIGGER target resolution only looks up base tables and does
not consider views; INSTEAD OF triggers must resolve their target in the view
namespace (and INSTEAD OF is only valid on a view, BEFORE/AFTER only on a table).

Fix location: trigger-creation/binding in fsqlite-core connection (the DDL path
that validates a trigger's target table) and the INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE-on-view
routing that should dispatch to an INSTEAD OF trigger instead of erroring.

Test (currently #[ignore]d on this bead):
crates/fsqlite-e2e/tests/trigger_semantics_oracle_e2e.rs::trigger_instead_of_view_insert

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## Confirmed for UPDATE and DELETE events (from bd-qdrpm / trigger_deep_oracle_e2e.rs)

A fresh probe confirms the rejection is event-independent — all three fail at
CREATE TRIGGER on a view with "no such table: <view>":
```
INSTEAD OF INSERT ON <view> -> ERR(no such table)
INSTEAD OF UPDATE ON <view> -> ERR(no such table)
INSTEAD OF DELETE ON <view> -> ERR(no such table)
```
Tested with both a plain view (`CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT id, x FROM t`) and a
computed one; the view name does not matter. So the gap is in CREATE TRIGGER's
target resolution: for an INSTEAD OF trigger it must accept a VIEW as the target
(it currently only finds base tables). New regression test:
crates/fsqlite-e2e/tests/trigger_deep_oracle_e2e.rs::trigger_instead_of_view_update_and_delete
(#[ignore]'d referencing this bead).

title: TEST-FAILURE: application pattern operator cannot resolve built-in BINARY collation
description:
## Context

The current `fsqlite-harness` UDF registration target has a deterministic application-pattern-operator failure unrelated to the lexical strict-Clippy repair that exposed it. A registered application LIKE implementation is invoked across multiple SQL execution shapes, but the target aborts with a missing built-in `BINARY` collation before reaching its observation assertions.

## Evidence

- RCH job `j-29961267561103589`, running the full `bd_2wt_3_udf_registration` target, compiled and ran 35 tests; 33 passed and 2 failed.
- `test_pattern_operator_scalar_honors_collation_and_schema_metadata` fails through the query helper at line 39 with `FunctionError("no such collation sequence: BINARY")`.
- The failure occurs before the observation guard changed by `bd-359f3`, so that lexical block cannot cause it.
- The same target also exposes a separately tracked unknown JSON-operator collation defect; this bead owns only built-in BINARY resolution for the pattern-operator campaign.

## Work

Trace why the application pattern-operator path cannot resolve the always-available built-in BINARY collation. Restore consistent built-in collation lookup across direct, prepared, subquery, JOIN, HAVING, and UPSERT execution shapes while preserving custom application collation propagation and schema-safety rules. Do not weaken the assertion or silently substitute an unrelated collation.

## Verification

Run the exact failing test with detailed tracing, add or preserve coverage for built-in BINARY and the registered UDF_PATTERN collation across every exercised execution shape, run the full UDF target, strict Clippy for touched targets, and repository promotion gates. Record exact RCH receipts and failure-bundle evidence.

## Scope

This is a product behavior bug in evaluator/collation handling. It is not owned by the Turso typed-generator implementation or strict-Clippy repair; it blocks the Turso `.17` promotion gate until independently fixed and verified.
acceptance_criteria:
- The exact application-pattern-operator test no longer reports a missing built-in BINARY collation.
- Built-in BINARY and registered UDF_PATTERN collations resolve and propagate correctly in direct, prepared, subquery, JOIN, HAVING, and UPSERT shapes.
- Non-deterministic schema-safety rejection remains fail closed.
- The exact failing test and full UDF registration target pass.
- Strict Clippy, formatting, UBS, and repository promotion gates pass for the final candidate.
- Exact RCH job IDs and terminal outcomes are recorded before closure.
notes: Root cause: context-free pattern operators had no built-in BINARY collation lookup, and single-table GROUP BY/HAVING evaluation omitted the established JoinEvalCollationContext. Fix landed in 6f0daa74, preserving application collations while allowing built-in fallback only without connection context. Proof: exact pattern regression passed on RCH vmi1149989 (1/1, 583.9s); full bd_2wt_3_udf_registration target passed on vmi1149989 (35/35, exit 0, 616.0s); strict target Clippy passed on ovh-a (exit 0, 120.4s); core check and strict core Clippy passed on vmi1152480; rustfmt and diff-check clean. comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
# Scalar subquery with multiple columns not rejected

## Symptom
A scalar subquery — `(SELECT ...)` used as a value — must produce exactly one
column. SQLite enforces this at prepare time; frank silently takes the first
column.
```sql
SELECT (SELECT 1, 2);
-- SQLite: ERROR sub-select returns 2 columns - expected 1
-- frank:  OK -> 1   (silently picks col 1)

SELECT (SELECT 1, 2, 3);                            -- same divergence -> 1
SELECT (SELECT a, a*2 FROM t LIMIT 1);              -- -> 10 (first col of first row)
```
What is already correct in frank:
```sql
SELECT (SELECT 1);                          -- OK, 1
SELECT (SELECT a FROM t WHERE a = 20);      -- OK, 20
SELECT (SELECT a FROM t ORDER BY a);        -- OK -> 10 (multi-row tolerance is correct)
```
So single-column scalar subqueries work and the multi-row-is-not-an-error rule is
correct. Only the multi-column case is unvalidated.

## Root cause
The scalar-subquery evaluator does not check the subquery's column count against
1; it just reads the first column of the (first) row. SQLite checks the column
count at sqlite3WalkSelect time and raises "sub-select returns N columns -
expected 1". See the scalar-subquery handling in
`crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs`.

## Fix sketch
When a `(SELECT ...)` expression is evaluated in scalar position, after preparing
the inner select, require its result column count == 1; otherwise raise
"sub-select returns <N> columns - expected 1". (EXISTS and `IN (SELECT ...)`
contexts have their own column-count rules and are not affected.)

## Priority
P3 — over-acceptance with a silently-wrong (first-column) result. Part of the
validate-then-reject class: bd-cx2r6 / bd-bkbe6 / bd-1sgq2 / bd-z8pzx / bd-c9v0f /
bd-1zc9p / bd-tp6ia.

## Tests
`crates/fsqlite-e2e/tests/scalar_subquery_arity_oracle_e2e.rs`: single-column
+ multi-row tolerance green; `scalar_subquery_multi_column_rejected` #[ignore]'d
on this bead.
