title: §2: Why Page-Level MVCC — Problem, Granularity, Isolation, Layered Solution
description:
SECTION 2 OF COMPREHENSIVE SPEC — WHY PAGE-LEVEL MVCC

The foundational rationale for the core MVCC innovation. Every implementor must understand this deeply.

§2.1 THE PROBLEM: In WAL mode, C SQLite allows multiple concurrent readers but only ONE writer. WAL_WRITE_LOCK (byte 120 of WAL index SHM) is an exclusive advisory lock. Any write attempt while another holds it → SQLITE_BUSY (or SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT when reader-turned-writer detects WAL snapshot conflict). For mixed read/write workloads across different tables/regions, this is needless bottleneck — two users inserting into unrelated tables should never wait.

§2.2 WHY PAGE GRANULARITY (not row or table):
  - Row-level (PostgreSQL-style): Minimal false conflicts BUT requires visibility map, per-row xmin/xmax, BREAKS file format, requires VACUUM.
  - Page-level (OUR CHOICE): Maps to B-tree I/O unit, preserves file format, simple version chains. Con: false conflicts when rows share a page.
  - Table-level: Trivial but nearly useless (most apps have few tables).
  Page-level is the sweet spot: maps directly to SQLite's B-tree page architecture (pages are already the unit of I/O, caching, WAL frames), preserves on-disk format, provides meaningful concurrency for real workloads where writers typically touch different leaf pages.

§2.3 THE ISOLATION LEVEL PROBLEM (CRITICAL):
  C SQLite provides SERIALIZABLE isolation trivially because writers are serialized.
  Page-level MVCC provides Snapshot Isolation (SI), which is WEAKER. SI allows WRITE SKEW anomaly.
  Example: Table (A=50, B=50), constraint sum>=0. T1 reads both, withdraws 90 from A→-40. T2 reads both, withdraws 90 from B→-40. Both commit. Sum=-80. Constraint violated. Under SERIALIZABLE one would see the other's write.
  THIS IS A DATA CORRUPTION RISK. SQLite users depend on SERIALIZABLE. We cannot silently downgrade.

§2.4 THE SOLUTION — LAYERED ISOLATION:
  LAYER 1 (Default): SQLite behavioral compatibility mode (single-writer, WAL semantics).
    - BEGIN / BEGIN DEFERRED: DEFERRED. No write lock at BEGIN. First write → acquire global write mutex → proceed as single writer.
    - BEGIN IMMEDIATE / BEGIN EXCLUSIVE: Acquire global write mutex at BEGIN.
    - This is default. Existing SQLite apps observe SERIALIZABLE for writer interactions without sacrificing concurrent readers.
    - Interop boundary: Hybrid SHM (foo.db.fsqlite-shm) — legacy SQLite processes supported as readers only; legacy writers excluded (SQLITE_BUSY while coordinator alive).

  LAYER 2: MVCC concurrent mode with SSI (Serializable by Default).
    - BEGIN CONCURRENT: New non-standard syntax (matching SQLite's experimental branch). Page-level MVCC with SSI — not merely SI.
    - Multiple concurrent writers, first-committer-wins on page conflicts, plus SSI to prevent write skew.
    - Conservative Cahill/Fekete rule at page granularity ("Page-SSI"): no committed txn may have both incoming AND outgoing rw-antidependency edge. Prevents serialization cycles.
    - 3-7% throughput overhead (OLTP, Ports & Grittner VLDB 2012; up to 10-20% synthetic micro without read-only opts) — acceptable for correctness.
    - PRAGMA fsqlite.serializable = OFF → explicit opt-out to plain SI for benchmarking/apps that tolerate write skew. NOT default.
    WHY SSI SHIPS BY DEFAULT:
    - SI silently downgrades correctness. SQLite users depend on SERIALIZABLE.
    - Page-SSI rule (has_in_rw && has_out_rw => abort) is simple: two boolean flags per txn plus witness plane.
    - PostgreSQL proven SSI viable since 2011, 3-7% OLTP overhead, ~0.5% false positive abort rate. Page granularity higher false positives but safe write-merge ladder (§5.10) compensates.
    - Starting with SSI from day one = no correctness regression. Can reduce abort rates later (finer witness keys, better victim selection) but can't retroactively fix apps that relied on SI.

  LAYER 3 (Future refinement): Reduced-abort SSI.
    - Reduce false positive aborts via witness refinement: Cell(btree_root_pgno, cell_tag) and/or ByteRange(page, start, len) for point ops; KeyRange(...) for range scans.
    - Smarter victim selection (not always aborting committing pivot).
    - VOI-driven investment: VOI = E[ΔL_fp] * N_txn/day - C_impl. Only invest when VOI > 0.

## UNIT TEST REQUIREMENTS
- test_single_writer_serializable_trivially: Under Layer 1 (default), writers are serialized by global write mutex; verify execution is equivalent to some serial order (SERIALIZABLE)
- test_page_level_mvcc_provides_si: Under Layer 2 (BEGIN CONCURRENT), page-level MVCC provides Snapshot Isolation; verify concurrent readers see consistent snapshots
- test_write_skew_detected_by_ssi: Classic write-skew anomaly (§2.3 sum constraint example) is detected and aborted by SSI under BEGIN CONCURRENT
- test_page_granularity_false_conflict: Two transactions writing different rows on the same page produce a false page-level conflict; verify first-committer-wins behavior
- test_layer1_begin_deferred_upgrades_on_write: BEGIN/BEGIN DEFERRED acquires no write lock at BEGIN; first write attempt acquires global write mutex
- test_layer1_begin_immediate_acquires_mutex: BEGIN IMMEDIATE acquires global write mutex at BEGIN (writer-intent)
- test_layer2_pragma_serializable_off: PRAGMA fsqlite.serializable = OFF downgrades to plain SI; verify write skew is NOT detected
- test_legacy_reader_interop: In Hybrid SHM mode, legacy SQLite processes can read but legacy writers get SQLITE_BUSY while coordinator is alive

## E2E TEST
test_e2e_layered_isolation_full_stack: Exercise all three isolation layers in sequence: Layer 1 (single-writer compatibility), Layer 2 (BEGIN CONCURRENT with SSI), and verify Layer 3 refinement hooks exist. Run the §2.3 write-skew scenario under each layer. Verify: Layer 1 serializes, Layer 2 detects and aborts, PRAGMA OFF permits write skew.

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] Layer 1 (default mode) provides SERIALIZABLE isolation via single-writer serialization
- [ ] Layer 2 (BEGIN CONCURRENT) provides SERIALIZABLE via SSI with 3-7% OLTP overhead
- [ ] Write-skew anomaly (§2.3) is provably prevented under both Layer 1 and Layer 2 (SSI on)
- [ ] PRAGMA fsqlite.serializable = OFF explicitly opts out to plain SI (not default)
- [ ] Legacy SQLite reader interop works via Hybrid SHM; legacy writers are excluded with SQLITE_BUSY

## Success Criteria

- [ ] Isolation model layers are implemented as specified: Layer 1 (serialized writer compatibility), Layer 2 (BEGIN CONCURRENT + SSI), Layer 3 (refinements), with clear PRAGMA controls.
- [ ] Write-skew and SSI anomaly suites run end-to-end through the public API and pass deterministically under the lab runtime.
- [ ] Compatibility-mode interop with C sqlite3 is validated where required (busy semantics, lock protocol, snapshots).
- [ ] Logging requirements implemented for SSI edges/aborts and regime changes; failures capture minimal repro artifacts.
- [ ] Spec coverage audit complete for the embedded §2 extract.

## §2 Full Spec Text (Verbatim Extract)
Source: COMPREHENSIVE_SPEC_FOR_FRANKENSQLITE_V1.md lines 333-456

## 2. Why Page-Level MVCC

### 2.1 The Problem

In WAL mode, C SQLite allows multiple concurrent readers but caps the number
of simultaneously active reader locks via `WAL_NREADER` in the wal-index shared
memory (default: 5). It still allows only ONE writer at a time. The
`WAL_WRITE_LOCK` (byte 120 of the WAL index shared memory) is an exclusive
advisory lock. Any connection attempting to write while another holds this lock
receives `SQLITE_BUSY` (or `SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT` when a reader-turned-writer
detects a WAL snapshot conflict: the wal-index header has changed since the
read transaction started, so upgrading to a writer would create a fork).

For applications with mixed read/write workloads across different tables or
different regions of the same table, this is a needless bottleneck. Two users
inserting into unrelated tables should never wait for each other.

### 2.2 Why Page Granularity

| Granularity | Pros | Cons |
|-------------|------|------|
| **Row-level** (PostgreSQL) | Minimal false conflicts | Requires visibility map, per-row xmin/xmax, breaks file format |
| **Page-level** (our choice) | Maps to B-tree I/O unit, preserves file format, simple version chains | False conflicts when rows share a page |
| **Table-level** | Trivial implementation | Nearly useless (most apps have few tables) |

Page-level is the sweet spot: it maps directly to SQLite's B-tree page
architecture (pages are already the unit of I/O, caching, and WAL frames),
preserves the on-disk file format, and provides meaningful concurrency for
real-world workloads where writers typically touch different leaf pages.

### 2.3 The Isolation Level Problem (CRITICAL)

**C SQLite provides SERIALIZABLE isolation** -- trivially, because writers are
serialized by the WAL_WRITE_LOCK. Every execution is equivalent to some serial
ordering of transactions.

**Page-level MVCC provides Snapshot Isolation (SI)**, which is weaker. SI allows
the **write skew anomaly**: two transactions T1 and T2 each read overlapping
data, each writes to a different item based on what they read, and both commit
successfully -- but the combined result is inconsistent.

**Example:** Table has two rows (A=50, B=50), sum=100. Constraint: sum >= 0.
T1 reads both (50, 50), decides safe to withdraw 90, writes A = 50-90 = -40.
T2 reads both (50, 50), decides safe to withdraw 90, writes B = 50-90 = -40.
Both commit. Sum is now -40 + -40 = -80. Constraint violated. Under
SERIALIZABLE, one would have seen the other's write and aborted.

**This is a data corruption risk.** SQLite users depend on SERIALIZABLE. We
cannot silently downgrade.

### 2.4 The Solution: Layered Isolation

**Layer 1 (Default): SQLite behavioral compatibility mode (single-writer, WAL semantics).**
- `BEGIN` / `BEGIN DEFERRED`: DEFERRED. No writer-exclusion lock is acquired at
  `BEGIN`. Readers do not block readers. On the first write attempt, the
  transaction MUST upgrade to a Serialized writer by acquiring the global write
  mutex (§5.4) and then proceed as the single writer.
- `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` / `BEGIN EXCLUSIVE`: Acquire the global write mutex at
  `BEGIN` (writer-intent). This provides the usual "single writer" behavior
  while allowing concurrent readers (WAL semantics).
- This is the default mode. **Within FrankenSQLite**, existing SQLite
  applications observe SERIALIZABLE behavior for writer interactions (writers
  are serialized) without sacrificing concurrent readers.
- **Interop boundary:** When running Hybrid SHM (`foo.db.fsqlite-shm`), legacy
  SQLite processes are supported as readers only; legacy writers are excluded
  and will observe `SQLITE_BUSY` while the coordinator is alive (§5.6.6.1,
  §5.6.7).

**Layer 2: MVCC concurrent mode with SSI (Serializable by Default).**
- `BEGIN CONCURRENT`: New non-standard syntax (matching SQLite's own
  experimental `BEGIN CONCURRENT` branch). Uses page-level MVCC with
  **Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)** -- not merely Snapshot Isolation.
- Multiple concurrent writers, first-committer-wins on page conflicts, plus
  SSI validation to prevent write skew anomalies.
- SSI implements the conservative Cahill/Fekete rule at page granularity
  ("Page-SSI"): no committed transaction may have both an incoming AND
  outgoing rw-antidependency edge. This prevents serialization cycles.
- Applications that opt in get **SERIALIZABLE** concurrent writes. The 3–7%
  throughput overhead measured on OLTP benchmarks with PostgreSQL 9.1+ (Ports &
  Grittner, VLDB 2012; up to 10–20% on synthetic microbenchmarks without
  read-only optimizations) is acceptable for correctness.
- `PRAGMA fsqlite.serializable = OFF` provides an explicit opt-out to plain
  Snapshot Isolation for benchmarking or applications that tolerate write skew.
  This is NOT the default.
- This is where the concurrency innovation lives.

**Why SSI ships by default (not deferred):**
- SI silently downgrades correctness. SQLite users depend on SERIALIZABLE.
  Shipping SI-only concurrent mode creates a correctness trap where applications
  that switch from `BEGIN` to `BEGIN CONCURRENT` get weaker guarantees without
  warning.
- The conservative Page-SSI rule (`has_in_rw && has_out_rw => abort`) is
  simple to implement: two boolean flags per transaction plus a witness plane
  that makes read/write evidence discoverable across processes (§5.6.4, §5.7).
  Hot-plane overhead is bounded by `TxnSlot` count and hot bucket capacity
  (bitsets over slots); cold-plane evidence is append-only but GC-able by
  `safe_gc_seq` horizons.
- PostgreSQL has proven SSI viable in production since 2011 with 3–7% OLTP
  overhead (up to 10–20% on microbenchmarks) and ~0.5% false positive abort
  rate. At page granularity, our false positive
  rate will be somewhat higher, but the safe write-merge ladder (Section 5.10)
  compensates by turning many apparent conflicts into successful merges.
- Starting with SSI from day one means we never ship a correctness regression.
  We can always *reduce* abort rates later (finer witness keys + refinement,
  better victim selection), but we cannot retroactively fix applications that
  relied on SI and experienced silent write skew.

**Layer 3 (Future refinement): Reduced-abort SSI.**
- Reduce false positive aborts via witness refinement:
  - point operations: `Cell(btree_root_pgno, cell_tag)` and/or `ByteRange(page, start, len)`
  - range scans: leaf-page `Page(leaf_pgno)` witnessing remains required for phantom protection,
    but MAY be refined with `KeyRange(...)` witnesses when implemented (§5.6.4.3)
- Smarter victim selection (instead of always aborting the committing pivot).
- These are optimizations of SSI, not correctness changes.
- **Value of Information (VOI) for granularity investment:** The decision to
  invest engineering effort in cell/byte-range witness refinement should be
  data-driven. Compute `VOI = E[ΔL_fp] * N_txn/day - C_impl`, where `E[ΔL_fp]`
  is the expected reduction in false positive abort cost (measured by the SSI
  e-process monitor INV-SSI-FP in §5.7), `N_txn/day` is daily transaction volume,
  and `C_impl` is the amortized implementation cost. Only invest when VOI > 0.
  This prevents premature optimization of witness granularity.

title: Implement Layer 1: SQLite Behavioral Compatibility Mode (§2.4)
description:
Implement Layer 1 — the default single-writer, WAL-semantics mode that provides SQLite behavioral compatibility.

TRANSACTION SEMANTICS:
- BEGIN / BEGIN DEFERRED: DEFERRED mode. No writer-exclusion lock at BEGIN. Readers don't block readers. On first write attempt, transaction MUST upgrade to Serialized writer by acquiring global write mutex (§5.4), then proceed as single writer.
- BEGIN IMMEDIATE / BEGIN EXCLUSIVE: Acquire global write mutex at BEGIN (writer-intent). Single writer behavior while allowing concurrent readers (WAL semantics).
- This is the DEFAULT mode. Existing SQLite applications observe SERIALIZABLE behavior for writer interactions without sacrificing concurrent readers.

INTEROP BOUNDARY:
- When running Hybrid SHM (foo.db.fsqlite-shm), legacy SQLite processes supported as readers only
- Legacy writers excluded and will observe SQLITE_BUSY while coordinator is alive (§5.6.6.1, §5.6.7)

RATIONALE: This is the safe default. Applications that don't explicitly opt into concurrent mode get exactly the same behavior as C SQLite. This is critical for drop-in compatibility.

CRATE: fsqlite-mvcc (transaction state machine), fsqlite-wal (WAL integration), fsqlite-core (connection API)
ACCEPTANCE: All C SQLite conformance tests for transaction behavior pass in this mode. BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK/SAVEPOINT work correctly. Single writer serialization verified.

## Acceptance Criteria

title: Implement Layer 2: BEGIN CONCURRENT with SSI (§2.4)
description:
Implement Layer 2 — MVCC concurrent mode with Serializable Snapshot Isolation, activated by BEGIN CONCURRENT.

TRANSACTION SEMANTICS:
- BEGIN CONCURRENT: Non-standard syntax (matching SQLite's experimental branch). Uses page-level MVCC with SSI.
- Multiple concurrent writers, first-committer-wins on page conflicts
- SSI validation: Conservative Cahill/Fekete rule at page granularity ("Page-SSI"): no committed transaction may have both incoming AND outgoing rw-antidependency edge
- Expected 3-7% throughput overhead on OLTP (Ports & Grittner, VLDB 2012; up to 10-20% on synthetic micro without read-only optimizations)
- PRAGMA fsqlite.serializable = OFF: Explicit opt-out to plain SI for benchmarking/apps tolerating write skew. NOT the default.

WHY SSI SHIPS BY DEFAULT (key design rationale to remember):
1. SI silently downgrades correctness — SQLite users depend on SERIALIZABLE
2. Page-SSI rule (has_in_rw && has_out_rw => abort) is simple: two boolean flags per txn plus witness plane
3. PostgreSQL proven viable since 2011, 3-7% OLTP overhead, ~0.5% false positive abort rate
4. At page granularity, higher false positive rate but safe write-merge ladder (§5.10) compensates
5. Starting with SSI from day one = no correctness regression ever

IMPLEMENTATION COMPONENTS:
- Parser: recognize BEGIN CONCURRENT syntax
- MVCC: page-level version chains, concurrent snapshot management
- SSI: rw-antidependency tracking via witness plane (§5.7), two boolean flags per transaction (has_in_rw, has_out_rw)
- Conflict resolution: first-committer-wins + safe write merge (§5.10)
- PRAGMA: fsqlite.serializable pragma implementation

CRATE: fsqlite-mvcc (core), fsqlite-parser (syntax), fsqlite-vdbe (transaction handling), fsqlite-core (connection API)
ACCEPTANCE: Concurrent writers commit in parallel when touching different pages. Write skew anomaly detected and aborted. PRAGMA fsqlite.serializable = OFF allows write skew. SSI overhead < 15% on OLTP benchmark.

## UNIT TEST REQUIREMENTS
- test_begin_concurrent_parsed: Parser recognizes BEGIN CONCURRENT syntax and creates a Concurrent-mode transaction object
- test_concurrent_disjoint_writes_both_commit: T1 writes page P1, T2 writes page P2; both commit successfully with no conflict
- test_concurrent_same_page_first_committer_wins: T1 and T2 both write page P1; first to commit succeeds, second gets conflict error
- test_ssi_write_skew_detected_and_aborted: Classic write-skew scenario (§2.3 two-account sum constraint); SSI detects dangerous structure and aborts one transaction
- test_ssi_dangerous_structure_both_flags: Transaction with both has_in_rw and has_out_rw boolean flags set is aborted at commit validation
- test_ssi_rw_antidependency_tracking: Verify rw-antidependency edges are correctly detected: T1 reads K, T2 writes K after T1's snapshot -> incoming edge on T1
- test_pragma_serializable_off_allows_skew: With PRAGMA fsqlite.serializable = OFF, BEGIN CONCURRENT uses plain SI and write skew is NOT detected
- test_concurrent_mixed_with_serialized: Connections using BEGIN CONCURRENT and BEGIN IMMEDIATE coexist correctly with proper mutual exclusion

## E2E TEST
test_e2e_begin_concurrent_correctness_and_throughput: Run a curated SQL corpus exercising concurrency-critical semantics under BEGIN CONCURRENT. Verify all results are serializable (no anomalies). Compare throughput of BEGIN CONCURRENT vs BEGIN IMMEDIATE under disjoint page writes. Log SSI false positive abort rate and commit latency distribution.

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] BEGIN CONCURRENT syntax is parsed and activates page-level MVCC with SSI
- [ ] Concurrent writers commit in parallel when touching different pages
- [ ] Write-skew anomaly is detected and aborted under SSI (default)
- [ ] PRAGMA fsqlite.serializable = OFF explicitly allows write skew
- [ ] SSI overhead < 15% on OLTP benchmark vs single-writer mode
close_reason: Layer 2 MVCC tests (8/8), PRAGMA fsqlite.serializable ON/OFF, SSI gating in commit pipeline

title: Plan Layer 3: Reduced-Abort SSI Refinement (§2.4)
description:
Layer 3 — Future refinement to reduce SSI false positive aborts.

APPROACHES:
1. Witness refinement: Cell(btree_root_pgno, cell_tag) and/or ByteRange(page, start, len) for point ops (currently Page-level).
   - Range scans: Leaf-page Page(leaf_pgno) witnessing remains required for phantom protection
   - MAY refine with KeyRange(...) witnesses when implemented (§5.6.4.3)
2. Smarter victim selection: Instead of always aborting the committing pivot, choose the transaction whose abort costs least.

DECISION FRAMEWORK (VOI-driven):
- VOI = E[ΔL_fp] * N_txn/day - C_impl
- E[ΔL_fp]: expected reduction in false positive abort cost (measured by SSI e-process monitor INV-SSI-FP in §5.7)
- N_txn/day: daily transaction volume
- C_impl: amortized implementation cost
- Only invest when VOI > 0 — prevents premature optimization of witness granularity

NOTE: This is an optimization, not a correctness change. Layer 2 is correct without this.

PRIORITY: P3 (backlog) — implement only after Layer 2 is proven stable and abort rates measured.
CRATE: fsqlite-mvcc (witness refinement), fsqlite-btree (finer witness registration)

## UNIT TEST REQUIREMENTS
- test_cell_witness_reduces_false_positives: Compare SSI false positive abort rate with Page-level witnesses vs Cell-level witnesses on identical workload; Cell-level must show lower rate
- test_byte_range_witness_finer_than_page: ByteRange(page, start, len) witnesses cover smaller scope than Page(pgno); verify fewer false conflicts on point operations
- test_refinement_preserves_no_false_negatives: Finer witnesses must not introduce false negatives (missed real conflicts); property test with known conflict schedules
- test_voi_framework_computes_actionable_score: VOI = E[DeltaL_fp] * N_txn/day - C_impl; verify framework produces a numeric score and recommends invest/skip based on VOI > 0
- test_keyrange_phantom_protection: Range scans with KeyRange(...) witnesses still detect phantom insertions (no phantom anomaly)
- test_smarter_victim_selection: When SSI detects dangerous structure, victim selection considers abort cost rather than always aborting the committing pivot

## E2E TEST
test_e2e_layer3_refinement_abort_reduction: Run a representative workload and compare abort rates with Layer 3 refinement disabled (Page-level only) vs enabled (Cell/ByteRange witnesses). Verify correctness unchanged (no false negatives) while false positive abort rate measurably decreases.

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] Cell-level and/or ByteRange witness types are implemented and registerable during B-tree operations
- [ ] VOI framework exists and produces actionable investment recommendations for granularity refinement
- [ ] Finer witnesses provably do not introduce false negatives (property-tested)
- [ ] False positive abort rate decreases measurably when refinement is enabled vs Page-level only
- [ ] Phantom protection preserved for range scans via leaf-page or KeyRange witnesses

title: Implement Write Skew Detection Test Suite (§2.3)
description:
Create a comprehensive test suite that verifies write skew detection works correctly.

THE CANONICAL WRITE SKEW EXAMPLE (from §2.3):
Table has two rows (A=50, B=50), constraint sum>=0.
T1 reads both (50, 50), withdraws 90, writes A = 50-90 = -40.
T2 reads both (50, 50), withdraws 90, writes B = 50-90 = -40.
Under SI: both commit → sum = -80 → constraint violated → DATA CORRUPTION.
Under SSI: one detects rw-antidependency cycle → aborts → constraint preserved.

TEST CASES:
1. Classic write skew (above example) → verify one transaction aborts under BEGIN CONCURRENT
2. Same scenario under BEGIN (Layer 1) → verify serialized execution prevents skew
3. Same scenario with PRAGMA fsqlite.serializable = OFF → verify both commit (SI behavior)
4. Non-conflicting concurrent writes → verify both commit successfully

title: Implement Isolation Level Switching PRAGMA (§2.4)
description:
Implement PRAGMA fsqlite.serializable to control SSI behavior in concurrent mode.

BEHAVIOR:
- PRAGMA fsqlite.serializable = ON (default): Full SSI enforcement for BEGIN CONCURRENT transactions
- PRAGMA fsqlite.serializable = OFF: Explicit opt-out to plain Snapshot Isolation — allows write skew, for benchmarking or applications that tolerate it
- This pragma has NO effect on Layer 1 (BEGIN/BEGIN IMMEDIATE/BEGIN EXCLUSIVE) which are always serialized by the global write mutex

IMPORTANT: OFF is NOT the default. This is deliberate to prevent silent correctness downgrades.

IMPLEMENTATION:
- Add to PRAGMA parser and handler
- Store setting per-connection (not per-database)
- SSI validation checks this flag before performing rw-antidependency analysis
- When OFF, skip SSI validation entirely in commit path (pure first-committer-wins)

CRATE: fsqlite-vdbe (PRAGMA handling), fsqlite-mvcc (SSI validation gate)
ACCEPTANCE: PRAGMA changes behavior correctly. Default is ON. Tests verify both modes.

- [ ] E2E test suite covers Layer 2 SSI vs SI mode and validates that anomalies are prevented/allowed as expected.
- [ ] Logging requirements implemented: INFO for mode at BEGIN, DEBUG for PRAGMA changes and SSI edges, INFO/WARN for aborts and false-positive drift.

title: U1: Dirty bitmap + deferred WAL flush — track dirty pages as bits, batch-flush at commit
close_reason: Deferred: :memory: mode already skips WAL/journal. The write_set HashMap is the per-page cost (~50ns insert). A dirty bitmap would save ~49ns per page but requires significant pager refactoring. Better to focus on S1 (Rc swap) for immediate impact.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## What
Add a dirty-page bitmap to the transaction state. On page write: set the bit. On commit: iterate set bits, flush those pages to WAL.

## Implementation
File: crates/fsqlite-pager/src/pager.rs

1. Add to transaction state: `dirty_bitmap: Vec<u64>` (bit per page)
2. On write_page: `dirty_bitmap[pgno / 64] |= 1 << (pgno % 64)` — 1 CPU cycle
3. Check before write: if bit already set, skip journal/notification — instant return
4. On commit: `for word in dirty_bitmap { for bit in set_bits(word) { flush_page(pgno) } }`
5. For single-connection :memory: mode: skip group commit queue entirely

## C SQLite Pattern
sqlite3PagerWrite checks `pPg->flags & PGHDR_WRITEABLE`. We check `dirty_bitmap[pgno/64] & (1 << pgno%64)`. Same O(1) check, different representation.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Page write after first dirty: < 5 cycles (from current 100-500)
2. UPDATE benchmark: ≥ 10% improvement
3. DELETE benchmark: ≥ 10% improvement
4. No data loss on crash (WAL flush at commit is unchanged)
5. conformance_oracle_s55 passes

## Risk & Fallback
Risk: The bitmap must be consistent with actual dirty state. If a page is dirtied but bitmap not set, data loss.
Fallback: Keep existing write path as fallback; bitmap is an optimization layer on top.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## FINDING (Review): Group Commit May Already Be Skipped for :memory:

Line 652 in pager.rs: `if vfs.is_memory() { ... }` — :memory: mode likely has a different commit path that skips group commit.

### Revised U1 Scope
Before implementing the dirty bitmap, FIRST verify:
1. Does :memory: mode already skip group commit queue coordination?
2. What is the actual per-write overhead for :memory: B-tree page modifications?
3. Profile: where does the time actually go during page writes?

If :memory: already skips group commit, U1's dirty bitmap helps only FILE-BACKED databases (which is still valuable for the autocommit benchmark).

### The bitmap itself remains useful
Even for :memory:, a bitmap is cheaper than HashMap for tracking dirty pages:
- HashMap insert: ~50ns (hash + probe + store)
- Bitmap set: ~1ns (bit OR)
- For 10K rows modifying ~100 unique pages: saves ~5 µs total (modest)

### Priority: Profile FIRST, then decide if bitmap is worth it for :memory:

title: T2/W11: Persistent rightmost-leaf state for full BTREE_APPEND parity
description:
## What
C SQLite BTREE_APPEND flag positions the cursor at the rightmost leaf in O(1) by caching the rightmost page. FrankenSQLite currently does a FULL root-to-leaf seek on every INSERT even when the append fast-path fires, because table_insert (not table_insert_prechecked_absent) is called.

The profiling agent confirmed: the append fast-path correctly sets exists=false but then calls table_insert which does a full seek (~500-850ns per insert).

## Why
This is ~500-850ns per row — the single largest B-tree bottleneck. At 100K rows, that is 50-85ms of pure waste.

## How
1. After the append fast-path determines the row is new (exists=false, rowid > last_successful), position the cursor at the rightmost leaf ONCE (via cursor.last())
2. Cache the rightmost leaf page number in the StorageCursor
3. On subsequent appends: if cursor is already at the rightmost leaf AND the new rowid > last rowid, insert directly at the end without any seek
4. This matches C SQLite BTREE_APPEND behavior: btreeInsertInto with seekResult=-1 appends at current position

## Key Implementation Detail
table_insert_prechecked_absent expects the cursor to be at the correct position from a prior seek. For append mode, the cursor needs to be at the END of the rightmost leaf. Call cursor.last() once, then use table_insert_prechecked_absent for all subsequent appends.

The challenge: table_insert_prechecked_absent calls table_insert_from_current_position which reads from the cursor stack. After cursor.last(), the stack has the rightmost leaf. This is EXACTLY where we want to insert.

## Files
- crates/fsqlite-vdbe/src/engine.rs — Insert opcode handler, append fast-path
- crates/fsqlite-btree/src/cursor.rs — table_insert_prechecked_absent, append optimization

## Estimated impact
~500-850ns per row → 50-85ms at 100K rows. ~10-17% of total gap.
acceptance_criteria: Persistent rightmost-leaf state eliminates redundant seek on verified append shapes only; non-append, gap, split, and rebalance cases fall back conservatively; Track T tests plus zero-seek counters prove parity.

title: Differential Privacy for aggregate queries (§12.5)
description:
Implement differential privacy mechanisms for aggregate queries. Differential privacy adds calibrated noise to query results such that the inclusion or exclusion of any single row changes the output distribution by at most a factor of e^epsilon (the privacy budget).

## Mathematical Foundation
(epsilon, delta)-differential privacy: for any two databases D and D-prime differing in one row, and any set of outputs S: Pr[M(D) in S] <= e^epsilon * Pr[M(D-prime) in S] + delta, where M is the mechanism.

For COUNT queries: add Laplace noise with scale 1/epsilon.
For SUM queries: add Laplace noise with scale (max_value - min_value)/epsilon.
For AVG queries: use noisy SUM / noisy COUNT.

Privacy budget tracking: each query consumes epsilon from the budget. When budget is exhausted, no more queries allowed (or answers become very noisy).

## Application in FrankenSQLite
- PRAGMA differential_privacy = ON (enable per-connection)
- SET privacy_budget = 1.0 (total epsilon budget)
- Aggregate queries automatically add calibrated noise
- Privacy budget tracked and enforced per-session

## Alien CS Reference
Dwork and Roth 2014 The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy: comprehensive textbook covering Laplace mechanism, composition theorems, and budget tracking. McSherry 2009 Privacy Integrated Queries PINQ: practical system for differentially private SQL queries with automatic sensitivity analysis. Wilson et al. 2020 Differentially Private SQL with Bounded User Contribution: Google implementation addressing multi-row user contributions.

## Rust Implementation Guidance
- Implement LaplaceMechanism with sample method using rand::distributions::Open01 for Laplace sampling
- Privacy budget: PrivacyBudget { total_epsilon: f64, remaining_epsilon: AtomicF64 } per connection
- Sensitivity analysis: implement for COUNT (sensitivity=1), SUM (sensitivity=max-min), AVG (derived)
- Hook into aggregate execution: after computing exact aggregate, add calibrated noise before returning
- Use opendp crate as reference for noise calibration correctness
- Feature-gate behind differential-privacy Cargo feature flag

## Logging Requirements
- Log privacy budget allocation at tracing::info level: connection_id, total_epsilon
- Log each query privacy cost at tracing::info level: query_hash, epsilon_consumed, remaining_budget
- Log budget exhaustion at tracing::warn level: connection_id, queries_served
- Never log the actual noise values (that would leak privacy)

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Laplace mechanism for COUNT, SUM, AVG
- [ ] Privacy budget tracking and enforcement
- [ ] Pragma-based enable/disable
- [ ] Correctness: noise calibration matches theoretical bounds
- [ ] Utility analysis: query accuracy at various epsilon values
acceptance_criteria: 1. Implementation is complete and behaviorally correct against explicit invariants and edge-case requirements, including fault and recovery paths where applicable. 2. Comprehensive unit/property tests cover normal, boundary, and adversarial conditions with deterministic fixtures and regression seeds. 3. End-to-end scenario scripts validate integrated behavior in real execution flows and include deterministic replay instructions. 4. Structured logging/metrics (traceable IDs, timing, counters, error context) are emitted and validated so failures are diagnosable and auditable.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
A multi-statement explicit transaction (`BEGIN ... COMMIT`, promoted to BEGIN
CONCURRENT) that performs an UPDATE or DELETE of a pre-existing row panics in
the prepared-direct write path:

  panicked at crates/fsqlite-mvcc/src/begin_concurrent.rs:1308:5
  "prepared page writes must retain their page lock before staging bytes"
  (debug_assert on handle.holds_page_lock(page))

Repro (FrankenSQLite; rusqlite handles all of these fine):
```sql
CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, v INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1,10),(2,20);
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO t VALUES (3,30);
UPDATE t SET v = 99 WHERE id = 1;   -- panics here / in COMMIT staging
COMMIT;
```

Observed in 3 scenarios, all of which contain an UPDATE or DELETE of an existing
row inside an explicit BEGIN:
  - BEGIN; INSERT; UPDATE; COMMIT
  - BEGIN; INSERT; SAVEPOINT sp; INSERT; UPDATE; ROLLBACK TO sp; ...; COMMIT
  - BEGIN; SAVEPOINT outer; INSERT; SAVEPOINT inner; INSERT; UPDATE; ROLLBACK TO outer; ...
INSERT-only explicit transactions, DDL-in-txn rollback, and SAVEPOINT-based
implicit transactions (no explicit BEGIN) all PASS — so the trigger is
UPDATE/DELETE staging inside an explicit multi-statement transaction.

Severity: debug_assert fires in debug/test builds; in release the invariant is
violated silently (the prepared write is staged without the page lock held),
which risks lost updates / corruption under the page-level MVCC scheme.

Fix location: the prepared-direct UPDATE/DELETE write path under BEGIN CONCURRENT
must acquire/retain the page lock before staging bytes (begin_concurrent.rs
around the prepared-write staging at :1300-1312), or the assertion's precondition
is being bypassed for the explicit-transaction case.

crates/fsqlite-e2e/tests/transaction_savepoint_oracle_e2e.rs:

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
# 5F.2: End-to-end storage stack test script with structured logging

## What

A comprehensive integration test that exercises the ENTIRE Phase 5 pipeline from database
creation to concurrent writers, with detailed structured logging at every step. This is the
definitive "does the storage stack work?" test.

## Test structure

The test follows a real-world database lifecycle:

### Stage 1: Database creation and DDL (validates 5A)
```
[E2E][stage=1_ddl][step=create_db] Creating fresh database at {path}
[E2E][stage=1_ddl][step=create_table] CREATE TABLE users(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, email TEXT UNIQUE)
[E2E][stage=1_ddl][step=verify_sqlite_master] sqlite_master entries=1 root_page=2
[E2E][stage=1_ddl][step=create_index] CREATE INDEX idx_email ON users(email)
[E2E][stage=1_ddl][step=verify_sqlite_master] sqlite_master entries=2 idx_root_page=3
[E2E][stage=1_ddl][step=schema_cookie] cookie_value=2 (incremented twice)
```

### Stage 2: Write operations (validates 5B)
```
[E2E][stage=2_write][step=insert_batch] Inserting 1000 rows via autocommit
[E2E][stage=2_write][step=insert_progress] inserted=100/1000 elapsed_ms=12
...
[E2E][stage=2_write][step=insert_complete] inserted=1000 total_ms=87 rows_per_sec=11494
[E2E][stage=2_write][step=update_batch] Updating 500 rows
[E2E][stage=2_write][step=delete_batch] Deleting 100 rows
[E2E][stage=2_write][step=verify_counts] expected=900 actual=900
```

### Stage 3: Read operations (validates 5C)
```
[E2E][stage=3_read][step=full_scan] SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY id
[E2E][stage=3_read][step=full_scan_result] rows=900 elapsed_ms=5
[E2E][stage=3_read][step=index_seek] SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'user500@test.com'
[E2E][stage=3_read][step=index_seek_result] rows=1 elapsed_ms=0
[E2E][stage=3_read][step=aggregate] SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(id) FROM users
[E2E][stage=3_read][step=aggregate_result] count=900 sum=expected_sum
[E2E][stage=3_read][step=join] SELECT u.name FROM users u WHERE u.id IN (SELECT id FROM users WHERE id < 10)
[E2E][stage=3_read][step=join_result] rows=9
```

### Stage 4: Transaction lifecycle (validates 5D)
```
[E2E][stage=4_txn][step=begin] BEGIN
[E2E][stage=4_txn][step=insert] INSERT INTO users VALUES (10001, 'txn_user', 'txn@test.com')
[E2E][stage=4_txn][step=rollback] ROLLBACK
[E2E][stage=4_txn][step=verify_rollback] SELECT WHERE id=10001 → rows=0 ✓
[E2E][stage=4_txn][step=begin] BEGIN
[E2E][stage=4_txn][step=insert] INSERT INTO users VALUES (10001, 'txn_user', 'txn@test.com')
[E2E][stage=4_txn][step=savepoint] SAVEPOINT sp1
[E2E][stage=4_txn][step=insert] INSERT INTO users VALUES (10002, 'sp_user', 'sp@test.com')
[E2E][stage=4_txn][step=rollback_to] ROLLBACK TO sp1
[E2E][stage=4_txn][step=verify] id=10001 present ✓, id=10002 absent ✓
[E2E][stage=4_txn][step=commit] COMMIT
[E2E][stage=4_txn][step=verify_commit] id=10001 present ✓
```

### Stage 5: Persistence and reopen (validates 5D + WAL)
```
[E2E][stage=5_persist][step=checkpoint] PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)
[E2E][stage=5_persist][step=checkpoint_result] pages_checkpointed=N
[E2E][stage=5_persist][step=close] Connection::close()
[E2E][stage=5_persist][step=reopen] Connection::open({path})
[E2E][stage=5_persist][step=verify] SELECT COUNT(*) = 901 ✓
[E2E][stage=5_persist][step=verify_data] Spot-checking 10 random rows... all match ✓
```

### Stage 6: Concurrent writers (validates 5E)
```
[E2E][stage=6_mvcc][step=setup] Creating accounts table with 100 rows, balance=1000 each
[E2E][stage=6_mvcc][step=spawn] Spawning 4 concurrent writer threads
[E2E][stage=6_mvcc][step=thread_0] commits=250 retries=12 restarts=3 elapsed_ms=340
[E2E][stage=6_mvcc][step=thread_1] commits=250 retries=8 restarts=5 elapsed_ms=360
[E2E][stage=6_mvcc][step=thread_2] commits=250 retries=15 restarts=1 elapsed_ms=310
[E2E][stage=6_mvcc][step=thread_3] commits=250 retries=10 restarts=4 elapsed_ms=350
[E2E][stage=6_mvcc][step=verify_conservation] SUM(balance)=100000 ✓ (expected=100000)
[E2E][stage=6_mvcc][step=verify_no_locks] Lock table empty ✓
```

### Stage 7: Final integrity check
```
[E2E][stage=7_integrity][step=pragma] PRAGMA integrity_check
[E2E][stage=7_integrity][step=result] ok ✓
[E2E][stage=7_integrity][step=page_count] total_pages=N
[E2E][stage=7_integrity][step=freelist] freelist_pages=M
[E2E][stage=7_integrity][step=summary] ALL 7 STAGES PASSED | total_elapsed_ms=1234
```

## Implementation

This test lives in `tests/e2e_storage_stack.rs` as an integration test.

Key requirements:
- Uses `tempdir()` for isolated test databases
- Each stage is a separate function that returns `Result<StageReport>`
- `StageReport` contains timing, assertion results, and structured log entries
- On any failure, dump full diagnostic state before panicking
- Print final summary with timing breakdown per stage
- Can be run standalone: `cargo test --test e2e_storage_stack -- --nocapture`

## Diagnostic dump on failure

When any assertion fails, before panicking:
```rust
fn dump_diagnostics(conn: &Connection, path: &str) {
    eprintln!("[DIAG] Database path: {path}");
    eprintln!("[DIAG] Page size: {}", conn.pragma_query_value("page_size"));
    eprintln!("[DIAG] Page count: {}", conn.pragma_query_value("page_count"));
    eprintln!("[DIAG] WAL file size: {} bytes", fs::metadata(format!("{path}-wal")).map(|m| m.len()).unwrap_or(0));
    eprintln!("[DIAG] Journal mode: {}", conn.pragma_query_value("journal_mode"));
    eprintln!("[DIAG] Integrity check: {}", conn.pragma_query_value("integrity_check"));
    // Dump sqlite_master
    for row in conn.query("SELECT * FROM sqlite_master") {
        eprintln!("[DIAG] sqlite_master: {row:?}");
    }
}
```

## Tests

- The e2e script IS the test — it's self-verifying at each stage
- `test_e2e_storage_stack_full`: Run all 7 stages end-to-end
- `test_e2e_storage_stack_stage_N`: Individual stages for targeted debugging

title: PRAGMA assignment must emit no rows for bool-toggle pragmas (oracle divergence)
description:
Verified empirically against sqlite3 3.46.1:

```
PRAGMA trusted_schema=ON;      -> (no rows)   bare -> 0
PRAGMA read_uncommitted=ON;    -> (no rows)   bare -> 0
PRAGMA cell_size_check=ON;     -> (no rows)   bare -> 0
PRAGMA checkpoint_fullfsync=ON;-> (no rows)   bare -> 0
PRAGMA automatic_index=ON;     -> (no rows)   bare -> 1
PRAGMA reverse_unordered_selects=ON; -> (no rows)
PRAGMA cache_spill=OFF;        -> (no rows)
```

vs. pragmas that DO echo a row on assignment:
```
PRAGMA locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE; -> exclusive
PRAGMA secure_delete=ON;       -> 1
PRAGMA threads=4;              -> 4
PRAGMA soft_heap_limit=N;      -> effective limit
PRAGMA hard_heap_limit=N;      -> effective limit
```

`apply_bool_toggle` in crates/fsqlite-vdbe/src/lib.rs:1686 returns `PragmaOutput::Bool(enabled)` on assignment, which crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs:50707 turns into a one-row result. C SQLite returns zero rows. This affects all five pragmas listed in that fn's doc comment (GH #282, #278, #262, #281, #283 — all currently closed as fixed).

Fix requires a new `PragmaOutput::NoRows` variant (`Unsupported` cannot be reused — it falls through to further dispatch in connection.rs) mapped to `Ok(vec![])`, and `apply_bool_toggle` returning it for the assignment arm.

Note: `PRAGMA trusted_schema` bare readback is 0 on the Ubuntu 3.46.1 oracle build (SQLITE_TRUSTED_SCHEMA=0 at compile time) but ConnectionPragmaState::default() has `trusted_schema: true`. Confirm which is intended before touching it — that is a build-flag difference, not necessarily a bug.
close_reason: STALE BEAD — already fixed by the has_value result-columns gate. The filed diagnosis (apply_bool_toggle returns Bool -> connection.rs emits a one-row result on assignment) predates the has_value-gated block in pragma_result_columns (connection.rs ~4643): for trusted_schema/read_uncommitted/cell_size_check/checkpoint_fullfsync/automatic_index, has_value=true (assignment) returns &[] columns, so the Bool arm hits result_columns.is_empty() -> Ok(Vec::new()) = ZERO rows; bare query (has_value=false) falls through to the one-column arm -> one 0/1 row. No PragmaOutput::NoRows variant needed. Oracle-verified vs rusqlite (SQLite 3.46.1) for all 5 pragmas: assignment=0 rows, bare=1 row. Keeper: crates/fsqlite-core/tests/bd_ji5oe_bool_toggle_pragma_no_rows.rs (1 passed) locks the parity and guards against dropping a name from the has_value list.

title: JSONB numeric payloads encoded as raw big-endian binary — not byte-compatible with SQLite JSONB (silent cross-engine numeric misread)
description:
## SUMMARY
FrankenSQLite's JSONB encoder writes INT and FLOAT node payloads as raw
big-endian binary, but SQLite's JSONB format stores numeric payloads as
ASCII text. Our blobs are internally round-trip consistent, yet a JSONB
blob stored in a table by FrankenSQLite and later read by stock SQLite
(or vice versa) silently misinterprets every numeric payload — a
silent-wrong-value interop hazard that violates the project's
file-format-compatibility mandate ("a UTF-8 FrankenSQLite database
remains readable by C SQLite without conversion").

## EVIDENCE (verified at HEAD 2026-08-14)
- crates/fsqlite-ext-json/src/lib.rs, `encode_jsonb_value` (~lines
  929-968): INT payload = `i64::to_be_bytes` (~936/939), FLOAT payload =
  `f64::to_bits().to_be_bytes()` (~942/948).
- SQLite's JSONB format (and our own closed spec bead bd-3cvl, "KEY DATA
  STRUCTURES": node types int(0x3)/int5(0x4)/float(0x5)/float5(0x6))
  stores numeric payloads as the ASCII text representation of the number
  (canonical RFC-8259 text for 0x3/0x5; JSON5 text for 0x4/0x6), NOT
  fixed-width binary.
- The header-nibble layout (4-bit type + payload-size-size) DOES match
  the spec, which makes the divergence extra dangerous: stock SQLite
  parses the envelope fine and then decodes garbage numbers instead of
  erroring.

## WHY IT MATTERS
Any workflow where jsonb() output lands in a stored column and the file
is later opened by stock SQLite (the documented interop path: checkpoint
+ sequential hand-off) yields wrong numeric values with no error. Also
breaks json_valid(X, 0x08) strict-JSONB cross-checking vs the oracle.

## FIX SKETCH
1. Emit ASCII-decimal payloads for INT/FLOAT on encode; decide via
   differential test against rusqlite's jsonb()/json() output whether to
   accept legacy binary payloads on decode during a transition or do a
   strict cutover.
2. Audit decode paths for the same assumption.
3. CHANGELOG note: JSONB blobs written by earlier fsqlite builds need a
   json(jsonb_blob) re-encode round-trip.

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] Differential test: for a corpus of ints/floats (i64 extremes,
      -0.0, exponents, non-finite rejection), fsqlite `jsonb(?)` bytes
      == rusqlite `jsonb(?)` bytes, and rusqlite `json(fsqlite_blob)`
      reproduces the original minified text (and vice versa).
- [ ] Stock sqlite3 CLI reads a table of fsqlite-written JSONB blobs and
      `json_extract` returns correct numeric values.
- [ ] Existing internal round-trip tests remain green.
- [ ] Oracle e2e added under crates/fsqlite-e2e/tests/ AND wired into a
      CI workflow allowlist (bd-ohk1x class — a local-only keeper does
      not count as done).

## PROVENANCE
Found during frankensqlite-mega-skill codebase research (2026-08-13/14);
recorded in the skill's EXTENSIONS-AND-VTABS reference and research pack
(je_private_skills_repo).
close_reason: Fixed in 0.3.1 wave, verified at HEAD: encode_jsonb_value now emits ASCII numeric payloads (Number::to_string for INT incl. u64>i64::MAX staying INT-typed; {:?} shortest round-trip for FLOAT) plus direct-size-nibble and escaped-text-element fixes beyond this bead's scope (5f6602db6/9e5c90ffe, 457 insertions). Acceptance met: test_jsonb_bytes_match_sqlite3_oracle does rusqlite byte-for-byte comparison; escaped-string round-trip + stock-escape decode + JSON5 numeric decode tests added; inline lib tests are CI-covered by the unit-test --lib shards (not subject to the bd-ohk1x tests/ allowlist hole). Legacy caveat documented in skill: pre-fix blobs carry raw-BE numerics and need json(jsonb_blob) re-encode.

SCOPE GREW under the byte-level oracle — the bead's claim that the envelope matched the spec was WRONG: live hex(jsonb(...)) capture from sqlite3 3.46.1 showed THREE divergences, all fixed: (1) numeric payloads now ASCII text (decimal for ints incl. u64>i64::MAX which stock keeps INT-typed; shortest-round-trip {:?} text for floats — '1e300'/'-0.0'/'0.1' byte-identical to stock for canonical inputs; Number::to_string's '1e+300' was itself non-canonical and is also fixed in our json() renderer); (2) header size nibble now encodes payload size DIRECTLY for 0..=11 with 12/13/14/15 as 1/2/4/8-byte length prefixes (the old scheme wrote a spurious length byte stock parsed as payload — every 1-11-byte payload was envelope-corrupt, not just numerics); (3) strings now TEXT when clean / TEXTJ with RFC-8259 escapes when needed (raw-TEXT quotes previously made stock render invalid JSON), and the decoder resolves TEXTJ/TEXT5 escapes + tolerates INT5/FLOAT5/TEXTRAW reading stock blobs. comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## BUG: printf — %u and %* unimplemented (emit literal); %c semantics differ from SQLite

Oracle parity vs rusqlite (bundled ~3.46). scalar_function/string_function show
%d/%x/%o/%i/%e/%g/%f/%s/%q/%Q/%w and width/precision/flags (%-Nd, % d, %.Ns) all
work. Three gaps remain:

```sql
SELECT printf('%u', 42);      -- frank: '%u'      csql: '42'   (unsigned int unimplemented -> emitted literally)
SELECT printf('[%*d]', 5, 42);-- frank: '[%*d]'  csql: '[   42]' (dynamic '*' width unimplemented -> emitted literally)
SELECT printf('%c', 65);      -- frank: 'A'       csql: '6'
```

- `%u`: not recognized, so it falls through to the "output the conversion
  literally" path. Should format the integer argument as an unsigned decimal
  (for 42 that is just '42').
- `%*d`: the `*` (take the field width from the next argument) is not handled;
  the whole conversion is emitted literally. Should consume the next arg (5) as
  the width and right-justify (`'   42'`).
- `%c`: frank treats the argument as a Unicode code point (65 -> 'A'); SQLite's
  SQL printf takes the argument's TEXT form and emits its first character
  (65 -> text "65" -> '6'). frank's result diverges from SQLite's.

### Fix area
crates/fsqlite-func/src/builtins.rs — the printf/format specifier dispatch (the
same match that handles %d/%x/%o/%g and has an "unknown specifier: output
literally" fallback around builtins.rs:2440). Add `%u` and `%*` handling, and
align `%c` with SQLite's first-character-of-text semantics.

### Test
crates/fsqlite-e2e/tests/printf_advanced_oracle_e2e.rs —
printf_quote_q, printf_quote_Q_and_w, and the %o/%i/%e/%g + width/precision/flag
cases pass; the %u/%c and %* cases are isolated (#[ignore]) on this bead.

A compound SELECT whose branches have different numbers of result columns is
silently accepted by FrankenSQLite; SQLite rejects it at prepare time.

Repro (FrankenSQLite returns rows; rusqlite errors):
```sql
CREATE TABLE a (x INTEGER, y INTEGER);
INSERT INTO a VALUES (1,2);
SELECT x FROM a UNION SELECT x, y FROM a;
```
frank => OK (returns rows; arity not validated)
csql  => Error: SELECTs to the left and right of UNION do not have the same
         number of result columns

Applies to UNION / UNION ALL / INTERSECT / EXCEPT. All branches of a compound
must produce the same number of columns; the mismatch must be a prepare-time
error.

Fix location: compound-SELECT validation in fsqlite-planner/parser (or codegen)
must check that every arm has equal output arity and raise the standard error.

title: Fixture selection UX: tags/filters + stable db_id resolution
description:
## Goal

Make fixture selection ergonomic and unambiguous for humans and automation.

## Requirements

- Every fixture has a stable `db_id` (manifest-driven) that is used across:
  - CLI flags (`--db <db_id>`)
  - JSON reports
  - TUI UI

- Add filtering by:
  - tag (`--tag beads`)
  - size range
  - requires header_ok
  - has_wal_sidecar_at_capture

- Resolve ambiguity:
  - if user passes a stem that matches multiple, show all candidates and fail with a clear error.

## Acceptance

- `realdb-e2e run --db <id>` never silently picks the wrong DB.
- `realdb-e2e corpus scan` output aligns with the IDs the rest of the harness uses.
acceptance_criteria:
Acceptance Criteria

1. Stable db_id resolution:
   - CLI commands (`realdb-e2e run`, `bench`, `corrupt`, `verify`) accept `--db <db_id>` and resolve via the corpus manifest/metadata.
   - If a user-provided identifier is ambiguous, the CLI prints all candidates and exits non-zero (no silent choice).

2. Filtering UX:
   - Support filtering fixture selection by at least:
     - tag (taxonomy defined in `bd-1n0i`)
     - size range or size bucket
     - header_ok

title: BUG-P1: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN reports SEARCH for IN(...) while the emitted VDBE program is a full Rewind/Next scan
description:
EQP text is rendered from the planner directive in connection.rs, not from the program codegen actually emits. Ground truth via EXPLAIN on the same DB (t(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, k INTEGER, v TEXT), idx_t_k on k):

  SELECT * FROM t WHERE k = 2                     EQP: SEARCH   opcodes: SeekGE, IdxRowid, SeekRowid   (truthful)
  SELECT * FROM t WHERE k IN (SELECT id FROM r)   EQP: SEARCH   opcodes: Rewind, Next ONLY             (FALSE)
  SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t WHERE k = 2              EQP: SCAN     opcodes: Rewind, Next                  (truthful)

Impact: (1) IN(list) and IN(subquery) never index-seek despite EQP claiming SEARCH; (2) any planner/index work validated against EQP output is unverified, because EQP can report a seek for a program that contains no seek opcode. Conformance or perf work that greps EQP for 'SEARCH' will pass while the engine full-scans.

Fix direction: derive EQP from the emitted program (or from the access path codegen actually took), not from the planner directive, so the two cannot diverge. Until then, validate index work with EXPLAIN opcode assertions, not EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN text.

Found while investigating bd-2dgf5. Filed by cc_fsq 2026-07-09.
close_reason: Fixed in 5268f25b (opcode-fact helpers) + 8d940d7d (verification gate in execute_explain_query_plan + regression test). EQP now renders seek claims only when the emitted program performs them; compile failure cannot vouch (RusticBasin review applied). 25/0 tests incl. C-parity suite. Perf half (make IN-subquery actually seek) continues as bd-g5ys1.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## cc_fsq 2026-07-10 — HALF fixed by d1306c7b. The original case still lies.

Fixed: the AGGREGATE branch. EQP for an aggregate is now read off the emitted program
(explain::aggregate_index_seek_facts): SEARCH iff a Seek* positions an index cursor,
COVERING iff no IdxRowid on that cursor feeds a SeekRowid. Verified on the same schema:

  SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t WHERE k IN (1,2)
    EQP: 'SCAN t'          opcodes: Rewind, Next        -> TRUTHFUL (was a lie)

STILL LYING: the non-aggregate branch, which is your original repro. It renders from
the planner directive, which I did not touch:

  SELECT * FROM t WHERE k IN (1,2)
    EQP: 'SEARCH t USING INDEX idx_t_k (k=?)'   opcodes: Rewind, Next ONLY  -> FALSE

Why I scoped it that way: the directive path feeds EQP for most queries, so replacing
it moves text engine-wide and belongs in this bead, not in a perf lever.

title: §14.6 ICU Extension: Unicode Collation + Tokenization
description:
E2E Test:
- test_e2e_bd_jzjn_compliance: concrete E2E identifier for structure lint compliance.

## SUMMARY
Implement the ICU extension (crate: fsqlite-ext-icu) providing Unicode-aware string operations using the ICU (International Components for Unicode) library. Features: locale-aware collation creation via icu_load_collation(locale, name) which creates a named collation using ICU's ucol_strcoll for linguistically correct sort order; locale-aware case conversion via icu_upper(X, LOCALE) and icu_lower(X, LOCALE) providing full Unicode case folding (unlike built-in upper/lower which handle ASCII only); and ICU tokenizer integration with FTS3/4/5 for language-aware word breaking using UBreakIterator, critical for CJK languages where words are not space-delimited.

## KEY DATA STRUCTURES / ALGORITHMS
- ICU collation: wraps ICU's UCollator (ucol_open + ucol_strcoll). Each registered collation holds a locale identifier and an open collator handle.
- icu_load_collation(locale, name): creates a collation from an ICU locale identifier (e.g., 'de_DE', 'zh_CN', 'ja_JP'). The collation uses ucol_strcoll for comparison.
- icu_upper(X, LOCALE) / icu_lower(X, LOCALE): uses ICU's u_strToUpper / u_strToLower with locale-specific rules. Handles full Unicode case folding including: German sharp-s (ss<->SS), Turkish dotted/dotless I, Greek final sigma, etc.
- ICU FTS tokenizer: implements Fts5Tokenizer (and FTS3/4 tokenizer interface) using ICU's UBreakIterator with word-break rules for the specified locale. Usage: tokenize='icu zh_CN'. Critical for Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and Thai where word boundaries are not marked by spaces.
- UBreakIterator: ICU's boundary analysis API. UBRK_WORD mode identifies word boundaries according to Unicode UAX #29 rules plus locale-specific exceptions.

## NORMATIVE INVARIANTS
1. icu_load_collation creates a named collation usable in ORDER BY, WHERE, GROUP BY, DISTINCT, and index creation.
2. The collation uses ICU's ucol_strcoll, not a simplified comparison.
3. icu_upper/icu_lower handle full Unicode case folding, not just ASCII.
4. icu_upper/icu_lower require a LOCALE parameter; it is not optional.
5. The ICU FTS tokenizer uses UBreakIterator with UBRK_WORD mode.
6. The ICU tokenizer locale parameter determines word-break rules (critical for CJK).
7. ICU collations produce linguistically correct sort order for the specified locale (e.g., German umlauts sort correctly in de_DE).
8. The ICU extension has a heavyweight dependency (libicu); it must be independently feature-gated.

## UNIT TEST REQUIREMENTS
1. test_icu_load_collation_basic: icu_load_collation('en_US', 'english') creates collation
2. test_icu_collation_order_by: ORDER BY col COLLATE english uses ICU comparison
3. test_icu_collation_german: German locale sorts umlauts correctly (ä near a, not after z)
4. test_icu_collation_case: ICU collation handles case according to locale rules
5. test_icu_collation_accents: accented characters sort according to locale rules
6. test_icu_upper_basic: icu_upper('hello', 'en_US') = 'HELLO'
7. test_icu_upper_unicode: icu_upper('café', 'fr_FR') = 'CAFÉ'
8. test_icu_upper_german_sharp_s: icu_upper('straße', 'de_DE') = 'STRASSE'
9. test_icu_upper_turkish_i: icu_upper('i', 'tr_TR') = 'İ' (dotted capital I)
10. test_icu_lower_basic: icu_lower('HELLO', 'en_US') = 'hello'
11. test_icu_lower_turkish_I: icu_lower('I', 'tr_TR') = 'ı' (dotless lowercase i)
12. test_icu_lower_greek_sigma: icu_lower('ΣΟΣΟΣ', 'el_GR') handles final sigma
13. test_icu_fts5_tokenizer_english: tokenize='icu en_US' tokenizes English text correctly
14. test_icu_fts5_tokenizer_chinese: tokenize='icu zh_CN' segments Chinese text into words
15. test_icu_fts5_tokenizer_japanese: tokenize='icu ja_JP' handles Japanese text
16. test_icu_fts5_tokenizer_thai: tokenize='icu th_TH' handles Thai text (no spaces)
17. test_icu_fts5_search_cjk: FTS5 with ICU tokenizer finds Chinese/Japanese terms
18. test_icu_collation_in_index: CREATE INDEX with ICU collation works

20. test_icu_collation_in_group_by: GROUP BY with ICU collation groups correctly

- test_e2e_bd_jzjn_compliance: concrete E2E identifier for structure lint compliance.
Create databases with multilingual text data (English, German, French, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Thai, Turkish, Greek). Register ICU collations for each locale and verify sort order matches expected linguistic rules. Test icu_upper/icu_lower with locale-specific case folding edge cases (German sharp-s, Turkish I, Greek sigma). Create FTS5 tables with ICU tokenizer for CJK languages and verify search queries find correct documents. Compare all results against C sqlite3 with ICU extension.

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
1. icu_load_collation creates working collations from ICU locale identifiers.
2. ICU collations produce linguistically correct sort order for tested locales.
3. icu_upper/icu_lower handle full Unicode case folding with locale specificity.
4. ICU FTS tokenizer correctly segments CJK text into words.
5. ICU tokenizer works with FTS3/4/5.
6. Extension is independently feature-gated with ICU as an optional dependency.

comments.text:
# Audit: CellSlotCache hit rate on the write-append hot path

Ran `audit_cell_slot_cache_hit_rate_write_vs_read` (release, `MemPageStore`,
10_000 rows of 35-byte payload) after commit 4b061dcc dropped `parse_cell_at`
from interior `child_page_at`. Global `CellSlotCache::get` counters wired
unconditionally (Relaxed atomics, single increment per call) so any workload
can read ground-truth hit/miss data.

## Raw measurements

| Scenario | hits | misses | total | hit-rate | calls/op |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| monotonic_append (10k `table_insert`) | 0 | 1 | 1 | 0.00% | ~0.0001 |
| random_insert (10k `table_insert`) | 0 | 12 | 12 | 0.00% | ~0.001 |
| read_heavy_after_append (40k `table_move_to`) | 0 | 0 | 0 | — | 0 |
| reverse_seek_preloaded (500 `table_move_to`) | 0 | 0 | 0 | — | 0 |
| delete_all_after_append (10k seek+delete) | 98 | 10_000 | 10_098 | **0.97%** | ~1 |
| index_random_insert (10k `index_insert`) | 64_416 | 66_852 | 131_268 | **49.07%** | ~13 |

## Findings

1. `parse_cell_at` is effectively **cold on the table-insert hot path**. Every
   `table_insert` on a monotonic rowid short-circuits through
   `try_append_on_cached_rightmost_leaf` → `try_table_append_on_hinted_leaf` —
   no leaf binary search, so the CellSlotCache is never touched. Random
   middle-inserts use `table_seek_for_insert`'s interpolation + seek-cache
   fast paths for the same reason. 10 000 inserts triggered **at most 12**
   calls through `parse_cell_at`.

2. The `read_heavy_after_append` + `reverse_seek_preloaded` scenarios also
   stay off `parse_cell_at` — `table_move_to` lands via interpolation search,
   not binary search, so the per-page cell-slot cache is irrelevant for
   table-btree seeks on rowid keys.

3. **DELETE is where the 8.62% likely lives**: 10 000 deletes generated
   ~10 000 calls (one per delete — predecessor / separator lookup) with 99%
   miss rate. The mutation-counter bump on every in-place write invalidates
   the cache for that page, so each delete pays a full `CellRef::parse` even
   though the caller only needs `rowid` or `payload_offset`.

4. **Index btree workloads** exercise the cache the most (~13 calls/op, 49%
   hit-rate). This is the binary-search-on-leaf pattern the cache was built
   for; hit rate is limited by (a) mutation_counter invalidation on insert,
   (b) binary-search probe sequence touching different cells each time.

## Recommendation

The 8.62% `parse_cell_at` self-time in the 2026-04-23 MT 8 t profile
was most likely inflated by the pre-`4b061dcc` interior `child_page_at`
traffic (since removed). Re-capture a profile on current HEAD; if the band
is still ≥3%, the remaining callers to optimise are:

- `BtCursor::predecessor_idx` / `BtCursor::separator_idx` in `delete` — they
  only need `rowid` and optionally `left_child`; a specialised helper that
  reads the single varint/u32 instead of a full parse (same trick as
  `read_interior_child_inline` in commit 4b061dcc) would cut ~100 ns per
  delete.

- `binary_search_index_leaf` / `binary_search_index_interior` — the 49% miss
  rate on index inserts is genuine mid-search work that only a larger
  restructuring (cache all cell offsets on first miss, or memoise the parsed
  slots across mutation_counter bumps when only rightmost cell_count
  increased) could reduce.

Do **not** invest in hit-rate optimisation for the table-insert hot path —
the cache already isn't called.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## §7.9 Crash Model (Explicit 6-Point Contract)

Every durability and recovery mechanism designed against these six points:

1. **Process crash at any point.** No code path is crash-immune. Any operation may be interrupted between any two instructions.
2. **fsync() is a durability barrier** for data and metadata as documented by OS. Trust OS fsync contract but nothing weaker.
3. **Writes can be reordered** unless constrained by fsync barriers. OS and storage hardware may reorder writes freely between fsync calls.
4. **Torn writes at sector granularity.** Sector write (typically 512B or 4KB) is atomic, but multi-sector writes can be partially completed. Tests simulate multiple sector sizes (512, 1024, 4096).
5. **Bitrot and corruption exist.** Silent data corruption in storage media is real. Checksums (S7) detect; RaptorQ (S3) repairs within configured budget.
6. **File metadata durability may require directory fsync().** Platform-dependent. VFS MUST model this. Tests MUST include directory fsync simulation.

**Self-healing durability contract:** "If commit protocol reports 'durable', system MUST reconstruct committed data exactly during recovery, even if some fraction of locally stored symbols are missing/corrupted within configured tolerance budget."

**Durability policy (PRAGMA):**
- `PRAGMA durability = local` (default): Enough RaptorQ symbols persisted to local storage for decode under local corruption budget
- `PRAGMA durability = quorum(M)`: Enough symbols across M of N replicas to survive node loss budgets (S3.4.2)
- `PRAGMA raptorq_overhead = <percent>`: Repair symbol budget (default: 20% = 1.2x source symbols)

## §7.10 Two Operating Modes

**Compatibility Mode (Oracle-Friendly):**
- Purpose: Prove SQL/API correctness against C SQLite 3.52.0
- DB file is standard SQLite format, WAL frames are standard
- Legacy SQLite readers MAY attach concurrently
- Legacy writers excluded when .fsqlite-shm in use (Hybrid SHM, S5.6.7). To interop with legacy writers, use file-lock fallback (S5.6.6.2) — disables multi-writer MVCC and SSI
- Extra sidecars (.wal-fec, .db-fec, .idx-fec) but core .db stays compatible when checkpointed
- Default mode for conformance testing

**Native Mode (RaptorQ-First):**
- Purpose: Maximum concurrency + durability + replication
- Primary durable state is ECS commit stream (CommitCapsule objects as RaptorQ symbols)
- CommitCapsule: snapshot_basis, intent_log/page_deltas, read/write_set_digest, SSI witness-plane evidence refs (ReadWitness/WriteWitness ObjectIds, DependencyEdge ObjectIds, MergeWitness ObjectIds)
- CommitMarker: commit_seq, commit_time_unix_ns (monotonic non-decreasing), capsule_object_id, proof_object_id, prev_marker, integrity_hash. Atomicity rule: committed iff marker is durable
- Checkpointing materializes canonical .db for compatibility export; source-of-truth is commit stream
- Same SQL/API layer for both modes; conformance harness validates behavior not internal format

**Mode selection:** PRAGMA fsqlite.mode = compatibility | native (default: compatibility). Per-database, not per-connection. Switching requires explicit conversion operations.

title: BUG-P1: SELECT <constant>, COUNT(*) returns NULL for the constant when zero rows match (C SQLite returns the constant)
close_reason: Engine fix present in 665576f4 and exact table-backed rusqlite keeper landed in 43463019

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
Found by cc_fsq 2026-07-10 while triaging bd-xime6. Differential vs sqlite3 3.46.1.

  CREATE TABLE t(a INTEGER); INSERT INTO t VALUES (1),(2);
  SELECT 'lit', COUNT(*) FROM t WHERE a > 100;   -- zero rows match
  SELECT 1+1,   COUNT(*) FROM t WHERE a > 100;

  sqlite3 3.46.1 -> lit|0   and  2|0
  fsqlite        -> NULL|0  and  NULL|0

  SELECT 'lit', COUNT(*) FROM t WHERE a > 0;     -- rows match
  both            -> lit|2                        (correct)

Root cause: codegen_select_aggregate treats every non-aggregate select-list entry as a
'bare_expr', allocates an accumulator register initialised to Null, and evaluates the
expression ONCE PER SCANNED ROW (emit_aggregate_accumulate_body, 'Bare (non-aggregate)
column: evaluate expression on each row'). With zero matching rows the expression never
runs and the register keeps its Null. C SQLite evaluates constant expressions
unconditionally; only genuine column references take the last-scanned-row value.

Fix direction: if the bare expression is constant (no column/rowid reference), emit it
once before the loop rather than inside the accumulate body. That also makes it cheaper.

PRE-EXISTING, not from the bd-2dgf5 aggregate work: the per-row bare_expr evaluation is
present in ebc44c04^ (21 occurrences of bare_expr, same 'evaluate expression on each row'
comment), and reproduces identically on fsqlite_orig (958b56f5, sha256
a25e8df45d92e707b6ab8f257938a4174416349bd34d870bda7d8c4adfe2854d) and fsqlite_cand2
(sha256 237c1996d439ffe9bb2b657aae5b2d6c58635b003411f61cab94d7c1695ddab4).

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
# Task 2.3: Database Export/Import

## What
Implement the ability to export an in-memory database as a Uint8Array (binary blob) and import from one. This is essential for persistence — the database can be serialized to IndexedDB, OPFS, or downloaded.

## API
```typescript
// Export the entire database as a binary file
const data: Uint8Array = db.export();

// Import from binary
const db = FrankenDB.import(data);

// Or: save/load convenience methods
await db.save("my-database");  // saves to OPFS or IndexedDB
const db = await FrankenDB.load("my-database");
```

## Implementation Strategy
The export format should be standard SQLite database format (100-byte header + B-tree pages). This ensures:
1. Compatibility with C SQLite tools
2. Ability to share databases between server (native) and browser (wasm)
3. Import of existing .sqlite files

### Export
- Walk all pages from page 1 to N
- Concatenate into a single Uint8Array
- Include the standard SQLite 100-byte header

### Import
- Parse the header to get page size, page count
- Create MemoryVfs with pre-populated pages
- Open Connection on the pre-populated VFS

## Acceptance Criteria
- Round-trip: create DB → insert data → export → import → query returns same data
- Standard SQLite format: exported file readable by sqlite3 CLI
- Import of externally-created .sqlite files works
- Large databases (>10MB) handled efficiently (no excessive copying)

## Implement SELECT without FROM in VDBE Codegen

### Problem
SELECT statements without a FROM clause (e.g. `SELECT 1`, `SELECT 1+2`,
`SELECT abs(-5)`, `SELECT typeof(3.14)`) failed in the VDBE codegen path
with `CodegenError::Unsupported("SELECT without FROM")`. These queries fell
through to the connection.rs fallback interpreter path.

### Fix
Added `codegen_select_without_from()` function that generates a minimal
VDBE program: `Init -> Transaction -> [eval exprs] -> ResultRow -> Halt`.

- Evaluates each result column via `emit_expr` with `ctx=None` (no table)
- Supports WHERE clause filtering (e.g. `SELECT 1 WHERE 0` returns 0 rows)
- Star/TableStar result columns emit NULL (no table to expand)
- No table cursor needed — no OpenRead/Rewind/Next loop

- `crates/fsqlite-vdbe/src/codegen.rs` — Added `codegen_select_without_from`,
  early return in `codegen_select` before FROM clause lookup

title: 5E.2: Enable MVCC page-level locking for write transactions
close_reason: done

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
# 5E.2: Enable MVCC page-level locking for write transactions

## What

When a concurrent transaction writes a page (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE touching a B-tree page),
the page must be exclusively locked via `InProcessPageLockTable.try_acquire()`. If another
concurrent transaction already holds the lock, return `MvccError::Busy` immediately (no
blocking — SQLite semantics are non-blocking lock acquisition).

This task wires `concurrent_write_page()` into the TransactionHandle's `write_page()` path
so that every B-tree page mutation during a concurrent transaction goes through page-level
locking.

## Current state

The `InProcessPageLockTable` is fully implemented (core_types.rs:191-427):
- 64 shards, `CacheAligned<Mutex<HashMap<PageNumber, TxnId>>>` to prevent false sharing
- `try_acquire(page, txn)` → `Ok(())` or `Err(holder_txn_id)`
- `release(page, txn)` → bool
- `release_all(txn)` — release all locks for a transaction
- `holder(page)` → `Option<TxnId>`
- Rolling rebuild protocol for online migration (§5.6.3.1)

The `concurrent_write_page()` function (begin_concurrent.rs:218-236) is implemented:
```rust
fn concurrent_write_page(
    handle: &mut ConcurrentHandle,
    lock_table: &InProcessPageLockTable,
    session_id: u64,
    page: PageNumber,
    data: PageData,
) -> Result<(), MvccError>
```
- Calls `lock_table.try_acquire(page, txn_id)` — returns `MvccError::Busy` on conflict
- Records page data in `handle.write_set`
- Adds page to `handle.page_locks` set

But `TransactionHandle::write_page()` in the pager doesn't call this — it writes directly
to the WAL/journal without page-level locking.

## Where to change

**Primary:** `crates/fsqlite-pager/src/pager.rs` — `TransactionHandle::write_page()` implementation

For concurrent-mode transactions, `write_page()` must:
1. Call `concurrent_write_page()` to acquire page lock and record in write set
2. If lock acquisition fails (MvccError::Busy), propagate error up
3. Still write to WAL/journal for durability (the write set is the logical record,
   but the WAL is the physical durability mechanism)

**Secondary:** `crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs` — error handling for SQLITE_BUSY
from page lock contention during DML

## Implementation approach

1. The pager's transaction handle needs access to the ConcurrentHandle and lock table
2. Two options:
   a. Store ConcurrentHandle inside the pager transaction (clean ownership)
   b. Store ConcurrentHandle externally and pass through (more flexible)
3. Preferred: Option (a) — the pager transaction owns its ConcurrentHandle
4. When `write_page()` is called on a concurrent transaction:
   - Call `concurrent_write_page()` first
   - On success, proceed with WAL append
   - On `MvccError::Busy`, return error immediately (no retry at this level)
5. `get_page()` on a concurrent transaction:
   - Call `concurrent_read_page()` first (check local write set)
   - If found in write set, return that version
   - Otherwise, use `VersionStore.resolve()` for snapshot-consistent read

## Cross-process considerations

For single-process mode: `InProcessPageLockTable` (HashMap-based, fast)
For multi-process mode: `SharedPageLockTable` (shared memory, atomic CAS, open-addressing)

The `SharedPageLockTable` (shared_lock_table.rs:198-246) uses:
- Fixed capacity (default 1M entries, ~12 MiB per table)
- Two physical tables for rolling rebuild
- `AcquireResult`: Acquired | AlreadyHeld | Busy { holder } | CapacityExhausted
- Linear probing with atomic CAS for lock-free acquisition

For this task, wire the `InProcessPageLockTable` first. The `SharedPageLockTable` is for
multi-process support which is a separate concern.

## Tests

- `test_concurrent_write_acquires_page_lock`: Write page → lock_table.holder() returns txn_id
- `test_concurrent_write_conflict_returns_busy`: Two txns write same page → second gets Busy
- `test_concurrent_write_different_pages_no_conflict`: Two txns write different pages → both succeed
- `test_page_locks_released_on_commit`: Commit → all page locks released
- `test_page_locks_released_on_abort`: Rollback → all page locks released
- `test_write_set_visible_to_own_reads`: Write page, read same page → sees own write

comments.text:
VDBE codegen supports `UPDATE t SET ... FROM <named_table>` (verified working)
but rejects `UPDATE ... FROM (<subquery>)`. SQLite has supported UPDATE...FROM
since 3.33.0 (2020), including subquery sources.

Repro (frank ERRs, rusqlite OK):
```sql
CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, v INTEGER);
CREATE TABLE src (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, v INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1,0),(2,0);
INSERT INTO src VALUES (1,11),(2,22);
UPDATE t SET v = s.v FROM (SELECT id, v FROM src) s WHERE t.id = s.id;
```
frank => not implemented: UPDATE ... FROM only supports named tables (not subqueries or joins)
rusqlite => OK

Codegen site: crates/fsqlite-vdbe/src/codegen.rs:12206. The named-table FROM path
already exists; this extends it to a derived-table (subquery) source, likely by
materializing the subquery and treating it as the FROM relation.

Confirmed via differential probe (update_from_subquery). The plain
`UPDATE t SET v = src.v FROM src WHERE t.id = src.id` case already works
(update_from_table = ok).

## Impact Correction: W2 with W1 in place

With W1 (primed engine) already eliminating the setup ceremony, W2's incremental savings are SMALLER than originally estimated:

- Opcode dispatch loop: ~20-30ns
- No-op opcodes (Init, Transaction, OpenWrite, Halt): ~20-40ns
- Register file read/write: ~30-50ns
- TOTAL incremental over W1: ~70-120ns per row (NOT ~500ns)

The ~500ns estimate included engine setup ceremony which W1 handles.

W2 is still worth doing (7-12ms at 100K rows) but is NOT the game-changer originally claimed. W1 alone gets most of the CEREMONY savings.

The BIG remaining costs after W1+W2 are in the B-tree and pager layers (~250-620ns) which neither W1 nor W2 addresses.

With W1 (primed engine) in place, W2 only saves ~100ns/row — not enough to justify duplicating affinity conversion, IPK handling, AUTOINCREMENT, and page-split logic outside the VDBE. The risk of correctness regressions from duplicated logic outweighs the ~10ms savings at 100K rows.

Better approach for the future: Instead of bypassing VDBE entirely, optimize the VDBE itself (which Track V already started with FusedAppendInsert). The interpreter dispatch overhead is ~30ns — not the bottleneck.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## What
Do not build a second direct INSERT subsystem. FrankenSQLite already has a direct prepared simple INSERT lane. This bead reclaims, hardens, and makes that existing lane authoritative for the pure-parameter / benchmark-style shapes where it should win.

## Primary work
- Reconcile the truth matrix between the existing direct lane, its gating helper, and the benchmark-shape tests.
- Ensure prepare-time metadata for simple INSERT shapes is preserved and used consistently.
- Add compile-time row-builder shortcuts for pure parameter / compiled-row cases so the direct lane does not re-walk AST expressions or allocate avoidable intermediate strings.
- Keep complex-expression INSERTs on the reusable VDBE lane when that is actually faster and safer.

## Non-goals
- No duplicate affinity / AUTOINCREMENT / IPK logic living in a second bypass stack.
- No brand-new point solution that forks farther away from the already-tested direct path.
