title: RaptorQ decode/repair engine with BLAKE3 proofs
description:
Implement the RaptorQ decode/repair engine that detects corruption and automatically repairs pages using available repair symbols. This is the heart of self-healing durability.

Detection:
1. Each page carries a BLAKE3 checksum in its header
2. On page read, verify BLAKE3 checksum
3. On mismatch: page is corrupted, trigger repair

Repair:
1. Gather available symbols for the corrupted page (source symbols from surviving data + repair symbols from WAL/snapshot catalog)
2. If available symbols >= k (source block size): invoke RaptorQ decoder
3. Decoder uses inactivation decoding (O(k * log k)) to recover original source symbols
4. Reconstruct page from decoded source symbols
5. Verify reconstructed page against expected BLAKE3 checksum (from page header or parent page pointer)
6. If verification passes: write repaired page, log repair action to evidence ledger
7. If verification fails: escalate — data loss beyond repair capacity

BLAKE3 witness proofs:
- Before repair: hash of corrupted page
- After repair: hash of repaired page
- Expected hash: from metadata
- Witness triple (corrupted_hash, repaired_hash, expected_hash) logged to evidence ledger

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Corruption detection via BLAKE3 checksum on every page read
- [ ] Automatic repair using RaptorQ decode
- [ ] BLAKE3 witness proof for every repair action
- [ ] Handles: single-page corruption, multi-page corruption, contiguous range corruption
- [ ] Graceful degradation when repair capacity exceeded
- [ ] Unit test: corrupt 1, 5, 10, 20% of symbols, verify repair success/failure boundary
- [ ] Benchmark: decode latency for 4KB page (target < 1ms)
close_reason: Implemented unified repair engine with BLAKE3 corruption detection, RaptorQ-powered repair via InactivationDecoder, and RepairWitness proof triples. 15 tests pass covering checksums, single/multi/contiguous corruption, boundary percentages, batch repair, and compliance gate.

title: Evidence ledger integration for RaptorQ repair actions
description:
Integrate the RaptorQ repair engine with the EvidenceLedger for full auditability of all repair actions. Every repair event must be recorded as a galaxy-brain card with:

1. Timestamp (monotonic + wall clock)
2. Page identifier (page_id, database file offset)
3. Corruption signature (BLAKE3 hash of corrupted data, bit error pattern if detectable)
4. Repair source (WAL repair symbols, snapshot repair symbols, or both)
5. Symbols used (how many source + repair symbols consumed out of available)
6. BLAKE3 witness triple (corrupted_hash, repaired_hash, expected_hash)
7. Repair latency (time from detection to verified repair)
8. Confidence level (repair symbols available / minimum required — higher = more confident)

The evidence ledger enables:
- Post-incident forensics (what was corrupted, when, how it was repaired)
- Durability health monitoring (frequency and severity of corruption events)
- Capacity planning (are we running low on repair headroom?)
- Regulatory compliance (provable data integrity chain)

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Every repair action produces an evidence ledger entry
- [ ] Ledger entries contain all 8 fields listed above
- [ ] Ledger is append-only and tamper-evident (BLAKE3 chain)
- [ ] Query interface: list repairs by time range, page, severity
- [ ] Integration test: trigger repair, verify ledger entry

title: Async RaptorQ repair symbol generation off critical path
description:
Move RaptorQ repair symbol generation off the critical write path to ensure zero impact on write latency. Architecture:

1. Write path: page write -> WAL append -> fsync -> return to caller (NO encoding on this path)
2. Background thread(s): continuously process a queue of recently-written pages
3. Queue: lock-free SPSC or MPSC channel (crossbeam-channel)
4. Encoding thread: batch-encode pages (e.g., 64 pages per batch for amortized overhead)
5. Write encoded symbols to repair sidecar file
6. Backpressure: if encoding falls too far behind writes, optionally throttle writers (configurable policy)

Durability window: Between a page write and its repair symbol generation, the page has NO repair capability. This window should be bounded (configurable, default: 100ms or 1000 pages, whichever comes first). The window is documented as 'repair latency' in the durability model.

Thread management:
- Dedicated encoding thread (not from the query thread pool)
- CPU affinity hints for NUMA locality
- Graceful shutdown: drain queue before exit

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Write path latency unaffected by RaptorQ encoding (< 1% overhead)
- [ ] Background encoding thread processes queue continuously
- [ ] Backpressure policy prevents unbounded queue growth
- [ ] Repair latency window bounded and configurable
- [ ] Graceful shutdown drains pending pages
- [ ] Benchmark: write throughput with and without async encoding (target < 5% difference)
close_reason: Completed async RaptorQ repair generation pipeline hardening: verified off-critical-path enqueue, bounded backpressure behavior, graceful shutdown drain semantics, and commit-path overhead benchmark coverage (<1% in synthetic critical-path model).

title: E2E test: corrupt random pages, verify automatic repair

End-to-end integration test that validates the complete RaptorQ self-healing pipeline: write data -> generate repair symbols -> corrupt pages -> detect corruption -> repair -> verify integrity.

Test scenarios:
1. Single page corruption: flip random bits in one page, verify repair
2. Multi-page corruption: corrupt 5% of pages randomly, verify all repaired
3. Contiguous corruption: corrupt a contiguous range of pages (simulating sector failure)

title: V1.2: Eliminate page cache get_copy 4KB memcpy — return Arc<PageData> directly
description:
## What
`ShardedPageCache::get_copy()` (pager.rs page_cache.rs) returns `Vec<u8>` by COPYING the cached page bytes. The caller then wraps this in `PageData::from_vec()` creating a NEW Arc. This is a 4KB memcpy + Arc allocation on every cache-hit page read.

## Why
The page cache already stores `PageBuf` (page-aligned buffer). Every `get_page()` call through the pager results in `cache.get_copy(page_no)` → `Vec<u8>` (4KB copy) → `PageData::from_vec()` (Arc wrap). This is the #2 ranked bottleneck at ~50-200ns per page read.

C SQLite returns a pointer to the cache buffer directly (zero-copy) because the page cache owns the buffers and pages are pinned during use.

## How
Two approaches:
A. **Return `PageData` from cache**: Change `get_copy` to `get_shared` returning a pre-computed `PageData` (Arc) stored alongside the `PageBuf`. First access creates the Arc from the PageBuf bytes; subsequent accesses clone the Arc (cheap refcount bump). This is the `OnceLock<PageData>` pattern already used in `StagedPage::published_page()`.

B. **Pin-based zero-copy**: Return a `PageRef` handle that pins the cache entry and provides `&[u8]` access without any copy. When the handle is dropped, the page is unpinned. This matches C SQLite's `sqlite3PagerGet` → `sqlite3PagerUnref` pattern. More complex but truly zero-copy.

Option A is recommended — it fits the existing Arc-based PageData ecosystem and requires minimal changes to callers.

## Files
- `crates/fsqlite-pager/src/page_cache.rs` — ShardedPageCache, FastPageArray, get_copy → get_shared
- `crates/fsqlite-pager/src/pager.rs` — SimpleTransaction::get_page and callers
- `crates/fsqlite-types/src/lib.rs` — PageData (already Arc-based)

## Estimated impact
50-200ns per page read × ~250 page reads per 10K INSERT = 12.5-50µs saved
At 100K rows: ~125-500µs  
Also benefits ALL read operations (SELECT, JOIN, etc.)

## Verification
- Page cache unit tests pass
- Conformance oracle suite
- Benchmark sections 1 (INSERT) and 5 (read-after-write)

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## BUG: REINDEX <collation-name> not supported (only table/index targets resolve)

Oracle parity vs rusqlite.
```sql
CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT COLLATE NOCASE);
CREATE INDEX idx_name ON t(name);
REINDEX NOCASE;
  -- frank: ERROR("internal error: unable to identify the object to be reindexed")
  -- csql:  OK   (rebuilds every index that uses the NOCASE collation)
```
`REINDEX <name>` accepts a collation name as well as a table or index name; when
given a collation, SQLite rebuilds all indexes that use that collating sequence.
frank's REINDEX target resolution only looks for a table or index named <name>,
so a collation name fails.

### What works
- REINDEX (no arg) rebuilds everything; REINDEX <table>; REINDEX <index> — all OK.
- ANALYZE keeps query results correct and creates the sqlite_stat1 table.

### Fix
crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs `resolve_reindex_targets` (~:37668, which
raises "unable to identify the object to be reindexed"): when the name is not a
table or index, check whether it is a known collation; if so, rebuild every
index whose key uses that collation. Also drop the "internal error:" prefix from
this user-facing message (cf. bd-ujuzr).

### Test
crates/fsqlite-e2e/tests/maintenance_oracle_e2e.rs::reindex_collation_name
(#[ignore]'d on this bead). The other maintenance cases (ANALYZE, REINDEX
table/index, REINDEX after DML) pass.

comments.text:
FINDING + RELEASE (deeper than triaged; NOT a P2 error-taxonomy fix).

ORACLE: sqlite3 PERMITS "VACUUM INTO" on a read-only source connection (it writes a NEW target and
only reads the source) while plain VACUUM errors SQLITE_READONLY. fsqlite currently rejects VACUUM
INTO with ReadOnly at the read-only guard in execute_statement_dispatch_impl (connection.rs ~32412,
matches Statement::Vacuum wildcard).

LAYERED BLOCKERS (each investigated to code level):
  1. Guard rejects ALL Statement::Vacuum -> must exempt VACUUM INTO (into.is_some). NECESSARY but
     NOT sufficient.
  2. execute_vacuum_main (~55472) checkpoints the source in WAL mode (~55491) -- a read-only source
     cannot checkpoint; must skip on is_readonly.
  3. THE REAL BLOCKER: execute_vacuum_main -> quiesce_pager_export_state (16185) returns
     FrankenError::Busy because it rejects active_txn being set (16187), and a read-only
     (open_schema_only) connection RETAINS a read snapshot in active_txn.
     invalidate_cached_read_snapshot only clears the SEPARATE cached_read_snapshot field, not
     active_txn. So VACUUM INTO on a read-only conn hits Busy even on a FRESH connection.

CONCLUSION: full parity requires the vacuum quiesce to release/tolerate the read-only connection's
retained read snapshot (a connection-txn rework), NOT an error-taxonomy fix. Shipping the guard
exemption alone regresses ReadOnly -> Busy (a LESS-distinguished kind), so both partial edits (guard

title: Lexer: support underscore digit separators in numeric literals (SQLite 3.46+)
description: FrankenSQLite's lexer rejected numeric literals containing '_' digit separators (e.g. 1_000, 0xFF_FF, 1.0_5, 1e1_0) which C SQLite 3.46+ accepts. Found via differential divergence_hunt_probe vs the rusqlite oracle. Rule: a '_' is consumed only when surrounded on both sides by a digit of the appropriate class (decimal, or hex after 0x); leading/trailing/doubled/adjacent-to-(./e/sign) underscores are rejected as unrecognized tokens, matching SQLite. Fixed in crates/fsqlite-parser/src/lexer.rs (lex_number + new consume_decimal_digit_run helper; underscores stripped before numeric parse). Gated by 18 accept/reject cases in divergence_hunt_probe.rs.

comments.text:
## Triage finding 2026-06-28 (Opus 4.8): bd-nao48 is an INTENTIONAL, ALREADY-DOCUMENTED divergence touching the project's #1 invariant — needs a product decision, must NOT be "fixed" toward single-writer WAL. Reverted to open (not mine to close or implement).

### Premise confirmed (frank vs sqlite3 3.46.1 CLI)
- New file default journal_mode: sqlite3 = `delete`; frank = `wal` (connection.rs:13557 `bootstrap_journal_mode_from_storage`, storage_was_empty → "wal"). Existing file → "delete"/actual (13559); `:memory:` → "memory" (13545), matching sqlite which also reports "memory" and ignores `=wal`.
- `journal_mode=wal` in frank runs under concurrent MVCC by default: `concurrent_mode_default = RefCell::new(true)` (connection.rs:9083/9390); every BEGIN auto-promotes to BEGIN CONCURRENT (14350-14351, 12595). SQLite's WAL contract is single-writer (one writer at a time via WAL_WRITE_LOCK). So frank reports `wal` but does NOT enforce SQLite's single-writer WAL semantics — exactly as the bead title states.

### Why this is BY DESIGN, not a bug to fix
- Replacing SQLite's single-writer WAL_WRITE_LOCK with page-level MVCC concurrent writers is the ENTIRE PURPOSE of FrankenSQLite (README TL;DR; AGENTS.md "CRITICAL: Concurrent-Writer Mode is the ENTIRE POINT — DO NOT TOUCH"). `concurrent_mode_default` MUST stay `true`. An agent who set it false + added single-writer file locking on 2026-02-10 destroyed the core innovation and required an emergency revert. Implementing this bead's implied fix (honor SQLite's single-writer WAL contract when journal_mode=wal) is therefore FORBIDDEN.
- The divergence is ALREADY DOCUMENTED as the contract: docs/concurrency-contract.md (436 lines) states supported shapes and divergences explicitly — single-writer multi-reader WAL parity is offered as a comparison/fallback path (lines 211-246), while concurrent MVCC is the default. README links this doc as the source of truth for callers before they "write any workaround."

### The only legitimate residual question (a PRODUCT decision)
The bead's word is "silently". The divergence is documented in the contract doc, but the PRAGMA surface itself does not signal that `wal` here means MVCC-concurrent-WAL, not single-writer WAL. Resolution options (all preserve the invariant):
  A. Close as intentional-divergence/wontfix-by-design — the behavior is correct and documented; this mirrors how the project resolved bd-hrz7y (DQS) and bd-9sf3q (premise-N/A).
  B. Add an HONEST-SIGNAL introspection surface (no behavior change): e.g., surface the active concurrency model via the existing PRAGMA fsqlite_txn_* introspection family, or a dedicated `PRAGMA fsqlite.concurrent`/`PRAGMA fsqlite.write_concurrency` readback, so callers can see "wal+concurrent" without reading the doc.
  C. Keep open as a docs-prominence enhancement only.

Recommendation: B (a read-only introspection surface) is the only option that meaningfully addresses "silently" without violating the invariant; A is acceptable if the team considers the concurrency-contract doc sufficient. Escalating to the human because this is invariant-adjacent (AGENTS.md mandates asking before concurrency-behavior changes) and the close-vs-enhance choice is a product call.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: WhiteDeer/Opus 2026-07-23 ARCHITECTURAL ANALYSIS + DESIGN (the skip-scan-architecture lane deliverable). GAP CONFIRMED: analyze_skip_scan_candidate (planner lib.rs:3327) detects the classic skip-scan shape (composite index >=2 cols, leading col UNCONSTRAINED, second col constrained by eq/range/between/in/likeprefix, estimate_skip_scan_leading_distinct <= SKIP_SCAN_MAX_LEADING_DISTINCT) and uses it ONLY for cost estimation (probe_multiplier at lib.rs:1943-1948). TWO IMPLEMENTATION APPROACHES: (A) planner+codegen: add SkipScan AccessPathKind, emit it when the stats-gated candidate wins, codegen emitter consumes it. Correct + stats-gated (no high-cardinality regression) but cross-crate. (B) codegen-only ADAPTIVE (reuses the DISTINCT loose-scan pattern): iterate distinct leading values (SeekGT past each leading run) and per value find the second-col constraint; use the loose-scan's adaptive-Next degradation so a near-unique leading column falls back to a full index WALK (at-worst = full scan, no regression) WITHOUT needing stats. comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
`ALTER TABLE ... DROP COLUMN <c>` removes the column from the schema but does
NOT repack the stored row image: columns after the dropped one continue to read
the dropped column's bytes (off-by-one column shift).

Repro (FrankenSQLite vs rusqlite, both `:memory:`):

```sql
CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, a TEXT, b INTEGER, c REAL);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 'x', 5, 1.1), (2, 'y', 6, 2.2);
ALTER TABLE t DROP COLUMN b;
SELECT id, a, c FROM t ORDER BY id;
```

frank: `[1,'x',5], [2,'y',6]`   <- `c` is reading dropped column `b`'s values
csql : `[1,'x',1.1], [2,'y',2.2]`

Expected: after DROP COLUMN the persisted records (and any in-memory row mirror)
must drop the column slot so trailing columns realign. SQLite repacks each row
(or records the logical->physical mapping). FrankenSQLite leaves the old record
layout, so `c` resolves to `b`'s old position.

title: Parallel WAL — Silo/Aether Style (§15.4)
description:
Durability scaling for concurrent writers via parallel logging. The current single WAL is a serialization bottleneck — all concurrent writers must serialize their WAL appends. Score 5.3 in the opportunity matrix. Critical for the concurrent-writer story that page-level MVCC enables.

## Background
SQLite's WAL uses a single-writer model (WAL_WRITE_LOCK). FrankenSQLite's page-level MVCC allows concurrent writers at the MVCC layer, but the WAL becomes the new bottleneck if it remains single-writer.

## Key Papers
- Tu, Zheng, Kohler, Liskov, Madden 2013: 'Speedy Transactions in Multicore In-Memory Databases' (Silo — epoch-based parallel logging)
- Johnson, Pandis, Stoica, Athanassoulis, Ailamaki 2010: 'Aether: A Scalable Approach to Logging' (consolidation-based group commit)

## Architecture
Silo-style parallel logging:
1. Per-core log buffers: each worker thread writes to its own log buffer (no contention)
2. Epoch-based ordering: global epoch advances periodically. All log records within an epoch are equivalent for ordering purposes.
3. Epoch boundary = durability boundary: at each epoch advance, all log buffers are flushed to persistent storage
4. Recovery: replay all log buffers in epoch order (within an epoch, order does not matter for committed transactions)

Aether-style group commit with consolidation:
1. Writers add their log records to a consolidation buffer
2. A designated 'flusher' thread (or the first writer in a group) performs the actual I/O
3. All writers in the group are notified when the flush completes
4. Amortizes fsync overhead across multiple transactions

Combined approach:
- Per-core buffers for zero-contention logging
- Periodic epoch advance triggers consolidation and group flush
- Single fsync per epoch covers all writers

## Expected Impact
- Write throughput scales linearly with cores (currently bottlenecked at 1 core)
- Group commit reduces fsync overhead (dominant cost for small transactions)
- Latency: individual transaction commit latency bounded by epoch interval (configurable, default 10ms)

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Per-core WAL buffers with zero-contention writes
- [ ] Epoch-based ordering across buffers
- [ ] Group commit with consolidation
- [ ] Recovery correctly replays multi-buffer WAL
- [ ] Write throughput scales with cores
- [ ] Commit latency bounded by epoch interval
- [ ] Benchmark: parallel WAL vs single WAL throughput

## Success Criteria
Epic completion requires all child beads to satisfy their structured acceptance criteria, including explicit unit/property coverage, deterministic e2e evidence, and structured logging/metrics validation.

title: Design per-core WAL buffer architecture
description:
Design the per-core WAL buffer architecture for parallel logging. Each worker thread has a dedicated log buffer that it writes to without any synchronization.

Design considerations:
1. Buffer allocation: pre-allocate per-core buffers at startup (size: configurable, default 4MB per core)
2. Buffer format: sequence of (txn_id, epoch, page_id, before_image, after_image) records
3. NUMA locality: allocate buffer memory on the same NUMA node as the core
4. Overflow handling: when a buffer is full before epoch advance, either block the writer or allocate overflow buffer
5. Thread-to-buffer mapping: use thread-local storage or core affinity to map threads to buffers
6. Buffer lifecycle: buffers are recycled after flush (double-buffering: write to buffer A while flushing buffer B)

Integration with MVCC:
- Each MVCC write generates a WAL record in the writer's per-core buffer
- The WAL record includes the MVCC version information (txn_id, begin_ts, end_ts)
- On commit, the transaction's WAL records are 'sealed' (marked as committed) in the buffer

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Design document with buffer format, allocation strategy, and lifecycle
- [ ] NUMA-aware allocation strategy documented
- [ ] Overflow handling policy specified
- [ ] Double-buffering scheme for concurrent write/flush
- [ ] Integration points with MVCC write path identified
- [ ] Prototype: per-core buffers with concurrent writers (no contention)

Logging contract for the design specifies required structured fields and automated conformance checks to catch drift early.

title: Implement epoch-based ordering across per-core buffers
description:
Implement the epoch-based ordering mechanism that provides a total order across per-core WAL buffers. This is the key insight from Silo: within an epoch, the order of operations across cores does not matter for correctness.

Epoch management:
1. Global epoch counter: atomic u64, advanced periodically (configurable interval, default 10ms)
2. Epoch advance protocol: 
   a. Increment global epoch E_new = E_old + 1
   b. Wait for all active transactions to observe E_new (fence)
   c. All log records written before the fence are tagged with E_old
   d. Log records after the fence are tagged with E_new
3. Durability guarantee: when epoch E is flushed, all transactions that committed in epoch <= E are durable

Transaction commit protocol:
1. Writer seals log records in per-core buffer with current epoch
2. Writer waits for its epoch to be flushed (group commit)
3. Epoch flush: collect all sealed records from all per-core buffers for epoch E, write to persistent storage, fsync
4. Notify all waiting writers that epoch E is durable

Recovery ordering:
- Replay log records in epoch order (ascending)
- Within an epoch: apply all committed transactions (order does not matter due to MVCC isolation)
- Uncommitted transactions within an epoch: discard during recovery

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Global epoch counter with periodic advance
- [ ] Log records correctly tagged with epoch
- [ ] Group commit: flush all per-core buffers per epoch
- [ ] Writers correctly block until their epoch is durable
- [ ] Recovery replays in epoch order
- [ ] Correctness: concurrent transactions committed in different epochs maintain serial order
- [ ] Fence correctness: no log records straddling epoch boundaries

title: Implement group commit with consolidation
description:
Implement Aether-style group commit with consolidation to amortize fsync overhead across multiple transactions. fsync is the dominant cost for small transaction commits (1-10ms per call). Group commit batches multiple transactions into a single fsync.

Consolidation protocol:
1. Writers add their sealed log records to a consolidation queue
2. Consolidation phases: FILLING (accepting records) -> FLUSHING (writing to disk) -> COMPLETE (notify waiters)
3. The first writer to enter FILLING state becomes the 'flusher'
4. Subsequent writers add records and wait on a condition variable
5. Flusher: when epoch advance triggers, collect all records in FILLING state
6. Flusher: write consolidated batch to WAL file, fsync
7. Flusher: notify all waiting writers, transition to COMPLETE
8. Next epoch begins a new FILLING phase

I/O optimization:
- Consolidated write: single writev() syscall with scatter-gather of all per-core buffers
- io_uring for async write+fsync on Linux (with fallback to synchronous)
- Direct I/O to bypass page cache (WAL is write-once, page cache is wasted)

Tuning:
- Group size target: configurable (default: wait up to 1ms for additional writers before flushing)
- Maximum group delay: bounded to ensure tail latency (default: 10ms)

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Consolidation protocol correctly batches multiple writers
- [ ] Single fsync per group commit
- [ ] writev() scatter-gather for efficient I/O
- [ ] io_uring integration (with fallback)
- [ ] Commit latency bounded by max group delay
- [ ] Benchmark: commits/second with group commit vs individual fsync
- [ ] Correctness: all committed transactions durable after group fsync

title: Benchmark: parallel WAL vs single WAL throughput
description:

Workloads:
1. Small transactions (1 page write each): 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 concurrent writers
2. Medium transactions (10 page writes each): same concurrency levels
3. Large transactions (100 page writes each): same concurrency levels
4. Mixed: 80% small + 15% medium + 5% large at 32 concurrent writers

- Transactions committed per second (the primary metric)

- WAL write throughput (MB/s)
- fsync frequency (fsyncs/s)
- CPU utilization per core
- I/O wait time

title: E2E test: crash recovery with parallel WAL multi-buffer replay
description:
End-to-end test validating crash recovery correctness when using the parallel WAL with per-core buffers. Parallel WAL recovery is more complex than single-WAL recovery because log records are distributed across multiple buffers and must be replayed in epoch order.

## Test Scenarios

1. Crash mid-epoch: Kill process during an active epoch (some per-core buffers flushed, others not). Expected: recovery replays all committed transactions from flushed buffers. Unflushed committed transactions may be lost (within the documented durability window).

2. Crash during epoch flush: Kill process while the group commit flusher is writing per-core buffers to disk. Expected: partial flush produces a valid WAL (each buffer flush is atomic via aligned writes).

3. Crash with mixed epoch records: Multiple epochs in the WAL (some fully flushed, latest partially flushed). Expected: all fully-flushed epochs recovered completely.

4. Crash with concurrent SSI aborts: Kill process while SSI abort is rolling back writes. Expected: recovery correctly identifies and discards uncommitted (aborted) transactions.

5. Multi-buffer ordering correctness: After recovery, verify that the recovered state matches what would result from serial replay of all committed transactions in epoch order.

## Alien CS Reference
Tu et al. 2013 Silo: Section 4.2 describes epoch-based recovery protocol for parallel logging. Zheng et al. 2014: recovery ordering guarantees for distributed log buffers. Johnson et al. 2010 Aether: group commit crash recovery semantics and partial-flush handling.

## Rust Implementation Guidance
- Use the fail crate for crash injection at specific code points in the WAL flush path
- Implement crash scenarios as integration tests with #[test] and fork: use std::process::Command to spawn child process, then kill with SIGKILL at injection point
- Use tempfile::TempDir for isolated test databases (cleanup on drop)
- Recovery verification: compute BLAKE3 checksum of database state post-recovery, compare against expected state from known committed transactions
- Use crossbeam::scope for concurrent writer threads in test setup

## Logging Requirements
- Log every crash injection point and the state at crash time at tracing::info level
- Log recovery replay decisions: which epochs replayed, which transactions recovered/discarded at tracing::info level
- Log final verification result with expected vs actual checksums at tracing::info level
- Log partial-flush detection and handling at tracing::warn level
- Log any data loss events (unflushed committed transactions) at tracing::warn level

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All 5 crash scenarios implemented and passing
- [ ] Recovery produces consistent database state in all scenarios
- [ ] No committed data lost (within documented durability window)
- [ ] No uncommitted data visible after recovery
- [ ] Multi-buffer replay ordering verified deterministic
- [ ] 50 randomized crash points per scenario
- [ ] CI integration (nightly, due to time cost)

title: Unit tests: per-core WAL buffer correctness and epoch ordering
description:
Unit tests for per-core WAL buffer correctness and epoch-based ordering guarantees. These tests validate the foundational mechanisms of parallel WAL before integration testing (bd-ncivz.5).

## Test Categories

1. Per-core buffer isolation: Verify that writes from different threads go to different buffers with no cross-contamination. Spawn N threads, each writing unique log records, verify each buffer contains only its thread records.

2. Epoch tagging correctness: Verify that log records are tagged with the correct epoch. Write records across an epoch boundary, verify records before the boundary have epoch E and records after have epoch E+1.

3. Buffer overflow handling: Fill a per-core buffer to capacity, verify overflow handling (either blocking or overflow buffer allocation) works correctly without data loss.

4. Double-buffering: Verify that write-to-A while flush-B works correctly. Simulate concurrent write and flush, verify no data corruption or loss.

5. Epoch advance fence: Verify that the epoch advance fence correctly separates records. All active transactions must observe the new epoch before any new records are tagged with it.

6. Sealed record integrity: Verify that sealed (committed) records cannot be modified. After transaction commit, the corresponding log records must be immutable.

7. Abort cleanup: Verify that aborted transaction log records are correctly marked as discarded and not replayed during recovery.

## Alien CS Reference
Tu et al. 2013 Silo: Section 4.1 specifies the per-core logging invariants and epoch fence protocol. The double-buffering scheme follows standard WAL buffer management from Mohan et al. 1992 ARIES.

## Rust Implementation Guidance
- Use std::thread::scope for structured concurrency in multi-threaded tests
- Verify buffer isolation with unique per-thread markers (thread::current().id() or custom u64)
- For epoch boundary tests: use std::sync::Barrier to synchronize threads at epoch advance points
- For double-buffering: use crossbeam::channel to simulate concurrent write/flush timing
- Use proptest to generate random write/commit/abort sequences for unit test coverage
- Each test should run in < 1 second (unit test performance requirement)

## Logging Requirements
- Log test setup at tracing::info level: test_name, num_threads, buffer_size
- Log epoch transitions observed during tests at tracing::debug level
- Log assertion details on failure at tracing::error level: expected_epoch, actual_epoch, record_details

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All 7 test categories implemented and passing
- [ ] Multi-threaded tests use structured concurrency (no detached threads)
- [ ] Buffer isolation verified under 8+ concurrent writers
- [ ] Epoch boundary correctness verified with barrier synchronization
- [ ] No data loss under any tested scenario
- [ ] All tests complete in < 5 seconds total
- [ ] Integrated into CI test suite (cargo test)

## MECHANISM ANALYSIS 2026-07-26 (GreenBirch): B-tree balance/split, NOT WAL

The engine's own diagnostic localises this precisely. From
crates/fsqlite-btree/src/cursor.rs (~3890-3925), `table_seek` raises

    table rowid seek on root {R} missed scan-visible rowid {K} on successor page {P}

only when tree DESCENT concluded "absent / past the end" (`!res.is_found()`
and `at_eof`) but then `advance_next` — a linear scan — lands on a leaf cell
whose rowid EQUALS the target. Descent and scan disagree about a row that is
demonstrably present. That is an interior-key/leaf-content inconsistency: an
interior separator or child pointer sends the search down the wrong side of a
boundary the row actually lives on.

`PRAGMA integrity_check` agrees and adds where:

    Tree 2 page 2 cell 0: Rowid 986 out of order
    Tree 8 page 8 cell 4: Rowid 3528 out of order
    Tree 8 page 8 cell 3: Rowid 2671 out of order

Mapping tree numbers to the schema (sqlite_master rootpage):
    tree 2 / page 2 = table `issues`   (root)
    tree 8 / page 8 = table `comments` (root)

So in both damaged trees the offending cells are ON THE ROOT PAGE, and the root
of a 3,235-issue table is an interior page. The failure is out-of-order cells
written into an interior root — i.e. the split/balance path that propagates
upward into (or re-creates) the root produced a wrong cell order or wrong
separator keys. Compare the standing warning already in that file on
`find_child_slot_by_page_no`: "Upward split propagation cannot trust the stale
cursor-stack cell_idx after a lower-level balance rewrites the tree shape
underneath it." This defect is in exactly that family.

Why the merge triggers it and the export flush does not: `br sync --merge
--force` does bulk INSERT/UPDATE across issues + dependencies + labels +
comments in one transaction, driving enough growth to split leaves and
propagate to the roots of several trees at once. The open-time export flush
only rewrites `export_hashes` rows and never splits those roots.

### Consequence for the release
This localises the defect to fsqlite-btree. The v0.1.19 squash (v0.1.18 plus
one commit) touches NO fsqlite-btree source — nor wal/pager/mvcc/vfs. So the
prediction is that **v0.1.19 does NOT fix this**. Being tested directly by
building br against the v0.1.19 tree via [patch.crates-io] (v0.1.19 is still
the sync API, so br compiles unmodified) and running the reproducer.

### Consequence for prior analysis
The "rollback-surviving damage => WAL/checkpoint page-application defect"
inference is superseded. It was derived from the wrong operation (the
rolled-back export flush) and the evidence now points at btree balance under a
committed multi-table write instead.

## HARNESS TRAP (cost me a false result; read before bisecting)

`[patch.crates-io]` is only honoured when the patched version SATISFIES the
dependency requirement. br requires `fsqlite = "0.1.18"`, so patching in an
OLDER tree (v0.1.15, v0.1.16, ...) is silently DISCARDED: cargo emits only a
`patch ... was not used in the crate graph` warning and resolves crates.io
0.1.18 instead. A test of an old revision then measures 0.1.18 and reports it
CLEAN with full confidence.

I hit exactly this on the first v0.1.15 attempt and caught it only because the
build log said "Compiling fsqlite-core v0.1.18" against a v0.1.15 worktree.

Required for any revision-under-test:
  1. rewrite every `fsqlite* = "0.1.18"` dep line to `= "=<rev version>"`
  2. write the [patch.crates-io] table pointing at the worktree
  3. FAIL CLOSED on both:
       grep "was not used in the crate graph" build.log   -> must be empty
       strings target/release/br | grep <worktree>/crates/fsqlite-core -> must hit

The v0.1.18 and v0.1.19 results are NOT affected: both satisfy ^0.1.18, and I
verified each binary's linked worktree path with `strings` at the time.

Recipe with these steps is committed at
crates/fsqlite-e2e/fixtures/bd105ga/README.md (90555c0f).

## SECOND OBSTACLE: asupersync API drift blocks building old revisions

Pinning the fsqlite deps correctly (see harness trap above) gets the right
source compiling, but old revisions then fail against the CURRENT asupersync:

    v0.1.15 declares asupersync = "0.3.5"
    ^0.3.5 resolves to 0.3.9, which changed Bulkhead::try_acquire from
    (weight) to (weight, now: Time)
    => fsqlite-core v0.1.15 fails: E0061 this method takes 2 arguments but 1
       argument was supplied

So a semver-compatible asupersync upgrade is source-breaking for old fsqlite.
Any revision-level bisect must ALSO pin asupersync to the version that
revision declared:

    [dependencies]
    asupersync = { version = "=0.3.5", default-features = false }

v0.1.18/v0.1.19 are unaffected (they already declare 0.3.9).

Expect further drift the further back you go; if pinning asupersync is not
enough for a given revision, the practical alternative is to stop bisecting
by release tag and instead test the four candidate btree commits directly by
cherry-picking them onto v0.1.15 (or reverting them from v0.1.16) with the
scratchpad/attrib-br.sh pattern, which applies file subsets to a worktree and
rebuilds br against it.

## SOURCE-LEVEL CONFIRMATION (GreenBirch 2026-07-26): mechanism is documented in-tree

The mechanism I derived empirically is already written down in
crates/fsqlite-btree/src/cursor.rs (~line 11057), added by c57499fb, and it
matches the reproducer's damage exactly:

    "The caller's positioning seek may have gone through the table seek-cache
     fast path (`try_table_seek_cache`), which rebuilds the stack as just the
     landing leaf with no path from the root. Deleting from such a rootless
     stack used to silently disable `balance_for_delete` (depth one was
     treated as 'the leaf IS the root'), the pre-delete anchor capture, and
     separator repair -- so a leaf drained to zero cells stays referenced by
     its parent interior page, a shape stock SQLite rejects as 'database disk
     image is malformed' (bd-kwei8; the INSERT OR REPLACE conflict path hits
     this because the failed insert's seek primes the cache and
     `native_replace_row`'s follow-up `table_move_to` then lands on the fast
     path)."

Point-by-point against what the bd-105ga reproducer produces:
  - "INSERT OR REPLACE conflict path" == br's merge upserts (its import does a
    per-issue existence probe then INSERT or UPDATE across 4 tables).
  - "separator repair skipped" / "leaf stays referenced by its parent interior
    page" == damage localised to INTERIOR ROOT pages (tree 2 `issues`,
    tree 8 `comments`), cells out of order.
  - "stock SQLite rejects as 'database disk image is malformed'" == the exact
    engine error string the reproducer emits, and the exact class bd-kwei8
    reports.
  - descent-vs-scan disagreement in table_seek is the read-side symptom of a
    parent pointing at the wrong child boundary.

CONSEQUENCE FOR bd-kwei8: its description attributes the corruption to
"MVCC WAL publication emits frames computed against a stale base". The in-tree
comment and this reproducer both point instead at the btree seek-cache /
rootless-stack path. Whoever owns bd-kwei8 should re-read that attribution --
the fixes that actually landed for it (3e81ad0a, d1a543e3, c57499fb) are all
cursor rebuild-on-mutation guards, not WAL publication changes. If bd-kwei8 is
still reproducing for downstream jsm, the remaining instance is more likely
another unguarded mutation path reachable from the seek cache than a WAL issue.

CAVEAT: this is corroboration by reading, not proof. The revert experiment
(remove these guards from the known-clean v0.1.18 and re-run the reproducer)
is what would prove it.

## TEST-COVERAGE GAP + concrete spec for the real regression guard

Existing coverage (crates/fsqlite-btree/src/cursor.rs ~14030),
`test_balance_choke_points_reject_nonroot_single_entry_paths`:
  - hand-builds a 3-page tree, manually pushes a rootless leaf onto the cursor
    stack, asserts balance_for_insert / balance_for_delete BOTH fail closed
    with "…cursor path starts at page 3 instead of root 2".
  - i.e. it pins the CHOKE POINT (balance refuses a rootless stack).

What it does NOT cover, and what bd-105ga actually exercised:
  1. that real workloads never ARRIVE at balance with a rootless stack --
     the pre-fix bug was that mutation paths reached balance without the
     guard at all, so a "fail closed" assertion cannot see it;
  2. the rebuild-before-mutate path added by 3e81ad0a / d1a543e3 / c57499fb
     actually rebuilding the root-to-leaf path correctly;
  3. any end-to-end check that the resulting FILE is stock-SQLite-valid.

So today a regression that reintroduces an unguarded seek-cache mutation path
would keep this unit test green.

### Spec for the guard worth writing (no 5 MB fixture needed)
An e2e test in fsqlite-e2e that synthesizes the shape instead of shipping the
corpus:
  1. create a rowid table with a secondary UNIQUE index (mirrors
     export_hashes / issues: TEXT PRIMARY KEY => sqlite_autoindex);
  2. insert enough rows that the root becomes an INTERIOR page (multi-level);
     a few thousand small rows is enough -- confirm via depth or page count,
     do not assume;
  3. drive INSERT OR REPLACE conflicts on EXISTING keys in a loop inside one
     transaction, so the failed insert's seek primes try_table_seek_cache and
     native_replace_row's follow-up table_move_to lands on the fast path --
     this is the entry condition named in the c57499fb comment;
  4. interleave deletes so balance_for_delete runs on drained leaves;
  5. commit, close, then assert stock integrity via rusqlite
     `PRAGMA integrity_check` == "ok" (NOT the engine's own checker -- the
     whole point is an independent verdict).

Suggested assertion beyond "ok": also assert no row loss, since bd-kwei8
recorded silent table emptying during heal attempts.

This is the deliverable that bd-7m1ep could not honestly ship (its corpus is
inert). It would have caught bd-105ga, is cheap to run, and needs no fixture.

## REVERT EXPERIMENT #1 (GreenBirch 2026-07-26): narrows 4 candidates to 2

Setup: known-CLEAN v0.1.18 worktree, reverse-applied the btree commits, rebuilt
br against it (binary verified to link the worktree; no unused-patch warning),
ran the reproducer on a fresh pristine copy.

Reverted successfully: c57499fb, e021f1f7
Could NOT reverse-apply: d1a543e3, 3e81ad0a (later changes touch the same
regions; would need 3-way revert)

RESULT: **CLEAN**. Merge COMPLETED ("Base snapshot updated. JSONL exported."),
DB grew 19 MB -> 34.2 MB, beads.base.jsonl written, 8 issues with fresh
updated_at, stock sqlite3 integrity_check = ok. Verified by reading the DB
directly, not just the script's verdict (see caution below).

CONCLUSION: c57499fb and e021f1f7 are NOT the fix, at least not on their own.
The fix is in the pair I could not revert -- **3e81ad0a and/or d1a543e3** --
which are exactly the two bd-kwei8 commits whose messages name the delete and
INSERT OR REPLACE paths, and which match the in-tree seek-cache/rootless-stack
comment. Candidates narrowed 4 -> 2, and the surviving 2 are the predicted ones.

### CAUTION: my harness printed a FALSE "CORRUPT" for this run
The verdict logic compared `[ "$CV" = "ok; " ]` while `tr '\n' '; '` actually
yields `ok;` with no trailing space, so the comparison never matched and the
script would report CORRUPT for ANY result. Caught because the same output block
showed `sqlite3: ok` immediately above `VERDICT=CORRUPT`, and I checked the
database directly.

No previously reported result is affected: the 0.1.12 / v0.1.18 / v0.1.19
verdicts were all read manually from sqlite3 output, not produced by these
scripts. Fixed in all harness scripts to `case "$CV" in ok*)`.

Lesson worth keeping: every automated verdict in this investigation must print
the raw evidence next to the verdict, so a broken comparison is visible rather
than authoritative.

3-way revert d1a543e3 + 3e81ad0a from v0.1.18 (`git revert -n` rather than
reverse-apply, since plain reverse-apply conflicts), rebuild, re-run. Expect
CORRUPT. That would pin the fix to the bd-kwei8 pair and confirm bd-105ga and
bd-kwei8 are one defect.

title: Database Cracking / Adaptive Indexing (§8.8)
description:
Implement database cracking (Idreos et al. 2007) for adaptive, zero-admin indexing. Database cracking incrementally sorts data in response to queries, so each query partially sorts the data in the regions it accesses and frequently queried ranges become progressively faster.

## Mathematical Foundation
After Q queries on a column, the column is partitioned into O(Q) sorted segments. Lookup cost decreases from O(N) to O(N/Q) as more queries crack the data. In the limit, the column becomes fully sorted (equivalent to a sorted index) but without any upfront sort cost.

## Application in FrankenSQLite
- Auto-indexing for ad-hoc analytics (no CREATE INDEX needed)
- Columnar storage cracking for vectorized scans
- Adaptive to actual query patterns (indexes emerge where needed)

## Alien CS Reference
Idreos, Kersten, Manegold 2007 Database Cracking: original paper with amortized cost analysis. Idreos et al. 2011 Merging What is Cracked, Cracking What is Merged Adaptive Indexing in Main-Memory Column-Stores: adaptive merging optimization that reduces worst-case crack overhead. Halim et al. 2012 Stochastic Database Cracking: probabilistic analysis of cracking convergence under different query distributions.

## Rust Implementation Guidance
- Implement CrackedColumn<T: Ord> wrapping a Vec<T> with a BTreeMap<T, usize> crack index
- Crack operation: on range query [lo, hi], partition the column at lo and hi using std::slice::partition_point
- Crack index: BTreeMap mapping crack boundaries to positions in the underlying Vec
- For vectorized integration: crack operates on columnar batches, producing selection vectors for cracked ranges
- Use std::slice::select_nth_unstable for efficient in-place partitioning (O(n) expected)

## Logging Requirements
- Log crack operations at tracing::debug level: column_name, crack_key, partition_size
- Log crack index growth at tracing::info level periodically: num_cracks, avg_segment_size
- Log full-sort convergence at tracing::info level when column becomes fully sorted

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Cracking prototype for single-column range queries
- [ ] Progressive refinement: repeated queries on same range get faster
- [ ] Benchmark: cracking vs explicit index vs full scan
- [ ] Integration with vectorized scan operator
- [ ] Correctness: cracked data produces same results as uncracked data
acceptance_criteria: 1. Implementation is complete and behaviorally correct against explicit invariants and edge-case requirements, including fault and recovery paths where applicable. 2. Comprehensive unit/property tests cover normal, boundary, and adversarial conditions with deterministic fixtures and regression seeds. 3. End-to-end scenario scripts validate integrated behavior in real execution flows and include deterministic replay instructions. 4. Structured logging/metrics (traceable IDs, timing, counters, error context) are emitted and validated so failures are diagnosable and auditable.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
# ALTER ADD COLUMN NOT NULL rejected on an empty table

## Symptom
`ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN b TEXT NOT NULL` (no default) is rejected by frank
even when `t` has no rows; this SQLite build accepts it on an empty table.
```sql
CREATE TABLE t (a INTEGER);                    -- empty
ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN b TEXT NOT NULL;
-- SQLite: OK     frank: ERROR(internal error: Cannot add a NOT NULL column without a default value)
```
When the table HAS rows, both engines reject it (back-filling NULL into a NOT NULL
column is impossible) — frank is correct there:
```sql
CREATE TABLE t (a INTEGER); INSERT INTO t VALUES (1);
ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN b TEXT NOT NULL;      -- ERROR on BOTH (agreement)
```
So frank applies the NOT-NULL-needs-default rule unconditionally, while the
reference only enforces it when existing rows would be back-filled with NULL.

## Secondary issue
frank's error text carries a stray `internal error:` prefix
("internal error: Cannot add a NOT NULL column without a default value"). Even
once the empty-table case is allowed, the rows-exist error message should not be
prefixed `internal error:` (cf. bd-ujuzr for the same stray-prefix pattern).

## What is already correct
- `ADD COLUMN ... PRIMARY KEY` -> rejected by both.
- `ADD COLUMN ... UNIQUE` -> rejected by both.
- `ADD COLUMN ... NOT NULL` (no default) on a NON-empty table -> rejected by both.
- legal additions (nullable, constant DEFAULT, NOT NULL + non-null DEFAULT) -> OK.

## Fix sketch
Gate the "NOT NULL column requires a non-NULL default" rejection on the table
having at least one existing row (matching the reference): if the table is empty
there is nothing to back-fill, so the column may be added. Also drop the
`internal error:` prefix from the rows-exist rejection message.
See the ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN handler in `crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs`.

## Priority
P3 — frank is over-strict (rejects an operation the reference accepts on an empty
table). Opposite direction from the over-acceptance class, but same conformance
bucket.

## Tests
`crates/fsqlite-e2e/tests/alter_add_column_restrictions_oracle_e2e.rs`: PK/UNIQUE
rejection green; NOT-NULL-no-default with rows green;
`add_not_null_without_default_empty_table` #[ignore]'d on this bead.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
# §4.19.1 Remote Named Computations + Idempotency + Sagas

## Spec Reference
COMPREHENSIVE_SPEC_FOR_FRANKENSQLITE_V1.md lines 5430–5510 (§4.19, §4.19.1–§4.19.5)

## Overview
Tiered storage (L3) and replication are fundamentally remote effects. FrankenSQLite
adopts asupersync's remote contract so remote behavior is cancellable, bounded, and
auditable. All remote operations must be named (no closure shipping), idempotent,
lease-backed, and saga-wrapped for multi-step workflows.

## Global Remote Bulkhead (Normative)
All remote operations (fetch, upload, anti-entropy RPCs) MUST run under a global
remote bulkhead with concurrency cap `PRAGMA fsqlite.remote_max_in_flight`
(0 = auto; §4.17.1). Prevents retry storms and kernel-level overload on many-core
machines when remote tiers degrade.

## §4.19.1 Explicit Remote Capability (Required)
- All remote operations MUST require `RemoteCap` in `Cx`.
- Without it: no network I/O (compile-time or runtime refusal).
- Native mode still functions under `durability = local`.
- Prevents silent network I/O from arbitrary SQL code paths.
- Lab contexts simply omit RemoteCap to test without network.

## §4.19.2 Named Computations (Required for Auditing)
Remote work MUST be specified by `ComputationName` + serialized input bytes.
Runtime MUST NEVER serialize arbitrary closures.

### Normative Remote Computation Names (Minimum Set)
1. `symbol_get_range(object_id, esi_lo, esi_hi, ecs_epoch)` — fetch range of symbols
2. `symbol_put_batch(object_id, symbols[], ecs_epoch)` — upload batch of symbols
3. `segment_put(segment_id, bytes, ecs_epoch)` — upload segment blob
4. `segment_stat(segment_id, ecs_epoch)` — stat a remote segment
5. No closure shipping: all are named + serialized inputs only.

## §4.19.3 Lease-Backed Liveness (Required)
- Remote handles MUST be lease-backed.
- If lease expires: local region MUST escalate (cancel, retry, or fail).
- Event MUST be trace-visible.
- Avoids "hung remote fetch" as unbounded tail-latency failure.

## §4.19.4 Idempotency (Required)
All remote requests that might be retried MUST include an IdempotencyKey:
```
IdempotencyKey = Trunc128(BLAKE3("fsqlite:remote:v1" || request_bytes))
```
Remote receivers MUST deduplicate by IdempotencyKey (asupersync IdempotencyStore):
- Duplicate with same computation name + inputs → return recorded outcome.
- Duplicate with same key but different computation inputs → conflict, MUST reject.

## §4.19.5 Sagas for Multi-Step Publication (Required)
Any multi-step remote+local workflow that would leave partial state on
cancellation/crash MUST be expressed as a Saga (forward steps + deterministic compensations).

### 3 Normative Sagas
1. **L2→L3 eviction:** upload segment → verify remote → retire local copy.
2. **Compaction publish:** write new segments → publish → update locators/manifests.
3. **Cross-region replication:** (implied) multi-step replication workflow with
   compensation on partial failure.

Sagas are deterministic and replayable: given same inputs, same sequence of steps
and compensations occurs, evidence recorded for debugging.

## Unit Test Specifications

### T1: remote_cap_required
Attempt remote operation without RemoteCap in Cx. Verify compile-time or runtime refusal.

### T2: remote_cap_enables_network
Provide RemoteCap in Cx. Verify remote operation proceeds (mock endpoint).

### T3: named_computation_serialization
Create each of the 4 normative computation names with inputs. Verify they serialize
to ComputationName + bytes, not closures.

### T4: idempotency_key_deterministic
Compute IdempotencyKey for same request_bytes twice. Verify identical Trunc128(BLAKE3) output.

### T5: idempotency_dedup_same_inputs
Submit same request twice with same IdempotencyKey. Verify second returns recorded outcome.

### T6: idempotency_conflict_different_inputs
Submit request with same IdempotencyKey but different computation inputs.
Verify rejection (conflict error).

### T7: lease_expiry_escalation
Set up remote handle with short lease. Let lease expire. Verify escalation
(cancel/retry/fail) and trace visibility.

### T8: saga_l2_l3_eviction_forward
Execute L2→L3 eviction saga forward path: upload → verify → retire.
Verify all steps complete and evidence recorded.

### T9: saga_l2_l3_eviction_compensation
Simulate failure at verify step of L2→L3 eviction. Verify compensation
rolls back upload and local state remains intact.

### T10: saga_compaction_publish_forward
Execute compaction publish saga: write segments → publish → update locators.
Verify complete and evidence recorded.

### T11: bulkhead_concurrency_cap
Set remote_max_in_flight=2. Launch 5 concurrent remote ops. Verify at most
2 are in flight simultaneously.

### T12: saga_deterministic_replay
Replay same saga with same inputs. Verify identical step sequence.

## Dependencies
- §3.5 (RaptorQ symbols), §4.17.1 (PRAGMA remote_max_in_flight), §4.15 (governor/bulkhead),
  §7.13 (compaction), §5.6.2 (leases)

## Testing Requirements for §4.19.1 Remote Named Computations

### Unit Tests (fsqlite-core or fsqlite-remote crate)

**RemoteCap requirement:**
1. **test_remote_op_requires_remote_cap**: Without RemoteCap in Cx, remote operations refuse (compile-time or runtime). Verify no silent network I/O.
2. **test_lab_omits_remote_cap**: Lab contexts omit RemoteCap to test without network. Verify remote ops return appropriate error.
3. **test_native_mode_without_remote**: Under durability=local, system functions fully without RemoteCap.

**Named computations:**
4. **test_symbol_get_range_named**: `symbol_get_range(object_id, esi_lo, esi_hi, ecs_epoch)` is a named computation with serialized inputs.
5. **test_symbol_put_batch_named**: `symbol_put_batch(object_id, symbols[], ecs_epoch)` is named with serialized inputs.
6. **test_segment_put_named**: `segment_put(segment_id, bytes, ecs_epoch)` is named.
7. **test_segment_stat_named**: `segment_stat(segment_id, ecs_epoch)` is named.
8. **test_no_closure_shipping**: Verify runtime NEVER serializes arbitrary closures. Only ComputationName + serialized input bytes.

**Idempotency:**
9. **test_idempotency_key_derivation**: IdempotencyKey = Trunc128(BLAKE3("fsqlite:remote:v1" || request_bytes)). Verify correct computation.
10. **test_idempotency_dedup_same_request**: Same computation + same inputs → same IdempotencyKey → duplicate returns recorded outcome.
11. **test_idempotency_conflict_different_inputs**: Same IdempotencyKey but different computation inputs → conflict, MUST reject.
12. **test_idempotency_key_unique_per_request**: Different request bytes → different IdempotencyKeys (BLAKE3 collision resistance).

**Lease-backed liveness:**
13. **test_lease_expiry_escalates**: Remote handle lease expires → local region escalates (cancel, retry, or fail). Not a silent hang.
14. **test_lease_expiry_trace_visible**: Lease expiry event is trace-visible (appears in evidence ledger or logs).
15. **test_no_unbounded_remote_fetch**: Remote fetch that exceeds lease time is terminated. No "hung remote fetch" scenario.

**Sagas for multi-step publication:**
16. **test_saga_compensates_on_failure**: Multi-step remote+local workflow fails at step 3. Steps 1-2 are compensated (rolled back).
17. **test_saga_idempotent_compensation**: Compensation actions are themselves idempotent (safe to retry).
18. **test_saga_partial_state_impossible**: After saga completes (success or compensated failure), no partial state remains.

**Global remote bulkhead:**
19. **test_remote_bulkhead_concurrency_cap**: All remote ops run under global bulkhead. Concurrent ops capped at PRAGMA fsqlite.remote_max_in_flight.
20. **test_remote_bulkhead_zero_means_auto**: remote_max_in_flight=0 → auto-derived default.
21. **test_remote_bulkhead_prevents_retry_storms**: When remote tier degrades, bulkhead prevents runaway retry storms.

### Integration Tests
22. **test_remote_symbol_fetch_end_to_end**: Tiered storage scenario: fetch symbols from remote → decode → return page data.
23. **test_remote_saga_upload_compaction**: Multi-step: upload compacted segments → update locator → publish. Verify saga discipline.

### E2E Tests
24. **test_e2e_remote_failure_recovery**: Remote tier fails mid-operation. Verify saga compensation, bulkhead prevents cascade, local operations unaffected.

### Logging Requirements
- DEBUG: Named computation dispatch, IdempotencyKey derivation, lease renewal
- INFO: Remote operation completion (latency, computation name)
- WARN: Lease expiry, bulkhead saturation, idempotency conflict
- ERROR: Saga compensation failure (should be rare with idempotent compensators)

title: RefCell re-entry audit across fsqlite-core: partial automation + Q2 audit doc + sub-bead per risky site
description: After bd-NEW-3.2 fixes the known site, sweep the entire fsqlite-core crate for analogous risks. Define risky precisely, automate the call-graph extraction, classify each site, file follow-ups.
design: Define risky precisely: a RefCell is risky iff there exists a call path from a publicly-reachable function (Connection::execute, Connection::prepare, etc.) such that the borrow happens, control then re-enters the same module (via callback, trait dispatch, or panic-unwind path), and another borrow of the same cell occurs before the first borrow's guard drops. Partial automation: a script tests/audit/refcell_audit.rs (or a cargo-deny custom rule) that uses syn/quote to walk fsqlite-core/src/, for each RefCell::borrow*() call captures the enclosing function and the call sites it reaches transitively. Emit a JSON report listing every (cell_site, reachable_caller, depth) tuple. A human (or AI) then classifies each as Safe (no re-entry possible) or RefactorNeeded (re-entry possible) and the verdict is recorded in docs/internal/refcell-audit-2026-Q2.md. For every RefactorNeeded site, file a sub-bead with the cell location and the suspected re-entry path.
acceptance_criteria: (1) tests/audit/refcell_audit.rs script emits a JSON report listing every RefCell::borrow*() site and its reachable callers. (2) docs/internal/refcell-audit-2026-Q2.md captures verdicts for every site (Safe vs RefactorNeeded with a re-entry-path sketch). (3) A sub-bead exists for every RefactorNeeded site, linked under bd-zywqc or bd-nkfbj depending on whether it overlaps with #70 work. (4) The audit script is added to CI (advisory, not gating) so any newly-introduced RefCell is flagged in PR review.
notes: This bead is the prophylactic: prevent the next instance of this class of bug. Advisory CI rather than gating because true safe RefCells are common (e.g. interior mutability inside a structure that is never re-entered).

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
# Reality Check — Concurrent-Writer MVCC Claims (2026-04-24)

Narrow-scope `reality-check-for-project` pass against the
concurrent-writer MVCC claims in `README.md` + `COMPREHENSIVE_SPEC_FOR_FRANKENSQLITE_V1.md`,
contrasted against the write-side evidence in
`tests/artifacts/perf/cumulative-verify-20260424T2033Z/` and the
read-side `mt_read_bench` data shipped in commit `ad899fac`
(2026-04-24).

**Bottom line:** the concurrent-writer write-side story holds.
The single-threaded and read-side parity claims do NOT.

---

## 1. What the docs claim

### 1a. Core pitch (README L26, L36, L184)

| Claim | Location | Stance |
|---|---|---|
| "MVCC Concurrent Writers. Multiple writers commit simultaneously as long as they touch different pages." | README L26 | ✅ SUPPORTED by evidence |
| "Concurrent writers: Many (page-level MVCC with SSI)" | README L36, feature table | ✅ SUPPORTED |
| "page-level versioning sits at the right point in the complexity/concurrency tradeoff" | README L57-65 | ✅ ARCHITECTURAL, not directly benchable |

### 1b. Performance table (README L1147-1173) — the measurable claims

| # | Workload | Claimed speedup | Source line |
|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | 8 threads, different tables | **~8× C SQLite** | L1151 |
| P2 | 8 threads, same table, different row ranges | **2–6×** | L1152 |
| P3 | 8 threads, same table, same hot rows | ~1× (page conflicts) | L1153 |
| P4 | Mixed 90/10 read/write | "Lower p99 read latency" | L1154 |
| P5 | **Single-threaded writes** | **~0.95×** | L1155 |
| P6 | **Single-row INSERT (1 writer)** | **"Comparable to C SQLite"** | L1168 |
| P7 | Single-row INSERT (8 writers, separate tables) | **~8× C SQLite** | L1169 |
| P8 | **Point SELECT by rowid** | **"Comparable to C SQLite"** | L1170 |
| P9 | Full table scan | "Comparable to C SQLite" | L1171 |
| P10 | Reader throughput under write load | "Higher (no aReadMark contention)" | L1173 |

---

## 2. What the benches actually show

### 2a. Write side — `mt_mvcc_bench` cumulative verify (HEAD `03c4988612`, 2026-04-24T20:33Z)

`--rows-per-thread=500 --iters=10 --threads=1,2,4,8 --apples-to-apples`,
3 repeats per thread count. Source:
`tests/artifacts/perf/cumulative-verify-20260424T2033Z/summary.md`.

| Threads | fs_wps (median) | sq_wps (median) | ratio |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 407 381 | ~727 k | **0.56×** |
| 2 | 241 420 | ~536 k | 0.45× |
| 4 | 218 436 | 210 k | **1.04×** |
| 8 | **176 747** | **54 551** | **3.24×** |

Write-workload shape: one table `bench(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, payload
TEXT)`, each thread inserts into a disjoint rowid range in the same
table (not separate tables).

### 2b. Read side — `mt_read_bench` shipped in `ad899fac` (2026-04-24)

`--rows=5000 --reads-per-thread=20000 --threads=1,2,4,8`. Prepared
`SELECT payload FROM bench WHERE id = ?1` with random rowids.

| Threads | fs_rps | sq_rps | ratio |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 18 931 | 288 428 | **0.07×** |
| 2 | 49 392 | 384 124 | 0.13× |
| 4 | 95 721 | 440 139 | 0.22× |
| 8 | 128 548 | 422 902 | **0.30×** |

Per-read wall-clock: ~53 µs (fsqlite) vs ~3.5 µs (sqlite) at 1t.

### 2c. Tests on clean HEAD

* `prop_index_btree_structural_invariants_hold_after_random_mutations`
  fails on clean HEAD in the fsqlite-btree lib suite (pre-existing, not
  caused by any btree work this session). Shrinks to a 2-insert
  minimal case.
* Cell-slot cache (bd-9e3xf audit): 0 % hit rate on `index_random_insert`
  under MemPageStore after `1be6ee30` swapped the cache key from
  xxh3 to `PageData::image_token`; production pager preserves tokens
  across reads so the 49 % hit rate captured pre-`1be6ee30` should
  carry over to real workloads, but this is not yet re-validated.

---

## 3. Gap analysis — claim by claim

| # | Claim | Evidence | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | 8t / different tables / ~8× | **No bench measures "different tables" — mt_mvcc_bench uses one table with disjoint rowid ranges.** | **UNPROVEN** |
| P2 | 8t / same table / different row ranges / 2–6× | `mt_mvcc_bench` 8t = **3.24×** | ✅ SUPPORTED (in range) |
| P3 | 8t / same table / hot rows / ~1× | Not measured in current bench matrix | UNPROVEN |
| P4 | Mixed 90/10 p99 | `mt_read_bench` is reads-only; `mt_mvcc_bench` is writes-only; no mixed harness | **NO BENCH** |
| P5 | 1t write ~0.95× | `mt_mvcc_bench` 1t = **0.56×** | ❌ **OVERSTATED** |
| P6 | 1 writer INSERT "comparable" | Same 0.56× | ❌ **OVERSTATED** |
| P7 | 8 writers separate tables ~8× | Not measured with separate tables; same-table 3.24× at 8t | **UNPROVEN** |
| P8 | Point SELECT by rowid "comparable" | `mt_read_bench` 1t = **0.07×** | ❌ **SEVERELY OVERSTATED** (15× slower) |
| P9 | Full table scan "comparable" | Not measured in current bench matrix | **NO BENCH** |
| P10 | Reader under write-load higher throughput | Not measured | **NO BENCH** |

Supported (2): P1 shape, P2.
Overstated (3): P5, P6, P8.
Unproven / no bench (5): P1 "different tables" angle, P3, P4, P7, P9, P10.

### 3a. The honest headline vs the README headline

README frames the project as "SQLite with concurrent writers so you
get ~8× on write-heavy parallel workloads AND comparable performance
everywhere else." The evidence says:

* Write concurrency beats SQLite at 4t+ and reaches 3.24× at 8t under
  same-table contention — **this is real and reproducible**.
* Single-threaded writes and single-threaded rowid reads are
  materially slower than C SQLite (0.56× and 0.07× respectively).
  A user whose app isn't multi-threaded gets a perf regression vs C
  SQLite, not "comparable".

The 1t-read gap is the single largest unreported finding; the 15×
ratio is well past "comparable".

---

## 4. Corrective beads

File the following as beads so the drift is tracked in the triage
graph and addressed. Each proposes either (a) updating the doc to
match evidence, or (b) shipping a bench + fix that earns back the
claim.

### B1 — `bd-doc-P5-P6-P8` (P0, doc correction)

**Title:** `PERF-DOCS: correct README 1t-write and 1t-read "comparable" claims against current bench evidence`

**Body:**
Three performance-table claims in `README.md` (L1155, L1168, L1170)
do not match the 2026-04-24 bench evidence:

* L1155 "Single-threaded writes ~0.95×" — measured 0.56× in
  `cumulative-verify-20260424T2033Z`.
* L1168 "Single-row INSERT throughput (1 writer) Comparable to C SQLite"
  — same 0.56×.
* L1170 "Point SELECT by rowid Comparable to C SQLite" — measured
  0.07× at 1t in `mt_read_bench` (commit ad899fac).

Action: rewrite these three cells as "1t fs/sq ratio ≈ {0.56, 0.07}
as of 2026-04-24" plus a one-line pointer to the bench that
produced it (`mt_mvcc_bench --threads=1` and `mt_read_bench`). Do NOT
drop the claims entirely — flag them as "gap we intend to close, here
is current measured ratio and the benches that track it".

Also: add a Documentation Invariants subsection to `AGENTS.md`
requiring that every numeric performance claim in README reference a
bench name that actually measures it.

### B2 — `bd-bench-different-tables` (P1, missing harness)

**Title:** `PERF-BENCH: add mt-mvcc-bench --separate-tables mode to validate "different tables" ~8x claim`

**Body:**
The README "8 threads writing to different tables Parallel (up to 8×)"
claim (L1151, L1169) has no corresponding harness. The existing
`mt_mvcc_bench` spins all threads on the same `bench` table with
disjoint rowid ranges. That measures the "same table, different row
ranges" shape (L1152), not the "different tables" shape.

Action: extend `mt_mvcc_bench` with a `--separate-tables` flag that
CREATEs N tables (one per thread) and inserts into the thread's own
table. Capture the ratio and either (a) confirm ~8× or (b) file the
delta as a doc correction. Ship in the same artifact-dir convention
as `cumulative-verify-20260424T2033Z`.

### B3 — `bd-bench-mixed-oltp` (P1, missing harness)

**Title:** `PERF-BENCH: mixed-read-write OLTP bench for the 90/10 and reader-under-load claims`

**Body:**
README L1154 claims "Mixed read/write (90% reads, 10% writes) →
Lower p99 read latency" and L1173 claims "Reader throughput under
write load → Higher (no aReadMark contention)". Neither has a
harness. `mt_mvcc_bench` is writes-only; `mt_read_bench` is
reads-only.

Action: add `mt_oltp_bench` that combines the per-connection
template of `mt_read_bench` with a mix ratio argument, reports both
read p99 under write load and write p99 under read load at 1/2/4/8/16
threads. Gate acceptance: "lower p99 read latency" should be
verifiable with a concrete number vs C SQLite in WAL mode.

### B4 — `bd-1t-read-latency-root-cause` (P0, root-cause)

**Title:** `PERF-READ: root-cause 15x 1t SELECT-by-rowid latency gap; ship fix or doc correction`

**Body:**
`mt_read_bench` shows fs/sq 1t = 0.07× on prepared `SELECT payload
FROM bench WHERE id = ?1`. ~53 µs per read vs ~3.5 µs for C SQLite.
The pinned-read WAL-adapter commits (d9c410bb, 7e4a5409) addressed
the pager layer and MT scaling is near-linear, so the 50 µs gap lives
upstream. Candidates (not yet profiled):

* `SimpleProjectedRowidLookup` fast-path (b86cd4e6) — verify it
  actually engages for this query shape.
* VDBE dispatch overhead on PK-equality SELECT.
* Column decode of a 64-byte TEXT into `SqliteValue::Text(Arc<str>)`
  that the caller discards.
* Per-SELECT autocommit-txn acquire/release on the Connection.

Action: capture a samply flamegraph on `mt_read_bench --threads=1
--reads-per-thread=200000` and file the top-1 hot function as a
follow-up bead with an ownership label. Target: close the 1t
ratio to ≥ 0.6× OR correct the README "comparable" claim per B1.

### B5 — `bd-proptest-index-structural-invariants` (P1, test regression)

**Title:** `BTREE-TEST: repair prop_index_btree_structural_invariants_hold_after_random_mutations`

**Body:**
Pre-existing failure on clean HEAD in the fsqlite-btree lib test
suite. Shrinks to a 2-insert minimal case. Spec L11 of the README
tries to stand on "MVCC snapshots are consistent under arbitrary
transaction interleavings" and this proptest exercises the
structural guarantee one level below that. A failing invariant
proptest on main is a credibility drain on the MVCC correctness
story.

Action: resolve or `#[ignore]` with a bead reference — currently it
fails silently in CI and noisily in any local `cargo test -p
fsqlite-btree --lib`.

### B6 — `bd-cache-hitrate-production-pager` (P2, validation)

**Title:** `PERF-BTREE: validate CellSlotCache hit rate on production pager (post-1be6ee30)`

**Body:**
Commit 1be6ee30 swapped the cache key from xxh3(page-bytes) to
`PageData::image_token`. Under `MemPageStore` (the audit harness),
image_token refreshes on every `read_page_data` because each read
allocates a fresh `Vec`, so the cache records 0 % hit rate
post-1be6ee30. The production pager preserves image_token via its
page-cache `Clone` path, so the 49 % hit rate measured pre-1be6ee30
on `index_random_insert` should carry over — but this has not been
validated on the production pager.

Action: run the bd-9e3xf audit bench against the production pager
(not MemPageStore) and confirm hit rate ≥ 40 % on
`index_random_insert`. If not, file the regression. Attach result as
a comment on bd-9e3xf.

---

## 5. Summary scorecard

| Claim class | Count | Supported | Overstated | No-bench |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Write concurrency core | 3 | 3 | 0 | 0 |
| Write perf / measurable | 4 | 1 | 2 | 1 |
| Read perf / measurable | 3 | 0 | 1 | 2 |
| **Total** | **10** | **4** | **3** | **3** |

**Recommendation:** land B1 (doc correction) within the current
release cycle; B2/B3/B4 can be phased. Without B1 the project
overclaims read-side and single-threaded performance parity that
benches do not support.

## 6. Reproduction

```
# Write side
/path/to/mt-mvcc-bench --rows-per-thread=500 --iters=10 --threads=1,2,4,8 --apples-to-apples

# Read side (shipped in ad899fac)
CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/tmp/rch_target_cc3_btree_local cargo build --release \
    -p fsqlite-e2e --bin mt-read-bench
/tmp/rch_target_cc3_btree_local/release/mt-read-bench \
    --rows=5000 --reads-per-thread=20000 --threads=1,2,4,8

# Btree test state
CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/tmp/rch_target_cc3_btree_local cargo test \
    -p fsqlite-btree --release --lib -- --test-threads=1
```

## 7. Artefact roots

* `tests/artifacts/perf/cumulative-verify-20260424T2033Z/summary.md` — write-side source of truth
* commit `ad899fac` — mt_read_bench binary + bd-eyh2e bead comment
* commit `d98e9e31` — counter gating
* bead `bd-9e3xf` — cell-slot cache classification (comment captures pre/post 1be6ee30)

Fix keeps rows where root_page==0 && is_virtual_table_sql(sql); still drops real tables + all indexes. Oracle-first keeper (tests/bd_o01lp_vacuum_into_fts5_vtab_gh357.rs, ext-fts5) reads the OUTPUT's raw sqlite_master via rusqlite: RED (search vtab entry missing) -> GREEN (survives: type=table/rootpage=0/CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE sql; shadow tables keep positive rootpages; ordinary row round-trips; reopen+MATCH returns indexed rowid). Full -p fsqlite-core --lib: 3755 pass / 5 pre-existing unrelated fails (dk9ra fts5 + recursive-trigger + pager_routing select-structure), 0 regressions. Distinct from #340/#347 (both fixed).

comments.author: SageBluff
comments.text: VERIFIED FIX READY, handed to CobaltHarbor (connection.rs holder, mail 9304). Root cause: NOT the vacuum.rs/compat_persist.rs copy path (the issue's/my hypothesis) — it's the extra_master_entries COLLECTOR vacuum_extra_sqlite_master_entries @connection.rs:~16464, which filtered out EVERY type='table' row including the rootpage-0 vtab. Contentless FTS5 'search' is a TableSchema root_page=0; the persist schema loop skips it (db.get_table(0)=None, correct — no b-tree) and copies the positive-root shadows, but the collector then dropped the CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE row → orphaned shadows. FIX (23+/5-): preserve rootpage-0 vtab rows in the collector (skip index; skip table UNLESS root_page==0 && is_virtual_table_sql(sql)), mirroring how views/triggers (also rootpage-0) survive; CREATE never re-run. title: O1: SIMD record serialization — AVX2 bulk varint encoding for fixed-width columns

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## What
For tables with all-INTEGER columns (the most common case), use AVX2 to serialize 4 column values into the record buffer simultaneously:
1. Load 4 i64 values from registers into a __m256i
2. Compute serial types (varint sizes) via parallel shift+compare
3. Write header varints via packed store
4. Write payload bytes via sequential store (already sequential in record format)

## Where
- crates/fsqlite-types/src/record.rs: add simd_serialize_integer_record()
- crates/fsqlite-vdbe/src/engine.rs: MakeRecord handler calls SIMD path for all-integer tables

## Acceptance Criteria
1. MakeRecord microbenchmark: ≥ 20% faster for INTEGER-only tables
2. Correct output matches scalar serialization (proptest: 10K random records)
3. Runtime CPU feature detection: falls back to scalar on non-AVX2 platforms

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## BLOCKER (cc_fsq 2026-07-10): un-implementable as specified under the workspace unsafe policy.

I pulled this as the top ready in-lane PERF bead (skipping WASM bd-hnzcr; write_single is cod's).
Profiling-then-lever ran into a hard architectural wall.

### 1. The AVX2 approach this bead specifies requires `unsafe`, which fsqlite-types forbids.
Cargo.toml sets `unsafe_code = "forbid"` workspace-wide; only fsqlite-vfs and fsqlite-c-api
override it. Both `core::arch::x86_64::_mm256_*` intrinsics and `#[target_feature(enable="avx2")]`
are `unsafe` and cannot be used in crates/fsqlite-types/src/record.rs. So steps 1-4 of this
bead ('Load 4 i64 into __m256i', 'packed store', etc.) cannot be written here. This is WHY the
repo has zero `_mm256_` intrinsics and zero `#[target_feature(enable)]` fns anywhere.

### 2. The existing 'SIMD' scaffolding is a scalar no-op stub.
crates/fsqlite-types/src/record.rs:1286
  fn classify_integer_block_simd(values: [i64; 4]) -> [IntegerEncoding; 4] {
      values.map(scalar_integer_encoding)   // <- NOT simd; a scalar map
  }
The `avx2_available()` runtime check (criterion 3 of this bead) gates a path that is scalar
either way. `nightly-simd` is not enabled in any bench or the default build.

### 3. The safe escape (core::simd portable) does not deliver AVX2 either, without a separate decision.
`core::simd::Simd<i64,4>` is SAFE and would satisfy #![forbid(unsafe_code)], but portable SIMD
lowers only to the target's ENABLED features. release-perf builds at the x86_64 default
(sse2 only; see the 2026-07-10 ISA baseline audit in perf-negative-results.md), so Simd<i64,4>
emits 2x SSE2, not one AVX2 op. Reaching AVX2 needs a whole-binary target-cpu/target-feature
floor, which has a measurement-integrity cost (release stays opt-level=z/portable, so a
release-perf-only AVX2 flag would benchmark a faster binary than ships).

### Recommended re-scope (pick one, it is a project decision, not a code task):
(a) Implement classify via core::simd::Simd (SAFE, no unsafe), enable nightly-simd, AND set a
    documented target-feature floor (e.g. x86-64-v2/v3) on BOTH release and release-perf so the
    portable SIMD actually widens and the shipped binary matches the benched one. Then the '>=20%
    faster' criterion is testable.
(b) Grant fsqlite-types a scoped unsafe exception (like vfs/c-api) for a runtime-dispatched
    #[target_feature(enable="avx2")] path. Contradicts the current 'unsafe only in vfs/c-api'
    design; needs sign-off.
(c) Close as won't-do: SQLite core is scalar C with no SIMD, the comparison is already fair, and
    the DELETE hot path has zero SIMD frames — so the ROI is confined to INTEGER-heavy INSERT
    serialization only.

I did NOT force a workaround or a noise-level micro-lever. Blocked pending a scope decision.
Full ISA context: perf-negative-results.md '2026-07-10 ISA baseline audit'.

title: VDBE Dataflow Automata
description:
**Goal:** Modify the VDBE execution graph to process `(Row, Weight)` tuples, enabling full algebraic differential dataflow including complex joins.
**Implementation:** 
- Add a new execution mode/opcode variants carrying algebraic weights (e.g. +1 for insert, -1 for delete).
- Implement delta-aware operators for Projection, Filter, Group By, AND Joins (e.g., ΔLeft ⨝ Right ∪ Left ⨝ ΔRight).
- Ensure the automata can be initialized from an existing VDBE program for a `SELECT` statement.
**User Ergonomics:** Update `EXPLAIN` to optionally output the differential dataflow graph for debugging.
**Testing & Logging:**
- Unit Tests: Test +1/-1 arithmetic for all VDBE operators, especially multi-way joins. Detailed `tracing::debug` logging of row transformations.
- E2E Tests: Script `tests/e2e_differential_automata.sh` verifying dataflow output vs standard VDBE execution for complex queries.
- **Schema Evolution:** Tests must verify that if the underlying table schema changes (e.g. `ALTER TABLE`), the automata safely halts and signals subscribers to re-bootstrap.
**Success Criteria:** VDBE correctly outputs a stream of weighted rows when fed a stream of weighted input rows, matching the derivative of the query.
