title: WASM 4.5: Query result streaming via AsyncIterator for large result sets
acceptance_criteria: Query result streaming exposes AsyncIterator over large result sets with bounded memory; backpressure documented; a test streams a result larger than the chunk size and verifies order and completeness.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
# Task 4.5: Query Result Streaming

## What
For large result sets, provide AsyncIterator support to stream rows without loading everything into memory.

## API
```typescript
const stream = db.stream<User>('SELECT * FROM large_table');
for await (const row of stream) {
    process(row);
    if (done) break;  // Early termination supported
}
```

## Implementation
Uses Worker message protocol with chunked delivery. Worker sends rows in batches (e.g., 100 at a time) and pauses until the consumer is ready for more (backpressure).

## Acceptance Criteria
- AsyncIterator protocol compliance
- Backpressure support (Worker doesn't buffer unbounded)
- Early termination (break/return) properly cleans up
- Memory-efficient for million-row result sets

title: V1.5: PageData layout — Arc<[u8]> flat allocation replacing Arc<Vec<u8>>
description:
## What
`PageData` is currently `Arc<Vec<u8>>` (types/lib.rs:278) — double indirection: Arc pointer → Vec header → heap data. Replace with `Arc<[u8]>` which is a single contiguous allocation: Arc header + data bytes.

## Why  
Every page access follows two pointer chases: Arc→Vec→data. With `Arc<[u8]>`, it is one chase: Arc→data (contiguous). This saves one L1 cache miss per page access (~3-5ns). More importantly, `Arc<[u8]>` is smaller (16 bytes vs 24 bytes for Arc<Vec<u8>>) and does not carry Vec capacity metadata.

## Caveat — previous attempt failed
A prior attempt to change PageData to Arc<[u8]> was abandoned because `Arc::make_mut` requires `Sized` (Arc<[u8]> is unsized). The solution: for mutations, convert to `Vec<u8>` first, mutate, then re-wrap. Or use `Arc::get_mut()` which returns `Option<&mut [u8]>` for sole-owner cases.

## How
1. Change `PageData { data: Arc<Vec<u8>> }` to `PageData { data: Arc<[u8]> }`
2. `PageData::from_vec(v: Vec<u8>)` → `Arc::from(v)` (this allocates a contiguous block)
3. `as_bytes()` → `&*self.data` instead of `&**self.data`
4. `as_bytes_mut()` — cannot use Arc::make_mut on unsized. Use: check `Arc::get_mut()` (sole owner), else clone to Vec, mutate, re-wrap. This is rare (only B-tree page modifications).
5. Grep for all 574 PageData references and update

## Files
- `crates/fsqlite-types/src/lib.rs` — PageData struct
- ~574 references across all crates

## Estimated impact
3-5ns per page access × 250 pages per 10K INSERT = 750ns-1.25µs. Small.
But eliminates Vec metadata overhead and improves cache locality across ALL operations.

## Risk
HIGH — 574 references. Must be done carefully with extensive testing.
Consider: do this LAST, after V1.1-V1.4 and V2 are landed and verified.

title: MVCC visibility race: BEGIN CONCURRENT snapshot misses pre-seeded committed rows (balance query returns 0 rows) — capture-independent, gates workspace gate
description: Surfaced while fixing bd-gmqxy (receipt channel). comments.author: RubyJaguar
comments.text:
[bd-o81ov] batch_pending — reproduced + root-caused + fix applied (verification disk-blocked)

REPRO (disk-safe, no rebuild): ran the orchestrator's warm preflight fsqlite lib binary
(/data/tmp/claude-1000/preflight-target/.../out/fsqlite-569b24cc849bf75d, has the test) in a loop:
`<bin> --exact tests::concurrent_writers_stress_conservation` x12 -> 3/12 FAIL, each
"balance query returned 0 rows for account N" (N varies: 91, 21, 21) — matches the bead's 1-3/10.
The account varies because the worker's FIRST SELECT after a bad BEGIN picks a random id and the WHOLE
table reads empty (snapshot bound too low), not because a specific account is corrupted.

ROOT CAUSE (connection.rs concurrent_snapshot_from_publication, ~17388): the concurrent-BEGIN snapshot
commit seq is capped to the connection-local finalized floor:
    finalized = current_global_commit_seq()   // = stable_commit_seq (Arc<AtomicU64>, from shared_mvcc_state)
    requested = publication.visible_commit_seq .max( local_visible_commit_seq )
    snapshot  = if requested > finalized { finalized } else { requested }
`publication.visible_commit_seq` is read from the pager PUBLICATION plane (refresh_published_snapshot),
which only advances on FINALIZED commits — it correctly reflects the seed rows (committed+closed by the
setup connection before workers opened). But a FRESH worker connection's finalized floor
(stable_commit_seq) can still LAG that seed commit (it is raised by align_commit_clock_floor /
set_memdb_visible_commit_seq_from_publication on refresh/commit paths — bd-#70 territory — which race
against this snapshot bind under concurrent BEGIN traffic). When finalized < publication_commit_seq, the
cap pulls the bound snapshot BELOW the durable committed state, so BEGIN CONCURRENT binds a snapshot that
excludes the seed -> the whole accounts table is invisible -> "0 rows". Intermittent because it depends
on whether a prior refresh/commit raised the shared floor before this BEGIN.

FIX (applied, connection.rs concurrent_snapshot_from_publication): never cap below the durable published
committed state — the publication seq is itself a valid finalized floor:
    let finalized_commit_seq = self.current_global_commit_seq().max(publication_commit_seq);
This makes snapshot_commit_seq >= publication_commit_seq >= seed_seq in all cases (seed always visible),
while still capping a connection-local execution image that is legitimately AHEAD of the durable state
down to the durable finalized floor (the original cap's purpose). Minimal, side-effect-free (no shared
state mutation).

STATUS: fix is applied but NOT yet verified/committed — DISK IS AT 100% (7.6G free) and the RC-gate
guidance is not to rebuild under pressure. Once space is freed I will: rebuild fsqlite --lib nodebug,
re-run the repro loop (expect 0/N), then commit with receipts. FLAGGING DISK PRESSURE to the operator.

comments.author: RubyJaguar
comments.text:
[bd-o81ov] CORRECTION — root cause is PAGE-LEVEL MVCC version visibility, NOT the snapshot-seq cap

My first hypothesis (concurrent_snapshot_from_publication caps the snapshot below the durable published
seq) was WRONG and has been REVERTED. Evidence: I built the candidate fix (warm target, -j8, nodebug —
compiled clean) and looped the fixed binary 15x -> still 4/15 FAIL (~unchanged rate). Capturing ALL
failing accounts (not just the first) shows the failures are PAGE-CLUSTERED:
  - fixed binary:    runs failed on accounts [77,78,79,80] and [92]
  - original binary: run4 [21,24], run5 [22,24]
Adjacent account ids share a leaf page (100 accounts x 512B payload => ~7-8 accounts/leaf), so a whole
leaf page's rows go invisible together. The affected leaf VARIES per run. A whole-snapshot-too-low bind
would hide the ENTIRE table (every id), not a single leaf — so it is not the snapshot commit-seq.

REVISED ROOT CAUSE: the workload only does in-place balance UPDATEs (no INSERT/DELETE), so the b-tree
STRUCTURE is stable and every committed version of a leaf still contains all its accounts. For a reader
to get "0 rows" for a leaf's accounts, its snapshot must resolve that specific leaf page to a PRE-SEED
(empty) or otherwise stale version while other pages resolve correctly — i.e. inconsistent PER-PAGE
visibility under concurrent UPDATE traffic. Prime suspect: the published-page-plane vs fallback
resolution (page_plane_visible_commit_seq deliberately lags visible_commit_seq on metadata-only fast
paths, pager.rs ~10391-10394) and/or the per-page MVCC version-chain lookup racing a concurrent
copy-on-write update to that page. Definitive attribution needs page-read tracing (which page version,
from which source, at what seq) for the failing leaf — that requires an instrumented rebuild.

STATUS: reproduced reliably (disk-safe via preflight binary; ~3-4/12-15). Precise fix BLOCKED on an
instrumented rebuild — DISK IS AT 2.4G (100%). Per RC-gate guidance I will not rebuild under this
pressure. FLAGGING DISK to the operator; will instrument + fix once space is freed.

comments.author: RubyJaguar
comments.text:
[bd-o81ov] refined root-cause hypothesis — reader's WAL pinned-read misses a committed frame -> all-zero page

Read-path trace (read-only): a concurrent-BEGIN SELECT reads a leaf page via
read_committed_page_copy (pager.rs:8202):
  1. WAL mode -> read_page_from_wal_backend (5049) -> wal.read_page_pinned(page_no) — the SHARED-LOCK
     concurrent WAL read (bd-db300.3.8.7). No snapshot-seq bound; it should return the page's latest
     committed frame.
  2. If that returns None -> fall back to the main db file. But the seed is still in the WAL (uncheckpointed
     after the setup connection closed), so the main db file is at its PRE-SEED size, and
     `if offset >= file_size { return Ok(vec![0; page_size]) }` (pager.rs:8225) returns an ALL-ZERO page.
An all-zero leaf has no cells -> the b-tree seek finds no row -> "0 rows" for every account on that leaf
(explains the page-clustered, whole-leaf-invisible signature).

So the defect is: under concurrent append_frames (8 workers committing), a reader's shared-lock
`read_page_pinned` intermittently MISSES the committed frame for a specific page (returns None / stale),
and the main-db fallback is empty because the seed is uncheckpointed -> zero page. It is a WAL pinned-read
vs append race in the WAL backend, surfaced as a visibility miss.

CONFIRMATION NEEDED (instrumented, rebuild-blocked by disk): trace read_page_pinned for the failing leaf —
does it return None while the WAL index holds a committed frame for that page? Candidate fixes once
confirmed: (a) make read_page_pinned observe frames appended-and-committed before the reader's pin
(index/horizon publish ordering), or (b) when the pinned read misses, fall back to a WAL-consistent read
under the shared/write barrier rather than to the raw (possibly-uncheckpointed-short) main db file.

STATUS: reproduced reliably (disk-safe preflight binary, ~3-4/12-15, page-clustered). First fix
(snapshot-seq cap) was WRONG and reverted (built+looped: no rate change). Precise fix needs an
instrumented rebuild. DISK AT 2.0G (100%) — halting heavy work per RC-gate guidance; flagging to operator.
Will instrument read_page_pinned + land the fix once space is freed.

comments.author: RubyJaguar
comments.text:
[bd-o81ov] consolidated analysis (emergency disk pause — read-only) + instrumentation plan

WHERE THE ZERO ROWS COME FROM (read-path, layered):
- File-backed concurrent SELECT resolves rows from the connection's MEMDB MIRROR, which is (re)built by
  the BEGIN-CONCURRENT reload (refresh_concurrent_begin_from_open_txn -> reload_memdb_from_txn/pager).
- The reload reads committed pages via the pager. A committed page read is read_committed_page_copy
  (pager.rs:8202): WAL-first (read_page_from_wal_backend, 5049) then main-db fallback.
- Failure shape = a whole LEAF's accounts vanish together, leaf varies per run => that leaf page was read
  as an ALL-ZERO page during the reload, so the mirror has an empty leaf and every account on it is gone.
- All-zero arises when the WAL read returns None for that page AND the main-db fallback hits
  `offset >= file_size -> Ok(vec![0; page_size])` (pager.rs:8225) because the seed is still in the
  UNCHECKPOINTED WAL (setup connection committed+closed; main-db file is at pre-seed size).

WHY INTERMITTENT / PAGE-CLUSTERED: the deterministic part is the short main-db fallback (seed uncheckpointed
-> main db too small for high page offsets). The intermittent part is the WAL read
(read_page_from_wal_backend -> wal.read_page_pinned / read_page) MISSING that page's committed frame while
8 workers concurrently append_frames. When the WAL read serves the frame, the page is correct; when it
misses (races the append / index publish), the read falls through to the short main db -> zero page ->
whole leaf empty. A worker's committed UPDATE to that leaf is likely what marks it "changed" and forces the
reload to re-read it right as another append is in flight.

comments.text:
[bd-o81ov] DEFINITIVE ROOT CAUSE — durable B-tree interior corruption (duplicate child pointer) from concurrent UPDATE commits; the bead's "snapshot visibility" framing is WRONG

I instrumented the failure end-to-end and the previous "snapshot misses committed rows" / "zero-page" hypotheses are DISPROVEN. New evidence (fsqlite lib test binary, DK9RA_O81OV diagnostic added at the "0 rows" branch in the test, loop to first fail):

SYMPTOM DECOMPOSITION at the failing SELECT (worker in a live BEGIN CONCURRENT txn):
  DK9RA_DIAG worker=3 from_id=15 snap_count=101 snap_min_max=[0,99]
  DK9RA_DIAG_FRESH from_id=15 fresh_count=101 point=Some(0) range=Some(0)
    cluster=[11,12,13]  dups=[12,13,70,71,72]
    integrity="database disk image is malformed: page 20 is referenced multiple times
               (table `accounts` root -> child[3]; table `accounts` root -> child[14])"

- COUNT(*) / MIN / MAX (full table scan) SEE all rows (count 100/101, ids 0..99) — the rows are
  physically present; nothing is "invisible to the snapshot".
- SELECT ... WHERE id = N (rowid point seek) returns 0 rows for a CLUSTER of ids — both the point
  form (`= N`) and the range form (`>= N AND <= N`) return 0.
- A FRESH connection (its own latest snapshot) reproduces the SAME 0-row point-seek and the SAME
  inflated count → the corruption is DURABLE in the committed image, not a per-snapshot artifact.
- PRAGMA integrity_check names it exactly: the accounts B-tree ROOT interior page references the same
  child page (page 20) from TWO different child slots (child[3] AND child[14]).

WHY THIS PRODUCES EVERY SYMPTOM:
- Point seek: the root's divider-key binary search (cursor.rs search on interior keys, then leaf
  search_table_leaf at crates/fsqlite-btree/src/cursor.rs:1385) routes key 15 to child[3]→page20,
  but page20 physically holds the key range that child[14] is supposed to cover, so key 15 is not on
  the landed leaf → Ok(None) → 0 rows. (search_table_leaf's binary search is correct; it is fed the
  wrong leaf by the corrupt parent.)
- Full scan: OP_Rewind/OP_Next walks every child slot in order and therefore visits page20 TWICE →
  count inflated to 101 and dups=[the rows physically on page20]. (dups=12,13,70,71,72 are page20's
  resident rowids, enumerated on both visits.)

ZERO-PAGE / FREELIST RED HERRING RETRACTED: with the same DK9RA probes present and firing-enabled,
this failing run produced ZERO WALADP_ZERO / RCPC_WAL_ZERO / GETPAGE_WAL_ZERO / ZEROFILL /
FREELIST_* output. No page is ever served as zeros. The earlier "RCPC_WAL_ZERO page=17" was an
unrelated benign read of an empty terminal freelist trunk. The real bug never involves a zero page —
it is a corrupt interior child-pointer array.

CLASSIFICATION: this is a concurrent-writer B-tree WRITE-path corruption: two concurrent UPDATE
commits under page-level MVCC leave the accounts root interior page with a duplicated child pointer
(page20 linked at two slots). Candidate mechanisms to pin next: (i) concurrent page ALLOCATION race —
two committing txns hand out the same physical page number and each links it into the tree at a
different position; or (ii) interior child-array MERGE/REBASE duplication — the deterministic rebase
(crates/fsqlite-mvcc/src/deterministic_rebase.rs) re-applies a rebased structural op and the parent's
child array gets one pointer inserted twice. The corruption is durable, so the bad interior image is
COMMITTED, not transient.

REPRO (disk-safe, no rebuild): instrumented fsqlite lib binary at
  /data/tmp/cargo-target/debug/build/fsqlite/d190dd841ea510c7/out/fsqlite-d190dd841ea510c7
  DK9RA_O81OV=1 <bin> --exact --nocapture tests::concurrent_writers_stress_conservation  (loop; ~1-3/25 fail)
On failure the DK9RA_DIAG_FRESH line prints integrity_check = "page N referenced multiple times".

throwaway (to be reverted); the earlier pager.rs 20577 zero-fill gate is unrelated to this root cause

comments.author: RubyJaguar
comments.text:
[bd-o81ov] CONFIRMED root cause + fix design: cross-connection EOF page DOUBLE-ALLOCATION (WAL group-commit misses it, incl. intra-epoch)

Added an ALLOC_EOF probe to SimpleTransaction::allocate_page (EOF arm) logging thread id + page +
db_size. Captured a failing run:

  integrity: "page 18 is referenced multiple times (accounts root -> child[...]; ...)"
  ALLOC_EOF: page=18 allocated by ThreadId(11), ThreadId(5), ThreadId(9) — all mode=Concurrent, all db_size=17
             page=20 allocated by ThreadId(10), ThreadId(6)

=> Multiple worker CONNECTIONS (each its own PagerInner, hence its own next_page = committed db_size
17 + 1 = 18) each hand out the SAME EOF page number 18, write different B-tree content into it, and
all commit. The committed accounts B-tree therefore links page 18 from more than one child slot →
"page N referenced multiple times". This is the whole bug. It is durable, page-clustered (the aliased
leaf's rowids), and it makes point-seeks fail while full scans double-count (see prior comment). The
"snapshot visibility" and "zero-page" framings are both wrong; no page is ever served as zeros.

WHY same-size balance UPDATEs allocate EOF pages: still to be fully traced, but empirically every
failing run shows Concurrent-mode allocate_page handing out fresh EOF pages during the transfer loop
(likely btree leaf churn / copy-forward under MVCC). The allocation itself is fine; the defect is that
two connections' concurrent commits are allowed to BOTH keep the same freshly-allocated EOF page.

WHY THE EXISTING GUARDS MISS IT:
- Rollback-journal mode HAS a guard (pager.rs ~18335-18414, bd-9inpb): under the EXCLUSIVE commit
  lock it reads the committed page-1 db_size; if it grew past this txn's snapshot original_db_size and
  the write_set contains any page in (original_db_size, committed_db_size], it aborts BusySnapshot →
  caller retries against the refreshed size. The comment there DESCRIBES THIS EXACT BUG.
- WAL mode (our default) relies only on conflicting_pages_since_batch_snapshots →
  wal.conflicting_pages_since_snapshot (pager.rs ~19427). A freshly EOF-allocated page has no
  pre-snapshot baseline, and — decisively — the process-global group-commit queue
  (GROUP_COMMIT_QUEUES keyed by PathBuf, pager.rs ~5094) batches DIFFERENT connections' commits into
  ONE epoch. Within an epoch the batches do not observe each other's db-size growth, so two batches
  that both allocate page 18 both pass the since-snapshot check and both commit. => WAL mode has NO
  effective cross-connection EOF-alias guard, and the missing check must cover the INTRA-EPOCH case,
  not just "peer already committed".

FIX DESIGN (fail-safe, abort→retry; mirrors the accepted journal-mode guard but epoch-aware):
Two complementary options; (A) is the smaller change, (B) is the robust one.
  (A) At the WAL commit critical section (pager.rs ~19424, after refresh_published_snapshot, under the
      append gate): for each batch, if the current committed db_size (from the refreshed published WAL
      snapshot) > that batch's snapshot db_size and the batch writes any page in
      (batch_snapshot_db_size, committed_db_size], abort BusySnapshot. Requires threading each batch's
      begin-time db_size onto TransactionFrameBatch (it currently carries only the WAL
      generation/frame conflict_snapshot, not db_size). This catches cross-EPOCH aliasing but NOT two
      batches in the same epoch.
  (B) Add an INTRA-EPOCH EOF-overlap check when assembling/finalizing the group-commit epoch: compute
      each batch's set of freshly-allocated pages (pages in its write_set with page_no >
      batch_snapshot_db_size, i.e. allocated_from_eof) and, if two batches in the epoch claim
      overlapping EOF page numbers, keep the first and abort the rest with BusySnapshot (they retry and
      re-allocate against the grown size). This is the check that actually fixes the observed failure.
  Recommended: implement (B) (intra-epoch overlap) and fold in (A)'s cross-epoch db-size guard for
  completeness. Net effect: two connections can never commit the same EOF page; the loser retries and
  allocates the next free page, exactly as EOF growth is meant to serialize.
  Alternative (heavier, not recommended first): coordinate EOF allocation across connections via a
  shared per-file-identity next_page so double-allocation never happens at alloc time — larger blast
  radius (rollback/quarantine of unused reservations), riskier.

VERIFICATION PLAN before commit: build fsqlite --lib nodebug (warm target), loop
tests::concurrent_writers_stress_conservation ≥40x expecting 0 fails + integrity_check clean; then run
the full concurrent-writer suite (fsqlite-e2e, pager concurrent tests) to confirm no new BusySnapshot
starvation / regression. This touches the core first-committer-wins commit path (AGENTS.md: the
concurrent-writer machinery is the project's entire point), so it must be verified broadly, not just on
the one repro.

        commit is not yet durable/published when this one checks. `committed_db > snap_db` is false,
        so page 19 is never flagged.
The guard is CORRECT and DOES fire when commits serialize (observed `EOFGUARD snap_db=18
committed_db=19` on unrelated update commits, with no false positives), but it is structurally unable
to catch two EOF allocations that commit concurrently/in parallel WAL epochs — neither's frame is
visible to the other's pre-append conflict scan. The existing intra-epoch cross-batch check
(conflicting_pages_across_group_commit_batches, pager.rs ~19143) also does not catch it in practice
(the colliding commits are not both present as fresh-page frames in a single epoch's batch set at that
point — likely parallel epochs / lane-staged frames).

EPOCH STRUCTURE (decisive, instrumented): every group-commit epoch in this workload is SINGLE-BATCH
(`EPOCH n_batches=1` for all 19 sampled epochs). The two colliding commits (e.g. page 18, two writers
each `per_batch=[(snap=17, maxframe=18)]`) land in SEPARATE, concurrent single-batch epochs. Therefore
the intra-epoch cross-batch check (conflicting_pages_across_group_commit_batches) can NEVER catch this
— there is only one batch per epoch, so there is nothing to compare it against — and the two epochs
run concurrently (parallel WAL lanes), so neither commit is durable/visible to the other's pre-append
conflict scan. This RULES OUT the smaller intra-epoch fix.

CONCLUSION: this cannot be fixed by any commit-time conflict scan that reads the durable WAL, because
the competing allocation is in-flight in a concurrent single-batch epoch and invisible. The fix must
PREVENT the double-allocation at the source.

RECOMMENDED FIX (source-level allocation coordination): give EOF allocation a shared, per-file-identity
monotonic high-water mark. All connections to one file already share a process-global GroupCommitQueue
(GROUP_COMMIT_QUEUES keyed by PathBuf, pager.rs ~5094) reachable from SimpleTransaction
(`self.group_commit_queue`). Add an `AtomicU32` next-EOF-page to that queue; in
`SimpleTransaction::allocate_page` (pager.rs ~20908) concurrent-mode EOF arm, reserve via
`fetch_max(inner.db_size)` then atomic increment (CAS loop) instead of the connection-local
`inner.next_page`, so two connections can never hand out the same physical page. Rollback semantics
match today's "never rewind next_page" (uncommitted reservations become holes above committed
db_size). Excludes memory bump-alloc + non-WAL. This removes the race entirely; the commit-time guard
becomes a belt-and-suspenders backstop (keep it — it is correct and false-positive-free) but is no
longer load-bearing.
ALTERNATIVE (smaller, perf-costly): force any EOF-growing commit onto the serialized (non-parallel-WAL)
append path so the existing guard's `committed_db_size` reflects the prior grower and the retry
re-allocates — serializes only growth commits, preserves parallel WAL for pure updates. (The
intra-epoch-check alternative is dead: epochs are single-batch here.)

RECOMMENDATION: implement the shared per-file-identity EOF high-water mark (source-level coordination).
It is the only option that closes the race regardless of parallel-epoch timing.

be committed as-is — it is an incomplete foundation, not a working fix. DK9RA_O81OV eprintln probes
(ALLOC_EOF/CPBS/EOFGUARD/EPOCH in pager.rs, WALADP in wal_adapter.rs) and the DK9RA_DIAG integrity
dump in fsqlite/src/lib.rs test remain in-tree to support the repro. Nothing committed this pass

title: CI-P1: 259 of 269 fsqlite-e2e integration tests are compiled but NEVER executed by any workflow (allowlist drift)
notes:
Found 2026-07-26 by GreenBirch while wiring a regression guard for the
bd-105ga/bd-kwei8 corruption class.

## The gap, measured
    crates/fsqlite-e2e/tests/*.rs                      269 files
    distinct e2e integration tests any workflow runs    10
    => 259 (96%) are COMPILED but NEVER EXECUTED in CI.

The ten that do run:
    bd_073kf_swarm_harness
    bd_2yqp6_6_1_ssi_serialization_anomaly_differential
    bd_2yqp6_6_2_busy_retry_error_semantics_matrix
    bd_2yqp6_6_3_crash_recovery_corruption_matrix
    bd_2yqp6_6_5_concurrent_mode_defaults
    bd_3v5ci_connection_not_sync
    bd_aiica_integrity_check
    correctness_concurrent_writes
    golden_integrity
    mvcc_concurrent_writers

## Why it happens (two independent mechanisms)
1. `.github/workflows/concurrent-platform-matrix.yml` runs
   `cargo test -p fsqlite-e2e --no-run` (BUILD ONLY) and then executes an
   explicit allowlist of `--test <name>` targets. New tests/*.rs files are
   therefore compiled and silently skipped by default.
2. `.github/workflows/unit-test-shard-matrix.yml:92` runs
   `cargo test -p "${crate}" ${test_target}` with `test_target="--lib"` for
   every crate except fsqlite-cli (`--bins`). fsqlite-e2e IS in that shard's
   crate list (line 33) but `--lib` never touches tests/.

So "fsqlite-e2e is covered by two workflows" is true and misleading: one
builds without running, the other runs only the crate's lib unit tests.

## Why this matters more than the raw number
fsqlite-e2e is where the differential, conformance, corruption and MVCC
integration tests live. A regression in any of the 259 is invisible to CI. It
also means adding a test to that directory provides no protection unless the
author also edits a workflow allowlist -- which is not documented anywhere and
is easy to miss (I only noticed because I went looking before landing a guard).

## Also found
README.md's CI badge points at
`.../actions/workflow/status/Dicklesworthstone/frankensqlite/ci.yml?branch=main`
but `.github/workflows/ci.yml` DOES NOT EXIST. The badge cannot reflect any
real workflow. Existing workflows are: concurrent-platform-matrix,
unit-test-shard-matrix, verification-gates, semver-check, windows-vfs-interop,
fsqlite-wasm-ci, release.

## Suggested direction (owner's call)
- Decide deliberately: either run the suite (`cargo test -p fsqlite-e2e`,
  possibly sharded/nightly for runtime) or keep an allowlist that is
  MECHANICALLY CHECKED -- e.g. a gate that fails when a tests/*.rs exists that
  no workflow names. A drifting allowlist is worse than an explicit small one
  because it looks like coverage.
- Point the README badge at a workflow that exists, or remove it.
- Immediate, narrow ask: add `--test bd_105ga_replace_conflict_guard` (and
  `--test bd_105ga_replay_regression`) to the allowlist, or the P0 corruption
  class this session investigated has no executing regression guard.

title: Track M: Epoch-Based Reclamation — Replace Arc<> with Zero-Cost Epoch Pinning
close_reason: Safe thread-local value slab fallback verified and landed

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## Problem (from alien-graveyard §14.10)
Every SqliteValue::Text and SqliteValue::Blob uses Arc<> for reference counting. Arc::clone() costs ~5 ns (atomic fetch_add with SeqCst). Arc::drop() costs ~5 ns (atomic fetch_sub + possible dealloc). For a 3-column row, that's 6 atomic operations = ~30 ns of pure reference counting overhead.

## Solution: crossbeam-epoch Pinning
Replace Arc<str> with epoch-pinned raw pointers. Readers pin the current epoch (1 atomic store, amortized across many reads). Values are retired to epoch garbage lists. When all readers advance past the epoch, values are freed in bulk. Per-access cost: ~1 ns (epoch check) vs ~10 ns (Arc clone+drop).

## Why This Is Safe
crossbeam-epoch is already a dependency (used for MVCC). The epoch pinning API is well-tested. Values allocated in an epoch arena are guaranteed to live until all readers advance. This is the same pattern used by LeanStore, Silo, and Hekaton.

## Expected Impact: -0.03 to -0.07 µs per row (eliminates all atomic ref counting in hot path)

## Fallback
If epoch pinning proves too complex for SqliteValue, keep Arc but use a thread-local cache of recently freed values (slab allocator) to amortize alloc/dealloc costs. This is simpler and still saves ~0.02 µs.

title: Correctness test: MVCC isolation — snapshot reads during concurrent writes
close_reason: done

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## Acceptance Criteria
- Test validates MVCC snapshot isolation during concurrent read/write operations
- Reader threads see consistent snapshots unaffected by concurrent writers
- Writer commits become visible only to new transactions started after commit
- Tests at least 3 concurrent readers and 2 concurrent writers

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## Task: Correctness test — MVCC isolation: snapshot reads during concurrent writes

### What
Demonstrate FrankenSQLite's MVCC advantage: readers see a consistent snapshot even while writers are actively modifying data. C SQLite's WAL mode allows this too, but with different characteristics.

### Test Design

**Phase 1: Writer thread**
- Begins a transaction
- Inserts 10,000 rows in batches of 100
- Commits after each batch
- Signals "done" when complete

**Phase 2: Reader thread (concurrent)**
- Opens a read transaction (BEGIN)
- Reads the table repeatedly during writer activity
- Verifies snapshot isolation:
  - Row count is consistent within a single read transaction
  - No partial batch visible (either all 100 rows from a batch or none)
  - No torn reads (half of a row's columns from old version, half from new)

**Phase 3: Verification**
- Writer completes all 10,000 rows
- Reader sees its snapshot (potentially stale — that's correct behavior)
- Reader closes transaction, re-reads — now sees all 10,000 rows
- Compare final state between backends

### MVCC-Specific Assertions
1. **Read stability**: Within a read transaction, repeated SELECTs return the same result (no phantom reads)
2. **No dirty reads**: Uncommitted writer changes are never visible to reader
3. **Snapshot freshness**: New read transaction after writer commits sees all changes

### Why This Is a Key Demo
This test directly demonstrates the MVCC advantage from §5 of the spec. C SQLite's WAL mode provides snapshot isolation for readers, but writers still serialize via WAL_WRITE_LOCK. FrankenSQLite's MVCC page-level versioning allows true concurrent readers and writers without the write serialization.

### Acceptance Criteria
- Snapshot isolation verified: reader sees consistent state throughout transaction
- No phantom reads within a read transaction
- No dirty reads
- Final state matches between backends after all transactions complete
- Test runs with both 1 writer + 1 reader and 1 writer + 4 readers

title: BUG-P2: WHERE a=? ORDER BY b (non-unique, no tiebreaker) streams off (a,b) index but diverges from C SQLite on tie order
description: SELECT id,b FROM t WHERE a=? ORDER BY b ASC LIMIT k on a composite (a,b) index streams off the index (no sorter) and returns a DIFFERENT tie representative/order than C SQLite: ORDER BY b ASC LIMIT 1 -> frank id=93 vs sqlite id=293 (both b=1); LIMIT 3 differs in order and rows. Bare ORDER BY b (no unique tiebreaker) has implementation-defined tie order; frank uses index rowid order, C SQLite differs -> byte-exactness gate violation for this common top-k-per-group shape. Repro: where_eq_orderby_limit_probe.rs. Consequence: a 'top-k per group off the index, no sorter' perf lever is byte-exact-unsafe (DESC case currently sorts+matches; streaming it would risk the same divergence). Fix options: decline index-order streaming when the ORDER BY is not fully determined (no trailing unique key), or match C SQLite's tie order.

title: julianday->calendar conversion diverges at extreme Julian day (datetime(0) gives -4712-01-01 vs SQLite -4713-11-24)
close_reason: jdn_to_ymd now proleptic Gregorian matching SQLite computeYMD (commit 54f75573)

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
# julianday->calendar conversion diverges at extreme Julian day

## Symptom
At Julian day number 0, frank's JDN->calendar conversion is wrong by ~1 year/38d.
```sql
SELECT datetime(0, 'auto');
-- SQLite: '-4713-11-24 12:00:00'   frank: '-4712-01-01 12:00:00'  (WRONG)
```
This is NOT an `'auto'` bug: `'auto'` correctly classifies 0 as a Julian day
(not a Unix timestamp), and normal-range conversions are correct:
```sql
SELECT datetime(1686836730, 'auto'); -- OK (unix)
SELECT datetime(2460111.0, 'auto');  -- OK (julian, modern date)
SELECT date(2460111, 'auto');        -- OK
```

## Root cause (suspected)
`crates/fsqlite-func/src/datetime.rs` `jdn_to_ymd` — the proleptic
Gregorian/Julian calendar conversion diverges from SQLite's algorithm at very
small (pre-historic) JDN values near 0. SQLite places JDN 0 at -4713-11-24 12:00
(proleptic Gregorian). frank's formula gives -4712-01-01 there. Likely an
off-by-era / proleptic-calendar-boundary difference that only manifests at
extreme dates; modern dates are unaffected.

## Scope / priority
Narrow extreme-date edge (JDN at/near 0, i.e. years before ~-4712). Unlikely to
affect real workloads, but a clean-room conformance gap. Verify against SQLite's
`computeJD`/`computeYMD` in date.c for the exact boundary constants.

title: I1: Retained write transaction for autocommit — hold txn open across statements
close_reason: Committed in e2582062: retained autocommit transaction for file-backed databases

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## What
In Connection::execute_statement(), when in autocommit mode, instead of begin/commit per statement:
1. If no retained txn exists: begin one
2. Execute statement within the retained txn
3. Mark dirty (needs eventual flush)
4. On next statement: reuse the retained txn
5. Flush (commit+reopen) every 64 statements or on read-after-write

## Where
- crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs: execute_statement_impl_after_background_status()
- Add field: `retained_autocommit_txn: Option<TransactionState>`
- Add field: `retained_stmt_count: u32`

## Why This Is The Biggest Single Win
Current autocommit: 10K rows × 30 µs/cycle = 300 ms
With retained txn: 10K rows × 1.7 µs/row + 156 flushes × 30 µs = 21.7 ms
Speedup: 300ms → 21.7ms = **13.8x improvement on autocommit alone**

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Autocommit 10K rows benchmark: ≤ 5x slower than C SQLite (from 31.52x)
2. Read-after-write returns correct data within same connection
3. Connection close flushes all pending writes
4. ROLLBACK properly undoes retained changes
5. conformance_oracle_s55 passes (no behavior change visible to user)

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## Risk & Fallback
**Risk 1 (CRITICAL)**: Read-after-write inconsistency. If the retained txn doesn't flush before a read, the user sees stale data.
**Mitigation**: Flush BEFORE any SELECT/pragma/read operation on a dirty table. The dirty-table tracking (from Track J) serves double duty here.

**Risk 2**: Retained txn accumulates too many dirty pages, causing commit to be slow.
**Mitigation**: Hard cap at 1000 dirty pages. Beyond that, force-flush even mid-write workload.

**Risk 3**: Connection close without flush loses data.
**Mitigation**: Connection::drop() MUST flush. Add a debug_assert that retained_txn is None at drop time.

**Rollback**: PRAGMA fsqlite.autocommit_retain = OFF disables the optimization. Default ON.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## IMPORTANT (Review Pass 4): Existing Autocommit Optimizations
The codebase already has autocommit optimization work:
- `memory_autocommit_fast_path_begins` counter (connection.rs:386) — fast path for :memory: autocommit
- `prepared_direct_insert_autocommit_*` metrics (connection.rs:435-438) — prepared INSERT autocommit path

### Before implementing I1, FIRST:
1. Understand what the existing fast path does (read the code around those metrics)
2. Profile whether the existing fast path already covers our use case
3. If the existing fast path reduces ceremony but still does begin/commit per statement, I1 adds the RETAINED transaction on top
4. If the existing fast path already retains a transaction, I1 may be partially redundant — adjust scope

### The 31x gap suggests the existing fast path is NOT fully effective
If it were, autocommit would be much closer to single-txn performance (3-5x, not 31x). So I1 is likely needed, but should BUILD ON the existing fast path, not duplicate it.

title: Corruption Injection + RaptorQ Repair Demo for SQLite DB Files
description:
## Goal
Create a dramatic, *real-file* durability demo:

1. Take a real SQLite DB (fixture).
2. Produce a correct mutated version (via workload harness).
3. Make an **encoded safety sidecar** (RaptorQ repair symbols + checksums).
4. Intentionally corrupt the DB copy (bit flips, truncation, torn-page simulation).
5. Show baseline `sqlite3` cannot self-heal (integrity check fails, data inaccessible).
6. Repair the corrupted DB using FrankenSQLite tooling that embodies “RaptorQ everywhere”.
7. Verify repaired DB matches the expected golden output (canonical sha256 match + integrity_check).

## Notes
- RaptorQ repairs *erasures*; for random corruption, we must detect corrupted chunks (checksums) and treat them as missing.
- Work at page/chunk granularity (default 4KB pages) to align with SQLite storage reality.

## Deliverables
- Corruption injector tool (safe: operates only on copies)
- Encoder tool producing sidecar symbols
- Repair tool that reconstructs missing/corrupted chunks
- End-to-end script that runs the full story and produces a report

## Acceptance
- At least 2 corruption modes demonstrated end-to-end.
- `sqlite3` integrity check fails before repair and passes after repair.
- Repaired canonical image sha256 matches the uncorrupted expected canonical image.

title: Track V: VDBE Interpreter Acceleration — Close 8-15x Single-Thread Gap
description:
## Context

After eliminating the O(n²) memdb refresh bug (230x improvement) and landing 5 constant-factor optimizations (~10% cumulative), FrankenSQLite single-thread INSERT remains 8-15x slower than C SQLite. The gap is now dominated by three structural costs:

1. **VDBE dispatch overhead** (~3-15ns/opcode): 181-arm cold-path match, per-opcode ceremony (bounds check, metrics, trace flag), register access overhead (NaN normalization, subtype HashMap probe)
2. **Page access overhead** (~50-200ns/page read): Arc<Vec<u8>> double indirection, cell pointer heap allocation per page load, 4KB memcpy in page cache get_copy(), first-access copy in StagedPage::published_page()
3. **MVCC per-operation ceremony**: Mutex locks for concurrent handle, HashMap probes for write_set/freed pages, RefCell borrow overhead in SharedTxnPageIo

## Strategy — Three Radical Approaches (ordered by EV)

### V1: Zero-Copy Page Access (highest EV, moderate complexity)
Eliminate unnecessary page copies and allocations in the B-tree cursor hot path.

### V2: Superinstruction Fusion for INSERT (high EV, moderate complexity)  
Fuse common opcode sequences (NewRowid+MakeRecord+Insert, OpenWrite+Last) into single "superinstructions" that bypass the interpreter dispatch loop entirely.

### V3: Speculative JIT for Prepared DML (high EV, high complexity)
Compile hot prepared INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE programs to native Rust closures that bypass the VDBE interpreter entirely. The JIT infrastructure stubs already exist (JitDecision enum, hot threshold tracking, plan hash caching at engine.rs:5874-6009).

## Target
- V1: 2-3x improvement on page-heavy operations (INSERT, full scan)
- V2: ~30-50% improvement on small prepared DML (fewer opcodes, less dispatch)
- V3: 3-5x improvement on prepared DML tight loops (eliminate interpreter entirely)
- Combined: close gap from 8-15x to 2-4x on single-thread DML

## Non-regression constraint
All optimizations must pass existing conformance oracle suite (928+ ext, 644+ s55).
Benchmark: comprehensive-bench sections 1-6 must show improvement or no regression.

## Key measurements before starting (baseline)
- 10K tiny INSERT single-txn: C=2.7ms, F=39.5ms (14.6x)
- 100K tiny INSERT: C=28ms, F=434ms (15.5x)  
- Per-opcode: ~5.6µs per INSERT row (7 opcodes × ~800ns avg)
- C SQLite per-opcode: ~0.4µs per INSERT row

title: DOC-INVARIANT VOID: .gitignore excludes tests/artifacts/perf/**/* so EVERY artifact path cited in README.md is unverifiable — including the headline 40.99x concurrent-writer claim
description:
Found 2026-07-25 while executing the campaign's 're-measure concurrent-writers and republish' assignment.

AGENTS.md 'Documentation Invariants for Performance Claims' requires: 'Every numeric performance claim in README.md must name the benchmark or artifact that measures it, including the artifact path or commit and the date of the run.'

.gitignore line 230 is:
    tests/artifacts/perf/**/*

So no perf artifact is ever committed. Every artifact path in README.md resolves to nothing for anyone who did not personally run the benchmark on the machine that produced it.

CONCRETE CASE: README cites the headline concurrent-writer numbers (the marquee 40.99x at 8 threads, and the shared-table 3.42x table) to
    tests/artifacts/perf/may8-current-gap-audit-20260508T2330Z/
    (mt-mvcc-separate-tables.json and mt-mvcc-shared-table.stdout)
That directory does not exist in the working tree and 'git log --all -- <path>' returns nothing: it was never committed. git check-ignore confirms .gitignore:230 is the reason.

The campaign doc quotes '40.99x at 8T' as this repo's honest marquee result. Per the repo's own invariant that number is currently uncitable.

I COMMITTED THE SAME DEFECT: my commit dd84b4d7 cites tests/artifacts/perf/dml-observer-3way-20260725T2205Z/ as its evidence. 'git ls-files' on that path is empty - my 'git add' was silently skipped by the same ignore rule. The message references files that are not in the repo.

WHY THIS IS P1: it silently voids the entire evidence chain the perf campaign is built on. An agent reading a README claim cannot check it; an agent reading a ledger entry's 'Evidence artifacts:' line cannot check it either (the ledger cites these paths constantly). It also means artifact-based reproduction across machines is impossible, which is precisely how the bd-zavyn instrument drift went unnoticed.

RESOLUTION OPTIONS (owner decision - do not change .gitignore unilaterally, it was set deliberately and perf artifacts can be large):
1. Narrow the ignore to large binaries and commit the small JSON/summary artifacts that claims actually cite (the three JSONs + log for my run total ~215 KB).
2. Keep the ignore, and change the invariant to cite a commit + exact reproduction command instead of a path, so claims are reproducible rather than merely referenced.
3. Publish artifacts to a separate retained location and cite that.

Option 2 is cheapest and matches what the campaign's harness contract already wants (self-reporting ELF sha + exact command). Option 1 is the only one that makes existing citations resolve.

Until this is resolved, no README perf claim in this repo is independently checkable, and that should be stated plainly rather than left implicit.

notes: INVESTIGATION (2026-06-26, this session). Confirmed via codegen_gap_probe: update_from_join AND update_from_comma_tables both still error 'UPDATE ... FROM with JOIN clauses is not yet supported' at fsqlite-vdbe/src/codegen.rs codegen_update_from (the single dispatch path; codegen_update -> codegen_update_from when stmt.from.is_some(); NO interpreted fallback). ROOT CONSTRAINT: codegen_update_from is a hand-rolled nested loop with a SINGLE secondary (ScanCtx.secondary: Option<SecondaryScan> = one table+alias). A JOIN/comma FROM needs MULTIPLE secondaries (e.g. src.w AND k.k must both resolve), which one secondary cannot express. Also vdbe codegen has NO FROM-subquery/relation materialization anywhere (emit_scalar_subquery itself only handles named tables). TWO viable approaches: (a) extend ScanCtx to Vec<SecondaryScan> + emit N nested loops in codegen_update_from + multi-table column resolution (deeper, touches shared resolution); (b) materialize the entire FROM relation (join result) into an OpenEphemeral table and drive the existing single-secondary loop against it, with a synthetic schema — but qualified refs (src.w, k.k) can't map onto one ephemeral table's columns, so (b) still needs multi-alias resolution. SIBLING bd-kkfok (subquery FROM source, NO joins) was handled THIS session via collision-safe subquery FLATTENING in connection.rs (try_flatten_update_from_subquery) — that does NOT generalize to joins (it bails when from.joins is non-empty). DEFERRED: needs (a) multi-secondary support. The flatten currently makes single-source subquery FROM work; p0xje remains for multi-source.

title: Stateful B-tree cursor persistence for sequential inserts: skip seek for monotonic keys (C SQLite BtreeInsert append fast-path)
close_reason: Implemented: last_successful_insert_rowid tracking on StorageCursor. When new rowid > last, skip table_move_to seek. Matches C SQLite BTREE_APPEND. 938 ext oracle tests pass.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: Background: C SQLite BtreeInsert has a BTREE_APPEND fast path -- when cursor is at end and key is larger than all existing keys, insert without seeking. FrankenSQLite StorageCursor seeks from root on every insert. Fix: After a successful table_insert, if the key was appended (larger than previous), remember cursor position. On next insert, if new key is larger, skip seek and insert at cached position. Files: btree/src/cursor.rs (add cached_position, try_append_fast_path), vdbe/src/engine.rs (pass BTREE_APPEND hint from codegen when keys are monotonic). Tests: cursor_append_fast_path_sequential_keys, cursor_append_fallback_random_keys, cursor_append_correctness_after_page_split, benchmark_sequential_insert_with_append. Success: sequential INSERT throughput improved by skipping B-tree seek per row.

title: RELEASE-P0: bound page-cache victim selection at pool ceiling (GH #326)
description: At pool saturation, ShardedPageCache::take_clean_buffer builds page_snapshots for the entire resident cache, sorts all snapshots by access_count and page number, then removes one clean buffer. GH #326 reports deterministic collapse in a 2.9 GiB downstream rebuild at the configured ceiling, with about 96% CPU in page_snapshots and no effective size-tuning workaround. Current main confirms the O(n log n) per-allocation path. Replace it with bounded or amortized O(1)-ish clean-only victim selection that preserves GH #131 invariants: never discard dirty data, never reclaim a foreign-pool buffer, never expose a duplicate tier image, retain flat-slot ABA safety, and make progress under concurrency. Add a deterministic structural keeper that fails if the saturated reclaim path rebuilds a diagnostic snapshot, plus focused flat/overflow/dirty/foreign/concurrent coverage and citation-grade before/after evidence. Before implementation, check the performance negative-results ledger and recent verified history; if a candidate is rejected by the matrix, record it durably. No release waiver.
acceptance_criteria: 1. The saturated clean-buffer path does not call page_snapshots or sort the full resident set. 2. Victim discovery is bounded or amortized O(1)-ish for the steady-state clean read workload and has no O(n log n) per-allocation fallback. 3. Dirty pages, foreign-pool buffers, duplicate-tier images, and flat-slot ABA races remain fail-closed. 4. Deterministic keepers cover fast-array, flat-slot, overflow-shard, dirty-only, foreign-buffer, and concurrent-race shapes without timing-only assertions. 5. Focused pager tests, full pager tests, strict Clippy, rustfmt, diff hygiene, and UBS pass remotely. 6. Before/after release-perf evidence on a ceiling-crossing scan is retained with source, host, profile, and raw samples; any rejected candidate is added to the negative-results ledger.

title: fsqlite-parser::semantic resolver is engine-unused (false-green fix trap) — wire it, document it as standalone, or remove with authorization
description:
## SUMMARY
crates/fsqlite-parser/src/semantic.rs implements a complete name-
resolution layer (Resolver/Schema/Scope) that nothing in the engine
uses: zero imports of `fsqlite_parser::semantic` exist anywhere in the
workspace outside the parser crate itself, and only semantic_test.rs
exercises it. Actual name resolution happens in fsqlite-core's
connection.rs via connection-owned resolver types
(SelectRelationResolver / SelectStructureResolver /
SelectColumnReferenceResolver / CteResultMetadataResolver, ~37006+).

## WHY THIS IS A TRAP (not just dead weight)
An agent asked to fix a resolution bug can plausibly land a "fix" in
fsqlite_parser::semantic, watch semantic_test.rs go green, and change
engine behavior not at all — a false-green class this repo has been
bitten by before. The module also inflates the parser crate's apparent
surface for anyone auditing coverage.

## EVIDENCE (verified during skill research, re-verify before work)
- `rg "fsqlite_parser::semantic|parser::semantic" --type rust` across
  the workspace: hits only inside crates/fsqlite-parser/.
- connection.rs performs its own resolution (grep the resolver type
  names above).

## FIX SKETCH (decide, then do ONE)
A. WIRE IT: if the long-term plan is to move resolution down into the
   parser layer (cf. bd-1dp9.3.x semantic-closure waves and the
   fsqlite-planner "no name resolution" boundary), make this module the
   real substrate and migrate connection.rs callers — that is a large
   epic; if chosen, split into its own bead tree and close this one as
   superseded.
B. DOCUMENT IT: add a module-level doc header stating it is a
   standalone/reference implementation not used by the engine, pointing
   at connection.rs as the live resolver — cheap, kills the trap.
C. REMOVE IT: requires operator deletion authorization (AGENTS.md
   Rule 1) and loses a possibly-useful future substrate.

Default recommendation: B now (one doc comment), leaving A as an
explicit future decision.

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] The zero-external-use claim re-verified at fix time.
- [ ] One of A/B/C executed; if B, the doc header names the live
      resolution path in connection.rs and this bead id.
- [ ] fsqlite-mega-skill note (SQL-FRONTEND-VDBE "orphaned resolver"
      trap) still accurate afterward or updated.

## PROVENANCE
Found during frankensqlite-mega-skill SQL-frontend research; recorded as
frontend gotcha #3 ("dead code from Connection's perspective — a
stale-test trap") in the skill.

Zero-external-use claim re-verified at close time (rg across crates/ excluding fsqlite-parser: no hits). Option A (wire it as the real resolution substrate) remains an explicit future decision for the bd-1dp9.3.x semantic-closure program; fsqlite-mega-skill's trap note updated to reflect the self-documenting header.

title: GH #280 PRAGMA soft_heap_limit / hard_heap_limit: implement process-global set/get
description:
GH issue https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/frankensqlite/issues/280 — verified OPEN, zero implementation.

## Exact C SQLite 3.46.1 semantics (empirically derived, matches pragma.c + malloc.c)

Both limits are **process-global**, not per-connection. Confirmed: `ATTACH ':memory:' AS b; PRAGMA soft_heap_limit=12345678; PRAGMA b.soft_heap_limit;` -> 12345678.

Both forms (bare and assignment) emit exactly one integer row = the value AFTER any mutation (`returnSingleInt(v, sqlite3_*_heap_limit64(-1))`).

**soft_heap_limit = N**  (`sqlite3_soft_heap_limit64`)
- N < 0 -> no change.
- otherwise: if `hard > 0 && (N > hard || N == 0)` then N is clamped to `hard`; then `soft = N`.

**hard_heap_limit = N**  (pragma.c guard, then `sqlite3_hard_heap_limit64`)
- pragma.c only calls the setter when `N > 0 && (prior_hard == 0 || prior_hard > N)` — i.e. from SQL the hard limit can only be **lowered**, never raised, and never set from a non-positive value.
- the setter also does: `hard = N; if (N < soft || soft == 0) { soft = N; }` — lowering hard retroactively lowers soft.

Non-numeric text -> `sqlite3DecOrHexToI64` fails -> no mutation, just readback. Hex (`0x2000000`) is accepted.

## Measured oracle transcript
```
bare soft / bare hard                          -> 0 / 0
hard=10000000; soft=50000000; bare soft        -> 10000000 / 10000000 / 10000000   (soft clamped to hard)
hard=50000000; soft=10000000; bare soft        -> 50000000 / 10000000 / 10000000
soft=90000000; hard=30000000; soft; hard       -> 90000000 / 30000000 / 30000000 / 30000000  (hard lowers soft)
soft=-5; bare                                  -> 0 / 0
soft=80000000; soft=0; bare                    -> 80000000 / 0 / 0
hard=80000000; hard=0; bare                    -> 80000000 / 80000000 / 80000000   (0 cannot clear hard)
hard=30000000; hard=50000000; bare             -> 30000000 / 30000000 / 30000000   (cannot raise)
soft=0x2000000; bare                           -> 33554432 / 33554432
```

## Wiring
Store as two process-global `AtomicI64`s in crates/fsqlite-vdbe/src/lib.rs (NOT in `ConnectionPragmaState` — per-connection storage would diverge on the multi-connection differential test the issue describes). Add `apply_soft_heap_limit` / `apply_hard_heap_limit` and dispatch arms next to `apply_threads`.

FrankenSQLite has no malloc-alarm mechanism, so like `PRAGMA threads` this is a faithful set/get surface with no allocator enforcement — say so in the doc comment rather than pretending it caps memory. Note C SQLite genuinely aborts with SQLITE_NOMEM once a hard limit is exceeded (`PRAGMA hard_heap_limit=1000` makes the very next statement fail with 'out of memory'); we deliberately do not replicate that.
close_reason: IMPLEMENTED (fsqlite-vdbe pragma + connection.rs result_columns). PRAGMA soft_heap_limit / hard_heap_limit are now process-global set/get, mirroring C SQLite 3.46.1 (sqlite3_soft/hard_heap_limit64). Two module-level AtomicI64 statics (SOFT_HEAP_LIMIT/HARD_HEAP_LIMIT, 0=unlimited) in the pragma module; apply_soft_heap_limit + apply_hard_heap_limit dispatched from apply_connection_pragma; both names added to pragma_result_columns so both bare and assignment emit exactly one integer row = value-after-mutation. Algebra (all 7 oracle scenarios + raise-block + non-numeric no-op verified): soft N<0 no-op; soft clamps to hard when hard>0 && (N>hard || N==0); hard lower-only (set iff N>0 && (prior==0 || prior>N)); lowering hard drags soft down when N<soft || soft==0; non-numeric arg = no-op readback. SCOPE: set/get surface only (no allocation enforcement, per bead); two independent Relaxed atomics (no mutex) — a pathological concurrent set-both could read a torn clamp, acceptable for advisory state. Keepers: fsqlite-vdbe test_connection_pragma_heap_limits_gh280 (full oracle replay w/ reset helper) + fsqlite-core tests/bd_pgdi6_heap_limit_pragma_gh280.rs (Connection::query row emission + cross-connection process-global). clippy clean, ubs-clean production code, 11/0 vdbe pragma tests + 1/0 core integration.

title: CRITICAL: In-transaction prepared INSERT takes 324-line slow path — add fast path for explicit txn
close_reason: Committed: in-transaction fast path skips ~90ns ceremony per prepared INSERT row.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## Problem
The benchmark INSERT path: BEGIN → 10K prepared inserts → COMMIT.

`try_execute_precompiled_prepared_insert_autocommit_direct_simple_fast` (line 9575) returns None when `in_transaction` is true. This forces ALL in-transaction inserts through the 324-line slow path (execute_precompiled_prepared_insert at line 9347).

The slow path includes ~125ns of ceremony per row:
- 20+ tracing::enabled!() checks (~40ns)
- Multiple RefCell borrows (~15ns)
- Statement savepoint checks (~20ns)
- Schema validation (~30ns)
- MemDB refresh checks (~20ns)

C SQLite: direct sqlite3BtreeInsert() with ~0 ceremony.

## Fix
Create a fast path for in-transaction prepared INSERT that:
1. Schema hasn't changed since prepare → skip schema validation (already checked at prepare time)
2. No triggers on this table → skip trigger collection
3. No statement savepoint needed (within explicit txn, not autocommit) → skip savepoint
4. No trace subscribers → skip all tracing checks
5. Go directly to: bind params → execute VDBE program → update counters

## Expected Impact: -125ns per row = -1.25ms per 10K rows = ~25% of the 3.34x gap

## Where
File: crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs
Add fast path at the top of execute_precompiled_prepared_insert_fast (line 9669)

title: JSONB binary format diverges from SQLite (numbers as raw be-bytes; header size-nibble misencoded)
description: fsqlite-ext-json lib.rs:908-979: integers/floats are encoded as raw 8-byte big-endian payloads and the header upper nibble stores the COUNT of length bytes, whereas SQLite JSONB stores numbers as ASCII text and uses the upper nibble as the literal payload size for 0..=11 (12/13/14/15 signal 1/2/4/8 trailing size bytes). Oracle: sqlite hex(jsonb(5))='1335'; frank produces '13080000000000000005'-style blobs. Round-trips internally but is NOT interchangeable with C SQLite; decode_jsonb_value rejects genuine SQLite JSONB integers (requires payload.len()==8). Fix = re-encode/decode to the documented SQLite JSONB format; keep a migration/read path for previously-written franken-JSONB blobs if any persisted.
close_reason: Already fixed by bd-t75hg (SQLite-spec JSONB: ASCII numeric payloads + direct size-nibble headers + escaped-text elements, 9e5c90ffe). Encoder (encode_jsonb_value ~1040) writes numbers as decimal/float ASCII text with the correct nibble header (append_jsonb_node ~1114: 0..=11 direct, 12/13/14/15 escape to 1/2/4/8 size bytes); decoder (decode_jsonb_value ~1169) parses ASCII-text INT/FLOAT payloads — no payload.len()==8 requirement. title: PRAGMA data_version approximated via schema cookie — misses other-connection data commits, false-positives on own DDL (stock-semantics divergence)
description:
## SUMMARY
`PRAGMA data_version` is approximated using the schema cookie
(connection.rs ~59656-59664: "In SQLite this changes when another
connection modifies the DB. We approximate it using the schema cookie."),
which diverges from stock semantics in both directions:

- MISSES data-only changes: another connection committing ordinary
  INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE bumps stock data_version but does NOT bump the
  schema cookie — callers polling data_version for cache invalidation
  (a documented SQLite pattern) never see the change.
- FALSE POSITIVES from own-connection DDL: stock data_version is
  unchanged by commits made on the SAME connection, while the schema
  cookie bumps on own DDL — so a caller sees "external change" signals
  for its own schema edits.

## EVIDENCE (verified at HEAD 2026-08-14)
- connection.rs "data_version" arm returns `self.schema_cookie()` with
  the approximation comment in place.
- Stock contract (sqlite pragma docs): data_version differs across
  connections; unchanged by commits on the same connection; bumped by
  other connections' data commits.
- Dedupe: the only tracker mention is incidental inside bd-2yqp6.4.2;
  no bead tracks this divergence specifically. It is also not listed as
  a divergence row in docs/contracts/supported_surface_matrix.toml's
  PRAGMA surface (worth confirming while fixing).

## WHY IT MATTERS
data_version is the canonical cheap "did someone else change the DB"
poll for connection pools and caches — the exact multi-Connection
workload FrankenSQLite exists to serve. A wrong signal here causes
stale caches (missed invalidation) or spurious refreshes.

## FIX SKETCH
Track a per-connection last-seen commit change counter: stock semantics
are (file change counter observed at transaction start, per connection,
excluding own writes). Candidates: derive from CommitSeq
(stable_commit_seq Arc<AtomicU64>) snapshotted per connection and
compared against last value returned, excluding commits attributed to
self; or read the header file-change-counter through the pager. Add the
divergence to the parity taxonomy if the fix is deferred.

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] Oracle parity test vs rusqlite covering: (a) other-connection data
      commit bumps it, (b) own commit does not, (c) own DDL does not,
      (d) reopen behavior — fsqlite matches stock on all four.
- [ ] Test wired into a CI workflow allowlist (bd-ohk1x class).
- [ ] If deferred instead of fixed: divergence row added to
      parity_taxonomy/supported_surface_matrix with rationale, and the
      approximation comment upgraded to cite this bead.

## PROVENANCE
Found during frankensqlite-mega-skill PRAGMA-catalog research; recorded
in the skill's PRAGMA-REFERENCE ("approximated via schema cookie, NOT a
true cross-connection change counter").

Acceptance fully met: crates/fsqlite-core/tests/pragma_data_version_oracle.rs (149 lines) covers all four cases (a) other-connection data commit bumps, (b) own data commit doesn't, (c) own DDL doesn't, (d) reopen behavior — differential vs rusqlite stock_dv; wired into .github/workflows/verification-gates.yml in the same commit.

title: R1: Reusable record buffer in VdbeEngine — clear+refill instead of alloc per row
close_reason: Committed in 707bb028: Arc::from(&buf[..]) + clear() instead of take(). Eliminates ~10K Vec allocs per 10K-row INSERT.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## What
Add `record_scratch: Vec<u8>` field to VdbeEngine. In MakeRecord opcode: clear() the scratch (keeps capacity), serialize directly into it, then pass a slice to the Insert opcode.

## Implementation
File: crates/fsqlite-vdbe/src/engine.rs

1. Add field: `record_scratch: Vec<u8>` (initialized with capacity 256)
2. In MakeRecord handler (execute_make_record_hot):
   - record_scratch.clear() (O(1), keeps allocation)
   - Write header size varint
   - For each column: write serial type varint, accumulate body size
   - For each column: write value bytes
3. Store result as `SqliteValue::Blob(Arc::from(&record_scratch[..]))` or pass by reference

## Key Insight from C SQLite
C SQLite's `pOut->z = pOut->zMalloc` reuses the Mem's internal buffer. The buffer grows as needed but NEVER shrinks, so repeated MakeRecord calls for same-schema rows do zero allocations after the first.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Zero Vec<u8> allocations during steady-state INSERT (after first row)
2. MakeRecord microbenchmark: ≥ 40% faster
3. INSERT 10K rows benchmark: ≥ 10% improvement
4. conformance_oracle_s55 passes (record format unchanged)

## Risk & Fallback
Risk: The scratch buffer must be properly lifetime-managed (not borrowed across yields).
Fallback: If lifetime issues arise, use a per-MakeRecord Cell<Vec<u8>> instead.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## CORRECTION (Review): make_record_buf Exists But Isn't Actually Reused

The VdbeEngine already has `make_record_buf: Vec<u8>` (line 10117) and `serialize_record_iter_into()`. BUT the current code does:
```rust
let blob = std::mem::take(&mut rec_buf);  // Takes all data, leaves empty Vec
self.make_record_buf = rec_buf;           // Puts back EMPTY Vec (capacity 0!)
```

This means the buffer is allocated fresh every row because `take` moves the allocation into `blob`, leaving `rec_buf` with capacity 0.

### Revised R1 Fix
Instead of `std::mem::take`, use `Arc::from(&rec_buf[..])` to create the blob, then `rec_buf.clear()` (keeps capacity) before returning:

```rust
// FIXED: Keep buffer capacity for reuse
let blob = Arc::from(&rec_buf[..]);  // Copy bytes into Arc (or use Bytes crate)
rec_buf.clear();                     // Clear but keep allocation
self.make_record_buf = rec_buf;      // Put back Vec WITH capacity
self.set_reg(target, SqliteValue::Blob(blob));
```

This single change eliminates ~10K Vec allocations per 10K-row INSERT.

### Exact Location
File: crates/fsqlite-vdbe/src/engine.rs, line 10148
Change: `let blob = std::mem::take(&mut rec_buf)` → `let blob: Arc<[u8]> = Arc::from(&rec_buf[..]); rec_buf.clear();`

title: BUG: INDEXED BY <nonexistent index> silently accepted instead of erroring "no such index" (hint name not validated)
close_reason: Fixed (commit pending): validate_select_ordinals_and_hints rejects out-of-range ORDER BY/GROUP BY ordinals (incl. signed -1/0) and unknown INDEXED BY. Tests un-ignored & passing; fmt+clippy clean.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## BUG: INDEXED BY <nonexistent index> is silently accepted (no "no such index" error)

Oracle parity vs rusqlite. Table t(id PK, a, b) with `CREATE INDEX idx_a ON t(a)`.
```sql
SELECT id FROM t INDEXED BY no_such_index WHERE a = 20;
  -- frank: [2, 3]   (hint ignored, query runs)
  -- csql:  ERROR("no such index: no_such_index")
```
`INDEXED BY name` requires that `name` be an existing index on the table; SQLite
rejects an unknown index name at prepare time. frank parses the hint
(IndexHint::IndexedBy) and plumbs it through (connection.rs references
index_hint.is_some() at ~26410/26581/27672/27017 as fall-back guards) but never
validates the index name, so a bogus INDEXED BY is silently ignored and the
query runs as if no hint were given.

### What works
- INDEXED BY <real index> with equality/range -> correct results (hint doesn't
  change the result set).
- NOT INDEXED -> correct results (full scan).
- INDEXED BY in UPDATE/DELETE -> correct results.
- INDEXED BY idx_a WHERE id=1 (constraint not on the indexed column) -> matches
  SQLite (both allow a full index scan; no error).

So the only observable divergence is the missing validation of a nonexistent
forced-index name. (Whether the planner actually honors a valid hint is a plan
concern not visible in oracle results.)

### Fix
When resolving a table reference carrying `IndexHint::IndexedBy(name)`, look the
index up in the table's schema and raise FrankenError ("no such index: name") if
it is absent — at prepare/codegen time, mirroring SQLite.

### Test
crates/fsqlite-e2e/tests/indexed_by_oracle_e2e.rs::indexed_by_nonexistent_index_errors
(#[ignore]'d on this bead). The equality/range, NOT INDEXED, UPDATE/DELETE, and
unusable-index cases all pass.

title: Forbid raw XOR merge on SQLite structured pages: runtime guard + fuzz harness + CI ast-grep
description: Per README and bd-zppf: raw byte-range XOR merges are forbidden for SQLite structured pages. Add a runtime guard at the merge entry, a fuzz harness that beats on it, and a CI ast-grep that prevents new callers from passing non-Overflow pages.
design: Add a debug-assertions runtime assertion at the entry point of every merge function that handles a raw byte-range XOR — assert page.kind == PageType::Overflow (or PageType::Free, where applicable; document allowed kinds inline with a comment citing README + bd-zppf). Anything else routes through intent-replay or the structured-patch ladder. In release builds the assertion elides via debug_assert!. Additionally, ship a fuzz harness under fuzz/fuzz_targets/xor_merge_guard.rs that feeds random PageType + arbitrary bytes to the merge path and verifies the guard rejects non-Overflow without panicking the process (the guard MUST return an error, not panic, in release mode — Rust panic-via-debug_assert is fine for debug, but release path uses a Result<(), MergeError>). In-code documentation block above the assertion explains why XOR is unsafe for structured pages: page header CRC would be desynced (different XOR cancellation), b-tree pointer corruption is undetectable until the next read, freelist trunk/leaf pointer mangling silently shares pages across trees (exactly the failure mode observed in the corrupted .beads/beads.db page 3552/123). Cite the README invariant. Add a forbidden-pattern grep in CI (ast-grep run -l Rust -p '$X.xor_merge($$$_)') checking that no caller passes a non-Overflow page; the only allowed callers are inside the merge module itself.
acceptance_criteria: (1) Runtime guard fires in debug + returns Result::Err in release on every non-Overflow PageType. (2) Fuzz harness fuzz/fuzz_targets/xor_merge_guard.rs runs 10M iterations green under cargo fuzz (in CI nightly). (3) CI ast-grep scans the workspace and fails if a non-Overflow xor_merge call exists outside the merge module itself. (4) Inline documentation explains the invariant with a citation to README + bd-zppf. (5) Audit complete: a PR-description list of every existing xor_merge call site with their page-type verdicts.
notes: Page header CRC desync is the diagnostic 'tell' for accidental XOR on a structured page. The CI grep is a backstop; the runtime guard is the real correctness bound.

title: §10.5 Query Planning: Cost Model, Index Selection, Join Ordering
description:
## SUMMARY

Implements the query planner: cost-model estimation, index selection, and join ordering. The cost model estimates access path costs primarily in page reads, using ANALYZE statistics (sqlite_stat1/sqlite_stat4) when available or heuristic fallbacks otherwise. Index usability rules determine which WHERE terms can exploit indexes. Join ordering uses bounded best-first beam search (NGQP-style, after C SQLite's wherePathSolver) with configurable mxChoice beam width, NOT exhaustive N! enumeration.

## KEY DATA STRUCTURES / ALGORITHMS

- **Cost model (page-read estimates)**:
  - Full table scan: `cost = N_pages(table)`
  - Index scan (range): `cost = log2(N_pages(index)) + selectivity * N_pages(index) + selectivity * N_pages(table)`
  - Index scan (equality): `cost = log2(N_pages(index)) + log2(N_pages(table))`
  - Covering index scan: `cost = log2(N_pages(index)) + selectivity * N_pages(index)`
  - Rowid lookup: `cost = log2(N_pages(table))`
- **Index usability rules**:
  - Equality (`col = expr`): usable if col is leftmost column of index.
  - Range (`col > expr`, `col BETWEEN`): usable as rightmost constraint.
  - IN (`col IN (...)`): expanded to multiple equality probes.
  - LIKE (`col LIKE 'prefix%'`): usable if prefix is constant.
- **Join ordering (beam search)**:
  - Maintain up to `mxChoice` best partial join paths at each level (lowest estimated cost).
  - `mxChoice` values: 1 (single-table), 5 (two-table), 12 or 18 (3+ tables; star-query heuristic may raise to 18).
  - Worst-case complexity: `O(mxChoice * N^2)` candidate expansions (bounded beam, not N!).
  - Based on C SQLite's `computeMxChoice` and `wherePathSolver()` in where.c.
- **Statistics sources**: `sqlite_stat1` (row counts, index selectivity), `sqlite_stat4` (distribution samples). Fallback: heuristic estimates when ANALYZE has not been run.

## NORMATIVE INVARIANTS

1. Cost model formulas use page reads as the primary cost unit (simplified for V1; C SQLite is more nuanced with CPU cost estimates).
2. Index equality usability requires the column to be the LEFTMOST column of the index.
3. Range constraints are usable only as the RIGHTMOST constraint in an index scan.
4. Join ordering uses bounded beam search, NOT exhaustive N! permutation.
5. mxChoice beam width is derived from join complexity (1/5/12/18), not a fixed constant.
6. There is no exhaustive N! search path -- beam search is the V1 strategy.

## UNIT TEST REQUIREMENTS

1. `test_cost_full_table_scan` -- Cost estimate for full scan equals N_pages(table); verify for tables of 1, 100, 10000 pages.
2. `test_cost_index_scan_range` -- Range scan cost includes log2(index pages) + selectivity * index pages + selectivity * table pages.
3. `test_cost_index_scan_equality` -- Equality scan cost is log2(index pages) + log2(table pages).
4. `test_cost_covering_index` -- Covering index scan omits table page lookups.
5. `test_cost_rowid_lookup` -- Rowid lookup cost is log2(table pages).
6. `test_index_usability_equality_leftmost` -- Only leftmost index column usable for equality.
7. `test_index_usability_range_rightmost` -- Range constraint usable only as rightmost constraint.
8. `test_index_usability_in_expansion` -- IN clause expands to multiple equality probes.
9. `test_index_usability_like_prefix` -- `LIKE 'abc%'` usable; `LIKE '%abc'` not usable.
10. `test_join_ordering_two_tables` -- Two-table join uses mxChoice=5; picks lower-cost order.
11. `test_join_ordering_three_tables` -- Three-table join uses mxChoice=12; beam search prunes suboptimal paths.
12. `test_join_ordering_star_query` -- Star-query heuristic raises mxChoice to 18 for 3+ table star joins.
13. `test_planner_uses_sqlite_stat1` -- When sqlite_stat1 exists, planner uses actual row counts instead of heuristics.
14. `test_planner_heuristic_fallback` -- Without ANALYZE, planner uses heuristic estimates and still produces valid plans.
15. `test_planner_selects_covering_index` -- When a covering index exists, planner prefers it over non-covering index + table lookup.

## E2E TEST

Create a multi-table schema with indexes and populated sqlite_stat1. Run `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` for various queries (single-table scan, indexed lookup, two-table join, three-table star join). Verify planner output matches expected access paths. Compare plan choices with C SQLite's EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN output for the same schema and data.

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA

- Cost model correctly estimates page-read costs for all five access path types.
- Index usability rules correctly identify which WHERE terms can use which indexes.
- Beam search join ordering produces optimal or near-optimal plans for 2-table and 3+ table joins.
- mxChoice scales correctly with join complexity (1/5/12/18).
- ANALYZE statistics are consumed when available; heuristic fallback works without them.
- EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN output is human-readable and shows chosen access paths.
- No N! blowup: 10-table joins complete in bounded time.
close_reason: Implemented cost model (5 access path types), index usability analysis (equality/range/IN/LIKE prefix), and bounded beam search join ordering (mxChoice scaling 1/5/12/18, star-query heuristic, CROSS JOIN enforcement). 34 new tests, 56 total in planner crate. Clippy clean.
