description: Downstream (mcp_agent_mail_rust) issues PRAGMA journal_size_limit on every pooled connection (schema.rs conn pragmas) and re-applies it on a schedule (integrity_guard), and documents a WAL cap via DATABASE knobs — but the pragma name is absent from both fsqlite pragma dispatchers and falls to the silently-ignored arm (fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs ~59699). WAL size is actually bounded only by wal_autocheckpoint plus explicit TRUNCATE checkpoints. Either implement journal_size_limit (truncate WAL to the limit after checkpoint, canonical semantics) or reject unknown pragmas under a strict mode so consumers stop believing no-op green. Downstream will annotate or remove its knob meanwhile. Related: unrecognized-PRAGMA-silently-succeeds is a general footgun (a green PRAGMA proves nothing).
notes: PART A LANDED (ab7a7a9f3): PRAGMA journal_size_limit is now RECOGNIZED + stored + returned (fsqlite-vdbe ConnectionPragmaState.journal_size_limit, default -1, negatives=no-limit verbatim; apply_journal_size_limit mirrors apply_mmap_size; unit test 16/0). No longer silently Unsupported. PART B (ENFORCEMENT = truncate WAL to the limit after checkpoint) = bd-2rsuf (blocks this bead) — the checkpoint-hot-path WAL truncation, deliberately NOT rushed at session tail. Until Part B lands, the pragma stores-but-does-not-enforce (tracked, not silently misleading). Kept in_progress pending bd-2rsuf.
close_reason: FULLY RESOLVED: Part A (recognition, ab7a7a9f3 — pragma stored+returned, fsqlite-vdbe) + Part B (enforcement, 2a4c85c13/11d727dbd — WAL truncated to the cap on auto-checkpoint). PRAGMA journal_size_limit is no longer silently ignored: it reports its value AND bounds the WAL (97KB capped vs 12.7MB uncapped in the enforcement test). No concurrent_mode change, no new/writer-blocking locks; behavior-neutral at the default -1.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: Background: C SQLite calls sqlite3PagerBegin once per transaction, not per statement. Journal file created lazily only when first page is dirtied. FrankenSQLite calls pager begin+commit for every autocommit write statement. Fix: For consecutive autocommit writes on memory databases, defer the commit -- keep the write transaction open and only commit when a read or explicit COMMIT arrives. This amortizes pager ceremony across multiple writes. Must be opt-in or auto-detected (consecutive write pattern). Files: connection.rs (detect consecutive write pattern, defer commit), pager.rs (support deferred commit mode). Tests: write_batching_consecutive_inserts, write_batching_interleaved_read_write, write_batching_explicit_commit_flushes, benchmark_batched_vs_per_stmt_commit. Success: 10K autocommit INSERTs pay 1 pager begin+commit instead of 10K.

title: §2 SSI Performance Validation: OLTP Overhead < 7% + False Positive Rate
description:
## SUMMARY

Validate the performance characteristics of Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) at page granularity for FrankenSQLite's MVCC concurrent writer mode (BEGIN CONCURRENT). Per spec §2.4 (Layer 2): SSI adds 3-7% throughput overhead on OLTP benchmarks (Ports & Grittner, VLDB 2012; up to 10-20% on synthetic microbenchmarks) and achieves ~0.5% false positive abort rate at row granularity in PostgreSQL. At page granularity, the false positive rate will be higher (spec §5.7 baseline: 0.5-5%), but the safe write-merge ladder (§5.10) compensates. This bead establishes the benchmark harness, performance gates, and the SSI e-process monitor (INV-SSI-FP) that continuously tracks false positive abort rates using anytime-valid statistical methods.

## KEY DATA STRUCTURES / ALGORITHMS

- **Page-SSI rule** (§2.4): Conservative Cahill/Fekete rule at page granularity — no committed transaction may have both an incoming AND outgoing rw-antidependency edge. Implemented via two boolean flags per transaction (`has_in_rw`, `has_out_rw`) plus the witness plane (§5.6.4).
- **Witness plane** (§5.6.4): Hot-plane witness index stores read/write evidence as bitsets over TxnSlots. Cold-plane evidence is append-only, GC-able by `safe_gc_seq` horizons. Witness keys: `WitnessKey::Page(pgno)` for range scans, `WitnessKey::Cell(btree_root_pgno, cell_tag)` for point reads (§5.6.4.3).
- **INV-SSI-FP e-process monitor** (§4.3, §5.7): Anytime-valid sequential test using KL divergence with calibrated baselines. Continuously estimates the false positive abort rate with optional-stopping-safe confidence intervals. Baseline expectation: 0.5-5% at page granularity.
- **VOI (Value of Information) formula** (§2.4 Layer 3): `VOI = E[DeltaL_fp] * N_txn/day - C_impl`. Determines when to invest engineering effort in witness granularity refinement (cell/byte-range witnesses). Only invest when VOI > 0.
- **Read-only transaction optimization**: Read-only transactions (no writes before COMMIT/ROLLBACK) MUST NOT participate in SSI validation — they cannot create dangerous structures (rw-antidependency requires a write).
- **PRAGMA fsqlite.serializable = OFF**: Explicit opt-out to plain Snapshot Isolation for benchmarking. NOT the default.

## NORMATIVE INVARIANTS

1. **INV-SSI-OLTP-OVERHEAD**: SSI witness registration + commit-time validation MUST add no more than 7% throughput overhead on OLTP-like workloads (mixed read-write, multiple concurrent writers via BEGIN CONCURRENT) compared to the same workload with `PRAGMA fsqlite.serializable = OFF`.
2. **INV-SSI-MICRO-OVERHEAD**: On synthetic microbenchmarks (single hot page, high contention), SSI overhead MUST be below 20%.
3. **INV-SSI-FP-RATE**: False positive abort rate MUST be below 5% for OLTP workloads. Target is < 2%. The e-process monitor (INV-SSI-FP) continuously validates this.
4. **INV-SSI-READONLY-EXEMPT**: Read-only transactions MUST incur zero SSI overhead and zero SSI aborts. They are exempt from the has_in_rw/has_out_rw validation.
5. **INV-SSI-DEFAULT-ON**: SSI MUST be enabled by default for BEGIN CONCURRENT transactions. Disabling requires explicit `PRAGMA fsqlite.serializable = OFF`.

## UNIT TEST REQUIREMENTS

- **test_ssi_overhead_oltp_below_7_percent**: Run a standardized OLTP workload (N=1000 transactions, W=4 concurrent writers, mixed reads/writes across 100 pages) with SSI enabled and disabled. Assert `throughput_with_ssi >= 0.93 * throughput_without_ssi`.
- **test_ssi_false_positive_rate_below_5_percent**: Run 10,000 BEGIN CONCURRENT transactions with random read/write sets across 1000 pages (W=8 writers). Count aborts that are false positives (aborted transaction's actual row-level read/write set did not conflict). Assert `false_positive_aborts / total_aborts < 0.05`.
- **test_read_only_txn_zero_ssi_overhead**: Run 10,000 read-only transactions (BEGIN CONCURRENT + SELECT only + COMMIT) concurrent with active writers. Assert zero SSI aborts for read-only transactions.
- **test_ssi_overhead_microbenchmark_below_20_percent**: Single hot page, 8 concurrent writers all reading and writing the same page. Measure throughput with SSI on vs off. Assert `throughput_with_ssi >= 0.80 * throughput_without_ssi`.
- **test_ssi_fp_eprocess_monitor_tracks_rate**: Instantiate the INV-SSI-FP e-process monitor. Feed it 1000 commit decisions (950 true positive aborts, 50 false positive aborts = 5% rate). Verify the monitor estimates the false positive rate within the anytime-valid confidence interval.
- **test_ssi_voi_computation**: Given `E[DeltaL_fp] = 0.001`, `N_txn/day = 1,000,000`, `C_impl = 500`. Compute `VOI = 0.001 * 1_000_000 - 500 = 500`. Assert VOI > 0 recommends investing in witness refinement.

## E2E TEST

- **test_e2e_ssi_overhead_and_false_positive_budget**: Run a TPC-C-like OLTP benchmark under BEGIN CONCURRENT with multiple concurrent writer connections. Measure throughput overhead vs. serialized baseline (PRAGMA fsqlite.serializable = OFF) and false positive abort rate. Assert overhead < 7% and false positive rate within the 0.5-5% envelope. On failure, emit actionable diagnostics (witness refinement suggestion, merge ladder stats).

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA

- [ ] OLTP benchmark harness implemented and measuring SSI-on vs SSI-off throughput
- [ ] OLTP overhead confirmed < 7% on representative mixed read-write workload
- [ ] Microbenchmark overhead confirmed < 20% on single-hot-page contention scenario
- [ ] False positive abort rate measured and confirmed < 5% for OLTP workloads
- [ ] Read-only transactions confirmed exempt from SSI validation (zero aborts, zero overhead)
- [ ] INV-SSI-FP e-process monitor wired and producing anytime-valid confidence intervals
- [ ] VOI computation implemented and returns correct recommendation for sample inputs
close_reason: Implemented/stabilized SSI perf validation compliance harness in crates/fsqlite-harness/tests/bd_yvhd_ssi_perf_validation_compliance.rs with concrete unit+E2E identifiers, bd-1fpm logging markers, and tuned deterministic workload parameters; validated via cargo test/check/clippy/fmt and UBS.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
# §2 SSI Performance Validation: OLTP Overhead < 7% + False Positive Rate

## Scope

This bead covers the performance validation requirements for Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) at page granularity, as specified in §2.4 (Layered Isolation, Layer 2) and §5.6.4/§5.7 (SSI Witness Plane).

## Spec References

- §2.4: "3-7% throughput overhead measured on OLTP benchmarks with PostgreSQL 9.1+ (Ports & Grittner, VLDB 2012; up to 10-20% on synthetic microbenchmarks without read-only optimizations)"
- §2.4: "~0.5% false positive abort rate [PostgreSQL]. At page granularity, our false positive rate will be somewhat higher"
- §2.4: "safe write-merge ladder (§5.10) compensates by turning many apparent conflicts into successful merges"
- §2.4 Layer 3: "VOI = E[ΔL_fp] * N_txn/day - C_impl. Only invest when VOI > 0"
- §5.7 (INV-SSI-FP): "false positive rate has an EXPECTED baseline of ~0.5-5%"

## Requirements

### Performance Targets
1. **OLTP overhead**: SSI witness registration + commit-time validation MUST add no more than 7% throughput overhead on OLTP-like workloads (mixed read-write, multiple concurrent writers via BEGIN CONCURRENT)
2. **Microbenchmark overhead**: Up to 10-20% overhead is acceptable on synthetic microbenchmarks (e.g., SIBENCH-like single-page hot contention)
3. **False positive abort rate**: Target < 2% for OLTP workloads. PostgreSQL achieves ~0.5% at row granularity; page granularity will be higher. The spec sets baseline expectation at 0.5-5%

### Benchmark Suite
4. **OLTP benchmark**: Implement a TPC-C-like benchmark harness using BEGIN CONCURRENT that measures throughput with SSI enabled vs PRAGMA fsqlite.serializable=OFF
5. **Contention microbenchmark**: Single-table hot-page contention scenario measuring abort rate and throughput under varying writer counts (2, 4, 8, 16)
6. **Read-only transaction fast path**: Read-only transactions (those that perform no writes before COMMIT/ROLLBACK) MUST NOT participate in SSI validation -- they cannot create dangerous structures. Verify this optimization with benchmarks showing ~0% SSI overhead for pure readers

### SSI e-Process Monitor
7. **INV-SSI-FP monitor**: Wire the anytime-valid e-process (§4.3, §5.7) to continuously track the false positive abort rate. The monitor uses KL divergence with calibrated baselines per §4.7
8. **VOI computation**: Implement the Value of Information formula for witness refinement investment decisions: VOI = E[ΔL_fp] * N_txn/day - C_impl

## Unit Test Specifications

### Test 1: `test_ssi_overhead_oltp_below_7_percent`
Run a standardized OLTP workload (N=1000 transactions, W=4 concurrent writers, mix of reads and writes across 100 pages) with SSI enabled and disabled. Assert that throughput_with_ssi >= 0.93 * throughput_without_ssi.

### Test 2: `test_ssi_false_positive_rate_below_5_percent`
Run 10,000 BEGIN CONCURRENT transactions with random read/write sets across 1000 pages (W=8 writers). Count the number of aborts that are false positives (i.e., the aborted transaction's read/write set did not actually conflict at the row level). Assert false_positive_aborts / total_aborts < 0.05.

### Test 3: `test_read_only_txn_zero_ssi_overhead`
Run 10,000 read-only transactions (BEGIN CONCURRENT + SELECT only + COMMIT) concurrent with active writers. Assert that zero SSI aborts occur for read-only transactions (they must be exempt from the has_in_rw/has_out_rw check).

### Test 4: `test_ssi_overhead_microbenchmark_below_20_percent`
Single hot page, 8 concurrent writers all reading and writing the same page. Measure throughput with SSI on vs off. Assert throughput_with_ssi >= 0.80 * throughput_without_ssi.

### Test 5: `test_ssi_fp_eprocess_monitor_tracks_rate`
Create the INV-SSI-FP e-process monitor. Feed it 1000 commit decisions (950 true positive aborts, 50 false positive aborts = 5% rate). Verify the monitor correctly estimates the false positive rate within the anytime-valid confidence interval.

### Test 6: `test_ssi_voi_computation`
Given a measured false positive abort cost reduction of 0.001 (ΔL_fp), a daily transaction volume of 1,000,000, and an implementation cost of 500 units, compute VOI = 0.001 * 1_000_000 - 500 = 500. Assert VOI > 0 recommends investing in refinement.

title: Parser rejects DEFAULT keyword in INSERT ... VALUES list ("unexpected token: KwDefault")
close_reason: Not a bug: SQLite rejects DEFAULT inside a VALUES tuple (verified sqlite3 CLI 3.46.1 + rusqlite); frank already correctly rejects it. Bead premise was wrong. Test converted to validate-then-reject parity assertion.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
The explicit `DEFAULT` keyword as a value in an INSERT VALUES list is rejected
by the parser; SQLite accepts it (the column takes its declared default).

Repro (FrankenSQLite errors at parse; rusqlite OK):
```sql
CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, a INTEGER DEFAULT 11, b INTEGER DEFAULT 22);
INSERT INTO t(id, a, b) VALUES (1, DEFAULT, 200);   -- a uses its default (11)
INSERT INTO t(id, a, b) VALUES (2, 100, DEFAULT);   -- b uses its default (22)
```
frank => SQL error: unexpected token in expression: KwDefault
csql  => OK (rows (1,11,200) and (2,100,22))

Per the SQLite INSERT grammar, each value in a VALUES row may be the literal
keyword `DEFAULT`, meaning "use this column's default value" (or NULL if the
column has no default). Fix location: the parser's VALUES-row / expression
grammar in fsqlite-parser must accept `DEFAULT` as a value token, and the
INSERT path must substitute the column default for it.

Test (currently #[ignore]d on this bead):
crates/fsqlite-e2e/tests/default_value_oracle_e2e.rs::default_explicit_keyword

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
INVALID PREMISE — verified false against ground truth. Real SQLite does NOT accept the bare DEFAULT keyword inside a VALUES tuple:
  sqlite3 CLI 3.46.1:  INSERT INTO t(id,a,b) VALUES (1, DEFAULT, 200) => Error: near "DEFAULT": syntax error
  bundled rusqlite:    same 'near "DEFAULT": syntax error'
Only the whole-row form 'INSERT ... DEFAULT VALUES' is valid SQLite (frank supports it via InsertSource::DefaultValues; covered by default_values_insert). The bead's claim 'csql => OK' is wrong — likely confused with MySQL/Postgres which DO accept DEFAULT in a VALUES list.
frank ALREADY correctly REJECTS DEFAULT-in-VALUES (parse error), matching SQLite. Accepting it (as the bead asked) would diverge from the C-SQLite parity target. Implemented acceptance end-to-end (Expr::Default variant + parser + codegen substitution across ~40 sites) then fully reverted after oracle check; net change is only the test.
Rewrote crates/fsqlite-e2e/tests/default_value_oracle_e2e.rs::default_explicit_keyword (was an impossible accept-test whose rusqlite setup panicked on the syntax error) into a validate-then-reject parity test: asserts BOTH engines reject 'VALUES (1, DEFAULT, 200)'. 6/6 tests pass.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## What
Instead of immediately removing cells and rebalancing on DELETE, mark cells as deleted (set a flag byte) and defer the actual rebalancing to:
1. When the page is > 50% deleted cells (lazy cleanup)
2. At transaction commit (batch rebalance)
3. During checkpoint

This eliminates the expensive per-delete rebalancing that causes the 5.60x slowdown.

## Alien Graveyard Reference: §5.4 Bε-trees (write-optimized) — batch modifications before applying

## Where
- crates/fsqlite-btree/src/cursor.rs: delete_cell() → mark_deleted()
- crates/fsqlite-btree/src/balance.rs: skip rebalance for marked-deleted cells
- Add cleanup_deleted_cells() called at commit time

## Expected Impact: -0.15 to -0.25 µs per DELETE (eliminates immediate rebalancing)

## Acceptance Criteria
1. DELETE benchmark: ≥ 25% faster
2. Reads correctly skip deleted-marked cells
3. Cleanup correctly removes marks and rebalances
4. No space leak (deleted space is reclaimed at commit)

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## COMPATIBILITY WARNING: Delete-Marks and SQLite File Format
SQLite's B-tree page format does NOT support delete-marked cells. If we write a page with delete-marked cells to disk, a C SQLite reader would see corrupted data.

### Safe Implementation Strategy:
1. **In-memory only**: Delete-marks exist only in the in-memory page image. They are never written to WAL or database file.
2. **On flush/commit**: Before writing any dirty page, compact it (remove all delete-marked cells and rebalance). This ensures on-disk format is always valid SQLite.
3. **Effect**: DELETE within a transaction is fast (mark-only). Commit is slightly slower (batch cleanup). Net effect: still faster because we avoid per-delete rebalancing during the transaction.

### Alternative: If this proves too complex, implement K2 as "batch rebalance at commit" instead of per-delete rebalance. Same net effect, simpler implementation, no format concerns.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## COMPLEXITY WARNING (Review Pass 5): Delete-Mark Is Non-Trivial

The B-tree delete path (cursor.rs:3634) involves:
1. Interior node key replacement with successor
2. advance_next() to find successor in right subtree
3. Re-seek and replace interior key in-place
4. Remove successor from leaf
5. balance_for_delete() to rebalance if underflow

A simple "mark as deleted" approach would need to handle:
- Interior nodes still referencing marked cells (can't just skip them)
- balance_for_delete() deferred = pages may be underfull for extended periods
- Cursor scans must skip marked cells (affects ALL scan paths: next/prev/seek)
- Index B-trees: marked cells in interior nodes affect key routing correctness

### Revised K2 Strategy: Deferred Leaf-Only Delete
Only defer deletion for LEAF cells in table B-trees (not index B-trees, not interior nodes).
- Leaf cell "delete" = zero out the cell pointer entry (shift remaining pointers)
- Skip defragmentation and balance_for_delete() until commit or page becomes > 50% waste
- This is simpler and avoids the interior node complication

### Alternative: Just Optimize balance_for_delete()
Instead of deferring, make balance_for_delete() cheaper:
- Only rebalance if page is < 25% full (vs current threshold)
- This reduces rebalancing frequency without the mark-skip complexity
- Simpler to implement, easier to verify correctness

### Priority: Downgraded to P1 (from P0) given complexity/risk ratio
K1 (scan-and-update) is still P0 and provides most of the UPDATE benefit.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
VERIFY/triage 2026-06-29 (Opus 4.8): K2's deferred-delete goal is SUBSTANTIALLY IMPLEMENTED — the bead premise ("immediately removing cells and rebalancing on DELETE") is OUTDATED. Do NOT apply the proposed "simplest fallback" — it would be redundant and a REGRESSION (see below).

CURRENT STATE (cursor.rs):
- DELETE removes a leaf cell via `remove_table_cell_from_leaf_deferred` (the deferred leaf-only delete) and only calls `balance_for_delete` when the leaf becomes COMPLETELY EMPTY (`new_count == 0`, cursor.rs ~10439/10472/10502). So per-delete rebalancing does NOT happen — rebalance is deferred to the empty-page case only. This already realizes the bead's "Revised K2 Strategy: Deferred Leaf-Only Delete".
- Extensive compact-defrag machinery exists: `materialize_deletions_compact_descending_single_pass`, `has_compact_cell_area`, OPT-A4 reusable defrag scratch buffers (defrag_ptrs_scratch / defrag_cells_scratch). Space is reclaimed via defragmentation, not leaked.

WHY THE PROPOSED FALLBACK IS WRONG NOW: the bead's "only rebalance if page < 25% full (vs current threshold)" assumes balance_for_delete runs on EVERY delete. It does NOT — it runs only when a page hits 0 cells. Adding a "<25% full" gate would make balance_for_delete fire MORE often (whenever a page drops below 25%, not just at empty) — i.e. a regression vs the current empty-only deferral.

GAP TO CLOSE (bench-gated): AC1 "DELETE benchmark >= 25% faster" + AC4 "no space leak (deleted space reclaimed at commit)". These need a DELETE throughput bench (degraded rch) or a deterministic rebalance-/defrag-operation-count proof showing balance_for_delete fires only on empty. The IMPLEMENTATION work is effectively done; this is a verify+bench, like bd-3wop3.5.

RECOMMENDATION: keep open as a verify+bench candidate (NOT from-scratch). When closing, add a deterministic proof (e.g. a metrics counter that balance_for_delete invocations == empty-page transitions, far fewer than DELETE count) rather than only a wall-clock bench. Do NOT implement the <25% gate.

title: frankensqlite: SQLITE_DEFAULT_FOREIGN_KEYS diverges from stock SQLite defaults
description:
frankensqlite compiles with SQLITE_DEFAULT_FOREIGN_KEYS which sets PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON by default for every new connection. This differs from standard SQLite behavior where foreign_keys defaults to OFF.

This caused a production outage in mcp-agent-mail where every am CLI command failed with "FOREIGN KEY constraint failed" because: (a) the libsqlite3.a produced by frankensqlite has DEFAULT_FOREIGN_KEYS compiled in, (b) mcp-agent-mail did not explicitly set PRAGMA foreign_keys = OFF since stock SQLite defaults to OFF, (c) orphan data in the DB caused cascading FK failures on every DML.

The fix should ensure frankensqlite compile flags match stock SQLite defaults. Specifically:
- Remove SQLITE_DEFAULT_FOREIGN_KEYS from the compile flags (or set it to 0)
- Audit all other SQLITE_DEFAULT_* compile options to confirm they match stock SQLite

Callers that WANT FK enforcement should explicitly set PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON, matching the standard SQLite contract.

Discovery: `strings /data/tmp/cargo-target/release/am | grep DEFAULT_FOREIGN` → `DEFAULT_FOREIGN_KEYS` confirmed in the binary. System sqlite3 (not frankensqlite) does NOT have this flag.

Workaround already deployed: mcp-agent-mail now explicitly sets PRAGMA foreign_keys = OFF in all 5 connection init paths. But frankensqlite should still fix its defaults to avoid surprising other consumers.
close_reason: foreign_keys already defaults to false in Rust code (lib.rs:572). No code change needed. Audited all SQLITE_DEFAULT_* defaults. See comment for full audit report.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## Audit: SQLITE_DEFAULT_FOREIGN_KEYS and Pragma Defaults (BrownCliff)

### Foreign Keys Default
**Status: ALREADY CORRECT** — `foreign_keys: false` at `crates/fsqlite-vdbe/src/lib.rs:572`

The Rust implementation correctly defaults `foreign_keys` to `false` in `ConnectionPragmaState::default()`. The `Connection::open()` method uses this default at `crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs:982`. The existing test at `connection.rs:15694` verifies `PRAGMA foreign_keys;` returns 0 for new connections.

The `DEFAULT_FOREIGN_KEYS` string in the `am` binary came from the C SQLite reference source (in `legacy_sqlite_code/`) or a separately-compiled `libsqlite3-sys` crate, not from FrankenSQLite's Rust code.

### Other Default Audits

| Pragma | FrankenSQLite Default | Stock SQLite Default | Match? |
|--------|----------------------|---------------------|--------|
| `journal_mode` | `"wal"` | `"delete"` | **DIVERGES** (by design — FrankenSQLite is WAL-first) |
| `synchronous` | `"NORMAL"` | `"FULL"` (delete mode) / `"NORMAL"` (WAL mode) | Matches in WAL mode |
| `cache_size` | `-2000` | `-2000` | ✓ |
| `page_size` | `4096` | `4096` | ✓ |
| `busy_timeout` | `5000` | `0` | **DIVERGES** (intentional: production-friendly default) |
| `temp_store` | `0` | `0` | ✓ |
| `mmap_size` | `0` | `0` | ✓ |
| `auto_vacuum` | `0` | `0` | ✓ |
| `wal_autocheckpoint` | `1000` | `1000` | ✓ |
| `user_version` | `0` | `0` | ✓ |
| `application_id` | `0` | `0` | ✓ |
| `foreign_keys` | `false` | `false` | ✓ |
| `recursive_triggers` | `false` | `false` | ✓ |

### Known Intentional Divergences
1. **`journal_mode = "wal"`**: FrankenSQLite is a WAL-first engine. Stock SQLite defaults to rollback journal (`"delete"`). This is a core architectural choice.
2. **`busy_timeout = 5000`**: Stock SQLite defaults to 0 (immediate SQLITE_BUSY). FrankenSQLite defaults to 5s for production ergonomics.

### Conclusion
The foreign_keys default is correct. No code change needed in FrankenSQLite. The production outage in mcp-agent-mail was caused by a separately-compiled C SQLite library with `SQLITE_DEFAULT_FOREIGN_KEYS` enabled, not by FrankenSQLite's Rust implementation.

## E2E Integration & Benchmarking Suite — Top-Level Epic

### Goal
Build a production-grade end-to-end integration test suite that proves FrankenSQLite's correctness, performance, and resilience advantages over C SQLite using **real-world databases** (beads.db files from 86+ projects in /dp).

### Three Pillars

**Pillar 1 — Correctness**: Massively concurrent write workloads produce bit-for-bit identical results (SHA-256) when run through FrankenSQLite vs. C SQLite. This proves the MVCC page-level versioning (§5) and WAL implementation are semantically equivalent.

**Pillar 2 — Performance**: Benchmark suite measuring write throughput, read latency, and mixed workloads. FrankenSQLite's MVCC eliminates WAL_WRITE_LOCK contention (wal.c:3676), which should show measurable improvement under concurrent load.

**Pillar 3 — Resilience**: Intentional corruption demos showing C SQLite loses data permanently while FrankenSQLite recovers via RaptorQ erasure coding (§3). WAL-FEC self-healing, DB-FEC page repair, and graceful degradation all demonstrated.

### Architecture
- All tests are Rust integration tests under a new `crates/fsqlite-e2e/` crate
- Golden copies stored in `sample_sqlite_db_files/` (never modified)
- TUI dashboard using frankentui for real-time visualization
- Criterion benchmarks in `benches/` for reproducible perf measurements

5. **TUI Dashboard Visualization** — frankentui real-time display of all above

### Key Technical References
- §3 RaptorQ (spec lines 457-3693): Erasure coding, WAL-FEC, DB-FEC, ECS
- §5 MVCC (spec lines ~4000+): Page-level versioning, conflict detection

title: RCU/QSBR for hot metadata paths (§14.8)
description:
Implement Read-Copy-Update (RCU) with Quiescent State Based Reclamation (QSBR) for hot metadata paths that are read-mostly. RCU provides wait-free reads with deferred writer synchronization, perfect for metadata like schema cache, configuration, and statistics that are read millions of times per second but updated rarely.

## Mathematical Foundation
RCU provides linearizable reads with O(1) overhead (no locks, no atomics on the read path). Writers create a new copy of the data, atomically swap the pointer, and defer freeing the old copy until all readers that could have observed it have completed (quiescent state).

QSBR: readers periodically report quiescent states (points where they hold no RCU references). Writers can free old copies after all readers have reported at least one quiescent state since the swap.

## Application in FrankenSQLite
- Schema cache: read on every query parse, updated on DDL (rare)
- Statistics cache: read on every query plan, updated by ANALYZE (rare)
- Configuration: read on every operation, updated by PRAGMA (rare)
- Transaction table: read for SSI conflict detection, updated on begin/commit

## Alien CS Reference
McKenney and Slingwine 1998 Read-Copy Update: Mutual Exclusion for Linux. McKenney 2004 Exploiting Deferred Destruction: formal QSBR analysis and amortized overhead bounds. Hart et al. 2007 Performance of Memory Reclamation for Lockless Synchronization: comparative benchmarks showing RCU achieves zero-overhead reads vs hazard pointers (1 atomic) and epoch-based (1 atomic).

## Rust Implementation Guidance
- Use arc-swap crate for the atomic pointer swap (ArcSwap<T> provides wait-free reads via load())
- QSBR integration: treat transaction commit/abort as quiescent points (natural fit with EBR epochs)
- For schema cache: define SchemaSnapshot as an Arc<Schema> swapped via ArcSwap
- Read path: let snapshot = schema_cache.load(); -- zero atomics beyond the initial Arc load
- Write path: schema_cache.store(Arc::new(new_schema)); then defer old schema drop via crossbeam-epoch
- Alternative: implement custom RCU with crossbeam-epoch for tighter integration with existing EBR
- Test with loom for model-checking concurrent reads during writer swap

## Logging Requirements
- Log RCU swap events at tracing::info level: cache_name, old_version, new_version
- Log QSBR quiescent state reports at tracing::trace level (high frequency)
- Log deferred deallocation at tracing::debug level: cache_name, deferred_count
- Log read contention (if using fallback path) at tracing::warn level

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] RCU read-side with zero overhead (no atomics on read path)
- [ ] QSBR integration with transaction commit as quiescent point
- [ ] Schema cache using RCU
- [ ] Statistics cache using RCU
- [ ] Benchmark: RCU vs RwLock for schema cache access under contention
- [ ] Miri clean: no use-after-free
acceptance_criteria: 1. Implementation is complete and behaviorally correct against explicit invariants and edge-case requirements, including fault and recovery paths where applicable. 2. Comprehensive unit/property tests cover normal, boundary, and adversarial conditions with deterministic fixtures and regression seeds. 3. End-to-end scenario scripts validate integrated behavior in real execution flows and include deterministic replay instructions. 4. Structured logging/metrics (traceable IDs, timing, counters, error context) are emitted and validated so failures are diagnosable and auditable.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
# AUTOINCREMENT accepted on a non-INTEGER PRIMARY KEY

## Symptom
`AUTOINCREMENT` is only legal on a column declared exactly `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY`
(a rowid alias). frank accepts it on a non-INTEGER PRIMARY KEY:
```sql
CREATE TABLE t (a TEXT PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT);
-- SQLite: ERROR AUTOINCREMENT is only allowed on an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY
-- frank:  OK   (WRONG)
```

## What is already correct in frank
- valid form accepted by both: `CREATE TABLE t (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT)`.
- AUTOINCREMENT with no PRIMARY KEY is rejected by both (parse-level):
  `a TEXT AUTOINCREMENT`, `a INTEGER AUTOINCREMENT`, `a AUTOINCREMENT`.

So the gap is narrow: a PRIMARY KEY is present but the column type is not INTEGER
(here TEXT). frank fails the "must be INTEGER PRIMARY KEY" semantic check.

## Root cause
The CREATE TABLE / column-constraint validation accepts AUTOINCREMENT whenever a
PRIMARY KEY constraint is present, without verifying the column's declared type is
INTEGER (i.e. that it is a genuine rowid alias). See the CREATE TABLE handler in
`crates/fsqlite-core/src/connection.rs`.

## Fix sketch
When a column carries both PRIMARY KEY and AUTOINCREMENT, require the declared
type to be exactly `INTEGER` (the rowid-alias rule — note `INT`, `BIGINT`, etc. do
NOT count; only `INTEGER` makes a PK a rowid alias). Otherwise raise
"AUTOINCREMENT is only allowed on an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY".

## Priority
P3 — over-acceptance (frank creates a table SQLite refuses). Same
"validate-then-reject" class as bd-1sgq2 / bd-c9v0f / bd-1zc9p / bd-tp6ia.

## Tests
`crates/fsqlite-e2e/tests/autoincrement_placement_oracle_e2e.rs`: valid
INTEGER-PK form green; no-PK misplacements green (both reject);
`autoincrement_on_non_integer_pk_rejected` #[ignore]'d on this bead.

title: §5.6.5 GC Coordination: Horizon, Scheduling, Incremental Pruning
description:
## §5.6.5 GC Coordination: Horizon, Scheduling, Incremental Pruning
Spec location: Lines 8012-8147 of COMPREHENSIVE_SPEC_FOR_FRANKENSQLITE_V1.md

### Overview
The garbage collection coordination subsystem for MVCC version chains. This is critical for preventing unbounded memory growth. Covers gc_horizon computation, GC scheduling policy, raise_gc_horizon() algorithm, and coordination with sentinel states (CLAIMING/CLEANING).

### gc_horizon (SharedMemoryLayout)
- gc_horizon is a monotonically increasing CommitSeq safe-point: `min(begin_seq)` across all active transactions
- Since begin_seq derives from monotonically increasing published commit_seq, gc_horizon never decreases
- gc_horizon is authoritative ONLY when advanced by the commit sequencer (other processes read-only)

### GC Scheduling Policy (Alien-Artifact Discipline)
```
f_gc = min(f_max, max(f_min, version_chain_pressure / target_chain_length))
```
- f_max = 100 Hz (never GC more often than every 10ms)
- f_min = 1 Hz (always GC at least once per second)
- version_chain_pressure = observed mean version chain length (BOCPD-tracked)
- target_chain_length = 8 (from Theorem 5: R*D+1 for R=100, D=0.07s)
- WHO runs GC: commit coordinator runs raise_gc_horizon() after each group commit batch
- Only the process holding WAL write lock (coordinator) runs GC — avoids thundering herd
- Other processes observe updated gc_horizon on their next read

### raise_gc_horizon() Algorithm (Normative Pseudocode)
```
raise_gc_horizon():
    old_horizon = shm.gc_horizon.load(Acquire)
    global_min_begin_seq = shm.commit_seq.load(Acquire)
    for slot in txn_slots:
        tid = slot.txn_id.load(Acquire)
        if tid == 0: continue
        if decode_tag(tid) != 0:
            // CRITICAL: Sentinel-tagged slots (CLAIMING/CLEANING) are horizon blockers.
            // A claiming slot may have captured snapshot but not published real txn_id.
            global_min_begin_seq = min(global_min_begin_seq, old_horizon)
            continue
        global_min_begin_seq = min(global_min_begin_seq, slot.begin_seq.load(Acquire))
    new_horizon = max(old_horizon, global_min_begin_seq)  // monotonic
    shm.gc_horizon.store(new_horizon, Release)
```

### Normative Rules
1. gc_horizon MUST be monotonically non-decreasing (new_horizon = max(old, computed))
2. CLAIMING/CLEANING sentinel-tagged TxnSlots MUST block horizon advance
3. GC frequency formula MUST use the specified constants (f_max=100Hz, f_min=1Hz, target=8)
4. Only the commit coordinator (WAL write lock holder) runs GC
5. gc_horizon uses Acquire/Release memory ordering for cross-process visibility

### Error Conditions
- No active transactions: safe point = latest commit_seq (all versions beyond gc reclaimable)
- Sentinel-tagged slot race: horizon pinned to old_horizon to prevent premature version reclamation
- Coordinator crash: gc_horizon persists in SHM; new coordinator reads with Acquire ordering

### Logging Requirements
- DEBUG: GC horizon computation: oldest_active_begin_seq, horizon, blocked_by
- INFO: pruning batch summary: pages_pruned, versions_dropped, duration_ms
- WARN: GC lag beyond budget with suggested mitigation

### Child Bead
- §5.6.5.1 In-Process Version Pruning (bd-3t3.10): The actual memory reclamation implementation

### Dependencies
- Depends on: §5.6.1 SharedMemoryLayout (bd-3t3.5) for SHM region
- Depends on: §5.6.2 TxnSlot (bd-3t3.6) for slot scanning and sentinel states
- Related to: §6.5-6.7 ARC cache (ghost lists, eviction rules)

Crate: fsqlite-mvcc

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] GC horizon is correctly computed as the minimum active read timestamp across all live transactions
- [ ] Incremental pruning reclaims obsolete page versions without blocking concurrent readers
- [ ] GC scheduling avoids starvation under high write load while maintaining bounded memory growth
- [ ] SHM region memory layout (bd-3t3.5) is correctly used for slot scanning and sentinel states
- [ ] No version visible to any active transaction is ever reclaimed (safety invariant)

### What This Implements
The garbage collection coordination subsystem for MVCC version chains. This is critical for preventing unbounded memory growth.

**gc_horizon** in shared memory is a monotonically increasing safe-point in CommitSeq space: `min(begin_seq)` across all active transactions. Only advanced by the commit sequencer. Other processes treat it as read-only.

**GC Scheduling Policy (quantitative, not "periodically"):**
```
f_gc = min(f_max, max(f_min, version_chain_pressure / target_chain_length))
```
- f_max = 100 Hz (cap: never GC more often than every 10ms)
- f_min = 1 Hz (floor: always GC at least once per second)
- version_chain_pressure = observed mean version chain length (BOCPD-tracked)
- target_chain_length = 8 (from Theorem 5: R*D+1 for R=100, D=0.07s)

**Who runs GC:** Commit coordinator after each group commit batch (piggy-backing on commit critical section). Only the coordinator process runs GC. Other processes observe the updated gc_horizon on next read.

**raise_gc_horizon() pseudocode (normative):**
- Default: if no active txns exist, safe point is latest commit_seq
- Scan TxnSlots: CRITICAL — treat CLAIMING/CLEANING sentinel-tagged slots as horizon blockers
- new_horizon = max(old_horizon, global_min_begin_seq) — monotonic guarantee

### §5.6.5.1 In-Process Version Pruning (Required)
Advancing gc_horizon defines which versions are reclaimable (Theorem 4) but doesn't reclaim memory. MUST implement incremental, touched-page-driven pruning with strict work budgets:
- GcTodo queue: VecDeque<PageNumber> + HashSet for dedup
- on_publish_or_materialize_version(pgno) → enqueue
- gc_tick(): pop pages, prune chains under VersionArena write guard
- Work budgets (normative): pages_budget=64, versions_budget=4096
- prune_page_chain walks from head, finds oldest version <= horizon, frees everything older

**ARC interaction:** Removed versions must be eligible for eviction from ARC indexes and ghost lists.
**I/O boundary:** prune_page_chain is pure in-memory work. MUST NOT perform file reads.

### Unit Tests Required
1. test_gc_horizon_monotonic: Verify horizon only increases
2. test_gc_sentinel_blocking: CLAIMING/CLEANING slots block horizon advance
3. test_gc_scheduling_frequency: f_gc formula correctness at min/max/normal
4. test_incremental_pruning_budget: Verify work budget limits are respected
5. test_pruning_frees_arena_slots: Freed VersionIdx slots go to free_list
6. test_arc_eviction_on_prune: ARC ghost lists cleaned after version pruning
7. test_no_io_during_prune: Verify prune_page_chain never issues file reads

### E2E Test
Spawn N writers, M readers. Run for duration D. Verify:
- Memory usage stays bounded (version chains don't grow unboundedly)
- No version visible to any active snapshot is pruned
- GC frequency adapts to write pressure

## GC Scheduling Policy (Alien-Artifact)
- f_gc = min(f_max, max(f_min, version_chain_pressure / target_chain_length))
- f_max = 100 Hz (never GC more often than 10ms)
- f_min = 1 Hz (always GC at least once per second)
- version_chain_pressure = observed mean chain length (BOCPD-tracked)
- target_chain_length = 8 (from Theorem 5: R*D+1 for R=100, D=0.07s)
- WHO runs GC: commit coordinator runs raise_gc_horizon() after each group commit batch
- Only the process holding WAL write lock (coordinator) runs GC -- avoids thundering herd
- Other processes observe updated gc_horizon on their next read

## raise_gc_horizon() Algorithm (normative)
- Default: if no active txns, safe point = latest commit_seq
- Scan all TxnSlots:
  - Skip tid==0 (empty)
  - CRITICAL: Sentinel-tagged slots (CLAIMING/CLEANING) are horizon blockers
    - Use min(global_min_begin_seq, old_horizon) for sentinel slots
    - Reason: claiming slot may have captured snapshot but not published real txn_id yet
  - For real TxnId slots: min with slot.begin_seq
- new_horizon = max(old_horizon, global_min_begin_seq) -- monotonic
- Store with Release ordering

## In-Process Version Pruning (§5.6.5.1, REQUIRED)
- Advancing gc_horizon defines reclaimable versions (Theorem 4) but doesn't reclaim memory
- MUST implement incremental, touched-page-driven pruning with strict work budgets
- FORBIDDEN: naive scan-everything-under-VersionArena-write-guard (stop-the-world pauses)

### GcTodo Queue
- GcTodo { queue: VecDeque<PageNumber>, in_queue: HashSet<PageNumber> }
- on_publish_or_materialize_version(pgno): enqueue if not already present
- gc_tick(): pop pages from queue and prune their version chains

### Work Budgets (normative)
- pages_budget = 64
- versions_budget = 4096
- Lock VersionArena.write() only during actual pruning work

### prune_page_chain(pgno, horizon) Algorithm
- Walk chain from head down through versions newer than horizon
- Find committed version <= horizon -> becomes new tail
- Everything older is reclaimable by Theorem 4
- Sever chain: arena[cur].prev_idx = None
- Free all nodes beyond the severed point to free list

### ARC Interaction (normative)
- When committed version removed from chain, its cache entry MUST be eviction-eligible
- Remove (pgno, commit_seq) from ARC indexes and ghost lists (§6.7 coalescing + §6.6 durability)

### I/O Boundary (normative)
- prune_page_chain is pure in-memory work, MUST NOT perform file reads
- If pruned version later needed by old snapshot, resolve() consults durable store (§5.2, §7.11)

title: §5.10.2.1 Index Regeneration on Rebase: Partial Indexes + UNIQUE Enforcement
description:
Implement the 7-step index regeneration algorithm executed during deterministic rebase, handling partial indexes, expression indexes, UNIQUE enforcement, and overflow pages (spec lines 10240-10272).

SCOPE: During rebase, IndexDelete/IndexInsert ops associated with an UpdateExpression carry stale key bytes from the original snapshot. These MUST be discarded and regenerated from the schema and rebased row images. The rebase engine has access to the full schema at rebase time.

ALGORITHMS:
- 7-step Index Regeneration:
  (1) Discard stale index ops matching (table, rowid) of the rebased UpdateExpression
  (2) Enumerate secondary indexes from schema (ordinary, expression, UNIQUE, partial; MAY skip if provably independent of updated columns)
  (3) Compute participation for base and updated rows: ordinary indexes always true; partial indexes evaluate WHERE predicate against row
  (4) Compute index key bytes using SQLite affinity + collation rules matching VDBE/B-tree encoding
  (5) Emit index ops based on participation delta: base-only -> IndexDelete; updated-only -> IndexInsert; both with key change -> Delete+Insert; both with same key -> no-op
  (6) UNIQUE constraint re-validation: each IndexInsert enforces uniqueness against the new committed base snapshot; violation aborts rebase with SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_UNIQUE (true conflict, no silent merge)
  (7) Overflow and index chain mutation: handle overflow pages correctly for both IndexDelete (free chains) and IndexInsert (allocate chains)

INVARIANTS:
- Affinity coercion MUST use schema's declared column affinities
- Collation sequences MUST match index declarations
- Expression evaluation for expression indexes MUST be deterministic
- Skip optimization (Step 2) MUST be conservative: if in doubt, regenerate
- UNIQUE violations during rebase are true conflicts and MUST abort, not merge

TEST REQUIREMENTS (8 unit + 1 E2E):
- test_index_regen_ordinary_index_key_change, test_index_regen_partial_index_participation_change, test_index_regen_partial_index_entry_to_entry, test_index_regen_unique_constraint_violation_aborts, test_index_regen_expression_index, test_index_regen_no_op_when_key_unchanged, test_index_regen_multiple_indexes_same_table, test_index_regen_overflow_key_handling
- E2E: test_e2e_index_regeneration_on_rebase_partial_unique (concurrent writes with UNIQUE partial index, verify C sqlite3 behavior match)

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA:
1. Stale index ops from original intent log correctly discarded for rebased rows
2. Partial index participation evaluated correctly for both base and updated rows
3. UNIQUE constraint violations abort with SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_UNIQUE
4. Expression indexes produce correct keys matching VDBE encoding
5. Overflow page chains correctly freed/allocated during index ops
6. Generated index ops match what a fresh VDBE encode would produce

comments.text:
# §5.10.2.1 Index Regeneration on Rebase: Partial Indexes + UNIQUE Enforcement

**Spec reference:** COMPREHENSIVE_SPEC_FOR_FRANKENSQLITE_V1.md, lines 10240–10272

## Overview

During rebase, any `IndexDelete`/`IndexInsert` ops from the original intent log that are
associated with an `UpdateExpression` (same table, same rowid) carry **stale key bytes**
derived from the original snapshot. These MUST be discarded. The rebase engine MUST
regenerate index operations from the schema and the rebased row images using the 7-step
algorithm below.

## 7-Step Index Regeneration Algorithm

### Step 1: Discard stale index ops
All `IndexDelete`/`IndexInsert` ops in the original intent log that match the same
(table, rowid) as the UpdateExpression being rebased MUST be dropped entirely.

### Step 2: Enumerate secondary indexes from schema
Enumerate the table's secondary indexes from the schema, including:
- Ordinary indexes
- Expression indexes
- UNIQUE indexes
- Partial indexes (indexes with WHERE predicates)

The engine MAY skip an index **only** if it can prove the index's key and partial
predicate are independent of the updated columns.

### Step 3: Compute participation for base row and updated row
For each index, determine whether the **base** row (before update) and the **updated**
row (after update) participate in the index:
- **Ordinary/expression indexes:** participation is always `true`.
- **Partial indexes:** evaluate the index WHERE predicate against the row;
  participation is `true` iff the predicate evaluates to `true` (SQLite semantics).

### Step 4: Compute index key bytes
If participation is true, compute the index key bytes by evaluating the index key
definition against the row:
- **Ordinary index:** use the indexed column values.
- **Expression index:** evaluate the index expressions.

Key construction MUST apply **SQLite affinity + collation rules** for that index,
and MUST match the normal VDBE/B-tree index encoding.

### Step 5: Emit index ops based on participation delta
- If base participates and updated does NOT → emit `IndexDelete(index, old_key, rowid)`.
- If base does NOT participate and updated does → emit `IndexInsert(index, new_key, rowid)`.
- If both participate:
  - If `old_key != new_key` → emit `IndexDelete(old_key)` then `IndexInsert(new_key)`.
  - If `old_key == new_key` → no-op.

### Step 6: UNIQUE constraint re-validation (normative)
For UNIQUE indexes, each `IndexInsert` MUST enforce uniqueness against the **new committed
base snapshot**. If a conflicting key exists for a different rowid, rebase MUST abort with
the appropriate constraint error (true conflict). The engine MUST NOT "merge" the violation
or silently skip it.

### Step 7: Overflow and index chain mutation
Index key bytes may overflow a single B-tree cell. The engine MUST handle overflow pages
correctly during both `IndexDelete` (freeing overflow chains) and `IndexInsert` (allocating
new overflow chains). The engine uses the schema (needed for affinity coercion) and MUST use
it to enumerate indexes and evaluate index predicates/expressions deterministically.

## Implementation Requirements

- The rebase engine has access to the full schema at rebase time.
- Affinity coercion MUST use the schema's declared column affinities.
- Collation sequences MUST match those declared on the index.
- Expression evaluation for expression indexes MUST be deterministic.
- The skip optimization (Step 2) MUST be conservative: if in doubt, regenerate.

## Unit Test Specifications

### Test 1: `test_index_regen_ordinary_index_key_change`
Rebase an UPDATE that changes an indexed column. Verify the old index key is deleted
and the new index key is inserted. Confirm the generated ops match what a fresh
VDBE encode would produce.

### Test 2: `test_index_regen_partial_index_participation_change`
Create a partial index with `WHERE active = 1`. Rebase an UPDATE that sets `active = 0`.
Verify an `IndexDelete` is emitted (row exits the partial index) and no `IndexInsert`
is emitted.

### Test 3: `test_index_regen_partial_index_entry_to_entry`
Partial index with `WHERE score > 50`. Rebase an UPDATE that changes `score` from 60 to 70.
Verify `IndexDelete(old_key)` + `IndexInsert(new_key)` are emitted since participation
stays true but key changes.

### Test 4: `test_index_regen_unique_constraint_violation_aborts`
UNIQUE index on column `email`. Rebase an UPDATE that changes email to a value that
already exists (for a different rowid) in the new committed base. Verify rebase aborts
with `SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_UNIQUE` and does NOT silently merge.

### Test 5: `test_index_regen_expression_index`
Expression index on `lower(name)`. Rebase an UPDATE that changes `name` from 'Alice'
to 'Bob'. Verify old key `lower('Alice')` is deleted and new key `lower('Bob')` is
inserted, with correct affinity and encoding.

### Test 6: `test_index_regen_no_op_when_key_unchanged`
Rebase an UPDATE that changes a non-indexed column. Verify no index ops are emitted
for indexes whose keys and partial predicates are independent of the changed columns.

### Test 7: `test_index_regen_multiple_indexes_same_table`
Table with 3 indexes (ordinary, unique, partial). Rebase an UPDATE that affects all
three. Verify correct ops are emitted for each index independently, in the correct order.

### Test 8: `test_index_regen_overflow_key_handling`
Index key that exceeds the B-tree cell payload threshold. Verify overflow pages are
correctly freed on `IndexDelete` and correctly allocated on `IndexInsert` during rebase.

title: Wire WAL & MVCC as default execution backend
description: The core innovation of FrankenSQLite is page-level MVCC replacing SQLite's WAL_WRITE_LOCK. Currently, fsqlite-core::Connection relies on MemDatabase. We must replace this by instantiating the full Pager/WAL/MVCC/B-Tree stack when opening a connection. BEGIN must auto-promote to BEGIN CONCURRENT. Ensure the concurrent_mode_default flag remains true. This involves routing VDBE cursor operations through BtreeCursor.
acceptance_criteria:
1) Connection open path instantiates real Pager/WAL/MVCC/B-Tree backend by default for parity/runtime mode and routes VDBE cursors through Storage/BtreeCursor paths.
2) Plain BEGIN continues default promotion to BEGIN CONCURRENT (`concurrent_mode_default == true`) with anti-regression tests proving no default-off regressions.
3) Parity harness and release verification run against the real backend path by default; MemDatabase fallback is disallowed in certifying runs.
4) Deterministic differential tests prove equivalence and durability behavior on the default wired backend, with first-failure diagnostics and replay artifacts.

Cross-cutting quality contract (mandatory):

description:
## Goal
Restore the synthetic persistent Criterion benchmark as a trustworthy FrankenSQLite-vs-SQLite signal by fixing the current FrankenSQLite commit-path failure.

## Evidence
- On 2026-03-21 local Criterion runs, SQLite 2-thread completed, but FrankenSQLite crashed during the 2-thread group before producing a stable estimate.
- Error signature: `COMMIT failed: Io(Os { code: 9, kind: Uncategorized, message: "Bad file descriptor" })`.
- Crash surface in `crates/fsqlite-e2e/benches/concurrent_write_persistent_bench.rs` around the worker commit/join path.
- Real-fixture matrix is currently usable, but this synthetic persistent benchmark remains blocked and should not be used for current performance claims until fixed.

## Why This Matters
This benchmark was the explicit target of recent many-core WAL/commit-path work. Until it runs cleanly, we do not have a trustworthy score for this benchmark family and we cannot separate performance regressions from correctness/FD-lifetime regressions.

## Acceptance Criteria

2. Focused reproduction exists and passes reliably.
3. The full Criterion persistent benchmark completes for FrankenSQLite and produces stable estimates for at least the currently targeted thread groups.

comments.text:
## Root Cause Identified — IronVault (claude-opus-4-6)

### Diagnostic Evidence
Instrumented UnixFile::write() caught the exact failure:
```
WRITE_FAILED fd=5 arc_strong=3 closed=false path=…/-wal offset=16512
```

### Key Facts
1. The failing fd is 5 (the InodeInfo canonical fd for the WAL file)
2. Arc strong count is 3 (InodeInfo + 2 worker connections)  
3. UnixFile.closed is false — close() was NOT called
4. write_at(fd=5, offset=16512) returns EBADF despite the Arc being alive

### Diagnosis
The fd was invalidated at the OS level despite the Rust Arc<File> still holding it.
Bug manifests after Criterion iterations of setup/teardown. Most likely cause:
asupersync io_uring backend fd lifecycle issue (H3 from fault matrix).

### Next Steps
1. Test with io_uring disabled to confirm H3
2. Add proper io_uring op drain before fd close
3. Add fd validity guard in WAL write path

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## ROOT CAUSE CONFIRMED AND FIXED — IronVault (claude-opus-4-6)

### Root Cause
**The WAL file was opened READONLY and the canonical fd was shared to writers.**

`install_existing_wal_backend_with_vfs()` (connection.rs:1174) and
`wal_file_present_with_vfs()` (connection.rs:1205) both opened the WAL file
with `VfsOpenFlags::READONLY | VfsOpenFlags::WAL`. On the first open for an
inode, the global `InodeInfo` table installs this READONLY fd as the canonical
fd. All subsequent connections that clone this fd via the fast path inherit
the read-only fd.

When the WAL group commit flusher calls `file.write_at()`, the `pwrite()`
syscall on a read-only fd returns `EBADF` on Linux. The fd is valid
(fcntl F_GETFD returns 1, /proc/self/fd exists), but writes are forbidden
because the fd was opened O_RDONLY.

### Diagnostic Evidence
```
[bd-zna34] WRITE EBADF DIAGNOSTICS:
fd=6 closed=false path=/tmp/.tmpSBeP7K-wal
fcntl(F_GETFD)=1 /proc/self/fd exists=true
Arc<File> strong=3 Arc<InodeInfo> strong=3
```
The fd is VALID but READONLY → pwrite returns EBADF.

### Fix (2 changes in connection.rs)
1. `install_existing_wal_backend_with_vfs`: Changed from READONLY-first to
   READWRITE-only. The READONLY fallback was defensive but poisoned the
   InodeInfo canonical fd.
2. `wal_file_present_with_vfs`: Changed probe to open READWRITE first,
   falling back to READONLY only if READWRITE fails (e.g., read-only FS).

### Verification
Ran the full Criterion 2-thread persistent benchmark 14+ iterations with
zero EBADF errors. Previously failed consistently within 3-5 iterations.

### Non-regression
- Concurrent writer mode: UNCHANGED (ON by default)
- No writer serialization introduced
- WAL append/sync path: UNCHANGED
- Fix is in connection setup, not in hot path

title: §5.8 Conflict Detection and Resolution: First-Committer-Wins + Conflict Response
description:
Implement the First-Committer-Wins conflict detection and resolution pipeline, including page lock table operations, CommitIndex validation, serialized/concurrent mode interaction, and conflict response handling (spec lines 8981-9167, also 9168-9195).

SCOPE: Core commit validation ensuring that when two transactions modify the same page(s), the first to commit wins and the second detects the conflict. Covers both the in-process reference implementation (64-shard InProcessPageLockTable) and the cross-process SharedPageLockTable in shared memory.

DATA STRUCTURES:
- InProcessPageLockTable: 64-shard parking_lot::Mutex<HashMap<PageNumber, TxnId>>; shard selection via pgno & (SHARDS - 1)
- SharedPageLockTable in foo.db.fsqlite-shm (section 5.6.3): canonical cross-process lock table
- CommitIndex: maps page numbers to latest commit_seq
- serialized_writer indicator in SharedMemoryLayout (token, lease, pid, pid_birth)

ALGORITHMS:
- Conflict detection pipeline: (1) acquire exclusive page locks for write_set, (2) CommitIndex check: for each page, if CommitIndex[pgno] > T.begin_seq then conflict, (3) attempt deterministic rebase (section 5.10) if conflict pages overlap, (4) SSI validation (section 5.7.3) even if rebase succeeds, (5) commit on success or SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT on failure
- Page lock operations: try_acquire (vacant->insert, occupied->check same txn or SQLITE_BUSY), release (remove entry, panic if not held), release_all (iterate per-txn set, may group by shard)
- Crash cleanup: shared-memory scan release_page_locks_for(txn_id) since crashed process has no in-process set
- Serialized/Concurrent mode interaction: serialized writer blocks concurrent page locks; concurrent page locks block serialized writer acquisition; check_serialized_writer_exclusion() CAS loop (detailed in bd-1e9x)

INVARIANTS:
- ALL page-level writer exclusion MUST use SharedPageLockTable in cross-process mode, NOT in-process HashMap
- Normal commit/abort uses fast-path per-txn lock set; crash cleanup uses slow-path shared-memory scan
- CommitIndex check is mandatory; without it, first-committer-wins has false negatives
- Compatibility mode MUST exclude legacy writers via WAL_WRITE_LOCK for coordinator lifetime

TEST REQUIREMENTS (5 unit + 1 E2E):
- test_first_committer_wins (T1 commits, T2 detects conflict), test_no_conflict_different_pages, test_conflict_with_successful_rebase, test_conflict_response_sqlite_busy (SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT), test_commit_index_lookup_correctness
- E2E: test_e2e_first_committer_wins_conflict_response (two concurrent writers on same page, deterministic outcome)

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA:
1. First committer always wins; second transaction gets SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT
2. Non-overlapping page writes never conflict
3. Rebase successfully resolves commuting operations on same page
4. SSI validation runs even after successful rebase
5. Serialized/concurrent mode mutual exclusion enforced correctly
6. Crash cleanup via shared-memory scan releases all locks held by dead process
close_reason: Implemented FCW conflict detection with GF(256) disjoint rebase pipeline. Modified commit_concurrent to: (1) collect conflicting pages via CommitIndex check, (2) check merge_decision - AbortRetry aborts immediately, (3) attempt try_rebase_page using XOR disjoint deltas (base/ours/theirs), (4) re-run SSI validation after successful rebase. Added 5 unit tests (test_first_committer_wins, test_no_conflict_different_pages, test_conflict_with_successful_rebase, test_conflict_response_sqlite_busy, test_commit_index_lookup_correctness) + 1 E2E (test_e2e_first_committer_wins_conflict_response). All 94 lifecycle tests pass.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## §5.8 Conflict Detection and Resolution: First-Committer-Wins + Conflict Response

### Spec Content (Lines 9168-9195)
First-committer-wins: When T2 attempts to commit and discovers T1 already committed modifications to the same page(s), T2 MUST detect this via CommitIndex lookup. The response depends on whether deterministic rebase (§5.10) can resolve the conflict.

Conflict detection pipeline:
1. Lock acquisition: T2 acquires exclusive page locks for its write_set
2. CommitIndex check: For each page in write_set, if CommitIndex[pgno] > T2.begin_seq → conflict
3. Rebase attempt: If conflict pages overlap, attempt deterministic rebase (§5.10)
4. SSI validation: Even if rebase succeeds, still run SSI check (§5.7.3)
5. Resolution: Commit on success, SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT on failure

### Unit Tests Required
1. test_first_committer_wins: T1 commits first, T2 detects conflict
2. test_no_conflict_different_pages: T1 and T2 touch different pages → both commit
3. test_conflict_with_successful_rebase: Same page but commuting ops → both commit
4. test_conflict_response_sqlite_busy: Non-rebasable conflict → SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT
5. test_commit_index_lookup_correctness: CommitIndex correctly tracks latest commit per page

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
SECTION: §5.8 (spec lines ~8981-9167)

PURPOSE: Implement page lock table, FCW commit validation, and serialized/concurrent mode interaction.

## Page Lock Table Implementation (normative)

### Concurrent Mode (cross-process)
- SharedPageLockTable in foo.db.fsqlite-shm (§5.6.3) is THE canonical lock table
- ALL page-level writer exclusion MUST be enforced via shared-memory table, NOT in-process HashMap

### Normal commit/abort (fast path)
- Release page locks by iterating in-process page_locks set (touch only locked pages)

### Crash cleanup (slow path)
- MUST use shared-memory scan release_page_locks_for(txn_id) (§5.6.3) -- crashed process has no in-process set

## Single-Process Reference Implementation (NOT cross-process safe)
- 64-shard InProcessPageLockTable (parking_lot::Mutex<HashMap<PageNumber, TxnId>>)
- Shard selection: pgno.get() as usize & (LOCK_TABLE_SHARDS - 1)
- try_acquire: vacant→insert, occupied→check same txn (idempotent) or SQLITE_BUSY
- release: remove entry, panic if not held by txn
- release_all: iterate per-txn lock set (O(W) where W = write set size)
  - Production MAY group by shard to reduce lock acquisitions

## Commit Validation Algorithm (First-Committer-Wins)
- validate_commit(T, commit_index):
  - For each page in write_set: if commit_index.latest_commit_seq(pgno) > T.snapshot.high → conflict
  - On conflict: attempt algebraic merge (§5.10)
    - If merge possible: perform_merge
    - If not: return SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT (retryable)

## Serialized ↔ Concurrent Mode Interaction

### While Serialized-mode writer is Active (holding global write mutex):
- Concurrent txns MAY BEGIN and read normally
- Any Concurrent-mode page write lock attempt MUST fail with SQLITE_BUSY
  (allowing concurrent writers would violate SQLite single-writer contract)

### While any Concurrent-mode writer is Active (holds any page locks):
- Acquiring Serialized writer exclusion (BEGIN IMMEDIATE/EXCLUSIVE/DEFERRED upgrade) MUST fail with SQLITE_BUSY
- DEFERRED read-only begins remain permitted; only writer upgrade excluded

### Cross-Process Implementation
- SharedMemoryLayout maintains serialized_writer indicator (token + lease)
- Set when Serialized txn acquires writer exclusion, cleared at commit/abort
- Concurrent-mode write paths MUST check this indicator before acquiring page locks

### check_serialized_writer_exclusion(shm) Algorithm
- Load token (Acquire); if 0 → Ok
- Check expiry + process_alive(pid, birth)
- If alive and valid lease → SQLITE_BUSY
- If stale (lease expired or owner dead): CAS clear + retry loop
  - CAS failure means token changed (someone else cleared or new writer installed)
  - MUST retry to avoid returning Ok while new serialized writer is active

### Serialized Writer Acquisition Ordering (5 steps)
1. Acquire global serialized writer exclusion
2. Publish shared indicator (serialized_writer_token != 0, Release ordering)
3. Drain concurrent writers: wait until no outstanding page locks from Concurrent-mode txns
4. Perform writes
5. On commit/abort: CAS clear indicator + release global exclusion

### External Interop Hook (Compatibility mode)
- Concurrent-mode exclusion meaningless if legacy writer bypasses .fsqlite-shm
- Compatibility mode with .fsqlite-shm MUST exclude legacy writers (§5.6.6.1, §5.6.7)
- FORBIDDEN: multi-writer MVCC while legacy writers permitted

PARENT EPIC: bd-3t3
DEPENDS ON: bd-3t3.8 (SharedPageLockTable), bd-3t3.3 (Transaction Lifecycle), bd-3t3.1 (Core Types)

Dependencies:
  -> bd-3t3 (parent-child) - §5: MVCC Formal Model (Revised)
  -> bd-3t3.8 (blocks) - §5.6.3 SharedPageLockTable: Cross-Process Exclusive Locks
  -> bd-3t3.3 (blocks) - §5.4 Transaction Lifecycle (Begin/Read/Write/Commit/Abort)
  -> bd-3t3.1 (blocks) - §5.1 MVCC Core Types

Dependents:
  <- bd-1h3b (blocks) - §5.10.2-5.10.4 Deterministic Rebase + Physical Merge + Merge Policy
  <- bd-1onb (blocks) - §5.9.1-5.9.2 Write Coordinator Sequencers (Native + WAL Paths)

title: PERF-P2: connection SimpleFullTableScan fast-path bypasses codegen index-range seek for secondary-index ranges

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
Found by cc_fsq 2026-07-10 (commit c2119b49). SELECT ... WHERE <secondary indexed col> <range> (>, <, BETWEEN) full-scans in the connection while C SQLite covering-seeks. The VDBE codegen index-range seek already works (test_codegen_select_with_index_range), and it's covering-aware (resolve_covering_output_sources). But the connection classifies these SELECTs into PreparedQueryFastPath::SimpleFullTableScan (connection.rs ~line 29993) which BYPASSES codegen entirely, so no codegen routing can fire.

Measured: SELECT id,k WHERE k BETWEEN a AND a+50 (51-row selective range) = 0.985x vs NOT INDEXED scan (both ~9000us) — the seek never fires.

The connection has SimpleRowidRangeScan but no secondary-index-range fast path. Fix direction: add a SimpleIndexRangeScan fast path in the classifier, OR declassify covering secondary-index ranges from SimpleFullTableScan so they route to codegen (where the seek is ready and covering-gated for regression safety). This is a connection-layer change (prepared-query classifier), not codegen.

Contrast: IN-list queries win (100x+) because IN is NOT classified into a direct fast path and reaches codegen. Ledger: perf-negative-results.md '2026-07-10 NON-WIN: covering secondary-index range'.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: RESOLVED via codegen (not a connection fast-path). Premise was WRONG: SimpleFullTableScan only fires for SELECT * WHERE <none>; secondary-index ranges reach codegen. Real cause: index_range_fast_path_is_safe gated the seek on (cmp_p5 & !0x80)==0, but every INTEGER/REAL/NUMERIC column carries NUMERIC comparison affinity (0x43) vs a literal -> seek NEVER fired for numeric cols -> full scan, despite EQP saying SEARCH USING INDEX (diagnosed at bytecode: 0 Seek, 1 Rewind). FIX (codegen.rs): accept when affinity is NUMERIC AND bound is a numeric literal (int/real/negated) -- NUMERIC coercion of a numeric literal is the identity (same subset as IN-list seek); placeholders/text decline. Also broadened is_index_range_constant for negated literals. Proof: index_range_seek_matches_sqlite (~40 queries bit-identical vs rusqlite) + opcode gate; A/B release-perf 84.63x (33us vs 2808us), null 0.907x. FOLLOW-UP: placeholder-bound ranges still scan. Ledger: perf-negative-results.md 2026-07-11 WIN.

title: PERF-P1: composite index prefix+range seek (WHERE a=? AND b>?) full-scans
description:
Profile-confirmed gap (by reasoning): SELECT ... WHERE <eq-prefix cols> AND <next index col> <range> on a composite index(a,b,...) FULL-SCANS. extract_column_range_target rejects the 'a = 5' equality conjunct (only handles Ge/Gt/Le/Lt), so the codegen index_range local is None; the planner emits MultiColumnEquality{trailing_constraint:Range} -> IndexRange directive, but codegen's IndexRange arm reads the single-column index_range local (None) -> bypass -> codegen_select_full_scan. Very common shape (composite indexes with eq-prefix + range suffix, e.g. WHERE status=? AND created_at>?). HIGH value.

DESIGN (reuse existing infra, low from-scratch risk):
- Detection: new extractor combining extract_index_equality_prefix_exprs(index,...) (crates/fsqlite-vdbe/src/codegen.rs:18821 — extracts the eq-prefix for a composite index) for the leading a=<lit/param> conjuncts + extract_column_range_target for the trailing (equality_prefix_len-th) index column's range. Require the prefix cols to be the leading index key terms and the range col to be the next key term.
- Codegen (new path or extend codegen_select_index_range_scan): build a multi-column probe like codegen_select_index_ordered_scan (codegen.rs:4987-5041): probe_key_regs[0..prefix_len]=prefix exprs (IsNull->done), probe[prefix_len]=range_lower (or Null for lower-open), trailing=Null, rowid=i64::MIN; MakeRecord; SeekGE. Loop bound: IdxGT(index_cursor, prefix_probe, done, P5=equality_prefix_len) to stop when the eq-prefix changes (this is the key primitive), PLUS the trailing-range upper stop (Gt/Ge on the range col like the single-column seek) and exclusive-lower skip. Covering via resolve_covering_output_sources / IdxRowid+SeekRowid like the single-column path.
- Affinity: coerce placeholder prefix/range bounds to the respective column affinities (reuse bound_matches_affinity/Affinity op from bd-u6tbr/bd-v79yz).
- HARD GATE: differential vs rusqlite — eq-prefix + range (>,>=,<,<=,BETWEEN), multi-col prefix (a=? AND b=? AND c>?), covering+non-covering, placeholder binds of all types, NULL prefix, empty ranges, ORDER BY, and declines (prefix not leading, range not next col, NOT INDEXED). Opcode gate: SeekGE + IdxGT(P5=prefix_len) + IdxRowid.
- NOTE: needs iterative dev; degraded rch fleet (~8min/build) blocked one-shot this session. Ledger: perf-negative-results.md range-seek family (bd-zq6dp/u6tbr/xiojw/v79yz).

title: CORRECTNESS: composite prefix+range seek (WHERE a=v AND b<range>) silently drops a residual predicate on a non-key column
description: bd-zqkrp regression. composite_index_prefix_range_target's genuine-range branch used extract_named_column_range (which ignores every non-range conjunct) with NO residual guard, so 'SELECT ... title: WAL integrity cross-check via stock C SQLite (with raw-page fallback) after every concurrency test
description: Many of the corruption fingerprints from issue #70 are WAL anomalies (frame-order, short-header-read, WAL page-index integrity failure). Every test under tests/concurrent/ and tests/swarm/ must call verify_with_c_sqlite (bd-bpnnx) on the resulting .fsqlite. On any failure, capture a full artifact bundle so triage does not need the original machine.
design: verify_with_c_sqlite(path) returns a structured VerifyReport (defined in bd-bpnnx). After every test in tests/concurrent/ and tests/swarm/, call it on the resulting .fsqlite file. Tiered fallback: (a) primary path opens read-only via rusqlite, runs PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE), then PRAGMA integrity_check; (b) if rusqlite cannot open the file (e.g. WAL header missing or truncated), fall back to a raw-page-walker (fsqlite-pager in read-only fsck mode) and emit a structured raw-fsck report; (c) if BOTH fail, capture the full WAL (not just first 32 frames) and the full main db header + first-32-pages dump into the failure artifact. title: BUG: correlated IN-subquery returns no rows (scalar = form works); doubly-nested correlation over-matches (inner EXISTS not bound to middle level)
close_reason: Fixed: (A) correlated x IN (SELECT...) now routes to interpreted fallback (per-row outer-ref substitution); (B) doubly-nested correlated EXISTS no longer over-matches (try_direct_exists_probe bails on subquery residual). 2 repro tests un-ignored, full subquery regression green.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## Two correlated-subquery divergences (oracle parity vs rusqlite)

Data: `emp(id PK, dept TEXT, salary INTEGER)` =
(1,eng,100),(2,eng,120),(3,sales,80),(4,sales,60),(5,eng,80),(6,hr,150).
dept max: eng=120, sales=80, hr=150.

### A. Correlated IN-subquery returns NO rows (the scalar `=` form works)
```sql
SELECT id FROM emp e1
 WHERE salary IN (SELECT max(salary) FROM emp e2 WHERE e2.dept = e1.dept);
  -- frank: []        csql: [2,3,6]
```
The IDENTICAL correlated+aggregate subquery via scalar `=` is CORRECT:
```sql
SELECT id FROM emp e1
 WHERE salary = (SELECT max(salary) FROM emp e2 WHERE e2.dept = e1.dept);
  -- frank: [2,3,6]   csql: [2,3,6]   (works)
```
And a NON-correlated IN-subquery works:
```sql
SELECT id FROM emp WHERE salary IN (SELECT max(salary) FROM emp);  -- frank == csql == [6]
```
So correlation is threaded correctly into the scalar-subquery path but NOT into
the `x IN (SELECT ...)` path: the correlated IN subquery appears to be evaluated
once with no outer binding (yielding an empty/constant set), so nothing matches.
(Related to but distinct from bd-l2si0, which was row-value `(a,b) IN (SELECT)`;
this is a scalar correlated IN.)

### B. Doubly-nested correlation over-matches (inner EXISTS referencing the middle level)
```sql
-- a(id)=1,2,3 ; b(id,aid)=(10,1),(11,2) ; c(id,bid)=(100,10)
SELECT id FROM a
 WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM b WHERE b.aid = a.id
                AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM c WHERE c.bid = b.id));
  -- frank: [1,2]     csql: [1]
```
Only a=1 should qualify (its b=10 has a matching c=100). a=2's b=11 has no c, so
the inner EXISTS should be false — but frank includes a=2, i.e. the innermost
`EXISTS (... c.bid = b.id)` is not correctly bound to the middle query's `b.id`
(it evaluates true regardless). Single-level correlated EXISTS works
(correlated_exists_and_not_exists passes); only the two-level nesting fails.

### Fix area
Subquery correlation/evaluation in the VDBE codegen + connection subquery path:
(A) the `InSet::Subquery` lowering must re-evaluate the subquery per outer row
with the correlation bound (as the scalar-subquery path already does);
(B) nested EXISTS must thread the enclosing (middle) query's row values into the
innermost correlated subquery, not just the outermost.

### Tests
crates/fsqlite-e2e/tests/correlated_subquery_oracle_e2e.rs —
correlated_scalar_in_select_list / correlated_exists_and_not_exists /
self_correlated_above_group_average PASS; correlated_in_top_per_group and
doubly_nested_correlation are #[ignore]'d referencing this bead.

title: BUG-P1: durable commit can be reported as Err and never published — execute_commit_with_cx gates CommitIndex/SSI publication on commit_res.is_ok() while the group callback can return Err AFTER the epoch is durable
description: Surfaced by EmeraldPrairie's read-only boundary audit (bd-i0tn6 thread msg 4560, 2026-07-28). Mechanism: fsqlite-pager's own deterministic test test_fault_during_phase_c_returns_error_and_wal_frames_survive (pager.rs ~25173) encodes the contract 'commit returns Err after WAL frames are durable'; in production the group-commit callback can complete an epoch durably and still return a local publication/lock-restoration error (pager.rs ~13484-13509). Connection::execute_commit_with_cx (connection.rs ~50451-50526) publishes CommitIndex/SSI/session/clock ONLY when commit_res.is_ok(), then propagates the Err. Consequence: a durable-on-disk commit is (a) reported to the caller as failure and (b) never published to CommitIndex/SSI — recovery replays it as committed while the live system believes it rolled back. Result<()> conflates NotCommitted / InDoubt / DurableNeedsPublication. FIX = bd-i0tn6 S1a (typed pager physical outcome enum + DB-root exact receipt + checkpoint fence, per the TxnBoundaryReceipt state machine in msg 4560): DurableThenFailed{interval} must route to publication (monotonic), not rollback. Related hazard in the same audit: finalize_prepared_session_state warns on missing/inactive session while still applying CommitIndex/lock-table side effects (begin_concurrent.rs ~1829-1853) — stale-receipt/ABA unsafe. OWNERSHIP: RusticBasin's correctness lane (connection.rs+pager leased); this bead exists so the finding is durable outside mail. Deterministic repro shape: the existing phase-C fault test extended through the connection layer — assert that after the injected post-durable Err, either publication completes or the connection reports InDoubt, never clean rollback.
